en: Sūta said: Thus has this most auspicious path been revealed by Śiva himself—the supreme path that grants immediate liberation to men bound by the cycle of worldly existence. || 1 ||
Now, for men of dull intellect who are ineligible for the Vedas, for women, for those related to the twice-born, and for all embodied beings— (2)
This is the common path that directly accomplishes absolute liberation; it is practiced by great sages and highly honored even by the gods.
The hearing of the discourse of Śambhu destroys the fear of saṃsāra; it bestows immediate liberation, is praiseworthy, and is purifying for all embodied beings.
This lamp bestows the attainment of knowledge upon those blinded by the darkness of ignorance; it is the supreme medicine to be well-served by those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
It is as terrible as a thunderbolt-strike against the mountains of great sins, the parching of the seeds of karma, and the means for attaining all prosperity. (6)
Those who always hear the story of Śambhu, which purifies the world, are indeed Rudras themselves among men in this world; of this there is no doubt.
For those virtuous ones who hear the verses of Śūlin and likewise recite them, the sages have declared that the very dust of their feet is the true sacred ford.
Therefore, those embodied beings who desire to attain the supreme good should always listen with devotion to this Puranic narrative concerning Śiva.
If a man is unable to listen to the Puranic narrative constantly, he should listen for even a single muhūrta every day with a self-controlled mind.
Now, if a person is unable to listen to it every day, [they may do so] during meritorious months, on auspicious days, or even on sacred lunar dates.
He who hears this delightful narrative proclaimed by the Purāṇas crosses over saṃsāra, having burnt away the great forest of karma.
Those who always listen with devotion for even a moment, half a moment, or an instant to this purifying discourse, for them there is no miserable rebirth.
Whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—that fruit a man obtains by hearing a Purāṇa even once.
In the Kali age, especially, there is no higher dharma for men than listening to the Purāṇas, nor is there any other path to liberation.
There is no recitation superior to listening to the Purāṇas of Śambhu; for this very reason, it is the great fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree for human beings. (16)
In the Kali age, mortals will have short lifespans, be weak, and oppressed by fatigue; they will be dull-witted, partakers of suffering, and devoid of righteous conduct.
Having reflected thus, out of compassion, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa prepared for their benefit the nectar-like essence known as the Purāṇa.
By drinking this nectar with effort, one becomes free from old age and death; the nectar of Śambhu’s story shall make one's entire lineage free from old age and death.
Whether he be a child, a youth, poor, old, or even weak, one who knows the Purāṇas is always to be saluted and honored by those seeking the fruits of meritorious deeds.
One should never entertain a low opinion of one who knows the Purāṇas, from whose lotus-like mouth speech flows like a wish-fulfilling cow for all embodied beings. (21)
There are gurus in the worlds by virtue of birth as well as by virtue of their qualities; yet among all of them, the knower of the Purāṇas is the supreme guru.
Having been born again and again throughout thousands of millions of existences, one suffers; who else is a greater teacher than he who grants the state of no-return? (23)
One who knows the Purāṇas, who is pure, self-controlled, peaceful, and has conquered envy—the wise, virtuous, compassionate, and eloquent man—should recount the sacred story.
When a twice-born reciter of the Purāṇas has ascended the seat of Vyāsa, he shall not bow down to anyone until his discourse is concluded.
One should never speak of this story in the presence of those who are rogues, those of wicked conduct, or others who are seekers of victory through deceitful means. (26)
A wise person should not recount sacred stories in a place crowded with wicked people, nor in a region infested with Śūdras and beasts of prey, nor in a gambling house. (27)
In a good village crowded with virtuous people, in a fertile field, in a temple of the gods, or on the holy bank of a river or stream, the wise man should speak of meritorious stories.
Those who are endowed with devotion to Śiva, who have no longing for other activities, who are restrained in speech, well-disciplined, and composed, such listeners partake in merit. (29)
Those lowest of men who listen to the meritorious narrative without devotion have no fruit of merit; they shall experience suffering birth after birth. (30)
Those who listen with devotion to the Purāṇas after first honoring them with offerings such as betel leaves and other gifts shall not be impoverished, nor shall they be sinful.
Those men who depart elsewhere while the narrative is being recited will have their wives and wealth perish in the midst of their enjoyments.
Those lowest of men who listen to this purifying discourse while wearing turbans on their heads are reborn as cranes.
Those who listen to the purifying discourse while chewing betel-leaf, the servants of Yama cause them to eat their own excrement in hell.
And those hypocrites who, seated upon high thrones, listen to the discourse, shall experience inexhaustible hells and indeed become crows.
Those heroes who are seated in the vīrāsana posture and those who are situated upon couches, provided they listen to the sacred narrative, indeed become trees with straight trunks.
Those who listen without bowing down become poison trees; men who listen while lying down become pythons.
He who listens to the discourse of the speaker while occupying the same seat incurs a sin equal to that of violating the preceptor’s bed and shall go to hell. || 38 ||
Those mortals who revile one who knows the Purāṇas or the sin-removing narrative shall indeed become dogs for a hundred births.
Those lowest of men who speak while a discourse is in progress are born as donkeys, and after that, as lizards.
Those men who never at any time listen to the meritorious narrative, having experienced terrible hells, become wild boars in the forest.
Those best of men who rejoice in this narrative being recited—even those who do not hear it—go to the eternal, supreme state.
Those deceitful ones who create obstacles while this narrative is being recited shall, after suffering in hells for ten million years, become village pigs.
Those who cause human beings to hear this meritorious ancient narrative shall dwell in the abode of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Those men who provide a seat for one who knows the Purāṇas—whether it be a woolen blanket, a deerskin, garments, a couch, or even a wooden plank—[attain great merit]. (45)
Having reached the heavenly world and enjoyed pleasures as they desired, and having dwelt in the worlds of Brahmā and the other gods, they attain the state that is free from all affliction.
Those who give new cotton garments to one who knows the Purāṇas become enjoyers of pleasures and endowed with knowledge in birth after birth. || 47 ||
Those who are joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), by the mere hearing of the Purāṇas, they go to the supreme state.
O best of the twice-born, here I shall recount a highly meritorious history, which destroys all sins for those who hear it, and which is wonderful and very captivating. (49)
In the middle of the southern region, there is indeed a village known as Bāṣkala; all the people there are deluded and devoid of [proper] action.
There, the practices of the Brahmins were averse to the Śruti and Smṛti; they were devoid of silent recitation and Vedic study, and were obsessed with the wives of others.
Peasants, weapon-bearers, godless men, and those of crooked conduct do not know the supreme dharma characterized by knowledge and dispassion.
And women are devoted to sin, wanton, and greedy for lust; they are evil-minded, crooked in their ways, and devoid of virtuous conduct. (53)
There was a certain wicked-souled man named Vidura, the lowest of Brahmins; he was the husband of a courtesan and, though possessed of a wife, he followed an evil path. (54)
Abandoning his own wife named Bandulā every night, he likewise resorts to the house of a courtesan and, tormented by passion, takes his pleasure there.
That woman also, being separated from him at night and still in the bloom of her youth, being unable to endure the onset of passion, took her pleasure united with a lover.
Once, seeing her of wicked conduct united with a paramour, her husband, out of anger, rushed toward her in haste.
When the paramour had fled, that evil-minded man seized his wife and, striking her with his clenched fist, beat her again and again.
Afflicted by her husband, that woman, filled with anger, spoke fearlessly: "You take pleasure with a courtesan every night; what recourse is there for me? (59)
I am a beautiful woman, endowed with fresh youth; how shall I endure, afflicted by desire, deprived of union with you? (60)
Thus addressed by that slender woman, that lowest of Brahmins replied: "What you have said is indeed appropriate; therefore, I shall speak for your benefit. (61)
"Extract wealth from your lovers and give them supreme pleasure; give all that wealth to me, for I shall give it to the courtesans. (62)
"In this way, O fair-faced one, my desire shall also be fulfilled. "So be it," the bride accepted her husband's words. (63)
Thus, as that couple persisted in their wicked conduct, that Brahmin who was the husband of the Vṛṣalī met his death in the course of time.
When her husband had died, that woman, her youth having somewhat passed away, dwelt for a very long time in her own home together with her sons.
Once, by the turn of fate, when an auspicious festival arrived, that woman went to the sacred field of Gokarṇa together with her kinsmen.
Having bathed there in the water of a sacred ford, he heard a meritorious Puranic narrative concerning the foremost of the gods in a certain temple.
For women who are attached to paramours, the servants of Yama cast a red-hot iron club into their private parts in hell.
Having heard these words concerning dharma spoken by the reciter of the Purāṇa, she, being afraid, spoke in secret to that bull among Brahmins.
"O Brahmin, out of ignorance, a terrible sin was committed by me; it was perpetrated through lustful conduct in my youth and driven by deceit. (70)
Having heard these words of yours, which expand upon the meaning of the Purāṇas, a great fear has arisen within me, and my body trembles repeatedly. (71)
Fie on me, who am attached to wicked senses, sinful, and deluded by passion; for the sake of a trivial pleasure, I shall go to a terrible state of woe. (72)
How shall I behold the terrifying messengers of Yama at the time of death? How shall I find composure while being forcibly bound by their nooses around my neck? (73)
How shall I endure in hell the cutting of my body into pieces? And again, how shall I fall, tormented, into the caustic mire?
And how is it that I wander incessantly among hundreds of thousands of wombs—among worms, insects, birds, and the like—being tormented by a flood of suffering? (75)
And how can food please me from this day forward? And how shall I, overwhelmed by suffering, enjoy sleep at night? (76)
Alas, alas! I am ruined, I am consumed by fire, and my heart is rent asunder! O Fate, having bestowed such intelligence upon me, you have cast me down into great sin! (77)
The terrible suffering that arises for a living being as he falls from the peak of a lofty mountain while pierced by a spear is ten million times greater than mine.
Even by performing ten thousand horse-sacrifices or bathing in the Gaṅgā for a hundred years, purification generally does not arise from my exceedingly heavy sin. (79)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Or whom shall I take as my refuge? Who in this world will protect me as I fall into the ocean of hell? (80)
"You alone are my preceptor, O Brahman; you are my mother and you are my father. Lift me up, lift me up—I am wretched and have come to you alone for refuge. (81)
Thus, having raised up with compassion that woman who had fallen at his two feet, filled with world-weariness, the wise bull among the twice-born spoke.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "By good fortune you have awakened at the proper time after hearing this great narrative. Do not fear; I shall tell you of your destiny, which brings happiness. (83)
Merely by hearing the excellent discourse, such an understanding arose in you; there was detachment from the objects of the senses and great remorse. (84)
For repentance is the supreme atonement for all sins; by that alone does a wise man immediately perform his expiation. (85)
Even after performing all the prescribed expiations according to the rules, women who harbor no remorse do not attain the supreme goal.
By constantly listening to sacred discourses, one attains the supreme goal; and from dwelling in a holy field, purification of the mind arises. (87)
Just as one constantly attains the supreme goal through sacred discourse, so too the highest wisdom does not arise for a living being through other virtuous vows.
Just as a mirror becomes stainless when polished again and again, so too the mind attains supreme purity through the discourse on the sublime. (89)
When the minds of men are purified, meditation on Umāpati is perfected; through such meditation, everything defiled by mind, speech, and body is cleansed. (90)
Having immediately shaken off [all bonds], the perfected ones go to the supreme state of Śambhu; therefore, for those who have renounced merit, the discourse on the Truth is the supreme means.

Through discourse, meditation is perfected; from meditation comes supreme liberation. He who hears this discourse without having mastered supreme meditation shall attain meditation in another birth and reach the highest goal.
By merely uttering the Name while chanting the mantra, Ajāmila, filled with remorse, attained the supreme goal. (93)
For all men, listening to the sacred teachings is the seed of all that is auspicious; he who is devoid of it is a mere beast—how could such a one be liberated from bondage? (94)

Therefore, you too, with your intellect withdrawn from all sense-objects and having established supreme devotion, should always listen to the sacred narrative (satkathā). By constantly listening to the sacred narrative, your mind will attain purity.
Therefore, meditate upon the Lord of the Universe; from that, you shall attain liberation. For one who meditates on the lotus feet of Śiva, liberation is attained in a single birth. (96)
"It will happen, there is no doubt; I speak the truth, the absolute truth," said that brahmin to the woman, who was choked with tears. (97)
Having fallen at his feet, she said, "I have achieved my purpose," from that very best of brahmins in that same great sacred field.
She listened to the virtuous, excellent discourse that bestows the fruit of liberation; then that brahmin spoke to her a story enriched with the spirit of detachment.
Upon hearing which, a person would immediately abandon the latent impressions of sensory objects, so that his mind becomes pure and attuned to the essence of dispassion. (100)

Thus the twice-born one spoke a Śaiva narrative imbued with devotion; in whatever manner her mind attained serenity, in that very manner he gradually instructed her in the yoga of meditation upon Śambhu.

Gradually, the heart of the Brahmin woman—its impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* destroyed, its attachment to the enjoyment of all the senses and physical form liberated—entered into meditation on the form of the Lord of the Universe, the pure reality.
Thus, having taken refuge in the true guru, that woman attained right understanding and meditated again and again upon the body of Śambhu, which consists of consciousness and bliss.
Constantly bathing in the waters of sacred fords, wearing matted hair and bark garments, her entire body smeared with ashes, she was adorned with rudrākṣa beads.
Devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names, restrained in speech, moderate in eating, seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), undistracted, and eager to hear sacred discourses. || 5 ||
Devoted to the service of her guru and having renounced her children and friends, she thus gratified Śiva through the yoga taught by her guru.

O Lord of the Universe, cause of the dissolution, maintenance, and birth of the universe; O Śiva, the sole object of worship for the universe, eternal one whose form is the universe; O glorious Maheśa, who has destroyed the appearance of the qualities that are contrary to [the nature of] time—bestow upon me the glance of your compassionate eye.

O Śambhu, whose crest is adorned with the moon, O peaceful-formed one, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the best of immortals and who bears the Gaṅgā; O you whose ornaments are the lords of serpents, O Lord whose abode is on the king of mountains, O destroyer of the afflictions of devotees, cast upon me a glance of compassion! 8.

O Śrī Viśvanātha, O mine of compassion, O wielder of the trident, O Lord of beings, O Bharga, O you whose fame is sung throughout the three worlds; O Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, O destroyer of Madana, O universal form, O Lord of Gaurī, bestow upon me your compassionate glance. 9.
Thus, praying to Maheśvara with devotion every day and properly listening to the sacred stories, she completely severed the bonds of karma.
Then, in due course, that woman, having cast off her body, was led by the attendants of Maheśa and reached the abode of Śiva.
There, Mahādeva was being served by the gods, together with Umā, Gaṇeśa, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and others, as well as Vīrabhadra, Īśvara, and the rest.
He beheld Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gaurī, who was being worshipped, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, three-eyed, five-faced, and blue-throated.
Seeing him bearing Gaurī on his left lap—she who possesses a luster like lightning and the moon—that woman, filled with agitation, bowed down to him again and again.
Drenched with tears of joy, her hair standing on end with thrill, she was honored with compassion by both Pārvatī and Śaṅkara.
Having obtained an unshakable dwelling in that eternal world, which is a mass of supreme bliss and light, he attained unassailable happiness. || 16 ||
Once, having approached the goddess Umā and bowed down to her, she asked: "To what destination has my husband gone? (17)
The Great Goddess said to her: "That husband of yours, evil-minded as he was, having experienced the miseries of hell, has been born as a Piśāca on the Vindhya mountains. (18)
Again that woman asked the goddess, the sovereign of the three worlds: "By what means may my husband attain a good state? (19)
The Goddess said: "If he should ever hear this highly meritorious account of ours, having crossed over all misfortune, he shall go to this world. (120)
Having heard these words of Gaurī, that woman, with palms joined in reverence, entreated the goddess for the purification of her husband’s sins.
Being thus repeatedly entreated by her, Pārvatī, filled with compassion, summoned the Gandharva named Tuṃburu and then spoke as follows.
"O Tumburu, may you be blessed; go with her to the Vindhya mountain. There dwells a Piśāca who is her evil-minded husband. (23)
Having recounted before him the most meritorious narrative endowed with our own virtues, bring him, who is liberated from miserable states, into the presence of Śiva.
Thus commanded by the Goddess, Tumburu bowed to her and, together with her, went swiftly to Mount Vindhya in a celestial chariot.
There he saw a Piśāca of massive body, with red eyes and a large jaw, laughing, weeping, and leaping about. (26)
Having seized him by force, bound him with cords, and confined him, Tumburu, lute in hand, sang the story of the Lord of Gaurī.
Having heard this highly meritorious discourse on the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), that Piśāca shook off all impurity and regained his memory within seven days.
Having cast off that piśāca body and attained his own divine form, he himself sang the glorious life-story of the Lord of Pārvatī.

Having ascended the celestial chariot, assuming a divine form, and accompanied by his beloved with Tumburu at his side, he sang of the enchanting qualities of Maheśa and went to the eternal state of Kaivalya.
Sūta said: Thus has been told this meritorious narrative, which destroys sins, brings pleasure to Maheśvara, and is a means for attaining pure knowledge. 31.
Whatever mortal, being composed, should hear or recite this wonderful narration of Śambhu’s qualities, which destroys all sins. (32)

It generates supreme bliss and is the great medicine for the disease of worldly existence; having enjoyed various pleasures here, one who has consumed it attains liberation and goes to the highest state. || 33 ||
Sūta said: O most excellent sages, you are indeed highly fortunate and have achieved your life's purpose, for you always partake of the ever-fresh nectar of Śambhu’s stories.

Truly, those alone are partakers of true birth in the world of the living whose minds meditate upon the Lord of the Universe, whose speech praises His qualities, and whose two ears listen to His stories; they cross over the cycle of existence.

I take refuge in Supreme Śiva, who is dense with infinite bliss, whose form is eternally untouched by the various distinctions of qualities, who is equal in majesty whether within or without the world, who sports in his own splendor, and who is far beyond the reach of the functions of speech and mind. (136)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Hearing the Purāṇas," in the third section, the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Thus ends the third section, the Brāhma-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Purāṇa. || 3 ||
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa! We meditate upon that Maheśāna, the beloved child of Maheśānī, the Lord of the Gaṇas, whose face is like the lord of elephant-herds, and who is free from all ailment. (1)

Though situated on the earth, she is not of this world; though standing below, she is higher than even the third heaven. She bestows liberation upon those bound to the earth, and for living beings who die within her, there is immortality. That Kāśī—the city of the enemy of Tripura, which is eternally served by the gods on the banks of the river that purifies the three worlds—may she protect the universe from calamity. || 2 ||
Salutations to that Great Lord, through the pretext of whose three junctions (saṃdhyās) the lords of the three worlds incessantly perform their coming and going.
The son of Satyavatī, the author of the eighteen Purāṇas, related this sin-destroying narrative in the presence of Sūta.
Śrī Vyāsa said: Once the illustrious Nārada, having bathed in the waters of the Śrī Narmadā, worshipped the glorious Oṃkāra, which bestows everything upon all embodied beings.
As he proceeded, he beheld before him the Vindhya mountain, which destroys the torments of worldly existence and is adorned by the waters of the Revā.
By means of its two forms—the stationary and the moving—and through its manifest splendor, it makes this earth truly worthy of its name "Vasumatī" (the possessor of wealth).
It was an abode of flavors with its mango trees, a remover of grief through its ashoka trees; it was graced everywhere by palmyra, tamala, hintala, and sala trees.

With *khapura* fruits it was indeed like a city of the sky (*khapura*), with *śrīphala* fruits it possessed the splendor of Lakṣmī (*śrī*), with *aguru* it had great fragrance, and with *kapittha* fruits it was tawny like a monkey.
It was enchanting with lakuca trees shaped like the breasts of the forest’s beauty, and it was illuminated by plantain trees that rivaled the finest fruits of heaven.
It was adorned with beautiful orange trees like a pavilion for the limbs [of the earth], and it was filled with reeds, citrons, and pomegranates.

It was, as it were, performing the *hallīsaka* dance with the *kaṅkola* creepers swaying in the wind, while the *lavalī* trees served as the abode of the play of dancing through their various graceful movements.
With the gentle swaying of its camphor plantain leaves, it seemed to beckon travelers overcome by fatigue, inviting them to rest.
Like a *punnāga* tree with its *punnāga* sprouts, he seemed to bear upon his trembling sprout-like hands the breasts that were clusters of *mallikā* blossoms.
With its split pomegranates, it seemed to reveal its own heart full of passion, as if embracing a mādhavī creeper in the form of a lover within the forest.
With its udumbara trees reaching into the sky and garlanded with infinite fruits, it seemed to bear millions of cosmic eggs on all sides like the Infinite One himself.

It was covered with jackfruit trees resembling the noses of forest elephants, and with śukanāsa and palāśaka trees that seemed to have shed their leaves as if out of grief for those separated from their lovers because of eating them.
Seeing the *nīpa* trees as if they were bristling with horripilation, he beheld [the mountain] shining on all sides with clusters of *kadaṃba* and *kadaṃbaka* trees.
It shone with *nameru* trees like the lofty peaks of Mount Meru, and with *rājādana* and *madana* trees like the palaces of lovers.
On its banks, it was surrounded by high cloth tents with clever thatched roofs, shining with clusters of *kuṭaja* flowers as if presided over by white *baka* cranes.
With *karamarda*, *karīra*, *karaja*, and *karaṃbaka* trees, it shone like the thousand-rayed sun, as if with hands extended to welcome supplicants.
It was as if consecrated by the radiant buds of the royal campaka trees, and with its flowering śālmalī trees, it surpassed the splendor of a lotus pond.
In some places it was beautiful with high trees having trembling leaves, in some places with golden ketaka trees, and in various spots with kṛtamāla and naktamāla trees.
It was resplendent with *karkaṇḍu*, *bandhujīva*, and *putrajīva* trees; and with *satiṇḍuka*, *iṅguda*, and *karuṇa* trees, it was an abode of compassion.
He was Hara, who had assumed the form of the Earth, appearing as if he were incessantly worshipping with the falling flowers of the madhūka tree using pearls released from his own hand.
It was as if being fanned by fans made from the seeds of *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *añjana* trees; and with coconuts and dates, it was as if a parasol were held aloft in the sky.
With *amanda*, *picumanda*, *mandāra*, and *kovidāraka* trees; with *pāṭala*, *atiṃtiṇī*, *ghoṇṭā*, *śākhoṭa*, and *karahāṭaka* trees. || 27 ||
With its head marked by *tilaka* with *uddaṇḍa*, *śehuṇḍa*, *eraṇḍa*, *guḍapuṣpaka*, *bakula*, and *tilaka* trees.
It was adorned with *akṣa*, *plakṣa*, *śallakī*, *devadāru*, and *haridruma* trees, as well as trees and creepers that were perpetually in flower and perpetually in fruit.
It was covered with groves of cardamom, cloves, black pepper, and *kuluñja* trees, and adorned with rose-apple, hog-plum, marking-nut, *śelu*, and *śrīparṇī* trees.
It was delightful with groves of śāka and conch trees, and with sandalwood and red sandalwood; it was adorned with forests of harītakī, karṇikāra, and dhātrī trees.
It was covered with hundreds of vines of grapes, betel-nut, and long pepper, and was fragrant with jasmine, yūthikā, kunda, and madayantī flowers.
It was adorned with mālatī flowers accompanied by swarms of wandering bees, as if Kṛṣṇa had arrived under the guise of the bees to sport with the gopīs many times over.
It was crowded with various herds of wild animals, resounded with the cries of various birds, and was surrounded on all sides by various rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds.
It was filled on all sides by various hosts of gods who had come from the celestial realms, having abandoned their hollow splendors, and were dwelling there out of a desire for worldly enjoyments.
It seemed as if it were scattering offerings of leaves and flowers here and there, while indeed welcoming [the guest] from afar with the cries of peacocks.
Then the mountain saw Nārada in the sky, illuminating the heavens with a brilliance like a hundred suns, and went out from afar to meet him.
The splendor of the body of the son of Brahmā had dispelled all darkness; seeing him approaching, the darkness in his mind was cast away.
Arisen from the splendor of Brahman, filled with awe and performing the hospitable rites for the virtuous, he indeed abandons even his hardness and assumes gentleness. (39)
Seeing his gentleness even in that dual form, Nārada rejoiced exceedingly; for the virtuous have minds that are won over by humility. (40)

Upon seeing a teacher approaching his home, whether he be a true preceptor or not, he who is unworthy of being called a teacher yet maintains humility is truly a teacher; one who does not is no teacher at all.
In response, that mountain, though its peaks were high, bowed its neck even lower; with its crest touching the earth, it prostrated before the great sage.
Having raised him up with the tips of his hands and greeted him with blessings, he took the seat indicated by him, which was loftier even than the mind.
He worshipped him with eightfold offerings consisting of curd, honey, clarified butter, water, moist unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and flowers.

Having received the guest-offering (arghya), the mountain, seeing that [the sage] was weary and had been relieved of his fatigue by the massaging of his feet and other services, spoke while bowing down. (45)
Today, at once, the dust of worldly passion has been cast off by the dust of your feet; and the inner darkness has been instantly dispelled by the splendor clinging to your body.
"O Sage, today is a day of fruitful success for me, and today is a blessed day for me; today, the fruits of my long-accumulated past meritorious deeds have borne fruit. (47)
"Today my status as the bearer of the earth shall be honored by the wielder of the thunderbolt. Having heard this, the sage then sighed slightly and remained silent.
The best of the Kulis, his mind overcome with agitation, spoke again: "O Brahmin, skilled in all matters, tell me the cause of this sighing. (49)
If there is anything unseen or unheard by you that is desired within the three worlds, and if you have compassion for me here, let it be told; I am bowed before you.
My voice has become difficult to restrain due to the floods of joy born from your arrival; it is not at all possible for me to speak repeatedly, yet I shall say this one thing. (51)
The capacity to support the earth has been described by former sages as residing in Meru and other mountains collectively; yet I alone uphold the earth.
Because he was the father of Gaurī, because he was the lord of the mountains, and because he was the kinsman of Paśupati, he alone was the one honored by the virtuous.

The gods said: Salutations to the one of golden form, to Brahman who has the form of Brahman; to him whose true nature is unknown, to Kaivalya and to the Immortal.
Salutations to that Self of Consciousness, which the gods do not perceive, wherein even the mind is blunted, and where speech does not extend.
Salutations to that glorious Brahman, whom yogis, remaining motionless through their resolve, behold in the space of the heart as the form of light. || 32 ||
Salutations to the one who transcends time, to Time itself, to the Puruṣa who acts by His own will, whose nature consists of the three qualities, and who has Prakṛti as His form. || 33 ||
To Viṣṇu, who is the form of *sattva*; to Vedhas (Brahmā), who is the form of *rajas*; and to Rudra, who is the form of *tamas*, the cause of maintenance, creation, and destruction. || 34 ||

Salutations to the one whose nature is consciousness; salutations to the one who has manifested as the threefold ego; salutations to the one whose form consists of the five subtle elements and whose essence is the five organs of action.

Salutations to you whose nature is the mind, who are the essence of the five sensory faculties; salutations to you who possess the fivefold form of earth and the other elements, the very soul of the sense objects.

With soft couches provided with cotton-rolls, with lamps, mirrors, and seats; with palanquins, male and female servants, celestial chariots, livestock, and houses.

With bells, water-pots, jars, and other vessels used for bathing, with white wiping cloths, and with fragrant yakṣakardama pastes; || 23 ||
By means of recitations, burnt offerings, the chanting of hymns, the utterance of the exalted names of Śiva, and by movements accompanied by the Rāsa dance and circumambulations; || 24 ||

The lice, looking again and again, would devour them with the tips of their teeth; there were leaders of herds of dark-bodied monkeys with red faces. (39)
Having abandoned the envy inherent in their own species, they take delight together; even the hares play with those wolves, repeatedly rolling on their backs.

This gavaya and this porcupine both stand together here, having cast aside their intense malice and being restrained by the spiritual power of the sage.
Both Huṇḍa and Muṇḍa, desiring victory, were not prepared for battle; even a jackal touches a young deer gently with its paw. (49)
Beasts of prey devour grass, shrubs, and the like, making them the abode of calamity; for the consumption of meat causes suffering in both worlds—fie upon it!
He who, deluded by sin, cooks meat for his own sake shall dwell in hell for as many years as there are hairs on his body.

For those of wicked intellect who nourish their own lives with the lives of others, having suffered in the hells until the end of the kalpa, they are in turn devoured by those very beings here once again.
One must not eat the flesh of a living being even if one's own life-breaths have reached the throat; if one must eat, then one should eat only one's own flesh and not that of another.
O son of Mitrāvaruṇa, these wild beasts are indeed better, for their minds are not set on violence, unlike those men who are devoted to harming others. || 54 ||

On one side are all kinds of meat, and on the other is fish-meat; yet, though they say "it is the tradition, it is the tradition," these people nevertheless abandon the fish.
Even a hawk, upon seeing a quail, turns its face away; yet it is a marvel that even here, the bees, with their dark intentions, continue to wander about.
Having suffered in the hells for a very long time, those addicted to drinking liquor—mere drinkers of honeyed wine—possessed by delusion, sing [of their past] again and again.
Therefore, this verse is celebrated in the Purāṇas as having a clear meaning, once the knowers of the Purāṇas have understood the reality of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Where is meat and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is liquor and where is the worship of Śiva? For those who delight in liquor and meat, Śaṅkara remains far away.
Indeed, without the grace of Śiva, delusion never perishes anywhere; therefore, these bees wander about, deprived of Śiva.
Having seen even the animals dwelling in the hermitage as if they were sages, the gods thus realized that this power is born of the sacred field (kṣetra). 62.
For this reason, even these animals dwelling here are to be liberated by Viśveśvara at the time of their death through the instruction of the Savior (Tāraka).
Having understood the greatness of this sacred field, whoever dwells there with firm resolve—Viśveśa delivers him, whether he be living or dead.
Men who possess knowledge are liberated even if they do not know the secret doctrine; even ignorant animals are liberated when their sins have been removed.
While the gods, overcome with wonder, were proceeding toward the hermitage of the sage, they rejoiced even more upon seeing the flock of birds.
The crane, having placed its neck motionlessly around Lakṣmaṇā’s neck, we believe it is not sleeping but is surely meditating upon the Lord of the Universe.
Scratching with the tips of her beak, the female crane would ward off the longing male swan by shaking her wings.
O best of lovers, as the wheel is being stopped by the sounds of "krek-kreṃ" uttered by the felloe, what does it say here? "I am desired," it says. (69)
"The sweet-throated cuckoo, dwelling in the bower, warbles longingly; the sage, absorbed in meditation, will hear it, thinking it is a dove"—thus [the bird] is warned.
Abandoning its cry of "kekā," the peacock remains silent out of fear of him; and the cakora bird, the consumer of moonlight, has as if undertaken a vow of fasting at night.
"O parrot, listen! Śiva is the one who grants the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, which has no near or far bank. Thus did the sārikā, reciting the essence, awaken the parrot. (72)
The cuckoo, uttering soft notes and warbling its sweet melody, speaks thus to those staying in Kāśī who are experiencing the strife of the Kali age: "Do not [fear]! (73)
Having thus witnessed the behavior of the beasts and birds, the gods greatly censured heaven for its distress caused by this untimely downfall.
Better indeed are these birds, wild animals, and domestic beasts dwelling in Kāśī, for whom there is no return [to rebirth], than even those gods who are not yet free from rebirth.
We, who dwell in heaven, are never equal to those fallen ones residing in Kāśī; for there is no fear of falling from Kāśī, whereas in heaven there is great fear of falling.
Dwelling in the city of Kāśī through practices such as month-long fasts is better than a kingdom free of enemies under the shade of various royal umbrellas elsewhere. (77)
That state which is attained effortlessly even by rabbits and mosquitoes in Kāśī is not attained elsewhere even by yogis through the practice of yoga.
Better is a beggar in Vārāṇasī who is free from fear even of Yama; we are not gods, for such is our condition that even a mountain [weighs] upon us.
In the eighth part of a day of Brahmā, the realm of Indra perishes, along with the world-protectors, the sun, the moon, the planets, and the stars.
Even when two parārdhas have passed away, he who resides in Kāśī does not perish; therefore, with every effort, one should pursue the highest good in Kāśī.
The happiness found here in residing at Kāśī does not exist even within the pavilion of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa); if it did, how is it that everyone would long to dwell in Kāśī?
Through the exchange of that merit which has been accumulated over thousands of previous births, residence here in Kāśī is obtained. (83)
Even if one has attained success, it may not endure if the Three-eyed Lord should become angry; therefore, one should always seek refuge in Viśveśvara, the protector.
The fourfold aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are indeed found in their entirety at Kāśī, but not so anywhere else. (85)
Even if one should go from his home to the temple of Viśveśvara out of mere laziness, he shall gain a merit at every step that exceeds that of the horse sacrifice.
For one who, having bathed in the northward-flowing river, proceeds at the sight of Viśveśa with supreme faith, there is no end to his spiritual welfare.

From seeing, touching, bathing in, sipping the water of, performing the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) in, chanting prayers in, offering libations in, and worshipping the deities in the celestial river (Svardhunī); || 88 ||
And from beholding the five sacred fords (tīrthas), and then from seeing Viśveśvara, through faith, touch, and worship, and by the offering of incense, lamps, and so forth; || 89 ||
With circumambulations, hymns of praise, recitations, prostrations, and dances, [they call out] "O God of gods, Mahādeva! O Śambhu! O Śiva, Śiva! (90)
"O Dhūrjaṭi, O Nīlakaṇṭha, O Lord, O wielder of the Pināka bow, O moon-crested one, O trident-bearer, O Lord of the Universe! Protect me, protect me!"—with such utterances [he prayed]. || 91 ||
And by entering the pavilion of liberation for even half a moment, as well as through discourse on the Dharma and the hearing of the Purāṇas there, [one attains the goal].
Through the performance of daily and other obligatory rites, as well as by honoring guests and rendering assistance to others, dharma becomes progressively superior.
Just as the moon waxes bit by bit during the bright fortnight, so does the mass of merit increase step by step for those residing in Kāśī.

Faith is its seed, watered by the water from the feet of the Brahmins; the four branches are the ten branches of knowledge; the flowers are the [four] goals of life, and the two fruits are the gross and the subtle—liberation and desire. This is the venerable tree of Dharma.

Bhavānī is the bestower of all goals here, and Ḍhuṇḍhi shall fulfill all desires here; Viśveśa shall liberate all living beings at the time of death through the instruction of the mantra into the ear. 96.

In Kāśī, Dharma exists in its fourfold form; in Kāśī, Artha is also found in its many varieties. In Kāśī, Kāma is the sole ground of all happiness; in Kāśī, Śreya is found—what, then, is there that is not present here? 97.

Where Viśveśvara resides, it is no wonder that the forms of dharma, artha, kāma, and amṛta are present; for he is the embodiment of his own nature and the universal form. Therefore, there is nothing in the three worlds equal to Kāśī. 98.
Speaking thus, the gods beheld the hermitage of the sage, rich with the fragrance of the smoke from sacrificial offerings and surrounded by many young students.
It was adorned by young fawns following the daughters of the sages, who held handfuls of śyāmāka grain as offerings and whose mouths were filled with darbha grass used for support.
It was covered on all sides with moist bark-garments and loincloths hanging from the branches of trees, as if it were surrounded by snares set to capture obstructive deer.
Beholding the courtyard of the leaf-hut marked by the footprints of Lopāmudrā—the crest-jewel of devoted wives—the gods bowed down in reverence.

Beholding Agastya at their head, all the gods, including Indra, with joyful countenances, cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory! (4).
The sage rose, seated them all as was appropriate, and after greeting them with blessings, he asked the reason for their arrival.
Vyāsa said: Having heard this most meritorious narrative with devotion, and having read it or caused it to be read before those possessed of faith in the vow; || 6 ||
Having shaken off all sins, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, one shall certainly go to the city of Śiva by means of a swan-colored vehicle.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Description of Agastya’s Hermitage," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: O great sage, when the gods were thus questioned by the muni, what did those blessed ones say? For the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, please relate that now.
Śrī Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of Agasti with great respect, the gods gazed upon the face of Bṛhaspati, the lord of wisdom.
Vākpati said: Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya, to the cause of the gods' arrival. You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are worthy of honor even by the great.
O best of sages, are there not ascetics in every hermitage, at every mountain, and in every forest? Is your state not indeed something quite unique?
The splendor of asceticism resides here in you; the luster of Brahman is firmly established in you. The supreme fortune of merit is in you; generosity is in you, and a noble mind is in you.
This auspicious Lopāmudrā is a devoted wife and a partner in dharma; she is like a shadow to your body, for her very story brings merit.
By Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, Anasūyā, Śāṇḍilī, Satī, Lakṣmī, and Śatarūpā—all of whom were devoted to their husbands.
By Menā, Sunīti, Saṃjñā, and likewise Svāhā—just as she is described as preeminent, so it is certain that no other is.
O Sage, she eats when you eat, she stands when you stand; she sleeps when you sleep, and she awakens first.
She should never show herself to you without being adorned; even when away on some business, she should be devoid of all ornaments.
One should not utter your name for the sake of increasing one's lifespan; nor should one ever utter the name of another person.
Though reviled, she does not revile in return; though struck, she remains serene. And when told, "Do this," she says, "O Master, consider it done. (12)
"Summoned, she leaves her household duties and goes in haste. For what reason was she called, O Lord? May your favor be bestowed. (13)
He does not remain long at the door, nor does he frequent the gateway; furthermore, he gives nothing to anyone unless it has been given by you.

She herself should prepare all the articles for worship that have not been specifically mentioned, as well as the ritual restraints, water, sacrificial grass, leaves, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth.
Indeed, whatever is appropriate for the occasion, one should present it all with a mind free from agitation and appearing exceedingly joyful, while awaiting the right moment.
She partakes of the remnants of her husband’s desired food, such as fruits and the like; saying "Great Grace," she accepts what has been offered to her. (17)
One should not eat without having first distributed [the food] among the gods, the ancestors, guests, the circle of attendants, the cows, and the community of mendicants. (18)
With household utensils kept in order, skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure, she should not perform fasts, vows, and the like without being permitted by you.
She should avoid from afar the sight of communal festivals; she should not go to pilgrimages or to witness weddings and the like. (20)
Whether her husband is sleeping comfortably, sitting at ease, or enjoying himself as he pleases, she should never wake him even for matters concerning her own internal affairs.
A woman in her menses must not show her own face for three nights, nor should she let anyone hear her voice until she has bathed and become pure.
Having bathed well, she should look at the face of her husband and never that of another; or else, having meditated on her husband in her mind, she may look at the sun.
Turmeric, saffron, vermilion, and collyrium, as well as a bodice, betel, and auspicious, beautiful ornaments. (24)
Desiring long life for her husband, a devoted wife should not have her hair dressed in braids, nor should she remove her earrings or other ornaments from her ears.
A virtuous woman never forms a friendship anywhere with a dyer, nor with a sorceress, nor likewise with a female ascetic, nor even with an unfortunate woman.
She never converses with a woman who hates her husband; she is never alone anywhere, nor does she ever bathe naked. (27)
A virtuous woman should never sit upon a mortar, nor on a pestle, nor on a water-jar, nor even on a grinding stone; nor should she sit on a mechanical device or on the threshold. || 28 ||
She should never display boldness except at the time of sexual union; wherever her husband finds pleasure, there she should always be full of love. (29)
This alone is the vow of women; this alone is their supreme virtue: this is their sole worship of the deity—that they do not transgress the word of their husband. (30)
Whether he be impotent, in a miserable state, diseased, or even aged; whether well-off or ill-situated—one must never disregard her husband alone.
Whether her beloved is joyful or not joyful, or has a dejected face, that virtuous woman should always remain of one and the same disposition in both prosperity and adversity.
Even when ghee, salt, oil, and other provisions are exhausted, a devoted wife should not tell her husband "there is nothing," nor should she involve him in arduous tasks.
A woman seeking the merit of bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) should drink the water from her husband’s feet; for a woman, her husband alone is superior even to Śiva or Viṣṇu.
She who performs vows, fasts, and religious observances in defiance of her husband takes away his lifespan; upon death, she goes to hell. (35)
That woman who, intent on anger, gives a retort when she has been addressed, is born as a dog in a village or as a jackal in a lonely forest.
"For women, indeed, one supreme rule has been proclaimed: having worshipped the feet of her husband, she should eat with firm resolve. (37)
One should not frequent high seats, nor should one go to the houses of others; nor should words that cause shame ever be spoken. (38)
One should not speak slanderously and should abandon quarreling from afar; one should never speak loudly nor laugh in the presence of one's gurus. (39)
That evil-minded woman who, having abandoned her husband, wanders about in secret, is born as a cruel female owl dwelling in the hollow of a tree.
If she who has been beaten desires to strike back, she becomes a tigress or a cat; and she who casts a sidelong glance at another indeed becomes squint-eyed. || 41 ||
She who abandons her husband and eats sweet food alone shall become a village dweller, or even a beggar woman who eats the excrement of dogs.
She who speaks ill-willed and unpleasant words is indeed born mute; she who is envious of her co-wife becomes unfortunate again and again. (43)
She who, having violated the sight of her husband, looks upon another man, is born blind in one eye, with an averted face, or even deformed. (44)
Seeing him approaching from outside, she quickly attended to him with water and food, as well as with betel leaves, fans, the massaging of his feet, and other services. || 45 ||
Likewise, she who, being herself delighted, pleases her beloved with flattering words and the removal of his weariness, has thereby pleased the three worlds. (46)
For a father gives in limited measure, a brother gives in limited measure, and a son gives in limited measure; one should always honor the husband, who is the giver of the unlimited.
The husband is a god, the husband is a guru; he is dharma, the sacred ford, and the vows. Therefore, setting aside everything else, she should worship her husband alone. (48)
Just as a body devoid of life becomes impure in an instant, so too a woman deprived of her husband is always impure, even if she has bathed well. (49)
Among all inauspicious things, the widow is the most abandoned of auspiciousness; from the sight of a widow, success never arises anywhere at any time. (50)
A wise person should abandon even his mother if she is devoid of all auspiciousness; he should likewise reject her blessing, for it is like a venomous serpent.
"At the time of the maiden's marriage, the twice-born should cause her to recite: 'May you be the companion of your husband, whether he be living or even deceased. (52)
A husband must always be followed by a wife like her own body or a shadow, just as the moon is accompanied by its moonlight, or as a cloud is accompanied by lightning. (53)
She who joyfully follows her husband from the home to the cremation ground undoubtedly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step. (54)
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too does a virtuous wife, having transcended her messengers, lead her husband to heaven.
The messengers of Yama flee from afar upon seeing Satī, abandoning even her husband, however evil his deeds may be. (56)
We, the messengers, do not fear fire nor lightning as much as we do when we behold a devoted wife rushing toward us. (57)

The sun, though it scorches intensely, is itself scorched; even fire, though it burns, is itself consumed. All luminous bodies tremble upon beholding the great splendor of her devotion to her husband.
For as many tens of millions of years as there are hairs on her body, that devoted wife, sporting with her husband, enjoys the bliss of heaven. (59)
Blessed is that mother in the world, blessed is that father, and blessed is that illustrious husband in whose house there dwells a devoted wife.
Three generations on the father’s side, three on the mother’s side, and three on the husband’s side—these nine enjoy the pleasures of heaven through the merit of the devoted wife.

Those of evil conduct who break their vows of morality cause the three lineages—their father’s, their mother’s, and their husband’s—to fall; they shall suffer misery both in this world and in the next.
Wherever the foot of a devoted wife touches the earth, she considers that very spot to be the sacred ground; there is no burden too great for her purifying power.
Even the sun fears to touch a devoted wife; likewise, the moon and the wind do so as well, for the sake of their own purity and not otherwise.
The waters, ever devoted to their Lord, always long for His touch; today our dullness has been destroyed, and today we have become purifiers of others.
In every house, are there not women proud of their beauty and charm? Yet, it is only through devotion to the Lord of the Universe that a woman who is devoted to her husband is obtained.
The wife is the root of the householder; the wife is the root of happiness. The wife is the fruit of dharma; the wife is for the increase of progeny.
This world and the next world are both won through a wife; one who lacks a wife is not fit for the performance of rites such as those for the gods, ancestors, and guests. (68)
He alone should be known as a true householder in whose home dwells a devoted wife; otherwise, another woman devours him step by step, either as a demoness or through old age. (69)
Just as the body becomes purified by bathing in the Gaṅgā, so too does it become purified by the auspicious glance of a devoted wife.
Even if, by some stroke of fate, she does not follow her husband, she must still protect her virtue; for through the violation of virtue, one falls low.
Due to her misconduct, even the husband falls from heaven, and not otherwise; the same applies to her father, mother, and her circle of brothers.
Furthermore, that woman who, upon her husband's death, maintains the state of widowhood anywhere, attains her husband once more and enjoys the pleasures of heaven. (73)
The binding of hair in a braid by a widow leads to the bondage of her husband; therefore, a widow must always perform the shaving of her head.
One should always take only one meal, never a second; or [one may observe] a fast for three nights, five nights, or even a fortnight-long vow. (75)
Or he may perform a month-long fast, or even the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; or he may perform the Varāka-kṛcchra, or even the Taptakṛcchra.
One should maintain one's life-sustenance by means of barley-meals, or by subsisting on fruits, vegetables, or milk-vows, until the vital breath departs of its own accord.
A woman who sleeps on a bed while her husband is living will cause him to fall; therefore, she should sleep on the ground out of a desire for her husband's happiness. (78)
A widow must never perform the rubbing of unguents on her limbs, nor should she ever apply fragrant substances. (79)

Every day, the libation for the husband should be performed with water containing kusa grass and sesame seeds, preceded by the mention of his name and lineage, as well as those of his father and his grandfather.
The worship of Viṣṇu must be performed with the thought that he is her husband, and not otherwise; she should always meditate upon Hari, who bears the form of Viṣṇu, as her very husband.
Whatever is most beloved in the world and whatever is desired by her husband, that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtuous qualities, with the desire to please the husband. 82.
In the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha, one should observe special religious observances: bathing, giving gifts, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and the frequent chanting of Viṣṇu’s names.
In the month of Vaiśākha, water-pitchers; in Kārtika, lamps filled with ghee; and in Māgha, the offering of grain and sesame seeds—these are especially distinguished in the heavenly world.

In the month of Vaiśākha, a water-shed should be constructed and a water-dripping vessel should be offered to the Lord; likewise, sandals, a fan, an umbrella, fine garments, and sandalwood paste should be given. (85)
Betel-leaf with camphor, as well as offerings of flowers, numerous water-vessels, and likewise flower-houses; || 86 ||
Various drinks, grapes, and plantain fruits should be given to the foremost of the twice-born with the thought, "May my husband be pleased. (87)
For the sake of vigor, one should eat food made of barley or perhaps rice; however, one should avoid eggplant, the surana root, and the shuka-shimbika bean.
In Kārttika one should avoid oil; in Kārttika one should avoid honey; in Kārttika one should avoid bell-metal, and in Kārttika also that which is mixed [with impurities]. 89.
During the vow of silence in the month of Kārttika, one should cause a beautiful bell to be given; one who eats from leaves should present a bronze vessel filled with clarified butter.

For one observing the vow of sleeping on the ground, a smooth bed with a cotton mattress should be given; for the renunciation of fruit, fruit should be given, and for the renunciation of juice, that juice should be given.
Upon the renunciation of grain, that grain—or alternatively, śāli rice—is prescribed; one should diligently give cows adorned with ornaments and accompanied by gold.
On one side are all gifts whatsoever, and on the other side is the gift of a lamp; the former do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a lamp during the month of Kārttika.
When the sun has slightly risen, one should perform the Māgha bath; and according to one's ability, the performer of the Māgha bath should observe the prescribed rules.

One should feed the Brahmins, as well as ascetics and practitioners of austerity, with cooked foods such as sweetmeats (laḍḍukas), fried cakes (pheṇikās), and balls of meat or dough (vaṭakas and iṇḍarikās).
With samīracas fried in ghee, scented with pure camphor, filled with sugar in their centers, pleasing to the eyes, and fragrant; || 96 ||
One should provide loads of dry fuel to ward off the cold, as well as a cotton-filled jacket, a cotton mattress, and a fine upper garment. (97)
Madder, red garments, as well as cotton cloth, nutmegs, cloves, and many betel leaves. 98.
Variegated woolen blankets, windless dwellings, soft foot-protectors, and fragrant unguents; || 99 ||
With offerings of ghee and blankets preceded by a great ceremonial bath, and with the burning of black aguru and other incenses within the inner sanctum; 100.
With thick-wick lamps and various kinds of food offerings, one should utter: "May the Blessed One, whose nature is that of the Lord (Bhartṛ), be pleased. || 1 ||
In this manner, a widow should pass the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha by means of various such observances and vows.
One should not mount a bullock even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat; one should not wear a bodice, nor should one put on discolored clothing.
Devoted to her husband, she should do nothing whatsoever without first consulting her sons; one who is thus constantly engaged in such conduct is considered auspicious even if she is a widow.
Thus, a devoted wife who remains faithful even after her husband's death and is endowed with righteousness attains the worlds of her husband; she shall never experience suffering anywhere.
There is no difference between that Gaṅgā and the woman who regards her husband as a deity; she is Umā and Śiva in person. Therefore, a wise man should worship her.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lopāmudrā, O great mother, O you who gaze upon the lotus-feet of your husband, this very sight of you has yielded the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā."
Having thus praised the highly fortunate princess, devoted to her husband, and having prostrated before her, the Guru, who is skilled in all matters, spoke to the sage.
"You are the Praṇava; this is the Śruti; you are patient; you are austerity itself; this is the virtuous rite; you are indeed the fruit; you are blessed, O great sage! (9)

This is the splendor of devotion to your husband, and you are the supreme splendor of Brahman; even in that regard, this splendor of your asceticism—what is there that is impossible for you to achieve?
Nothing is unknown to you; nevertheless, I shall speak. Listen now, O Sage, to the purpose for which the gods have come here.
This glorious Śatamakha, the slayer of Vṛtra whose weapon is the thunderbolt, indeed beholds the eightfold supernatural powers at his door with a gracious glance.
In the vicinity of that city, herds of wish-fulfilling cows roam; its citizens always rest in the shade of the Kalpa trees.
Those which stand in the streets are but pebbles compared to the cintāmaṇi; this is Agni, the source of the world, and this, moreover, is Dharmarāja.
Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Śrīdara, Rudra, and these other lords are worshipped through their conducts for the sake of all desired objects. (15)
These petitioners of mine are to be entreated by you for the sake of the world; that which brings benefit to the universe is achievable for you through a mere effort of speech. (16)
There is a certain mountain named Vindhya which obstructs the path of the sun; it has grown out of rivalry with Meru—please put a stop to its growth.
Those who are inherently stubborn, those who obstruct the path, and those who increase through rivalry—their growth has increased my own impurity. (18)
Having heard these words of his guru, the great sage, without hesitation and having composed himself for a moment, replied, "So be it."
"I shall accomplish your purpose," saying this, he dismissed the denizens of heaven; then Agastya, becoming intent on reflection once more, became absorbed in meditation.
Vedavyāsa said: Having heard this chapter on the devoted wife, whether a woman or even a man, shall cast off the cloak of sin and proceed to the world of Śakra.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Devoted Wife," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Parāśara said: Then, having beheld the Lord of the Universe through meditation, that lord of sages, O Sūta, spoke these words to the auspicious Lopāmudrā. (1)
"O lady of beautiful hips, look! What is this that has arisen? Where is that task at hand, and where are we, who follow the path of the sages? (2)
How could he, by whom the opposing lineages were effortlessly shattered by the "Lineage-Splitter," have his power blunted even against something as large as a mountain? (3)

He whose courtyard possesses the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) and whose weapon is the thunderbolt (kuliśa), and at whose gate resides the eightfold supernatural powers (siddhyaṣṭaka)—such a person should seek success from that twice-born one.

"Alas, my beloved, the mountains are being thrown into turmoil by the forest fire! Where has that power of the consumer of wood (fire) gone, which was capable of increasing and then checking its own growth?"
Is he, the Lord who wields the rod of punishment and is the controller of all beings, not capable of punishing that single person who is nothing more than a stone?
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Tuṣitas along with the hosts of Maruts, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, and whatever other dwellers of heaven there may be—|| 7 ||
O beloved, are they not capable of preventing the growth of the mountain, they by whose mere glance even the worlds fall?
That cause has been understood and that well-spoken word has been remembered—the song which was sung concerning Kāśī by the sages who perceive reality.
Those seeking liberation must never abandon Avimukta under any circumstances; however, obstacles will arise for the virtuous who dwell in Kāśī.
"O auspicious lady, this great obstacle has arisen here; it cannot be averted, for the Lord of the Universe has turned his face away. (11)

Alas! Whether seeking liberation or not seeking it, who would abandon that [attainment] once obtained through the blessings of the twice-born of Kāśī? Such a person, with a deluded mind, casts away the delicious morsel held in his hand and licks his own elbow. 12.

Alas, people, like children, why would they abandon this Kāśī, the singular mass of merit? Is a lotus-root easily obtained at every immersion [in water]? Is this [Kāśī] likewise so easy to attain? 13.

Having reached Kāśī after overcoming a mass of merit accumulated over many other births through great hardships, why indeed do those of deluded intellect desire to go elsewhere, as if they were seeking to rise toward a miserable state?

Where is the *Kāśikā*, the illuminator of all words, and where is any other task that is so exceedingly painful? Therefore, why would a learned man go elsewhere; for does a pumpkin fruit ever travel toward the face of a goat? (15)
Alas, would a man quickly abandon Kāśī—the illuminator, the mass of accumulated merit? Surely my own heart reveals that his own merit is not at all deficient. (16)
If a man here does not abandon Kāśī—the sole heap of merit and the companion of every living being—then no one else who strives to go elsewhere shall remain free from disease. 17.

Those who have not been liberated do not abandon Gaṅgā—she whose sins are terrified away by the gods, who is difficult for even the thirty deities to attain, who possesses eternal waters, who destroys the curse of the bonds of worldly existence, who is never forsaken by Śiva, and who is the unique oyster shell for the nectar of immortality—even though they have already enjoyed liberation.

"O friends, why are you so dejected? Having been deceived by an excessive burden of toil, even after reaching Kāśī—the sole commodity for which abundant merit is the price—where are you now prepared to go, having abandoned it? (19)

Oh, the dullness of people that their minds do not go elsewhere after leaving Kāśī—even though it is held upon the tip of the trident of the Enemy of Kāma and is delightful with the shimmering waters of the Gaṅgā even at the time of cosmic dissolution! 20.

O people whose worlds are defiled by sin, why do you abandon Kāśī—the boat that drowns out and puts to sleep all opposing sins—and instead fall into the midst of the ocean of the next existence, which is entirely filled with the waters of sorrow? (21)

O twice-born ones, Kāśī is not easily attained even by the path of the virtuous, nor by the application of yoga, nor by gifts, nor indeed by fierce austerities; oh, it is attained only through the blessings of the twice-born or by the grace of the Lord of the Universe.

Dharma is indeed carried away by the weight of prosperities, and wealth is surely lost through desires for abundant giving and enjoyment; everything else may be found elsewhere, but that one thing—liberation—is found in Kāśī alone, and not elsewhere in the same way as it is here.
For just as the field of Avimukta is pure, no other is so described by the Vedas, nor by the Dharmaśāstras, nor by those Purāṇas; therefore, Avimukta is indeed always a place of refuge. (24)
Jābāli said this to Āruṇi: "The iḍā is known as sirī; the piṅgalā is the nāḍī, and within that is Avimuktaka."
That supreme channel is the Suṣumṇā; this [city] Vārāṇasī is a triad [of powers]. Indeed, it is heard in the Śruti that for all living beings departing from here, Hara [is the goal].
"He explains the Tāraka Brahman; through that, they indeed become Brahman. Thus is this verse, so say the exponents of the Vedas. (27)
At the time of his passing, by means of instruction to Tāraka, the Blessed One will liberate the living beings residing here in Avimukta; of this there is no doubt.
There is no sacred field equal to Avimukta; there is no destiny equal to Avimukta; there is no *liṅga* equal to Avimukta—this is the truth, the truth, again and again. (29)
He who, having abandoned Avimukta, finds delight elsewhere, is like one who, letting go of liberation from the palm of his hand, seeks some other supernatural power.

Having thus firmly resolved upon the power of the sacred field based on the Śrutis and Purāṇas, the high-souled sage [declared]: "There is no Liṅga equal to Śrī Viśvanātha, nor is there a city like Kāśī within three crores of worlds. (31)

Then, having prostrated before Śrī Kālarāja, the best of eminent sages made this request: "I have come here seeking leave to depart, since you, O Lord, are the master of the illustrious city of Kāśī. (32)

Alas! On this eighth day of the dark fortnight, coinciding with the day of Mars and the Sun, you have appeared here as the King of Death. Why do you look upon me, who am innocent, with eyes fixed on offense, instead of honoring me with roots, fruits, and flowers? 33.

O Kālabhairava, do you not protect the people residing in Vārāṇasī by extending your hand and saying, "Do not fear," to those afflicted by fear from all sides, while assuming a formidable form that consumes bitter sins? 34.

O King of Yakṣas, maker of the night, you of beautiful form, leader of the sons of Śrīpūrṇabhadra, wielder of the staff! You indeed know all the suffering born of ascetic penance; why then do you lead me outside, O protector of the inhabitants of Kāśī? (35)

You are indeed the giver of food, you are the giver of life, you are the giver of knowledge, and you are indeed the giver of liberation as well; with your masses of matted locks and necklaces of lordly serpents, you provide the final ornament for all people.

Indeed, your two attendants, Gaṇas, are experts in investigating the circumstances of those who have fallen into agitation and delusion; by creating confusion, they momentarily drive away other wicked people from this sacred field. (37)

Listen, O Lord Ḍhuṇḍhivināyaka, to my words; I am distressed like one who is helpless. Indeed, all the multitudes of obstacles reside within you; why then do I stand here like a man of evil conduct? (38)
"Let these five Vināyakas listen, as well as the one named Cintāmaṇi and the one named Kapardin; let those two Vināyakas known as the Āśāgajas and this Siddhivināyaka listen. (39)

I have never uttered slander against others, nor have I committed any injury to others; I have never entertained thoughts of another's property or thoughts of another's wife—what ripening of karma is this? (40)

The Ganges has been attended by me three times a day, and Śrī Viśvanātha has always been beheld; pilgrimages have been performed everywhere on every auspicious occasion—what is this consequence that is the cause of my obstacle? (41)

O Mother, O large-eyed one, O auspicious one, O eldest sister, O beautiful bestower of good fortune! O Creator of the universe, O you whose arms are the universe, salutations to you, O Śrī Citraghaṇṭā, O Vikaṭā, and O Durgikā!
"Let these deities of Kila and Kāśī be witnesses; I am not departing for my own sake. Being entreated by the hosts of gods, I act—what is not performed for the benefit of others? (43)
Did Dadhīci not give his bones in the past? Did Bali not give the three worlds to the seeker? Were Madhu and Kaiṭabha not given up? And did Tārkṣya even become the vehicle of Viṣṇu? (44)

Having taken leave of all the sages dwelling there, including both the young and the old, and having circumambulated the city as well as all the grasses, trees, and creepers, the Lord of Sages departed.
For whom would success not manifest here upon beholding the Moon-crested Lord—even for one who has gone abroad, or even for one who wanders on a base path, provided he is filled with devotion? (46)

"Better indeed that the grasses, trees, and shrubs in Kāśī wander about; they do not commit sin, nor anything else. We are the foremost among those who wander, yet fie on us! Alas, we are leaving Vārāṇasī this day like lions. (47)
Touching his sword again and again, the sage, gazing all around at the rows of palaces, said: "O straight-eyed ones, look! Behold Kāśī; where are you two, and where indeed is this city? 48.
Let the hosts of spirits dwelling on the borders laugh at will today, clapping their hands and even grasping one another's hands; I am departing, leaving behind Kāśī, that singular heap of merit.

Having lamented thus many times, that sage Agastya—alas, like that pair of *krauñca* birds, now accompanied only by his wife—fell into a deep swoon; and as a lover separated from his beloved, he cried out: "O Kāśī! O Kāśī! Come back once more, and grant me your sight! (50)

Having stood for a moment and cried out, "Śiva! Śiva! Śiva! as long as you were saying, "O beloved, they are indeed hard-hearted," why do you not remember the Three-Eyed One, who is skilled in bestowing happiness upon the three worlds, since it was by his command that he sent Madana against you?

Just as he had taken three or four steps, his forehead becoming dappled with drops of sweat from exhaustion, the Earth—as if fearing for her own safety because I would no longer rise to greet him—contracted herself.
Having ascended, as it were, the vehicle of austerity, the sage, in half a blink of an eye, beheld before him that lofty Vindhya mountain obstructing the sky.
Upon seeing that sage Agastya standing before him with his wife—the enemy of Vātāpi and Ilvala—the mountain immediately trembled.
He was blazing intensely with three fires—those arising from austerity and anger, and that born of separation from Kāśī—like the fire of universal destruction.
The mountain, becoming smaller as if wishing to enter the earth, said, "Let the favor of your command be granted; I am your servant. || 56 ||
Agastya said: "O Vindhya, you are virtuous and wise; you know me in truth. If I am to return again, then become smaller than before."
Having spoken thus, the sage, that treasure of asceticism, made the southern quarter well-guarded by his own placement of footsteps together with that virtuous woman.
When that best of sages had departed, the mountain trembled; it looked as if longing for him, thinking, "If he had stayed, then all would have been well."
"Today I am born again, for I have not been cursed by Agastya; indeed, that mountain thought, 'No one is as fortunate as I. (60)
And at that time, Aruṇa, who knows the proper moments, urged on the horses; the world attained great well-being once more through the movements of the sun as before.
"Today, tomorrow, or even the day after, the sage will surely arrive"—with such great burdens of anxiety, he remained as if weighed down by a mountain.
"Even now the sage does not arrive; even now the mountain does not grow—just like the wish-fulfilling trees of wicked people. (63)
For that base person who, harboring malice toward others, desires to prosper—let alone talk of his future growth, even the possibility of his prior growth is in doubt. (64)
The desires of the wicked would not be fulfilled, and even those already achieved would surely perish; therefore, the universe remains safe, protected by the Lord of the Universe.
Just as the breasts of widows, rising up again and again, dissolve right within the heart, so too do the desires of the wicked rise up high there [only to vanish].
Just as a mountain stream might overflow its banks with even a small amount of rain, so too will the prosperity of a wicked person destroy his own family with even a small amount of fortune.
Without recognizing the capacity of another, he who displays his own capacity meets with derision; so too does this mountain here.
Vyāsa said: Even while wandering on the beautiful banks of the Godāvarī, the sage did not abandon that supreme anguish born of separation from Kāśī.
Stretching out his arms toward the north wind that touches the northern quarter, the sage embraced it and inquired after the welfare of Kāśī.
O Lopāmudrā, there is no such seal anywhere here on the surface of the earth that could be seen as belonging to Vārāṇasī, for its creator was not Brahmā.
Standing in one place, speaking in another, running in one place, stumbling in another, and sitting down in yet another—thus the sage wandered here and there.

Then, as he proceeded, the ascetic Puṇyarāśi beheld before him a woman of great beauty, whose radiance was like that of the shimmering moon, appearing like a fortunate man who has attained prosperity.
Having conquered the sun, which blazes even by day, she seemed to extinguish the continuous stream of heat within her own mind.
There Agastya beheld Mahālakṣmī, who had been standing for a very long time.
At night the lotuses close, while the moon sometimes moves toward the ocean; it is as if, out of fear of Mount Mandara, he has taken up residence here in the Milky Ocean.
Ever since Mādhava indeed began to cherish her with honor, she has surely remained [with him] as if under the influence of jealousy toward his other wives. (77)
Having slain the great asura who was terrifying the three worlds in the form of a boar, she remained there in that beautiful city of Kolāpura.
Then, having attained Mahālakṣmī and bowed down to her, the best of sages, his mind filled with joy, praised her—the granter of desired boons—with pleasing words. (79)

Agastya said: O Mother, I bow to you, O Kamalā, whose eyes are as broad as lotuses; O dweller in the lotus-heart of Śrī Viṣṇu, O Mother of the Universe! O Lakṣmī, born from the Milky Ocean, with a complexion as tender as the interior of a lotus, O Gaurī, be gracious to those who constantly bow to you, O refuge of all! 80.

You are Śrī in the abode of Upendra; O sole mother of Madana, you are the moonlight in the moon, O you whose face is as enchanting as the moon; you shine as radiance in the sun and you shine throughout the three worlds. O Lakṣmī, be gracious, O refuge for those who constantly bow to you! 81.

In you, O Jātavedas (Fire), the power of burning always resides; through you, the Creator fashions this manifold universe. Even Viśvambhara (the Sustainer of the World) is able to support everything because of you, O Lakṣmī; be gracious, O refuge of those who constantly bow to you! 82.

O Immaculate One, even Hara takes away that which has been abandoned by you; you protect, you destroy, you create, and you are both the supreme and the inferior. Even Hari became worthy of praise through his attainment of you, O Immaculate Lakṣmī; be gracious, O Refuge of those who constantly bow to you! 83.

He alone is a hero, he alone is virtuous, wise, fortunate, and worthy of honor through his collection of noble lineage, character, and arts; for he alone is a pure man in this entire world upon whom you, O auspicious one, cast a glance of compassion. (84)

In whatever you may dwell—for a moment—whether in a great man, an elephant, a horse, a woman, a blade of grass, a lake, a temple, a house, food, a jewel, a bird, an animal, a bed, or the earth—in all these things here, everything is indeed accompanied by beauty (or prosperity), and nothing else exists.

O Lakṣmī, everything touched by you alone attains purity, while everything abandoned by you is impure in this world; and wherever your name exists, O Consort of Viṣṇu, O Kamalā, O Dweller in the Lotus, there all is indeed most auspicious.

Where can there be suffering for those who constantly recite: "Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Kamalālayā, Padmā, Ramā, she whose hands hold a pair of lotuses, and me, the one born from the Ocean of Milk, the beautiful one holding a jar of nectar, the beloved of Viṣṇu"? 87.
