Having thus praised the Blessed Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, the sage, together with his wife, prostrated himself like a staff, performing the eight-limbed salutation (sāṣṭāṅga).
Śrī said: Arise, arise, may it be well with you, O you who were born of Mitra and Varuṇa! O devoted wife, arise, Lopāmudrā of auspicious vows! 89.
"O illustrious princess, I am pleased by this hymn of praise; let that which is desired in your heart be chosen. O pure one, sit here. (90)
"By these auspicious marks upon your limbs and by your most purifying vows, I desire to cool this body of mine, which has been scorched by the weapons of the Daityas. (91)
Having spoken thus and embraced that wife of the sage, the beloved of Hari affectionately adorned her with many ornaments signifying great good fortune.
Again he said: "O Sage, I know the cause of your heart's torment; the fire born of separation from Kāśī surely burns even one who possesses consciousness. (93)
When that Lord of the Universe went to Mandara in the past, he then fell into such a state due to the separation from Kāśī.
To ascertain the progress of that [battle], the wielder of the trident dispatched Brahmā, Keśava, the Gaṇas, Gaṇeśvara, and the gods.
Having reflected again and again upon all the virtues of Kāśī, they do not go anywhere else even today; for where is there a city such as that? || 96 ||
Having heard this, that illustrious sage then bowed down and replied to Śrī with these words filled with devotion: || 97 ||
If a boon is to be granted to me, and if I am worthy of a boon, then let this be my boon: that I may attain Vārāṇasī once again. || 98 ||
And those who shall always recite this hymn composed by me with devotion to you—may they never experience suffering, and may they never suffer from poverty. (99)
May there be no separation from loved ones, may there be no depletion of prosperity; may there be victory everywhere, and may there be no interruption to one's lineage. (100)
Śrī said: "O Sage, let it be exactly as you have described everything; the recitation of this hymn is the cause of my presence. (1)
Misfortune and Kālakarṇī shall never enter that house; for the sake of the peace of elephants, horses, and cattle, one should always recite this hymn. (2)
For the pacification of children overcome by child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), one should write [this] on birch bark and bind it around the neck.
This secret of the seed-syllable must be guarded by me with great effort; it should not be given to one lacking faith, nor should it ever be given to one who is impure.
And hear this further, O best of Brahmins: in the future Dvāpara age, you, O Brahmin, will become Satyavyāsa as the twenty-ninth [Vyāsa]. || 5 ||
Then, having reached Vārāṇasī, you will attain the desired perfection after having arranged the Vedas and Purāṇas and taught the Dharmas.
I shall tell you one thing that is beneficial; perform it now. Go a short distance from here and behold the Lord Skanda standing before you.
O Brahman, Ṣaṇmukha will relate to you exactly as it was spoken by Śiva—the secret of Vārāṇasī, which brings you satisfaction.
Having thus obtained the boon and having bowed down to Mahālakṣmī, he then departed for the place where Agasti and Kumāra Śikhivāhana reside.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Departure of Agastya," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Pārāśarya said: Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta, to this narrative which is a sister to the Vedas; indeed, by placing it within his heart, a man here becomes a partaker of the goals of human existence.
Then, having plunged into that river which flows with streams of the nectar of joy from beholding Śrīdarśana, the sage, together with his wife, attained supreme delight.
O Sūta, whose mind is pure and born from the sacrificial fire-pit, listen to this one wise saying that was uttered by the learned men of old.
For those virtuous ones in whose hearts the impulse to help others remains awake, their calamities perish and prosperity attends them at every step.

That purity is not attained by bathing at sacred fords, nor is that fruit gained through manifold gifts; it cannot be reached even by severe austerities, but is bestowed upon one who has rendered assistance.
The merit arising from benefiting others and the merit born of giving and other virtues were weighed together by the Creator in one scale; therein, the former was found to be your superior.
Having thoroughly churned the web of words, this alone has been determined: there is no dharma higher than helping others, and no harm greater than causing injury. (7)
This has become an illustration of the benefactor Agastya: where is such sorrow born from the son of Kaśyapa, and where is such a sight of the face of Śrī? (8)
Life is as fickle as the tip of an elephant's ear, and wealth is manifold; therefore, a wise person should perform at least one act of service for others.
A man is not satisfied anywhere merely by obtaining the name of Lakṣmī; let him behold Lakṣmī in person, for only then does the sage become one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Then, traveling at his own will, he beheld from afar Śrīśaila, where the Lord Tripurāntaka himself dwells.
Then the sage, with a joyful mind, spoke these words to his wife: "O beloved, remaining right here, behold the supreme and most lovely sight."
This is the glorious peak of Śrīśaila; by the mere sight of it, rebirth for human beings shall never again occur anywhere in this world.
This mountain is indeed eighty-four yojanas in extent; because it consists entirely of liṅgas, one should therefore perform circumambulation of it.
Lopāmudrā said: "I wish to make a certain request, provided that my husband grants me permission; for she who speaks without being authorized by her husband becomes fallen. (15)
Agastya said: "O Goddess, what do you wish to say? Speak the truth without hesitation; for the speech of women such as yourself never causes distress to their husband. (16)
Then that goddess, bowing down with humility before the sage, questioned him for the sake of the welfare of all and to dispel her own doubts.
Lopāmudrā said: "If, upon seeing the peak of Śrīśaila, there is no further rebirth—since this alone is the truth—then for what purpose is Kāśī sought?"
Agastya said: Listen, O lady of excellent hips; what you have asked, O pure one, is the truth. This has been determined more than once by sages who contemplate the ultimate reality.
There are many places of liberation, and a definitive conclusion has been reached regarding them as well; I shall describe them to you here, so be attentive for a moment.
First is the king of sacred fords (tīrtharāja), well-known by the name Prayāga; it is the most desirable of all holy sites, bestowing dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, Avantikā, Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Dvārakā, and Amarāvatī; || 22 ||
The confluence of the Sarasvatī and Sindhu, the meeting of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Kāntī, Tryambaka, and the banks of the seven Godāvarīs; || 23 ||
Kālañjara, Prabhāsa, as well as Badarikāśrama, Mahālaya, and likewise the sacred field of Oṃkāra and Pauruṣottama. || 24 ||
Gokarṇa, Bhṛgukaccha, Bhṛgutuṅga, Puṣkara, Śrīparvata and other holy fords (tīrthas), as well as Dhārātīrtha; || 25 ||
O beloved, mental holy places such as Truth and the like are indeed bestowers of liberation; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (26)
And as for that which is called the Gayā-tīrtha, which indeed grants liberation to the ancestors; by it, even the sons of one's grandfathers are freed from their debt.
Sadharmiṇī said: O high-minded one, you have mentioned even the mental holy places (*tīrthas*); you ought to explain here which ones those are. (28)
Agastya said: Listen, O sinless one, as I speak of the mental sacred fords (tīrthas), by bathing properly in which a man attains the supreme goal. (29)
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford; compassion for all beings is a sacred ford, and straightforwardness indeed is a sacred ford. (30)
Generosity is a sacred ford, self-restraint is a sacred ford, and contentment is said to be a sacred ford; celibacy is the supreme sacred ford, and speaking kindly is also a sacred ford. (31)

Knowledge is declared to be a sacred ford, fortitude is a sacred ford, and austerity is a sacred ford; yet among all sacred fords, that which is the supreme purity of the mind is the true sacred ford.
Bathing with the body merely drenched in water is not called true bathing; he alone is bathed who has bathed in self-restraint, being pure and cleansed of the impurities of the mind.
He who is greedy, malicious, cruel, hypocritical, and devoted to sensual objects—even if he has bathed in all the sacred fords, that sinner remains truly defiled.
A man does not become pure merely by discarding the impurities of the body; rather, when the impurities of the mind are discarded, he becomes perfectly pure within.
Leeches are born and die only in the waters; yet, because their minds are defiled by impurities, they do not go to heaven.
Excessive attachment toward sense objects is called the mental impurity; indeed, detachment from those very same objects is declared to be its purity. (37)
A mind that is corrupt within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords; it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor, even if washed with water a hundred times.
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, purity, visiting sacred fords, and likewise sacred learning—all these are non-sacred fords if one's inner disposition is not stainless. (39)
Wherever a man whose collection of senses is restrained may dwell, there for him are Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford, purified by knowledge and filled with the water of wisdom that removes the stains of passion and hatred, attains the supreme goal.
This, O Goddess, has been told to you—the characteristic of the mental holy site (mānasa-tīrtha). Now hear the cause for the merit even of those holy sites that exist on the earth.
Just as certain parts of the body are remembered as being most pure, so too certain regions on earth are remembered as being most meritorious.
The sanctity of sacred fords (tīrthas) is traditionally held to arise from the wondrous power of the earth, water, and fire, as well as from the acceptance [of their merit] by sages. (44)
Therefore, he who constantly bathes in both types of sacred sites—those on earth and those in the mind—attains the supreme goal.
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords, and without giving gold and cows, one is born indeed as a pauper.
One does not obtain that fruit by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees which one obtains by visiting sacred fords (tīrthas). || 47 ||
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown—he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is content with whatever comes, and who is free from egoism, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
He who is free from hypocrisy, free from worldly undertakings, moderate in diet, has conquered his senses, and is liberated from all attachments, attains the fruit of the sacred fords.

One who is free from anger, pure-minded, truthful, firm in his vows, and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords (tīrtha). A wise man who visits sacred fords with faith and concentration—even if he has committed sins—is purified; how much more so one who performs pure deeds? (52)
He shall certainly not go to the womb of an animal, nor is he born in a wretched land; he shall not be miserable, he shall partake of heaven, and he finds the means to liberation.
The faithless, the evil-minded, the nihilist, one whose doubts are not severed, and the one who relies solely on logic—these five do not partake in the fruit of the sacred ford.
Those wise men who wander among the sacred fords according to the prescribed rule, enduring all pairs of opposites, are partakers of heaven.
Desiring to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), one should first observe a fast at home and worship Gaṇeśa, the ancestors, Brahmins, and holy men according to one's ability.

Having completed the breaking of his fast, he should go forth joyfully, maintaining his observances; then, having returned and honored the ancestors, he shall partake of the fruits as previously described.

A twice-born man seeking food at sacred fords should not be examined; he is simply to be fed. And the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be made with barley meal, sacrificial porridge, and milk-rice.
A Śrāddha rite seen as appropriate by the sages, performed with oil-cakes and molasses, should be conducted there, excluding the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana). || 59 ||
Whether out of season or in season, the śrāddha and the libation (tarpaṇa) at a sacred site must be performed without delay; one should never allow an obstacle to arise.
Having reached a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform a bath at that ford even by chance; he obtains the fruit arising from bathing as well as that which pertains to the pilgrimage itself.

For men who have committed sins, there shall be the pacification of sin at a sacred ford (tīrtha); for men whose souls are filled with faith, the sacred ford shall yield the fruit as it has been described.
He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part [of the merit]; he who goes by chance obtains half the fruit of the sacred site.
Having fashioned an image out of kuśa grass, one should immerse it in the waters of a sacred ford; whoever is intended for that immersion shall indeed receive an eighth part [of the merit].
A fast at the sacred ford (tīrtha) must be observed, as well as the shaving of the head; for by shaving, the sins residing in the head depart. (65)
On the day before the day when one reaches the sacred ford (tīrtha), a fast must be observed; on the day of arrival, one should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha).

In connection with the discussion of sacred fords (tīrtha), I have also described to you before the constituent parts of a ford; this is indeed a means for attaining heaven and shall also be a means for liberation.
Kāśī, Kāntī, the one named Māyā, Ayodhyā, Dvāravatī, Mathurā, and Avantikā—these seven cities here grant liberation.
Śrīśaila bestows liberation in its entirety, while Kedāra is even greater than that; and beyond both Śrīśaila and Kedāra, Prayāga is the supreme bestower of liberation.
Avimukta is superior even to Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords; there is no doubt that nirvāṇa is not attained anywhere else as it is in Avimukta.

Having heard this [account] which causes one to attain Kāśī and which renders other places of liberation as such, a person with a restrained mind, having also caused the twice-born who are endowed with faith and devotion to hear it, [attains the goal]. (73)
A twice-born man becomes free from sin by making Kṣatriyas devoted to dharma, Vaiśyas who walk the path of the righteous, and Śūdras who are devoted to the twice-born. (74)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Holy Places," in the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: In Mathurā there was a certain twice-born man, the most excellent among the gods on earth; his son was of great splendor, renowned by the name Śivaśarman. || 1 ||
Having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules and having understood their meaning in its true essence, and having recited the Dharmaśāstras and mastered the Purāṇas; || 2 ||
Having practiced the auxiliary sciences and thoroughly scrutinized logic from all sides, having examined the two systems of Mīmāṃsā and delved into the science of archery; || 3 ||
Having investigated Āyurveda and exerted effort in the science of drama (Nāṭyaveda), he mastered numerous treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra) as well as the movements of horses and elephants.
He was well-practiced in the arts, proficient in the science of mantras, and having mastered the languages and scripts of various foreign lands.
Having acquired wealth through righteous means and enjoyed pleasures as they arose, and having procreated virtuous sons and distributed his property among them; || 6 ||
Knowing that youth is transitory and observing that old age had reached his ears, Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born, fell into deep reflection.
Time has passed for me in reciting [the scriptures] and likewise in acquiring wealth; yet Maheśāna, who is capable of uprooting karma, has not been propitiated.
I have not propitiated Viṣṇu, the remover of all sins, nor have I worshipped Gaṇeśa, who grants all desires to men.
Never indeed have I offered light to the sun, the dispeller of the mass of darkness; nor have I meditated upon Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world and the remover of the bonds of existence.
I did not gratify with all my sacrifices the gods who bestow prosperity; nor did I perform service to the Tulasī grove for the pacification of sin. (11)
I have not gratified the Brahmins with delicious foods and sweet flavors—those who serve as the means of crossing over calamities both in this world and the next.
Trees laden with many flowers and fruits, providing excellent shade and glossy foliage, yet not planted along the road, yield fruit neither in this world nor in the next. (13)

Those virtuous women who are not adorned here with fine silk garments, tunics suited to them, and ornaments for every limb—yet who grant excellent dwellings both in this world and the next—[are truly honored]. (14)
Land was not given to the twice-born, which wards off the realm of Yama; nor was gold given to one worthy of gold, that supreme remover of sin. (15)
A cow adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her calf, when bestowed upon a worthy recipient, quickly destroys sins in this world and brings happiness for seven lifetimes.
To discharge his debt to his mother, he did not have a reservoir of water constructed; nor did he ever satisfy a guest who could show him the path to heaven. (17)
Parasols, sandals, and water-pots were not bestowed upon the traveler; for these indeed grant the bliss of the path to heaven to one departing for Saṃyaminī. (18)
Nor have I bestowed wealth anywhere for the sake of a maiden's marriage; rather, I gave a divine maiden in heaven for the sake of attaining happiness and prosperity here. (19)
Out of greed, I did not bathe at the concluding purificatory bath of the Vājapeya sacrifice; nor have I enjoyed abundant food and drink in this life or in any other.
I have not established a linga by constructing an auspicious temple; for when that linga is installed, the entire universe becomes established. || 21 ||
I have not built a temple for Viṣṇu, which bestows all prosperity, nor have I had images of the Sun, Gaṇeśa, and Īśāna fashioned by me. (22)
Neither Gaurī nor Mahālakṣmī [is difficult to attain] even when drawn in a painting; and by making images of them, one becomes neither ugly nor unfortunate. (23)
Extremely fine, variegated, and though not brilliant, garments were also offered to the Brahmins for the sake of attaining an abundance of divine raiment.
Sesame seeds, anointed with ghee and purified by mantras, when offered into a well-kindled fire, indeed effect the removal of all sins. (25)
The Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamānī hymns, the Brāhmaṇa-maṇḍalas, the recited Puruṣasūkta, and the Śatarudriya are the enemies of sin. (26)

If one does not perform service to the Aśvattha tree on the thirteenth lunar day after abandoning the Arka plant, that [service] indeed instantly removes sin; however, it should not be done at night nor on a Saturday.
The bed was not discarded, nor was the soft mattress; it was provided with a leopard-skin rug and a mirror, bestowing the abundance of all enjoyments. || 28 ||
A goat, a mare, a buffalo, a ewe, a female slave, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, water-pots with parched grain, a seat, and soft sandals—[these are the gifts]. (29)
Massaging the feet, the offering of lamps, and especially the provision of water-stalls; as well as fans, clothing, betel-leaf, and other things that provide fragrance to the mouth. (30)
The daily śrāddha, the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali), and the honoring of guests—having given these and other praiseworthy gifts, they enter the abode of Yama.
Those partakers of merit do not see Yama, nor the messengers of Yama, nor even the torments; yet this was not brought about by me.
The Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances, as well as the vows of eating only at night, which effect the purification of the body, have never been performed by me anywhere. (33)
The daily fodder for the cow was not given, the scratching of her body was not performed, and the cow who bestows the bliss of Goloka was not rescued when she was sunk in the mud. (34)
For I have indeed fulfilled the desires of those who sought wealth with the very objects they requested; otherwise, I shall become one who cries out "Give! Give! in another birth. (35)
Neither the Vedas nor the scriptures, neither wealth nor wife, nor son, nor field, nor house and such will follow one to the end of illusion. (36)
Reflecting thus on the name Śivaśarman and applying his intellect in every way, he resolved in his mind: "This would be more secure for me. (37)
"As long as my body remains healthy and as long as there is no impairment of my senses, I shall undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords, which is the cause of my own spiritual welfare. (38)

Having thus passed five days at home, the twice-born man, on an auspicious lunar day, under an auspicious weekday, and with the strength of an auspicious astrological moment (lagna), [proceeded]. || 39 ||
Having observed a fast for one night and performed the Śrāddha ceremony in the morning, the wise man bowed to Gaṇeśa and the Brāhmaṇas, ate, and set forth.
Having thus resolved upon that supreme ladder to the state of Nirvāṇa for all living beings who abide therein, [he spoke]. (41)
Then, having traversed some distance along the road, that twice-born man rested for a moment on the way and reflected: "Where shall I go first? (42)
There are many sacred fords on earth, yet life is fickle and the mind is restless; therefore, one should go to the seven cities, for all sacred fords are present there.
Having gone to the city of Ayodhyā and bathed in the Sarayū, he gratified his ancestors at those various holy sites by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Having stayed for five nights and having fed the Brahmins, the twice-born man went to Prayāga, the king of holy fords, with great joy.
There, where the two best of rivers, the white and the black—difficult even for the gods to attain—flow together; there, a man who has bathed, though he be a sinner, attains the supreme Brahman.
The holy field of Prajāpati is difficult for all to attain; it is acquired through a store of merit, and not otherwise by means of heaps of wealth. (47)
Where the auspicious and holy celestial river, having arrived, meets with Damayantī, Kali, Kāla, and the beautiful daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā).
Prayāga is celebrated as preeminent among all sacrifices; for those who have performed sacrifice there, their bodies moistened by the waters of Prayāga, there is no returning again to this world.
Where Maheśvara himself is personally present as Śūlaṭaṅka, he is the instructor of the path to liberation for those beings who have bathed there.
There also stands the Akṣayyavaṭa tree, whose roots reach down to the seven netherworlds; even at the time of universal dissolution, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu dwelt there, having ascended it.
He should be known as Hiraṇyagarbha himself, manifest in the form of the banyan tree; by feeding the twice-born with devotion near it, one partakes in inexhaustible merit.
Where the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, having come from Vaikuṇṭha in the form of Śrī Mādhava, leads men to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The two excellent rivers, the white and the black, are celebrated by the Vedas; it is certain that those who bathe there attain the immortal state.

From the world of Śiva, from the world of Brahmā, and again from the excellent world of Umā; from the world of Kumāra, from Vaikuṇṭha, and from Satyaloka on all sides; from Tapoloka, Janaloka, and Maharloka—all the inhabitants of the heavenly worlds (Svarloka); and from Bhuvarloka, Bhūrloka, and likewise from the entire world of the Nāgas.
Mountains such as Acala, Himavat, and others, as well as the Kalpavṛkṣa and other celestial trees, come to Prayāga at dawn during the month of Māgha to bathe.
Even the breezes from Prayāga, for which the celestial damsels pray, will purify us; what can we do? For we are like the lame.
Sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha and the dust of Prayāga were once weighed by Brahmā; they [the sacrifices] were not equal to that dust. (59)
Even sinful deeds accumulated over many lifetimes, though deeply rooted within, are utterly destroyed by the mere hearing of the name of Prayāga; it is truly most wondrous.
This is the ford of Dharma; this is the supreme ford of the true goal; this is the ford that fulfills desires, and this is the certain ford of liberation.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin roar within embodied beings only so long as they do not immerse themselves in Māgha at Prayāga, the remover of sins.
"The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; this which is recited in the Veda is Prayāga, again and again. (63)

Sarasvatī is of the nature of rajas, the daughter of Kalinda (Yamunā) is of the nature of tamas, and Gaṅgā here is of the nature of sattva; together they lead one to Brahman, which is beyond all qualities.
This ladder of matted locks belongs to the living being whose body is purified, who has entered the path of Brahman, and who is immersed in both faith and lack of faith.

In this world, there is a certain woman renowned as Kāśī, whose eyes are as restless as those of Lolārka and Keśava; her pair of arms is this Varaṇā, and that which is called her braid here is the river Asi, the ground of imperishable bliss.
Agastya said: O virtuous lady, who here is capable of describing the qualities of that Prayāga, the king of holy places, which is served by all other sacred sites?

Aho! Since the sins of sinners have been forcibly washed away [by other holy sites], Prayāga is served by those very sites for the sake of their own purification; therefore, it is superior to them all. 68.
Having learned of the virtues of Prayāga, the wise brahmin Śivaśarman stayed there during the month of Māgha and then reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Upon entering, he beheld the Vināyaka at the threshold and then, with devotion, smeared him with a paste of ghee and vermilion.
Deceiving his own people by offering five modaka sweets as an oblation, he then entered the inner precinct of the sacred field to escape from the multitude of great calamities.

Having arrived and seen at Maṇikarṇikā the northward-flowing river that leads to heaven, she was surrounded by throngs of men whose non-meritorious deeds had been exhausted and who were like the attendants of Śiva.

Having bathed without delay in pure water along with his clothes, he—possessing stainless intellect and being a knower of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa)—should offer libations to the gods, sages, divine humans, and his own ancestors.

Having quickly performed the five-fold pilgrimage (pañcatīrthikā) and worshipped Viśveśvara according to his own custom, he gazed again and again at the city of the Enemy of Tripura, wondering in amazement, "Has this been seen by me before? || 74 ||

That city of yours does not possess even a partial similarity to the city of the gods, even if it were compared fairly; for it is like a copy of a book made from a different original, due to the difference in the composition and the failure to preserve the excellence of the fine script.

Even the nectar of the gods dwelling in heaven is rendered useless compared to the milk here, which possesses such inconceivable majesty; for if this milk were ever drunk, then the milk from a mother's breast would not even be tasted.

Those people who, through their pure contemplation, do not belong to the Lord except for the wielder of the Pināka bow; and who, though performing good deeds, do not perform them as mere ritual acts, but rather emulate the attendants of Śarva in every respect.

Indeed, by whom has this city of Kāśī not been praised, since for a living being dwelling here at the time of death, the Moon-crested Lord causes the syllable *Oṃ* to be uttered through the ripening of the burden of merits accumulated in the past? (78)
Since Śiva suddenly imparts that wish-fulfilling gem of saṃsāra—the liberating mantra—into the ear of a virtuous person at the time of death, it is therefore sung of as the "Maṇikarṇikā."
The great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) of the Fortune of Liberation is the jewel upon his two lotus feet; therefore, people call that which is there Maṇikarṇikā.
The womb-born, egg-born, soil-born, and sweat-born beings dwelling here do not equal those who partake in liberation, even compared to the gods for whom liberation is difficult to attain. (81)
My birth has been born in vain, for I am one of evil conduct and dull intellect; until this very day, I have not visited Kāśī, the illuminator of liberation. 82.
Making that field his guest again and again with his eyes—both wondrous and pure—he did not attain satiety.
And among the seven cities that bear the burden [of sanctity], I indeed extol Vārāṇasī, which is expert in bestowing perfect liberation. 84.
Nevertheless, I have not yet brought the other four within the range of my vision; even after learning their power, I shall return once more. (85)
Though he performed pilgrimages every day for nearly a full year, he did not reach all the sacred sites; for in Kāśī, there is a holy place at every grain of sesame.
Agastya said: O Goddess, although that twice-born man was well aware of the supreme qualities of this sacred field through various authoritative means, he nevertheless departed; oh, how strange! (87)
O beautiful one, what indeed can even authoritative scriptures accomplish against that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) who is destined to come? Who is capable of warding her off? (88)
Who could turn back the mind once it has been set in motion, or water once it has begun to flow? For the very nature of both is instability. (89)
Then Śivaśarman, traveling gradually from country to country, reached the city of Mahākāla, which is free from the influence of the Kali age.
He who, by his own sport, could dissolve the entire universe—which is like a stubborn thicket—at every kalpa; having himself measured that very Time (Kāla), he indeed became Mahākāla.
Protecting from evil, she is called Avanti; protecting the universe, she is known as Viśvavantī; in age after age she is known by various names, and in the Kali age she is Ujjayinī. (92)
Wherever a living being indeed passes away and clearly attains the state of a corpse, he does not experience a foul odor nor does he swell up anywhere. (93)
Indeed, the messengers of Yama never enter that place; there, millions upon millions of lingas exist at every step.
Hāṭakeśa, Mahākāla, and likewise Tārakeśa—having become threefold as the Single Liṅga (Ekaliṅga), it remains pervading the three worlds. || 95 ||
The light is at Siddhavaṭa; those twice-born ones who behold that light here, or those who behold the illustrious Mahākāla, become heaps of merit.
Those afflicted by suffering who have anywhere beheld that liṅga of Mahākāla are not touched by great sins, nor are they seen by the fierce messengers of Yama.
The horses, their backs touched by the tips of Mahākāla’s banners, momentarily rest from the lash of Aruṇa in the sky.
For one who constantly and repeatedly remembers "Mahākāla, Mahākāla, Mahākāla," [the two] who are the creator of desire and the ender of desire [grant their grace]. 99.
Having thus propitiated Mahākāla, the Lord of Beings, the twice-born man then went to the city of Kāntī, which is more beautiful even than the three worlds.
Lakṣmī’s beloved himself, being directly present there, certainly makes the creatures dwelling in that place lovers of Śrī both in this world and in the hereafter.
Having seen Kāntī, who was radiant and frequented by those full of splendor, he too became possessed of luster; there was no one there who lacked brilliance.
There, having performed whatever duty was to be done, he who knew all duties stayed for seven nights and then departed for the city of Dvāravatī.
Since there are gates on all sides for all four classes [of beings], it is therefore called Dvāravatī by the wise who know the truth. || 4 ||
Oh, how wonderful it is that even the bones of living beings there are marked with discus-signs; what wonder then could there be where hands are marked with conchs and discuses? (5)
The Ender (Antaka) repeatedly instructs his own messengers: "Those by whom even the name of Dvāravatī is grasped must be abandoned."
Where is that fragrance in sandalwood, or such a color in gold? Where indeed is that sanctity found in a sacred ford as it is in Gopīcandana?
"O messengers, listen: even one whose forehead is marked with cow-dung ash, though he may be like a blazing fire, must be avoided from afar with great effort. (8)
Those who are adorned with *tulasī*, those who chant the name of *tulasī*, and those who tend to groves of *tulasī*—these must be avoided from afar by soldiers.
In age after age, plundering the treasures of Dvāravatī on all sides, the ocean—the mine of jewels—is even now celebrated throughout the worlds. (110)
Those living beings who, impelled by time, die in Dvāravatī, shall become four-armed and wear yellow garments in Vaikuṇṭha.
There too, having gratified the ancestors along with the gods, sages, and humans, he bathed tirelessly in all those sacred fords.
Then he reached Māyāpurī, which is difficult for evildoers to attain, where that Vaiṣṇavī Māyā does not bind one with the snares of illusion.
Some said it was Haridvāra, others called it Mokṣadvāra; some spoke of Gaṅgādvāra, while others again named Māyāpura.
From her emerged the Gaṅgā, renowned on earth as Bhāgīrathī; by the mere utterance of her name, the sin of men is split into a thousand pieces.
People have declared Haridvāra to be the sole staircase to Vaikuṇṭha; men who bathe here go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having observed a fast at the sacred ford and likewise kept a vigil through the night, he should bathe in the Gaṅgā in the morning and offer libations to all those who are to be propitiated.
Just as that best of brahmins desired to break his fast, he was seized by a cold fever and trembled, being exceedingly distressed.
Being a foreigner, alone, and afflicted by a severe fever, he fell into great anxiety, wondering, "What is this that has come upon me? (19)
He became submerged in an ocean of anxiety, having abandoned all hope for his life and wealth, like a sea-faring merchant whose ship has been wrecked in the fathomless great ocean.
Where is my field, where is my wife, where are my sons, and where is that wealth? Where is that wonderful mansion, and where is that collection of books? (21)
Even now my lifespan is not exhausted, nor has grey hair appeared upon me; yet this terrible fever has come upon me, and Time itself is most cruelly aware of its hour.
Death has made its dwelling upon one's head, while the garment remains situated far away; when the fire has reached the top of the house, one should dig a well right here.
"What is the use of these futile thoughts of mine that cause such great distress? I shall instead meditate upon Hṛṣīkeśa and Śiva, who bestows auspiciousness. (24)
Alternatively, this one means to liberation has indeed been properly practiced by me alone; these seven cities of liberation have been made the objects of my own eyes. (25)
For one who possesses knowledge, it is certain that heaven and liberation must have one as their goal; if neither of these is achieved, one later suffers with remorse. (26)
Or rather, what is the use of this anxiety of mine regarding this miserable state? Death in battle or here at a sacred pilgrimage site is better for me.
"Shall I, like one of ill fortune, die now somewhere on a street? Today I shall die in the Bhāgīrathī; what cause for worry is there for me, like a fool? (28)
"By means of this body, which is but a collection of skin and bone, I shall certainly attain death here and surely achieve the ultimate perfection of liberation. (29)
As he was thinking thus, an exceedingly terrible pain arose within him; he reached a state like that of one bitten by ten million scorpions.
Everything that ought to have been remembered was forgotten; he did not know "where am I? or "who am I?"; having remained for forty-nine days, he met his death.
At that moment, a celestial chariot arrived from the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, upon which a very lofty banner marked by the emblem of Tārkṣya was raised.
It was overspread by a thousand beautiful young women dressed in golden silk garments, their hands busily occupied with chowries.
It was graced by two hosts of those with meritorious conduct and excellent virtue, possessing four arms and beautiful faces, and adorned with garlands of networks of small bells.
Then, having ascended that celestial chariot, the twice-born one—clothed in yellow garments, four-armed, and adorned with divine ornaments—graced the path of the sky.
Lopāmudrā said: O Lord of my life, I do not attain satiety from hearing this meritorious narrative concerning the holy city as it issues from your glorious mouth. || 1 ||
O Lord, tell me the reason why Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born, did not attain liberation even though he died in Māyāpurī, the city of liberation.
Agastya said: "O lady of sweet speech, liberation is not attained directly within these cities; however, with reference to this very matter, I have heard an ancient legend."
Listen, O beloved, to this story of wondrous meaning that destroys all sins, as told by Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla to Śivaśarman.
Śivaśarman said: "O meritorious attendants of Viṣṇu, with eyes like the petals of a lotus, I desire to make a certain request, having joined my palms in reverence."
I do not indeed know your names, nor do I know anything of you by your physical appearance; yet, you two must surely be named Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla.
The two Gaṇas said: "What remains unknown to those like you who are endowed with devotion to the Blessed One? For this very thing is our own name, as it has been spoken by your illustrious self. (7)
Whatever else you wish to ask in your mind, O one of great wisdom, inquire about it without hesitation; out of affection, we shall explain it to you.
Having heard these words spoken by the attendant of the Blessed One, which were exceedingly pleasing and heart-pleasing, he then replied to the two of them.
The divine twice-born said: "What is this world of meager splendor, inhabited by people of little merit? Who are these beings of deformed appearance? Tell me this. (10)
The two Gaṇas said: "This is the world of the Piśācas; here dwell flesh-eaters who, having given, are possessed by regret, or who do not give even after having made a promise. (11)
"O friend, having worshipped Śiva even once by chance, those whose minds are impure and who possess little merit and little fortune—these are indeed Piśācas."
Proceeding from there, he saw before him a place filled with joyful and well-nourished people, [guarded] by those with large bellies, thick faces, and voices as deep as thunderclouds.
The two attendants said: "O Śyāmalāṅga and Lomaśa, this world has been inhabited even by the worlds themselves; tell us, what world is this, and from where does its merit arise? (14)
The two Gaṇas said: "This is the world of the Guhyakas, and these indeed are known as the Guhyakas—those who, having acquired wealth by righteous means, conceal it on this earth. (15)

The householders will be rich in deep devotion to their own path, resembling Śūdras in their simplicity; they will be those who enjoy their food only after sharing it with others, and will be free from anger and envy. (16)

They never know the lunar day, nor the day of the week, nor the transits of the sun and so forth, nor the sacred festivals; they know neither unrighteousness nor righteousness, for they are always happy.
For they know only one [true] twice-born man who is honored by the family; to him they bestow cows, and they clearly consider his word as authoritative. || 18 ||
Indeed, even here, by that merit, the Guhyakas, possessing great prosperity, enjoy celestial pleasures like the gods, free from fear from any quarter. (19)
Then he surveyed that world which bestows bliss upon the eyes, [asking]: "Who are these people, and what is the name of this world? Tell me, O pair of speakers! (20)

The two Gaṇas said: "This world belongs to the Gandharvas, and these Gandharvas are observers of auspicious vows. They are the singers of the gods, as well as the Cāraṇas who recite hymns of praise. (21)
Those skilled in song please kings with their exquisite singing, and those deluded by greed for wealth praise the wealthy. (22)
Fine garments and wealth obtained through the favor of kings, as well as various fragrant substances such as camphor and the like—(23)
They bestow gifts upon the Brahmins and sing songs day and night; their minds are fixed solely on the Vedas, though they have exerted themselves in the science of dramaturgy (Nāṭyaśāstra).
By that merit, the world of the Gandharvas is distinguished for them, since the Brahmins were indeed gratified with wealth acquired through the science of song. (25)
By the power of his knowledge of music, the great celestial sage Nārada is indeed honored in the world of Vaiṣṇava and is exceedingly dear to Śrī Śambhu. || 26 ||
Both Tuṃburu and Nārada are exceedingly rare even among the gods; for Śiva himself is manifest as Sound (Nāda), and they both truly know the reality of Sound.
If a song has been sung anywhere in the presence of the glorious Hari and Hara, they say that its fruit is either liberation or proximity to those two.
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through singing, he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him. (29)
In this world, this very mindfulness is always proclaimed; by means of that garland of song, the two gods Hari and Hara are to be worshipped at all times. (30)
Hearing this, Śivaśarman reached another enchanting place in an instant; he then asked, "What is the name of this city? (31)
The two Gaṇas said: "This is the world of the Vidyādharas, who are experts in various sciences. These seekers of knowledge [deserve] food, sandals, clothing, and blankets. (32)
For even medicinal herbs grant relief from suffering, and those free from pride in their learning teach various arts. (33)
They look upon their disciple as a son, providing him with clothing, betel, and food; and they give away their well-adorned daughters in marriage according to dharma.
Constantly worshipping their chosen deities with a longing mind, these excellent Vidyādharas dwell here by virtue of their merits. (35)
While they were thus conversing, Dharmarāja, the lord of Saṃyaminī, arrived amidst the sounds of divine drums.
Possessing a gentle form, seated in his celestial chariot, and surrounded by those who know the Dharma, he was accompanied by three or four servants skilled in the duties of service.
The King of Dharma said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great intelligence, Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born! That which is appropriate for the lineage of brahmins has been set forth by you. (38)
In the past, you studied the Vedas and satisfied your gurus; you observed the dharma within the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas and adhered to it. (39)
Your body has been washed by the waters of the city of liberation; you alone are the wise one, both in life and beyond life.
This body, which is always a vessel of impurity with a putrid odor, has been perfectly fashioned by you through the merchandise of merit from sacred fords.
For this very reason, the wise hold learning in high regard; for those enlightened ones do not waste even a single moment, but rather spend their time purposefully. (42)
Living beings in the mortal world certainly live for five breaths [in a moment]; even during that time, they should not engage in contemptible sinful deeds. (43)
The body is always subject to certain decay, whereas wealth does not protect one at the time of death; why then, like you, does a fool not strive for that which is a mature and noble task? 44.
Life is fleeting and the world is overwhelmed by sorrow; therefore, the mind should be directed toward Dharma, as it has been by you, O most righteous one. (45)
This is the fruition of your virtuous deeds; oh, these two are worthy of my veneration as well, since they have attained friendship with you, who are both devotees of the Blessed One. (46)
Therefore, let my command be given; what assistance may I provide? Whatever ought to be done by those like me has indeed already been performed by you yourself.
Today I am most blessed here, since the two attendants of the Blessed One have been seen; let my service always be made known in the presence of their glorious feet. (48)
Then, sent forth by those two, Yama entered his own city; and when Yama had departed, the brahmin questioned those two attendants.
Śivaśarman said: "Indeed, this Dharmarāja is visibly of most gentle appearance; his words are entirely righteous and pleasing to the mind. (50)
This city Saṃyamanī is possessed of exceedingly auspicious characteristics; even upon hearing its name, sinners tremble intensely.
"O Gaṇas, people in the mortal world describe the form and complexion of Yama in one way, yet he has been seen by me in another way; tell me the reason for that."
By what means do they see this world, and who dwell here? What is its true nature, and what else is it? Please explain this. (53)

The two attendants said: "Listen, gentle one; this most gentle being seen here by those such as you is the very embodiment of Dharma, appearing by his very nature like a heap of merit to those who are free from doubt. (54)
For this very one has tawny eyes, with the corners of his eyes red with rage; his face is formidable with fangs, and he is terrifying like flickering lightning.

With hair standing erect and limbs exceedingly black, possessing a voice like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, he held the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa) raised in his hand, his face contorted with a frown.
"Bring him here! Strike him down! Bind him! Do not release this one who is difficult to subdue! Slay this man of wicked conduct with heavy iron clubs upon his head! (57)
Seize this one of evil conduct by his feet and strike him against the surface of a stone; place your foot upon his throat and pluck out his eyes.
Quickly split open his swollen cheeks with a razor; having bound his neck with a noose, hang him from a tree. (59)
Tear open his head with a saw as if it were wood; crush his mouth with terrible blows from your heels.
"Cut off the hand of this sinner that reaches out for another's wife; and sever the feet of him who goes to the house of another's wife."
Pierce the body of that evil-minded man everywhere with needles at every pore—him who drew rows of nail-marks upon the limbs of another’s wife.
Spit indeed into the mouth of him who has kissed the face of another's wife; thrust a sharp stake into the mouth of the speaker of slander against others.
Roast him like a chickpea in hot sand and in earthen pans, O Vikaṭavaktra, you who cause torment to others! 64.
O Krūralocana, always cast the charge of fault upon the faultless; plunge his face into the mire of pus and blood. 65.
O fierce one, repeatedly drenching the hand-like sprout of him who seizes the property of others that was not given, cook it in heated coals with oil! 66.
For one who speaks slander against their guru, who reviles the gods, cast terrifying red-hot iron rods into their mouth. 67.
And for him who touches the vital secrets of others and exposes their flaws, drive well-heated iron spikes into all his joints. 68.
"Others, being evil-doers, would not have forbidden their own property when it was being given away; cut off the tongue of this foul-mouthed man who seizes the livelihoods of others! (69)
"Quickly tear open the belly of this one who eats the property of the gods and the property of Brahmins, and fill it with excrement-worms! (70)

O Andhaka, one should never cook food for the sake of the gods, nor for the sake of Brahmins, nor for the sake of guests; that person who cooks solely for his own sake shall be cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
O Ugra, quickly lead this slayer of children, this betrayer of trust, and this ungrateful man to Mahāraurava and Raurava.
The slayer of a Brahmin goes to Andhatāmisra; the drinker of liquor to Pūyaśoṇita; the thief of gold to Kālasūtra; and the violator of the Guru’s bed to Avīci.
Those who associate with them shall likewise remain for a year in the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana), and these great sinners [shall remain] in a cauldron of boiling oil.
"Having plunged again and again, dwell there for an entire eon with those most sinful ones who are constantly being tormented by crows with wicked fangs and iron beaks. (75)
Hang for a long time, with your feet upward and your head downward, upon the Kūṭaśālmali tree—there you shall hang as a killer of women, a killer of cows, and a killer of friends.
O mighty-armed one, tear away his skin with pincers; and for the sake of purification, pluck out the arms of him who embraces the wife of his friend.
Cast this man into that most terrible hell, Jvālākīla, who burns another's field or another's dwelling with fire.
Cast the poisoner into Kālakūṭa, the one who speaks false testimony into Kūṭasākṣya, and the one who deceives with measures and weights into Kaṇṭhamoṭa.

One who drinks saliva is difficult to look upon; lead away the one who spits at sacred fords. One who causes the miscarriage of an embryo is destroyed when his own food is cooked; one who causes pain to others is destroyed when his own food is cooked on a spit. (80)
Crush the Brahmin who sells liquor in a sugarcane press; cast down the king who oppresses his subjects into a blind well.
O Halāyudha, [he cursed] the seller of sesame seeds and horses, that lowest of the twice-born, and the seller of mātulānī liquor.
"Let the Vaiśya be threshed again and again with pestle and mortar; and the Śūdra who insults the twice-born and serves at their feet while they are present. || 83 ||
And in the downward-facing hell, having crushed [them] with long necks; || 84 ||
A Śūdra who defeats a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya who considers himself a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya who acts as a priest, and a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Vedas—(these are to be avoided). || 85 ||
One who sells lac, salt, meat, oil, poison, clarified butter, weapons, or products of sugarcane—that lowest of the twice-born—[should be avoided]. (86)
"O you who hold nooses and whips in your hands, bind these men firmly by the feet, strike them with lashes of the whip, and lead them to the Taptakardama hell! (87)
"Quickly join this woman—a harlot and a stain upon her family—with that paramour, made of glowing red-hot iron. (88)
"O Durādharṣa, lead him who, having himself undertaken a vow, abandons it because his senses are unsubdued, to a place full of many stinging bees."
Thus Yama is heard from afar by those of evil conduct as he utters such chatter; yet he is seen as terrifying by the wicked who are apprehensive for their own deeds.
Those kings who protect the subjects here as if they were their own biological sons, and who punish them according to righteousness, are the members of his assembly.
Those kings in whose kingdom the castes and stages of life perform their own duties, and who meet their death in due time, are his members of the assembly.
Those kings in whose kingdom no one is seen to be dejected, ill-behaved, beset by calamity, or overcome by grief—they are his members of the assembly.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas are always devoted to their own duties; others as well, who are self-restrained, dwell in Samyaminī.
Uśīnara, Sudhanvan, Vṛṣaparvan, Jayadratha, Raji, Sahasrajit, Kukṣi, Dṛḍhadhanvan, and Ripuñjaya. || 95 ||
Yuvanāśva, Daṃtavaktra, Nābhāga, Ripumaṅgala, Karaṃdhama, Dharmasena, Paramarda, and Parāntaka. || 96 ||
These and many other kings who abide by political wisdom, knowing how to discern between righteousness and unrighteousness, sit together in Sudharmā.
Furthermore, we shall tell you that by which they behold the son of the Sun, as well as his messengers with fierce faces, who sometimes carry raised staffs and nooses in their hands.

"O Govinda, Mādhava, Mukunda, Hare, Murāri; O Śambhu, Śiva, Īśa, Moon-crested One, Trident-bearer; O Dāmodara, Acyuta, Janārdana, Vāsudeva—these names must never be abandoned before a soldier," so they constantly declare. (99)

"O Gaṅgādhara, enemy of Andhaka, Hara, Nīlakaṇṭha, Vaikuṇṭha, enemy of Kaiṭabha, you whose hands hold the tortoise and the lotus; O Bhūteśa, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Mṛḍa, Lord of Caṇḍikā—these [names] must be abandoned by the soldier," so they constantly advise him. (100)

"O Viṣṇu, O Nṛsiṃha, O Madhusūdana, O wielder of the discus; O Lord of Gaurī, O Giriśa, O Śaṃkara, O moon-crested one; O Nārāyaṇa, O destroyer of Asuras, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow—these [names] must always be invoked for the warrior," so they declare. (1)

"O Conqueror of Death, O Lord with fierce and piercing eyes, O Enemy of Kama, O Shauri who is as dark as a cloud yet clad in yellow garments, O Sole Lord of the Gods who wears the hide of an elephant—these [enemies] must be abandoned by Your soldiers," so they constantly declare.

"O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Enemy of Madhu, O Supreme Person, O Primordial One, O Śrīkaṇṭha, O Sky-clad One, O Peaceful Wielder of the Pināka bow, O Root of Bliss, O Supporter of the Earth, O Lotus-navelled One! These [objects] must be abandoned to the soldier"—thus he constantly admonishes. (3)

"O Lord of All, Destroyer of Tripura, God of Gods, Friend of Brahman, whose banner is Garuḍa, O you who hold the conch in hand! O Three-eyed One, adorned with serpents, whose crown is the young moon—your soldiers must never be abandoned," so they constantly declare.

"O Śrīrāma, Rāghava, Supreme Lord, Enemy of Rāvaṇa; O Bhūteśa, Foe of Manmatha, Lord of the Pramathas; O Cāṇūramardana, Hṛṣīkeśa, Murāri—these [names] must be constantly invoked by the warrior. Thus he continually instructs. (5)

"O wielder of the trident, Lord of the Mountain, Moon, ornament of the arts, destroyer of Kaṃsa, eternal slayer of Keśin, Bharga, Three-eyed One, Source of Existence, Lord of Beings, Enemy of Tripura—the soldiers must be abandoned," so they constantly declare.

"O Lord of the Gopīs, O Lord of the Yadus, O Son of Vasudeva, O You whose forehead-eye is like the camphor-white bull-bannered Śiva, O Cowherd who lifted Govardhana and are preeminent in the burden of righteousness—these [enemies] must be abandoned by Your soldiers," so they constantly declare.

"O Sthāṇu, O Three-eyed One, O Wielder of the Pināka bow, O Enemy of Smara, O Destroyer of the sins of Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, and Kamalākara; O Lord of the Universe, whose mass of matted locks is moistened by the triple-pathed river—'He is to be abandoned,' so they constantly declare to the soldier. (8)

He who places around his neck this garland—composed of one hundred and eight beautiful names, woven with a cluster of lovely jewels, possessing a noble thread and firm strings—he, alas, shall not behold Yama.

Thus, O best of the twice-born, that Dharmarāja should always instruct his own groups of servants who dwell upon the earth; furthermore, O wonder, those others on earth who bear the marks of Hari and Hara must be avoided from afar.

Agastya said: That steadfast man who daily recites here this garland of names—composed by Dharmarāja, beautifully structured, and the destroyer of the seeds of all sins—of the wearer of the Kaustubha gem and the one adorned with the moon, shall never again drink the milk from a mother’s breast.
Thus listening to this delightful and faultless story, Śivaśarman, with a joyful countenance, beheld before him the city of the Apsarases.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Yama," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śivaśarman said: Who are these women, who are treasuries of beauty, charm, and good fortune, wearing divine ornaments and endowed with celestial enjoyments? (1)
The two Gaṇas said: "These are courtesans who bring pleasure to those entitled to sacrificial offerings; they are experts in song, skilled in dance, and proficient in the art of instrumental music."
They were experts in the arts of amorous play, proficient in the science of gambling, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, perceivers of inner emotions, and clever in appropriate speech.
They were experts in the particularities of various regions, highly skilled in diverse languages, proficient in signs and local lore, and they moved about joyfully in various independent ways.
Expert in playful jests and well-versed in charming conversation, these women constantly delight the hearts of the young with their natural gestures.
Formerly, from the Ocean of Milk as it was being churned, these celestial nymphs emerged—the mind-born goddesses of the god of love, who are the enchanting weapons that conquer the three worlds.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Candralekhā, Tilottamā, Vapuṣmatī, Kāntimatī, Līlāvatī, and Utpalāvatī.
Alambuṣā, Guṇavatī, Sthūlakeśī, Kalāvatī, Kalānidhi, Guṇanidhi, Karpūra, Tilakā, and Urvarā. (8)
Anaṅgalatikā, as well as Madanamohinī, Cakorākṣī, Candrakalā, and Munimanoharā; || 9 ||
Grāvadrāvā, Tapodveṣṭī, Cārunāsā, Sukarṇikā, Dārusaṃjīvinī, Suśrī, Kratuśulkā, and Śubhānanā. || 10 ||

Himāvatī is one whose bride-price is austerity, whose bride-price is pilgrimage, and whose bride-price is charity; she is the fruit of fifty horse-sacrifices and likewise desires the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Likewise, there were those who performed the eightfold fire-sacrifice and those born from a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; such was the foremost thousand of Apsarases, numbering sixty thousand.
In this world of Apsarases, there dwell other women as well, whose beauty never falters and whose youth never declines. (13)

Clad in divine garments, adorned with divine garlands, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, they were fully endowed with divine enjoyments and could assume forms according to their own will.
Having undertaken month-long fasts, they stumble from their celibacy—either once, twice, or thrice, by the turn of fate.
These divine enjoyments, consisting of the perfection of beauty and charm, dwell in the world of the Apsarases, endowed with all objects of desire. (16)

Having performed their desired vows along with all their constituent parts according to the prescribed rules, they become women who act according to their own will; having come here, they become objects of enjoyment for the gods.
O twice-born one, women who are sustained by devotion to their husbands, even when held by force by a powerful man, may sometimes take pleasure in him, perceiving him as their husband. (18)
Those beautiful-eyed women who always observe the vow of celibacy while their husbands are away from home—even they, by some chance, once fall into transgression. (19)
Fragrant flowers, well-scented sandalwood, very white camphor, and extremely fine garments.
The leaves were straight, star-shaped, withered, and hard; they had pointed tips, were golden-colored, and possessed thick blue veins.
O best of the twice-born, they were richly furnished with excellent garments and utensils, adorned with betel vines, provided with wonderful beds and ornaments, and suitable for the chamber of love.
Having honored many objects of curiosity and the Brahmin couple, this desirable gift of enjoyment is for the transit of the Sun.
Or else, for every Vyatīpāta occurring within the span of a single year, that woman of excellent complexion shall give [the gift] with the mantra beginning, "Who will give? (ko dāt).
"May the God who assumes any form at will be pleased"—speaking thus, that woman shall dwell here for a kalpa among the most excellent of the Apsarases.
A certain woman, assuming the form of a maiden, was enjoyed by someone somewhere; from that time forward, she has remained a celibate student (brahmacāriṇī) in the form of a goddess.
Meditating upon that very conduct, she meets her death in due course of time; assuming a divine form, she is born here as one who enjoys divine pleasures.
Hearing that this was the cause for reaching the world of the Apsarases, that foremost of the twice-born, traveling by celestial chariot, then reached the solar world in an instant.
Just as a kadamba flower is completely enveloped by its filaments, so indeed does it shine brilliantly on all sides with the rays of the sun.
Having recognized from afar the sun bearing its two lotuses, he [approached] by way of a path measuring nine thousand yojanas.
With a variegated single wheel, yoked to seven horses, and presided over by Anūru who held the reins in front; || 31 ||
Accompanied by Apsarases, Munis, Gandharvas, Sarpas, Grāmaṇīs, and Nairṛtas, he bowed with joined palms from his exceedingly swift chariot.
Having granted him permission with a movement of his eyebrows, even the god, after receiving his salutation, traversed the path of the sky to a great distance in an instant.
When the sun had traveled far away, Śivaśarman, filled with great joy, said to the two devotees of the Blessed One: "How can the station of the Sun be attained? (34)
I desire to hear this; please explain it before me. Friendship among the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; therefore, impelled by that friendship, [speak]. (35)

The two attendants said: "Listen, O twice-born one of great wisdom; there is nothing that should not be told to you. It is only through the company of the virtuous that the sacred discourse of the holy ones proceeds. (36)
The sole supreme cause, the controller of all beings, who is nameless, devoid of lineage, and free from form and the rest. || 37 ||
He alone—the Soul of All, the Person of the Veda—constantly declares that manifestation and concealment are the dancing movements of His own being. (38)
"He who is that person in the sun, he am I"—thus clearly; but those who worship another enter into blinding darkness. (39)
O best of the twice-born, having ascertained this meaning of the Veda, the Brahmins repeatedly approach that One, having reached a firm conclusion. (40)
And he who, having received the Sāvitrī, does not worship it at the supreme time—three times a day—for seven days, shall fall; of this there is no doubt.

One should remain standing while reciting the morning prayers until half of the sun has risen; then, seated and observing silence, one should continue the recitation until the stars have disappeared from view.
One should recite the prayers during the midday twilight while facing the sun; one must not let the proper time lapse, and therefore one should wait for that specific time.
Herbs bear fruit in their season, trees blossom in their season, and clouds rain in their season; therefore, one should not transgress the appointed time.
For the sake of destroying the bodies of the Maṇḍehas, the Sun at sunrise and sunset longs for the three handfuls of water consecrated with mantras offered by the twice-born. (45)
If three handfuls of water enriched with the Gāyatrī mantra are offered at the proper time to Savitṛ by someone, what is there that has not been given by him in the three worlds?
What does the Sun not produce when properly worshipped at the right time? Longevity, health, sovereignty, and wealth, along with cattle. (47)
Friends, sons, wives, and various fields; the eight kinds of enjoyments, as well as heaven and even liberation. || 48 ||
Among the eighteen branches of learning, Mīmāṃsā is the most venerable; even greater than that are the treatises on logic (tarka-śāstra), and the Purāṇa is more venerable even than those. (49)
Even greater than those, O twice-born one, are the Dharmaśāstras; greater than them is the Śruti; even greater than that is the Upaniṣad, and Gāyatrī is superior even to that.
Among all mantras, the Gāyatrī accompanied by the Praṇava is difficult to obtain; nothing superior to the Gāyatrī is proclaimed within the three Vedas.
There is no mantra equal to the Gāyatrī, no city equal to Kāśī, and no Liṅga equal to Viśveśa; this is the truth, the truth, again and again. (52)
Gāyatrī is the mother of the Vedas; Gāyatrī is the progenitor of the Brāhmaṇas. Because she protects the singer (gātāram), she is therefore called Gāyatrī. || 53 ||
The relationship between the expressed and the expresser exists between Gāyatrī and Savitṛ; Savitṛ is directly the expressed, while Gāyatrī is the other, the expresser.
By the power of the Gāyatrī alone, the self-controlled Kṣatriya Kauśika abandoned his status as a royal seer and attained the rank of a Brahmin seer.
She attained an exceedingly great capacity for the creation of another world; what indeed would Gāyatrī not bestow when worshipped correctly in this manner? (56)

A man does not become a Brāhmaṇa by reciting the Vedas, nor even by studying the Śāstras; one becomes a Brāhmaṇa by practicing the worship of the Goddess at the three times of day, and not otherwise. (57)
Gāyatrī alone is the supreme Viṣṇu; Gāyatrī alone is the supreme Śiva; Gāyatrī alone is the supreme Brahmā; therefore, Gāyatrī is the threefold Veda itself.
That Blessed One, the sun-god garlanded with rays, is the triad of deities, a mass of all splendors, and the impeller of the time of time.

Constantly referring to Arka, those inhabitants of our world who discern between the essential and the non-essential cite this Vedic revelation: The sun is the eye of the universe; he is the soul of all beings. He moves within the worlds, pervading everything with his rays. (60)

This God indeed pervades all directions; He was born first, and He is within the womb. He alone has been born, and He is yet to be born; facing all beings, He stands with faces on every side. || 61 ||
Those who, unwearied, always worship here with the Saura hymns and offer salutations, those Brahmins, O Brahmin, are equal to the Sun himself.

O twice-born one, whether on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, or on a Sunday coinciding with Hastā, or Mūla, or Uttarā, whatever task is performed then certainly bears fruit; it is not otherwise.
O observer of noble vows, he who bathes at sunrise on a Sunday in the month of Pauṣa, and performs charity, fire-offerings, and recitation while worshipping the Sun, [attains great merit].
Endowed with faith, devoted to the One, and free from desire and anger, he shall dwell here, radiant and possessed of enjoyments, together with the Apsarases.
Those of virtuous vows who bestow great gifts during the solstices, the equinoxes, the six *aśītimukha* periods, or at the *viṣṇupadī*, [attain the highest reward].
Those wise ones who offer sesame seeds with clarified butter into the fire, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and perform the Śrāddha ceremony dedicated to the ancestors; || 67 ||
And those who perform great worship and recite the great mantras, they shall possess a splendor equal to the Sun in this world of Vaikartana.
Those who are devoted to the Sun at the transitions [of the zodiac] are neither poor nor afflicted by suffering, nor oppressed by disease; they are neither deformed nor unfortunate. (69)

Those by whom no gifts were given at the sacred junctions (saṃkrama), nor bathed in the waters of holy fords (tīrtha), and who did not perform special fire-offerings with sesame seeds soaked in the clarified butter of a tawny cow; || 70 ||
They are seen at every door, their eyes and faces disfigured, wearing rags and crying out, "Give! Give! to those who possess bodies. (71)
The virtuous person who gives gold, even if only the weight of a *kṛṣṇalaka*, at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, shall dwell here as a partaker of merit.
When the sun is seized by Rāhu, all water is equal to the Gaṅgā, all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā, and every gift is equal to gold.

Whatever has been given, recited, offered in sacrifice, bathed in, or whatever else has been well-performed, such as the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and so forth, during a solar eclipse—that is the cause [of merit], O Sun, because of Your presence. (74)
If a solar transit (saṃkrānti) or an eclipse occurs on a Sunday, then whatever merit is earned at that time becomes inexhaustible in this world. || 75 ||
When Sunday occurs on the sixth or the seventh lunar day, then whatever meritorious deed is performed is experienced here [in this world]. (76)
Haṃsa, Bhānu, Sahasrāṃśu, Tapana, Tāpana, Ravi, Vikartana, Vivasvat, Viśvakarmā, and Vibhāvasu. (77)
Viśvarūpa, Viśvakartā, Mārtaṇḍa, Mihira, Aṃśumān, Āditya, Uṣṇagu, Sūrya, Aryaman, Bradhna, and Divākara. (78)
The twelve-fold one, the seven-horsed, the maker of light, the sun, the sky-goer, the god, the source of radiance, the illustrious one, the eye of the world, and the lord of the planets. (79)
The Lord of the three worlds, the witness of the world, the enemy of darkness, the eternal, the pure; he whose hands are rays, the one of intense beams, the sun, the great source of light.

The jewel of the sky, the one with bay horses, the sun, the radiant one, the destroyer of fear; he whose horses are the Vedic meters, the one known through the Vedas, the shining one, the nourisher, and the bull-like monkey.

Mitra, the possessor of the single-wheeled chariot, the enemy of the Mandehas, the destroyer of darkness; the slayer of Daityas, the remover of sins, and the illuminator of dharma and adharma. || 82 ||
Helika, Citrabhānu, Kalighna, Tārkṣyavāhana, Dikpati, Padminīnātha, Kuśeśayakara, and Hari. (83)
The Sun, the son of Kaśyapa, possesses fierce rays and is difficult to behold; by these seventy meritorious names of the Sun— || 84 ||
Uttering each name preceded by the syllable *praṇava*, ending in the dative case, and accompanied by a salutation (*namaskāra*), while looking at the sun as he gazes upon it. (85)
Holding a very pure copper vessel with both hands, having knelt upon the ground, and having filled it with water; 86.
With flowers such as the *karavīra* mixed with red sandalwood paste, along with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), which have been placed into the center of the vessel.
One should offer the *arghya* to the priceless Savitṛ preceded by meditation, having brought that vessel near the crown of the head, with one's gaze and mind fixed on nothing else.
At both sunrise and sunset, one should pay homage to the Sun with each individual mantra, using this "Seventy Names" which is the secret of the great mantras.
A person acting in this way shall never be poor nor a partaker of suffering; he is liberated from even the most terrible diseases acquired in previous births.
Without medicines, without physicians, and without the observance of a wholesome diet, he who meets his death in due time is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Thus, O best of beings, only a single portion of this world of the Sun, a treasury of great splendor, has been described; alas, who indeed can comprehend its full distinction? 92.
Making this meritorious narrative the object of his own ears, he beheld the great city of Mahendra in an instant.
Agastya said: Having heard this account of Saurī together with the world of the Apsarases, how could one ever become poor, or ever engage in unrighteous acts? (94)
This supreme narrative should be constantly heard by Brahmins; it bestows the fruit of that merit which is gained through the recitation of the Vedas. (95)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who hear this supreme chapter shall cast off their sins here and attain the unsurpassed goal.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of the Apsarases and the Sun," in the first half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śivaśarman said: Who is this woman who so intensely delights the mind, and to which lord does she belong? She is the most excellent city, bestowing a multitude of delights upon the eyes.
The two attendants said: "O illustrious Śivaśarman, O tree bearing fruit from excellent holy places, people here rejoice, O Brahmin, for this is indeed the city of the Thousand-eyed One."
Created by Viśvakarman through his great power of asceticism, even by day the moonlight resorts to the beauty of its rows of palaces.
When the treasury of digits (the moon) becomes invisible somewhere on the new moon day, it would then hide its beloved moonlight within these palaces.
Seeing her own reflection on a translucent wall and suspecting it was another woman, the innocent girl quickly entered her picture-gallery, even though it was clearly a painting.
In the palaces constructed here of sapphire gems, darkness remains even during the day, fearlessly assuming its own deep blue hue.
Taking only the pure water that has just flowed from the collection of moonstone slabs there with their jars, the people do not desire any other water.
There are no weavers here, nor are there any who steal from one's sight; for here, the Kalpavṛkṣa tree provides garments and ornaments.
"Calculators skilled in the science of calculation do not exist here; for the Wish-Fulfilling Gem (Cintāmaṇi) quickly understands the thoughts of everyone. || 9 ||
There are no cooks here skilled in the art of flavoring, because the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) yields all various tastes from her own milk.
His fame, like the horse Uccaiḥśravas, is supreme among all rows of steeds; here, that jewel Uccaiḥśravas is preeminent in manly prowess among horses.
Airāvata, the best of elephants with four tusks, shines here like a second Mount Kailāsa, moving and radiant as crystal.
The Pārijāta tree is the jewel among trees; Urvaśī is the jewel among women here; the Nandana grove is the jewel among forests; and the Mandākinī is indeed the jewel among waters.
The thirty-three crores of gods mentioned in the Vedas wait here every day for an opportunity to serve him.
In the heavens, nothing whatsoever would surpass the station of Indra; for whatever sovereignty exists within the three worlds is not equal to this.
What else could be equal to it, or even greater, as something pure that might be obtained in exchange for a thousand horse-sacrifices? (16)
Arciṣmatī, Saṃyaminī, Puṇyavatī, Amalāvatī, Gandhavatī, and Alakeśī—none of these are equal to her in terms of great supernatural powers.
He alone is the thousand-eyed one; he alone is the lord of day; he is the god Śatamanyu—these are his names according to their designations.
The seven guardians of the world who attend upon him, and the eminent sages such as Nārada and others, praise him with benedictions.
By the stability of this [mountain], the stability of all the worlds is desired; by the defeat of Mahendra, the three worlds would be defeated. (20)
Danujas, humans, and Daityas perform austerities with fierce self-restraint; Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas likewise do so, desiring to attain the station of Mahendra.
Sagara and other protectors of the earth, desiring to seize the sovereignty of Śakra, performed great efforts in the performance of horse sacrifices.
Whoever on earth performs a hundred sacrifices without hindrance and has conquered his senses, he obtains Pulomajā in Amarāvatī.
Kings who have not yet completed a hundred sacrifices dwell here, as do those twice-born ones who perform sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others.
Those pure-souled ones who bestow the sixteen great gifts, beginning with the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa, attain Amarāvatī.
Those kings who speak without timidity, who are steadfast, who do not turn their backs in battle, and who are courageous on the hero’s bed—these remain here. (26)
Thus has been briefly described the situation of the city of Mahendra; here dwell those who are constantly performing sacrifices and are experts in the science of ritual.
Behold this radiant and auspicious city of Vītihotra; those of noble vows who are devoted to Jātavedas dwell here.
Those of firm resolve who enter the fire, having conquered their senses, or women endowed with great courage—all of them possess the splendor of fire. (29)

Those Brahmins devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, as well as those who maintain the sacred fires and practice celibacy, and those who observe the vow of the five fires—they indeed possess the splendor of fire in the world of Agni.
He who provides loads of fuel to remove the cold during the winter, or establishes a sacrificial fire, shall dwell in the proximity of the fires.
He who, endowed with faith, performs the cremation rites for a destitute person, or if unable to do so himself, urges another to do it, is honored in the world of Agni.
That meritorious soul who gives an Agni-related medicine for the sake of increasing the digestive fire shall dwell for a long time in the world of Vahni (Fire). || 33 ||
He who gives sacrificial implements, materials, or wealth for the sake of sacrifice according to his ability shall indeed dwell in Arciṣmatī.
Fire alone is the supreme bringer of ultimate welfare for the twice-born; fire is certainly determined to be the teacher, the deity, the vow, and the sacred ford for all.
All impure things become pure in an instant through contact with fire; therefore, he is remembered as Pāvaka (the Purifier). || 36 ||
Even if he has mastered the Veda, that Brahmin who, having abandoned Jātavedas (the sacrificial fire), fixes his delight elsewhere, is not a knower of the Veda.
For this inner self is directly perceived as the fire itself; it digests morsels of meat within the belly, yet not the flesh-embryo of women.
The fiery form of Śambhu is directly perceived as being of the nature of fire; it is the creator, the destroyer, and the protector—without this, what else could be seen? (39)
This Citrabhānu is the manifest eye of the Lord of the three worlds; in this world filled with blinding darkness, who else could be its illuminator without him? (40)
Incense, lamps, food offerings, milk, curd, ghee, and sugarcane juice—all the inhabitants of heaven consume these when they have been partaken of [as offerings]. (41)
Śivaśarman said: "Who is this Kṛśānu? Whose son is he? And how was this fiery state attained by him? Tell me all this in my presence. (42)
The two attendants said: "Listen, O highly wise one; we shall describe exactly as it happened how this man reached the city of Jyotiṣmatī, who he was, and by what means."
Formerly, on the beautiful bank of the Narmadā in the city of Narmapura, there lived a meritorious sage named Viśvānara, who was a devotee of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).

Established in the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), always devoted to the sacrifice of sacred knowledge (brahmayajña), belonging to the Śāṇḍilya lineage, pure, a treasury of Brahmanic luster, and self-controlled. || 45 ||
