Having mastered the meaning of all the scriptures and being proficient in worldly conduct, he once meditated upon Maheśvara in his heart and reflected thus.
Of all four stages of life, this is by far the most excellent for the virtuous, since when it is fully mastered, one attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
"This is better, this is better, but this would be easier to perform"—having thus weighed all these considerations, he praised the life of a householder.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—the householder is the support for all of them, and not otherwise. (49)
Since the householder is daily sustained by gods, humans, ancestors, and animals, therefore the one in the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
The householder who eats without having bathed, or without having offered oblations, or without having given gifts, becomes a debtor to the gods and others and falls into hell.

One who eats without having bathed consumes impurity; one who does not recite prayers consumes pus and blood; one who eats without offering oblations consumes worms; and one who eats without giving [to others] consumes excrement, O Lord.
For the kind of celibacy found in the householder stage, which is free from conceptual construction—where could such a thing exist in a student whose mind is fickle by its very nature? (53)

Whether by force, out of fear of the world, or for one's own sake, if one who observes celibacy forms a mental resolve [for sexual intercourse], then even what has been performed is as if unperformed.
By abandoning the wives of others, by being content with his own wife, and by approaching her only during the proper season, a householder is said to be a celibate (brahmacārī). || 55 ||
He who is liberated from passion and hatred, and who is free from desire and anger—he, though possessing a sacred fire and his wife, is a householder who excels the forest-dweller.
Having abandoned his home out of dispassion, yet still dwelling on the duties of a householder in his heart, he would be fallen from both states—neither a forest-dweller nor a householder.
The householder who lives by a livelihood that presents itself unasked, and who is content with whatever he receives, excels the mendicant. (58)
If he should ever request anything whatsoever, even if it be difficult to obtain, or if he is not content with his food, that ascetic becomes fallen. (59)
Having thus deliberated upon merits and demerits, that twice-born Viśvānara married a noble maiden suitable for his family according to the prescribed rites.
Devoted to the service of the sacred fire, dedicated to the five great sacrifices, he was constantly engaged in the six duties and cherished the gods, the ancestors, and guests.
With his mind disciplined, he pursued virtue, wealth, and pleasure each at its proper time, ensuring that there was no mutual conflict between the husband and wife through their harmony.
Knowing the ritual section of the Vedas, he performed the rites for the gods in the forenoon, those for humans at midday, and those for the ancestors in the afternoon.
Thus, when much time had passed, that twice-born man’s wife, named Śuciṣmatī—a devoted partner who was faithful to her husband—[became pregnant]. (64)
Not seeing even a sprout of progeny, which is the means for attaining heaven, she recognized Śaṅkara as her beloved and, having prostrated before him, made this request: || 65 ||

Śuciṣmatī said: "O noble son, O one of noble intellect, O lord of my life, O you who are devoted to dear vows! There is nothing here that is difficult for me to obtain through the worship of your feet."
Those very enjoyments that are appropriate for women have been experienced by me, adorned through your grace; I shall describe them to you as well, in this context. (67)
Fine garments, beautiful clothing, a comfortable bed, a lovely wife, garlands, betel, food, and drink—these are the eight enjoyments for those who follow their own dharma.
O Lord, there is one request of mine that has long resided in my heart; you ought to grant me here that which is appropriate for householders. (69)

Viśvānara said: "O lady of beautiful hips, what indeed is there that cannot be given away by me, since you desire my pleasure and welfare? Therefore, O highly fortunate one, ask for it; I shall grant it to you without delay."
"O auspicious lady, by the grace of Maheśī, nothing is difficult for me to obtain, both in this world and the next, since she is the bringer of all that is auspicious. (71)
Having heard these words of her husband, she, who regarded her husband as a deity, spoke with a joyful countenance: "If a boon is to be granted to me... (72)
"O Lord, if I am worthy of a boon, I choose no other; O son of Maheśvara, grant me a son equal to Maheśvara. (73)
Having heard these words of Śuciṣmatī, he of pure vows, having entered a state of meditative absorption for a moment, reflected upon this within his heart.
"Oh, what is it that this slender maiden has sought, which is so exceedingly difficult to attain? Let it be far beyond the path of even one's desires; for He is the creator of all. (75)
Since Śambhu himself, abiding within her mouth in the form of speech, has uttered this, who would dare to make it otherwise? Let it be so.
Then the illustrious sage Viśvānara, established in the vow of devotion to a single wife, spoke to his wife: "O beloved, it shall be thus. (77)
Having thus consoled his wife, the sage departed for penance to the place where Viśveśvara, the Lord of Kāśī himself, resides.
Having quickly reached Vārāṇasī and beheld Maṇikarṇikā, he abandoned even the threefold suffering accumulated over hundreds of births. (79)
Having visited all the lingas, headed by Viśveśa, and having bathed in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), as well as in the oblong ponds, wells, and lakes; || 80 ||
Having bowed to all the Vināyakas and having prostrated before all the Gaurīs, and having fully worshipped Kālarāja Bhairava, the devourer of sins; || 81 ||
Having diligently praised the chief leaders of the Daṇḍa and the Gaṇas, and having gratified the Keśavas, foremost among whom is Ādikeśava; || 82 ||
Having bowed down again and again to the suns, foremost among whom is Lolārka, and having diligently performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at all the sacred fords (tīrthas), [he departed].
Having gratified the ascetics and Brahmins with a thousand meals and other offerings, and having worshipped the Lingas with devotion through the services of the great ritual (mahāpūjopacāra).
He reflected repeatedly: "What is the emblem that grants swift success, wherein penance may attain stability through the desire for a son? (85)
Or is it the illustrious Oṃkāranātha, or perhaps Kṛttivāseśvara? Or else Kāleśa, Vṛddhakāleśa, and indeed Kalaśeśvara? (86)
Or Kedāreśa, Kāmeśa, Candreśa, Trilocana, Jyeṣṭheśa, Jaṃbukeśa, or indeed Jaigīṣavyeśvara. || 87 ||
Daśāśvamedheśāna, Drumicaṇḍeśa, Dṛkkeśa, Garuḍeśa, Gokarṇeśa, and Gaṇeśvara; || 88 ||
[He visited] Dhundhyāśāgaja, Siddha, Dharmeśa, Tārakeśvara, Nandikeśa, Nivāseśa, Patrīśa, and Prītikeśvara. || 89 ||
Parvateśa, Paśupati, Brahmeśa, Madhyameśvara, Bṛhaspatīśvara, or indeed Vibhāṇḍeśvara; || 90 ||
Is it Bhārabhūteśvara, or perhaps Mahālakṣmīśvara; or Marutteśa, Mokṣeśa, Gaṅgeśa, or Narmadeśvara? || 91 ||
Mārkaṇḍa, Maṇikarṇīśa, or likewise Ratneśvara, or else the Yoginīpīṭha—these grant success specifically to the practitioner.
Yāmuneśa, Lāṅgalīśa, the all-pervading and glorious Viśveśvara, or else Avimukteśvara and Viśālākṣīśa as well.
Vyāghreśvara, Varāheśa, Vyāseśa, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Varuṇeśa, Vidhīśa, or Vasiṣṭheśa, and Śanīśvara. || 94 ||
Is it Someśvara, or Indreśa, or Saṅgameśvara who has merged into heaven? Is it Hariścandreśvara, or perhaps Harikeśeśvara? || 95 ||
[He visited] Trisaṃdhyeśa, Mahādeva, Upaśānti, Śiva, Bhavānīśa, Kapardīśa, Kaṇḍukeśa, and Makheśvara. || 96 ||
Having reflected for a moment, that wise sage Viśvānara thought: "Is this [child] named Mitrāvaruṇa, or is it one who bestows swift sons upon these [parents]? (97)
It has been understood; it was merely forgotten. My heart's desire has now borne fruit—this supreme Liṅga, frequented by the Siddhas, which bestows all perfections. (98)
Upon seeing or touching it, one's mind attains bliss; for there, indeed, the gateway to heaven stands forever open. (99)

Having petitioned the Lord of the Thirty-three for the sake of worship day and night, [he established it] upon the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of the five seals (pañcamudrā), which bestows success upon all living beings.
Where that goddess Vikaṭā is manifest in the form of Siddhi, and where for the devotees stationed there, Siddhivināyaka himself is present.
Having shaken off the entire web of obstacles, it bestows all spiritual accomplishments; for in the great field of Avimukta lies that supreme field of accomplishment.
Wherein the Vīreśvara Liṅga is considered the most supreme secret; in Kāśī, there is not even a space the size of a sesame seed that is anywhere without a Liṅga.
O Vīreśa, there is no other liṅga like you that bestows swift accomplishment; it perfectly grants dharma, artha, kāma, and likewise mokṣa.
Just as the Vīreśvara Liṅga in Kāśī is certainly without equal, so too the Gandharva Pañcasvara formerly attained supreme perfection here.
The Vidyādhara Svacchavidya and Vasupūrṇa, the king of the Yakṣas, were present; formerly, the preeminent Apsaras danced here with her own natural grace.
The cuckoos, with their melodious warbling, attained dissolution within the center of the Liṅga; meanwhile, the sage named Vedaśiras was indeed chanting the Śatarudriya.
Formerly, both Candramauli and Bharadvāja, the two best among the Pāśupatas, entered with their physical bodies into the Liṅga composed of the light of mantra.
Having worshipped Vīreśvara, the two of them sang and attained dissolution; for Śaṅkhacūḍa, the lord of the Nāgas, [shone] at night with the jewels on his own hoods.
In this place, the Kinnarī Haṃsapadī attained perfection within six months through many rites of lustration (nīrājana), together with her husband, who was indeed fond of the flute.
Singing with a beautiful voice, she has gone to the supreme stage of Nirvāṇa; thousands of incalculable Siddhas have attained perfection here.
Therefore, Vīreśvara is declared here to be the supreme Siddhaliṅga.
Having propitiated Vīreśvara, Jayadratha, the son of Videha, though deprived of his kingdom, slew his enemies and regained his realm without obstacle.
Then King Vidūratha, who was childless, became possessed of a son through the grace of Vīreśvara; he was the self-controlled lord of Magadha.
And here, after worshipping Vīreśa for a year, Ratnadatta obtained a merchant’s daughter who was like the daughter of Vasu. || 15 ||
I too, having propitiated Vīreśa here at the three times of day, shall swiftly obtain a son as desired by my wife.
Having thus formed this resolve, the wise and skillful brahmin Viśvānara, a performer of vows, bathed in the waters of the moon-well and undertook his religious observances.
For one month he took food once a day; for one month he ate only at night; for one month he subsisted on unsolicited food; and for another month he again abstained from food entirely.
For one month he observed the milk-vow; for one month he subsisted on vegetables and fruits; for one month his food was a handful of sesame seeds; and for one month his sustenance was water alone.

For one month he subsisted on the five products of the cow, for one month he observed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, for one month he consumed water from the tips of Kuśa grass, and for one month he lived by inhaling air alone.
Then, in the thirteenth month, having bathed in the waters of the triple-pathed river at the very break of dawn, that twice-born man arrived before Vīreśa.
Then the ascetic beheld in their midst a beautiful child-liṅga, eight years of age, adorned with sacred ashes.
With eyes reaching to his ears and deeply red lips, with a beautiful crown of tawny matted hair, naked, and with a smiling face. (23)
Wearing attire suitable for childhood, captivating the heart, reciting Vedic hymns, and laughing with his own playful charm.
Beholding him, his hair standing on end with joy, he offered praise, uttering "Obeisance to You! again and again with a voice faltering from intense emotion. (25)

Viśvānara said: Brahman alone is non-dual and the entire universe; this is the truth, the absolute truth—there is nothing whatsoever here that is manifold. Rudra is one; he did not exist as a second. Therefore, I take refuge in You alone, the Great Lord. (26)

O Śambhu, you alone are indeed the creator of all; though possessing many forms, your true form is one. Just as the sun, though singular, appears manifold in the various waters, therefore I take refuge in none other than you, O Lord.

Just as a snake [is imagined] in a rope, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a mirage in a desert, and a deer in a shimmering heat-haze, so too is this manifold world; I take refuge in that Great Lord who, when known, [dissolves it]. 28.

Coldness in water, burning power in fire, heat in the sun, and clarity in the moon; fragrance in the flower, and ghee within milk—that which exists therein, O Śambhu, is You; therefore, I take refuge in You. (29)

Though earless, you hear sound; though lacking a nose, you smell; though footless, you come from afar; though eyeless, you see; and though tongueless, you know tastes—who truly knows you? Therefore, I take refuge in you.

O Lord, neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator of all, nor the lords of yoga, nor the gods headed by Indra, know You directly; only Your devotee knows You. Therefore, I take refuge in You. || 31 ||

Neither your lineage, nor your birthplace, nor your name, nor your form, nor your conduct, nor your region is known; yet, being such as you are, you fulfill all the desires of the three worlds—I worship you, O Lord.

Everything comes from you; indeed, you are everything, O enemy of Smara! You are the Lord of Gaurī, and you are the naked one, supremely tranquil. You are the old man, you are the youth, and you are the child; whatever reality exists, it is not other than you—to you I bow.
Having thus offered praise, the brahmin fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff, exceedingly joyful; at that moment, that boy—the eldest of all the elders—spoke: "O god on earth, choose a boon."
Then, having risen with a joyful heart, the accomplished sage Viśvānara replied: "O Lord, what is unknown to you, who are all-knowing? (35)
O Blessed One, you are the inner self of all, the All, and the bestower of everything; why do you direct me, a lord, toward a request that causes such wretchedness?
Having heard these words of Viśvānara, who was pure and devoted to pure vows, the child-like god, smiling with a pure smile, spoke quickly.
The boy said: "O pure one, that desire which has been formed in your heart for Śuciṣmatī will, without doubt, be fulfilled in a very short time. (38)
"O high-minded one, you shall become the son of Śuciṣmatī, renowned by the name Gṛhapati, pure and beloved by all the immortals. (39)
This meritorious hymn of eight verses on longing has been recited by you; by reciting it three times a day for one year in the presence of Śiva, it grants all desires.
The recitation of this hymn, O son, bestows sons, grandsons, and wealth; it brings about all forms of peace and destroys all calamities. (41)
There is no doubt that this brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation; having risen early in the morning and bathed well, one should worship the Śambhu-liṅga.
Reciting this hymn for a year, one who is childless shall obtain a son, provided he observes special vows during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha.
Whoever recites this at the time of bathing shall obtain the entire fruit of the month of Kārtika; by my grace, I, the Imperishable One, [grant this]. 44.
I shall become your son; whoever else recites this *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka*, it must not be given to just anyone.

This must be guarded with great effort; it brings about the birth of even a woman who has long been barren. By means of this rite, whether by a woman or by a man, [the result occurs] through the constant presence of the liṅga. (46)
"If this hymn is recited for one year, it will grant a son; of this there is no doubt. Having said this, the boy vanished, and that Brahmin also went home.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worlds of Indra and Agni," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: Listen, O lady of beautiful hips, O fortunate one, to the account of the origin of Vaiśvānara, just as it was told by Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla to Śivaśarman.
Then, in due course of time, that woman became pregnant after he had duly performed the rite known as *garbhādhāna* (conception).
Then, before the fetus began to move, the wise man properly performed the *puṃsavana* rite for the sake of increasing the male quality, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.

In the eighth month, the parting of the hair (sīmanta), which brings about the full development of the form of the embryo and ensures a comfortable delivery, was performed by that knower of ritual procedures.

Now, therefore, when the moon was in conjunction with the auspicious constellation Puṣya, the Lord with the excellent countenance, whose face is like the moon, [spoke] while Jupiter was in a quadrant and the benefic planets were in odd houses from the ascendant.
A son named Ariṣṭa was born to that Śuciṣmatī; he kindled prosperity with his splendor and brought about the destruction of all misfortunes.
Immediately bestowing all happiness upon the inhabitants of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar, the winds carry fragrance and perfume the faces of the quarters, which are like brides.
Those dense clouds rained down showers of flowers with desirable fragrances; celestial drums resounded, and all directions became serene.
On all sides, the rivers were clear, along with the minds of living beings.
Tamas became utterly exhausted, and rajas also became free from passion.
At that time, all beings were endowed with goodness, and the earth was auspicious; everywhere, speech was virtuous and brought delight to all living creatures.
Tilottamā, Urvaśī, Raṃbhā, Prabhā, Vidyutprabhā, Śubhā, Sumaṅgalā, Śubhālāpā, and Suśīlā—these were excellent women endowed with virtuous character. || 11 ||
Joyfully making their palms into sounding vessels with tinkling bracelets, they held them filled with yakṣakardama paste and enriched with scattered pearls.
Lamps made of diamond and lapis lazuli, ointments of turmeric, objects of the singular form of emerald, as well as conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and curd; || 13 ||
They possessed rubies known as padmarāgas and coral, as well as gems such as kun-kuma; they shone with gomedas, topazes, sapphires, and beautiful garlands.
And thousands of Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, and Apsarases, with their hands busily holding chowries and carrying auspicious objects in their palms, [attended upon him]. || 15 ||
Numerous well-dressed women with beautiful voices, belonging to the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Yakṣas, arrived there while singing charming songs.
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and I, Vibhāṇḍaka, the son of Māṇḍavī. || 17 ||
Lomaśa, Lomacaraṇa, Bharadvāja, and Gautama; Bhṛgu, Gālava, Garga, Jātūkarṇya, and Parāśara. || 18 ||
