Having heard what was said by the pilgrim, the tawny-eyed soldier approached from a distance, saying, "Do not fear! Do not fear! (36)
Drawn by the threads of his own karma, the Bhilla, who was fond of the traveler, arrived there in an instant as if he were his own life-span quickly drawn near.
"Who is this person of wicked conduct? While I, Piṅgākṣa, am alive, who wishes to plunder the travelers who are as dear to me as my own life-breath and Liṅga? (38)
Having heard those words, his sinful paternal uncle Tārākṣa, out of greed for wealth, conceived a wicked thought toward Piṅgākṣa.
"Having cast aside the family dharma, this defiler of the lineage acts thus; today I shall undoubtedly kill him, as I have long contemplated. (40)
Having reflected thus, that evil-minded one, filled with rage, commanded his servants: "First, kill this man, and then these pilgrims."
Then all those men of wicked conduct fought with him alone; and he, by some means or other, led them to the vicinity of his own dwelling.
For had I been the master, I would have destroyed them when my bow was severed, my arrow cut down by shafts, and my armor shattered. (43)
While speaking thus, he gave up his life for the sake of others; those pilgrims also reached his hermitage, their fear having vanished.

Whatever state of mind one possesses at the time of death, one's destination corresponds accordingly; therefore, you attained the status of a Lord of the Quarters as the Sovereign of the Nairṛtas in the southwest.
Thus has its true nature been described by us both to you; beyond this lies the wonderful world of Varuṇa.
Those who construct wells, step-wells, and tanks with pure wealth are honored in this world and, possessing the splendor of Varuṇa, they dwell in the realm of Varuṇa.
In waterless regions, they are givers of water who remove the distress of others—those who bestow upon supplicants wonderful umbrellas and water-pots. (48)
They should construct water-stalls equipped with various utensils, and they should also give "vessels of dharma" filled with fragrant water. (49)
Those who water the *aśvattha* tree on the road, those who assist in planting trees, those who build rest-houses, and those who dispel the suffering of the weary; || 50 ||
At the onset of the heat, even fans made of peacock feathers and other materials, when decorated with colorful paintings, dispel the scorching summer heat.
During the summer months, they diligently provide flavorful, fragrant, and cooling drinks that grant complete satisfaction.
Having mentally resolved upon them, they give fields of sugarcane to the Brahmins, as well as many various kinds of sugarcane products.
Those who provide fresh milk products, as well as those who gift cows and buffaloes, those who construct water-shed pavilions, and those who create shady arbors; || 54 ||
Those who provide multi-streamed water-dripping vessels in temples, or those who seize the tolls at holy places, or those who cause the paths to the holy places to be overgrown; || 55 ||
Those who grant fearlessness to those whose hands are raised in distress, dwell and rejoice in the world of Varuṇa, free from fear.
Those meritorious ones who release those bound by the neck with nooses by the wicked dwell in this world, O wielder of the noose, free from fear from any quarter. (57)
O twice-born one, just as travelers cross over rivers and other waters by means of boats and such, so too do the citizens cross over the ocean of suffering there.

Those men who construct embankments with stones and other materials for rivers such as the Puṇyatāṭinī for the sake of achieving the happiness of those seeking water, become enjoyers of pleasures in that [heaven]. (59)
Those meritorious ones who satisfy the thirsty with cool waters become partakers of a continuous stream of happiness here in this world of Varuṇa.
He is the lord of all reservoirs of water; Pracetas is the master of aquatic creatures and the witness to all deeds.
Listen to the origin of this lord of the great-souled Varuṇa: there was a sage of immeasurable soul, [the son] of the progenitor Kardama. (62)
He had a son renowned as Śuciṣmān, who was well-bred and endowed with virtues such as steadfastness, sweetness, and fortitude.
He went with the boys to bathe in a clear lake; while he was absorbed in playing in the water, a crocodile seized him.
Then, after that son of the sage had been carried off by those children who were crying out in great distress, they gathered together and reported the matter before his father. (65)
Though he had heard of the calamity that befell his son, the mind of Harārcana did not waver from its state of unwavering self-absorption as he sat in meditation.
He practiced even more intensely, beholding the omniscient three-eyed Lord Śambhu while observing the fourteen worlds in his presence.
The various beings and elements contained within the cosmic egg, as well as the moon, the sun, the constellations, the stars, the mountains, the rivers, and the trees.
Indeed, [he saw] oceans, islands, vast forests, and lakes, as well as various hosts of deities and the many cities of the celestial dwellers in heaven.
[He saw] many ponds, wells, reservoirs, canals, and lotus-pools; and in a certain lake, those devoted to water-sports.
And he [honored] many young sages with baths consisting of immersion and emergence from the water, and by sprinkling them with streams of water released from his hands like mechanical contrivances.
Thus, many boys were engrossed in water-sports, making sounds by clapping their hands and filling the quarters with the noise of the water.
Then, while remaining in meditative absorption, Kardama beheld among them his own infant being carried away by a crocodile and rendered utterly distraught.
Then, a certain goddess of the waters forcibly led that cruel aquatic creature away from him and delivered it to the ocean; he saw it handed over.
Having rebuked the lord of rivers with a certain form of Rudra, one who held a trident in his hand and whose face was copper-red with rage, he spoke as follows.
O Lord of Waters, how could there be a son for this devotee of Śiva, the highly fortunate and wise Prajāpati Kardama? (76)
Not knowing Śiva’s power, you remained for a long time terrified by fear upon hearing those words from that ocean.
Having adorned that young *śiśumāra* with jewels and bound it, they brought it and presented it in the presence of the lotus feet of Śambhu.
Having bowed, he addressed him: "O Lord, I have committed no offense; O Lord of the Universe, protector of the helpless, destroyer of the calamities of your devotees. (79)
"O Śambhu, O wish-fulfilling tree for devotees! O Lord, this child of your devotee has been brought here by me from afar by this wicked aquatic creature. (80)
Then, having understood the intention of Śambhu, that host bound that aquatic creature with a noose and delivered it into the hand of the child.
"O attendant, take this son of yours by the command of Śaṅkara; go to your own abode, my child," said Kardama as he spoke thus.
At the time of meditative absorption, the one of noble intellect, hearing the word "all," opened his eyes and released his formal concentration. (83)
He beheld the child right before him and gazed intently at him; he saw the child held by Śiśumāra, who had his ears adorned.
With the tips of his crow-feather tufts moist with water, the corners of his eyes reddened, his skin somewhat parched, trembling with agitation, and his mind overcome by distress.
Embracing him as he prostrated, and smelling his lotus-like face, he regarded him as if born again, gazing at him again and again.
Five hundred years passed while Kardama remained established in his vow, worshipping Śambhu at that time.
And at that moment, Kardama also understood their brief union, for Time has no power in the presence of Mahākāla.
Then, having questioned his father and prostrated before him, the son departed quickly for the glorious city of Vārāṇasī in order to perform austerities. (89)
Having performed severe penance there and installed a Śambhu-liṅga, he remained for five thousand years as motionless as a stone.
Then Mahādeva appeared, pleased by that austerity, and said to Kārdrava: "Speak; what supreme boon shall I grant you? (91)
Kārdami said: "O Lord, compassionate toward your devotees, if you are pleased with me, grant me sovereignty over all waters and aquatic creatures."
Having heard this, the Great Lord, the Sovereign who grants all that is desired, consecrated him there in the supreme station of Varuṇa.
Of gems born from the ocean, of oceans, of rivers, of lakes, of ponds, and furthermore, of tanks, water, and streams; 94.
Be the sovereign of all reservoirs of water and of Vaidiśa in the west; wielder of the noose, may you be beloved by all the immortals. (95)
I grant another boon as well, which shall bring benefit to all: this Liṅga installed by you shall be known by your name. (96)
Known as Varuṇeśa, it bestows excellent siddhi in Vārāṇasī; it is situated in the south-western direction from the Maṇikarṇeśa Liṅga. || 97 ||
Worshiped constantly by men, it effects the destruction of all dullness; for those who are devotees of Varuṇeśa, there is no fear of water anywhere.
For them there is no fear of distress, nor is there ever the suffering of death or rebirth in a lower realm; they have no fear of dropsy, nor indeed any fear of thirst anywhere.
O Lord Varuṇa, upon the remembrance of you, even tasteless foods and drinks will become flavorful; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and Varuṇa too, along with his kinsmen, remained from that time forward adorning this world, O twice-born one.
Thus has the true nature of Varuṇa’s world been described to you; having heard this, a man is never again afflicted by any calamities.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Worlds of Nirṛti and Varuṇa," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
The two Gaṇas said: O twice-born one, O treasure-house of great fortune, behold this meritorious city of Gandhavatī, situated on the northern side of Vāruṇī.
In this [quarter], the lord of the world’s vital breath and the guardian of the direction named Prabhañjana attained the status of a world-protector after propitiating Śrī Mahādeva. || 2 ||
Formerly, the son of Kaśyapa, renowned as Pūtātman, performed extensive penance in the capital city of Dhūrjaṭi.
In Vārāṇasī, the illustrious one established a great, purifying Liṅga named Pavaneśvara for ten million years.
By the mere sight of whom a man becomes purified in soul, casting off the mantle of sin, he shall dwell in that holy city.
Then, by virtue of his fierce austerity, Śiva, the bestower of the fruits of penance, the Great Lord Maheśvara, manifested from that linga in the form of light.
And he, whose soul was serene and who was an ocean of the nectar of compassion, said: "Arise, arise, O pure-souled one of noble vows; choose a boon."
"O you of purified soul, through this fierce austerity and the worship of the Liṅga, there is nothing unattainable for you in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile."
The Purified Soul said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness upon the gods; O you who grant the status of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Indra! || 9 ||
O Lord, even the Vedas do not know what your true nature is; though they have reached the state of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, they speak only of "not this, not this."

O Lord, how could one such as I be capable of praising the Lord of the Pramathas, who is beyond the reach of the speech of even Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and even beyond that of the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati)? || 11 ||
O Lord, my devotion forcibly compels me to the act of praising You. O Master of the World, what can I do? My senses are not under my control.

The universe is you; indeed, there is no duality, because you alone are all-pervading. You are the object of praise, the praiser, and the act of praising; you are both possessed of attributes and devoid of attributes.
Before creation, you alone existed, devoid of form and name; even yogis do not find your true nature in its ultimate sense.
O Lord who moves at your own will, when you were unable to enjoy yourself alone, that desire arose within you, and Śakti became yours to be served.
You alone have attained duality through the distinction between Śiva and Śakti; you are the Lord whose nature is knowledge, while your own will is the very form of Śakti.
By both of you, Śiva and Śakti, through your own divine play, the power of action (kriyā-śakti) was produced; from that, this entire universe arose.

O Lord, you are the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), Umā is remembered as the power of will (icchā-śakti), and this entire universe is the power of action (kriyā-śakti); therefore, you are its cause.
Your right side is Brahmā and your left side is Acyuta; you have the moon, sun, and fire as your eyes, and your breath is the three Vedas.
The oceans are born from your sweat; the wind is your sense of hearing; the ten directions are your arms; and the Brāhmaṇas are remembered as your mouth.
O Lord, those excellent kṣatriyas are Your arms, the vaiśyas are born from Your thighs, the śūdra is from Your feet, and the clouds, O Īśāna, are Your hair. (21)
In the past, you created the cosmic egg in the form of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti; within that cosmic egg is this entire universe, consisting of all things mobile and immobile.
Therefore, O you who consist of the universe, I do not consider anything to be distinct from you; all beings reside in you, and you are composed of all beings. (23)
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again! O Lord, may this alone be my boon: may my mind remain steadfast in you.
When the lord of the gods had spoken thus to that pure-souled one, the Lord, having invested him with His own form, established him in the station of a guardian of the quarters.
Pervading all through my form, the awakener of all reality, you alone shall become the embodiment of the life-span of all beings. || 26 ||
Those men who behold this divine linga of yours here shall be enriched with all enjoyments and shall partake in the happiness of your world.

Having worshipped the Pavamāneśvara Liṅga in the center according to the prescribed rite, with fragrant baths and other offerings, a man who does so even once in his lifetime [attains the goal]. || 28 ||
One who worships with fragrant sandalwood and flowers is honored in my world; [this place is] to the west of Jyeṣṭheśa and to the north of Vāyukuṇḍa.
"By propitiating Pāvamāna, one becomes purified at that very moment. Having granted these boons, the God merged into that Liṅga. || 30 ||
The two attendants said: "Thus has the true nature of the city of Gandhavatī been described to you. To its east lies this glorious city of Alakā, belonging to Kubera."
Through the yoga of devotion, her lord attained friendship with Śambhu; by worshipping Hara, he became both the giver and the enjoyer of treasures, chief among which is Padma.
Śivaśarman said: Who is he, whose son is he, and what kind of devotion did he have toward Sadāśiva, by which he attained friendship with Dhūrjaṭi, the God of gods?
Thus my mind, made slow by its heart's fullness from tasting the nectar of your speech, has come within the range of my hearing.

The two Gaṇas said: "O Śivaśarman, O highly wise one, O lord whose senses are completely purified, whose great impurities born of all previous births have been washed away by visiting excellent sacred fords! (35)
To you, a friend endowed with affection, nothing remains unspeakable; for conversation with the virtuous leads to the increase of all that is most auspicious. (36)
In the city of Kāmpilya, there lived a consecrated priest named Yajñadatta, born into a family of Soma-sacrificers and an expert in the science of sacrifice.

He was proficient in the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the meaning of the Vedas, skilled in the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, honored by kings, possessed of great wealth, munificent, and a vessel of fame.
Devoted to the service of the sacred fire and intent upon the study of the Vedas, he had a son named Guṇanidhi, whose appearance was like the orb of the moon.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, he then acquired extensive knowledge; subsequently, unknown to his father, he became addicted to the practice of gambling.
Having repeatedly taken much wealth from his mother, he gave it to gamblers and formed friendships with them.
He had abandoned the conduct of a Brahmin, was averse to the twilight prayers and ritual bathing, and was a reviler of the Vedas and Shastras, as well as a slanderer of the gods and Brahmins.
Devoid of mindfulness and proper conduct, he indulges in the diversions of song and instrumental music, maintaining a continuous succession of attachments for actors, heretics, and jesters.
Though urged by his mother, he did not go near his father; the initiated one was preoccupied with other household duties for the sake of his initiated wife.
Whenever that son, a treasury of virtues, would ask her: "She is not seen by me in the house; where does she go, and what does she do? (45)
Then she should say, "At such and such a time," [adding] "but now he has gone outside, having bathed and worshipped the gods for all this time. (46)
Having finished his studies, he went with two or three friends for the purpose of further study; meanwhile, his mother deceived the initiated one, saying, "He is my only son. (47)
That initiated one knows nothing of that ritual action nor of that conduct; and he, having performed the tonsure ceremony for him, then at the sixteenth year—
He had his son take her hand according to the ritual prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras; every day, his mother would gently [attend] to that son, who was a treasure-house of virtues.
"Your father, whose heart is softened by affection, will surely rebuke you for your anger; if he learns of your conduct, he will beat both you and me. (50)
I shall always conceal your misconduct before your father; for your father is honored by the world because of his virtuous conduct, and not indeed because of his wealth. (51)

O son, the wealth of Brāhmaṇas consists of true knowledge, association with the virtuous, those who are well-versed in the Vedas, those who have studied them thoroughly, those who are consecrated, and those who perform the Soma sacrifice.
Thus did your ancestors of old attain their established status here; having abandoned association with the wicked, be devoted to the company of the virtuous. (53)
Bestow the auspicious knowledge upon me; practice the conduct of a Brahmin, which is worthy of you in its form, age, lineage, and character. (54)
"You are nineteen years of age, and she is sixteen; she is your wife, O treasure-house of virtues—a virtuous woman who speaks with sweetness. (55)
Restrain this [speech] which is well-behaved, and be endowed with devotion to your father; for your father-in-law also is to be honored by you in every respect due to his virtues and character.
Therefore, why do you not feel shame? O child, abandon your wicked conduct! My sons, your maternal uncles are incomparable in learning, character, lineage, and other virtues. (57)
"You do not fear even them; you are pure on both sides of your lineage. Behold these young Brahmins living as your neighbors. (58)
"Look at these disciples of your father in this house, who are worthy of discipline; O son, when the king hears of your wicked conduct,"
"Having abandoned faith, he will cause the loss of your father's livelihood; even today, people still say that this was merely the behavior of a child. (60)
Immediately thereafter, they will laugh, saying, "It is fitting that you have been initiated"; indeed, everyone will revile both you and me, O Brahmin.
"Does a son bear his mother's character through ill-spoken words? Is a father not even more sinful than a sinner, according to the path of the Śruti and Smṛti? (62)
Maheśvara is the witness for me, whose mind is fixed upon his feet; even though I have bathed at the end of my menstrual period, I have not gazed upon the face of this wicked man here.
"Ah! How powerful is fate, by which you were born!"—thus being instructed at every moment by his mother, he became exceedingly arrogant.
And he did not abandon that way of life, for he was addicted and difficult to reform; [he indulged] in hunting, liquor, slander, prostitutes, theft, and gambling. (65)
Who here has not been ruined by these vices, including adultery? That evil-minded man takes whatever he sees within his house and carries it away.
One should cause the gamblers to surrender their clothing and other items along with their base metals, as well as the mother’s ring made of the nine gems from her hand and the father’s signet ring.
Once, while she was sleeping, he took [her ring] and placed it in the hand of a gambler; on another occasion, as he was returning from the royal palace, [he found] his own seal-ring.

The Dīkṣita, having recognized it, asked the gambler who had found it by chance: "From where did you obtain this ring? Being thus questioned and pressed repeatedly, he replied: "What [is the point]? (69)
"O Brahmin, why do you revile me so harshly for the act of theft? This seal was obtained by your son and presented to me. (70)
For my mother’s cloth was indeed won and taken away the day before yesterday; furthermore, this ring has been surrendered to me as well. (71)
He bestowed abundant wealth upon other gamblers, including jewels, base metals, fine silken garments, golden jars, and other such items.
Various vessels made of bronze and copper are stripped bare and bound [as stakes] every day by gamblers. (73)
O Brahmin, until this very day, there has been no gambler on the face of the earth equal to you, the crest-jewel of those who play with dice.
"How was it that my son, who was skilled in both discipline and policy, was not recognized?"—hearing this, his neck bowed low under the weight of shame. (75)
Having covered his head with a garment, he entered his own palace; then, addressing his wife, who was a woman of great devotion to her husband, he spoke to her.
"O Dīkṣitāyinī, where are you? Where is your son, that treasury of virtues? Or rather, let him be; what is the use of him? Where is that auspicious ring of mine? (77)
"Bring quickly that ring made of nine gems which was taken from my finger by you at the time of massaging my limbs, and give it back to me. (78)
Having heard those words, that initiated wife became afraid and said, "Now, let her complete the midday rites."
"I am occupied with the rites of offerings and the like for the worship of the gods; O you who are dear to guests, the proper time for guests might pass by. (80)
"Only this moment ago, while I was busy preparing cooked food, I placed it in some vessel; I do not know where it has been forgotten. (81)
The initiated one said: "O mother of a virtuous son, O you who always speak the truth! Whenever I ask you, 'Where has my son gone? (82)
"You should say, 'He has gone out just now for the purpose of study, accompanied by two or three friends. (83)
"O wife, where is that madder-dyed garment which was given to me by you? It hangs from the cloth-holder; tell me the truth and cast away your fear. (84)
Now that very water-pot adorned with jewels is no longer seen; and where is that triple-clothed garment made of silk thread presented by the king? (85)
Where is that southern bronze vessel, and where is that Bengal copper jar? And where is that ivory couch for pleasure and amusement? (86)
Where is that mountain-born lamp, fashioned from moonstone, with its tip held eagerly in hand, and adorned like a statue on a pillar? (87)
What is the use of saying more? I am angry with you, though you are of noble birth, for no reason at all. I shall eat [only] when I take you as my wife. 88.
"I am childless because of that wicked defiler of the family; arise, bring darbha grass and water so that I may offer him a handful of sesame seeds. (89)
It is better for men to have no son at all than a wicked son who brings disgrace upon the family; one should abandon a single individual for the sake of the lineage—this is the eternal law.
Having bathed and performed his daily rites on that very day, the initiated one took the hand of the daughter of a Vedic scholar in marriage.
Having heard that account of his own past and having reproached himself, the son of the Dīkṣita looked toward a certain direction and departed.
He fell into great anxiety: "Where shall I go? What shall I do? I have not mastered the sciences, nor do I possess any wealth. (93)
For in another land there is wealth, and one with true learning prospers in happiness; yet there is fear of thieves regarding wealth, whereas one possessed of learning is fearless everywhere. (94)
My birth was in a family of perpetual sacrificers, yet where is this calamity of mine? Oh, how powerful is destiny, which pursues one's future karma! 95.
I do not know how to beg, nor have I any acquaintances anywhere; nor is there any wealth by my side—what, then, could be my refuge? (96)
The sun has always risen for me, my mother provides me with pure food; what more could I ask for today? My mother here asks nothing of me.
While he was thinking thus, the sun went to the mountain of setting; at that very moment, a certain man devoted to Maheśvara appeared.
Having taken great offerings, he went outside the city, having fasted on Śivarātri, in order to worship Īśāna.
Smelling the fragrance of cooked food, he followed after it, hungry; [he thought: "This food, prepared for Śiva at night, must be taken by me."
Having thus taken hold of hope, he then sat down at the door of Śambhu and beheld a great worship performed by that devotee.
When the devotees, having performed the dancing, singing, and other rites, fell asleep for a moment, he then entered the inner sanctum to offer the food offering (naivedya).
Seeing the lamp’s light fading as he looked for cooked food, he gave a wick from the hem of his own garment and rekindled it.
Then, as he was going outside in haste taking cooked food with him, someone who was asleep woke up from the blow of his foot.
"Who is this? Who is this? This is a thief; seize him!"—as he spoke, the city guards arrived and [seized] him. || 5 ||
Fleeing, he was struck down and in an instant met his death; yet, by the power of his future merit, he did not consume the sacrificial offering (naivedya).
Then, bound by hideous soldiers who had arrived with nooses and mallets in their hands, he was led away by the Yama-guards desiring to take him to Saṃyaminī.
Meanwhile, the attendants of Śiva, trident-bearers, arrived bringing a divine celestial chariot adorned with a network of tinkling bells, in order to lead him away.
Beholding the attendants of Śambhu, those servants of Yama, terrified and bowing down, spoke thus: "O Gaṇas, this twice-born man is a man of wicked conduct."
He acts contrary to family tradition and turns his back on the words of his parents; he has fallen away from truth and purity, and is devoid of the twilight prayers and ritual bathing.
Let his other deeds be set aside; behold him here directly as one who carries away the offerings made to Śiva—he is untouchable for those such as you. (11)
Those who consume the offerings made to Śiva, those who step over the offerings made to Śiva, and those who give away the offerings made to Śiva—their touch indeed brings about demerit.
Whether one stirs up poison and drinks it, or whether fasting is the supreme good, the wealth of Śiva must be served; life, even when it has reached the throat, is not to be preserved at its expense.
"You are the authority regarding these matters, not we. If there is even a trace of dharma in him, O members of the assembly, then let us hear it."
Having heard his words in this manner, the attendants then spoke: "O servants of Śiva's dharma, those who are subtle are indeed like you. (15)
How can those who are visible to those with coarse vision be perceived by those with subtle insight? Listen here to what karma has been performed by this or that person.
As the shadow of a lamp was falling upon the top of the linga, he prevented it at night by placing the wick of his own lamp within the fold of his garment.
Furthermore, another supreme dharma has arisen there for him: even while merely hearing the names of Śiva, he grasps them through incidental association. || 18 ||
The worship being performed according to the rules with devotion was observed by him, who remained firm-minded while fasting until the end of the day.
"O messengers, this best of the twice-born shall now become the King of Kaliṅga, his sins shaken off; you may go back as you came. (120)
That twice-born one was liberated from the messengers of Yama by the attendants; he was Dama, the son of Kaliṅgādhi, the subduer of enemies.
Then, having obtained the kingdom in due course after his father had passed away, the young King Dama—the difficult-to-subdue—knew no other duty.
O twice-born one, apart from the offering of lamps in all the shrines of Śiva, he summoned the lords of the villages and all those residing within his own domain. (23)
Thus he commanded me: "He shall be punished by me—whosoever [neglects] as many temples of Śiva as there are on all sides around his village. (24)
In each and every place, the lamp must always be lit without hesitation; otherwise, by the fault of violating my command, I shall undoubtedly cut off your head. || 25 ||
Thus, out of fear of him, lamps were lit at every temple of Śiva; by this very merit, King Dama lived for the rest of his life.
Having attained great supernatural power through the Dharma, he passed away under the sway of the law of time, having indeed kindled many lamps from the oil and wicks of his own lamp.
The lord of Alakā became the refuge for the flames of jewel-lamps; thus, O Śivā, even that which is done in small measure bears fruit in due time.
Knowing this, those who seek their own welfare should practice devotion to Śiva; where is that heir of the initiated, who has turned his back on all dharma? (29)

Resplendent like a lamp illuminating his own purpose, with the crest-jewel of his emblem removing all darkness, he attained sovereignty over the region of Kaliṅga, always delighting in righteousness. (130)

"O Śivaśarman, look! Having lit lamps in the temple of Śiva due to the awakening of former impressions, where is this status of a world-guardian that is now being enjoyed here by this one who possesses only human nature? (31)
The two Gaṇas said: O Brahmin, listen with a focused mind as we relate how he also came to attain friendship with Śiva at all times. (32)
O Brahmin, formerly in the Pādma Kalpa, Viśravas was born from Pulastya, the mind-born son of Brahmā; Vaiśravaṇa was his son.
Therefore, this city of Alakā was enjoyed by him; it was created by the Architect of the Universe after he had propitiated the three-eyed God in the past through exceedingly fierce austerity.
When that kalpa had passed and the Meghavāhana kalpa had begun, this Yājñadatti, the son of Uśanas, performed most difficult penance.
Having recognized the power of devotion to Śambhu through that mere lamp, he reached Kāśī, the city of the Enemy of Tripura, which illuminates consciousness.
Having awakened the lamp of variegated jewels—the singular Śiva—[he made it] rich with the oil of exclusive devotion and steady through the great meditation upon Him. (37)
It is the great vessel of union with Śiva, nourished by the fire of asceticism, and free from the strikes of the moths that are the great obstacles of desire and anger. || 38 ||

Having established the Śāmbhava Liṅga—which is free from the wind of breath-restraint, stainless, and perceived by the stainless eye—and having worshipped it with the flower of true being (sadbhāva), [he should remain]. || 39 ||
He performed that austerity until his body was reduced to mere skin and bone, for a period of ten million years.
Then the Lord Viśveśvara himself, together with the large-eyed goddess, beheld the lord of Alakā with a gracious inner soul.
Having fixed his mind upon the Liṅga and remaining as motionless as a pillar, he said, "O Lord of Alakā, I am the giver of boons; enough of this asceticism."
As soon as that ascetic opened his eyes and looked, he beheld one whose splendor exceeded a thousand rising suns.
He first beheld Śrīkaṇṭha, the moon-crested lord of Umā; his own eye-sight being overwhelmed by that splendor, he closed his eyes.
He spoke to the Lord of the gods of gods, who transcends the path of thought: "Now, by the sight of your own feet, grant me the power of vision. (45)
O Lord, this alone is the boon—that you are beheld directly before my eyes; what need is there for any other boon, O Master? Salutations to you, O moon-crested one! 46.
Having heard those words, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, touched him with the palm of his hand and granted him the power of vision.
First extending her eyes, she gazed only at Umā; for this woman beside Śambhu was beautiful in every limb.
"What penance has she performed? Even my own penance is surpassed by hers! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what love! Oh, how great is the splendor of her good fortune! (49)
As he gazed with a cruel look, speaking this again and again, his left eye burst open due to that malevolent glancing.
Then the Goddess said to the God: "Why does this wicked ascetic, looking at me repeatedly, speak while disparaging the power of my asceticism? (51)
Again and again he looks at me with his right eye, envying my beauty and the perfection of my love and good fortune.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, the Lord laughed and said to her: "O Umā, this is your son; he has not looked with a cruel eye."
"Beholding your ascetic splendor, how indeed could one describe it? Having thus addressed the Goddess, the Lord spoke to him again:
"I grant you boons, my child, for I am gratified by this asceticism. You shall be the sovereign lord of the treasures (Nidhis) and the master of the Guhyakas. (55)
O you of noble vows, be the king of the Yakṣas and Kinnaras, the sovereign of kings, the lord of the Puṇyajanas, and the giver of wealth to all. (56)
I shall always maintain friendship with you and dwell in your presence, like one near Alakā, for the sake of increasing your joy.
"Come, fall at her feet; she is indeed your mother. Having thus granted these boons, the divine Śiva spoke again to Śivā: "O Queen of the Gods, show favor toward this ascetic daughter of yours."
The Goddess said: "O child, may your devotion to Bhava be unwavering forever. Let there be a single eye on your face by means of my left eye, which has burst open. (59)
"May the boons granted to you by the god remain exactly as they were. O son, because of my jealousy regarding your beauty, you shall be known by the name Kubera. (160)
"This Liṅga established by you shall be known by your name; it will grant success to practitioners and is the supreme remover of all sins. (61)
The man who beholds the Kubereśvara Liṅga shall never be deprived of wealth, nor of friends, nor of kinsmen. || 62 ||
To the south of Viśveśa, one should worship Kubereśa; such a person shall not be tainted by sins, nor by poverty, nor by miseries.
Having thus granted these boons, the Lord Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, then entered the supreme abode of Viśveśvara belonging to the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
The two attendants said: "In this manner, this giver of wealth attained supreme friendship with the illustrious Śambhu; and here near Alakā is Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara."
Thus has the true nature of those lords of the Yakṣas in the city been described; having heard this, a person shall undoubtedly be liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Gandhavatī and Alakā," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 13.

The two attendants said: In the northeastern quarter of the city of Alakā, there is the great and prosperous Mahodayā; in this place dwell those whose wealth is penance, who are constant devotees of Rudra. (1)
Constantly absorbed in the remembrance of Śiva, devoted to the vows of Śiva, having dedicated all their actions to Śiva, they were always intent upon the worship of Śiva.
Full of longing, they perform austerities here with the thought, "May there be enjoyment in heaven for us"; those men, assuming the form of Rudra, dwell here in this beautiful city of Rudra.
The eleven Rudras, headed by Ajaikapād and Ahirbudhnya, are indeed the sovereign lords here, with tridents raised in their hands.
Indeed, they protect the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) from the wicked who hate the gods; those excellent ones constantly grant boons to the people who are devotees of Śiva.
Having reached the city of Vārāṇasī, these [sages] also performed penance after installing the great, auspicious-bestowing Liṅga known as Īśāneśa.
By the grace of Īśāneśa, the eleven lords of the directions in the northeastern quarter indeed move alone, adorned with crowns of matted hair.
With an eye in their forehead, blue throats, pure limbs, and the bull as their emblem—those Rudras who exist upon the surface of the earth are innumerable by the thousands.
Residing in this city, which is presided over by Īśa, they possess the abundance of all enjoyments; having worshipped Īśāneśa in Kāśī as well as in other regions, [they attain these fruits].
Due to that merit, they are born as those who possess no enemies or priests; and those who worship Īśāneśa on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days [attain this].
Those very ones are to be known as Rudras here and in the hereafter without a doubt, having performed a vigil at night in the presence of Īśāneśvara.
Having observed a fast on any such lunar day, a man shall not again enter a womb; thus he hears the account regarding the path to heaven as it is proclaimed by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
Even by day, Śivaśarman beheld the moonlight shining intensely, delighting his mind along with all his senses in manifold ways.
Marvelling again and again, Śivaśarman asked those two attendants of Hari, "Who is this world? and they spoke to that brahmin.
The two attendants said: "O illustrious Śivaśarman, this world belongs to the moon, the storehouse of digits, by whose nectar-showering rays the universe is nourished. (15)
O sage, the venerable Ṛṣi Atri, the father of Soma, was born in the beginning from the mind of Brahmā, who desired to bring about the creation of beings. (16)
We have heard that in former times he performed a penance called Anuttara for three thousand divine years. (17)
His semen ascended upwards and attained the state of Soma; it flowed forth from his two eyes, illuminating the ten directions.
Then, commanded by the Creator, ten goddesses took up that embryo according to the prescribed rite; having come together, they bore it, for individually they were not at all able to do so.
When those quarters were no longer able to sustain that embryo, Soma fell together with them to the earth.
Beholding Soma fallen, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
With that preeminent chariot, Druhiṇa circumambulated the earth, bounded by the oceans, twenty-one times.
That radiant energy of his which overflowed and reached the earth gave rise to the medicinal herbs by which the world is sustained.
Having attained great splendor and being personally encouraged by Brahmā, the illustrious one performed penance for one hundred and ten padmas of years, O fortunate one.
Having reached the supremely purifying field of Avimukta, he installed a nectar-like Liṅga named Candreśa, according to his own name.
Through the grace of the God of gods, the Lord of the Universe, the wielder of the Pināka bow, he became the king of seeds, medicinal herbs, waters, and the twice-born. (26)
There, having constructed a single well known as Amṛtoda, by drinking its water and bathing therein, a person is liberated from ignorance.
He who was personally worn upon his own crown by the gratified God of gods, having taken that one supreme digit which causes the world to flourish; 28.
Even though cursed by Dakṣa later on, and having reached waning for one month less, this moon is again replenished by that very same digit.
Having obtained that great sovereignty, Soma, the best among those who possess the Soma-plant, performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, for which the sacrificial fee consisted of a hundred thousand cows.
"O twice-born one, we have heard that Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those foremost Brahman-sages and to the members of the assembly. (31)
Where Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahmā, Atri, and Bhṛgu served as the officiating priests (ṛtvij), Hari was present there as a member of the assembly (sadasya), accompanied by many sages.
Taṃsinī, Kuhū, Dyuti, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Vasu, Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī—these nine goddesses waited upon him.
Having gratified Rudra together with Umā through the sacrificial rite, he attained the renown of "Soma," a name bestowed upon him by Śambhu, who was himself Soma.
In that very place, Soma performed most difficult penance; and in that same spot, he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice before Candreśvara.
Right there, the delighted Brahmins said this to that treasury of arts: "Soma is the king of us Brahmins, for whom the three worlds are a sacrificial fee."
Right there, he attained the state of being the eye of the God of gods; by the God, with a pleased mind, for the sake of bringing joy to the three worlds. (37)
"You have been declared by him to be my supreme form; through the power of that austerity, the world, having attained its rise from you, shall experience the dawning of happiness. (38)
Touched by your hands, which consist of nectar, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings shall cast off its extreme exhaustion caused by the heat of the sun. (39)
Having said this, Maheśāna joyfully granted other boons: "O king of the twice-born, this most fierce penance which has indeed been performed by you here—" (40)
And as for that sacrifice and its performance which was announced by you to me, and this Liṅga named Candreśvara which has been installed—41.
Therefore, in this Liṅga bearing your name, I, assuming the form of Soma and Somārdha, shall remain entirely hidden every month on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
"I shall dwell for a day and night endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds; therefore, even a very small meritorious act performed here on the full moon day [shall yield great fruit]. (43)
Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, meditation, giving gifts, feeding Brahmins, and the great ritual of worship—these will surely bring me great delight. (44)
The restoration of dilapidated [shrines] and similar works, the offering of dance, instrumental music, and so forth, the rite of hoisting the flag, and the honoring of ascetics and mendicants; 45.
Whatever is performed at Candreśvara then becomes infinite in its merit. Furthermore, O Moon, listen as I shall tell you another secret. (46)
It must not be told to one who is not a devotee, nor to an atheist, nor to one who harms the Vedas. O Soma, when the new moon occurs on a Monday... (47)
Then, O Soma, having performed the daily obligatory rites on the thirteenth day, the virtuous should respectfully observe a fast on the fourteenth day; listen! (48)
Having worshipped the Liṅga named Candreśvara on the occasion of Śanipradoṣa, and having observed the fast at night on the thirteenth lunar day while undertaking the prescribed restraints; || 49 ||
Having fasted on the fourteenth day and kept a vigil throughout the night, one should bathe in the waters of the Candrodaka at dawn during the conjunction of the moon with the new moon (Kuhū).

Having performed the twilight devotions according to the rules and completed all the water-rites, he should duly perform the Śrāddha ceremony at the sacred bathing places on the banks of the Candroda river.

One should diligently offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) without the rites of invocation (āvāhana) or the water-offering (arghya), representing the three persons who are the embodiments of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the sons of Aditi.
Having likewise intended for his maternal grandfathers and others born of his lineage, the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should utter the names of his gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen.
Performing a śrāddha at this sacred site with faith, one uplifts all [ancestors], just as the ancestors are gratified by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Gayā.
Likewise, in this Candrodakuṇḍa, ancestors are satisfied by Śrāddhas; and just as a man is liberated from all debt to his forefathers at Gayā, so too is he here.
Likewise, one is liberated from debt by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Candroda; and whenever any preeminent man should go to behold Candreśvara. (56)
Then his great-grandfathers will dance with joy, thinking: "This man will perform the libation for us at this Candroda-tīrtha."
If, due to our misfortune, he does not do so, then our satisfaction will come from the mere touch of that sacred ford. || 58 ||

When even a dull-witted person merely touches it, he shall behold [the deity] for his satisfaction. Having thus performed the Śrāddha and touched Caṇḍreśvara, the observer of the vow, after satiating the Brahmins and ascetics, should then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
When such a vow has been performed at Kāśī on a Monday coinciding with the new moon, one shall be liberated from the three debts through my grace, O deer-marked one (O Moon).

On this occasion of the Great Caitrī festival, a pilgrimage must be undertaken by the residents of the sacred field; it serves to remove obstacles from the field and leads to the attainment of the knowledge of the Tāraka.
Having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara, even if one is situated elsewhere, one shall pierce through the mass of accumulated sins and attain the world of Soma.
In the Kali age, the greatness of Candreśa is not understood due to misfortunes; furthermore, O Lord of Night, I shall tell you another supreme secret.
This seat (pīṭha) of the Lord of Siddhas and Yogins bestows success upon the practitioner, even among the gods, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, and vidyādharas.
Among the rākṣasas, guhyakas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and humans, there are seventy million perfected ones (siddhas) who have attained perfection here before me.
Meditating here upon the Sovereign of the Universe while restricting his food for six months, he beholds the Siddhas who have arrived before him to worship Caṇḍreśvara.
The Siddhayogīśvarī herself becomes the direct bestower of boons upon him; for you too, great accomplishment arises from the sight of Siddhayogīśvarī. (67)
There are many sacred sites on earth for the accomplishment of the practitioner; however, none bestows success as swiftly upon the surface of the earth as the seat of Yogīśvarī.
O Moon, this very place where you have installed this Caṇḍeśvara Liṅga is indeed that sacred seat (pīṭha), which remains invisible to those who have not disciplined their souls.
Those who have conquered desire, conquered anger, and conquered greed, longing, and pride, behold the Yogīśvarī, my supreme and benevolent Śakti.
But those people who, being purified in mind, shall worship on every eighth and fourteenth day at the Siddhayogīśvarī-pīṭha; || 71 ||
To them, she who is invisible in form, auspicious, tawny-hued, and the bestower of all accomplishments, will manifest through incense, food offerings, lamps, and other such gifts.
O twice-born one, having thus granted boons to that Moon, the Great Lord Śambhu vanished there in the city of Vaiśveśvara.
From that time forth, he became the sovereign lord of the twice-born in this world, dispelling the darkness of the quarters with his own spreading rays.
Men who perform the Monday vow and are devoted to the drinking of Soma indeed go to the world of Soma by means of a vehicle as radiant as the moon.
The man who listens with devotion to the origin of Candreśvara as well as to the lunar penance shall be honored in the world of the Moon.

Agastya said: While the two attendants were narrating this auspicious story on the divine path—bestowing happiness upon Śivaśarman and removing his fatigue—they then proceeded to the world of the stars (Uḍuloka).

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Soma," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 14 ||
Agastya said: Listen, O illustrious wife Lopāmudrā, my partner in dharma; this is the story told by Viṣṇu and his attendant to Śivaśarman.
Śivaśarman said: "O Gaṇas, this wonderful account of the Moon has been heard; O you who are experts in narrating all manner of stories, tell me now the celebrated tale of the world of the stars."

The two Gaṇas said: In ancient times, from the back of the thumb of the Creator who desired to bring forth creation, there was born the Prajāpati Dakṣa, who was skillful in the fashioning of progeny. He had sixty daughters, adorned with the beauty of ascetic penance; they were auspicious, increasing all loveliness, and headed by Rohiṇī.
Having performed intense penance by means of those [goddesses] and reached the city of Viśveśvara, they propitiated Mahādeva, Soma, who is adorned with the moon.
When this Lord was pleased, he approached to grant a boon; with a gracious soul, he said, "Ask for an excellent boon."
Then, having heard the words of Śambhu, those maidens said: "O Śaṅkara, if a boon is to be granted to us, we are worthy of a boon."
"O Mahādeva, may he who removes the suffering of worldly existence, and who is equal to you in form, become our husband. (8)
Having installed a very great Liṅga known as Nakṣatreśvara on the beautiful bank of the Vāraṇā, in the vicinity of Saṃgameśvara.
For a thousand divine years, they performed a great penance known as the "man-like posture" (puruṣāyita), which is difficult even for men to accomplish.
Thereupon, Viśveśa, being pleased, granted an excellent boon to all those women who were devoted to a single husband and possessed steady minds: ||| 11 ||
The illustrious Viśveśvara said: "Indeed, such intense austerity as this has never before been endured by other women; therefore, your name here shall truly be Nakṣatra."
"Because you have recently performed penance under the misconception that it was for the sake of acting as men, you shall therefore possess masculinity according to your desire. (13)
"In this entire circle of luminaries, you shall become preeminent; you are the supreme sources of origin for the zodiac signs beginning with Aries. (14)
He who is the lord of herbs, of nectar, and of the Brāhmaṇas—by him as your husband, O fair-faced ladies, may you become wives possessed of husbands.
This Linga of yours, known by the name Nakṣatreśvara—having worshipped it, a man shall go to your supreme world. || 16 ||
Above the moon, there shall be a world for you to dwell; and among all the stars, you shall be honored.
And those who worship the constellations and observe the vows of the constellations shall dwell in your world, possessing a radiance equal to that of the stars.
Those who behold Nakṣatreśvara in Kāśī shall never suffer any affliction from the constellations, planets, or zodiac signs. (19)
Agastya said: Then the world of Budha became the guest of the eyes of Śivaśarman, as he related the conversation between the two Gaṇas, Bhagaṇa and Viṣṇucetas.
Śivaśarman said: "Whose world is this incomparable one? Tell me, O two attendants of the Blessed Lord; it gladdens my mind exceedingly, like the light of the moon. (21)
The two attendants said: "O Śivaśarman, listen to this story which removes sin, which serves as a diversion on the path to heaven, and which destroys the threefold suffering. (22)
That one of great splendor whom we previously described has attained the status of sovereignty; O King of the Twice-born, he stands before you. (23)
He who performed the Rajasuya sacrifice for which the three worlds were made his sacrificial fee, and who practiced most intense austerity for one hundred million lotuses.
He who was born from the eye of Atri, the grandson of Brahmā, the lord of all medicinal herbs and indeed the master of the luminaries.
He who is celebrated as the treasury of stainless arts, and who, rising up, would seize the oppressors of others by the throat with his own rays; || 26 ||
He who brings joy to the night-lotuses along with the entire world, serving as a circular mirror for the beautiful adornment of the women of the quarters.
Of what use are other accumulations of virtues? Even these are not equal to the Moon, upon whose own head the Omniscient One wears it as an ornament.
Deluded by the intoxication of power, he [approached] the wife of Bṛhaspati, even though he was his domestic priest, his elder, and his brother, the son of Aṅgiras.
Though he was repeatedly restrained by the gods and many divine sages, that handsome man swiftly carried off Tārā, who was endowed with exquisite beauty.
This is certainly not the fault of that moon, the king of the twice-born; for whom has their mind not been wounded by Kāma, who disregarded the Three-eyed One? (31)

This darkness spreading on all sides has been created by Fate for the sake of its own cessation; it is no more than a great medicine consisting of the lamp and the rays of the sun, yet it possesses no power over the [spiritual] darkness.

One deluded by the intoxication of power does not perceive the beneficial and auspicious welfare of Hari, just as a person of pure intellect does not touch a mind that is hostile due to baths in sacred fords performed by the wicked.

Fie, fie upon this activity of excessive pride, which is revealed even by his walking and his gaze; for he looks for a moment with an ungraceful eye, a foot that has been struck down and is a stepping-stone to calamity.

Alas! Who has not been conquered by desire, even by that flower-armed god who rules the three worlds? Who has not fallen under the sway of anger, and who has not been utterly deluded by greed? Who, with a heart pierced by the arrows of women's glances, has not met with calamity? And who, having attained the glory of sovereignty, has not reached the path of blindness—even though possessing clear eyes? (35)

Sovereignty and prosperity are exceedingly fickle, and even if they are attained here through one's own exertion, they are indeed unstable; therefore, that which is truly beneficial—whether it be great or small—should always be performed with noble conduct.
When that fierce one did not release Tārā to the descendant of Aṅgiras, Rudra then seized his heel, having taken up the Ājagava bow.
Then that supreme weapon named Brahmaśiras was discharged by the high-souled one who had approached the God of gods; it was subsequently destroyed by him.
Between those two, there occurred that terrible battle concerning Tāraka; then Brahmā became afraid of the sudden destruction of the cosmic egg.
Having restrained Rudra, who possessed the splendor of the fire of universal destruction, from the battle, the Grandfather himself gave Tārā back to the descendant of Aṅgiras.
Then, perceiving the embryo within her, Bṛhaspati said to Tārā: "The embryo must not be retained by you in my womb under any circumstances."
Having approached a clump of reeds, she cast off the fetus; as soon as he was born, that Blessed One surpassed the splendor of the gods.
Then, fallen into doubt, those best of gods said to Tārā: "Tell us the truth; whose son is he—Soma’s or Bṛhaspati’s? (43)
When Tārā, overcome with extreme shame, did not speak even though questioned by the gods, she was then about to be cursed by Kumāra, who possessed exceeding splendor.
Having restrained him, Brahmā then questioned Tārā regarding his doubt; with palms joined in reverence, she spoke to the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) concerning Soma.
Then King Prajāpati, having smelled the head of that wise child, gave him the name Budha.
Then, surpassing all the gods in splendor, form, and strength, Budha took leave of Soma and resolved to go into exile for the sake of asceticism.
He went to Kāśī, the abode of the mass of liberation protected by Viśveśa; having installed there a Liṅga named Budheśvara after his own name. (48)
Practicing intense austerity while meditating upon the fierce Śiva—the ornament of the young moon—in his heart, the boy performed this for ten thousand years. (49)
Then the glorious Lord of the Universe, the Master of All and Creator of the World, appeared from the great Liṅga Budheśvara with great majesty.
And the Great Lord, whose form is light, spoke with a serene soul: "O one of great intelligence, O wise one, best among the learned, choose a boon. (51)
"O most gentle one, I am pleased with this great austerity of yours and with your constant devotion to the *liṅga*; there is nothing that cannot be granted to you."
Having heard these words, which were as deep in sound as a thundercloud and like the reviving of crops withered by drought, he then [acted].
As soon as the boy opened his eyes and looked ahead, he then beheld the three-eyed, moon-crested Lord upon the linga.
Budha said: Salutations to you, the pure-souled one; salutations to you whose form is light. Salutations to you, the universal form; salutations to you who transcend all forms.
Homage to the one who destroys all suffering for those who bow down, whose nature is auspiciousness; homage to you, the omniscient one; homage be to you, the creator of all. 56.

Salutations to you, the compassionate one; salutations to you who are accessible through devotion; and salutations to you, the bestower of the fruits of austerities, whose very form is austerity. || 57 ||
O Śambhu, O Śiva, O beloved of Śivā, O you of peaceful splendor, O bearer of the throat and the trident, O moon-crested one, O Lord Śarva, O Lord Śaṅkara, O Dhūrjaṭi! || 58 ||
O wielder of the Pināka bow, O Lord of the Mountain, O blue-throated one, O Sadāśiva! O Mahādeva, salutations to you; O God of gods, let there be salutation to you.
O Maheśvara, lover of praise, I do not know how to offer hymns; may I possess undivided devotion toward the pair of your lotus feet.
O Lord, O Sovereign, if you are pleased, this alone is the boon [I seek]: I choose no other boon from you, O ocean of the nectar of compassion. (61)
Then Maheśāna, gratified by that hymn of praise, said: "O highly fortunate son of Rohiṇī, O ocean of exceedingly gentle speech!"
Your world shall be above the world of the stars; and you shall receive supreme worship in the midst of all the planets.
O gentle one, this Liṅga established by you bestows intelligence upon all; it removes evil-mindedness and grants residence in your own world.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Śambhu vanished right there; and by the grace of the God of gods, Budha went to his own celestial realm.

The two attendants said: O moon to the eyes of the virtuous, a man who has attained wisdom through the worship of Budheśvara in Kāśī, having entered the fathomless ocean of worldly existence, would not sink; rather, with a beautiful countenance, he shall dwell here in this world of the wise.
Having beheld the Budheśvara Liṅga in the eastern direction from Candreśvara, a living being is never deprived of his intellect, even at the time of death.
While the two Gaṇas were thus conversing with the woman of the world of the wise, a celestial chariot arrived at the unsurpassed realm of Śukra.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worlds of the Nakṣatras and Budha," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 15.
The two Gaṇas said: "O Śivaśarman of great intelligence, this is the wonderful world of Śukra; here dwells Kavi, the preceptor of the Dānavas and the Daityas. (1)

In the case of those who are foolish and without allies, fortune acts as a helper; whether in the vast forest, in battle, or at home, fortune is indeed the cause.
Where is the young prince, and where is that dense forest? O Destiny, who forcibly makes [all things] your own, salutations to you!
For wherever and for whomever that which is destined to happen—whether auspicious or indeed inauspicious—is to occur, the inevitable rope drags it there and causes it to be delivered.
This mortal man ordains things otherwise through the power of his intellect; however, the Lord Fate would ordain them otherwise by means of destiny.
Neither youth nor beauty, nor even a wondrous deed performed for oneself, nor strength nor exertion are the causes for men; rather, it is that which was done in a previous life.
Then, seeing the seven seers, who possessed the intense splendor of seven suns and seemed as if drawn and brought there by the threads of destiny, he rejoiced greatly.

With their excellent foreheads marked by the *tilaka*, their fingers grasping the ritual *kuśa* grass, seated upon black antelope skins, and adorned with sacred sacrificial threads (*yajñasūtra*). (85)
With rosary beads in their hands and their eyes slightly closed, they were clad in well-washed, fine saffron-colored robes and upper garments.
It was marvelous that even at an untimely moment, the seven highly fortunate oceans had met, as if desiring to rescue all creatures who were submerged in calamity.
Approaching him with humility, Dhruva joined his palms in reverence and, bowing down, addressed these charming words: (88)
Dhruva said: "O best of sages, know me to be Dhruva, born from the womb of Sunīti, the son of Uttānapāda, whose mind is filled with world-weariness."
This forest, having been reached by you, now has its protector in your feet; it was previously ignorant of everything, yet now its mind dwells in great spiritual power.
Having seen that boy, full of vigor, whose appearance was naturally sweet, whose eyes and attire were priceless, and who spoke with soft yet profound words; || 91 ||
Having seated the child nearby, they spoke, greatly amazed: "O child of large eyes, O great king, O little prince! (92)
Even after reflecting, we do not understand; tell us the cause of your despondency. For today we have no anxiety for wealth, nor any insult from our mother’s house.
What indeed is the cause for the perfection of a healthy body not being attained? For men whose desires remain unfulfilled, dispassion arises. (94)
How is it that you, a prince of the king who rules over the seven islands, do not have this [thought] in your mind, given that the nature of this world is inherently diverse? (95)
"Indeed, it would be possible for [this] to be understood by a youth, an elder, or even a child. Having heard these words of theirs, which were overflowing with natural affection, [he replied: 96.
Then that child, whose aspirations were lofty, grasped these words. Dhruva said: "O lords of sages, I have been sent by my mother for the purpose of serving the king."
For, wishing to ascend the royal throne, he was rebuked by Suruci; yet he held me and my mother in the highest esteem. (98)
Having reproached themselves, they praised this very reason for their world-weariness; and having heard these words of the child, they looked at one another.
On that day, they praised only the warrior code; alas, there was no forbearance even toward a child.
The sages said: "O, what must be done by us? What is your desire? Let that first be known to us; bring it within the range of our hearing. (1)
Dhruva said: "O sages, he who is my kinsman—supreme and most excellent—should occupy that most excellent and auspicious throne bestowed by my father."
"O you of excellent vows, I desire this assistance rendered by you; for, due to my childhood, I likely do not know it myself—therefore, let that instruction be spoken. (3)
How could that which was enjoyed by no other king, which is superior to all others, which is difficult even for Indra and the gods to attain, and which is hard to reach, be obtained?
I do not desire what is bestowed by my father; I desire that which is won by my own arms—something, alas, that would surpass even the father's wildest dreams.
Those who merely enjoy their father’s wealth generally do not possess the riches of fame; however, those who perceive their father as superior are to be known as the best of men.
May there be only death for those of wicked mind who destroy the fame, learning, and wealth acquired by their father.
Having heard those words of his, which were well-reasoned and powerful, the sages headed by Marīci replied truly and resolutely, exactly as it was.
Marīci said: "How can one who has not worshipped the feet of Acyuta attain his state? O dear one, you have spoken the truth exactly as it is; I do not speak anything that is untrue."
Atri said: One who has not tasted the essence of the pollen from the lotus feet of Govinda cannot attain that vast state which transcends the path of the mind.
Aṅgiras said: Not far from here is the station of all prosperity in this world for him who would cultivate with a virtuous disposition the lotus-feet of the beloved of Kamalā’s beloved.
Pulastya said: By the mere remembrance of him, the succession of great sins attains the supreme end; he is Viṣṇu, the eternal bestower of all.
Pulaha said: That which they call the Supreme Brahman, beyond both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, by whose Māyā all this is pervaded—that Acyuta shall grant everything.
Kratu said: What is there that Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice, Janārdana, who is to be known through the Vedas and is the inner soul of this world, would not grant when he is pleased?

Vasiṣṭha said: O prince, since even the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) that move within the dance of his eyebrows [are attained] by worshipping that Hṛṣīkeśa, liberation (apavarga) is likewise not far off.

Dhruva said: "O lords of sages, what you have spoken regarding the propitiation of Viṣṇu is true; however, let it be taught how the Lord is to be worshipped and according to what ritual procedure. (16)
The sages said: Whether standing or walking, whether sleeping or waking, and likewise while lying down or sitting, Nārāyaṇa should always be recited in prayer.
Who has not attained perfection by meditating upon the four-armed Viṣṇu and chanting the twelve-syllable mantra which consists of Vāsudeva? 18.
Who on this earth does not attain perfection by beholding for even a moment Acyuta, who resembles the flax flower and is clad in yellow garments, the soul of all? (19)
A mortal who chants the name of Vāsudeva undoubtedly attains everything—sons, wife, friends, kingdom, heaven, and liberation. 120.
Even for those people who have committed sins, if they are intent on the recitation of Vāsudeva, neither obstacles nor the terrible messengers of Yama shall touch them.
This great mantra was also practiced by my grandfather, Manu, who possessed great prosperity and was devoted to Viṣṇu, as he desired sovereignty. || 22 ||
You too, by means of this mantra, become devoted to Vāsudeva; O best of beings, quickly attain whatever prosperity you desire. (23)
Having spoken thus, all those high-souled lords of sages vanished; and Dhruva, having fixed his mind upon Vāsudeva, departed for ascetic penance.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Dhruva," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the description of the world of Dhruva. || 19 ||
The two Gaṇas said: O twice-born one, having emerged from that forest, the son of Uttānapāda reached the beautiful Madhuvana on the great bank of the Yamunā.
The first abode of the Blessed One, that merit of Hari-medhas—by reaching it, even a sinful creature certainly becomes sinless.
Chanting the name of Vāsudeva, the supreme Brahman free from all affliction, he—his eyes stilled by meditation—beheld the entire universe as being composed of that alone.
Hari is in all directions; Hari is in the rays of the sun; Hari, in the form of the auspicious deer, the lion, and other creatures, dwells in the forest.
In the waters, the Lord Hari appears in the form of the śālūra-frog, the tortoise, and others; and even in the stables of kings, Hari exists in the form of horses and such.
In Pātāla he is Anaṃtarūpa, and in the sky he is known as Ananta; though he is one, he has attained infinity through his infinite varieties of forms.
He who dwells eternally among the gods, for he is indeed the abode of the gods—he is Vāsudeva; wherever he may sport, it is by the power of his own latent impressions (vāsanā).

The root *viṣlṛ* signifies "pervasion," and it is this root that has acquired its meaningful application in the name *Viṣṇu*, for His essential nature is indeed characterized by the pervading of all things.
Because he is the lord of all the senses (hṛṣīka), he is celebrated as Hṛṣīkeśa; he who is thus known is established everywhere.
Because his devotees do not fall even when the great dissolution occurs, he alone is Acyuta (the Unfallen) in all the world—the omnipresent and imperishable one.
He who, by his own effortless play, sustained this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, sustains the whole world here through the perfection of his own nature as the servant.
In his vision, they behold nothing other than the foot of Viṣṇu; therefore, by rule, the lotus-eyed Lord alone is to be beheld, and no one else.
His two ears for perceiving sound do not perceive any other sound, even when sounds are present, except for "Mukunda," "Govinda," and "Dāmodara, O four-armed one. (13)
Without performing service to the worship of Govinda’s feet—which is his beloved deed—his two hands, marked with the conch and discus, shall perform no other work.
His mind, having abandoned all other thoughts, meditated upon the pair of feet of Hari—which move without duality—and indeed attained a state of perfect stillness.
Having abandoned his feet, which are the refuge of Viṣṇu, for the courtyard of Nārāyaṇa, he now wanders elsewhere, performing intense penance.
My speech is made authoritative in the description of Govinda’s virtues; therefore, let it remain silent as I practice that which is of great essence through austerity.
Her tongue, savoring the nectar-like essence of the name "Beloved of Kamalā" (Viṣṇu), has no desire for any other flavor.
Delighted by the fragrance of the lotus-like pair of feet of the glorious Mukunda, his sense of smell does not quickly perceive any other scent. 19.
Having touched the two feet of the enemy of Madhu, the sense of touch attained all the pleasures of sensation belonging to that one born from the earth.
Having reached Dāmodara, the supreme essence who is the substratum of objects such as sound, our senses then became fulfilled.
At the rising of that ascetic heat, all the splendors of the moon, the sun, fire, and the stars were eclipsed as the three worlds were set ablaze.
Indra, Candra, Agni, Varuṇa, Samīraṇa, and the Lord of Wealth, as well as Yama and Nairṛta and the other chiefs, were born, apprehensive for their own positions. (23)

Likewise, other celestial dwellers, foremost among whom was Vasu, as well as the inhabitants of the celestial mansions, became terrified of Dhruva; their anxieties were increased by the fear of losing their own offices.
Wherever Dhruva set his foot upon the surface of the earth, the earth, overcome by his weight, indeed sank down in those very places.
Oh! Even the waters, having abandoned their dullness upon contact with her limbs, become flavorful and, remaining in their places, quiver elsewhere out of fear of her.
As many objects of diverse splendors and perfected forms and qualities as there were, all became guests of his eyes through the power of that asceticism. (27)
"Oh, how wonderful! By the constant touch of its own inherent quality, the wind has made my skin perceive [the fragrance], even though it resides in a distant land."
Even the sky, though possessing the quality of sound, with the intent to worship Dhruva, has sought refuge in his ear for the sake of the entire multitude of sounds.
Though he was honored daily even by the five elements, he, whose mind was dedicated to Govinda, considered asceticism alone to be supreme.
With his heart illuminated by the Kaustubha gem and wearing yellow silk garments, the prince beheld the entire universe as consisting of light through meditation.
A very great anxiety was seized by Marutvān out of fear of his ascetic power; had Dhruva desired my station, he certainly would have attained it.
The host of Apsarases is capable of restraining the self-restraints of ascetics; yet he has power over a youth, not over this child—what can I do in this matter?
"Desire and anger, those two who assist me in destroying the asceticism of the practitioners of austerity—those two shall certainly not prevail over this child, Dhruva. (34)
"Indeed, there shall be only one means by which I can prevail over this fool: I shall dispatch here a terrifying Bhūta-ali to frighten him. (35)
"He will surely abandon his asceticism, terrified by the spirits due to his youth"—having thus decided, Vāsava dispatched a host of spirits.
With all his limbs shaped like a bear and a long, camel-like neck, a certain creature with hideous teeth rushed toward that boy.
A certain being with the face of a tiger, possessing a body as tall as an elephant and a hideous countenance, approached him while repeatedly roaring and opening his mouth wide. || 38 ||
Then, a certain creature with formidable tusks, having seen him eating the meat, rushed at him in a rage as if threatening him. (39)
Tearing apart the high riverbanks with the tips of his exceedingly sharp horns and cleaving the earth with the points of his hooves, the great bull bellowed loudly.
For someone, having become a female serpent, terrifying with the expansion of her hood and possessing an exceedingly flickering double tongue, hissed repeatedly.
And another, in the form of a buffalo, hurling mountains from the tips of his horns and striking the earth with his tail, reached him with the force of his breath.
Another, appearing with a gaping mouth, struck terror into him as he stood there, his two thighs resembling a date-palm tree licked by a forest fire.
Scratching his head against the clouds, with a long and emaciated belly and sunken, tawny eyes, a certain being terrified him. (44)
With sword in hand and mouth agape, holding a skull-cup in his left hand, a certain fierce man rushed toward that boy while letting out a terrible roar.
Taking up a massive sala tree and letting out a "kila-kila" cry, someone approaches him from all sides like Time bearing his staff.
Bearing darkness as his dwelling, a tiger as his great mouth, and the terrifying form of the God of Death, a certain being approached him.
Assuming the form of an owl, someone certainly terrified Dhruva with extremely dreadful hissing sounds that made the heart tremble.
A certain yakṣiṇī, having brought the weeping child of someone, drank the blood from his belly and ate the bones as if they were lotus stalks.
"Thirsty today, I shall certainly drink even his blood; having chewed the bones of this child just as [I did] before," so she spoke. (50)
Having strewn grass and wood all around, one woman ignited a forest fire that was fanned by a rising wind.
Assuming the form of a Vetālī, one [of them] shattered trees and mountains, obstructing the path of the sky while violently shaking it.
Another woman, appearing in the form of a wise counselor, beheld him from afar and, afflicted with extreme grief, wept while striking her chest again and again.
And she spoke words of flattery, fashioned with much guile, while manifesting an exceeding tenderness full of compassion and affection. (54)
"O child, alas, Death seeks to slay me, who have you as my sole refuge! Protect me, protect me, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek your shelter, for my life is departing! (55)
In every village, in every city, on every road, in every forest, in every hermitage, and at every mountain, she has grown weary, longing for the sight of you.
O child, from the very day you departed for asceticism, from that same day I have set out to behold you.
Just as you, O child, are pained by those various wicked words of your co-wife, so too am I deeply tormented by the fire of her speech.
I do not sleep, nor do I wake; I neither eat nor do I drink. I meditate on you alone, like a female yogi separated from her beloved.
With eyes deprived of sleep, I, unfortunate as I am, cannot behold your face—which brings me such joy—in even my dreams; this is so in every way.
The moon, the counterpart to your face, was gazed upon by me, who am distressed and desirous of casting off my feverish heat, even though it was rising.
Even the warbling of the cuckoo, which emulates the sweet conversation of your speech, was not heard by me, whose ears were filled with the sound of anklets.
Sweet with the touch of your limbs and surely purifying my ailments, not even the wind was embraced by me anywhere while I rested so intensely.
O Dhruva, what countries, what rivers, and what mountains have not been traversed by me, the king’s wife, as I followed behind your feet? (64)
"Seeing that all this is indeed impermanent, I have become blinded; O son, protect me, your mother, now that you have obtained the status of a staff for the blind. (65)
"Where are these tender limbs of yours, and where is this asceticism, O bull among men? This [asceticism] is harsh, achievable by men with coarse bodies. (66)
"O child, what is the use of this asceticism to you? Tell me now, is there anything superior to being the son of a lord of the earth? (67)
"At this age, O child, you ought to play incessantly with other toys, together with children of your own age. (68)
Then, having attained youth, you, being devoted to contemplation, must indeed become one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.
Having reached youth, you shall enjoy many pleasures—the objects of the senses such as women, garlands, sandalwood, and the like—fulfilling your desires. (70)
Then, having procreated many virtuous sons who are devoted to the Dharma, and having transferred your royal fortune to them, you may then practice asceticism.
Why this exertion now in penance while still in your childhood? When shall the fire of cow-dung under your big toe reach your head? (72)

"By someone who has been humiliated by adversaries, whose pride has been taken away, or even by one fallen from prosperity—you must exert yourself against them; who are you to be concerned with them? (73)
Having heard these words, "One whose pride has been taken away must perform penance," Dhruva sighed long and hot, and again meditated upon Hari within his heart.
Without speaking to his mother and casting aside all fear of living beings, Dhruva once again became solely intent on meditating upon Acyuta.
That host of spirits, displaying terror with their many terrifying ornaments, beheld the Sudarśana discus all around him.
O Adhokṣaja, for her protection against the Rākṣasas, you created a halo around the sun, appearing like a circular aura and shining with intense radiance.
Beholding him, the Bhūtāvalī saw that Sudarśana discus, which was intensely blazing with garlands of flames and was certainly protecting [him] firmly on all sides.
