With a heart exceedingly free from trembling and a mind dedicated to Govinda, he was like a sprout of asceticism that had burst through the earth and risen upward.
She too, becoming terrified upon seeing him—Dhruva, whose resolve was firm—paid him homage and departed as she had come, her desires rendered fruitless.
Just as a mass of thundering clouds in the sky, though agitated, becomes useless upon encountering even a slight movement caused by the wind; (81)
Then, O twice-born one, all the gods, terrified along with Jambhāri, consulted together and went in haste to Brahmā for refuge.
Having bowed and offered praise, they addressed the Grandfather, seeking an opportunity to speak once they had been asked the reason for their arrival. (83)
The gods said: "O Creator, by the son of Uttānapāda, who is possessed of great splendor, all the inhabitants of the three worlds have been scorched by his heat. (84)
"O father, we truly understand that this is not the wish of Dhruva; desiring to abandon his station, for what reason would that great ascetic seek refuge among us? (85)
Thus addressed by the gods, the four-faced one smiled and then replied to them all, whose minds were filled with fear for Dhruva.
Brahmā said: "O gods, you who seek the eternal state need not fear Dhruva; let all of you go free from anxiety, for he does not desire your position."
Therefore, one should never fear anyone on account of that devotee of the Blessed One; it is certain that those who are devotees of Viṣṇu do not cause suffering to others.
Having propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, and having obtained from him his own desired object, he will also establish the positions of all of you in a stable state.
Having heard these words uttered by Brahmā, the gods bowed down and, filled with joy, returned to their own celestial abodes.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, seeing that boy of firm mind who sought no other refuge, approached him on his chariot drawn by Tārkṣya and spoke.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "I am pleased, O highly fortunate one, O observer of noble vows; choose a boon. Cease from this austerity, for you have been weary for a long time, my child."
Having heard those nectar-like words, he opened his eyes and beheld a mass of light like that of a sapphire.
With clusters of freshly blooming blue lotuses, she made both heaven and earth appear on all sides like a lake in full bloom.
Dhruva then beheld everything within the space between heaven and earth as if it were gazed upon by the floods of glances from the goddess Lakṣmī.
Before him appeared Kṛṣṇa, dressed in yellow garments, possessing a luster like a streak of lightning in the midst of a rising bank of clouds; he was thus made a guest of his eyes.
Just as the sky is a touchstone marked with the streak of gold that is Mount Meru, so was the one whose vehicle is Garuḍa beheld by Dhruva at that time.
Then he beheld Hari, who was adorned with a beautiful crescent moon and clad in yellow garments, like the deep blue sky graced by the moon.
Then, having prostrated like a staff and rolled about on the ground in every direction, he wept for a long time like a distressed infant who has finally beheld its father.
The best among yogis was highly praised by Nārada, Sanandana, and Sanaka, as well as by other yogis such as Sanatkumāra and others.
With his lotus-like eyes moistened by tears of compassion, the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) certainly raised him up, supporting him with his hand.
Then Hari touched that body, which was grey with dust, with his two very calloused hands due to his constant handling of scriptures.
From the touch of the God of gods, an auspicious speech, refined and beautiful, issued from his mouth; then Dhruva praised Hari.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Blessed One," in the Narrative of Dhruva within the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 20 ||
Dhruva said: Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, the ordainer of all creation; salutations to you, Hiraṇyaretas, the bestower of excellent gold. (1)
Homage to the one whose nature is Hara, the agent of the destruction of beings; homage to the one who has become the self of the great elements, the lord of all beings. || 2 ||
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, the all-powerful sustainer; to Kṛṣṇa, who removes craving and endures the great burden.
Salutations to the one whose nature is like a forest fire to the great forest of the Daityas; salutations to you, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is the axe for the trees that are the Daityas.
Salutations to the wielder of the mace, whose fingertips are occupied with the Kaumodakī; salutations to the destroyer of the great Danujas, the bearer of the Nandaka sword. || 5 ||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Śrī; salutations to the wielder of the discus; to the Supreme Self in the form of the Boar, the upholder of the earth.
Salutations to you who hold a lotus in your hand, the beloved of Kamalā; salutations to you who take the forms of the Fish and others; salutations to you whose chest bears the Kaustubha gem.
Salutation to the one known through Vedānta; salutation to the wearer of the Śrīvatsa mark. Salutation to the one whose nature is the qualities, who possesses qualities, yet is devoid of qualities.
Salutations to you, O Padmanābha, and to the bearer of Pāñcajanya; salutations to you, O Vāsudeva, the joy of Devakī.
Salutation to you, Pradyumna; salutation to you, Aniruddha. Salutation to the destroyer of Kaṃsa, and salutation to the crusher of Aṇūra.
O Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Gopījana-vallabha, Acyuta, Mādhava, Upendra, O enemy of Kaiṭabha, slayer of Madhu, Adhokṣaja! (11)
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the remover of hell and the destroyer of sin; salutations to you, Vāmana, to Hari, and to Śauri. || 12 ||
Salutations to you, the infinite, and to you who recline upon the infinite; salutations to you, the husband of Rukmiṇī, and to the subduer of Rukmin.
Salutations to You, the slayer of Caidya, the enemy of the Dānavas and the foe of the Asuras; to Mukunda, the supreme bliss, and the beloved of Nandagopa.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, the slayer of the lords of the Danujas; salutations to the one who assumes the form of a cowherd and plays the flute. 15.
Salutations again and again to the beloved of the Gopīs, the slayer of Keśin, and the upholder of Govardhana; salutations again and again to Rāma, the Lord of the Raghus, the descendant of Raghu.
O enemy of Rāvaṇa, salutations to you, the protector of Vibhīṣaṇa; to the unborn one who takes the form of victory, skilled upon the field of battle.

Salutations to you, who are the form of time consisting of moments and the like, who possess manifold forms, who bear the Śārṅga bow, the mace, and the discus, and who are the crusher of the hosts of Daityas.
Salutations to Bala, to Balabhadra, and to the beloved of Balarāti; O crusher of Bali’s sacrifice, salutations to you, the bestower of boons upon devotees! 19.
O you who tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu, O lover of battle! Salutations to the God who is devoted to Brahman, and to the benefactor of cows and Brahmins. 20.
Salutations to you whose form is Dharma, and salutations to the one whose quality is sattva; salutations to the Supreme Puruṣa who possesses a thousand heads.
O thousand-eyed one, O thousand-footed one, and to the one with a thousand rays; O thousand-formed one, O beloved of Śrī, salutations to you, O Yajñapuruṣa!

Salutations to the one whose essential nature is the Veda and its objects of knowledge, to the lover of the Vedas, to the Veda itself, to the expounder of the Vedas, and to the traveler upon the path of righteous conduct.
Salutations to you, O Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to you, Viṣṭaraśravas; salutations to the one who rides upon Garuḍa.
O Viṣvaksena, salutations to you, O Janārdana who pervades the universe! Salutations to Trivikrama, to the Truth, and to the one who is fond of truth.
Salutations to you, O Keśava, the wielder of Māyā, the singer of the Veda; salutations to you, whose form is austerity, the bestower of the fruits of austerities. || 26 ||

Salutations to you who are the object of praise, whose form is praise, and who delights in the praises of your devotees; salutations to you who are the embodiment of the Vedas and who are dear to those whose conduct accords with the Vedas.

Salutations to you who are born from an egg; salutations be to you who are born from sweat; salutations to you whose nature is the womb-born; salutations to you who have the form of that which sprouts from the earth.
Among the gods you are Indra; among the planets you are the radiant one. Among the worlds you are Satyaloka; among the oceans you are the Milky Ocean. || 29 ||
Among rivers you are the Surāpagā; among lakes you are Lake Mānasa; among mountains you are the Himavat; and among cows you are the Kāmadhuk. (30)
Among minerals you are gold; among stones you are crystal; among flowers you are the blue lotus; and among trees you are the tulasī. (31)
Among all stones worthy of worship, you are indeed the Śālagrāma stone; among the fields of liberation, you are Kāśī; and among the series of sacred fords, you are Prayāga.
Among colors you are white; among bipeds you are the Brāhmaṇa; O Lord, among birds you are Garuḍa; and in worldly dealings you are speech. (33)
Among the Vedas, you are the Upanishads; among mantras, you are the Praṇava; among letters, you are the syllable 'A'; and among sacrificers, you assume the form of Soma.
You are the fire for those who are majestic; you are the forbearance of the forbearing; you are the rain-cloud for the givers; you are the supreme among purifiers. || 35 ||
Among all weapons you are the bow; among the swift you are the wind; among the senses you are the mind; and among those who are fearless, you are the hand. (36)
O Lord, you are indeed the supreme self among all selves that pervade the sky; you are the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) within all eternal rites.
Among sacrifices, you are the Aśvamedha; among gifts, you are the granting of fearlessness; among gains, you are the gain of a son; and among seasons, oh, you are the spring.

You are the first of the ages (yugas), and you are indeed the new-moon day (kuhū) among lunar days; you are Puṣya among the host of constellations, and the transition (saṃkrānti) among all festival occasions.
Among yogas you are indeed the Vyatīpāta, and among grasses you are the Kuśa; for you, O Lord, are the final liberation (nirvāṇa) of all who exert themselves.
O Unborn One, among all intellects here, the intellect of Dharma is supreme; the Ashvattha is supreme among all trees, and the Soma creeper among all creepers.
O Prāṇāyāma, among all pure means of accomplishment, you are indeed the best; O Śrīmad Viśveśvara, you are the giver of everything among all sacred emblems. 42.
For you are the wife of friends, you are dharma among all kinsmen; O Nārāyaṇa, there is nothing else like you in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
You alone are my mother, you are my father, you are my son, and you are my great wealth; you alone are the perfection of happiness, you are my life-span, and you are the lord of my existence.

That discourse in which your name is found is true speech; that mind which is offered to you is a true mind; that action which is for your sake is true action; and that meditation which is the remembrance of you is true austerity.
That wealth of the wealthy is pure which has been spent for your sake; that alone is the complete time in which you, O Jiṣṇu, are worshipped.
Life is truly beneficial only so long as you abide within the heart; for by partaking of the water from your feet, all diseases come to rest.
O Govinda, even great sins accumulated over many lifetimes are instantly dissolved by the chanting of "Vāsudeva. (48)
Oh, what great delusion of men! Oh, what negligence of men! That they disregard Vāsudeva and exert their efforts elsewhere. 49.
For this alone is auspiciousness, this alone is the acquisition of wealth, and this is the very fruit of life: the chanting of the praises of Dāmodara. (50)
There is no dharma higher than Adhokṣaja; there is no artha higher than Nārāyaṇa; there is no kāma other than Keśava; and there is no apavarga without Hari.
This indeed is the supreme loss, this indeed is the greatest affliction, and this is the ultimate misfortune—that one should not remember Vāsudeva. (52)
Alas, what does the worship of Hari not accomplish for men? It bestows sons, friends, wives, wealth, sovereignty, heaven, and even liberation.
It removes sin, destroys diseases, subdues mental afflictions, swiftly increases righteousness, and grants one's heart's desire. (54)
The pair of the Blessed One’s feet is the supreme, conflict-free meditation; even by a sinner, through mere association with it, his own highest welfare has been accomplished.
The chanting of the name of Hari, when accomplished through deeply absorbed meditation, removes even those sins of the wicked that entail great secondary consequences.
Just as even a spark of fire, if touched through negligence, may burn, so too the name of Hari, when merely touched by the lips, removes all sin.
If one were to cultivate a state of tranquility for even a moment toward the Beloved of Kamalā, Kamalā herself would surely become firmly established there.
This alone is the supreme dharma, this alone is the highest austerity, and this alone is the supreme sacred ford: that one should drink the water from the feet of Viṣṇu.
O Puruṣottama, he who serves your offering with devotion has surely served the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) itself through that person of great intelligence.

That man who, having placed the water from Viṣṇu’s feet into a conch shell, bathes with it, is indeed one who has performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and is one who has immersed himself in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
He who has worshipped a Śālagrāma stone with Tulasī leaves is worshipped with garlands of Pārijāta flowers in the abode of the gods.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even another, if he is endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu, he should be known as the most excellent of all. (63)
If one whose body is marked with the conch and discus, who bears a crest of flowers on his head, and whose limbs are smeared with Gopīcandana is seen, then whence can there be sin? (64)
He who worships twelve Śālagrāma stones every day, together with a stone from Dvāravatī, is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha.
The servants of Yama never approach that house where Tulasī is worshipped every day.
The followers of Yama shall not touch one whose face is adorned with the syllables of Hari’s names, whose forehead is marked with the earth of Vṛndāvana, and whose chest is garlanded with tulasī.
For one who possesses these five in their home—the Gopī-mṛttikā, Tulasī, a conch, a Śālagrāma stone with its discus, and [the aforementioned items]—whence can there be any fear of sin? (68)
Those moments, those instants, those divisions of time known as kāṣṭhās, and those twilights of the eye—whatever has passed without the remembrance of Viṣṇu, all that has been stolen by Yama.
Where could the two-syllable name of Hari blaze like a spark, and where is the vast heap of sins, which is like a tuft of cotton? (70)
O Govinda, Supreme Bliss, Mukunda, Madhusūdana! Abandoning You, I know nothing else; I do not worship it, nor do I remember it.
I do not bow, nor do I praise, nor do I behold with my eyes here; I do not touch, nor do I speak, nor do I sing—nothing at all without Hari. 72.
In water, on land, in the netherworld, in the wind, in fire, or in mountains; among Vidyādharas, Asuras, or gods—what need is there to mention humans or monkeys? (73)
In grass, in women, in stones, and in trees, shrubs, and creepers—everywhere I behold the dark-bodied one with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
For you alone are the dweller in the hearts of all and the direct witness; indeed, I know no other omnipresent being besides you who exists both within and without.
Having spoken thus, Śivaśarman Dhruva then became silent; the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, with a gracious gaze, spoke to him.
The Blessed One said: "O child, O large-eyed one, O Dhruva of steadfast resolve, O sinless one! I have fully understood the desire residing within your heart. (77)
Beings arise from food; food originates from rain; the sun is the cause of that rain; and the sun is supported by Dhruva—be firm, O Dhruva! (78)
You shall become the support for the entire wheel of luminaries—the planets, constellations, and so forth—which revolves eternally throughout the sky. (79)
"Having become the central pivot for all those bound by the snares of the vital breaths (vāyu), remain in that state until the end of the kalpa, causing the hosts of luminaries to revolve. (80)
In the past, having propitiated Śrī Mahādeva, this supreme state was attained by me; that very state is now offered to you through my ascetic penance.
O Dhruva, some remain for as long as four yugas, and others for a manvantara; but you shall indeed rule this station for an entire kalpa.
Even that station which was not attained by Manu—how much less by other human beings—is established for you, O Śakra, though it is difficult even for the gods to reach. (83)
"Pleased by this hymn of praise, I grant you other boons as well: your mother Sunīti shall also attend upon you."
The person who, being composed in mind, shall recite this supreme hymn at the three junctions of the day, their sin will go to complete destruction. (85)
Fortune will undoubtedly never abandon his home; nor shall there be separation from his mother, nor the arising of strife with kinsmen. (86)
This meritorious hymn of praise to Dhruva destroys even the greatest sins; even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified—what need be said, then, of other sinners? (87)
She is the mother of great merit, the bestower of great prosperity, the pacifier of great calamities, and the destroyer of great diseases. || 88 ||
He whose mind is pure and who possesses supreme devotion to me should recite this hymn of Dhruva, which brings me great delight. (89)
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he fully attains that same fruit by joyfully reciting this hymn.
There are many hymns that bring me joy, yet they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this Dhruva-stuti.
Even upon merely hearing this hymn with supreme faith and joy, a mortal is instantly liberated from sins and attains great merit.
Through the chanting of the praise of Dhruva, one who is childless obtains a son, one who is destitute obtains wealth, and one who lacks devotion attains devotion. (93)
Just as a man obtains various gains by giving many gifts and performing diverse vows, so too does he obtain them through this hymn of praise.
Having abandoned all other duties and having set aside numerous recitations, this hymn of praise to Dhruva should be recited; it bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
The Blessed One said: Listen attentively, O high-minded one; I shall declare what is for your benefit, by which this state of yours will become perfectly and immovably established. (96)
I was desirous of going to the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī, where Viśveśvara himself resides as the cause of liberation.
And where the Lord of the Universe himself whispers into the ears of beings who have fallen into misfortune, a whisper capable of uprooting their karma.
For this suffering of saṃsāra, which brings about all calamities, there is only one remedy: the blissful ground of Kāśī. 99.
"This is delightful, this is not"—this is the seed of the great tree of suffering. When that seed is burnt by the fire of Kāśī, whence can there be any occasion for suffering? (100)
That which, once attained, is never lost again, by which one no longer grieves, and which is the abode of supreme bliss—that is the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana).
If a person should dwell elsewhere after abandoning the abode of immortality, the Ānandakānana of Śambhu, how can there be the arising of happiness for him?
It is better to wander for alms with a begging bowl in hand through the streets of Cāṇḍāla dwellings in Kāśī than to hold sovereignty over other lands devoid of merit.
From the city of Vaikuṇṭha, I come daily to Kāśī according to my vow to worship Viśveśa, who is worshipped by the entire world.
The supreme power within me that is capable of protecting the three worlds—its cause is Maheśāna, the giver of the Sudarśana discus.
In former times, even Hara slew the Daitya Jālandhara, who caused even me to tremble, by creating a discus arising from a line on the tip of his big toe.
And that discus was obtained by me through the worship of the Lord’s lotus-eyes; it is indeed named Sudarśana, the crusher of the hosts of Daityas.
Therefore, for your protection, I have first dispatched this supreme dispeller of spirits; having done so, I have now come here.
"O Viśveśvara, I shall now go to Kāśī to behold you; today there is a great pilgrimage on the full moon of Kārtika, which bestows abundant merit."
Whoever beholds Viśveśa on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, after bathing in the northward-flowing river, shall have no return to this world.
Having spoken thus, Hari placed Dhruva, who was overflowing with bliss, upon Tārkṣya and reached Vārāṇasī, the abode of Śiva, in an instant.
Having reached the boundary of five krośas, Lord Janārdana descended from Vainateya, and then, taking Dhruva by the hand, [proceeded].
Having bathed at Maṇikarṇikā and worshipped Viśveśvara, the Blessed One spoke to Dhruva, desiring to bring about his welfare.
Establish the Liṅga with effort in this very field of Avimuktaka, so that the merit of establishing it in the three worlds may become inexhaustible for you.
Whatever fruit is obtained by establishing ten million lingas elsewhere, that same fruit is attained here by means of a single linga. || 15 ||
For him who carries out the restoration of that which has fallen into ruin over time, there is no end to his reward in this world, even at the time of universal dissolution.
Whoever, having abandoned stinginess regarding wealth, should cause a temple to be built here, by him the entire Mount Meru, extending for a million yojanas, would be considered as given. || 17 ||
Whoever here causes wells, step-wells, and tanks to be constructed according to his capacity, his merit from that act is ten million times greater than from constructing them elsewhere.
Whoever constructs a beautiful flower garden here for the purpose of sacrifice, for every single flower he receives a reward exceeding that of a golden flower.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who, having constructed a city of Brahmā here, bestows it upon Brahmins along with provisions for a year's sustenance. || 120 ||
The waters of the ocean may waste away, as may the motes of dust upon the earth; yet there is no exhaustion of that merit in the world of Śiva, in brief.
Having also caused monasteries to be built here for ascetics, he should provide them with the means of subsistence; he too shall partake in the fruits of the former [meritorious deeds].
Having performed great meritorious deeds, he who dedicates them here to Viśveśvara shall have no return to this terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
"This claim that I am infinite is sung here in the world; however, even by me, no end to the virtues of Kāśī can be found. (24)
Therefore, one should diligently seek the certain welfare in Kāśī; for in Kāśī, an inexhaustible fruit of welfare arises for men. (25)
The two Gaṇas said: Having instructed him, saying "It shall certainly be so," the one whose banner is Garuḍa departed; Dhruva, for his part, installed a Liṅga in the vicinity of Vaidyanātha.
Having constructed a very great palace and having made a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of it, he worshipped Viśveśvara and, his purpose accomplished, went home.
Having worshipped Dhruveśvara and performed the water-libation at the Dhruva-pit, a man attains the world of Dhruva, endowed with enjoyments. || 28 ||
Whoever reads or causes others to read this supreme narrative of Dhruva shall reach the world of Viṣṇu and become beloved of Viṣṇu. (29)
Even by merely recollecting the deeds of Dhruva in this context, a person shall not be overcome by sins and shall attain great merit. || 130 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Hymn of Dhruva," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śivaśarman said: "O Gaṇas, having heard this delightful narrative of Dhruva—which destroys great sins, produces great wonder, and is meritorious—I am satisfied."
Agastya said: While the twice-born was speaking thus, the celestial chariot, moving with the speed of the wind, reached Maharloka, which is most wonderful and superior even to Svarloka.
Then the twice-born one, seeing the world on all sides enveloped in splendor, replied to those two attendants: "What is this enchanting world? || 3 ||
Then those two said to the brahmin: "Listen, O high-minded one! This is indeed that Maharloka, most wonderful even compared to the Svarloka."
Those whose sins have been shaken off by austerity dwell here with a lifespan of an eon, their entire accumulation of afflictions completely destroyed through the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Having perceived the world as consisting of radiant light through sincere resolve, the supreme gods, endowed with great yoga, dwell here.
O beloved, while the two attendants of the Blessed One were thus conversing, that celestial chariot carried them to Janaloka in half a moment.
There dwell the stainless sons of Brahmā, the Mānasas, all those lords of yogis such as Sanandana and others, who are indeed perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
But those other yogis who are indeed unswerving in their celibacy, liberated from all dualities, dwell there exceedingly pure.
The world of Tapoloka was brought within the range of their vision by that aerial chariot, which traveled with the speed of thought, as it departed from Janaloka.
Where those gods dwell, free from the fear of burning, they are the Vairājas; those whose minds are fixed on Vāsudeva and whose actions are dedicated to Vāsudeva.
Having gratified Govinda through austerity and being free from all desire, those who have conquered their senses reach this world of Tapas and dwell there.
Those who subsist by gleaning grains, those who use their teeth as a mortar, those sages who grind with stones, and those who eat only withered leaves; || 13 ||
In summer they perform the penance of the five fires, in the rainy season they sleep on the bare ground, and during the half-year of winter and the dewy season, they spend their nights in the water.

Thirsty ascetics drank drops of water from the tips of blades of kusha grass; those who subsisted on air alone, being extremely hungry, touched the earth with only their big toes at the tips of their feet.

Those whose defects have been cast upward, who stand motionless like pillars for a single quarter of the sun's day, who indeed remain breathless by day, and those who breathe only once a month; || 16 ||
Those who observe the vow of fasting for a month, those who observe the Cāturmāsya vows, those who drink only water at the end of each season, and those who fast for six months; || 17 ||

Those who indeed cause rain and the blinking of eyes, those who provide the water of rain-showers for the thirsty, and those who have become like motionless pillars, providing the pleasure of being scratched by deer; (18)
And those birds who have made their nests within the hollows of the forest of matted locks, whose bodies are overgrown with moss, and whose heaps of bones are bound together by sinews; (19)
Their limbs were entwined on all sides by the spreading creepers, and grains had grown upon their bodies and remained there for a long time.

Thus, those whose bodies have been refined by such arduous penance, the ascetics whose wealth is their austerity, dwell in the world of austerity (Tapoloka) with the lifespan of Brahmā, free from fear from any quarter.
Just as that meritorious soul heard this from the mouths of the two attendants, so too did the brilliantly radiant Satyaloka become a guest of his eyes.
Hurrying there, those two attendants descended from the celestial chariot and, together with him, bowed down before the creator of all the worlds.
Brahmā said: These two wise brāhmaṇas were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; they were proficient in the conduct prescribed by the Smṛtis and were averse to sinful deeds.
O twice-born one of great wisdom, I know you, Śivaśarman; well done by you, my child, for giving up your life at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Everything that has been observed by you here is fleeting and transitory; due to the daily dissolution, I create it again and again.
Hara withdraws even the *pratipad* [verse] up to the *vairāja*; what then can be said of mortal men who are like gnats? || 27 ||
For among the four classes of living beings, there is indeed but one quality for human beings, and that is found only in that most excellent Bhārata-varṣa, the field of action.
Having conquered the fickle senses along with the mind, and having abandoned greed—the enemy of the entire multitude of virtues—(he remains).
Having analytically severed desire—which destroys the lineage of the Dharma, carries away the accumulation of wealth, and brings about old age and gray hair—[one should abandon it]. (30)
Having conquered through fortitude the enemy that is anger—the thief of asceticism, fame, prosperity, and even the body, and the leader to the path of darkness—[he remains steadfast]. (31)
Always abandoning intoxication, which is the sole ground for negligence and the sole refuge of negligence, and which brings about the loss of all prosperity. (32)
Having abandoned the ego which is the cause of lightness in all matters, he nevertheless exerts effort in attributing faults even to the virtuous.
Having abandoned delusion—which plants the seeds of great enmity, destroys the intellect, causes utter blindness, and reveals the blinding darkness (andhatāmisra)—|| 34 ||
Having ascended the staircase of dharma, which is proclaimed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas and has been well-trodden by great men, those who reach this state do so with ease.
O twice-born one, all the inhabitants of heaven strive for the land of action (karmabhūmi), because they are the enjoyers of what is acquired there in various high and low stations. (36)
There is no land as excellent as Āryāvarta; there is no city equal to Kāśī; and there is no Liṅga equal to Viśveśa anywhere within the entire sphere of the universe.
There are many kinds of heavens, entirely devoid of anything other than happiness; they are all the sole fruit of meritorious deeds and are endowed with every prosperity. (38)
Within the cosmic egg, there is nothing more beautiful than the world of the gods (Svarloka); for everyone strives for heaven through asceticism, charity, vows, and other such means. (39)
"Even the netherworlds (pātālas) are more delightful than the world of the gods," Nārada declared while in the midst of the inhabitants of heaven, having returned from the netherworlds. (40)
Who could equal that Pātāla, where brilliant, white, and radiant jewels, set as ornaments upon the bodies of serpents, provide such delight? (41)
In Pātāla, which is adorned here and there by the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas, who would not feel delight—even one who is liberated? (42)
There, the rays of the sun during the day spread forth radiance but not heat; and the moon at night serves only for illumination, not for cold. (43)
There, even the passage of time was not perceived by the Danujas and others; there were forests, rivers, and delightful lakes filled with water.
The notes of the male cuckoo, clean and fine garments, most delightful ornaments, and fragrant unguents such as scents and the like; (45)
The sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments, enchanting to the ear, [resound] where the great Liṅga Hāṭakeśa—indeed, the granter of all desires—is located.
These and other delightful objects fit for enjoyment are enjoyed by the Dānavas, Daityas, and Uragas who dwell within the depths of Pātāla.
O twice-born one, the region of Ilāvṛta is indeed more delightful even than the netherworlds; it is situated all around, resting upon the jeweled peak [of Meru].
O twice-born one, there the doers of good deeds always enjoy every luxury; there the fawn-eyed women are eternally endowed with fresh youth. (49)
This is declared to be a land of enjoyment, acquired through the exchange of merit; it is enjoyed by worlds such as yours, whose bodies have been cast off at sacred fords (tīrtha).

And by those who speak without timidity, yet who have not abandoned their sons, fields, and so forth; and by those whose stores of happiness, lifespan, and wealth are entirely consumed for the sake of helping others. (51)
Indeed, there are many islands situated between this shore and the further shore; yet, nowhere on the surface of the earth is there an island equal to Jambūdvīpa.
Even there, Bhārata consists of nine regions, and among them, this one is the most excellent; it is declared to be the land of action, difficult to attain even for the gods.
The eight [forests], beginning with Kiṃpuruṣa, are to be enjoyed by the gods; indeed, the inhabitants of heaven come from the celestial realm to take delight in them.
This first region, Bhārata, situated to the south of Meru, is nine thousand yojanas in extent.
Even there, the region between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains is supremely merit-bestowing; indeed, the Antarvedī between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is the highest part of the earth.
For Kurukṣetra is superior to all sacred fields; even more so than that is the Naimiṣa forest, the supreme means for attaining heaven.
Even compared to the Naimiṣa forest, this place is superior on the entire circle of the earth; indeed, as the king of holy sites, it excels all other sacred fords.
Bestowing both heaven and liberation, and granting the fruits of all desires, that great sacred field of Prayāga is remembered as the King of Tīrthas.
O twice-born one, all sacrifices were previously weighed by me on a scale; and that excellent, beautiful holy place (tīrtha) was found superior because it fulfills all desires.
Having seen that it excelled all sacrifices nourished by sacrificial fees and other offerings, Hari, Hara, and the other gods gave it the name Prayāga.
For one who remembers Prayāga by its name alone at the three periods of the day, sin never dwells anywhere within the body of that rememberer. (52)
There are many sacred fords that provide protection from sin; yet they are not capable of granting anything more than the purification of committed transgressions. (63)
The accumulation of sins committed over countless previous births is indeed extremely difficult to dispel by means of vows, gifts, austerities, or recitations. (64)
As he prepared to depart for the king of holy fords, that man of auspicious birth trembled violently in his limbs like a tree struck by the wind.
Then, for that man of firm resolve who has traversed half the path to Prayāga, the [soul] seeks another place to emerge from his body.
When the king of holy fords became the guest of his eyes through good fortune, the darkness of that great-souled one fled most swiftly, like darkness at the rising of the sun.
Whatever sins indeed exist within the physical body composed of the seven constituents, they reside in the hair; by shaving, even those depart.
Having thus become free from impurity, one should then bathe at the confluence of the white and dark waters; whatever desire one contemplates, that very thing one obtains—there is no other way.
He obtains a vast heap of merit and meritorious enjoyments according to his desire; through that merit, he attains heaven, and being free from desire, he shall attain liberation.
He who desires liberation and bathes there, having abandoned all other desires, shall also attain liberation from this king of holy places, the granter of all wishes.
He who, abandoning the king of holy fords (Tīrtharāja), desires his wish from another, will clearly not obtain that wish in this great region called Bhārata.
O twice-born one, I perceive no difference between Satyaloka and Prayāga; those there who perform auspicious deeds are the inhabitants of my world. (73)
There is no other sacred ford on the circle of the earth to be resorted to by mortals longing for holy sites, except for Prayāga, the king of tīrthas. (74)
O best of the twice-born, just as there is a difference between a king and his other servants, so too has this mere illustration been told regarding Prayāga and other holy places. (75)
Whoever gives up their life at this sacred ford by whatever means possible shall incur no guilt for self-destruction and shall attain all their desired goals.
O twice-born one, for that fortunate person whose bones remain here, not even a trace of suffering arises anywhere throughout any birth.

One who desires to perform expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin must, according to the words of the twice-born, serve Prayāga according to the prescribed rules; of this there is no doubt. (78)
O best of Brahmins, what is the use of speaking at length? One who desires great prosperity should resort to the preeminent pilgrimage site, white and black, upon the surface of the earth. (79)
Even compared to Prayāga, the lord of sacred fords, liberation from the exhaustion of the body at Kāśī occurs without effort throughout all the worlds.
Avimukta is indeed more delightful than even Prayāga; of this there is no doubt, for Viśveśvara himself presides there in person.
O Lord of the Universe, presiding over the great field of Avimukta, there is nothing anywhere in this entire cosmic egg that is more beautiful than this. 82.
This field, even though situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), is unliberated; it does not exist as being five krośas in measure anywhere within the cosmic egg.
For just as the water of the single ocean increases, so too does the Lord raise that field even beyond dissolution.

O twice-born one, this sacred field stands at the tip of the trident of the Wielder of the Trident; those of deluded intellect do not perceive it, for it is situated in the intermediate space and not upon the earth.
In this hermitage of Viśveśvara, it is always the Kṛta Yuga, and there is indeed always a great festival; there is no defect caused by the rising or setting of the planets.
There, the northern solstice is always present; there, there is always great prosperity; and there, where Viśveśvara resides, there is always auspiciousness. (87)
O Brahmin, just as there are thousands of cities upon the surface of the earth, Kāśī is not to be considered like them; for she is transcendent.
O best of Brahmins, the fourteen worlds were created by me; however, the Lord Viśveśvara himself is the architect of this city.
In ancient times, Yama, having performed very difficult austerities for a long duration, attained sovereignty over the three worlds after abandoning the city of Vārāṇasī.
Indeed, whatever actions are performed by all beings, both moving and stationary, fall within the domain of Citragupta, with the sole exception of those committed by residents of Kāśī.
O best of the twice-born, the messengers of Yama can never enter the city of Kāśī; there, its protectors—the hosts of [Śiva’s] attendants—stand guard everywhere.
The Lord of the Universe himself is the restrainer there in Kāśī for those who cast off their bodies; yet even there, Kālabhairava is the restrainer of those who have committed sins.
In that regard, one must not commit evil, for the torments of Rudra are terrible; alas, the state of being a *rudrapiśāca* is more unbearable even than the hells! (94)
If such is your mind that only evil must be done, then it should be done elsewhere with ease, for there is indeed a much vaster earth.
Even a creature overcome by passion protects its own mother; likewise, even a sinner must protect Kāśī alone if he seeks liberation. (96)
One who is habituated to slandering others and who lusts after the wives of others should not resort to Kāśī; for where is Kāśī, and where is he? [They are as far apart as heaven and hell. 97.
Those men who constantly desire wealth here through gifts, or even the property of others through deceit, should not resort to Kāśī.
One should always avoid actions that cause suffering to others while in Kāśī; for if such were the case, what would be the point of the residence in Kāśī for those of evil mind? 99.
Those who, having abandoned devotion to the Lord of the Universe, are devoted to other deities, must by no means reside in the capital city of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
But those Brahmins who seek wealth, and those men who seek objects of desire—by them this field of liberation, Avimukta, should not be resorted to. (1)
Those who are intent on censuring Śiva, those who are intent on censuring the Vedas, and those who act in opposition to Vedic conduct—by them Vārāṇasī is not to be resorted to.
For those whose minds are intent on harming others, those who act out of envy toward others, and those who truly cause suffering to others, Kāśī does not lead to their spiritual success.
Even in their minds, those of wicked intellect who do not rejoice in Kāśī—for such evil-minded ones, even the mention of liberation remains far away.
Nowhere on this earth is liberation found without knowledge; and that knowledge cannot be attained through vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others.
And by means of gifts, foremost among which is the tulāpuruṣa, offered with faith, at the proper place and time, according to the rules, and bestowed upon worthy recipients.
Not by restraints such as the *yamas* and *brahmacarya*, nor by observances such as worship and the like, nor by fierce mortifications of the body, nor by austerities, O best of the twice-born. (7)
Not by the recitation of great mantras imparted by gurus, nor by the prescribed private study of the Vedas, nor by the highest services rendered to the sacrificial fires.
Knowledge is not attained through service to gurus, nor by ancestral rites and worship of deities, nor by pilgrimages to various sacred fords.
There is no knowledge without yoga, and yoga is the cultivation of the meaning of reality through the path taught by the guru and by the power of constant practice. (110)
There are many obstacles to that [knowledge], such as hearing it from a great distance; therefore, knowledge is not attained through yoga and other means in a single lifetime.
O observer of noble vows, without austerity, recitation, and the like, and without yoga, the supreme good is attained in Kāśī in this very single birth.
O best of the twice-born, the future fruit of that merit which you, of pure intellect, have acquired in Kāśī is even greater than that merit itself.
Having spoken thus, the noble one ceased while those two attendants were listening; and that high-minded Śivaśarman also became filled with joy.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Praise of Kāśī by Brahmā," in the first half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 22 ||
Śivaśarman said: O Lord of Satyaloka, O Creator, Great-Grandfather of all! I desire to make a certain representation, yet I do not venture to speak out of fear. (1)
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, that which you intended to ask has been understood by me as being in your mind. Desiring to inquire about liberation (nirvāṇa), the two attendants will explain it to you."
Indeed, there is nothing here that is beyond the range of these two attendants of Viṣṇu; they know everything whatsoever that exists within the world of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, those attendants of the Lord were indeed honored by Brahmā; and having bowed to the Creator of the World, they too departed, filled with joy.
Once again, mounting their own vehicle, they departed toward Vaikuṇṭha; yet even as they were going, the twice-born man questioned the two attendants once more.
Śivaśarman said: "How far have we come, and how much further still must we go? I ask you another thing as well, O auspicious ones; please tell me that too with affection. (6)
Kāñcī, Avantī, Dvāravatī, Kāśī, Ayodhyā as the fifth, Māyāpurī, and Mathurā—these are the seven cities that grant liberation.
Having abandoned the other six cities, liberation was established by the Creator in Kāśī alone; why then should my liberation not be attained now?
"Thus, you two who are worthy of grace should relate everything before me. Having heard those words, the two attendants spoke with respect: ||| 9 ||
The two Gaṇas said: "O sinless one, we shall tell you exactly what has been asked by you; by the grace of Viṣṇu, we know the past, the future, and the present. (10)
O Brahmin, as far as the earth shines with the rays of the two suns, so far is the earth declared to extend, including its oceans, mountains, and forests.
Furthermore, at a height of two hundred thousand yojanas above the earth, the sun is situated, having a diameter and circumference equal to that distance.
One hundred thousand yojanas above the sun, the moon is visible; and the circle of the constellations is one hundred thousand yojanas higher than the moon.
O gentle one, two hundred thousand [yojanas] above the sphere of Uḍu (the lunar mansion) is Mercury; two hundred thousand from Mercury is Venus; and two hundred thousand from Venus is Mars.

Two hundred thousand yojanas above the son of the Earth (Mars), Jupiter is situated; and two hundred thousand yojanas above the priest of the gods (Jupiter), Saturn is located, with a height of two hundred thousand yojanas.
The constellation of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala) is ten times ten thousand yojanas above Saturn; and Dhruva is situated a hundred thousand yojanas above the Seven Sages.
Whatever object exists on the surface of the earth that can be traversed by foot—comprising oceans, islands, mountains, and forests—is known as Bhūrloka. (17)
From the Bhūrloka, the Bhuvarloka is declared to extend as far as the sun; from the sun up to Dhruva, O Brahmin, it is sung of as the Svarloka.
Maharloka is situated one crore [yojanas] above the earth; Janaloka is reckoned by people to be two crores from Bhūrloka. (19)
The realm of Tapas extends four crores of yojanas from the surface of the earth; it is said that Satyaloka is situated eight crores above the earth. (20)
Above Satyaloka is Vaikuṇṭha, which, measured by the standard of yojanas, is reckoned from Bhūrloka as being sixteen crores [of yojanas] in extent.
Where Śrīpati himself resides, bestowing fearlessness upon all; beyond that lies Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva, possessing sixteen times the qualities [of the former].
Where Śambhu dwells together with Pārvatī, Gajānana, Skanda, and Nandin—the Lord of the Universe, complete in all his aspects—he is known as the Supreme. (23)
This is the play (khela) of that God who assumes forms through his own divine sport; he is renowned as Viśveśa, and this entire world is the executor of his command.
He is the teacher of all, and there is no other teacher besides him; he himself creates all beings, he himself protects them, and likewise he consumes them. (25)
He alone is declared to be omniscient, his actions being subject to his own will; there is no one whatsoever who can impel him, nor anyone who can restrain him. (26)
That which is the supreme Brahman is formless, yet it is described in the Vedas as having form; it is all-pervading, eternally constant, the truth, and devoid of duality. || 27 ||
Higher than all causes, the supreme beyond the supreme, that bliss which the Vedas proclaim as the very form of Brahman.
That which the Vedas know as consciousness, Viṣṇu knows it, but the ritual injunction does not; for from Him words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach Him.
He is self-knowable, the supreme light, dwelling in the heart of all; accessible to yogis yet inexpressible, he is the sole object of valid cognition.
Though possessing manifold forms, he is formless; though all-pervading, he is not an object of the senses; though infinite, his body is the end-maker; he is the omniscient one, free from karma.
This is his sovereign form, adorned with a crescent moon as an ornament, with a throat dark as the tamāla tree and a throbbing eye upon his forehead.

He is the active half-female form of Śiva, who wears the auspicious remains of the serpent as an ornament; the slopes of his matted locks are perpetually washed by the excellent contact with the waves of the Gaṅgā.
His limbs were radiant, worshipped by the mass of pollen from the body of Smara; he wore great serpents as ornaments upon his variegated body.
He was mounted upon a great bull as his vehicle, wielding the Ājagava bow; he wore an elephant hide as an upper garment, possessed five auspicious faces, and was radiant.

He who has terrified the great hosts of Mṛtyu and his mighty retinue; he who provides protection to those seeking refuge; he who is the cause of Nirvāṇa for those who bow before him; he who transcends the path of the mind’s desires; and he who is solely intent upon granting boons. (36)
O twice-born one, that very essence, which transcends all forms, abides pervading everything in the form of Rudra, both the higher and the lower.
Though formless, Śiva alone is indeed the cause, possessing form; whether for liberation or for enjoyment, there is no giver of liberation other than Śiva. (38)
Just as he, though formless, has surrendered all this—the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, both visible and invisible—to the Lord of Pārvatī. (39)
Likewise, O Brahmin, having fashioned the entire world through the power of Viṣṇu, Mṛḍānī sports eternally with Him at Her own will through Her divine play.
As is Śiva, so is Viṣṇu; as is Viṣṇu, so is Śiva. There is not even the slightest difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Having first summoned all the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Vidyādharas, Uragas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas; || 42 ||
Having fashioned an auspicious throne equal to his own, he seated Hari upon it and held a beautiful parasol over him.
It was smooth, with a million spokes, fashioned by Viśvakarman; it had a white jeweled handle from which thick strings of pearls hung down.
It was resplendent above with a variegated pinnacle, extending for a thousand yojanas, auspicious, and composed entirely of all kinds of jewels.
It was adorned with beautiful chowries made of silk thread, and with all the substances required for a royal consecration, such as all medicinal herbs and other items. || 46 ||

With five beautiful jars filled with the waters of the manifest holy fords, along with white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, and dūrvā grass, and accompanied by mantras spontaneously present; || 47 ||
And having brought sixteen auspicious maidens each from among the gods, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, and even the serpent-beings.
With lutes, mṛdaṅgas, lotus-shaped drums, kettledrums, marus, ḍiṇḍimas, jharjharas, ānakas, cymbals made of bell-metal, and other such instruments, accompanied by charming songs; || 49 ||

When the courtyard of the sky was filled with the great resonance of the chanting of the Vedas, on an auspicious lunar day, at an auspicious moment, and endowed with the strength of the stars and the moon; || 50 ||
He was beautiful with his crown bound on, having performed the auspicious marriage rites; he had been adorned by Mṛḍānī and was endowed with exquisite splendor.
Having personally consecrated him in the pavilion of the cosmic egg, Maheśa bestowed upon him his entire sovereignty, which was his own and not shared with anyone else.
Then the Lord of Gods, together with the Pramathas, praised the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; he spoke these words to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds: ||| 53 ||
"Viṣṇu is worthy of my worship; you too must bow down to this Hari. Having said this, Rudra himself then bowed to the one who has Garuḍa as his banner.
Then [he was honored] by all the lords of the Gaṇas, by Brahmā, by the hosts of Maruts, by the yogis headed by Sanaka, and likewise by the Siddhas and the divine sages.
[He was worshipped] by the Vidyādharas along with the Gandharvas, the hosts of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Apsaras; by the Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, and Bhūtas; and by Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka.
Then, by all the winged beings, the kinnaras, and all things mobile and immobile, it was said: "Victory! Victory! and "Homage to you! Homage to you! (57)
Then, in that assembly of the gods, Hari was honored by Maheśa with these great and delightful sounds, as well as with supreme offerings of light.
You alone are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of all beings; you alone are the one to be worshiped by the worlds, and you alone are the Lord of the universe. || 59 ||
"You shall be a bestower of dharma, wealth, and pleasure; a teacher of those who act with misconduct; and indeed, you shall be invincible in battle even for me. (60)
The power of will, the power of action, and likewise the supreme power of knowledge—O Viṣṇu, accept these three powers offered by me. (61)
O Hari, your enemies must certainly be punished by me with great effort; O Viṣṇu, the supreme liberation must be granted by me to your devotees.
And take also this Māyā, which cannot be dispelled even by gods or asuras, by which the entire world, deluded, shall become ignorant of anything at all.
"You shall be my left arm, and that Grandfather (Brahmā) shall be my right; indeed, you shall be both the protector and the progenitor of this Creator."
Having thus attained the sovereignty of Vaikuṇṭha from Hari, Hara himself, the lord of Umā, sports at his own will on Kailāsa together with the Pramathas.
From that time forward, this Lord Hari—the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and the mace, the destroyer of the Dānavas—has ruled over the entire three worlds.
Thus, O Brahmin, the condition of the worlds has been described to you; now we shall speak of the cause of liberation through praise.
But whoever, with a concentrated mind, should hear this supreme narrative, will go to the world of the gods and thereafter attain nirvāṇa in Kāśī. || 68 ||
During a sacrifice, a festival, a wedding, and indeed all auspicious occasions, as well as at the time of a royal consecration and the ritual installation of a deity; || 69 ||
In all matters of granting authority and upon entering a new house, this should be recited with effort for the successful accomplishment of that task.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth becomes wealthy; the diseased is liberated from disease, and the bound is released from bondage.
This should be recited with effort and constantly by one seeking auspiciousness; it is the pacifier of all inauspicious things and is dear to Hari and Nārāyaṇa. (72)

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Consecration of the Four-Armed One," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 23.
The two attendants said: "O Śivaśarman, we shall tell you of your future; listen. Having enjoyed abundant pleasures here in this world of Viṣṇu," || 1 ||
For a full year of Brahmā, he shall sport with throngs of apsarases; indeed, this is by virtue of the remainder of merit acquired through death at a sacred pilgrimage site.
You shall become a protector of the earth in the city of Nandivardhana, having obtained a kingdom free from rivals and endowed with abundant forces and vehicles.

It was frequented by prosperous and well-nourished cultivators adorned with beautiful golden ornaments, who were constant performers of religious duties such as *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrifices and works of public utility).
It was a land where crops were always abundant, filled with fertile fields, a good country with excellent offspring, well-settled, rich in fine grass, and possessing great wealth of cattle.
It was adorned with rows of temples dedicated to the deities, where the villages were graced by beautiful sacrificial posts and resplendent with the abundance of great wealth.
Where the lands shine with artificial gardens of exquisite flowers, with trees that bear fruit at all times, and with lakes adorned with lotus ponds.
Nowhere was there a populace characterized by deceit, as if it were the courtyard of the king of rivers; there were only noble families, and no wealth acquired through injustice.
In that realm, there was never any delusion among women or among the learned, nor were the rivers crooked in their course, nor were the subjects so.
Wherein men do not abound during nights joined with darkness, nor women joined with passion, nor men who are abundant in righteousness during the dark fortnights.
There, wealth brings no joy, nor is there even food for the mind; there, disorder is the vehicle, and indeed, there is no royal official.
The staff [of punishment] was found only in rows of axes, mattocks, and yak-tail fans, and in parasols; it was never found anywhere else arising from the offense of anger. (12)
Nowhere was there lamentation, except among groups of gamblers; for everywhere one saw only gamblers with dice in their hands.
In that place, talk of dullness exists only in the waters; women alone are weak, for the mothers there possess hearts as hard as adamant, unlike ordinary men.
Where there is the application of the *kuṣṭha* herb only in medicinal drugs and not in humans; where piercing occurs only within precious gems and pain only in those who fashion images. (15)
Trembling arises from the *sāttvika* emotion and never from fear in anyone; fever is born of passion, while poverty belongs to the impure.
By what merit is anything ever difficult to obtain? Indeed, it is only elephants who, being intoxicated, engage in battle within a body of water.
Generosity exists only in elephants; thorns exist only in trees; indeed, pleasure gardens exist only among people—not on the chest of anyone. 18.
In arrows there is the separation from the string, in books there is firm binding, and the abandonment of oil is always present in the person of a Pāśupata. (19)
There, the livelihood of those who have performed the act of renunciation is always through the staff; their seekers of alms are indeed the mendicants and the celibate students.
Where only ascetics wearing soiled garments are seen, and where, for the most part, even the bees are fickle in their behavior.
"Thus, while you—who know the duties of a king and are endowed with the quality of heroism—rule the kingdom by righteousness in this land possessed of such virtues," (22)
Among beautiful women who possess good fortune, are rich in beauty, endowed with the virtues of heroism and generosity, and possess lovely splendor yet lack physical charm; || 23 ||
There will be ten thousand queens and three hundred princes; the eldest among them, known as Vṛddhakāla, will be fierce and a conqueror of enemy cities.
He had conquered many battles, his path was gratified by the goddess Śrī, he was filled with manifold virtues, and his splendor was like that of the full moon. || 25 ||
That bull among kings had his hair moistened by the final ablutions of the sacrifice; he was perfected in the protection of his subjects and had gratified the Brahmins with his treasury. || 26 ||
Meditating with unwavering mind upon the lotus feet of Govinda within his heart, he spent his days and nights entirely absorbed in conversation concerning Vāsudeva.
Once, O twice-born one, while he was seated in the midst of the royal assembly, he was seen from afar by some kārpaṭikas who had arrived from Vārāṇasī.
Then, he was greeted with many blessings by all those who resembled his own past deeds, O tiger among kings.
May the glorious Lord Viśveśvara, the teacher of all the worlds and the Master of Kāśī, grant you the abandonment of evil-mindedness.
May that Lord of Kāśī, who bestows the attainment of ultimate liberation even through mere remembrance, grant you knowledge free from all impurity.
By that merit through which you have obtained this vast kingdom free from thorns, may your mind be directed toward Viśvanātha by the remainder of that same merit.
May that Lord of the Universe be gracious, by whose grace long life, sons, garments, women, prosperities, heaven, and liberation are easily obtained.
May that Lord of the Universe, by the mere hearing of whose name the great sins are severed, abide in your heart. (34)
O King, having heard this succession of blessings, you, Vṛddhakāla, will then remember this account with your body marked by horripilation.
Having concealed his outward appearance and given them much wealth, and having secured an auspicious moment, he established his son in the kingdom.
Then, after giving abundant gifts and satisfying those who seek them, you shall go from there to Kāśī along with Queen Anaṅgalekhā.
Having installed there a Liṅga that causes liberation under his own name, he constructed a lofty temple there and an excellent well in front of it.
Having duly performed there the rites beginning with the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), [he offered] jewels, rubies, fine silk garments, elephants, horses, and cattle.
Having bestowed abundant divine requisites—great banners, flags, umbrellas, chowries, and mirrors—he became free from fatigue.
With your body thoroughly emaciated by vows, fasts, and observances, you will see a single ascetic there at midday in that solitary place.
His body was exceedingly aged and his matted locks were completely tawny; he was tall and captivating to the people, like Dharma itself incarnate.
Having entrusted the burden of her slender body to a sturdy staff, she emerged from the inner chamber and approached the performance arena.
Having sat down near you, he will question you in this sequence: "Who are you? Why are you here? And who is this second person who is like you? (44)
"By whom was this temple caused to be built? Tell me that; and what is the name of this Liṅga? Due to my old age, I generally do not know. (45)
O Lord, when you were thus questioned by that aged ascetic, you then said: "I am a king, known as Vṛddhakāla. (46)
Having arrived here from the south with this beloved wife, I meditate upon this Linga and pray for nothing at all.
"O matted-haired one, Śiva himself is the builder of this palace; however, I do not know for certain the specific name of this liṅga. (48)
Having heard these words of the king, the one wearing matted hair said: "You have indeed spoken the truth; however, you do not know even one name of the Liṅga. (49)
May I always behold you seated there, perfectly motionless; for by whomsoever this palace was caused to be built, he shall hear of your glory.
"Tell me that in my presence, if you know it according to reality. Having heard these words of his, he spoke again: "It is Bhava," he said. (51)
Śambhu is the doer and the one who causes others to act; what untruth could I possibly speak? Or rather, O ascetic, O Lord, what is the use of such worry to me?
While you remained thus silent, that aged ascetic spoke again: "I am thirsty; bring water quickly and give it to me. (53)
Thus urged by him, you shall bring water from the well and cause that aged ascetic to drink; and at that very moment, he— || 54 ||
From drinking that water, may he become as radiant as the full moon on a festival day, youthful, endowed with beauty, like a serpent freed from its slough.
Filled with wonder, you spoke to him once again: "O Blessed One, what indeed is this power by which you have [returned] once more? (56)
"Having cast off old age here, you do not shine at present; if there is still time for you, O one whose wealth is asceticism, then speak. (57)
The ascetic said: "O King Vṛddhakāla, I know you to be of great intelligence; and I also know this wife of yours to be devoted to her husband."
O King, from this birth she was the daughter of a brahmin named Turvasu, whose body was the Vedas; she was of auspicious conduct and a beautiful countenance. (59)
She was given by him for marriage to the high-souled Naidhruva; however, that Naidhruva fell under the power of Time before reaching his youth.
Having observed her vow of widowhood and died in Avantī while maintaining auspicious vows, she was born as the daughter of King Pāṇḍya by virtue of that merit.
O King, she who was married by you and who has always been devoted to her husband has arrived here with you; she shall attain unsurpassed liberation.
O King, [this may be done] in Ayodhyā, or in Avantī, or even in Mathurā; or in Dvāravatī, or in Kāñcī, or in Māyāpurī.
Even those who are sinners and have met their death in the course of time, having indeed come here from heaven, shall attain liberation in Kāśī.
I know you as well; you were a twice-born man in a previous birth. You were a resident of Mathurā named Śivaśarman, and having died in Māyāpurī, [you have been born here]. (65)
By virtue of that merit, having reached Vaikuṇṭha and enjoyed delightful pleasures, you were born as a king in Naṃdivardhana due to the remainder of that merit.
O King Vṛddhakāla, by that very same merit, you have reached this field of liberation; you shall attain unsurpassed liberation.
Moreover, O Indra among kings, listen to that which you have uttered: it is clear that Śambhu is both the builder and the one who causes the temple to be built. (68)
One should never, at any time, constantly proclaim one's own good deed; by saying "I have done it," that merit perishes instantly.
Therefore, with every effort, one should guard this like a treasure; for well-performed merit becomes useless through public proclamation, just like an oblation poured into ashes. (70)
O sinless one, I know for certain that you, impelled by Viśvanātha and having fulfilled your purpose, have indeed constructed this temple and other works here. (71)
O Lord of the Earth, know that this linga named Vṛddhakāleśvara is established from beginningless time; you are merely its instrumental cause.
By seeing, touching, worshipping, hearing of, or bowing down to that Vṛddhakāleśa Liṅga, one obtains everything desired. (73)
There is a well named Kālodaka which destroys old age and disease; by drinking its water, one no longer requires a mother’s milk.
Having bathed in the water of the constructed well and performed worship of this Liṅga, a man attains within a year the success he desires in his heart.
Neither leprosy, nor eruptive boils, nor ringworm, nor scabies shall remain for one who drinks from or touches the *Kālatamodaka*, which dispels phlegm. (76)
Neither indigestion, nor colic, nor urinary disorders, nor dysentery, nor difficulty in urination, nor skin diseases arise from the consumption and regular use of this [remedy]. (77)
Whatever fevers caused by spirits there may be, and whatever irregular fevers there may be, they are quickly pacified by the use of the water from this well.
"Before your very eyes, my old age and grey hair have vanished in an instant through this well-water, according to the prescribed rite; I have become young again. (79)
When the Vṛddhakāleśvara Liṅga is worshipped, there is no poverty, nor calamities, nor diseases, nor sin, nor the fruit born of evil deeds.
To the north of Kṛttivāsas in Vārāṇasī, the Liṅga Vṛddhakāleśvara should be visited with great effort by those desiring spiritual perfection.
Having spoken thus to that protector of the earth and taking him by the hand, the ascetic Sānaṅgalekhā merged into that liṅga along with the queen.
By chanting "Mahākāla, Mahākāla, Mahākāla," one is liberated from sins a hundredfold; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In this manner, your liberation shall come from the sight of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, after you have enjoyed manifold pleasures in the auspicious city of Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus, with the hair on his body standing on end from joy, that brahmin, having heard this from the mouth of the Lord’s attendant, beheld his own future destiny—the realm of Hari, as beautiful as ten million suns.
Maitrāvaruṇi said: O Lopāmudrā, that lord of sages, having enjoyed delightful pleasures in Māyāpurī, gave up his life there by the power of his merit. || 86 ||
Having come from the realm of Vaikuṇṭha to the city of Nandivardhana, he enjoyed earthly pleasures and begot handsome sons.
Having entrusted the kingdom to them and reached the city of Vārāṇasī, he worshipped Viśveśvara and attained the state of liberation.
Having heard this most meritorious narrative of the Brahmin Śivaśarman, one is liberated from sin and attains supreme knowledge. (89)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation by Śivaśarman," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O Sūta, I shall narrate the story of the one born from a water-jar (Agastya), by hearing which a man becomes free from passion and a vessel of knowledge.
Having circumambulated the mountain named Śrī, the pot-born Agastya, together with his wife, then beheld the great and beautiful Skandavana forest.
It was rich in flowers in every season, with trees bearing succulent fruits; it was well-suited for habitation, abounding in bulbs and roots, and possessed trees with excellent bark.
It was a place where herds of wild beasts roamed, surrounded by rivers and ponds, possessing clear and deep lakes—the supreme essence of the entire earth.
Resounding with the cries of various birds and inhabited by various groups of sages, it was like a single sanctuary for the practice of austerity, the very abode of all prosperities.
There is a mountain there named Lohita, possessing the luster of a golden mountain; it has beautiful caves and waterfalls, and its own ridges shine like peaks.
A single fragment of Kailāsa has come here to this land of action, as if to perform intense penance, endowed with various wonders.
There, the best of sages, Agastya, of great asceticism, beheld the six-faced god in person; together with his wife, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
He praised the son of Girijā with hymns originating from the Vedas, as well as with a self-composed eulogy, while joining his palms in reverence.

Agastya said: Salutations to the one whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, who is the moon of nectar, the six-faced one of immeasurable prowess, and the source of joy for the heart of Gaurī. (10)

Salutations to you, the destroyer of the distress of those who bow before you, the fulfiller of all desires, the giver of chariots, the supreme savior, and the slayer of the fierce asura Tāraka. || 11 ||

Salutations be to you, the one whose vehicle is the peacock, who are both formless and possessed of form, who possess a thousand forms, who are the quality and the possessor of qualities, who are higher than the highest, who are the shoreless and the shore, and who are both the transcendent and the immanent.

Salutations to you, the best among the knowers of Brahman, who are clothed in the directions and abide in the sky; salutations to the golden-hued one, to the golden-armed one, to the golden one, and to the one whose seed is gold.

Salutations to Him whose very nature is austerity, whose wealth is austerity, who bestows the fruits of austerity; salutations to the Eternal Youth, the destroyer of the enemy of the snowy mountain’s daughter, who has rendered sovereignty as insignificant as a blade of grass and remains free from passion. 14.

Even he who bathes in Maṇikarṇikā according to the prescribed rite, though lacking faith, attains supreme merit that brings about the attainment of heaven. (120)

Having bathed according to the rules with faith and having performed the libations for the gods and others properly with sesame seeds, kusha grass, and barley, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
One who is full of faith, purified by the prescribed rites, having performed all water-libations, and having worshipped the deities while reciting mantras, shall obtain the fruit of all mantras.
O Śivā, having bathed and beheld Viśveśa while observing silence and with senses restrained, one who maintains the vow of silence obtains the merit resulting from all religious observances.

One should diligently observe silence during bathing, worship of the deities, recitation of mantras, the voiding of urine and feces, as well as during the brushing of teeth and the performance of fire-offerings (homa).
Having worshipped Viśveśvara with excellent offerings according to the prescribed rules, one indeed obtains the fruit of worshipping Śiva for as long as one lives by doing so even once.
O Goddess of the Gods, having given even a small amount of wealth acquired through righteous means in my field of Avimukta, one shall never become poor.
Having acquired various kinds of wealth, he who does not bestow it upon Avimukta becomes a fool; having met his death, he grieves forever elsewhere.
Whatever delightful jewels, cattle, elephants, horses, and garments have been fashioned, they were made for the welfare of those dwelling in Avimukta.
He who, for the sake of pleasing the Lord of the Universe, acquires wealth or even incurs its loss through righteous means in Kāśī, is blessed and is a knower of dharma. (29)
O Umā, that Lord Viśveśvara who resides in the city of Kāśī, manifesting in the form of a Liṅga, is indeed the direct source of my welfare.
Avimukta is the great field, measuring five krośas; it should be known as that single Jyotirliṅga named Viśveśvara.
Just as the orb of the sun, though situated in one place, is seen by all as being omnipresent, so too is Viśveśvara in Kāśī.
Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere through unimpeded yoga cultivated over various births, that is obtained in Kāśī by one who casts off the body.
Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere by those who have conquered their senses after performing all types of austerities for a long time, that is obtained at Kāśī in a single night.
Even one who does not know the greatness of this field, or even one devoid of faith, becomes sinless upon entering Kāśī and, having died there, attains immortality in due course of time. (35)
Even after committing terrible sins, when he reaches Kāśī in the course of time and casts off his body, he shall attain me alone through my grace.
Without my grace, O large-eyed one, who indeed can attain Kāśī? Without the sun, who here is called the maker of the day? (37)
O Goddess, who could obtain perpetual happiness without reaching Kāśī, since even Brahmā and the other gods are constantly bound by the fetters of material nature? (38)
Bound at the neck with twenty-four strong nooses made of the three qualities and bound by karma, how can people be liberated without Kāśī? (39)
This yoga is beset by many obstacles, for austerity is indeed difficult to accomplish; one who falls from yoga or falls from austerity must again endure the suffering of the womb.
Even if one has committed sins in Kāśī, if one dies in Kāśī itself, even after becoming a Rudra-piśāca, one will again attain liberation.
For those beings who die in Kāśī—even if they have committed sins by fate—there is no fall into hell, because I myself am their teacher. (42)
Having understood that the body is fraught with suffering and remembering the pains of the womb, one should abandon even a vast kingdom and serve Kāśī continuously. (43)
The most terrible messengers of Yama, arriving unawares, will bind one with nooses and slay; therefore, one should quickly take refuge in Kāśī.
Who would not take refuge in that Kāśī, where there is no fear of sins, where there is indeed no fear of Yama, and where there is no dread of dwelling in a womb? 45.
Death is certain to be encountered either this morning or the day after; as long as there is delay in time, for that long one should take refuge in Kāśī. (46)
When death has arrived for men, there is rebirth and further death; therefore, a wise person should take refuge in Kāśī, the ground of no-return.
Having abandoned the illusion pertaining to Viṣṇu known as son, field, and wife—which takes many forms in other births—one should take refuge in Kāśī, which destroys worldly existence.

Skanda said: "Death is far from me; I am still young; this [sound] should not be held in mind"—thus one should quietly listen to the sound of the bells on the neck of the buffalo of Death (Kṛtānta). Having reached the manifest and intense assembly of exhaustion due to its proximity, and having quickly abandoned his worn-out leaf-hut, the one of sharp intellect should then go to the city of Dhūrjaṭi.
Vyāsa said: O Sūta, having related this story before Agastya—which pacifies all sins—Skanda spoke again.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Maṇikarṇikā," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 26 ||
Skanda said: I shall here relate how the grove of Ānandakānana became renowned as Vārāṇasī, just as it was spoken by the God of gods.
Īśvara said: Listen, O mighty-armed Viṣṇu, O beauty of the three worlds, to how Avimukta acquired the name Vārāṇasī. || 2 ||
Having heard that his ancestors, who had performed horse-sacrifices, had been consumed by the fire of Kapila’s wrath, Bhagīratha [acted].
In the solar dynasty there was a king of great splendor and supreme righteousness, who, desiring to propitiate Gaṅgā, resolved to perform austerities.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his ministers, that mass of glory went to Himavanta, the best of mountains, desiring to honor his ancestors.
O Viṣṇu, who other than the one who flows through the three paths (Gaṅgā) could lead creatures to heaven—even those scorched by the fire of Brahmā’s curse and fallen into the great states of misery?
She is my own supreme form, consisting of water and having Śiva as her essence; she is the support of countless cosmic eggs and the ultimate primordial nature (prakṛti).
She is the very nature of pure knowledge, the triple power whose essence is compassion; she is the form of the nectar of bliss and the embodiment of pure dharma.
I sustain with my own effortless play this very one who is the sustainer of the worlds, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, for the sake of protecting the universe.
Whatever holy fords and sacred fields exist throughout the three worlds, whatever dharmas exist everywhere, and all sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees; || 10 ||
O Viṣṇu, all austerities, the fourfold Veda with its auxiliary limbs, myself, you, whoever else there may be, and the hosts of deities—[all these are contained within you]. (11)
Indeed, all the goals of human life and whatever various powers exist—all these reside within the Gaṅgā in a subtle form.
He who resorts to the Gaṅgā has bathed in all sacred fords, is initiated into all sacrifices, and has fulfilled all vows.
He who serves the Gaṅgā has performed austerities, he is a giver of all gifts, and he has attained the discipline of yoga.

One who bathes in the Gaṅgā is superior to all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, as well as to those learned in the Vedas and those who have reached the further shore of the meaning of the scriptures. (15)
Even if a person is corrupted by many kinds of faults born of mind, speech, and body, upon beholding the Gaṅgā he becomes pure; there is no doubt in this matter.
