In the Kṛta age, sacred fords exist everywhere; in the Tretā age, Puṣkara is supreme; in the Dvāpara age, Kurukṣetra; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā alone is so.
O Hari, by the power of impressions from practice in previous lives and through my supreme grace, one shall have a dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
In the Kṛta age, meditation was the cause of liberation; in the Tretā, it was indeed austerity; in the Dvāpara, those two along with sacrifices; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā alone is the means.
He who does not leave the bank of the Gaṅgā until the fall of his body is indeed a yogi of Vedānta knowledge, always observant of the vow of celibacy.

In the Kali age, for those with defiled minds, whose souls delight in the wealth of others, and who perform actions devoid of scriptural injunctions, there is indeed no destination other than the Gaṅgā.
Misfortune, ill fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—indeed, by chanting "Ganga, Ganga," these do not remain.
For the Gaṅgā, O Viṣṇu, always bestows fruits upon all beings both here and in the hereafter, according to their inner disposition, and is ever beneficial to the entire world. (23)
O Hari, in the Kali age, sacrifices, charity, austerity, yoga, chanting, along with the observances and restraints, do not equal even a thousandth part of service rendered to the Gaṅgā.
What is the use of the eightfold yoga, what use are austerities, and what use are sacrifices? Indeed, dwelling by the Ganges alone is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman. (25)
Even for one who stands far away, who knows the greatness of the Gaṅgā, and even for one who is unworthy, the Gaṅgā becomes gracious through devotion to Govinda.
Faith is the supreme, subtle dharma; faith is the highest knowledge and the highest austerity. Faith is heaven and liberation; through faith, she is propitiated.
Due to ignorance, passion, greed, and other such traits, faith does not arise in the dharma for men whose minds are utterly deluded, and this is especially true regarding the Gaṅgā. (28)
Just as water situated outside enters within the coconut, so too does the Jāhnavī, the water of the Supreme Brahman, which exists outside the cosmic egg.
There is no other gain found anywhere superior to the gain of the Gaṅgā; therefore, one should worship the Gaṅgā, for the Gaṅgā herself is the Supreme Person.
O Hari, even for one who is capable, learned, virtuous, and charitable, birth is useless if he is devoid of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
In this Kali age, for one who does not devote themselves to the Gaṅgā, family life is in vain, learning is in vain, sacrifices are in vain, austerities are in vain, and gifts are in vain. (32)

The fruit obtained from honoring a worthy recipient endowed with virtues is not equal to the fruit gained by bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā and performing worship according to the prescribed rite.
This [mantra] contains within it my fiery splendor; it is perfectly encompassed by my virility. It is the burner of all defects and the destroyer of all sins.
Merely by remembering the Gaṅgā, the cage of the multitude of sins shatters into a hundred pieces, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
They say that the fruit for one who goes alone to the Gaṅgā and for one who rejoices with devotion is equal; in this matter, devotion alone is the cause.
Whether walking, standing, reciting prayers, meditating, eating, waking, sleeping, or speaking, he who constantly remembers the Gaṅgā shall indeed be liberated from bondage.
Whoever, out of devotion, should cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā milk-rice mixed with honey, along with jaggery, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, for the sake of the ancestors; || 38 ||
O Hari, his ancestors remain satisfied for a hundred years; being fully gratified, the grandfathers grant him various desires.
Just as when the Liṅga is worshipped, the entire world becomes worshipped, so too one obtains the fruit of all holy fords by bathing in the Gaṅgā.
A man who, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, daily worships the Liṅga, certainly attains supreme liberation in a single birth. (41)
The Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, vows, gifts, and austerities are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of a Liṅga at the Gaṅgā.
Having resolved to go to the Gaṅgā and having performed the Śrāddha and other rites at home, the ancestors of that man rejoice because of his perfect resolve.
And their sins weep quickly, crying out, "Alas! Where shall we go? and they deliberate again and again with greed, delusion, and the like.
We shall create such obstacles that he does not go to the Gaṅgā, and we shall act so that once he has reached the Gaṅgā, he will not bring about its destruction.
As he goes from his home to bathe in the Gaṅgā, his sins depart from his body at every step, leaving him utterly hopeless.
O Hari, by means of the merits performed in previous births, having abandoned greed and other vices and having cast aside the multitude of all obstacles, the meritorious person reaches the Gaṅgā.
Whether by association, by means of wealth, through trade, or even by service, a mortal who bathes in the Gaṅgā shall go to heaven, even if he is attached to sensual desires.
Just as fire, even when touched unintentionally, would burn, so too the Gaṅgā, even when bathed in unintentionally, would burn away evil. 49.
A living being wanders in saṃsāra only so long as it does not resort to the Gaṅgā; having resorted to the Gaṅgā, a creature no longer experiences the affliction of existence. || 50 ||
He who has bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā with devotion, having completely cast away all doubt—he, though bound by human skin, is a god; of this there is no doubt. (51)
If one who has set out for the purpose of bathing in the Gaṅgā dies midway on the journey, he too obtains the fruit of that Gaṅgā-bath; of this there is no doubt.
Those who hear and those who recite this majesty of the Gaṅgā are liberated from all great sins; there is no doubt about this. || 53 ||
O Viṣṇu, those of evil intellect, wicked conduct, rationalists, and those full of many doubts, being deluded, look upon Gaṅgā as if she were any other river.
Through gifts, austerities, observances, and vows performed in previous births, devotion to the Gaṅgā arises for men in this present life.
For the sake of those devoted to the Gaṅgā, the Self-born One himself constructed palaces with delightful enjoyments in cities such as that of Mahendra.

There are numerous supernatural powers (*siddhis*), signs of accomplishment (*siddhiliṅgas*), and many signs of touch (*sparśaliṅgas*); there are also palaces constructed of jewels and multitudes of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*).

Out of fear of the impurities of the Kali age, they remain within the waters of the Gaṅgā; therefore, in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā should indeed be resorted to, for she grants the fulfillment of all desires.
Like darkness at sunrise, like mountains from fear of a thunderbolt's fall, like serpents at the sight of Tārkṣya, or like clouds driven by the wind—[so did they flee]. 59.
Just as delusion vanishes through the knowledge of reality, and just as deer flee upon seeing a lion, so do all sins go to destruction by the mere sight of the Gaṅgā.
Just as diseases [are cured] by divine medicines, as virtues [are lost] through greed, and as the intensity of summer heat [is dispelled] by plunging into a deep lake; 61.
Just as a mountain of cotton is destroyed in an instant by a single spark, so too are all defects certainly annihilated by the touch of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Just as asceticism [is destroyed] by anger, as the intellect [is destroyed] by desire, as fortune [is destroyed] by injustice, and indeed as knowledge [is destroyed] by pride; || 63 ||
Just as dharma perishes through hypocrisy, crookedness, and deceit, so too do sins perish by the mere sight of the Gaṅgā.
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as flickering as a flash of lightning, he who serves the Gaṅgā has reached the supreme further shore of intelligence.
Those mortals who have shaken off their sins behold on earth Gaṅgā, whose nature is the supreme light and who resembles a thousand suns.
Those atheists, whose eyes are impaired by sin, behold the Gaṅgā as if it were an ordinary river filled with common water.
Out of compassion for people, I, the liberator from saṃsāra, have constructed a staircase to heaven in the form of the waves of the Gaṅgā.
On the banks of the glorious Jāhnavī, every moment is auspicious, every place is likewise auspicious, and every person is a worthy recipient of gifts. (69)
Just as the horse-sacrifice is among sacrifices, as the Himavat is among mountains, as truth is among vows, and as the granting of fearlessness is among gifts; || 70 ||
Just as breath control is the foremost among austerities, the syllable Om among mantras, non-violence among duties, and prosperity is the best among desirable things; (71)
Just as the knowledge of the Self is the foremost among all sciences, and as Gaurī is the most excellent among women, so are you, O Supreme Person, the greatest among all the hosts of gods.
Just as a devotee of Śiva is the most excellent among all worthy recipients, so too is the holy ford of the Gaṅgā distinguished above all other sacred fords.
He who does not create a division between us two is one of great intelligence; he should be known as a devotee of Śiva and a Mahāpāśupata. (74)
This Gaṅgā, the carrier of merit, is a great whirlwind for the dust of sin, an axe for the trees of evil, and a forest fire for the fuel of wickedness.
And the ancestors, appearing in various forms, always sing this verse: "Will there perhaps be someone in our family who will bathe in the Gaṅgā? (76)
Having fully gratified the celestial sages, the poor, the helpless, and the suffering, and having bathed according to the prescribed rite with faith, he will offer handfuls of water.
May there be born in our family one who possesses an equal vision toward Śiva and Viṣṇu, who builds temples for them with devotion, and who performs their cleaning and other services. (78)
Whether devoid of desire or full of desire, even if born among the animal realm, that mortal who dies in the Gaṅgā does not behold hell.
Those who, while staying on the banks of the Gaṅgā, praise other holy places and do not hold the Gaṅgā in high esteem, shall go to hell.
That lowest of men who hates me, you, and Gaṅgā shall go to a terrible hell along with his own people.
Sixty thousand hosts always protect the Gaṅgā; they create obstacles for the dwelling of non-devotees and sinners.
With sharp arrows such as desire, anger, great delusion, greed, and the like, they strike their minds and cause them to lose their stability therein.
He who takes refuge in the Gaṅgā is a sage and he is a scholar; he should be known as one who has accomplished his purpose regarding the four aims of human life.
One who bathes even once in the Gaṅgā obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; and by offering libations there to the ancestors, one delivers them from the ocean of hell.
The meritorious person who bathes continuously in the Gaṅgā for a month dwells in the world of Śakra as long as Śakra and his ancestors remain there.
That meritorious man who bathes continuously in the Gaṅgā for a year, having reached the world of Viṣṇu, shall dwell there in happiness.
That mortal who bathes in the Gaṅgā day after day for as long as he lives should be known as liberated while living; at the end of the body, he is indeed liberated.
One need not consider lunar days, constellations, festivals, or the like when in the waters of the Jahnavi; by the mere act of bathing in the Ganga, accumulated sin is destroyed. (89)
Even a learned man would be a fool, and even one endowed with power would be powerless, if he does not take refuge on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, which are so easy to enjoy. (90)
Of what use is long life free from disease, or even of what use is expanding prosperity, or even of what use is pure intellect, if one does not serve the Gaṅgā? (91)
The man who causes a shrine to be built for the image of the Gaṅgā, having enjoyed worldly pleasures, goes even after death to the same world as the Gaṅgā.
Those who constantly and with reverence listen to the greatness of the Gaṅgā obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā by pleasing the reciter with wealth.
He who bathes a Liṅga with the water of the Gaṅgā for the sake of his ancestors, his ancestors shall be satisfied, even if they have gone to a great hell.
The wise have declared that bathing with fragrant water from the Ganges, purified by cloth and over which mantras have been recited eight times, is superior even to the bath of clarified butter.
Whoever [offers] even once water from the Gaṅgā mixed with eight substances, measuring a *prastha* of Māgadha, and placed in a copper vessel; || 96 ||
One should offer the arghya to Bhānu together with one's own ancestors; such a person, by means of a radiant celestial chariot, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, ghee, honey, cow’s curd, red karavīra flowers, and red sandalwood as well—98.

This eightfold offering (arghya) which has been described is exceedingly pleasing to the Sun; O Viṣṇu, when performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā, it should be known as ten million times more effective than when using other water.

The wise person who, according to their capacity, should construct a temple on the bank of the Gaṅgā, shall obtain a fruit ten million times greater than the consecration of a temple at any other sacred site. || 100 ||

Whatever fruit is obtained by planting trees such as the *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *cūta*, and likewise by the construction of wells, large tanks, ponds, water-stations (*prapā*), and charitable feeding-halls (*satra*); || 1 ||
Whatever merit might arise elsewhere, that would be attained simply by the sight of the Gaṅgā; and even more than that is gained by touching the Gaṅgā with flower gardens and other offerings. (2)

Whatever merit is gained by the gift of a daughter in marriage, and whatever merit is gained from the gift of cows and food—that merit becomes a hundredfold by drinking a mouthful of water from the Gaṅgā.
O Janārdana, whatever merit may be gained by a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, one obtains a fruit even greater than that from drinking the nectar of the Gaṅgā.
O Hari, what other fruit can be spoken of for bathing in the Gaṅgā with devotion? It is either an imperishable residence in heaven or even liberation.
The man who daily worships the pair of sandals of the Gaṅgā obtains long life, merit, wealth, sons, heaven, and liberation.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā for destroying the impurities of the Kali age; O Hari, there is no field equal to Avimukta that bestows liberation.
Upon merely seeing a mortal devoted to bathing in the Gaṅgā, the servants of Yama flee in the ten directions, just as deer do upon seeing a lion.
One who is habitually devoted to the Gaṅgā and dwells on the banks of the Gaṅgā shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice by performing worship according to the prescribed rule.
By the gift of cows, land, and gold with devotion on the auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā, a man is not born again in this cycle of existence, which is thorned with suffering.
Longevity is attained through the gift of garments, knowledge through the gift of books, prosperity through the gift of food, and fame through the gift of a daughter in marriage. (11)
O Hari, whatever action is performed elsewhere—whether it be a vow, charity, recitation, or austerity—all that becomes ten million times more meritorious on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
O Viṣṇu, he who gives a cow with her calf on the bank of the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite shall possess all prosperity for as many yugas as there are hairs on the cow's body.
By the gift of a wish-fulfilling cow, one enjoys all desires—many various kinds of divine things—in Goloka or in my own world. || 14 ||
Having enjoyed even those things unattainable by the gods together with his kinsmen, ancestors, and friends, he was adorned with every kind of jewel.
Thereafter, he is born into a noble family abounding in wealth and grain, endowed with jewels and gold, and possessed of virtuous conduct and learning. || 16 ||
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures together with his sons and grandsons, he again reached the Ganges at Kāśī, where it flows northward. || 17 ||
Having propitiated Viśveśvara due to the impressions (vāsanā) from a previous birth, one reaches the end of the body in due course and thereafter attains Brahman.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that man who, with devotion, gives even two *vivartanas* of land on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī. (19)
Having enjoyed mind-pleasing delights in the worlds of Mahendra and Candra for as many Yugas as there are atoms in that land, [he shall attain liberation].
O Hari, having become the lord of the seven islands and being devoted to the great Dharma, he shall cause all his ancestors residing in hell to attain the third heaven.
Having liberated all his ancestors residing in heaven, that one of great luster finally severed the ignorance consisting of the five elements with the sword of knowledge.
Having attained supreme detachment and practicing the highest yoga, or having reached liberation, he attains the Supreme Brahman. || 23 ||
He who bestows even a mere measure of gold as gold upon Suvarṇa on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, [attains great merit]. || 24 ||
In a beautiful, all-pervading celestial chariot inlaid with gold and jewels, he was endowed with all sovereign powers and honored in all the worlds. || 25 ||
O Viṣṇu, being honored by all, he shall enjoy delightful pleasures within the interior of the cosmic egg until the dissolution of all beings.
Then, having become a powerful sovereign over Jambūdvīpa, he reaches the state of Nirvāṇa upon arriving at Avimukta. || 27 ||
If one performs a bath in the Gaṅgā with devotion on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), one is instantly liberated from the multitude of sins accumulated since birth. || 28 ||
A bath in the Gaṅgā during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha is very difficult to obtain; on the new moon day, the merit is a hundredfold, and at the sun's transit, it is a thousandfold.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, [the merit is] one hundred thousandfold; during Vyatīpāta, it is infinite; during the equinoxes, ten thousandfold; and during the two solstices, one millionfold.
A lunar eclipse on a Monday and a solar eclipse on a Sunday are known as the Cūḍāmaṇi parvan; bathing during those occasions yields merit beyond counting.
O Viṣṇu, whatever bathing, charity, recitation, or fire-offering is performed here on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī according to the Cūḍāmaṇi [Kalpa], all that becomes inexhaustible.
But one who, endowed with faith and devotion, bathes in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite—even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified; how much more so, then, any other sinner?
Even worms, insects, moths, and the like that die on the bank of the Jāhnavī, as well as the trees that fall from its shore, attain the supreme goal.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the tenth day conjoined with the asterism Hasta, a man or a woman on the bank of the Gaṅgā, with a spirit of devotion— || 35 ||
O Hari, one should keep a vigil at night by worshipping Gaṅgā with ten varieties of fragrant flowers, food offerings, and fruits, ten of each kind.
O Garuḍa-bannered Lord, the wise man should worship with ten lamps and ten-ingredient incense ten times according to the prescribed rite, with faith.
One should cast sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter into ten streams of the Gaṅgā, and one should offer ten balls made of jaggery and parched grain while reciting the mantras.
"Salutation to Śivā," first; then the word "Nārāyaṇī"; then the word "Daśaharā"; and finally "Gaṅgāyāi"—this indeed is the mantra. (39)

The mantra should consist of twenty syllables, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*. Worship, giving, recitation, and burnt offerings are prescribed to be performed with this very mantra. (140)
Having fashioned an image of Gaṅgā out of gold or silver according to one's means, [one should place it] upon a full water-pot whose mouth is covered with a cloth.
Having installed the Goddess, who has been purified with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship her—she who has four arms, three eyes, and is attended by rivers and streams.
Her slender body was dripping with the nectar of loveliness; her excellent hands displayed a full water-pot, a white lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Then one should meditate upon her who is exceedingly serene, possessing a luster equal to ten thousand moons, being fanned with chowries, and adorned with a white parasol.
Her surface was flooded with nectar, anointed with divine perfumes, her feet worshipped by the three worlds, and she was praised by the celestial sages.
Having meditated upon and worshipped me, you, Brahmā, the Sun, Himavat, and Bhagīratha with mantras, along with offerings of incense and lamps; || 46 ||
Having worshipped before the image those [offerings] fashioned from sandalwood and unbroken rice, one should respectfully give ten *prastha* measures of sesame seeds to ten Brahmins.
A pala, a kuḍava, a prastha, an āḍhaka, and a droṇa—these should be understood, according to the measure of grain, to increase fourfold in succession. (48)
Fish, tortoises, frogs, crocodiles, and other aquatic creatures; swans, kāraṇḍavas, cranes, cakravākas, ṭiṭṭibhas, and saras cranes. || 49 ||
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers according to his ability those [images] fashioned from gold, silver, or copper-backed materials, the observer of the vow should cast them into the Ganges.
Having performed it in this manner according to the prescribed rite, avoiding stinginess with wealth and observing a fast, one is liberated from the ten sins that will be described.
Taking what is not given, violence according to improper rules, and consorting with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold physical [karma]. (52)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and incoherent chatter—this constitutes the fourfold nature of speech. (53)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—these are remembered as the threefold mental [actions]. (54)
By these ten kinds of sins arising from ten births, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. This is the truth, the absolute truth, O Gadādhara.
One should rescue ten ancestors and ten descendants from the terrible hells by reciting this hymn to be described hereafter with faith at the edge of the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ, salutations to Śivā, to Gaṅgā; salutations again and again to the giver of auspiciousness. Salutations to you who possess the form of Viṣṇu; let there be salutations to you, the embodiment of Brahmā. (57)
Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations again and again to you, the consort of Śaṅkara. Salutations to her who embodies all the gods, to her whose form is the supreme medicine.
Salutations to you, the best of physicians for all diseases of every kind; salutations to you, the destroyer of poisons produced from both stationary and moving sources.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of the poison of saṃsāra and the giver of life; repeated salutations to you, the mistress of the vital breath who removes the threefold suffering.
Salutations to you, whose form is pure, who brings about the lineage of peace; salutations to her whose form is the enemy of sin, who effects the complete purification of all.
Salutations again and again to her who bestows enjoyment and liberation, the giver of auspiciousness; obeisance to you, Bhogavatī, who grants both worldly enjoyment and its full experience.

Salutations to you, O Mandākinī; salutations again and again to you, the giver of heaven. Salutations to the ornament of the three worlds; salutations again and again to you, the one who flows through the three paths.

Salutations again and again to her who abides as the three white [sacrificial fires], to her who is endowed with patience; salutations again and again to her who abides as the three sacrificial fires, to her who is possessed of splendor.
Salutation to Nandā, the bearer of the *liṅga*, whose essence is a stream of nectar; salutation to you, O Viśvamukhyā; repeated salutations to you, O Revatī.
Salutations to you, the Great One; salutations to you, the Sustainer of the World. Salutations to you, the Friend of the Universe; repeated salutations to you, Nandinī.
Salutations again and again to Pṛthvī, to Śivāmṛtā, and to Suvṛṣā; salutations again and again to you, Tārā, who are enriched by hundreds of higher and lower [states].
Salutations to you who cut through the net of bonds; salutations again and again to you who are indivisible, peaceful, most excellent, and the bestower of boons.
Salutations to you, O Ugrā, the one who provides easy sustenance, and Saṃjīvinī; salutations again and again to Brahmiṣṭhā, the giver of Brahman, and the destroyer of evil.
Salutations to you, the Mother of the World, who shatters the suffering of those who bow before you; salutations again and again to Maṅgalā, the adversary of all calamities. || 170 ||
O Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who are solely intent on protecting those who have come for refuge and those who are distressed and miserable; O remover of the suffering of all, salutations be to you! (71)
Salutations again and again to you, the stainless one, the destroyer of difficulties, the skillful one; salutations to Gaṅgā, who bestows liberation and who is both supreme and beyond the supreme.
O Gaṅgā, may you be before me; O Gaṅgā, stay behind me; O Gaṅgā, come to my sides; O Gaṅgā, let my very existence be in you.

In the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, you are everything; O auspicious one who has entered the earth, you alone are the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and indeed the supreme Puruṣa. O Gaṅgā, you are the Supreme Self and Śiva himself; salutations to you, O auspicious one.
Whoever recites this hymn, or even hears it with faith, is liberated in ten ways from the sins arising from body, speech, and mind. (75)

One afflicted by disease shall be freed from disease; one beset by calamities shall be freed from calamities; one who is bound shall be released from bondage; and one who is afraid shall be liberated from fear.
One obtains all desires and, after death, goes to the third heaven; having ascended a divine celestial chariot, one is fanned by divine women.
For one who always keeps this written in their home and wears it, there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor is there ever any fear of snakes and the like.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, the tenth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Hasta and joined with Wednesday destroys the three kinds of sin.
On that tenth day, whoever—whether poor or even powerless—stands in the waters of the Gaṅgā and recites this hymn ten times, [attains the fruit]. (180)
He too obtains that fruit which has been proclaimed as resulting from worshipping the Gaṅgā with effort according to the previously described procedure.
As is Gaurī, so is Gaṅgā; therefore, whatever ritual procedure is properly prescribed for the worship of Gaurī, that same one applies to the worship of Gaṅgā as well.
"As I am, so are you, O Viṣṇu; as you are, so indeed is Umā. As Umā is, so is Gaṅgā; this fourfold form is not divided. (83)
He who speaks of a difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra, or likewise between Śrī and Gaurī, or between Gaṅgā and Gaurī, is indeed a person of deluded intellect.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Daśaharā Stotra preceded by a Description of the Majesty of the Gaṅgā," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Umā said: "O Lord, desirous of asking something for the sake of dispelling my own doubt, please speak if it causes you no weariness, O Knower of the Wisdom of the Three Times."
At that time, where was King Bhagīratha and where was the Bhāgīrathī when Viṣṇu performed penance on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī? || 2 ||
Śiva said: "O large-eyed one, O ever-pure lady, no doubt should be entertained in this matter; for in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, the three divisions of time are proclaimed."
"What has been, what is to be, and what is now occurring—do not harbor doubt about these in vain. Having said this, the Lord spoke again concerning the supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā.
Agastya said: O son of Pārvatī, tell me again about the greatness of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) as it was described by the God of gods regarding Hari at that time.
Skanda said: O son of Mitrāvaruṇa, listen here to the greatness of the river that flows through the three paths, as it was spoken by the Lord; it destroys all sins.
Whoever, having reached the Trisrotas river, offers rice-balls even once, by means of those water-libations with sesame seeds, his ancestors are uplifted from the ocean of existence.
For as many sesame seeds as are taken by mortals for the ancestral rite, for that many thousands of years do the ancestors dwell in heaven.
Since the gods along with the ancestors are always present in the Gaṅgā, there is no need for their invocation or dismissal there.
Those who have died in the paternal lineage and likewise in the maternal lineage, as well as those who have died among gurus, fathers-in-law, kinsmen, and other relatives; || 10 ||
Whosoever have not yet cut their teeth, those who were aborted in the womb, those killed by fire, lightning, or thieves, and those slain by tigers or fanged beasts;

Those who died by hanging, those who fell [from a height], those who committed suicide, those who sold themselves, thieves, and likewise those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice; || 12 ||
Those who sell liquids, those who suffer from other diseases, arsonists, poisoners, and even those born in one's own lineage who kill cows—[these are excluded]. (13)
Those who have gone to the Asipatravana hell, and those who have gone to Kumbhīpāka; those who have gone to Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra; || 14 ||
Those who wander through thousands of different births by virtue of their own actions—whether as birds, wild animals, insects, trees, or climbing plants—[attain this state]. (15)
Countless and innumerable women have entered the womb, while those who were counted as auspicious have been brought to the realm of Yama by the most terrible servants of Yama.

Those who were non-relatives or relatives, those who were relatives in another birth, those whose names are unknown, and those who are born of one's own lineage but are childless—[may they all attain liberation]. (17)
Those who have died by poison, those who have been gored by horned animals, those who are ungrateful, those who kill their teachers, and likewise those who betray their friends; || 18 ||
Those who kill women or children, those who are betrayers of trust, those who are devoted to untruth and violence, and those who are always intent on evil; (19)
Those who sell horses, those who steal the property of others, the helpless, the wretched, and the miserable—these are unable to attain human birth. || 20 ||
Even those who have attained heaven, if they are once satiated by a person according to the prescribed rite with the waters of the Jāhnavī, go to the celestial realm and shall attain liberation.

He who, having recited these mantras, performs the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa), the ancestral rite (śrāddha), and the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍapradāna), is here called one who knows the ritual injunctions.
Whatever holy fords (tīrthas) exist throughout the three worlds that bestow desired objects, they all reside in Kāśī at the north-flowing river.
O Viṣṇu, the celestial river is meritorious in every respect and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin; it is especially so at Kāśī where it flows toward the north.
The hosts of gods, sages, and ancestors indeed sing this verse: "May the northward-flowing river be within the range of our vision in Kāśī. (25)
May we truly become that very nectar, satisfied by the nectar found therein and freed from the threefold affliction, through the grace of the Lord of the Universe. (26)
O Hari, it is determined that the Gaṅgā alone leads to liberation everywhere; however, it is especially so at Avimukta, due to the weight of my presiding presence there. || 27 ||
Having recognized the terrible Kali age, devotion to the Gaṅgā was well-concealed; people did not find the Gaṅgā, who is the sole provider of the paths to liberation.
Wandering through millions of births across various wombs, who indeed could attain liberation without resorting to the Jahnavi? (29)
O Viṣṇu, for men of small intellect whose minds are distracted, sin is like the Gaṅgā—the supreme medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
O Hari, he who repairs what is broken or dilapidated on the banks of the Gaṅgā shall enjoy inexhaustible happiness for a long time in my world.
He who, having set out for the sake of others or even for his own sake, does not go to the Gaṅgā due to extreme delusion, shall fall along with his ancestors.
O Hari, those embodied beings for whom all their rites are performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā are indeed immortal, even though they remain on earth as mortals.
Even in the final stage of life, he who resorts to the celestial river—even after committing many sins—shall attain an auspicious destination.
As long as the bones of humans remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that many thousands of years they are honored in the heavenly world.
Viṣṇu said: O God of gods, Lord of the world, O Master who brings welfare to the worlds! If, by fate, the bone of that wicked and evil-minded one should fall [upon you], [what will happen]? || 36 ||
O Lord, how can there be a supreme destination for one who has met an untimely death in the sinless waters of the celestial river? Let this be explained. (37)
Maheśvara said: In this regard, O Adhokṣaja, I shall relate an ancient account; listen with a focused mind, O Viṣṇu, concerning the twice-born Vāhīka. 38.
Formerly, in the land of Kaliṅga, there was a twice-born man who sold salt; he was devoid of the twilight ablutions and bereft of even a single syllable of the Vedas.
One named Vāhīka possessed nothing more than a sacrificial thread; his only possession was a young widow from the loom.
Then, afflicted by famine and deprived of his wife—a woman of the śūdra caste—he went from country to country for the sake of sustaining his life.
Then, in the middle of the Daṇḍaka forest, emaciated by hunger and devoid of companions, he was killed there by a tiger that was fond of human flesh.
A vulture seized his left foot and flew up from there; a fight ensued in the sky between him and another flesh-eating vulture.
Then, as two vultures, greedy for meat and desiring victory over one another, were contending, a foot and ankle fell from the beak of a *kaṅka* bird.
By the turn of fate, as he was engaged in combat, that Vāhīka Brahmin, slain by a tiger, fell into the middle of the Gaṅgā.
The very moment the leopard killed that Vāhīka who had come to the forest, at that same instant he was bound with nooses by cruel servants.
Struck excessively with whips and pierced all over with iron spikes, vomiting blood from his mouth, he was led by them before Yama.
Then, O Lord of Men, Citragupta was questioned by Dharmarāja: "Having deliberated upon the merit and demerit of this twice-born man, report it to me quickly. (48)
Then Citragupta, of wondrous intellect, who always knows all the deeds of all living beings, was questioned by Vaivasvata.
He spoke to the friend of the Yamunā about the wicked Vāhīka, a twice-born man whose conduct was inauspicious from the very day of his birth.
Citragupta said: "O Hari, no one has performed for him the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna); nor has his ignorant father performed the birth-rite (jātakarma)."

The pacification of sins committed in the womb is the cause that bestows a full lifespan and happiness; yet on the eleventh day, his naming ceremony was not performed according to the prescribed rite.
By whatever rite one becomes renowned everywhere as a purifier of rituals, that [rite] the dull-witted man did not perform for him during the fourth month.

On an auspicious lunar day and other favorable occasions, Janaka did not perform the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) according to the prescribed rites during the sixth month, which removes the obstacle of traveling abroad.
By that karma, he always eats sweet food during the month of Bhāskara; furthermore, his tonsure ceremony was not performed in the year according to family custom.
By that karma through which his hair would have been glossy and showering flowers, his progenitor did not perform the piercing of his ears at the auspicious time.

By means of which his two ears became excellent listeners, like those who grasp gold; and when the eighth year had passed, O Hari, there was also the binding of the girdle of muñja grass for him, which is the cause for receiving the Veda and for the increase of celibacy.
Not even a mention of the untying of the sacred girdle was made for him at birth; for it is better to attain the state of a householder immediately after that rite. (58)
Then his wife, who had been married by some means or other, was one who had abandoned her family and social standing; she was wedded to that husband of a low-caste woman, a thief of another's wife.
From the fifth year onwards, this man of wicked conduct became a thief of others' property and was devoted to gambling.
While he was living in Rumā, a one-year-old cow belonging to Hatāgaura was once killed by him with a firm staff while she was licking salt. (61)
He struck his mother many times with kicks of his feet; indeed, he never once carried out the word of his father.
This man, who is fond of quarreling, has repeatedly consumed poison; he is habituated to tormenting people and has caused his own belly to be torn open.
This evil-minded one would consume various poisons, such as those derived from the *dhattūra* and *karavīra* plants, merely for the sake of sport or a quarrel.
O son of Sūrya, he has been burnt by fire and swallowed by dogs; he has been pierced on all sides by horned beasts with the tips of their horns in great numbers. 65.
Bitingly stung by venomous serpents, wicked and censured by the virtuous, that most sinful man constantly brought harm upon his own self with pieces of wood, bricks, and clods of earth.
Moreover, that head which is always worshipped in many ways by the virtuous has been struck repeatedly by this evil-minded one.
For that dull-witted Brāhmaṇa, though he had indeed studied the Gāyatrī, had out of desire eaten fish and meat by this evil-minded one. (68)
For his own sake, he cooked milk-rice in many ways, together with lac, salt, and meat, along with milk, curd, and ghee.
That fool was always a seller of poisons, metals, and weapons, as well as female slaves, cows, and horses, and likewise of hair and hides. (70)

His limbs were nourished by the food of a Śūdra; he engaged in sexual intercourse on the sacred festival days; and this evil-minded man turned his back on the rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
He has killed birds and even more than a hundred deer; he is a cutter of trees without cause, always cruel-minded. (72)
He was constantly a source of anxiety even to his own kinsmen; he was perpetually a speaker of untruth and always devoted to violence. (72)
He took what was not given, was treacherous, and devoted himself to his genitals and belly; O son of the Sun, what need is there for much speaking? He was a personified form of sin itself.
In Raurava, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, Atiraurava, Kālasūtra, Kṛmibhuja, and in the mire of pus and blood; (75)
In the terrible Asipatravana hell, in Yantrapīḍa, Sudaṃṣṭraka, Adhomukha, Pūtigaṃdha, Viṣṭhāgarta, and Abhojana; || 76 ||
Furthermore, let him be cast for a number of kalpas into each of these hells: Sūcībhedya, Sandaṃśa, Lālāpa, and Kṣuradhāraka.
Having heard this from the mouth of Citragupta, Dharmarāja rebuked that man of evil conduct and commanded his servants.
Seized by a sign from her brow and led away, he was bound and taken to the abode of hell, where the loud cries of the sinners cause one's hair to stand on end.
Īśvara said: When Vāhīka had thus been established in extremely intense torments, [he was cast] into the stainless waters of the Gaṅgā, which yield the fruit of merit for that very moment.
For that [fruit] had fallen from the beak of a vulture into the mouth of that Vāhīka twice-born man; at that moment, Hari’s celestial chariot arrived from the abode of the gods.
Adorned with divine ornaments and wearing celestial attire, that twice-born man ascended a divine vehicle suspended with bells and crowded with hundreds of celestial women.
Fanned by throngs of apsarases and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, he went to the heavenly realm, O Hari, because his bones had fallen into the Gaṅgā.
Skanda said: O Pot-born one, this investigation into the power of things is truly marvelous; this supreme power of Sadāśiva is somehow of a liquid nature.
This Gaṅgā was indeed set in motion by Śambhu, the God of gods, who is filled with the nectar of compassion, for the sake of uplifting the world. 85.
Just as there are thousands of other rivers in the world filled with water, so too should this river that flows through the three paths not be compared by the wise.
O Sage, having ascertained the syllables of the Vedas, this Gaṅgā was indeed fashioned out of those very fluids by Śambhu, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, out of compassion.
Having extracted this essence from these Yoga-Upaniṣads, Śaṅkara, out of compassion for all living beings, created [this work] as the best among rivers.
Just as there are nights that hold no digits of the moon and trees that bear no flowers, so too are those lands where the celestial river does not exist.
O Hari, just as riches are useless without integrity and sacrifices are fruitless without sacrificial fees, so too are all lands and directions devoid of merit without the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Just as the courtyard of the sky without the sun, or a house at night without a lamp, or Brahmins who are ignorant of the Vedas, so too are the quarters of the earth when devoid of the Gaṅgā.
Between one who might perform a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances for the purification of the body and one who drinks the nectar of the Gaṅgā, the drinker of the Gaṅgā's water is superior.
If one were to stand on a single foot for a thousand years, and another were to drink the water of the Gaṅgā for a single year, the latter who drinks the Gaṅgā’s water is superior to the former.
O Hari, that man who would hang head-downwards for a hundred years is better off than one who lies upon a bed of sand from the Bhīṣma-sū river. 94.
Just as the Gaṅgā is the remover of the heat of sin for beings tormented by the heat of evil in this world, so too in the Kali age there is nothing else like her.
Just as two hooded serpents become devoid of venom by the mere glance of Tārkṣya, so too do sins lose their luster upon the sight of the Bhāgīrathī. 96.
The man who wears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā certainly bears the orb of the sun for the destruction of darkness. (97)
For one who is overwhelmed by calamities, destitute of wealth, and a sinner, the Ganges alone is said to be his refuge, and not otherwise. 98.
Whether heard of, longed for, seen, touched, drunk, or bathed in, the Gaṅgā delivers both lineages of men; of this there is no doubt. (99)

From chanting, from seeing, from touching, and from drinking or bathing in the Gaṅgā, one should know that the increase of merit and the destruction of demerit possess tenfold greater efficacy in each successive case.
Neither by sacred texts, nor by wealth, nor even by any other meritorious deed is that fruit obtained among mortals which is attained by reaching the Gaṅgā. || 1 ||
Those who, though capable, do not bathe in the Gaṅgā who bears liberation within her, are indeed born blind and lame; even while living, they are as good as dead.
Listen, O Hari, to the sacred revelation (Śruti) which speaks of the majesty of the Gaṅgā; having heard it, its meaning being certain, the best of men shall take refuge in the Gaṅgā.
Those who take refuge in Gaṅgā—who is full of refreshment, honey-sweet, rich in milk, the very form of nectar, and abounding in vigor; who is born from the third heaven—go to the third heaven.

Those who have with their whole being and with their minds taken refuge in the Jāhnavī—the river frequented by sages, the foot of Viṣṇu, ancient, and possessing most meritorious currents in this world—they go to the abode of Brahman.

She who, like a mother leading her sons, ever leads these worlds to heaven endowed with all virtues—Ganga should always be worshipped by those who desire the beloved abode of Brahma and who have themselves under their own control.

One who desires the purification of the self should take refuge in Gaṅgā—the beloved of Brahmā, immortal, served by the learned, the mother of Guha, the source of all forms, the bestower of nourishment, and the one cherished by the rays of the sun.
A man who, being celibate and composed, bathes in the Gaṅgā, becomes cleansed of sin and obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
The Gaṅgā always rescues those who are seized by impure deeds, sinking in the great ocean, and falling into hell, provided they have taken refuge in her.
Just as the world of Brahmā is the highest among all worlds, so too is the Jāhnavī the most excellent among rivers and lakes. (110)
Whatever fruit may be obtained by performing austerities for three years after forming a right resolve elsewhere, that same fruit is attained through devotion at Gaṅgā in even half a ghaṭikā.
Even for one dwelling in heaven and enjoying inexhaustible bliss, there is no such joy as that which men experience on the banks of the Gaṅgā when the moon rises at night.
But having cast away with fortitude like a blade of grass that corpse overcome by old age and disease into the waters of the Jahnavi, one may enter Amarāvatī.
Her lunar orb is constantly bathed by torrents of water, yet at the end of that day, it assumes an even greater splendor.
Upon casting offerings into her waters, one's sins are instantly destroyed, and the attainment of great spiritual welfare occurs at that very moment. (15)
O Acyuta, the waters offered with faith by those born of one's own lineage to the ancestors at this place provide supreme satisfaction for three autumns.
She delivers mortals from the earth and reptiles from the depths; she is the river that flows through the three paths, leading the inhabitants of heaven to the abode of Viṣṇu in heaven. 17.
It is the supreme holy place among all holy places, the best of rivers among all rivers; it bestows heaven upon all living beings, even those who have committed great sins.
O Viṣṇu, there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) everywhere—in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space—and they all exist in their entirety within the Ganges.
Whether he knows it or not, whoever meets his death in the Gaṅgā—provided he is not a suicide—shall go to heaven and shall not behold the hells.
The Gaṅgā alone is all sacred fords; the Gaṅgā alone is the forest of asceticism; the Gaṅgā alone is indeed the field of spiritual perfection—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (21)
O Pot-born One, there the trees yield fruits according to one's desires, the earth is made of gold, and those who bathe in the Ganges dwell there.
He who, having adorned a well-behaved and milch cow with garments and jewels on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, gives her to a Brāhmaṇa; || 23 ||
For as many hairs as there are on that sage and on his progeny, for that many thousands of years shall he enjoy the happiness of heaven.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 28.
Agastya said: For men, a birth is fruitless without bathing in the Gaṅgā; there is another means by which one may obtain the fruit of that bath.
And for those who are powerless, the lame, those whose souls are overcome by laziness, and those residing in distant foreign lands—how can they perform a bath in the Gaṅgā? (2)
Whether it be charity, or a vow, or a mantra, or the recitation of hymns; or bathing at other sacred fords, or the worship of deities. (3)
O Six-faced One, if there exists anything that bestows the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā through a mere alternative procedure, tell that to me who am prostrate before you.
O high-minded one, born from the womb of the Gaṅgā, no one other than you knows the supreme majesty of the celestial river.
Skanda said: "O Sage, there are lakes with meritorious waters and rivers here, as well as sacred fords (tīrthas) situated in various places inhabited by those who have conquered their own selves."
O you of great majesty, although these [other acts] produce visible results and possess great power, they do not equal even a ten-millionth part of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā).
By this very inference, O Pot-born One, understand that the Ganges was held upon his head by Śambhu, the God of gods.
At the time of bathing at other holy sites, people chant the name of the Jahnavi; for what else is capable of liberating one from sin except for the river that flows from Vishnu’s foot?
O Brahmin, the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā is obtained only in the Gaṅgā itself; just as the taste of a grape is found only in the grape and not elsewhere.
"But there is, O Sage, one means here by which the fruit of bathing in the celestial river may be obtained in its entirety—a most profound secret. (11)

To one who is a devotee of Śiva, who is peaceful, who is devoted to Viṣṇu, who is full of faith, who is a believer, and who desires not to dwell in a womb; (to such a person, [this should be told]). 12.
This supreme secret, which destroys even the greatest sins, must not be told by anyone to anyone else, anywhere. (13)
It is supremely conducive to great welfare, meritorious, the fulfiller of desires, a source of joy for the celestial river, and a continuous stream of satisfaction for Śiva.
This thousand names of Gaṅgā, the most beautiful among royal hymns, is the supreme recitation among all that is to be recited, equal to the Vedas and the Upaniṣads. (15)
One should recite it with effort, in silence and without a reciter, in pure places, being oneself pure, and with very distinct syllables. (16)

Skanda said: Om, salutations to the Goddess Gaṅgā! She is the embodiment of the syllable Om (Oṃkāra), ageless, incomparable, unyielding, and flowing with nectar; she is exceedingly noble, fearless, free from sorrow, the delight of Alaka, immortal, and stainless. || 17 ||

She is compassionate toward the helpless, unfailing, the source of the waters, and the bestower of immortality; she is characterized by the unmanifest, unshakeable, uninterrupted, and unconquered. || 18 ||

She is the protector of the protectorless, the bestower of the accomplishment of desired goals, the increaser of the god of love, the foundation of the powers such as *aṇimā*, the foremost among the most exalted, and the stealer of falsehood. || 19 ||

She is of inconceivable power, faultless, of wondrous form, and the remover of sins; she is the daughter of the King of Mountains, the bestower of the perfection of the eightfold yoga, and the infallible one.

Her power is unimpaired, she bestows life-force, she possesses infinite sacred fords, her waters are nectar; she is of infinite majesty, boundless, the giver of infinite bliss, and the provider of food.
She is the embodiment of all deities without exception, non-terrible, and of the nature of nectar; she is the pacifier of the web of ignorance and the bestower of a state beyond the reach of thought.
She is the destroyer of all obstacles without exception, she is woven with all virtues, and she is solely devoted to bestowing grace as the light that dispels the darkness of ignorance. 23.
Delightful, with faultless limbs, possessing infinite essence, and stainless; the giver of health, a creeper of bliss, and the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress. (24)

She is of wondrous form, bestowing long life, indeed wealthy, primordial, unattained, and served by the noble; she is nourishing, known for her attained wisdom, blissful, and the giver of consolation.

She is the destroyer of laziness, the remover of calamities, and the showerer of the nectar of bliss; she is Irāvatī, the giver of desired things, the beloved, and the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices and charitable works.

Her purpose is praised by history and the Vedas; she bestows auspiciousness in this world and the next; she is preeminent in sacrifice, virtuous conduct, and austerity; and she is worshipped by Indra and the other gods.
She who wears a garland of ornaments, whose beautiful abode is Indira, who is served by bees and others, and who is the beloved of the Lord of Lords; (28)
She who removes the fear of calamities, she whose conduct is worthy of praise, she who possesses supreme power, and she who moves within the circle of the most excellent stars.

She who sports in the world of the serpents with the risen path of the sky as her crest-jewel; she who possesses the earth of the bull as her lotus-vessel; she who is the liquid flowing from the feet of Upendra.
She is the cause of the fulfillment of desires, the increaser of noble enthusiasm, the destroyer of anxiety, the quencher of heat, and the beloved daughter of the Sun.
She is the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction; she moves above; she carries nourishment; she is the sustainer of nourishment; she is full of vigor; and she is garlanded with waves.

She is dear to those of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), whose path is upward; she possesses waves and bestows the higher state of existence. She is praised by hosts of sages, possesses supernatural power (ṛddhi), and destroys the three debts.

She is the bearer of truth (*ṛta*), the bestower of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the very embodiment of the *Ṛgveda*, and she who is fond of straightforwardness. She carries the constellations along the path of the stars, possesses the radiance of the stars, and reveals the straight path.

She has flourished through the fulfillment of all dharma and artha; she bestows the nectar of immortality one by one; she is the sacrifice whose very nature is to cause growth; and she has conquered all remaining sins.

She is indeed the bestower of sovereignty, the embodiment of sovereignty, the traditional lore, and the lunar splendor; she is the vigorous one, the field of medicinal herbs, and the giver of strength-bestowing food.

You are the giver of the height of nectar to the lips; you are the medicine for those diseased by worldly existence; you are the daughter of Indra, renowned for your generosity; you are fierce; and you possess the form of Umā’s son.

She who flows through the path of the sky, who is established in the excellent garland, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is Ambikā, whose great source is the waters, who bestows the waters of the firmament, and who removes the darkness of ignorance.

She is indeed Aṃśumālā and Aṃśumatī; she has accepted the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) as her son; she is the destroyer of the blinding darkness (of ignorance); she is the remover of the burden of the world; and she is the possessor of collyrium (Añjanāvatī).

She is the doer of good, the desirable one, fragrant with the scent of lotuses and water-lilies; she is the abode of white lilies, the bed of red lotuses, splendor itself, and the bestower of what is desired.

She is the golden-eyed one, the wish-fulfilling cow, the creator of fame, and the destroyer of affliction; she is the most excellent sacrifice, the fruit of sacrifice, and the breaker of the bonds of karma.
She has lotus-like eyes, she removes fatigue, her splendor is like that of the scorching fire, she is moist with compassion, auspicious, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age. 42.
She possesses the power of desire, form, and action; she is garlanded with lotuses and water-lilies; she is immutable, beloved by compassion, the vehicle of karma, and possessed of all arts.
She is the wish-fulfilling creeper for Kamalā, the destroyer of the darkness of Kali, lovely with her beautiful waters, and she who dwells upon the beautiful matted locks of Kapardin.
She is the pacifier of the black poison, fond of kadamba flowers; she is the playful one of the Kālindī river, possessing a garland of sweet-sounding waves.

She who has scratched away the itching of the three worlds, who is affectionate toward her son Kaṇḍu, who wields a sword, who possesses the luster of a sword’s edge, who moves through the sky, and who bears the crescent moon.

Moving through the sky, abiding in the sky, beloved by the one whose tilaka is the crescent moon; she who is the sky-farer among sky-farers, worthy of worship, renowned, and the bestower of renown. (47)

She who has shattered the flood of sins of those who bow before her; she who destroys the intellect of the wicked; she who has uprooted the entire mass of the bulbous roots of sin; she who wields the sword, the skull-topped staff, and the shield.
The Gaṅgā is the mine that quenches the intense heat of the harsh [world], a source of nectar-like waters; she is fragrant, fair-complexioned, and fond of the city of the Gandharvas.
She has profound limbs, is composed of virtues, is free from fear, and is fond of liberation; she is the Mother of the Lord of Ganas, celebrated in song, and praised through both prose and verse.
Gāndhārī, the pacifier of the womb, the bestower of a state upon those who have lost their way; Gomatī, the secret knowledge, the cow, the protector, and she who moves through the sky. || 51 ||

She who increases the lineage, she who possesses virtues, she who transcends qualities, she who is the foremost of virtues; she who is the Mother of the Cave, the Daughter of the Mountain, and she who has arisen from the feet of Govinda.
Her conduct is worthy of praise; she is Gāyatrī, the beloved of Giriśa. She is of hidden form, possessed of virtues, venerable, and the increaser of dignity.

Guṇḍrā removes the afflictions caused by malevolent planets; she is the destroyer of poison and is fond of song. She is the dispeller of heat, possesses the essence of clarified butter (ghṛta), and bestows satisfaction through that very essence. || 54 ||

She who loves the sound of the bell, the formidable one, the destroyer of the flood of sins; she who brings satisfaction to the sense of smell, the resonance, the one of dense bliss, and the beloved of the clouds.

She who destroys [sins], whose waters are terrifying, who has rubbed away the succession of transgressions, whose waters are drunk by millions of jars [of the gods], and who has brought about every auspiciousness.
Compassionate, a treasure-house of compassion, voracious, and sounding like an owl; saffron-colored, with a tawny body, she is the Gurgling One, possessing a gurgling voice.

She is the moonlight, the water of the moonstone, and she whose radiance moves like a shimmering flood; she consists of consciousness, is the very form of the intellect, and possesses ten thousand faces as bright as the moon.
She has eyes like campaka flowers, she is beautiful, with lovely limbs and a graceful gait; she is noble, the abode of virtuous conduct, a creator of wonders, and possessed of a wondrous form.
Campā is pure with sandalwood and water, worthy of constant worship, long-enduring, rich with beautiful campaka garlands, and one who has measured out all evil deeds. (60)
Flowing through the sky of consciousness, she is inconceivable; she is fanned by waving chowries; she has stolen away all sins; and she has traversed the entire circle of the world.
She has severed the entire flood of sins, she is the destroyer of deceit and the remover of guile; she covers the surface of the triple heaven and has loosened all bonds.

She who pours forth streams of nectar, she whose course is unimpeded by the destruction of sins, she who has made the flocks of swans her parasol, and she who has rendered her own nectar into a spray.

She is the Jāhnavī, the mother of the world, she who is to be recited, and she whose ripples move swiftly; she is victory, she who is dear to Janārdana, she who is to be cherished, and she who is the welfare of the world.

She is life itself, the vital breath of living beings, the eldest in the universe, and composed of the universe; she is the incomparable creeper that sustains all living creatures and eradicates birth after birth.
She who destroys dullness, the source of the universe, turbid with water; she who generates joy for the world, the lotus-born one, whose eyes are like lotuses. || 66 ||

She is nectar to the eyes of the people, she who sports upon the slopes of matted locks; she is victorious, the destroyer of those who mutter prayers mechanically, and the embodiment of generated wisdom. 67.

She is skilled in playing the jhallarī drum; she is surrounded by waters that gurggle and splash; she is to be worshipped by the jhiṃṭī flower; she produces the sound "jhāṃ"; and she possesses the jharjhara drum.

She has traversed the entire netherworld; she is capable of splitting mountains with her thunderbolt-like claws; her waves dance to the sound of her thundering; and her great banks are to be approached with reverence.
She is filled with flocks of royal swans gliding in magnificent flight; she holds a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in her hand, and she is the Great Egg (*mahāṇḍaka*) as proclaimed in the *Ḍāmara*.

She has brought forth all of nirvāṇa; she is the mother of the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa) who is sought after; she whose waters are stirred by the sound of the ḍhakka drum; and she who causes sins to be shattered and destroyed.

She is the one who satisfies through the sacred ford, the ford of fords; she who flows through the three paths, the sovereign of the thirty gods; the protector of the three worlds, the mistress of the waters, and she who is praised by all the three worlds.

She is the destroyer of the threefold suffering, the increaser of splendor and strength, the one with three targets, the savior, Tārā, who is worshipped by the hand of the Lord of Stars (the Moon). 73.

She is the purifier of the three worlds, meritorious, the giver of contentment, and the embodiment of contentment; she is the cutter of craving, the mother of all holy places, and born from the foot of Trivikrama.

Consisting of austerity, having the form of austerity, bestowing the fruits of the multitude of austerities, pervading the three worlds, she is satisfaction itself, the granter of satisfaction, and the embodiment of reality. || 75 ||

She is the beauty of the three worlds, the fourth state, and the bestower of the state beyond the fourth; she is the Fortune of the three worlds, the three-footed one, the truth, and the moonlight that dispels the darkness.

She whose essence is splendor, whose core is austerity, who dwells upon the head of the enemy of Tripura; she who is the embodiment of the three Vedas, who is slender, and who removes the fear of Yama, the son of the Sun. 77.
She has crossed over the enemy that must be traversed, she has satisfied all her ancestors, she is devoid of the scales [of deceit], and she is a fierce fire to the cotton-wool of evil deeds. 78.
She is the subduer of poverty, skillful, difficult to behold, adorned with divine ornaments; she possesses initiation, is hard to attain, and bears water as sweet as grapes.

She who displays manifold wonders, who removes the suffering that is difficult for the wicked to overcome, who takes away wretchedness, and who destroys sin—she is born from the lotus-feet of the enemy of the Dānavas.

She is the destroyer of the venom of biting serpents, the one who has torn asunder the continuous succession of the flood of evils; she is swift, hidden by trees, irresistible, and the slayer of the afflictions of sin.

She is the one to be grasped with firm resolve, the mother of the gods, the revealer of the world of the gods; she is the goddess beloved by the God of gods, the bestower of the station of the guardians of the quarters. || 82 ||
She bestows long life, she is long itself, the milch-cow, free from blemish; she flows with milk and water, she is to be milked, divine, and the giver of divine states.

The celestial river is the refuge for the wretched, the remover of the bodies of embodied beings, exceedingly long, the destroyer of feverish affliction, and the one who has destroyed the succession of sins.
She wanders through distant lands, difficult to approach, and is beloved by the gods; she destroys the wicked, is unfathomable, the reservoir of compassion, and merciful. || 85 ||
Difficult to approach, characterized by the virtue of generosity, the one who brings about transformation, praised by Brahmā, the purifier of Daityas and Dānavas, and the remover of evil intellect.
With generosity as its essence and compassion as its core, it pervades heaven and earth; it brings about the attainment of both seen and unseen fruits and is worshipped by hosts of deities. (87)

She who observes long vows, who possesses far-reaching vision, whose waters are radiant, who is difficult to attain; she who punishes, who is the science of punishment, and who is worshipped by those who wield the rod against the wicked.

She is the destroyer of gambling dens, the flame of forest fires, and the sole treasure-trove of liquid substances; she is the pacifier of the suffering of the wretched, the giver [of boons], and the enemy of affliction. || 89 ||
Devoted to rending mountain caves, self-controlled, and beloved by those who have subdued their senses; she has split the slopes of mountains, she is Durgā, who wanders through difficult forests.

She is the liquid of Dharma, the yoke of Dharma, the cow, the wise one, fortitude, and the eternal; she is touched by the fruit of the gift of cows, and she bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.

She carries the waves of Dharma, she is the foremost leader, the sustainer, and the ornament of the earth; she is endowed with righteousness, possesses a virtuous nature, and provides refuge at the tip of her bow.

She removes the sins of the meditator, she is the object of meditation, she is the purifier, and she has shaken off all impurity; she is the stream of Dharma, the essence of Dharma, the giver of wealth, and the increaser of prosperity. || 93 ||

She is the cutter of the qualities of merit and demerit, fond of the dhattūra flower; she is the mistress of dharma, the knower of the treatises on dharma, and the one who brings about the abundance of wealth and grain.

She is attainable through Dharma, whose waters are Dharma, and whose nature is the procreation of Dharma; her true form is accessible through meditation, and she is the Earth honored by the Sustainer. 95.
Dhūḥ, who resides in the matted locks of Śiva; Dhanyā, whose intellect possesses the power of retention; Nandā, the mother of liberation; Nandinī, who has cast away all sins. 96.

She who has warded off the entire multitude of obstacles, who manifests her own bliss, who moves through the expanse of the sky, who is worthy of praise, who is to be saluted, and who is lauded by Nārāyaṇa—[to her be my homage]. 97.
She is stainless, known as the Stainless One, the destroyer of the afflictions of asceticism, ever-restrained, the bestower of eternal bliss, and a great treasure-house of manifold wonders. || 98 ||
She is the mother of rivers, streams, and lakes; she is the leading lady and the celestial pool; she is the one whose intellect rescues the lost, and she bestows the joy of the Nandana grove.
Having cleansed all the worlds, she is free from attachment, free from affliction, without support, beyond phenomenal proliferation, and has destroyed all great impurities.

She who gives birth to stainless knowledge, who removes the suffering of all living beings without exception, who is eternally festive and eternally satisfied—she, the stainless one, is worthy of salutation.
She is established in perfection, free from fear, untainted, and of an immovable nature; she is irreproachable, effortless, and dwells upon the head of the Blue-and-Red One (Śiva).

Praised by hosts of Nandikeśvara and the Bhrṅgis, the daughter of the Mountain, who brings joy to the Nāgas, is free from obstacles; she is the celestial river and the long ship for crossing the ocean of hell.
Bestower of merit, containing merit within, meritorious, a river of even greater merit; vast, yielding abundant fruit, full, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before her.
The giver of life, the mother of all living beings, the mistress of life, whose form is life itself; she who dwells in the lotus, the Supreme Power, the most beloved of the Conqueror of Cities.
She is the attainment of the higher and lower fruits, the purifier, and the nourishing one; she is supreme bliss, the most excellent goal, the supreme foundation, and the protector.
Chanted in the Purāṇas, she is the beloved one whose form is the syllable Om (praṇava); endowed with love for Pārvatī, she is the liberator from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
She is the very nature of the Supreme Self, the illuminator of the Supreme Brahman; she is the vibration of supreme bliss and the embodiment of expiation.
She is the water and form of nirvāṇa, devoted to providing protection; she is a forest fire to the fuel of sin, the enemy of sin, and the destroyer of sin.

She is the mother of supreme sovereignty, wisdom itself, the wise one, both transcendent and immanent; she is the manifest Lakṣmī, the lotus-eyed goddess, who flows with the nectar of the supreme void.
She is of serene form, a pure vow, and a deity manifest before one's eyes; she is supremely pleased by the wielder of the Pināka bow and holds a water-pot like that of the Lord of Creatures.
Born from the water-offering at the feet of Padmanābha, she is garlanded with lotuses; she bestows supreme prosperity, grants nourishment, is wholesome, fulfills, and is radiant.
She is the purifier, the destroyer of the womb of the drinker, and the shatterer of the mountain of sin; she possesses fruit, holds fruit in her hand, and has eyes like blossoming lotuses.

The great field of her body was rent open; she was the ornament of the world of serpents; she drove away the elephants under the guise of foam; and she possessed the fragrance of blooming white water-lilies.
Resembling streams of clear water with froth upon them, they have utterly eradicated all sins; their waters are as sweet as molasses and are turbid with wholesome, infused decoctions.

The Mother of the Universe, the Sovereign of the Universe, the All-pervading, the Beloved of the Lord of the Universe; she who is devoted to Brahman, the Creator of Brahman, the Power of Brahman, most established in Brahman, and possessing pure waters.
She is Vibhāvarī, Virajā, Vikrāntānekaviṣṭapā, Viśvamitrā, Viṣṇupadī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vaiṣṇavapriyā.

She is the beloved of Virūpākṣa, the source of prosperity, and faces in every direction; she is the river Vipāśā, belonging to the gods, to be known, and the flowing essence of the syllables of the Vedas.
Vidyāvegavatī, Vandyā, Bṛṃhaṇī, Brahmavādinī, Varadā, Viprakṛṣṭā, Variṣṭhā, and Viśodhanī. || 19 ||
Vidyādharī, Viśokā, and Vayovṛndaniṣevitā; Bahūdakā, Balavatī, Vyomasthā, and Vibudhapriyā. (120)
Her speech is as sacred as the Vedas, her wealth is the river of Brahma-vidyā; its waters pervade millions of cosmic eggs, and she removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
She is the form of Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu; she is the intellect that increases prosperity, the Vaiśya woman who bestows the pleasures of enjoyment, the all-pervading one, and the source of virtue.
She whose abode is the crest of the bull-bannered god, who destroys the distress of those in calamity, she who is disciplined, humble, the daughter of the Sun, and endowed with modesty.
She is skilled in playing the lute, expert in the art of flute-playing, bestowing radiance, granting strength, and uprooting impurities by means of her power.
Free from sin, devoid of fear, and abandoned by conceptual construction; she is the bringer of rain, whose waters are rain, the ritual procedure itself, and whose bonds are severed. (25)

She is the embodiment of vows, the embodiment of wealth, the destroyer of many obstacles; she is the stream of riches (Vasudhārā), the earth (Vasumatī), the one of variegated limbs, and the source of light (Vibhāvasu).
Vijayā, Viśvabījā, Vāmadevī, Varapradā, Vṛṣāśritā, Viṣaghnī, Vijñānormi, and Aṃśumālinī. (27)

She is the capable one, the possessor of enjoyments, the auspicious one, Bhavānī, the creator of beings, the sustainer of all creatures, the remover of fear, and the destroyer of the poverty of her devotees. || 28 ||

She who bestows enjoyment and liberation; she who grants heaven and final emancipation to her devotees; she who flows from the chariot of Bhagīratha; she who is radiant as the sun; she who possesses fortune and enjoyment; she who is the support of all. || 29 ||

She who loves existence and yet hates worldly existence; she who bestows prosperity and is adorned with ashes; she who knows the inner intent of the one with the eye on his forehead (Śiva); she who is the sovereign of the past, the future, and the present.
She quiets delusive knowledge, she who has shattered the pavilion of the cosmic egg; she is the bestower of abundance, easily attained through devotion, and visible only to the eyes of the fortunate.

She who has shattered the host of calamities, who bestows the pleasure of various foods and edibles, who is to be sought as alms, the mother of mendicants, and whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence—(32).
Mandākinī, Mahānandā, Mātā, Muktitaṅgiṇī, Mahodayā, Madhumatī, Mahāpuṇyā, and Mudākarī. || 33 ||
Praised by sages, the destroyer of delusion, the great sacred ford, flowing with honey; belonging to Mādhava, proud, venerable, she who transcends the path of desires. (34)
She is the giver of liberation, the giver of intelligence, the foremost, and she is resorted to by people of great fortune; she possesses great speed, is pure, and is adorned with great majesty.
She is of great majesty, vast, with eyes as tremulous as a fish; she is filled with great compassion, possesses great supernatural power, and is like a great blue lotus.
She is the personified beauty of liberation, adorned with ornaments of gems and rubies; dressed in attire of pearl necklaces, she delights both the mind and the eyes.

She is the destroyer of heaps of great sins, she who takes half of Mahādeva’s body, she who wears a garland of great waves, she who is liberated, the Great Goddess, and she who transcends the mind. 38.

She is the moonlight that dispels the darkness of illusion, attainable through the arising of great merit; she is the Great Knowledge, the Great Illusion, the Great Intellect, and the Great Medicine. (39)
Wearing garlands, possessing great means, adorned with great serpents, she is the pacifier of great delusion and the most auspicious among all that is auspicious. || 140 ||
Moving within the orb of the sun, she is Mahālakṣmī, free from intoxication; she is Yaśasvinī and Yaśodā, the worthy one who is served by those with disciplined minds.

She bestows the perfection of yoga, she is worthy of worship, she is fulfilled by the Lord of Sacrifice; she is the Mistress of Sacrifice, the giver of the fruit of sacrifice, she who is to be worshipped, and the bringer of glory.

She who is to be worshipped, the source of yoga, the Yoginī who bestows disciplined intellect, the giver of the knowledge of yoga, she who is disciplined and endowed with the eightfold yoga beginning with restraint (yama). 43.
She restrains the movement of the flood of sins, wards off the realm of Yama, brings peace to the cycle of coming and going, and cuts asunder all forms of torment.
She is the moon of the night, pure with snow, free from the dharma of the ages; she is Revatī, the creator of delight, the beautiful one, the womb of jewels, Ramā, and Rati.
She is the vessel of love for the mine of jewels, the knower of flavors whose very form is nectar; she dwells within palaces of gems and is a most delightful river.
She is the radiance of jewels, the delight of Rudra, the destroyer of passion and hatred; she is Ramā, the beautiful woman of lovely form, who takes the form of a life-saving medicine for the sick.

She who creates delight, who is enchanting, who is beautiful, who is radiant, who removes disease; she who is like a royal swan, who possesses jewels, and whose rows of waves shine brilliantly. || 48 ||

She is the line of beauty, the enemy of pain, and the subduer of the wrath of disease; she is the one who pacifies the suffering caused by the digit of the moon, the delightful one, and the one whose voice resounds like a bumblebee.
She who delights Śiva, she who is a treasure-trove of beauty and loveliness, the mother of the world, honored by the world, and garlanded with shimmering waves. (150)
Līlāvatī is the ground of the world, the moonlight for the eyes of the people, a celestial river, charming, swift-moving, and the remover of [the sense of] lightness.
She whose hands are like waves of graceful dance, who moves with charming rhythmic breaks, the ornament of the world, the sustainer of the world, and exalted by supermundane virtues. || 52 ||
She is the welfare of the three worlds, the Goddess Lakṣmī marked by auspicious signs, whose liberation is characterized by divine play, and who showers the nectar of loveliness.
The Vaiśvānarī Vāsaveḍyā removes barrenness; she destroys the dust from the feet of Vāsudeva and wards off the thunderbolt of Indra.
She is the possessor of auspiciousness, the one whose fruits are auspicious, peace itself, and the beloved of Śāntanu; she holds the trident, possesses a youthful age, is cool, and flows with nectar.

She is the radiant one, possessed of virtue, who has dried up all sins; she is the refuge, the bestower of auspiciousness, the disciplined one, the mother of him who was born from a reed, and the auspicious one.
Śakti is as stainless as the moon, esteemed by the sister of Śamana; she is tranquility itself, the destroyer of the path to death, and the great beloved of the blue-throated Lord.

She is the pure one, the purifier, the remnant, and she who arose from the feet of the one who reclines upon the remnant; she is the sacred tradition of Śrīnivāsa, faith, the illustrious one, prosperity, and she whose vows are auspicious.

She is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā), the Whirlpool of Auspiciousness (Śubhāvartā), the Joy of Sacred Learning (Śrutānandā), and the Praise of the Vedas (Śrutistuti). She is the Destroyer of the Opposite of Śiva (Śivetaraghnī), the Śabara Woman (Śabarī), and the One who assumes the form of Śambarī (Śāṃbarīrūpadhāriṇī).
