She is the purifier of the cremation ground, the peaceful one, eternally praised by those who possess a hundredfold fortitude; she is the graceful one, rich with the splendor of rice, and she bears within her the one whose vehicle is the peacock.
Her conduct is praiseworthy, and she has eradicated all sins; she is endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers and is the embodiment of the Veda with its six limbs.
The river that removes impotence, the one with eight streams, the one flowing from the mountains, the lord of rivers, the best of streams, the flavorful one, the radiant one, and the celestial pond.
Sarasvatī is the celestial river, the destroyer of all suffering, the great medicine for all diseases, the attainable perfection, the virtuous woman, the eloquent speech, and the mother of Skanda.
She is the river of perfect attainment, worthy of praise, whose abode is upon the crest of Śiva; she bestows steadfastness, is auspicious and blissful, and grants good fortune among women.
She is the subtle ladder to heaven, the sacrificial offerings of *svadhā* and *svāhā*, and the water of nectar; she has the form of the ocean, belongs to heaven, and is the enemy of all sins.
Sītā is remembered as the remover of sins and a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence; she is Saubhāgyasundarī, the Twilight (Sandhyā), endowed with the essence of all things.

She who is dear to Hara, whose senses are under her control, who has the form of a swan, who is golden-hued; she who removes the multitude of sins, who acts for the benefit of others, who is effortless playfulness, and who destroys the pride of those whose sins have been removed.

Bestower of security, washer away of the flood of sins, dispeller of the base, and patient—O Pitcher-born One (Agastya), by reciting these thousand names of Gaṅgā correctly, a person shall obtain the full fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
It pacifies all sins, destroys all obstacles, is superior to the recitation of all hymns of praise, and is the purifier of all that purifies. (69)
O Sage, by reciting this even once with faith, one obtains the fruit of a single sacrifice; it bestows desired results and brings about the prosperity of the four aims of life.
Whatever fruit is declared for one who has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices, that same fruit is obtained from reciting this at the three times of day.
O Vāḍava, by reciting this with self-restraint at the three junctions of the day, one obtains the same fruit as the merit gained from all vows when they have been correctly performed.
O Sage, wherever one may recite this at the time of bathing in any body of water, the Ganges, which flows through the three paths, is surely present there.
One who seeks excellence attains excellence; one who seeks wealth attains wealth; one who seeks desires obtains desires; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation.
By reciting this with faith for one year at the three times of day, with a pure mind, and by approaching his wife during the proper season, a sonless man shall obtain a son. (75)
O Sage, for one who recites the thousand names of the Gaṅgā with faith, there shall be no untimely death, nor any fear of fire or thieves.
Having recited the thousand names of Gaṅgā, one should proceed to another village; one attains the accomplishment of one's purpose and enters one's home free from obstacles.

At that time, no defect arising from the lunar day, the weekday, the asterism, or the astrological conjunction shall prevail, provided that a person recites this hymn and then proceeds to another village.
The Thousand Names of Gaṅgā produce long life and health, destroy all calamities, and grant all perfections to men. (79)
Whatever sin has been fully accumulated over thousands of previous births shall go to its destruction through the recitation of the thousand names of Gaṅgā. (180)

O Sage, [these are]: the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief of gold, the violator of the Guru’s bed, one who associates with them, the killer of an embryo, the slayer of a mother, and the slayer of a father. (81)
A betrayer of trust, a poisoner, an ungrateful person, a slayer of friends, an arsonist, a killer of cows, and a thief of the teacher's property; || 82 ||
Even one joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) or even joined with minor sins (upapātaka), is liberated by reciting the Thousand Names of Gaṅgā with faith. 83.
Enveloped by mental and physical ailments and overwhelmed by terrible torments, one is liberated from all sufferings by reciting this hymn. (84)
One whose self is disciplined, reading with devotion for a year, shall obtain his desired perfection and be liberated from all sins. || 85 ||
Even for one whose mind is possessed by doubt, who hates the Dharma, who is hypocritical, or even violent, their heart may become intent upon the Dharma.
Whatever fruit one who follows the path of the castes and stages of life, being free from desire and anger, attains through knowledge, that he obtains by the recitation of this [text]. (87)
Whatever fruit is acquired by reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one shall obtain that entire result in its completeness by reciting this [text] just once correctly. || 88 ||
Whatever merit a virtuous person obtains by giving a cow to one learned in the Vedas, that same merit is fully declared to be gained from reciting this king of hymns even once.
Whatever merit a supreme man may acquire by serving his guru for as long as he lives, that same merit one obtains by reciting [the mantra] three times a day for a year.
Whatever merit is proclaimed here as resulting from the complete study of the Vedas, one obtains that by reciting [this text] at the three junctions of the day for six months.
By the daily study of this king of hymns to the Gaṅgā, one attains devotion to Śiva, or else becomes a devotee of Viṣṇu. (92)
Whoever recites the thousand names of Gaṅgā every day, the goddess Gaṅgā shall always remain by his side as his companion.
By reciting the hymn to the Jāhnavī, one becomes worthy of worship everywhere, victorious everywhere, and attains happiness everywhere. (94)
He who recites this hymn of praise should be known as one of virtuous conduct and indeed always pure; he has performed the worship of all the gods. (95)
When he is satisfied, the Gaṅgā becomes satisfied; there is no doubt about this. Therefore, with every effort, one should honor a devotee of the Gaṅgā.
Whoever should hear this King of Hymns, which flows from the Gaṅgā, or should recite it, or cause those devoted to it to hear it, being free from deceit and greed; || 97 ||
One is liberated from the three kinds of sins arising from mind, speech, and body; in an instant, one attains sinlessness and becomes dear to the ancestors.
Beloved by all the gods and honored by all the hosts of sages, he finally ascended a celestial chariot, surrounded by hundreds of divine women.
Endowed with divine ornaments and possessed of divine enjoyments, he rejoices at will like a god in the Nandana and other celestial groves.
While the Brahmins are eating, especially at the time of the Śrāddha ceremony, one who recites this great hymn brings about the satisfaction of the ancestors.
For as many grains of rice and as many drops of water as remain there, for that many years indeed do the ancestors rejoice in heaven.
Just as the ancestors are gratified by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at the Gaṅgā, so too shall they be satisfied by the recitation of this hymn during a śrāddha ceremony.
In whose house this hymn is written and worshipped, there is no fear of sin; that residence is always pure.
O Agastya, what is the use of speaking at length? Listen to my certain word; no doubt should be entertained here, for in a matter of uncertainty there is no fruit.
However many hymns and various networks of mantras exist in the mortal world, none of them are equal to this king of hymns dedicated to Gaṅgā’s son.
Whoever recites these thousand names throughout their life shall not enter a womb again, even if they die in the land of Kīkaṭa.
He who, being constantly observant of his vows, recites this supreme hymn—even if he perishes elsewhere, he shall die upon the banks of the Gaṅgā.
This most excellent and delightful hymn was formerly proclaimed by the wielder of the Pināka bow to Viṣṇu, his own devotee, as the locus of the seed-syllables of liberation.
This hymn uttered by me is a substitute for bathing in the Gaṅgā; therefore, a wise person desiring to bathe in the Jāhnavī should recite this hymn. (210)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand Names of Gaṅgā," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya; that King Bhagīratha, desiring to uplift his ancestors, propitiated the illustrious Mahādeva.
The best of royal sages, by means of great asceticism, brought back to the earth all those who had been utterly consumed by the curse of Brahmā and had gone to the third path.
Then, for the great benefit of all three worlds, the king brought the Gaṅgā to the place where Maṇikarṇikā was located.
Ānandakānana is the singular excellent field of the Supreme Brahman for Śambhu, and Cakrapuṣkariṇī is that of Hari; both bestow liberation through divine play.
The son of Dilīpa, walking ahead, led her to that Gaṅgā, where the city renowned as Kāśī stands, which reveals the light of liberation.
The great field of Avimukta has never been relinquished by Śambhu at any time; for it is itself, O Sage, like priceless, noble Jāmbūnada gold.
Furthermore, if even a diamond is joined with a superior gem, how much more so is the Cakrapuṣkariṇī tīrtha the very seat of all auspicious things?
Then, even more excellent than the jewel-ear-ornament of Śambhu, [is that which is] in that Avimukta, the abode of Śiva, within the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana).
Liberation was already fully accomplished even before that, yet it became even greater through contact with the Gaṅgā; from the moment that Gaṅgā arrived at Maṇikarṇikā. || 9 ||
From that time forward, even for the gods, that sacred field became difficult to attain, regardless of whether they had performed many auspicious or otherwise deeds.
Having cast those [impurities] away in an instant, one residing in Kāśī becomes immortal, even without the practice of *nididhyāsana* upon that which is to be known through the Vedāntas. || 11 ||
Established in Kāśī, one becomes immortal even without Sāṃkhya or Yoga, O Pot-born Sage, provided one possesses the knowledge that uproots karma.
By the grace of the Moon-crested Lord, one residing in Kāśī shall become immortal, whether by effort or without effort, upon casting off the body in due time.
By the instruction of Tāraka, one residing in Kāśī shall become immortal, even if bound by the material qualities (guṇas) perfected through many previous births. 14.

By means of the yoga of non-differentiation, one established in Kāśī becomes immortal. Indeed, the casting off of the body here is charity; indeed, the casting off of the body here is austerity. (158)

In this Kāśī, the renunciation of the body is indeed Yoga that brings about the bliss of Nirvāṇa; for even one who has committed most heinous sins, having reached Kāśī where the river flows northward, [attains liberation].
Having effortlessly abandoned their own [worlds], they would go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which the gods headed by Yama, Indra, and Agni behold as those intent upon the path of liberation.
Having gazed upon all of them, they all provided protection before the city; and they took up a sword of great form, which shatters evil thoughts and wickedness.
The gods created the river Dhunī, which shakes off those who enter with evil intent, and they established there the Varaṇā, which wards off obstacles to the sacred field.
O gods, having established the Varaṇā river on the southern and northern sides as the means for turning back both evil conduct and excellent conduct, O gods; (20)
May they obtain liberation, the final entrustment of the field, and peace; [one should worship] that Dehalīvināyaka in the western quarter of the field.
The moon-crested Lord himself took charge for the sake of protection, for those who had been granted permission to enter by the compassionate Viśveśvara.
They grant entrance [to such people] and never to others; for this purpose, I shall relate an ancient legend, most wonderful and supreme, which increases devotion to Kāśī. (23)
Skanda said: On the shore of the southern ocean, near the Setubandha, there was a certain merchant named Dhanañjaya who was endowed with devotion to his mother.
He acquired wealth by means of the path of merit; he satisfied seekers with his riches; his fame was spread abroad by those very seekers; and he was a worshiper of the son of Yaśodā. || 25 ||
Though elevated by his prosperity, he kept his neck bowed with humility; for even though he was a mine of virtues, he concealed his own excellence before those possessed of virtue.
Though possessed of noble physical perfection, he turned his back on the wives of others; though endowed with all auspicious marks, his rising was always free from stain.

O Sage, although he was by caste other than a Brahmin, he lived a life of both truth and falsehood, yet for the most part he was fond of truth; and though not of the highest rank, he was praised in the world as one whose appearance was like that of pure gold.
Though he was always engaged in virtuous conduct, traveling on easy conveyances, and accomplished in his duties, that wise man, despite not being poor, became one whose mind was impoverished by sin.
As he was living in this manner, after some time had passed, his mother met her end, having been afflicted by disease and overcome by extreme old age.
And by her, having attained youth—which is as fickle as the shadow of a cloud and like the flood of a river in the rainy season—her own husband was utterly deceived.
That woman who, having attained youth, deceives her husband out of delusion for even three or four days, shall go to an inexhaustible hell. || 32 ||
For even if a husband is devoted to righteousness, he will fall from the heaven earned through merit by violating the chastity of his wives; therefore, chastity must be guarded by a woman. (33)
The evil-minded person falls himself into the hell that is a pit of excrement; he remains there until the dissolution of all beings, after which he becomes a village pig.
Furthermore, she may be a *valgulī* that drinks its own excrement and hangs from trees; or she may be an owl (*ulūkī*) who is blind by day and dwells in the hollows of trees. (35)
This body, which is a vessel for meritorious deeds, must be protected with great effort from the touch of another woman—a touch that is unpleasant yet consists of a mere semblance of pleasure. (36)
Indeed, did not Satī, by the mere command of her husband, paralyze the rising sun with this very body that was offered for his sake? (37)
Did not Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, who was devoted solely to her husband’s vows, bear the three Vedas in her womb through the power of her devotion to her husband? (38)
In this world there is vast fame, as well as imperishable residence in heaven; through devotion to her husband, a woman may obtain these, along with friendship with Śrī herself. (39)
Having abandoned the eternal duty toward her husband through wicked conduct, she became a woman who acted according to her own whims and, upon death, ascended to hell.
And Dhanañjaya also, O Sage, having practiced penance together with a certain Śiva-yogin, thus became devoted to dharma.
The righteous Dhanañjaya, devoted to his mother, then took his mother's bones and set out upon the path toward the Gaṅgā. (42)

Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then indeed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), having smeared it with the yakṣakardama paste, and having worshipped it with flowers; || 43 ||
Then, having wrapped [it] with a cloth for the eyes, then indeed with a silken garment, then with a fragrant cloth, and then with a madder-dyed cloth.
Then, having placed the limbs of his mother in a copper casket using Nepalese blankets and pure clay, the merchant—oh!—[proceeded].
Untouched by low birth, pure, and sleeping on the bare ground, Dhanañjaya remained in the middle of the road even while afflicted by fever.
He made someone a carrier of his burden after giving him the appropriate wages; what more need be said, O Pot-born One? Thus, he indeed reached Kāśī.
Having taken up the porter for the sake of protecting the provisions, Dhanañjaya went to the market to fetch some goods such as food and other necessities.
Having found another capable of carrying the burden, he took a copper casket from the midst of his provisions; and having ascertained that it contained wealth, he went home.
Then, having returned to his dwelling and not seeing him, Dhanañjaya, observing that the preparations were missing the copper casket, became anxious.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! and beating his heart, he lamented intensely many times; having looked here and there for him, he followed after him.
Without having bathed in the Jāhnavī and without having beheld the Lord of the World, Dhanañjaya reached the dwelling place of that bearer of burdens.
Even Bhāravāṭ, having seen those bones within a copper casket in the middle of a vast forest, sighed deeply, abandoned them, and went home.
Then the merchant, having reached that house with his throat, lips, and palate parched, saw a piece of cloth inside the grass hut.
Taking heart with some hope, he questioned his wife: "Speak the truth; you need not fear. I shall certainly give you something else as well. (55)
"O Vasu, where has your husband gone? Give us these bones of your mother. We are pilgrims, O blessed lady; we shall not cause you any sorrow. (56)
"Out of ignorance and under the influence of greed, he took this casket of bones; this is his fault, O blessed lady, not mine, for such was my mother’s deed. (57)
Or rather, there is no fault in my mother; I am the unfortunate one, her son. O Bhilla woman, I have not attained that which ought to be accomplished by a son.
I have exerted my efforts, yet it has not succeeded due to my misfortune; let the forest-dweller come because of my truthful word, and let him not fear.
"Show me the bones quickly; I shall give you even more wealth than that. Thus addressed by him, the Bhilla woman spoke to her husband. (60)
Then, with his head bowed in shame, that Śabara reported the entire account and led Dhanañjaya into the depths of the forest.
Then, O Sage, the forest-dweller, having by fate forgotten that place, fell into confusion regarding the directions and wandered about in the forest.
From that forest he goes to another forest, and from that forest he proceeds further; wandering from forest to forest, that forest-dweller too becomes exhausted.
Leaving the middle of the forest, that best of pilgrims wandered for two or three days and went to his own settlement.
Emaciated by hunger, with his throat and lips parched, lamenting "Alas! Alas!", the merchant returned once more to the city of Kāśī with a withered countenance. (865)
O Sage, having heard that misfortune from the people, the pilgrim went to Gayā and Prayāga, and then returned to his own country.
O Pot-born Sage, even after entering Kāśī, those bones departed from that very moment without the permission of the Lord of the Universe.
Thus, even having entered Kāśī, a sinner does not obtain the fruit of the sacred field due to his association with unrighteousness; at that very moment, he is cast outside.
Therefore, the command of Viśveśvara alone is the cause for residing here in Kāśī; for both the Asi and the Varaṇā have been appointed there to guard the sacred field.
From that time on, O great sage, it became renowned as Vārāṇasī; having reached the confluence of the Asi and the Varaṇā, it is known as Kāśikā.

In this Vārāṇasī, where the divine form consisting of compassion has cast off its body with ease, may that path—which, having suddenly entered the splendor of the gaze of Viśveśvara, assumes that very form—be extended for you.

O living being, you have been born and died many times in various excellent holy places, yet never did peace come to you by immersing yourself there. Now, having heard the praise of Vārāṇasī, attain immortality and, by my power, become a disciple of the Subduer of Desire (Śiva).

A twice-born man who falls into the waters of any other sacred ford attains the state of a god or similar being, but not so in Kāśī; it is a marvel that one fallen here does not attain rebirth again—not even a Pulkasa, let alone one of noble birth.

This city is not the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence; rather, it is the City-Destroyer, the Foe of Tripura, who, desiring the supreme human goal within it, leads his succession of citizens to perfection.

A person who has bathed in various other sacred fords (tīrthas) and cast off his defiled body shall become a deity in heaven; however, having abandoned the body in the vicinity of Vārāṇasī, one becomes subject to doubt even regarding the attainment of a physical state [in the hereafter].

Vārāṇasī, by the mere act of making one equal to the gods (or through its contact), removes the suffering of common folk even for those who lack yoga; it brings that saving mantra within the range of their hearing, through which one perceives that Brahman for whom there is no rebirth.

Alas! Having abandoned in the vicinity of Vārāṇasī that slender form which grants desired objects and is the abode of dharma, artha, and kāma, you—exceedingly joyful at desiring some unknown, supreme state—have obtained a loss that has rendered even your very root void.

Surely the people dwelling in Āḥkāśī have been deceived by Him who possesses an eye upon His forehead and shares half His body with a woman; for, having taken away their cherished bodies which served as vessels for the performance of twilight rites, He bestowed upon them mere liberation from rebirth.

Vārāṇasī is the sole ground for the manifestation of boundless virtues; by the power of the Moon-bearer (Śiva) residing there, all embodied beings at the end [of their lives] become venomous in the throat, eye-possessing on the forehead, with beautiful bodies on the left half, and thereafter become bodiless.

This Ānandakānana has long been a bestower of happiness; there too is the Cakrasarasī lake, and then Maṇikarṇikā; furthermore, there is the confluence of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) and the supreme abode of the Lord of the Universe—what is there here that does not lead to liberation?

O Vārāṇasī, here you are—the most excellent river Varaṇā, the source that dispels the exhaustion of worldly existence, possessing the radiant splendor of the celestial Ganges; you are the immovable resting place for the glory of stainless liberation. Why, then, does the deluded creature neglect you and languish? 81.

Have you forgotten the mental distress born of the womb and the binding and beating inflicted by the messengers of Death? Why does a fool abandon Kāśī, which is obtainable through the acceptance of Śambhu’s grace, and go elsewhere when liberation is already in his hand? (82)

Other sacred fords instantly remove impurities, bestow great spiritual merit, and lead one to heaven through the acts of drinking their waters, bathing, and the abandonment of the body; but Vārāṇasī, alas, effects the destruction of the very root! 83.

In the vicinity of the city of Kāśī, at Maṇikarṇikā, embodied beings who cast off their bodies attain a form possessing an eye in the forehead, with blue splendor upon the neck, and a beautiful consort as half of their body—those whose harem was once separated from their lord. (84)

Having realized the incomparable power of Maṇikarṇikā, whoever casts off their person there—though it be reeking with impurities and pus—suddenly unites with the splendor of self-realization and shall never again fall into a state of separation, even throughout other kalpas.

Those whose minds are filled with defects such as passion and whose senses are agitated, who imagine the incomparable, divine city of Kāśī—possessing great majesty—to be equal to other holy places on all sides, are sinners; one should not even converse with them.

O fool, why do you depart for other directions, abandoning Vārāṇasī, the beloved capital of the Destroyer of Smara? Having attained the stable fortune of liberation—which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to obtain—why would you desire the fortune that is fickle by its very nature? (87)

Knowledge, wealth, dwellings, elephants, horses, servants, garlands, sandalwood, and most enchanting women—even heaven itself—is not unattainable here for men who possess effort; yet Vārāṇasī is difficult to reach, for it grants liberation even to moths and the like. Let the Creator, who held Vaikuṇṭha and other principal worlds on one scale along with Kāśī to test their weight, know that those worlds rose up due to their lightness, while this city remained here because of its gravity, being the abode of the four aims of human life.

Dwelling in the city of Kāśī, even gods and men, being honored with various offerings, become the one Rudra; casting off the burdens of suffering born of the nature of diverse afflictions and karma, they enter the abode of the Supreme Lord.

Having abandoned this body—which is subject to certain decay and is the abode of birth, death, and affliction—why, alas, does one not take hold of this Kashi? That deluded creature exchanges it for a body of radiant form, which is the abode of most stable supreme bliss, as if trading a manifest jewel for something worthless. (91)

Alas! Why does this world, its intellect utterly destroyed, endure grief here amidst the burdens of calamity—calamities that are substantial, certain to end in death, and which shatter all wealth? For while Kāśī exists upon the earth, where Śiva declares at the time of death, "Upon hearing [my name], one shall not enter again into the cave of the belly," why do people suffer?

Oh, how great is the distinction of a person residing in Kāśī! Even one who wanders in the forest, subsists on two or three mouthfuls of food, feeds only on air, moves about at will, and has conquered his senses—none of these possess such excellence as one who dwells in Kāśī.

For those who have performed evil deeds or those whose nature is virtuous, there is no distinction whatsoever in their destination when they reach the end in Kāśī; for the seeds produced by karma do not sprout when scorched by the fire of Śiva’s gaze upon that saline wasteland.
O Daughter of the Mountain, rabbits, mosquitoes, cranes, parrots, sparrows, wolves, jackals, horses, serpents, monkeys, and men who die in Kāśī attain the supreme nectar.

O Daughter of the Mountain King, those people residing constantly in Kāśī—who are adorned with non-terrifying rudrākṣas and lordly serpents, and who bear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the crescent moon—are considered by me to be your attendants.

However many living beings dwell here in Kāśī—whether moving in water or on land, such as fish, jackals, and the like—all of them, having attained the body of Rudra through my grace, enter into me upon the dissolution of their bodies.
O Goddess, those who are proclaimed as the Varṣeṣu Rudras in heaven, those who are the Vāteṣus in the intermediate space, and those who are the Anneṣus on earth, O Beloved; || 98 ||

The Rudras who are proclaimed by the exponents of the Vedas as being ten times ten, situated in the east, south, west, north, and those Rudras who abide in the upward direction—[all these are present]. (99)
Those thousands of Rudras who exist upon the surface of the earth are innumerable; yet all those beings in Kāśī who possess the form of Rudra are superior to them all.

Therefore, O Pot-born One, Avimukta is declared to be the abode of Rudra; consequently, one should worship those residing in Kāśī, whether they belong to the castes or to those outside the castes, and whether they belong to the [four] stages of life or otherwise.
A person who worships Rudra with faith and the understanding that he is the Lord partakes in the fruit [of that action]. || 2 ||
By the word *śma*, a corpse (*śava*) is expressed, and by *śāna*, lying down (*śayana*) is meant; O Sage, those skilled in the meaning of words explain the sense of *śmaśāna* in this way. (3)
Moreover, when the dissolution has arrived, even great beings lie here having become corpses; therefore, this is a truly great cremation ground.

The abundant water here goes to dissolution in the waters; the waters [go] into the fierce cave of the mouth of Aurva; the great fire goes into the wind; and the wind always perishes in the sky. || 5 ||

The ether also goes to dissolution in the ego; that [ego], together with the sixteen transformations, dissolves into the Great Principle known as the intellect (buddhi); here, the Great Principle becomes absorbed within primordial nature (prakṛti).

She, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), remains enveloping that qualityless Puruṣa; this twenty-fifth principle, the supreme Puruṣa, is the master of the house of the body, the individual soul (jīvaka).

This is called the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya), in which Hari, Rudra, and the swan-vehicled Brahmā are excluded; then the Supreme Lord, the embodiment of Time, effortlessly swallows even that Puruṣa.
He is indeed called Mahāviṣṇu by the wise; they proclaim him to be Mahādeva. That Śiva is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; he is the Lord of Śrī, and he is also the Lord of Pārvatī.

Furthermore, at the daily dissolution as well as the [great] pralaya, Hara, adorned with the great bones of Saṃvarta, lifts his own city up upon the tip of his trident and sustains it; therefore, Kāśī is indeed devoid of the influence of the Kali age.
Skanda said: O twice-born one, Ānandakānana is called Vārāṇasī, Kāśī, Rudrāvāsa, and likewise Mahāśmaśāna.

Thus was it proclaimed before the Goddess by Śambhu, the God of gods; just as it was previously told to Viṣṇu, so too have I heard it. And that great secret concerning Kāśī has been related by me in your presence.
Having recited this meritorious chapter, which destroys great sins, and having properly caused the twice-born to hear it, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
After this, O Pot-born one, what do you wish to hear? Tell me that; for the story of Kāśī being told brings me great satisfaction. (114)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Vārāṇasī," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||
Agastya said: O omniscient one, delighter of the heart, you who have crushed Tāraka, I do not reach satiety while listening to the story of Vārāṇasī.
If there is grace toward me, and if I am worthy to hear it, then tell me, O Lord Bhairava, the sacred narrative concerning Kāśī.
Who is this one named Bhairava established here in the city of Kāśī? What is his form, what is his activity, and what indeed are his names?
And how indeed is he propitiated so as to grant success to the practitioner? Where and at what time must Bhairava be propitiated so that he quickly bestows accomplishment? || 4 ||
Skanda said: O highly fortunate one, I consider that no one else possesses such love for Vārāṇasī as you do; therefore, I shall describe it to you in its entirety.
This is the manifestation of Bhairava, which destroys great sins; by hearing it, one shall obtain without obstacle the fruit of residing in Kāśī.

Having squeezed the entire cosmic egg between his two hands with great firmness and repeatedly wringing it out—resembling the lofty fruit of a ripe mango tree—the Great Bhairava, drinking those juices again and again from every side like one intoxicated, danced with the grandeur of a tāṇḍava, and thus brought the three worlds to their end.
O Pot-born One, even Vaikuṇṭha with his four arms and Viśvakṛt with his four faces do not truly know the majesty of the Great Lord.
O Brāhmaṇa, there is nothing surprising in this: the illusion of Bhava (Śiva) is difficult to transcend. Deluded by it, everyone fails to perceive even that Supreme Being.
If he were to reveal himself, he alone would be the Supreme Lord; then Brahmā and the others would find him by his own will, yet they do not know him.
Though all-pervading, that Great Lord, who delights in his own self, is not perceived; he who transcends mind and speech is understood by the deluded to be like a god.
Long ago, O Brahmin, on a peak of Mount Meru, the great sages bowed down to the Grandfather, the Lord of the World, and asked: "What is the one imperishable reality? (12)
By that [power] of Maheśa, which is equal [to his other attributes], the source of the world was deluded; not perceiving the supreme state, he called himself a sage.
I am the source of the universe, the sustainer, the self-existent, the sole Lord; I am the beginningless Brahman, and without worshipping me, one is not liberated. 14.
For I alone am the initiator of the worlds, and I alone am their withdrawer; there is no one else superior to me, truly none at all, O best of gods. (15)
While the Creator was speaking thus, Kratu, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa, spoke these words with a smile, his eyes copper-red with rage.
Without having realized the supreme reality, why is this being propounded? This ignorance on the part of one joined in yoga is not at all fitting for you. (17)
"I am indeed the creator of the worlds; the sacrifice is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme. O Unborn Brahmā, the life of the worlds does not exist apart from me. (18)

"Cast off these deceptive appearances without delay; behold this wonder as I immediately render her free from all affliction. (56)
Upon seeing this painted canvas, she immediately fell into a state of agitation; surely there is someone here who is the object of her love. (57)
Therefore, from the touch of the painted cloth, she will abandon her torment; and from the words of the personified intellect, her attendants [will do the same]. (58)
Placing it before her, they said: "O Kalāvati, look at this painting; there exists some beloved deity therein who will bring you joy. (59)
She too, as if receiving a sprinkling of nectar through the name of her chosen deity and the sight of that painting, cast off her fainting fit and rose up quickly. (60)
Like medicinal herbs withered by drought that are revived by showers of rain, she gazed once more upon Jñānadā, the pool of wisdom.
Having touched that pond, even though it was depicted in a painting, Kalāvatī obtained knowledge of her other existence, just as she had been in her previous birth.
He reflected once more upon the supreme majesty of the Vāpī: "Aha! Even this [image] depicted in the painting has been touched by the Jñānavāpī."
Then, delighted, the beautiful woman spoke before them: "He has generated in me knowledge arising from my previous existence. (64)
Kalāvatī spoke of her own account from a previous birth, born of the power of Jñānavāpī: "Prior to this birth, I was the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa. (65)
Having settled at the Lord of the Universe in Kāśī, by the Jñānavāpī, I rejoice with delight; my father is Harisvāmī and my mother is Priyaṃvadā.
"My name is Suśīlā," she said, and then a Vidyādhara carried me off; thus, in the middle of the path at midnight, I reached Mount Malaya.
The hero, being struck by the Rākṣasa, slew that Rākṣasa; and the Rākṣasa, being released from the curse, attained a divine body.
That Gandharva obtained birth from Malayaketu; I became Kalāvatī, the daughter of the King of Karṇāṭa.
"Thus has this knowledge arisen in me in an instant from the sight of the Pool of Knowledge. Having heard these words of hers, she too was the embodied Intelligence (Buddhi).
And those female attendants of hers then became joyful of countenance; they bowed down and spoke to that Puṇyaśīlā Kalāvatī.
"Aha! How indeed might she be obtained, she whose power is such as this? Fie on the birth of those in this mortal world who have not beheld the Pool of Knowledge! (72)
O Kalāvati, salutations to you; grant that we may fulfill our desire and make our birth fruitful by requesting the king on our behalf. (73)
And this is our resolve, O Kalāvati: from this day forward, having beheld that Pool of Knowledge, we shall enjoy great pleasures. (74)
That pool of knowledge must certainly be so by name, for it is a marvel that even when depicted here in a painting, it bestows wisdom upon you.
Having acknowledged their words and concealed her own true feelings, she, who was skilled in discerning the proper occasion, spoke after having done what was pleasing to the lord of the earth.
Kalāvatī said: "O Lord of my life, there is nothing anywhere more dear to me than you. O King, having obtained you as my husband, all my heart's desires have been fulfilled. (77)
"O noble son, there is one wish that I have here which deserves to be sought; it is highly beneficial and has entered the path of your own deliberation as well. (78)
But for me, who am dependent on you, this great desire is exceedingly difficult to attain; whereas for you, whose conduct is self-dependent, your wish is almost as good as accomplished. (79)
O Lord of my life, what is the use of speaking at length? If you have need of my life, then grant me my desire; otherwise, my life-breaths shall depart.
Having heard her words, which were dearer to him than his own life, the king spoke these words that were pleasing to both her and himself.

The king said: "O beloved, O beautiful woman, I see nothing here that cannot be given to you; even my very life has been purchased by you through the qualities of your character, arts, and virtues. (82)
"Speak without delay; consider it done, O Kalāvatī! For virtuous women such as you, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be attained. (83)
Who is to be entreated, what is to be entreated for, or who is the petitioner, my dear? O Kalāvati, our conduct is not at all like that of ordinary people.
The kingdom, the treasury, the army, the fortress, and whatever else there may be, O beautiful lady—all that is yours; I have nothing here except for mere sovereignty. (85)
And that sovereignty belongs to me alone, O mistress of my life, with the sole exception of you; O proud one, at your word I would renounce even this kingdom, treating it as a blade of grass. (86)
Having heard these words of King Mālyaketu, Kalāvatī spoke these charming words in a deep voice.

Kalāvatī said: "O Lord, in the beginning, various kinds of creatures were created by the Creator of Beings; for the welfare of those creatures, the four aims of human life (puruṣārthacatuṣṭaya) were established. (88)
Even birth devoid of that [virtue] is as futile as a bubble on the water; therefore, even a single [virtuous act] should be accomplished for the sake of happiness both in this world and the next.
"Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish; what has been stated by those who know the past is seen to be true. (90)
"You have a hundred slave-girls like me here in your palace; nevertheless, my lord’s love for me is seen to be exceedingly great. (91)
Even your maidservant is rich in enjoyments; how much more so she who dwells upon the expanse of your lap? Moreover, she possesses no other wealth, and her husband is under her own control. (92)

The wise man should accumulate wealth for the performance of *iṣṭa* and *pūrta* rites, for the sake of austerity so that his life may be free from obstacles, and for the sake of obtaining a wife and progeny. (93)
"O dear one, all this belongs to you here through the grace of Viśveśa; if my desire is to be fulfilled, then listen as I speak. (94)
O Lord, quickly send me toward the city of Viśvanātha; my life-breaths have already departed, and I remain as nothing but a physical body. 95.
Having clearly heard these words of Kalāvatī, King Mālyaketu reflected for a moment within his heart and spoke to his beloved.
"O dear Kalāvati, if you must indeed depart, what use have I for this fickle royal fortune when it is bereft of you? (97)
They do not call it a kingdom simply because it is a kingdom; royal splendor is certainly more dear. Even that seven-limbed kingdom, when bereft of her, is regarded as mere straw.
Having enjoyed the kingdom without rivals and pleasures without interruption, the objects of the senses were fully gratified, and constancy was maintained, O beloved. (99)
"Even though offspring have been born, what remains for me to do here? We two must certainly go to the city of Vārāṇasī. (100)
Having thus consoled his beloved and having made his resolve, Mālyaketu summoned the astrologers and honored the subjects.
Then, having entrusted the kingdom to his son and taking a certain amount of various jewels for the sake of his son, the king set out for Kāśī.

Upon seeing the city of Viśveśvara, the lord of men, his hair standing on end with joy, considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose and crossed to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
Due to the connection with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of her previous birth, Queen Kalāvatī herself recognized the paths to the city, as if she had come from another village.
Then, having bathed in Maṇikarṇikā and given abundant wealth as a gift, he worshipped Viśveśa with numerous varieties of jewels.
There too, having given jewels, elephants, horses, a herd of cattle, variegated silk garments, and articles for worship; || 5 ||
Golden and silver jars, lamps, mirrors, chowries, flagstaffs, banners, and variegated canopies.
Then, having circumambulated it, he entered the Muktimaṇḍapa; there, having heard the discourse on Dharma, he also gave excellent wealth.
Having again performed the great evening worship, the lord of the earth kept a vigil there with the great festivities of the triple symphony (tauryatrika).
Then, having risen at dawn and performed the rites of purification and sipping water, the king went to the Jñānavāpī pond by the path indicated by the queen.
The king, together with Kalāvatī, bathed there joyfully; then, having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), he satiated the ancestors with faith.
There, having bestowed silver, gold, and other such items upon the vessels, he gratified the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless with various kinds of precious jewels.
Having gratified [the ascetics], the king then performed his breaking of the fast; he consecrated the Jñānavāpī with jeweled staircases, O Kalāvatī.
There, the ascetic woman took delight with her husband through fasts on alternate days and sometimes through vows lasting three days.
Furthermore, by eating only every sixth mealtime, by the observances of half-months, by fasting for the other half of the month, and by month-long fasts and so forth; || 15 ||
Through the Cāndrāyaṇa vows, Kṛcchra penances, and even by serving her husband, that sinless woman passed the remainder of her life as if it were a mere moment.
Once, while the two of them were seated after bathing at dawn in the Jñānavāpī, a certain matted-haired ascetic arrived and placed sacred ash in their hands.
And with a serene countenance, having greeted them with blessings, he said: "Arise and prepare yourselves for magnificent attire this very day."
"The rising of the Tāraka [star] will occur for you both here in an instant"—even as the matted-haired ascetic was thus speaking these words before them, [the star rose]. (19)
Then, while all the worlds were looking on, the moon-crested Lord descended from his chariot onto a celestial vehicle that resounded with the tinkling of many small bells.
Having crossed over that [ocean], he himself imparted something ineffable into the hollow of his ear; and that supreme light departed at that very moment.
Illuminating the path of the sky, even the god departed for his own abode. Skanda said: From that time forward, Jñānavāpī has been preeminent in this world.
O Sage, she bestows direct knowledge more than all the principal holy sites; she consists of all knowledge, embodies all Lingas, and is auspicious.
The manifest form is composed of Śiva himself; it bestows knowledge and is a reservoir of wisdom. There are many other holy places that also bring immediate purification.

But they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the Jñānavāpī. Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to the origin of the Jñānavāpī, for him there shall never be any loss of knowledge at the time of death.
This great narrative is meritorious and destroys even the most heinous sins; it increases the great joy of Mahādeva and Gaurī. (26)

Having read it, or caused it to be read, or having heard it endowed with faith, one who possesses knowledge is honored in the world of Śiva by means of this auspicious narrative, which is a pool of wisdom.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of Jñānavāpī," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 34 ||
The Pot-born Sage said: Avimukta is the great sacred field, the cause of supreme liberation; it is the highest of all fields and the most auspicious of all auspicious things. || 1 ||
Of all cremation grounds, the cremation ground is the supreme and greatest; of all sacred seats, it is the supreme seat; and of all saline wastes, it is the great saline waste. (2)
It is the supreme producer of the mass of Dharma for those whose minds long for the Dharma; it is the illuminator of the ultimate truth for those who seek its meaning, like a fire-chariot.
It is heard that wherever this [work] exists, there is the supreme nectar: producing desire for those who seek desire, and bestowing liberation upon those who seek liberation.
O delighter of Gaurī’s heart, having heard this supreme account of the pool of knowledge situated in a single part of the sacred field, I think thus: [5]

Even that which is of atomic dimension, yet which shines forth as Kāśī within it—that earth should be known as most vast; for its sake, one should never strive in vain anywhere else for the attainment of perfection.
How many sacred fords (tīrthas) exist here upon this entire surface of the earth? Yet, where among them could there even be equality in weight with a single particle of dust from Kāśī?
O Mine of Jewels, how many joy-bestowing rivers do not flow here? Yet, what [river] could bear comparison with the celestial river at Kāśī? || 8 ||
O Six-faced One, how many fields of liberation are there upon this earth? Yet, alas, I consider that not even a ten-millionth part of Avimukta exists among them.
Since the triple set consisting of the Gaṅgā, Viśveśvara, and Kāśī remains ever awake, what wonder is there that the fortune of ultimate liberation is obtained there? (10)
O Skanda, how is this triad invariably attained by men, especially in the Kali Yuga, when the senses are exceedingly fickle? (11)

Where is such austerity in the Kali age? Where is such yogic practice in the Kali age? Where is such observance of vows, or where is such charity in the Kali age? Therefore, how can there be liberation in the Kali age?
O Six-faced Skanda, you have declared that liberation is attained in Kāśī even without austerity, without yoga, without vows, and without gifts. (13)
"O Skanda, tell me what specific conduct must be practiced to attain Kāśī? I believe that without virtuous conduct (sadācāra), one's desires cannot be fulfilled. (14)
Right conduct is the supreme dharma; right conduct is the supreme austerity. Indeed, through right conduct life is prolonged, and through right conduct evil is destroyed. (15)
Therefore, O Six-faced One, first explain the conduct itself; speak exactly as the God of gods spoke in your presence.
Skanda said: O son of Mitra and Varuṇa, I shall describe the conduct of the virtuous which is beneficial to the good; by practicing this constantly, a man shall attain all his desires. (17)
Immobile beings, worms, aquatic creatures, birds, animals, and humans—these become increasingly righteous in this order; indeed, the gods are more righteous than these.
The first is a thousandth part of the second in sequence; all these fortunate ones remain so until they attain liberation.
Among all four classes of beings, living creatures are by far the most excellent; and among living creatures, O Sage, those who subsist by means of intelligence are the best of all. (20)
Men are superior to the wise; among them, the Brāhmaṇas are superior. Among the Brāhmaṇas, the learned are superior, and among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected are superior. (21)

O Pot-born One, those who act for the sake of those whose intellects are perfected, and who are devoted to Brahman even more than those performers—there is no one else in the three worlds to be worshipped by them.
Indeed, they honor one another because there is no distinction between their austerity and knowledge; for the Brāhmaṇa was created by Brahmā as the lord of all beings. (23)

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa—and no one else—is entitled to all that exists in the world; for one who possesses good conduct is worthy of everything, whereas one fallen from conduct is not. Consequently, a Brāhmaṇa must always be characterized by a nature devoted to good conduct. 24.
O Sage, that which the wise, free from hatred and attachment, practice—the learned know that to be right conduct, the root of dharma. (25)
Even if one is devoid of auspicious marks, if he is devoted to right conduct, full of faith, and free from malice, that man shall live for a hundred years.
One should, without laziness, always practice the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti and serves as the root of dharma in one's respective duties.
In this world, a man who delights in misconduct becomes censurable; he is overcome by diseases, always short-lived, and a partaker of great suffering. (28)

Action dependent on others should be abandoned; the body should always be kept under one's own control. For one who is dependent on others is always miserable, while one who is self-dependent is always happy.
Whatever action causes the inner self to feel serene while it is being performed—that alone should be done; never its opposite.
Since the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) have been declared to be the very essence of dharma, one who desires dharma must indeed apply effort toward them alone. (31)
Truthfulness, forbearance, straightforwardness, meditation, non-cruelty, non-violence, self-restraint, serenity, gentleness, and mildness—these are the ten *yamas*.
Purity, bathing, austerity, charity, silence, sacrifice, study, vows, fasting, and control of the generative organ—these ten are remembered as the observances (niyamas). || 33 ||
Having conquered these six enemies—namely desire, anger, pride, delusion, envy, and greed—one shall be victorious everywhere. (34)
Little by little, he should accumulate dharma like an anthill, without causing pain to others, as a companion for the world beyond. (35)
In the hereafter, only Dharma shall be one's companion; neither wealth nor kin—neither father, mother, son, brother, wife, nor other relatives—will accompany one. (36)
A living being is born alone, and likewise dies alone; alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone one experiences the fruit of evil deeds. (37)
Having abandoned the body when it has reached its fivefold state, like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, kinsmen turn away and depart; only dharma follows one as they go.
A wise person should accumulate merit, for it is a companion in the world beyond; having obtained merit as a companion, one may cross over the darkness that is so difficult to traverse.
The wise man should always cultivate relationships with the most excellent among the excellent; having abandoned those who are base and the basest, he should lead his lineage to preeminence. (40)
Moving only toward the superior and the unsurpassed while avoiding the inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence; he does not fall to the state of a Śūdra through transgression.
Death afflicts that Brahmin who is habitually neglectful of Vedic study, who transgresses the rules of right conduct, who is indolent, and who eats improper food.
Therefore, a twice-born man should always practice good conduct with diligence; even sacred pilgrimage sites long for the company of those who possess good conduct. (43)
The half-yāma at the end of the night is called the Brāhma time; having risen during that period, a wise man should always contemplate his own welfare.

First, one should meditate upon the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa), then upon the Lord (Śiva) together with his Mother (Pārvatī), then upon Śrīraṅga accompanied by Śrī, and finally upon the Lotus-born (Brahmā) with Brahmāṇī.
[He beheld] all the gods beginning with Indra, the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, and all the mountains beginning with Śrīśaila.
The oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk, the lakes beginning with Lake Mānasa, the groves beginning with Nandana, and the cows beginning with the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenu.
He [created] trees such as the Kalpavṛkṣa, minerals primarily consisting of gold, celestial women headed by Urvaśī, and winged creatures such as Garuḍa.
And [he gave] the Nāgas headed by Śeṣa, the elephants headed by Airāvata, the horses headed by Uccaiḥśravas, and auspicious jewels such as the Kaustubha. (49)
He remembered the chaste wives, headed by Arundhatī, as well as the forests such as Naimiṣa and the cities, headed by the city of Kāśī.
The Liṅgas beginning with Viśveśa, the Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda, the Mantras beginning with Gāyatrī, and the yogis beginning with Sanaka—[all these he beheld].
[He saw] the great seed-syllable beginning with Om, as well as Nārada and other Vaiṣṇavas, the devotees of Śiva such as Bāṇa and others, and Prahlāda and others who were firm in their vows.
And having remembered Dadhīci and other such generous men, as well as kings such as Hariścandra, and the feet of one's mother—the most excellent of all sacred fords—[one should offer gifts].
Having meditated upon his father and his teachers with a tranquil mind, he should then proceed toward the southwest (nairṛtī) direction to perform his necessary duties.
One should go a hundred bows' length from a village and four times that distance from a city; having covered the ground with grass and veiled one's head with a cloth. (55)
Wearing the sacred thread over the right ear, facing north during the day and at the two twilights, one should void urine and feces in silence; at night, however, one should face south.
One should not [perform it] while standing, nor in water, nor facing a cow, fire, or the wind; nor on ground ploughed by a plowshare, nor on a surface used as a road.
One should not look at the quarters of the sky, the circle of luminaries, or the clear firmament; holding the penis with the left hand, one should rise up with effort.
Then, having taken earth that is free from insects and gravel—avoiding that which has been dug up by mice, that which is leftover from cleansing, and that which is not suitable for the family.
One should apply one portion of earth to the private parts, five portions to the anus, ten portions to the left hand, and seven portions to both hands.
One should apply one portion of earth to each foot and likewise three portions to the hands; thus a householder should perform purification until the odor and the smear are removed.

From this point forward, there is a doubling of the requirements in each of the three stages beginning with studentship; one should perform half of the purification prescribed for the day during the night.

Half of that [penance] is prescribed when one is afflicted by thieves and the like on the road, half of that again when women are afflicted, and even less when they are in good health; one should not perform less than this.
Even if one performs purification from head to foot with the waters of all rivers, heaps of earth, and cow dung, one who is corrupt in heart does not partake in purity.

Clods of earth the size of fresh *dhātrī* fruits are prescribed for purification; all sacrificial oblations (*āhuti*) and mouthfuls (*grāsa*) in the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance are likewise measured by this standard. Facing either the east or the north, seated comfortably on pure ground that is free from husks, charcoal, bones, and ashes, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*).

A Brāhmaṇa should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that is neither hot nor frothy, which reaches the heart, without haste, using the Brāhma-tīrtha, and which has been purified by his gaze.

A king would be purified by [water] reaching the throat, and one of the thighs by [water] reaching the palate; women and Śūdras, however, are purified even by the mere contact with [the water] in the mouth.

One who has covered his head or neck while in the water, or whose topknot is untied, or whose pair of feet has not been washed—even if he has performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)—is considered impure.
Having drunk water three times for the sake of purification, one should then cleanse the apertures of the body; with the base of the thumb, one should touch both the upper and lower lips twice each.
Afterwards, the wise one should touch his face with three fingers; then, he should repeatedly touch the nostrils with the tips of the index finger and the thumb.
With the tips of the thumb and the ring finger, one should repeatedly touch the eyes and ears; with the union of the little finger and the thumb, one should touch the opening of the navel.
Having touched the heart with the palm, one should touch the head with all the fingers; likewise, one should touch both shoulders with the tips of the fingers, sprinkling water everywhere.
Having sipped water once, one should sip again after walking upon a road; likewise, after bathing, eating, drinking water, or at the commencement of auspicious rites. (74)

Having slept, having put on a garment, or likewise having seen something inauspicious, or having touched an impure thing through negligence, one becomes pure by sipping water twice (performing *ācamana*).
Furthermore, one should take up a tooth-stick for the sake of purifying the mouth; for even after sipping water (ācamana), one remains impure if one has not cleansed the teeth.
On the first lunar day, the new moon, the sixth, the ninth, and on Sundays, the contact of a wooden stick with the teeth shall burn one’s family unto the seventh generation.
If tooth-sticks are unavailable, or if the day is prohibited for their use, twelve mouthfuls of water should be taken as gargles for the purification of the mouth.

The tooth-stick should be the size of the tip of the little finger, with its bark intact, free from blemishes, straight, twelve finger-breadths in length, and provided with a half-finger's length at the end. (79)

For other castes, it is proclaimed that [the length] should be reduced by one finger-width each; [the wood] may be derived from the mango, the hog-plum, the emblic myrobalan, the kaṅkola, or the khadira tree. (80)
[The fruits] produced from the śamī, apāmārga, kharjūrī, śelu, śrīparṇī, and pīlu, as well as the rājādana, nāraṅga, kaṣāya, kaṭuka, and kaṇṭaka [fruits]. 81.
Alternatively, a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree is highly recommended; one should also fashion an auspicious tongue-scraper in the shape of a bow.
"Spread yourselves out for the sake of food; let King Soma not come [to you]. His face shall be wiped clean by both glory and fortune. (83)
O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory. (84)
For one who performs the cleansing of the teeth while reciting these two mantras, Soma, residing within the trees, is forever pleased with him. (85)
Since a man becomes a partaker of impurity when his mouth has been stale, he should therefore diligently perform the cleansing of the teeth for the sake of purification. (86)
Even during a fast, one should not be guilty of using a tooth-stick, collyrium, perfumes, ornaments, fine garments, flower garlands, or ointments.
Then, after first cleaning one's teeth, one should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā), having completed the morning bath, especially at a pure sacred ford (tīrtha).
Since this body is always impure, it becomes purified through morning ablutions and the like; for, pierced by nine apertures, it indeed flows [with waste] day and night. (89)
Bathing at dawn is praised as it promotes enthusiasm, intelligence, good fortune, and the perfection of physical form, and serves as a cause for the clarity of the mind.
Since a person is drenched with sweat, saliva, and the like, and is under the sway of sleep, he becomes fit for the recitation of mantras, hymns, and other such rites only through the morning bath.
They say that the bath performed every morning when the beautiful dawn has appeared is equal to the Prājāpatya penance; it destroys even the greatest of sins.
The morning bath removes sin, misfortune, and exhaustion; it also dispels impurity and bad dreams, while bestowing contentment and nourishment. (93)
Indeed, the wicked do not approach those who bathe in the morning at any time; therefore, one should perform the morning bath, for it yields both seen and unseen fruits.
In this connection, O Pot-born One, I shall describe the procedure for bathing; for they say that bathing performed according to the prescribed rite is a hundred times superior to ordinary bathing.

Having taken pure clay, sacrificial grass (barhis), sesame seeds, and cow dung, and having placed them in a clean location, one should perform ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and then proceed with the bath.
The assistant, with his topknot tied, should enter into the midst of the water; having stirred the water in a clockwise direction with the mantra "uruṃ hi," he should proceed.

Having first recited those one hundred [verses] for the consecration of the water with the mantra "sumitriyā na āpaḥ," and having offered a handful of water, he should then cast it toward his enemy while reciting the mantra "durmitriyāḥ. || 98 ||
Having recited the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should smear the limbs with clay; having washed the head with one portion of clay, and likewise the area above the navel with two portions.
One should purify the area below the navel with three [repetitions] and the feet with six; one should immerse oneself facing the current while reciting the mantra "āpo asmān."
The mantra "ud id ābhyaḥ śuciḥ" is prescribed for emerging from the water; having recited "mā nas toke," one should smear one's limbs with cow dung.
The mantra beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" is for one's own self-consecration; likewise, "tattvāyāmi," "tvanno agne," "sa tvaṃ naḥ," and "uduttamam. (2)
One should mutter the verses beginning with "dhāmnodhāmnaḥ" and "tathā māpo mauṣadhīḥ," as well as those beginning with "yadāhuraghnyāḥ," "muñcantu mā," and "avabhṛtha."
These mantras, addressed to the deities of the months, are prescribed for one's own self-consecration; thereafter, the Brahmin [should perform it] with the Praṇava and then with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.

Then the wise and accomplished man should purify himself with the Gāyatrī; it is traditionally taught that purification is achieved by reciting each verse of the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. (5)
These purifying mantras are also: "idam āpo haviṣmatīḥ," "devīr āpaḥ," "apo devāḥ," and those known as "drupadād iva. (6)
"śanno devīr apaḥ," "devīḥ," as well as "apāṃ rasaṃ," and "punantu mā"—these nine are proclaimed as the Pāvamānī verses.
Then, having recited the Aghamarṣaṇa and the Drupadā, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rules, or otherwise recite [the mantra] while submerged within the water.

The wise man should either mutter the *praṇava* three times or meditate upon Viṣṇu. Having bathed in this manner and wrung out his garment, he should put on two clean washed clothes. Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should perform the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*) while holding *kuśa* grass. For a Brāhmaṇa, especially, must not fail to perform the twilight devotion.
While still alive, such a Śūdra is indeed reborn as a dog after death; being perpetually impure due to neglecting the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), he is unfit for all ritual acts.
Whatever other ritual act one performs, one shall not partake of its fruit. Having first meditated upon the Praṇava in the eastern direction, one should then provide a seat of Kuśa grass.
Having recited this mantra at the four corners, one should not have one's gaze or mind fixed on anything else.
Either facing east with his topknot tied or seated facing north, having sprinkled himself clockwise, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras), preceded by the seven vyāhṛtis and accompanied by the ten oṃkāras; this is called prāṇāyāma. || 15 ||
A Brahmin who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma) with his senses and mind restrained becomes instantly liberated from the sins committed during the day and night. || 16 ||
If ten or twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) have been performed while restraining the mind, then great austerity has been practiced by him. || 17 ||
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a fetus within a month.
Just as the impurities of the earthly elements are burnt away by smelting, so too the defects produced by the senses are consumed by the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma). 19.
Whatever fruit one may obtain by feeding a single Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rite, that same fruit is attained through twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed with faith.
Since the entire corpus of speech, beginning with the Vedas, is established in the *praṇava*, therefore the reciter of the Vedas should practice the *praṇava*, the beginning of the Vedas.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the Praṇava, as well as in the seven Vyāhṛtis and in the three-footed Gāyatrī, no fear arises anywhere.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity; and there is nothing more purifying than the Gāyatrī, O Pot-born One. (23)
Whatever sin one commits by deed, mind, or speech during the night, one should purify it upon rising at the morning twilight through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin one commits during the day through the actions of mind, speech, and body, one may remove that by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while seated during the evening twilight.
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should sit during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. (26)
Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night; sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by day.
He who does not attend to the morning [prayer] and he who does not perform the evening [prayer] should be excluded from all the rites of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (28)
Having approached the vicinity of water, one should perform the daily rites; having gone to the forest, one should recite the Gāyatrī with a concentrated mind. (29)

Since the twilight devotion performed outside possesses many more merits than that performed at home, it is better for a Brahmin to be one who has conquered his senses and merely practices the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Even one who knows the three Vedas is not to be honored by us if he eats all things and sells all things; he whose deity is Savitṛ, whose mouth is Agni, and who is three-footed.
Viśvāmitra is the seer, Gāyatrī is the metre, and it is preeminent; one should meditate upon Gāyatrī at dawn as red-hued, with Brahmā as her presiding deity. (32)
Mounted upon a swan, eight years of age, adorned with red garlands and unguents, she is the personification of the Rigveda, bestowing fearlessness and holding a rosary.
Praised by the sage Vyāsa in the Anuṣṭubh meter, this hymn, when meditated upon, removes the nocturnal sin of the goddess Uṣas.

The supreme sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed with the mantra beginning "sūryaśca," and thereafter one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
One should cast [the breath] nine times: on the ground, at the head, and in space; in space, on the ground, and at the head; and likewise at the head, in space, and on the ground.
By the word "ground" (bhūmi), the feet and the heart are remembered as the space; the word "head" (śiras) is declared by those skilled in purification to refer specifically to the head itself. (37)
This supreme Brāhma bath is superior even to the baths of Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and Indra, and even superior to the bath performed with mantras.
He who has bathed with the Brāhma-bath is pure both externally and internally; he attains fitness in all matters, such as the rites of worshiping the gods and so forth. (39)
Are fishermen pure simply by immersing themselves in water day and night? Likewise, even those who have bathed a hundred times are not purified if they are defiled by their inner disposition. (140)
May that divine power purify those whose internal organs are already pure; for what is the point of praising as holy those donkeys who are merely grey with ash? (41)
He has bathed in all sacred fords; he is free from all impurity. He whose mind here is stainless has performed hundreds of sacrifices.
O Sage, listen to how that very mind may become stainless; it shall be so only if the Lord of the Universe is pleased, and never otherwise. (43)
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, one should take refuge in the Lord of Kāśī; by taking refuge in Him, the impurities of the mind are certainly destroyed. (44)
With the impurity of pride completely destroyed through the supreme grace of the Lord of the Universe, he casts off this body and attains the Supreme Brahman. || 45 ||
Good conduct is considered the cause for the grace of the Lord of the Universe for human beings; therefore, one should follow that which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti. 46.
Then, having recited the Drupadā verse and taking water in his hand, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite with the mantra beginning with "Ṛtam."

If a wise man, having immersed himself in the waters, should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, that act for him is certainly equivalent to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
Whether in water or on land, whoever should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, that person's flood of sins shall perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Having then recited this mantra, the twice-born should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); some teachers desire this, while others do so according to the specific Vedic branch (śākhā).
You move within all beings, dwelling in their secret cave, facing every direction; you are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, you are the waters, light, essence, and immortality.
Standing, one should cast three handfuls of water with joined palms, reciting the Gāyatrī preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis and beginning with the Praṇava, while omitting the Śiras.
By that adamantine water, the Rākṣasas named Maṃdehas, who are enemies of the sun, are swiftly dissolved like mountains struck by a thunderbolt.
That twice-born man who does not offer three handfuls of water for the sake of assisting Vivasvat in order to destroy his own state as a *mandahe* shall himself become a *mandahe*.
In the morning, one should remain standing while reciting [the mantra] until the sun is seen; in the evening, one should recite while seated until the stars appear. (55)
A twice-born man desiring his own welfare must not omit the proper time; therefore, at the moment of half-rise or sunset, he should cast vajrodaka.

Even if performed according to the prescribed rules, the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) becomes fruitless if it is past its proper time; for this is indeed the illustration: just like sexual intercourse with a barren woman.
That twilight prayer which is performed by twice-born men while holding water in the left hand should be known as a *vṛṣalī*, which brings joy to the hosts of Rākṣasas. (58)
The mantras "ud vayaṃ tam," "ud u tyaṃ," "citraṃ devānām," and "tat puruṣāya," as well as "taccakṣur," are the prayers for worship that grant success to one who honors the Sun.
One should perform the ritual attendance (upasthiti) to the Sun-god with the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand times, or again one hundred times, or even ten times, using the Goddess's own mantra.
The Brahmin who recites the Gāyatrī—consisting of at most one thousand repetitions, at least one hundred, or no fewer than ten—is not defiled by sins. (61)
One should mutter either the *Vibhrāṭ* section, or the *Puruṣasūkta*, or the *Śivasankalpa*, or the *Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa*.
And these offerings, which bring delight to the Sun, are made with water mixed with red sandalwood, unbroken grains, flowers, and kusha grass.
One should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented with mantras declared in the Vedas or the Āgamas; by him by whom the Sun is worshipped, the three worlds are worshipped. (64)
When worshipped, Savitṛ procreates sons, cattle, and wealth; he removes diseases, bestows longevity, and fulfills even one's desires. (65)
For this Rudra is the Āditya, the golden-hued maker of day; he is Ravi, he is Hiraṇyagarbha, and as the embodiment of the Triple Veda, he is Aryaman.
By your gratification, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are satisfied, as are all the gods beginning with Indra and the great sages beginning with Marīci.
The descendants of Manu, headed by Manu himself, and the ancestors beginning with Somapa, having thus performed the worship of the Sun, should then commence the libation (tarpaṇa).
Taking nine, seven, or five blades of Darbha grass—complete with their tips and roots, uncut—the twice-born man should hold them in his right hand.
With his left hand held in the *anvārabdha* position, he should offer libations to the six Vināyakas, to all the gods beginning with Brahmā, and likewise to the sages beginning with Marīci. (170)
One should offer libations with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and fragrant flowers, as well as with pure water, while reciting the words, "May they be satisfied. (71)

Wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītin), the twice-born should satisfy Sanaka and the others, as well as human beings, with barley grains, having placed straight darbha grasses between his two thumbs.

One should satisfy the divine ancestors, beginning with Kavyavāḍ and Anala, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and using double-folded darbha grass mixed with sesame seeds.
A Brāhmaṇa seeking his own welfare should never perform the libation with sesame seeds on a Sunday, on a Friday, on the thirteenth or seventh lunar day, at night, or during the two twilights.
If he should perform it, then the skillful man should do so with white sesame seeds; afterwards, he should satisfy the fourteen Yamas while uttering their names.
Then, having uttered his own lineage, he should joyfully offer libations to his ancestors, kneeling with his left knee on the ground, using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, and remaining silent.
The gods desire one handful each, Sanaka and the others two each, the ancestors three, and women one handful each.

The divine (daiva) [region] is at the tip of the fingers; the ṛṣi [region] is at the base of the fingers; the brahma [region] is at the base of the thumb; and that of Prajāpati is in the middle of the palm. (78)
The wise declare that the space between the thumb and the forefinger is the ancestral (pitrya) tīrtha; reciting the nine verses, the learned man should perform the libation for the ancestors.
One should desire [the mantra] beginning with "udīratām aṅgirasa āyantv" and then recite [the verse] "ūrjaṃ vahantī pitṛbhyaḥ svadhāyibhyaḥ. || 180 ||
Likewise, for those ancestors who are here, he should recite the three verses beginning with "madhuvātā," say "namo vaḥ pitaraḥ," and pour water upon the ground.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, may the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, as well as all the paternal ancestors, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.
May this water mixed with sesame seeds reach the ancestors of ten million lineages dwelling in the seven continents, from the world of Brahmā down to the lower realms. (63)
And those born in our family who died childless or without heirs—may they all attain satisfaction through the water squeezed from this cloth. (84)

Then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should engage in the study of the Vedas. The study of the Śruti is fivefold: acceptance [of the text], reflection on the meaning, [recitation, teaching, and application]. || 85 ||

Furthermore, there is practice, as well as recitation, and the imparting [of the teaching] to disciples; this is for the sake of preserving what has been obtained and for obtaining what has not yet been obtained. (86)
One should indeed approach the giver and increase one's own status as a guru; this, O best of the twice-born, is declared to be the morning duty for the twice-born. 87.

Alternatively, having risen in the morning and performed the necessary duties, and having taken up ritual purification and sipping water (ācamana), one should use a tooth-stick for cleansing the teeth.
Having purified all his limbs, he should perform the morning twilight ritual (prātaḥsaṃdhyā) and study the meanings of the Vedas as well as various other scriptures. || 89 ||
He should teach pure disciples who are well-disposed and endowed with intelligence; and he should approach the Lord for the sake of attaining security and prosperity. 190.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the midday rites, one should perform the previously mentioned bath; having bathed, the wise person should perform the midday *saṃdhyā* worship.
Her limbs were bursting with fresh youth, she was as pure as clear crystal, associated with the Triṣṭubh meter, and had Sāvitrī as her deity and Rudra as her presiding god.
She is associated with the sage Kaśyapa, has the nature of the Yajurveda, consists of three syllables, is mounted upon a bull, and is the supreme goddess who grants fearlessness to her devotees. (93)
Having fully worshipped the deity, one should then perform the daily rite; having kindled the cooking fire, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
One should avoid niṣpāva, kodrava, māṣa, kalāya, and chickpeas; one should also avoid all cooked food prepared with oil and all that is mixed with salt.
One should avoid pidgeons, lentils, round beans, and *varaṭas*, as well as the remnants of a meal or anything that has become stale, during the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. (96)

Holding darbha grass in his hand, having sipped water for purification (ācamana) and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should then perform the sprinkling (paryukṣaṇa) with the mantra beginning "pṛṣṭo divi."
