Having sprinkled water clockwise and having strewn kuśa grass three times around, one should, with the mantra "eṣo ha deva," make the fire well-facing toward oneself.

Then, having worshipped Vaiśvānara with flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and clarified butter, one should offer three oblations beginning with "bhūḥ" and ending with "svāhā," preceded by the syllable Om.
The Brahmin should likewise offer an oblation with the mantra "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," and he should also offer six oblations beginning with "devakṛtasya. (200)
One [offering] should be made silently to Yama, and likewise two for Sviṣṭakṛt; then one should offer the bali-oblation on the ground to the Viśvedevas as well.

Then, to the north of that, he should offer salutations to all beings; and to the south of that, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should offer them to the ancestors.
One should offer the water used for rinsing and the food to Yakṣman in the northeast; thereafter, one should pay homage to the gods beginning with Brahmā in the north of that.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (nivītin), one offers to the ancestors beginning with Sanaka; wearing it over the left shoulder (apavītin), one offers to the Pitṛs. A mouthful consists of sixteen morsels, while four such mouthfuls are remembered as a "puṣkala."

Alms consisting of a single mouthful bestow merit upon the householder; likewise, the traveler, the one whose livelihood is exhausted, the seeker of knowledge, and the one who supports his teacher [are entitled to such alms]. || 5 ||

The ascetic and the celibate student—these six are considered religious mendicants; likewise, a guest, a traveler, and one who has mastered the Vedas and reached their further shore are to be known as such.
These two are worthy of honor by householders who desire the world of Brahmā; even when given to an outcaste or a dog, food never goes to waste.
When one seeking food arrives, one should not consider whether they are a worthy recipient or not—whether they be dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, or those afflicted by disease.
He should scatter food on the ground for the crows and the worms; [and for those] who belong to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Nirṛti.
"O crows, accept this ball of rice offered by me upon the ground; and [accept it for] the two dogs, the dark one and the brindled one, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata. (210)
"I shall offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) to those two so that they may become harmless; [for] gods, humans, animals, rākṣasas, yakṣas, uragas, and birds. (11)
The Daityas, Siddhas, Piśācas, Pretas, Bhūtas, and Dānavas—even the grasses and trees—have no desire for food given by me.
May this food indeed be for the delight of the worms, insects, moths, and others, who are bound by their karma and tormented by hunger; may it serve for their satisfaction.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation to the beings and waited for the duration of a cow's milking, he should then enter the dining hall while awaiting the arrival of a guest.

Without having offered the bali-oblation to the crows, one should perform the daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha). In the daily śrāddha, according to one's own capacity, one may offer to three, two, or even one [ancestor]. 15.

One who is weak should set aside [food] and give it for the sake of the ancestral sacrifice (pitr-yajña). The daily śrāddha (nitya-śrāddha) is devoid of the invocation of the gods (daiva-hīna) and is free from restrictive observances (niyama-ādi-vivarjita).

Having thus performed this ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), which is devoid of ritual fees (dakṣiṇā) and free from the vows of the giver and the eater, one whose mind is established and who is undistressed [should proceed]. (17)

Having occupied a seat that is not defective, he should eat together with children; being fragrant, cheerful, wearing a garland, and dressed in clean garments, he should be endowed with these two [sets of qualities].
One should eat the food offered to the ancestors facing either the east or the north.
Having made that food "not naked" by placing water above and below it according to the rule for *āpośana*, the wise twice-born man should eat.
Having uttered, "Svāhā to the Lord of the Earth, likewise to the Lord of the World, and to the Lord of Beings," one should offer three oblations upon the ground.
Having touched water once, with darbha grass in hand and a tranquil mind, he should offer the five oblations beginning with prāṇa into the fire of the stomach-pit.
But for one who eats with *darbha* grass in hand, no fault is found; he may eat even that which has become contaminated by hair, insects, and the like, provided he holds the *darbha*.
One should eat as much as one desires without speaking of its merits or defects; the ancestors partake of the food only so long as the merits and defects are not mentioned. (24)
Therefore, he who eats in silence eats nothing but pure nectar; thereafter, he may drink milk, buttermilk, or even water.
Having thus sipped the water once with the mantra "amṛtāpidhānam asi," one should pour the remainder of the water that was drunk onto the ground while reciting this mantra.
For one who has not washed his hands, from the base of the right thumb, [the water goes] to Raurava, the abode of demerit, for those dwelling in hundreds of millions of lotuses.
"May the water from the remnants of the meal remain inexhaustible for those who desire it. || 28 ||
Having sipped water again, the wise man, having become pure through diligent effort, should take water in his hand and recite this mantra: || 29 ||
The Person, the size of a thumb, residing within the thumb, is the Lord of the entire world; as the Master and the consumer of all, he brings satisfaction.
Having thus mentally resolved upon the food and having washed his feet and hands, he should then recite these mantras for the sake of the transformation of the food.
May Agni, impelled by the wind and granted space by the ether, nourish the earthly elements and digest [my food]; may there be happiness for me.
May there be nourishment for my vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—and may unimpeded happiness be mine. (33)
May the ocean, the submarine fire, the sun, and the son of the sun digest all that has been consumed by me without exception.

Then, having performed the purification of the mouth and passed the remainder of the day through activities such as listening to the Purāṇas, one should thereafter commence the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).

The twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) performed at home, in a cow-pen, or on a riverbank is tenfold more meritorious respectively; it is a hundredfold at the confluence of rivers, and indeed infinite in the presence of Śiva.
The external twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), when practiced, pacifies the sin of sexual intercourse during the day, the evil of speaking untruths, and even that arising from the smell of liquor.
She was the very embodiment of the Sāmaveda, accompanied by the sage Vasiṣṭha; she had a dark complexion, wore black garments, and her youth had slightly begun to falter.
One should meditate upon the supreme single-syllabled Sarasvatī, who rides upon Tārkṣya, who destroys obstacles, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu, and who is joined with the Jagatī meter. (39)
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra "agniśca," the wise man, facing west, should recite [the prayer] until the appearance of the stars.
Having honored a guest who arrives in the evening even with mere words, grass, and water, the wise man should thus prepare for the first watch of the night.
Having thus performed the duties of the day through the recitation and teaching of the Vedas, he, still not fully satiated, should then lie down upon a bed made of a single piece of wood.
Thus has this most eternal rule been declared in brief; a Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner never comes to grief. (243)

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Sadācāra" (Right Conduct), in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 ||
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, I shall further declare the specific details of right conduct (sadācāra), hearing which even a wise man shall not enter the darkness of ignorance.

The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—these three castes are known as the twice-born; they are born the first time from their mother and the second time from the initiation ceremony (upanayana). || 2 ||

For these [rites], the Vedic ritual procedure begins with the *niṣeka* (conception) and ends at the *śmaśāna* (funeral pyre). A wise man should perform the *garbhādhāna* (impregnation) during the menstrual period, avoiding the asterisms Mūla and Maghā.
Before the throbbing [of the fetus], the Puṃsavana rite is performed; after that, the Sīmantonnayana; then, in the sixth or eighth month, or upon birth, the Jātakarman rite is performed.

On the eleventh day from birth, the departure from the house [the *niṣkramaṇa*] takes place; in the fourth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*); and in the sixth month, or at the age of one year according to family custom, the tonsure (*cūḍā*).

In this manner, one should proceed with the pacification of the seed-born and the womb-born [impurities]. These rites for women are performed silently; however, the taking of the hand (marriage) is accompanied by mantras.
In the seventh or eighth year, a Brāhmaṇa is entitled to receive the Sāvitrī; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth, or according to family custom.
For the sake of increasing Brahmanic luster, a Brahmin deserves the girdle in the fifth year; a king seeking strength should wear it in the sixth, and a Vaiśya in the eighth.
Having initiated that disciple, the teacher should first teach him the Veda preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and he should also engage him in the rules of purification and proper conduct.

One should perform purification and likewise the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the previously stated rule; then, having cleansed the teeth and the tongue, one should effect the removal of bodily impurities.
Having bathed with mantras dedicated to the water-deities and having diligently performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should perform the worship of the Sun at both twilights.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should salute the Brāhmaṇas, saying: "I am of such-and-such a lineage; please accept my salutation."
For one who is habituated to saluting others and delights in serving the elderly, longevity, fame, strength, and intelligence increase more and more day by day. (13)
When summoned by the teacher, he should study; he should report whatever he has acquired to him; and he should always perform what is beneficial for him through deed, mind, and speech. (14)

They should be those who do not teach for the sake of wealth through unrighteous means, but rather give knowledge and wealth to the virtuous; they should be capable, grateful, pure, free from malice, and devoid of envy. (15)
He should carry a girdle, a staff, a sacred thread, and a deerskin; for his own sustenance, he should wander for alms among blameless Brāhmaṇas.

For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the practice of begging for alms—characterized by the word "bhavat"—should be performed in sequence at the beginning, middle, and end [of their respective stages].
Restraining his speech and permitted by his teacher, he should eat his food without disparaging it; he should not consume the food of a single person, except at a śrāddha or in times of distress.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven; it is meritless and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. (19)
A twice-born man of the highest order should never eat twice on the same day; knowing the procedure for the Agnihotra sacrifice, the twice-born should eat in the evening and in the morning. (20)
One should avoid honey, meat, injury to living beings, looking at the sun, [using] collyrium, women, stale food, leavings from another's meal, and slander. (21)
The time for the initiation ceremony (upanayana) for the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas is, at the latest, until the sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth year respectively.
Beyond this point, they are no longer eligible for sacraments; being fallen and excluded from the Dharma, they may only remove that state of degradation by means of the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.

One should not maintain social relations with those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī; furthermore, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are, respectively, the prescribed hides for the twice-born.

They should wear, in due order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool. The girdle of a twice-born man should be made of muñja grass, and that of one born from the arms (a Kṣatriya) should be made of bowstring; it should be threefold, even, and smooth. For a Vaiśya, however, it should be made of hempen threads.
In the absence of muñja grass, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja; it should be joined with one, three, or five knots.
According to the sequence for the sacred thread (upavīta), it may be made of cotton, hemp, or wool; it should be triple-stranded and twisted upwards, and that serves to increase one's lifespan.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; that of a King (Kṣatriya) from Nyagrodha or Bāla wood; and that of a Vaiśya from Pīlu or Udumbara wood. (28)
The staff for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should reach up to the crown of the head, the forehead, or the nose respectively; it must be solid and not damaged by fire.
Having circumambulated the fire and worshipped the sun, and being equipped with a staff, a deerskin, and a sacred thread, he should go about for alms as prescribed.
One's mother, maternal aunt, sister, and paternal aunt should be the first to be approached for alms; one should not utter the word "begging" (yācana) [at the outset].
As long as he studies the Veda and observes the Vedic vows, he remains a *brahmacārī*; thereafter, having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), he becomes a householder (*gṛhī*). || 32 ||

This first is declared to be the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home), while the second therein is the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong student). He should remain in the teacher’s family until the exhaustion of his life.
He who, having resorted to the householder stage of life, nevertheless maintains celibacy, is neither a forest-dweller nor an ascetic; he is excluded from all [specific] stages of life.
A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama; for he who remains without an āśrama must indeed perform penance.
One who performs recitation, fire-offerings, vows, charity, Vedic study, and libations for the ancestors, yet has fallen from his stage of life (āśrama), shall not obtain the fruit thereof.

The girdle, deerskin, and staff are the marks of the religious student (brahmacārin); for the householder, they consist of the Vedas, sacrifices, and so forth, as well as the maintenance of nails and hair, and dwelling in the forest.
In this context, the triple staff and so forth mentioned for the ascetic are indeed indicative; however, one who lacks these characteristics must perform penance day after day.
Having cast away into water a worn-out water-pot, staff, sacred thread, and deerskin, he should take up others according to the mantras.
One should perform the Keśāntakarman in the sixteenth year according to the sequence, and in the twenty-second or twenty-fourth year for the purpose of entering the householder stage.
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the cause for the attainment of the glory of the highest beatitude, surpassing all austerities, sacrifices, vows, and auspicious deeds. (41)
One should always employ the Praṇava at the beginning and at the conclusion of the Vedas; for that which is not preceded by Oṃ is fruitless, and even if recited, it does not lead to success.
Gāyatrī, consisting of three feet, is declared to be the supreme mouth of the Veda, together with the three great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable Om. || 43 ||
Chanting these three mantras more than a thousand times every day outside [the monastery] for one month, one is liberated even from great sin. (44)
He who practices this for more than a year, month by month, with undistracted mind, becomes one whose form is space, a pure soul, and attains the Supreme Brahman.
From the three-colored *oṃkāra*, the triad of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, and the three feet of the *Sāvitrī*, they milked forth the three Vedas.
A Brahmin learned in the Vedas who recites this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during the two twilights becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas. (47)

One enjoys the fruit of recitation (japa) that is ten times greater than the sacrifice performed according to ritual rules; the sacrifice of recitation is declared to be ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice.
The whispered recitation is a hundred times more effective than that, and the mental recitation is a thousand times more so than that. (49)
Having studied the four Vedas, two Vedas, or even one Veda according to his ability, the twice-born enjoys the fruit of gifting the entire earth filled with gold.
The best of the twice-born should always practice the study of the Vedas in order to perform austerity; for the study of the Veda is said to be the supreme austerity of a Brahmin. (51)
He who, having abandoned the study of the Veda, desires to read something else, is like one who, having let go of a milch cow, wishes to milk a village pig.
Having initiated the disciple, the twice-born man should teach him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas; the wise know such a person as an Ācārya.
He who would teach even a single portion of the Veda, or likewise its auxiliary sciences, for the sake of a livelihood, is celebrated by the learned as an Upādhyāya.
That twice-born man who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rules and honors [the student] with food is proclaimed here as a *guru*.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—he is here called that person's officiating priest (ṛtvij).
An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya, but a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya; a mother, however, exceeds even a father in respect by a thousandfold.

The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of those born of the arms (Kshatriyas) is by valor, that of Vaishyas is by grain and wealth, but that of those born of the feet (Shudras) is by birth alone. || 58 ||
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names. (59)
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during a dream, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."

And among those who are devoted to their own duties and perform the rites of the Vedas and sacrifices, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), being well-restrained, should daily go for alms at their houses.
Having failed to go for alms and having failed to kindle the sacrificial fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights.
He should not act according to his own whims while within the range of the teacher's vision, nor should he utter the teacher's name without an honorific prefix, even when the teacher is absent.
Wherever there is censure of the guru, or wherever there is slander, one should remain there with the ears covered, or else depart for another place.
By reviling his guru one becomes a donkey; by censuring his guru one becomes a dog. One who is envious becomes a small insect, and one who consumes [the guru's property] becomes a worm.
A young wife of the guru, being virtuous, should not be saluted by touching her feet even by one who is twenty years of age, provided he is capable of discerning virtues and faults.
The nature of women is fickle; therefore, this is considered a fault in men. Even the wise never become negligent regarding young women.
For they are able to overwhelm even the learned as if they were unlearned, or they bring them under their own control like a bird bound by a string. (68)
Neither with one's mother, nor with a daughter, nor even with a sister should one dwell in solitude; for the powerful senses delude even the wise in this world. (69)
Just as one who digs the earth with effort obtains water, so too does a disciple obtain knowledge through service to the teacher. (70)
If the sun should rise while the student is sleeping, or if it should set through negligence, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.
And since parents endure hardship for the sake of their son's birth, it is not possible to repay them even in a hundred years. (72)
Therefore, one should always do what is pleasing to those two and also to the guru; when these three are well-pleased, all austerity is fully accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity; whatever one does in disregard of them shall never succeed.
Having propitiated these three, that wise man shall conquer the three worlds; increasing their satisfaction, he shall sport like a god in heaven.

Through devotion to his mother he conquers the Bhūrloka; likewise, through devotion to his father, the Bhuvarloka; and through service to his guru, the virtuous man likewise conquers the Svarloka. (76)
This alone is declared to be the fourfold aim of human life for men; indeed, contentment with these is the goal, while anything else is called a secondary dharma.
Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or even all three Vedas in due order, the twice-born man, having maintained his vow of celibacy without fail, should then enter the stage of the householder.
One shall become one whose celibacy is unviolated through the grace of the Lord of All; and that supreme grace of the Lord of All brings about the attainment of Kāśī. (79)
Through the attainment of Kāśī, knowledge arises; from knowledge, one reaches Nirvāṇa. Indeed, for the wise, effort toward Nirvāṇa consists in right conduct.
Just as virtuous conduct is not found in other stages of life as it is in the home, so too, after studying the various branches of knowledge, one should take refuge in the householder stage of life.
There is nothing superior to the householder's stage of life if the wife is submissive; for the harmony between husband and wife is the cause for the arising of the three aims of human existence.
If one's wife is favorable, what need is there even for heaven? If one's wife is unfavorable, what need is there even for hell? (83)

The householder's life is for the sake of happiness, and that happiness is rooted in a wife; yet such a wife belongs to one who is disciplined, for discipline is certain to bring about the three goals of life.
Women are compared to leeches by those of dull intellect; yet, when analyzed, there is a vast difference between the fawn-eyed woman and the leech.
The leech, though ascetic, takes only blood; but a woman always gives away one's heart, wealth, strength, and happiness. (86)
Skillful, blessed with offspring, virtuous, pleasant-spoken, and submissive—endowed with these qualities, she was Śrī herself, assuming the form of a woman. (87)
Having bathed with the permission of his guru, and having completed his vows and the study of the Veda, he should then marry a wife of the same caste who possesses the marks of a virtuous woman.
Among people, however, a woman who is not of the same *rasagotra* as her mother and is not a *sapiṇḍa* is fit for marriage among the twice-born for the increase of righteousness. (89)

One should abandon a family that suffers from epilepsy, consumption, or leprosy, even if it has connections with women; likewise, one should abandon a family afflicted by a grave accusation or one that produces only daughters.
A twice-born man should marry a wife who is free from disease, has brothers, is slightly younger than himself, possesses a gentle countenance, and speaks softly. (91)

A wise man should not marry a girl whose name is derived from a mountain, a bear, or a tree; nor one named after a river or a serpent; nor one bearing the name of a bird, a snake, or a servant; however, he may marry one with an auspicious name.

Nor one with extra or missing limbs, nor one who is too tall, nor one who is emaciated; nor one who is hairless, nor one who is excessively hairy, nor one whose hair on the head is unsmooth or coarse. (93)
Out of delusion, one should not marry a girl from a low family; by marrying into a low lineage, even one's progeny falls into a state of degradation.
Having first examined the auspicious marks, one should then marry a maiden; for a girl endowed with good marks and virtuous conduct increases the lifespan of her husband. (95)
The conduct of a religious student (brahmacārin) has thus been proclaimed by you; now, O Pot-born One (Agastya), in this context, I shall describe the characteristics of women.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 36 ||
Skanda said: A householder always enjoys happiness if his wife possesses auspicious marks; therefore, for the sake of the abundance of happiness, one should first examine her marks.
Body, the scent of the body's whorls, complexion, disposition, voice, gait, and complexion—these eight are declared by the wise to be the ground of characteristics.
O Sage, listen as I describe in due order the auspicious and inauspicious marks, beginning from the soles of the feet up to the hair on the crown of the head.
First the soles of the feet with their lines, then the big toes, the other toes, and the nails; then the two insteps, the ankles, the heels, the shanks, the body hair, and the knees.
The thighs, waist, hips, buttocks, vulva, pubic region, bladder, navel, the two sides of the belly, the flanks, the abdomen, and the three folds [of skin]. || 5 ||
The line of body hair, the heart, the chest, the two nipples of the breasts, the collarbones, the shoulders, the armpits, the two arms, the wrists, and the two hands. || 6 ||
The back of the hand, the palm of the hand, the lines, the thumb, the fingers, and the nails; the back [of the neck], the nape of the neck, the throat, the chin, and the two jaws.
The two cheeks, the face, the lower and upper lips, the teeth, the tongue, the uvula, the palate, the smile, the nose, the sneeze, and the two eyes.

The eyelashes, eyebrows, ears, forehead, crown of the head, the parting of the hair, and the hair itself—these sixty-six [parts] constitute the mine of the sixty-four auspicious marks of a woman's body.
The soles of women's feet that are glossy, fleshy, soft, even, free from perspiration, warm, and reddish are said to be indicative of a life of great luxury.
That which is rough, discolored, harsh, with a broken reflection, shaped like a winnowing basket, and parched, indicates suffering and misfortune.
She on whose sole of the foot there are lines resembling a wheel, a svastika, a conch, a lotus, a banner, a fish, and a parasol, shall become the consort of a king.
If a line is joined to the middle finger of the upper hand for the sake of unbroken enjoyment, yet resembles a rat, a snake, or a crow, it indicates suffering and poverty.
A thumb that is elevated, fleshy, and round bestows incomparable prosperity; one that is crooked, short, and flattened destroys happiness and good fortune. (14)
A woman with a broad thumb will be a widow, and one with a long thumb will be unfortunate; soft, thick, rounded, and elevated fingers are praised. (15)
A woman with long fingers is unchaste; one with thin fingers is extremely poor; and one with short fingers has a short life, while one with crooked fingers follows a crooked path.
If the toes are flattened, she will become a servant; if they are widely spaced, she will be poor; indeed, her toes are said to be overlapping one upon another.
Even if she has killed many husbands, she then becomes a servant of another, she whose menstrual blood should rise up on the path as she travels. 18.
That woman whose little finger touches the ground as she walks shall give birth to a loose-living woman who destroys three families. (19)
That woman who, having slain her first husband, takes a second husband, is one whose ring finger and middle finger do not touch the ground. || 20 ||
The first [of these two] destroys one husband, and the second destroys three husbands; both of these cause the loss of a husband if they are deficient. (21)
If her ring finger is not distinct from her thumb, she shall be an unchaste woman even while still a maiden; this indeed is the certain conclusion. (22)
The auspicious toenails are glossy, elevated, copper-colored, and rounded. || 23 ||
The backs of the feet of women that indicate queenship are elevated, free from perspiration, devoid of prominent veins, smooth, and fleshy. (24)
A woman with a neck that is thin in the middle, veiny, and always sunken becomes a traveler; one with hairiness becomes a servant; and one who is fleshless becomes unfortunate. || 25 ||
The ankles that are hidden, devoid of visible veins, and well-rounded are said to belong to Śiva (the auspicious); whereas those that are uneven, flaccid, and visible indicate misfortune.
A woman with even heels is auspicious; one with broad heels is unfortunate. A woman with raised heels is unchaste, and one with long heels is a partaker of suffering. (27)
She whose shanks are hairless, symmetrical, smooth, gradually tapering, and as beautiful as the *viśira* flower becomes the wife of a king. (28)
A woman with a single hair in each pore is a queen; one with two hairs brings happiness; but she who has three hairs in her pores shall experience the suffering of widowhood. (29)
A pair of knees that are rounded and covered with flesh is praised; those that are fleshless belong to a woman who acts according to her own will, and those that are loose belong to a poor woman.
Those with thighs that are well-proportioned, shaped like the trunk of an elephant, smooth, firm, perfectly round, and hairless, shall become beloved of kings. (31)
Hairy [nipples] are said to indicate widowhood, while flattened ones indicate misfortune; those with a gap in the middle portend great suffering, and those with hard skin indicate poverty.
The hips of gazelle-eyed women are praised when they measure twenty-four finger-breadths, are elevated with prominent buttocks, and are well-proportioned and square.
A woman whose nose is flat, long, fleshless, and whose hips are narrow; who is short in stature and covered in hair, is an indicator of suffering and widowhood. (34)
The rounded hips of women that are elevated, fleshy, and broad are said to lead to great enjoyment; any other kind is considered to lead to misfortune.
The buttocks are like the fruit of the wood-apple (kapittha)—soft, fleshy, and firm; free from folds, they increase the pleasure of love.

The auspicious vulva resembles the back of a tortoise or the shoulder of an elephant; if the left side is elevated, it indicates the birth of a daughter, while if the right side is elevated, it indicates the birth of a son.
The penis is auspicious when it is hairy like a rat, with a hidden glans, well-knit, firm, broad, prominent, resembling a lotus petal, and shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha). || 38 ||
That which has the form of a deer's hoof, resembling the interior of a cooking pot, hairy, with a wide-open mouth and a visible nose, is extremely inauspicious. (39)
She whose vulva (bhaga) is shaped like a conch-spiral does not desire pregnancy here; a vulva that is flat and shaped like a skull-fragment brings the status of a servant. (40)
Resembling a bamboo or a cane-leaf, with a nose as high as an elephant's hair, deformed, crooked in shape, with pendulous cheeks, and thus inauspicious; || 41 ||
The forehead of Bhaga is broad, the hips are expansive, high, and fleshy; they are soft, rich with delicate hair, and praised for their clockwise whorls.
A hip that spirals to the left, is fleshless, and is bent indicates widowhood; one that is uneven, rugged, and rough always brings misery. (43)
A broad, soft, and slightly elevated vulva is praised; one that is hairy, veiny, or marked with lines is not auspicious at all. (44)
A navel that is deep and spirals to the right brings about happiness and prosperity; one that spirals to the left, is flat, or has distinct ridges is not auspicious. (45)
A woman with a broad belly gives birth to many sons who are a source of happiness; she whose belly resembles a frog shall give birth to a son who is a lord of the earth.
By means of a protruding, wrinkled, and even a coiled belly, women in this world become, respectively, barren, female renunciants, and slave-girls. (47)
A woman whose ribs are even, fleshy, soft, auspicious, and with the bones submerged will undoubtedly be a treasury of good fortune and happiness. (48)
She whose head and sides are invisible, elevated, and covered with hair, shall be childless, ill-behaved, and a treasure-house of suffering. || 49 ||
A woman whose belly is very small, hairless, and soft-skinned becomes rich in enjoyments and always partakes of sweet food. (50)
The belly of a poor woman becomes like that of a potter, or like a drum; it resembles a gourd or a barley grain, and remains difficult to fill. (51)
A woman with an excessively broad belly is childless and unfortunate; one with a pendulous abdomen destroys both her father-in-law and her husband's younger brother.
She whose line of hair is slender, straight, and marked with three folds, being auspicious, slender at the waist, and rich in enjoyments—that woman is the source of happiness and sport. (53)
A line of body hair that is tawny, crooked, thick, or broken brings about theft, widowhood, and misfortune for women in this world. (54)
She whose heart is hairless and even, devoid of depressions, shall obtain sovereignty, freedom from widowhood, and the love of her beloved. (55)
A woman with a broad chest who is unchaste and likewise merciless, and whose chest is covered in excessive hair, certainly kills her husband. || 56 ||
The chest, eighteen finger-breadths in width, should be fleshy and elevated for happiness; it becomes the source of suffering if it is hairy, uneven, or broad.

Breasts that are dense, rounded, firm, full, and symmetrical are praised; however, those with thick tips, that are sparse, or that are shriveled do not bestow happiness upon women of beautiful thighs.
A woman whose right breast is elevated is considered foremost among those who bear sons; one whose left breast is elevated gives birth to a daughter who is beautiful and fortunate.
Breasts resembling the buckets of a water-wheel indicate immoral conduct; those that are thick at the base with a wide space between them, and those with broad outer corners, are not auspicious. (60)
Breasts that are thick at the base, gradually tapering toward the tips, and pointed, grant happiness during the early period of life, but subsequently cause extreme suffering.
A pair of nipples that is very firm, dark, and well-rounded is auspicious; however, one that is sunken, elongated, and thin leads to suffering.
A woman with thick clavicles is a treasure-house of wealth and grain; one with loose, sunken, and uneven clavicles is poor.

Shoulders that are not bound together, not drooping, neither too long nor too thin, yet auspicious; or those that are crooked, thick, and covered with an abundance of hair—these indicate servitude and widowhood.

Shoulders with well-concealed joints and drooping tips are auspicious, while those that are well-knit and elevated at the tips bestow widowhood; those that are devoid of flesh cause extreme suffering. (65)
The armpits are auspicious when they have fine hair, are elevated, smooth, fleshy, praised, deep, free of visible veins, and moist with perspiration.
The two arms of the deer-eyed women are perfectly free from defects, possessing hidden bones and tender joints; they are without prominent veins or hair, and are straight. (67)
Arms that are hairy, short, and visible at the shoulders indicate widowhood and misfortune for women; they lead to great suffering. (68)
The two hands of deer-eyed women, joined together with the thumbs and fingers facing each other in the shape of a lotus bud, lead to great enjoyment. (69)
The palms of the hands, being soft, medium, or high, red, and without cracks, are praiseworthy; they are endowed with auspiciousness and glory when rich in excellent lines and possessing few lines.
A woman with a palm having many lines becomes a widow; with no lines, she is poor; and with a palm abounding in prominent veins, she indeed becomes a beggar.
A hand that is hairless, devoid of veins, praised, elevated on the back of the palm, yet excessively hairy—a cause for widowhood—and fleshless with prominent sinews, one should reject.
The lines on the hand of a woman that are red, distinct, deep, glossy, full, and circular are auspicious, according to her fortune. (73)
With the fish [mark], a woman becomes fortunate; with the svastika, she bestows wealth; with the lotus, she becomes the wife of a king and gives birth to a son who is a king. (74)
On the hand of a universal monarch’s wife, there is a clockwise *naṃdyāvarta* mark; these, along with the marks of a conch, a parasol, and a temple, indicate the status of being a king's mother. (75)
Lines in the form of a balance and a measure, caused by her being the wife of a merchant, and lines in the shape of an elephant, a horse, and a bull appear on the left hand of deer-eyed women. (76)
A line resembling a temple or a vajra indicates that he will have a son who is a Tīrthaṅkara; [a line] like a plow, a cart, or a yoke indicates she will be the wife of a farmer. (77)
One who has lines resembling a chowrie, a goad, or a bow will certainly become the wife of a king; a line emerging from the base of the thumb travels to the little finger. (78)

If she should be a killer of her husband, a wise man should abandon her from afar; for on this earth, by abandoning a woman with hips marked by lines in the shape of a trident, sword, mace, spear, or drum, one becomes renowned.
A hawk, a jackal, a frog, a wolf, a scorpion, a serpent, a donkey, a camel, and a cat—if these appear in her hand, they bring suffering to the woman. (80)
The thumb that is straight, round, with rounded nails, and soft, bestows auspiciousness. || 81 ||
The fingers have well-jointed, long, rounded, and gradually tapering nails; those that are flat, unevenly indented, rough, or covered with hair on the back are inauspicious. (82)
The fingers of women that are too short, thin, crooked, or sparse are caused by disease; those possessed of many joints lead to suffering. (83)

Nails that are reddish, possessed of a crest, elevated, and radiant with beautiful luster bring prosperity; whereas those that are sunken, discolored, resembling mother-of-pearl, or yellow, bestow poverty. (84)
White spots on the nails generally belong to a woman who is unchaste; men, too, become miserable when their nails are "flowered" (marked with such spots). || 85 ||
A back whose backbone is submerged within and which is fleshy is auspicious; however, with a hairy back, one certainly attains widowhood.
Even if bent, curved, or accompanied by a headache, the nape of the neck is best when straight, fleshy, and well-elevated. (87)
A neck that is dry, veiny, hairy, broad, and crooked is inauspicious; one that is fleshy, round, and four finger-breadths in circumference is praised.
A neck marked with three lines that is well-knit, with bones not protruding, free of flesh, flattened, and with long sockets does not bestow auspiciousness. (89)
A widow has a thick neck, a servant girl a crooked neck; a barren woman has a double-flattened neck, and one without sons has a short neck. (90)
A chin measuring two finger-breadths is praised; it should be round, plump, and very soft. One should reject a chin that is thick, divided into two parts, elongated, or hairy.
A jaw that is joined to the chin, hairless, and very dense is auspicious; however, one that is crooked, thick, thin, short, or hairy does not bestow good fortune.
The cheeks of a woman with beautiful eyes are praised when they are full, round, and well-elevated; one should avoid those that are hairy, rough, sunken, or devoid of flesh. (93)
A face that is symmetrical, fleshy, very smooth, fragrant, and round, possessing the luster of its progenitor’s own countenance, is born here for those who are fortunate. (94)
O Queen of the Earth, a lower lip that is pale-red, round, glossy, with its center adorned by lines, belongs to a woman named Sīmantinī and is beloved.
A lower lip that is thin, pendulous, cracked, and rough indicates misfortune; one that is dark-brown and thick portends widowhood and strife. (96)

The upper lip of a woman who is intoxicated with passion, if smooth and slightly elevated in the middle and hairless, bestows great enjoyment; the opposite characteristics bring about contrary results.
His auspicious teeth are thirty-two in number, glossy like cow’s milk, and beautiful; those below and above are even and slightly elevated. (98)
Teeth that are yellow or dark-brown, thick, long, unevenly aligned in two rows, shaped like mother-of-pearl, or widely spaced, are causes of suffering and misfortune. (99)
If the lower teeth are more numerous than the upper, she will clearly devour her mother; if they are protruding, she will be husbandless; and if they are sparse, she will be unchaste.
A tongue that is red, soft, and likewise black, while eating what is desired, brings about one's wishes; however, one that is mottled, of medium size, and protruding brings suffering. (1)
One with white [teeth] dies by water; one with dark [teeth] is fond of quarreling; one with fleshy [teeth] is poor; and one with long [teeth] eats what should not be eaten.
With a broad tongue, the woman experiences extreme intoxication; her palate is supple, praised, smooth, and has the luster of a red lotus. (3)

If it is pale on the palate, there will be widowhood; if yellow, she will become a wandering ascetic; if black, she will suffer from separation from her offspring; and if rough, she will have many dependents.

A bell that is thick at the neck, well-rounded, gradually tapering to a fine point, and deep red is auspicious; one that is not too long is also auspicious, whereas one that is thick and black brings suffering.
The smile of the fair-eyed women was excellent, with teeth barely visible and cheeks slightly blooming, while their eyes remained unblinking.
A nose with symmetrical nostrils and small openings brings auspiciousness; one that is thick at the tip, curved in the middle, or excessively elevated is not praised.

A nose with a curved and reddish tip brings the suffering of widowhood; one that is flat makes one a servant to others; one that is short brings misfortune, while one that is long makes one fond of strife.
A long sneeze is auspicious, as is one that is prolonged, simultaneous, or occurs in two or three clusters. The eyes are praised when they are beautiful, with red corners and black pupils.

She whose eyes are as white and bright as cow’s milk, very lustrous, and have black lashes, is long-lived; she whose eyes are protruding will be unchaste, and she whose eyes are round will be an adulteress. (110)

She with eyes like a ram's, she with eyes like a buffalo's, and she with squinting eyes are not auspicious; she who is utterly seized by lust, she with tawny eyes like a cow's, and she of very wicked conduct [are likewise inauspicious]. 11.
A woman with eyes like a pigeon's is ill-behaved; one with red eyes is a killer of her husband; one with sunken eyes is wicked; and one with eyes like an elephant's is not auspicious.
A woman who is left-eyed is unchaste, while one who is right-eyed is barren; a woman with honey-colored, tawny eyes is a delightful wife who possesses an abundance of wealth and grain.
A woman possessing eyelashes that are thick, glossy, black, and fine partakes in good fortune; one whose lashes are tawny, sparse, and coarse is censurable. (14)
The eyebrows of the slender woman are well-rounded, glossy, black, and not joined together; they are praised for having soft hairs and being shaped like a bow. 15.
A woman's eyebrow that is coarse-haired, broad, scattered, or straight is not praised; nor one that is joined together, long-haired, or tawny. (16)
Long ears with auspicious curls are givers of happiness and bestowers of good fortune; those lacking the ear-lobes (śaṣkulī), or which are veiny, crooked, or thin, are to be censured. || 17 ||
A woman’s forehead that is free of visible veins, hairless, resembling a half-moon, and measuring three finger-breadths in width without being depressed, is the cause of good fortune and health. (18)
A forehead with clearly visible svastika lines leads to the attainment of sovereignty; however, she whose head is excessively long certainly kills her husband's younger brother-in-law.
A woman with hairy, veiny, and tall legs is considered to be sickly.
A straight parting of the hair is praised, and a well-elevated crown of the head is praised; these, being rounded like the frontal globes of an elephant, indicate good fortune and sovereignty.
A widow has a thick head, and an unchaste woman has a long head; even with a broad head, one becomes a vessel for misfortune.
The hair has the luster of a swarm of bees; it is fine, glossy, very soft, with slightly curled tips, wavy, and exceedingly beautiful. (23)
Hair that is coarse, with split ends, thin, tawny, scanty, and rough brings about suffering, poverty, and bondage. (24)
A mole between the eyebrows or on the forehead indicates sovereignty; a red mole on the left cheek bestows sweet food upon a woman.
A tilaka or even a mole upon the heart is a cause of good fortune; she who has a red tilaka-mole on her right breast [is likewise blessed].
She gives birth to four daughters and three sons; she on whose left breast there is a red mark or mole. || 27 ||
If a woman has a *tilaka* on the right side of her private parts, she will first give birth to one son and thereafter become a widow. (28)
At that time, the king’s wife either gives birth to a son who is a ruler of the earth, or a red mosquito appears on the tip of the nose of the queen herself. (29)
That very mark on the abdomen is proclaimed as auspicious for a woman who has killed her husband, for an unchaste woman, or for one with a mole or a birthmark below the navel. (130)
A mosquito-like mark or mole at the region of the ankle causes poverty; however, if it should appear on the hand, the ear, the cheek, or the left side of the neck, [it brings prosperity]. (31)
Of these three, one indeed bestows a son within the womb even before [conception], having been fashioned by the Self-born One with a trident from his own forehead.
A woman may attain lordship over thousands of beautiful women; while sleeping, she shall grind her teeth against one another with a *kiṭikiṭā* sound.
Even if she possesses auspicious marks, she is not praised if she prattles at all; a clockwise whorl on the hand is righteous, while a counter-clockwise one is not auspicious. (34)
A clockwise curl (dakṣiṇāvarta) praised when located at the navel, the ear, or the chest brings happiness; likewise, one on the right side of the spine is auspicious. (35)
The inner surface of the back, level with the navel, increases longevity and progeny; it should be seen as clockwise-circling at the base of the vulva of a queen.

If there is a fracture of the cart (śakaṭabhaṅga), it bestows happiness through many offspring; however, if the fracture is at the hips (kaṭi), piercing the private parts causes the destruction of both husband and children. (37)
If there are two whorls on the back caused by piercing the belly, they are not auspicious; by one of them she kills her husband, and by the other she becomes unchaste.
A clockwise curl on the neck is a cause of suffering and widowhood; whether it appears on the parting of the hair or on the forehead, it should be avoided from afar with great effort. (39)
A woman who has a whorl of hair on her waist, whether turning to the right or to the left, kills her husband within a year. (140)
If one [crane] is on the head or two are on the left, moving toward the left, they are both slayers of the husband for ten days; therefore, they should be avoided from afar by one of sound intellect.

A woman with a whorl on her hip becomes unchaste; one with a whorl at the navel is devoted to her husband; and one with a whorl on her back becomes either a slayer of her husband or an unchaste woman. (42)

Skanda said: Though she possessed auspicious marks, she was ill-behaved and the crest-jewel of those with inauspicious traits; yet that virtuous woman, though lacking marks, became the embodiment of all auspicious characteristics.
A woman endowed with auspicious marks, virtuous conduct, self-restraint, and devotion to her husband as a deity is obtained in the home only through the grace of Viśveśa. (44)
Indeed, those women who, in their previous birth, remained at home without being adorned with various kinds of ornaments, become truly beautiful in this life. || 45 ||
Those women by whom the body has been cast off or exhausted at sacred bathing places (tīrthas) become possessed of beautiful marks here, with waves of loveliness. || 46 ||
Those women who worship the Mother of the Worlds, like the consort of Mṛḍa, become possessed of excellent conduct and have husbands under their own control. (47)
For those deer-eyed women of virtuous character who have husbands under their own control, heaven and liberation are found right here; for that is indeed the fruit of auspicious marks.
Through auspicious marks and virtuous conduct, women—who are the very abode of joy—make even a husband of short life-span one who possesses long life.
Therefore, a woman with auspicious marks should be married by the wise, after first examining her characteristics and rejecting those who possess inauspicious ones. (150)
I have described the characteristics for the welfare of householders; I shall now speak of the forms of marriage as well—learn of them, O Pot-born One. 151.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Women," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 37 ||
Skanda said: "The forms of marriage are the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, and likewise the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca is declared as the eighth."
Having invited an excellent Brāhmaṇa, where a well-adorned daughter is given [in marriage], his son shall sanctify twenty-one generations.

The Daiva marriage is that in which the bride is given to the officiating priest at a sacrifice; its offspring sanctifies fourteen generations. The Ārṣa marriage is that in which the bridegroom receives a pair of cattle as a boon; its offspring sanctifies six generations. (3)
Having said, "May both of you practice dharma together," where a daughter is given to a seeker, that is the Prājāpatya rite; its progenitor purifies six lineages.
These four are recorded as the lawful forms of marriage for Brahmins: the Āsura through the purchase with wealth, and the Gāndharva through mutual affection.
The Rākṣasa form is censured by the virtuous due to the forcible abduction of a maiden; the eighth, the Paiśāca, is despised for the abduction of a maiden through deception.
Generally, the Gāndharva, Āsura, and Rākṣasa forms are prescribed for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; this eighth one, however, is most sinful and occurs among the most sinful.
The hand should be grasped by a woman of the same caste; a bow should be held by a Kṣatriya woman; a goad should be held by a Vaiśya woman; and likewise, the hem of her garment by a Śūdra woman.
This rule is recorded and observed for marriage with women of a different caste; however, when marrying women of the same caste, the hand must be taken by all—this is the rule.

From righteous marriages are born children who are themselves righteous, possessing a lifespan of a hundred years; from unrighteous marriages are born those devoid of dharma, with meager fortune, wealth, and life-span.
Approaching one's wife during her fertile period is the supreme duty of a householder; however, it may also be according to her desire, keeping in mind the excellence of women. (11)

Approaching a woman during the day is considered most detrimental to the longevity of men; likewise, the day of a Śrāddha ceremony and all festival days (parvan) should be diligently avoided by a wise man.
Going there out of delusion toward a woman, one falls away from the supreme Dharma.
He who approaches his wife only during her fertile period and is devoted solely to his own wife should be known as a true celibate and a virtuous householder at all times. (14)

The season (*ṛtu*) consists of sixteen nights; among these, four are strictly forbidden. Of those remaining, the even-numbered nights produce sons, while the odd-numbered nights result in daughters. (15)

Having abandoned the ill-placed Moon (Candramas), and having avoided Maghā and Revatī (Pauṣṇa), one who is pure should approach his wife, especially under a male asterism; thus she shall give birth to a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human life.
The pair of cattle mentioned in the case of the Ārṣa marriage is not praised; even the slightest fee for a daughter constitutes the sin of selling a daughter. (17)
One who sells his offspring shall dwell for a kalpa in the hell Viṭkṛmibhojana; therefore, a father must not live off even the slightest wealth derived from his daughter.
Those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off the property of women in this world—not only they, but even their ancestors, go to hell. (19)
Where a woman is satisfied with her husband, and where a husband is satisfied with his wife, there Mahālakṣmī dwells, pleased by the enemy of the Dānavas.
Trade, service to a king, teaching the Vedas, improper marriage, and the omission of sacred rites are the causes of downfall for a family. (21)
A householder should perform the domestic rites daily in the nuptial fire, as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.

For a householder in the stage of life (gṛhasthāśramin), there are five slaughterhouses (sūnā) in his daily activities: the mortar for pounding, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom. (23)
And for the purpose of eliminating those five slaughter-houses, five sacrifices have been prescribed for the householder, which increase his spiritual welfare.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), libation is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛkratu), burnt offerings are the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña), the bali offering is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛkratu), in that order.
Seeking to bring satisfaction to his ancestors, a householder should perform the Śrāddha rite daily with food, water, milk, roots, or even fruits.
And whatever merit is gained by the gift of a cow to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rites, one shall obtain that same fruit by honoring a mendicant and giving him alms. || 27 ||

Offered into the fire of a Brahmin’s mouth, which is kindled by the fuel of austerity and knowledge, it shall deliver one from hosts of obstacles and even from the difficult-to-cross ocean of sin. (28)
If a guest departs from one's house unhonored and with his hopes frustrated, that person is instantly cast out from the merit accumulated since birth. (29)
Words preceded by conciliation, as well as ground, grass, and water for the sake of a bed—these too should always be offered for the satisfaction of a guest. (30)
A householder who subsists on the food of others will, after death, become the domestic animal of that person; for the giver of food shall receive the merit of one nourished by another's food.
A guest who arrives at sunset, brought by the sun, must be honored with great effort; if he departs elsewhere unhonored, he bestows abundant misfortune.
One who eats the food remaining after serving guests shall enjoy long life and wealth in this world; however, the householder who eats his food while having turned away a guest is a sinner.
One who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite is known as a Sūryoḍha guest; he has not arrived at the earlier time, nor has he been seen before anywhere.

If another guest arrives while the Brahmin has the vessel for the *bali* offering in his hand, he should offer food to that guest according to his ability, without first giving the *bali* offering to him. || 35 ||
Young boys, women living in their own homes, pregnant women, and those afflicted with severe illness—these should be fed even before the guest; there is no doubt about this. (36)
Having given to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, the householder eats nectar; he who cooks for his own sake eats only sin, being merely a filler of his own belly. (37)
The householder himself should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite at midday; his wife should offer the evening bali with prepared food, without the recitation of mantras.
This is called the Sāyaṃtana Vaiśvadeva in the householder's stage of life; one should perform the Vaiśvadeva with diligence both in the evening and in the morning. (39)
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from the rites of hospitality—all those should be known as Śūdras, even if they are twice-born men who have acquired the Vedas. (40)
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite shall be destitute of food in this world and thereafter enter the womb of a crow.
One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas without sloth; for by performing that according to one's ability, one shall attain the supreme, auspicious state.
Sin resides always in oil and meat on the sixth and eighth lunar days; likewise, it dwells in sexual intercourse and shaving on the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
One should not look at the sun when it has risen, nor when it is setting, nor when it is at midday; nor when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, nor when it is reflected in water.
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor run while it is raining; one should not step over a tethered calf, nor enter water naked. || 45 ||
A temple, a Brahmin, a cow, honey, clay from a sacred site, clarified butter, one aged by birth, one aged by years, one aged by learning, and an ascetic—[these should not be stepped over]. || 46 ||
While walking, one should circumambulate the Aśvattha tree, a sacred shrine-tree (caityavṛkṣa), one's teacher, a water-filled jar, prepared food, curd, and white mustard seeds.
One should not have intercourse with a woman during her menses, nor eat together with one's wife; one should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor eat while seated on a high seat. 48.
A twice-born man desiring luster should not look at a woman who is not eating; nor should he ever eat new food without first having gratified the ancestors and the gods.
One who desires to live for a long time should not eat cooked food containing meat, nor should one void urine in a cow-pen, on an anthill, or in ashes.

One should not void urine in pits containing living beings, nor while standing or walking; nor should one do so facing cows, Brahmins, the sun, the wind, fire, the moon, the stars, water, or one's teachers.
While looking ahead, one should not discharge feces or urine; having covered the ground with clods of earth, wood, leaves, grass, and the like.

Covering his head with a cloth, he should void excrement and urine while observing silence; at night he may face any direction that is comfortable, and during the day, he should do so in shade or darkness.
In times of fear or when one's life is threatened, one may discharge excrement; one should not blow on a fire with the mouth, nor look at a naked woman. (54)
One should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor cast impure things into it; one should not commit violence against living beings, nor eat during the two twilights.
One should not go to sleep during the twilight hours, even if one's head is turned toward the east or the north; nor should one who desires long life void excrement, urine, or spittle in water.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one display a rainbow. One should never sleep alone in a deserted place, nor should one awaken someone who is sleeping.
One should not travel alone on a road, nor drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not eat the cream of curdled milk during the day, nor consume curd at night.

He should not greet a woman in her menses, nor should he eat to satiety on the nights [of the dark fortnight]; he should not be fond of the triple symphony (song, dance, and music), nor should he wash his feet in a vessel of bell-metal.
If one who is devoid of knowledge eats at another's śrāddha after having already performed a śrāddha himself, the giver receives no fruit from the śrāddha, and the eater becomes a consumer of sin.
One should not wear clothing or shoes that have been used by another; one should not eat from a broken vessel, nor sit on ground defiled by fire or other such things.
One who desires to live long should avoid mounting upon the backs of cows, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming], the morning sun's heat, and sleeping during the day. (62)
Having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs; one should not release the topknot on the road; one should not shake the hands or the head; nor should one drag a seat with the foot.
One should never ever pluck out hair or nails with the teeth; one should avoid cutting nails with the fingernails and should refrain from cutting grass.
One should diligently abandon that action which leads to an auspicious state in the future; one should not enter one's own house or another's house by a way other than the door.
One should not play with dice nor sit with those who destroy dharma or those afflicted by disease; one should never sleep naked, nor should one ever eat from the hand.
One who eats with wet feet, hands, or face lives for a long time; one should not go to bed with wet feet, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from food.

A twice-born man should not eat, drink, or recite while lying on his bed; nor should he perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, nor should he drink from a continuous stream while standing.
One who desires well-being should not eat anything made of sesame seeds in the evening; one should not look at feces or urine, nor, while still impure from food remnants, touch the head.
One should not step upon husks, charcoal, ashes, hair, or potsherds; dwelling together with those who have fallen from their status leads only to one's own downfall. (70)
One should never cause a Vedic mantra to be heard by a Śūdra; the Brāhmaṇa falls from his status as a Brāhmaṇa, and the Śūdra falls from dharma.
Instruction in the Dharma would obstruct the spiritual welfare of Śūdras; for service to the twice-born is considered the supreme duty of Śūdras. (72)
Scratching the head with both hands is indeed considered inauspicious, as are striking it with the two hands, crying out, and plucking out the hair. (73)
A Brāhmaṇa who accepts a gift from a greedy king who does not abide by the scriptures goes, along with his lineage, to twenty-one hells.

During the rainy season, when there is lightning and thunder at an improper time, during a dust storm, and during the sound of a great wind, these are proclaimed as times of non-study (anadhyāya) even at night.

During the falling of meteors, earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, at midnight, during the two twilights, in the presence of a Śūdra, upon the death of a king, and during the impurity caused by an eclipse; 76.

Having accepted an offering for a Śrāddha on the new moon, on the Aṣṭakās, or on the fourteenth day (bhūtā), or even on the first day (pratipad) or the full moon, or when there is an interval caused by an elephant or a camel; 77.

When there is the simultaneous braying of donkeys, camels, and jackals; when one is weeping; during the Upākarma and Utsarga ceremonies; and when crossing a river, climbing a tree, or being in water. (78)
Even after studying the Āraṇyaka, as well as the Bāṇa and Sāman chants, a twice-born man should never study during these times of non-study (anadhyāya).

One should not recite [the Veda] when obstructed by a frog, a rat, a dog, a snake, or a mongoose; on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on the fifteenth, one should always remain celibate.
Approaching another's wife indeed shortens one's lifespan; therefore, that should be avoided from afar, as well as the service of enemies. (81)
One should not despise oneself for being deprived of former prosperity; for those who are always industrious, neither fortune nor knowledge is difficult to attain. (82)

One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant; nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant. This is dharma, O Pot-born One (Agastya). 83.

One should always speak what is auspicious, one should always contemplate what is auspicious; one should have association here only with those who are auspicious, and never with those who are inauspicious.
A wise man should not revile those who are deficient in beauty, wealth, or lineage; nor should he gaze at the host of luminaries while impure, even if they possess flowers.

One should avoid the impulse of speech, the impulse of mind, and the impulse of the tongue; one should abandon from afar wealth obtained through bribery, gambling, or acting as a messenger for the distressed.
One should never touch cows, Brahmins, or fires with hands that have food remnants on them; nor, unless one is ill, should one touch one's own nails without a specific reason.

Even the hair born from the private parts becomes impure by contact with them; likewise, water used for washing the feet, urine, and water from which food remnants have been removed [are impure]. (88)

One should cast spit and phlegm far away from the house. By reciting the Vedas day and night, by practicing pure conduct, and with a mind free from malice, the twice-born shall remember his former birth. (89)
One should respectfully salute the elders and offer them one's own seat; thereafter, with veins humbled by devotion, one should follow after them.
O King, one should never at any time utter censure against the Vedas, the brahmins, the gods, virtuous ascetics, or women devoted to their husbands.
One should not offer praise to men, nor should one disparage oneself; one should not repel one who is striving, nor should one utter the vital secrets of others. (92)
Through unrighteousness one prospers at first and may even subjugate those who hate him; yet, despite attaining universal well-being, he shall eventually perish along with his lineage.
Having drawn out five lumps of earth, one should bathe in another person's reservoir; by not doing so, one becomes a sharer in a fourth part of that reservoir-maker’s sin.
Whatever wealth is given with faith, having approached a worthy recipient at the proper place and time according to the prescribed rule, that leads to infinity.
The giver of land becomes a sovereign of a realm; the giver of food is happy everywhere; the giver of water is always satisfied; and the giver of silver becomes endowed with beauty.

The giver of a lamp attains clear vision; the giver of a cow reaches the world of the noble ones (Aryama); the giver of gold becomes long-lived; and the giver of sesame seeds shall have excellent offspring. (97)

The giver of a dwelling becomes the lord of lofty mansions; the giver of clothing attains the realm of the moon; the giver of a horse gains a divine vehicle; and the giver of a bull becomes possessed of prosperity.

One who gives a palanquin obtains a virtuous wife; one who provides an excellent couch becomes a donor of happiness; one who gives grain always attains prosperity; and one who grants fearlessness becomes a lord. (99)
The giver of Brahman is worthy of worship in the world of Brahmā; the giver of Brahman is considered the giver of everything. Even he who causes another to give Brahman by some means is equal to him.
He who receives with faith and he who gives with faith—both of them shall go to heaven; those who act without faith fall into the depths below.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; charity perishes through boasting; and the life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins.
Fragrance, flowers, kusha grass, a bed, vegetables, meat, milk, curd, a jewel, fish, a house, and grain—these, when offered, may be accepted.
Honey, water, fruit, roots, medicinal herbs, and the gift of safety—even from a lowly person, these should be accepted when offered.
A slave, a barber, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who plows half the field—these belong to the category of Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (5)

Having thus attained freedom from the debts owed to the gods, sages, and ancestors, and having distributed [his wealth] everywhere among his sons, he should take up a state of neutrality within the household.
One may practice knowledge even at home, or one may take refuge in Kāśī; liberation comes through perfect knowledge, or else in the abode of Viśveśa.
How could right knowledge arise for men in a single lifetime? In Vārāṇasī, liberation is certain merely by the casting off of the body. (8)

Whether today, tomorrow, the day after, or even after more than a hundred years, this body is fleeting and destined for destruction; yet, if one should attain immortality in Kāśī, that would be truly gained.
And that city of Vārāṇasī is always attainable by one who possesses good conduct; therefore, a wise man should never transgress good conduct even in his thoughts. (110)
Having heard this, Agastya then spoke again to the six-faced one: "Describe Kāśī once more—that which is sustained by righteous conduct."
O Skanda, tell me, who am asking you, what are the various sacred marks (liṅgas) in Vārāṇasī that bestow knowledge?
"Without Kāśī I have no pleasure; without Kāśī I have no delight. O Six-faced One, without Kāśī I am like a painted doll. (13)
I do not sleep, nor do I wake; I do not eat, nor do I drink water; for I drink only Kāśī, the nectar of two syllables. 14.
Having heard these words spoken by the son of Mitrāvaruṇa, Skanda began to describe the greatness of Avimukta.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 38.
Skanda said: Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya, to this sin-destroying narrative concerning Avimukta, which is the cause of the glory of ultimate liberation.

The Supreme Brahman, which is declared in the sacred tradition to be devoid of phenomenal expansion, without selfhood, free from conceptual construction, formless, unmanifest, and yet possessing both gross and subtle aspects—(2)
Alas! Although it is all-pervading, this [power] remains filling only this field; is he not capable of liberating living beings from worldly existence elsewhere?
Listen to how one may certainly liberate that very existence right here—either through great yogic methods or through great selfless gifts.
Or Śiva may release one elsewhere through very great austerities, but not by means of the great application of yoga, nor by great acts of charity.
One seeking welfare should not perform excessively long austerities for the sake of liberation at Kāśī, because [the Lord] does not separate one from Kāśī even during a great calamity.
This indeed is the supreme application of Mahāyoga here; for the Lord of the Universe, flowers, leaves, fruits, and water are [offered] as a matter of rule.
Whatever great gift is given here with a well-disposed mind, and whatever moment is spent sitting steadily in this pavilion of liberation; || 8 ||

Having bathed in the pure nectar of the Gaṅgā, this austerity performed here is supreme; yet, the gift of alms bestowed upon a mendicant with due honor in Kāśī is such that even the Tulāpuruṣa sacrifice does not equal a sixteenth part of it.
Having meditated upon the Lord of the Universe in one's heart, when the eyes are closed for even a moment on the right side of the Deity, this is the supreme Mahāyoga.
This alone is the most intense austerity: to remain in Kāśī while restraining the fickleness of the senses and disregarding hunger, heat, and other such afflictions. (11)
Whatever fruit is obtained month after month from the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, that same fruit is obtained here on another occasion by eating only at night on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
Whatever fruit is acquired through fasting for a month elsewhere, that shall undoubtedly be attained at Kāśī by means of a single fast performed with faith. (13)
Whatever great fruit is proclaimed elsewhere from the Cāturmāsya vow, that shall undoubtedly be attained at Kāśī by fasting on the Ekādaśī day. 14.
Whatever fruit one might obtain elsewhere through non-abandonment for six months, that is certainly attained at Kāśī by fasting on Śivarātri. (15)
O Sage, whatever fruit a practitioner of vows might obtain elsewhere by performing fasts for a year, that same fruit shall be obtained in its entirety at Kāśī in just three nights.

Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere by drinking water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month, that same fruit is attained at Kashi on the north-flowing river with a single mouthful.
Infinite is the greatness of Kāśī; who is capable of describing it? For a living being seeking liberation, the mere whispering [of its name] into the ear is auspicious.
Śambhu whispers something into the ear of a dying person; having heard that syllable, even one who has died attains immortality.
Remembering again and again the city of the enemy of Smara, just as Śaṅkara did for you, he went to Mandara many times in order to obtain her.
Agastya said: "O Lord, I have been driven out from the city of Kāśī by the exceedingly fierce gods, who are experts in their own affairs; how then could the Lord Hara abandon it?"
Is the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, dependent on others like me? Why did he abandon Kāśikā, which is a mass of jewels of liberation? (22)
Skanda said: O you who were born from Mitra and Varuṇa, I shall relate this story of how Sthāṇu abandoned Kāśī due to the obstruction of the piercing.
O Sage, just as you were requested by the gods for the sake of helping others, so too was Rudra, who is expert in protecting himself, requested by Druhiṇa.
Agastya said: O Six-faced One, tell me how that Lord Rudra, the ocean of compassion, was entreated by Druhiṇa, and for what purpose.
Skanda said: O Brahmin, in ancient times, during the Padma Kalpa within the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, there occurred a drought that caused all living beings to tremble.
But by her, who was sixty years of age, all living beings were oppressed; some [sought refuge] on the shores of the ocean, and others in mountain valleys.
In deep marshlands and riverbanks, people lived according to the way of sages; the vast wildernesses were born from the earth, devoid of villages and market towns.
In all cities and towns, as well as everywhere throughout the circle of the earth, there were only flesh-eating trees that reached toward the clouds. (29)
Thieves themselves are plundered here and there by great thieves; those who subsist on the trade of meat become the very protectors of the lives of living beings.
When a state of lawlessness arose in the world, portending great calamity, the effort of the Creator toward creation then became fruitless.
The Source of the World fell into great anxiety due to the destruction of his progeny; as the subjects were perishing, the rites such as sacrifices and the like declined.
When those [sacrificial offerings] were exhausted, all the partakers of the sacrifice became utterly depleted; then, as the Creator was reflecting, he beheld the most excellent of royal sages.
In the great field of Avimukta, that hero, born of the lineage of Manu, performed austerities with his senses motionless, like the Kṣatriya dharma incarnate.
There was a king renowned as Ripuñjaya, a conqueror of the cities of his enemies; then Brahmā approached him with great respect.
O King, he spoke these words to the high-minded Ripuñjaya: "O protector of the earth, rule over Ilā, together with its oceans, mountains, and forests. (36)
Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, will give you his daughter, named Anaṅgamohinī, who is adorned with virtuous character, to be your wife. (37)
O Great King, even the gods in heaven will bestow jewels and flowers upon you at every moment, being well-pleased with your protection of the subjects.
"Therefore, you shall obtain the name Divodāsa, renowned by that very title; and by my power, O King, may divine capability be yours. (39)
Having heard the words of Parameṣṭhin, that best of kings then praised the Creator many times and spoke these words: ||| 40 ||
The king said: "O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, on this earth crowded with people, why are there no other kings, and why is it that you speak thus of me? (41)
Brahmā said: "While you are exercising sovereignty, the god will provide rain; but when the king is devoted to sin, the god will not rain again."
The King said: "O Grandfather, O highly venerable one, capable of creating the three worlds! I have accepted your command upon my head as a great favor. (43)
I wish to say something; if you will do it for my sake, then I shall rule the kingdom on earth as one without a rival.
Brahmā said: "O King, speak that without delay; consider it already done. O mighty-armed one, there is nothing whatsoever that you should not give to me."
The king said: "O Grandfather of all the worlds, if I am the lord of the earth, then let the gods remain in heaven, O best of gods; let them not stay on the earth."
While the gods remain in heaven and I remain upon the earth, he shall obtain the happiness of his subjects through a kingdom free from rivals.
Having been told "So be it" by the Creator of the Universe, King Divodāsa caused a drum to be sounded, proclaiming: "O gods, go to heaven!"
"Let the Nāgas not come here; let men be at ease from this point on. While I rule the earth, let the gods also be at ease. (49)
In the meantime, as Brahmā, having prostrated before Viśveśa, was about to make his request, the Lord spoke to the Creator:
O Lord of the World, come! There is a mountain named Mandara; having come here from Kuśadvīpa, he shall perform difficult austerities. (51)
