Having said, "He has performed penance for a long time so that you may grant him a boon," the Lord of Pārvatī, preceded by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, [departed].
Mounting his bull, he went to where Mandara was situated; and the God of gods, whose banner is the bull, spoke with a gracious soul.
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you; choose a boon, O best of mountains! Then he, having heard [these words from] Maheśāna, the God of gods, the three-eyed one—
Having prostrated many times upon the ground, he made this request: "O Śambhu, who assumes a body for your divine play, sole treasure-house of compassion for those who bow before you! (55)
O protector of those who seek refuge, O knower of all occurrences, how is it that even you, the omniscient one, do not know my desire? (56)
O Śarva, the all-pervading creator of all, who brings joy to the hearts of everyone—if a boon is to be granted to me, whose nature is like a stone, [then grant it].
O destroyer of the suffering of those who bow down, I truly desire equality with the sacred field of Avimukta for this most pitiable beggar. (58)
O Lord, may Kuśadvīpa together with Umā and their retinue today take up residence upon my head; this is my boon. (59)

While Śambhu, the giver of everything to all, was reflecting for a moment, Brahmā, perceiving the opportune moment, approached and addressed Śambhu; having bowed down and come forward, he stood with his two hands joined upon his head. (60)
Brahmā said: "O Lord of the Universe, O Master of the worlds, I have been appointed by you as my master, O All-pervading One, to perform the fourfold creation through your bestowed grace. (61)
That creation was fashioned by me with great effort through your permission; however, due to a drought lasting sixty years, the progeny there perished upon the earth.
The world was without a king and fell into a state of great distress; then there arose a royal sage named Ripuñjaya, born of the lineage of Manu.
Having been consecrated by me as a royal sage and lord of men to protect the subjects, he too—possessed of great heroism and great ascetic power—made a solemn vow.
If, by your command, all the dwellers of heaven remain in heaven, and likewise the Nāgas in the world of the Nāgas, then I shall rule the kingdom.
"I said, 'So be it,' and let that be made authoritative; O Treasure of Compassion, let the boon be granted to Mandara in this very way. (66)
"May this desire of mine—to protect the subjects of that king—be fulfilled; for my two channels constitute his kingdom, as well as that of Śatakratu. (67)
What account can there be here of mortals who blink their eyes even for half a moment? Even a god, considering Mandara with its beautiful caves to be pure, [approached it]. (68)
Protecting the dignity of the injunction, Hara likewise accepted it; just as Kāśī in Jambūdvīpa always bestows the state of liberation. (69)
Likewise, for a very long time, that Mandara also became an island; and when the Lord, desiring to depart, went toward Mandara with its variegated caves, [he took it up].
This linga, consisting of his own form and unknown even to Brahmā, was established in order to be offered to those who had installed it, so that they might attain all supernatural powers.
And to bestow the glory of ultimate liberation upon beings who have fallen away, and to protect the sacred field for all those established here. (72)

Even though this field was left by the wielder of the Pināka bow while he had gone to Mount Mandara, it is remembered as Avimukta (the Unforsaken) because it was not abandoned in the form of the Liṅga.
Formerly, this sacred field was celebrated by the name Nandavana; from that time onwards, its name has been renowned on earth as Avimukta.
The name Avimukta belonged to both of these fields and lingas; having reached this pair, one shall not again be subject to rebirth in a womb.
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga in the sacred field of Avimuktaka, one becomes truly liberated from all bondage of karma.
All worship the Lord of All; the Creator of All worships the Lord of Avimukta, the Liṅga that bestows liberation upon the earth. (77)
In the past, no liṅga had ever been established by anyone anywhere for anyone; no one even knew what the form of a liṅga might be. (78)
Having seen the form of the Unliberated One, Brahmā, Acyuta, and others, as well as Vasiṣṭha and other sages, installed a *liṅga*. (79)
This great Avimukteśvara Liṅga is declared to be the primordial Liṅga; from it, other Liṅgas have arisen here upon the circle of the earth.
Upon merely hearing the name of Avimukteśa, a mortal shall be liberated in an instant from the sins accumulated over lifetimes; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (81)
Even if one has traveled far away, by remembering the Avimukteśvara Liṅga, one is liberated from the sins committed in two lifetimes in an instant.
Having beheld the Unliberated One in the great field of Avimukta, one shall abandon the sins produced over three lifetimes and become composed of merit. || 83 ||
Whatever sin has been committed during five births through the loss of knowledge, that shall surely perish by contact with the Lord of Avimukta, and not otherwise.
Having worshipped the great Liṅga Avimukteśvara here, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; he shall not undergo birth again—how could that be? (85)
Having praised, bowed to, and worshipped the Lord of Liberation in Avimukta according to one's capacity and intelligence, he is himself praised, bowed to, and worshipped. 86.
This sign (liṅga), which is beginningless and personally worshipped by Viśveśvara, should be diligently served at Avimukta in Kāśī for the sake of liberation. 87.
There are many lingas in sacred shrines; those lingas come here upon reaching the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha. 88.
By keeping a vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha at Avimukteśa, a yogi who is forever free from sleep shall attain the supreme goal.
Possessing various sacred sites and emblems, and bestowing the fourfold goals of human life, they worship Avimukta on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Why should a steadfast man fear the mountain-like heap of sins he has committed, if he possesses the thunderbolt of devotion to the Liṅga of Avimukteśa? 91.

Where is this great Liṅga of Avimukta, which yields the fruit of the four aims of life? And where is the small mountain of sin, O sinner, which is destroyed merely by the utterance of its name? || 92 ||
Those by whom the supreme Liṅga at Avimukta has not been seen are truly deluded; for that great field of liberation is presided over by Viśveśvara.
Upon seeing the beholder of Avimukta, Yama, the wielder of the staff, bows from afar with his palms joined in reverence.
Blessed is that creation of the eyes, and fulfilled indeed are those two hands, by which one has beheld or touched Avimukteśvara.
He who, being self-restrained and pure, recites [this mantra] to the Lord of Avimukta at the three junctions of the day, shall obtain the fruit of dying in Kāśī even if he perishes in a distant land.
Having beheld the great Liṅga of Avimukta, one may go to another village; having achieved the successful completion of his intended task, he shall enter his home in safety.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Avimukteśa," in the first half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 39 ||
Skanda said: "The greatness of Avimukteśa has been described by me before you. Now, what do you wish to hear? I shall tell that to you again."
Agastya said: Having heard again and again the greatness of Avimukteśa, my ears have become exceedingly well-pleased; nevertheless, I am not yet satiated.
O Ṣaṇmukha, tell me how the attainment of the Avimukteśvara Liṅga and the sacred field of Avimuktaka may come to be.
Skanda said: Listen, O Kuṃbha; I shall tell you how attainment may be achieved here for this giver of his own welfare who is liberated, O high-minded one.
The accomplishment of one's desired aims is obtained through the weight of merit; and that merit, O Brahmin, arises from honoring the path of the Vedas.
O Sage, for a man who follows the path of the Vedas, even the Kali age and Time itself, though ever seeking to strike him down by finding a vulnerability, perish upon contact with him.
Indeed, by the non-performance of what is prescribed and the performance of what is forbidden, even the two ages of Kali and Dvāpara strike the Brāhmaṇa upon seeing his vulnerability.
Therefore, I shall describe before you the practice of what is forbidden; by abandoning that from afar, a man shall not fall into hell.
Onion, village pig, śelu, garlic, gṛñjana, cow's colostrum, taṇḍulīya, and mushrooms should always be avoided.
One should avoid wood-sap, tree-resins, milk-rice, cakes, and fried pastries; likewise, one should avoid meat not offered to gods or ancestors, and the milk of a cow whose calf is absent.
Milk from a single-hoofed animal is to be avoided, as is that of a camel or a sheep; one should not eat curd at night, nor fresh butter by day.
One should avoid the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *kalaviṅka*, the swan, the ruddy goose, the water-fowl, all meat-eating birds, the crane, the cock, and the parrot.
Having seen web-footed khañjarīṭa birds that subsist on fish, one who eats fish is a consumer of all kinds of meat; therefore, one should avoid fish entirely.

The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish may be eaten when employed for offerings to gods (*havya*) or ancestors (*kavya*). Furthermore, these—hares, porcupines, and tortoises—may be eaten by those who consume meat.
The porcupine and the monitor lizard are praiseworthy, as are known deer and birds; however, those desiring long life and those desiring heaven should diligently avoid meat. (15)
The killing of animals for the sake of sacrifice leads to heaven, but never any other [killing]; one should discard all food that is stale and devoid of unbroken oiliness.

In a life-threatening emergency, during a sacrifice, at a funeral rite (śrāddha), for medicinal purposes, or at the request of a Brahmin—one who eats meat in this manner without greed incurs no fault. (17)
The sin incurred by one who desires the livelihood of a hunter would not be as great as that which accrues after death to one who, out of greed, consumes meat. (18)
The Brahmin who slays the animals, trees, deer, and herbs created by Brahmā for the sake of sacrifice is not a killer; his destination is indeed auspicious. (19)

For the sake of sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, and specifically for the purpose of the *madhuparka* offering, even violence therein shall be non-violence; elsewhere, violence is most difficult to overcome.
He who, weak in wisdom, harms living beings for the sake of his own nourishment—such a person of evil conduct finds no happiness anywhere, neither in this world nor in the next. (21)

The eater, the consenter, the preparer, the buyer, the seller, the injurer, the one who causes injury, and the one who facilitates injury—these are remembered as the eight types of perpetrators of violence. (22)
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the latter of these two is superior. (23)
Just as one views oneself, so should another be viewed by one who desires happiness; just as with oneself, so it is with others regarding pleasures and pains. (24)
Whatever is done for another, whether it be happiness or something else, all that which was performed will subsequently accrue back to oneself. (25)

Without affliction there is no substance; how can there be purposeful action in the absence of substance? How can there be dharma in the absence of action; and how can there be happiness in the absence of dharma? (26)
For happiness is desired by all, and that arises from dharma; therefore, dharma must be practiced here with effort by the four social orders.

With wealth acquired through righteous means, one should perform deeds for the sake of the next world; and gifts should be given according to the prescribed rule, at the proper time, to a worthy recipient, and with sincere devotion. (28)
If one gives a gift to an unworthy recipient in a manner contrary to the prescribed rules, not only does that gift go to waste, but his remaining merit is also destroyed. (29)

Whatever is given for the sake of relieving distress, for the sake of one's family, or for the sake of paying a debt, that becomes inexhaustible both in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt. (30)
He who, by means of his own wealth, performs the purificatory rites—such as the tying of the girdle and the taking of the hand—for one deprived of parents, attains infinite spiritual merit.
That supreme good which is attained by mortals when a single twice-born man is established in his duty cannot be achieved through Agnihotra sacrifices nor through rites such as the Agniṣṭoma. (32)
For that virtuous man who causes the hand of a destitute Brahmin to be taken [in marriage] attains happiness in this world and shall reach the imperishable heaven. || 33 ||
If an unmarried girl should see her menses while still in her father's house, her father is to be known as a killer of an embryo, and that girl is a *vṛṣalī*.
He who, out of delusion, should marry her would become the husband of a vṛṣalī; one must always avoid conversation with such a person, who is unworthy of sitting in the row for a meal.
Having understood the faults of both the girl and the groom, one should subsequently arrange the alliance; otherwise, the father incurs blame.
Women are eternally pure; they cannot be defiled by anyone. Month after month, their menstrual flow washes away their misdeeds.
In the past, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, the Gandharvas, and Agni; men enjoy them afterwards, yet they are not defiled by anyone. (38)
Soma gave women purity, and Pāvaka (Fire) granted them total sanctity; the Gandharvas gave them auspicious speech; therefore, women are always pure.
Agni enjoys a maiden during the period of her menses; Śaśin, upon the appearance of body hair; and the Gandharvas, at the budding of her breasts. Therefore, she should be given away even before that.

One whose hair is visible, one who destroys her offspring, one who destroys her family, one whose youth has fully emerged, and one who has manifested menses—one should avoid these women for marriage. (41)

Therefore, one who desires the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage should give her away while she is still unmarried; otherwise, there is no fruit for the giver, and the receiver falls into a low state.
By giving a maiden who has not been enjoyed by the Moon and other [planets], one obtains the fruit of the gift; but by giving one who has been enjoyed by the gods, the giver does not attain heaven.
Beds, seats, vehicles, a corpse, the face of a woman, kusha grass, and all sacrificial vessels—wise men are never defiled by these at any time. (44)
A calf is pure at the source of its mother's milk, a bird while falling from a fruit-bearing tree, women during the act of sexual union, and a dog while seizing a deer. (41)
The mouth of goats and horses is pure; cows are pure from their backs; Brāhmaṇas are pure from their feet; and women are pure in every respect. || 45 ||
Whether she has been enjoyed by force or has fallen into the hands of thieves, a beloved wife must not be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained. (47)
Copper is purified by sour substances, and bell-metal is purified by ashes; a woman is purified by her menses, and the river is pure through its current. 48.
For she who does not even in her mind think of another man here, enjoys happiness with Soma and is possessed of fame even in this world. (49)
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person who is of sound mind is the giver of the maiden. (50)
If he does not give her away at the proper time, he incurs the sin of killing an embryo; however, in the absence of givers, the maiden herself may choose a husband for herself.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.

Purification is prescribed after her menstrual period in the event of infidelity; however, in the case of pregnancy, abandonment is ordained—even in the event of great sin such as the killing of the fetus or the husband. (53)
The wife of a Śūdra is only a Śūdra woman; those two and his own [woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and his own for a Kṣatriya; and those three and his own for a Brāhmaṇa.
Having placed a Śūdra woman upon his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state; by procreating a son upon a Śūdra woman, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood itself. (55)
But he for whom the rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests are primarily characterized by that [negligence], the gods and others do not eat his offerings, and he does not go to heaven. (56)
Those households which female relatives, when not properly honored, curse, will undoubtedly perish as if destroyed by malevolent spells (kṛtyā). || 57 ||
Therefore, those desiring prosperity should always honor well-dressed women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at ceremonies and during festivals. (58)
Where women are delighted with ornaments, clothing, and food, there the deities reside; there all ritual actions bear fruit.
But where the wife is pleased with her husband and the husband is pleased with his wife, in that household prosperity shall prevail at every step.
The Ahuta, the Huta, the Prahuta, the Prāśita, and likewise the Brāhma-huta—these are the five auspicious sacrifices.

Japa is the ahuta offering; the fire sacrifice is the huta; the offering to the elements is the prahuta; the consumption [of food] is the satisfaction of the ancestors (pitṛsaṃtṛpti); and the worship of the twice-born is the brāhma offering. (62)
A Brāhmaṇa who performs these five sacrifices does not come to ruin; by failing to perform them, he incurs the guilt of the five slaughterhouses.

One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*), a Kṣatriya about his health (*anāmaya*), a Vaiśya upon meeting him about his happiness (*sukha*), and a Śūdra about his contentment (*saṃtoṣa*).
A child, from the moment of birth until eight years are completed, is considered to be such that he incurs no fault regarding what is fit or unfit to eat, as long as he has not yet been initiated.

The maintenance of those who are to be supported brings about both visible and invisible rewards; indeed, there is transgression in failing to support them, therefore they must be supported with diligent effort. (66)
Mother, father, the wife of a guru, one's own children, dependents, guests, visitors, and the sacred fire—these are the nine classes of those who must be supported. 67.
That man truly lives here who is supported by many; however, the man who fills only his own belly should be known as one who is dead while living.
One desiring prosperity should give to the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished; those who do not give gifts are born in future lives dependent upon the fortune of others.
One who is endowed with the virtue of generosity, compassionate, possessed of forbearance, and devoted to the gods and guests is considered a righteous householder. (70)
A Brāhmaṇa who sleeps during the two middle watches of the night and eats only the remnants of the oblation does not come to grief.
O gentle one, these nine things should always be made ready by a householder for a guest: excellent food, expenditure [of wealth], pleasant speech, a kind eye, and a gracious countenance. (72)
Rising from one's seat upon arrival, speaking with affection first, attending to guests, and following them as they depart—these are for the sake of the prosperity of the householder. (73)
Likewise, these nine duties should indeed be performed with some degree of expenditure: providing a seat, washing the feet, food according to one's ability, and a place on the ground. (74)
A bed, grass, water, anointing oil, and a lamp grant success in the householder's life; likewise, householders should avoid the nine forbidden acts.
Slander, adultery, malice, anger, falsehood, unkindness, hatred, hypocrisy, and deceit are indeed the bolts barring the path to heaven. (76)
Nine essential duties must be performed every day: bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), recitation (japa), burnt offerings (homa), study of the scriptures (svādhyāya), and worship of the deity.
The Vaiśvadeva offering, the hospitality for guests, and the ninth, the libation to the ancestors—O Sage, listen to those nine things that are to be kept secret here. (78)
One's birth star, sexual intercourse, mantras, domestic secrets, deception, lifespan, wealth, and insults—these, as well as one's wife, must never be disclosed under any circumstances. (79)

These nine matters are to be disclosed in private: a sin that is not blameworthy, a gift worthy of acceptance, the clearing of a debt, purchase and sale along with their lineages, the giving away of a daughter, and excellence of qualities; none of these should be discussed by anyone anywhere else. (80)
This gift bestowed upon these nine—worthy recipients, friends, the disciplined, those who assist the poor and the helpless, and one's mother, father, and teacher—is inexhaustible.
That which is bestowed upon a new-born infant, or upon a flatterer, a wandering minstrel, a thief, a quack physician, a gambler, a rogue, a cheat, a wrestler, or a bard, is fruitless.

Water must never be given away, nor these nine things under any circumstances; however, when there is a lineage, one may give away one's entire property, one's wife, and those who have come for refuge. (83)
He who gives away a deposit, the property of a wife, a son, or the livelihood of one dependent on him for maintenance—that deluded soul is purified only through penances. (84)
Having understood this group of nine, one shall obtain what is dear; furthermore, I shall speak of another group of nine that grants the path to heaven for all.
Truthfulness, purity, non-violence, forbearance, charity, compassion, self-restraint, abstention from theft, and control of the senses are the means for the practice of dharma for all. (86)
Having practiced these ninety [verses], which illuminate the path to heaven, are meritorious, and are esteemed by the virtuous, a householder does not come to grief. (87)
The wife, son, brother, friend, servant, and dependents—he who possesses these as being rich in discipline (vinaya) gains respect everywhere. (88)
Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at will], and living in another's house—these are the six vices that corrupt women. (89)
He who, having purchased grain at a low price, sells it at a high price, is indeed called a usurer; one should never consume his food. (90)
Having seen first a man who lives off his wife's paramour, then in the middle one who is the husband of a low-caste woman, and finally at the end a usurer, the ancestors depart in despair.
A woman who is unchaste is called a *mahiṣī*; he who desires that wicked woman is indeed known as a *māhiṣika*. || 92 ||
She who, having abandoned her own husband, takes pleasure in the bull of another, she indeed should be known as a *vṛṣalī*; a Śūdra woman does not become a *vṛṣalī* [merely by that]. (93)
As long as the food remains warm, as long as it is eaten in silence, and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, so long do the ancestors eat.
When a learned Brahmin endowed with knowledge and humility arrives at one's house, all medicinal herbs rejoice, thinking: "We shall go to the supreme goal."
When food is being given to a Brahmin who has fallen away from purity, conduct, and observances, and is devoid of Vedic knowledge, the food weeps: "What evil deed have I committed? (96)
He whose food, once it has entered his stomach, is digested through the study of the Vedas, delivers the donor—ten ancestors and ten descendants.
One should not perform the shaving of women's heads, nor should one follow after cows; one should not stay overnight in a cow-pen, nor should one recite Vedic scriptures [in such places]. 98.
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths; in this very manner, the shaving of the head for women should be performed.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, one should prescribe an expiation without having performed the shaving of the head. || 100 ||
For the sake of protecting the hair, one should prescribe a double vow; a double sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
He who considers himself a householder without having taken the nuptial fire—his food must not be eaten, for he is said to be one whose cooking is in vain. || 2 ||

He who, while his elder brother remains [unmarried], takes a wife, establishes the sacred fires, and undergoes initiation, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother is the *parivitti*. (3)
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, the woman with whom he marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest—the fifth—these all go to hell.
There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] if he is impotent, residing in another country, mute, an ascetic, mentally deficient, humpbacked, dwarfed, or fallen from his caste. || 5 ||
For as many syllables of the Veda as one might employ for the sake of worldly gain, so many instances of killing an embryo shall the seller of the Veda incur.
But he who, having become a renunciant, again indulges in sexual intercourse, is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.

The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together on the same seat as a Śūdra, and even the acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra—these may cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual merit.
Those ignorant twice-born men who, having procured the sacrificial offering from a Śūdra, cook it, go to a terrible hell, deprived of Brahmanic luster.
If one eats honey, molasses, vegetables, cow's milk products, salt, or ghee that have been offered by hand, one must fast for one day.
Oils, salt, and fans that are given with the hand do not reach the giver; rather, the eater consumes the sin.
If food is offered in an iron vessel, the eater consumes that which is equal to excrement, and the giver shall go to hell.
Using a finger as a tooth-stick, consuming visible salt, and eating clay—these are equal to the eating of cow-flesh.
One should not accept water, milk-rice, alms-food, clarified butter, or even salt when offered directly by hand; such acts are equal to the eating of cow-flesh.
A fool should dwell nearby, but one endowed with virtues should be kept at a distance; wealth should be given to the virtuous, for there is no transgression in doing so. (15)
There is no transgression against a Brahmin who is devoid of the Vedas; for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire. || 16 ||
Whoever bypasses a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby while studying, whether at a meal or at a gift-giving, shall burn his family unto the seventh generation.
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas. 18.
Families are swiftly destroyed by the misappropriation of divine property, by the seizure of a Brahmin’s wealth, and by the transgression against Brahmins. (19)
And he who says "do not give" regarding cows, fire, or Brahmins, having passed through a hundred births as animals, is born among the Cāṇḍālas. || 120 ||
Whatever has been promised by word but not fulfilled through action, that constitutes a debt bound by dharma, both in this world and in the next. (21)
One should always be an eater of vighasa and always an eater of amṛta; they know that amṛta is the remnant of a sacrifice, while vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten.

When the garment has slipped from the left shoulder and remains at the region of the navel, he is considered to be wearing only a single garment; one should avoid him in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Whatever merit the best of the twice-born obtains by satisfying the ancestors with water after bathing, by that alone he attains the entire fruit of performing the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
He who, having washed his hands, drinks mouthfuls of water after a meal, destroys the three: the gods, the ancestors, and himself. (15)
Having eaten the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a village priest, or the food of women during their first pregnancy, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man eats at the house of such an evil-minded person—whether it be once a fortnight or once a month—he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

For those engaged in a sacrifice, for those who have been consecrated, for ascetics, and for celibate students—for these, as well as for officiating priests while performing their duties, there is no impurity due to birth. (28)
When indigestion occurs, when wind rises, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, upon having a bad dream, or upon contact with a wicked person, bathing alone is prescribed. (29)

Having touched a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, one who eats the remains of offerings to Śiva, or a seller of the Vedas, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
One should indeed set aside one's sandals in the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of gods or Brahmins, while engaged in Vedic study, eating, or drinking. (31)
Grain found in a threshing floor or a field, water from wells or tanks, and milk found in a cow-pen—these may be accepted even if they come from an unapproachable source. (32)
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
Yātudhānas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas who perform cruel deeds steal the essence of the food that is devoid of the maṇḍala.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the great sages, beginning with Vasiṣṭha, subsist upon the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
For a Brāhmaṇa it should be square; for one born of the arms (a Kṣatriya) it should be triangular; for a Vaiśya it is declared to be circular; and for a Śūdra, sprinkling is prescribed. || 36 ||
One should not eat while sitting on one's lap, nor with the hands, nor on a rag; one should not eat from a seat or a bed, nor while afflicted by impurity.
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas, whatever they may speak—even in jest—that is remembered as the supreme Dharma. (38)
One who desires merit should not eat parched grain mixed with curd at night; for one who eats it, there shall be a loss of merit and he will be afflicted by diseases. (39)
Having given molasses, cow's milk, water, salt, honey, or sour gruel with his hand, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (140)
He who, knowing the Dharma, bestows perfumes, ornaments, and garlands, becomes fragrant and ever-joyful wherever he is born. (41)
One should avoid from afar any garment dyed with indigo; it becomes defiled by contact with the bedding used for sexual play with women. (42)
Through rearing, selling, and living off that occupation as his livelihood, a Brahmin becomes impure; he is purified by three *kṛcchra* penances. (43)
Bathing, charity, austerity, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and libations for the ancestors—all these great sacrifices of one who wears indigo-dyed clothing are in vain. (44)
If a Brahmin wears a garment dyed with indigo upon his limbs, he shall certainly dwell in hell for as many years as there are threads in the fabric.
Having fasted for a day and night, one becomes purified by means of the five products of the cow.
If one prepares food with a garment dyed with indigo, the eater consumes what is equal to excrement, and the giver shall go to hell. (47)
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is considered nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as milk; the food of a Vaiśya is indeed food; and the food of a Śūdra is remembered as blood. 48.
Through the Vaiśvadeva oblation, through the worship of the deities, and through recitations, food consecrated by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas becomes nectar for the Brahmins. (49)
But the milk that comes to a Kṣatriya from the protection of his subjects is that which is acquired through justice in accordance with worldly affairs. (150)
Whatever food one gives after having produced it by means of ploughing, yoking of oxen, and other such labors, that food of a Vaiśya is consecrated by the performance of the Sītā-sacrifice.
For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance and devoted to the drinking of liquor, blood flows; therefore, the food of a Śūdra is devoid of Vedic mantras.
A best among men should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter; for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. (53)
In matters concerning women, at a marriage, regarding the consumption of cattle, in the loss of wealth, and for the sake of assisting a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin in taking oaths. 54.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by the truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons, a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all sins.
Or one should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water; or one should make him touch the heads of his sons and wife, or even touch them individually.
They do not call Yama "Yama"; indeed, the Self is called Yama. What can Yama do to him by whom the Self has been restrained? (57)
Neither a sword so sharp, nor a serpent so difficult to overcome, nor an enemy ever perpetually enraged, is as [dangerous] as one's own self when it is poorly governed. (58)
There is but one fault among the forgiving, and never a second: that people consider one endowed with forgiveness to be weak. (59)

Liberation is not for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who is fond of pleasant dwellings; it is not for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one who takes pleasure in acquiring worldly wealth.

For one who is always of solitary conduct, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, whose mind is absorbed in the yoga of sacred study, and who is eternally non-violent, liberation is certain. 61.

Where is there for a man in this world the practice of solitude, where is there the cessation of sensory gratification, where is the application of yoga, and where is the worship of the deities? Yet, at Kāśī, liberation occurs by its very nature, even without these.

For the Lord of the Universe, constant devotion is itself yoga and austerity; residence in the city of the Lord of the Universe is the true vow, charity, observances, and restraints; and bathing in the celestial river that flows northward is the true ablution. (63)

Skanda said: Even a householder is liberated in this world if he possesses wealth acquired through righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites, and speaks the truth. (64)
Having given food especially to the poor, the blind, the miserable, and those who beg, and having performed his domestic duties, the householder shall attain the highest good.
For men who conduct themselves in this manner, the Lord of Kāśī becomes gracious; and through the grace of the Lord of Kāśī, the attainment of Kāśī itself brings about liberation.
He who has resorted to Kāśī has bathed in all sacred fords, he is initiated into all sacrifices, and he has indeed bestowed all gifts.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of a Householder," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 40.
Skanda said: Having thus lived in the householder stage, the Brahmin, beyond the second stage of life, and being endowed with wrinkles and grey hair, should enter the third stage.
Having seen the offspring of his offspring and having abandoned his village food, he should entrust his wife to his sons or enter the forest with his wife.
Wearing garments of skin and bark, maintaining the sacred fire, subsisting on the food of sages, he bore matted hair, bathed at dawn and dusk, and maintained his beard, nails, and body hair.
One should not neglect the five great sacrifices even with vegetables, roots, or fruits; one should honor mendicants and guests with water, roots, fruits, or alms.
Neither a taker nor a giver, he is self-controlled and devoted to the study of the Vedas; he should offer the Vedic Agnihotra sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.
He should offer sacrificial cakes made from the food of sages brought by himself; he should eat salt prepared by himself and oil extracted from fruits.
One should avoid śelu, śigru, mushrooms, meat, and honey; and in the month of Āśvina, one should discard whatever store of forest-food was previously accumulated.
He should renounce cultivated fruits and roots as well as food produced by the plow; he may either use his teeth as a mortar or use a stone for grinding.
He may either wash his food immediately after eating, or he may store it for a month; or he may collect grains, fruits, roots, and so forth, for three, six, or twelve months.
He may eat only at night, or eat only once every other day, or even eat only at every sixth meal-time; he may observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, or eat only once a fortnight, or even once a month.
Adhering to the Vaikhānasa doctrine, even if subsisting on fruits and roots, he should wither his body through austerity and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having established the internal fire within himself, he should wander without a fixed abode; for the sake of sustaining life, he should beg from ascetics dwelling in the forest.
Or, having brought food from a village, he may eat eight mouthfuls while dwelling in the forest; a Brahmin who lives thus in the forest hermitage is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having spent the third part of his life in the forest, he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth quarter of his life.
Without having cleared the three debts, nor having procreated sons, and likewise without having performed sacrifices, one who desires liberation goes downward. (15)
Since not even the slightest fear arises for him from living beings, all beings here always grant him freedom from fear.

One should always wander alone, without fire and without a fixed dwelling; for the sake of spiritual perfection, one should remain without companions, resorting to a village only for the purpose of food.
A renunciant should never desire either life or death; he should await his time alone, just as a servant awaits his orders. 18.
Empty of the sense of "mine" everywhere, endowed with equanimity everywhere, and making his abode at the foot of a tree—the seeker of liberation is praised here in this world. (19)
Meditation, purity, begging for alms, and constant practice of solitude—these are the four duties of an ascetic; a fifth does not exist.
A renunciant should not wander anywhere during the four months of the rainy season, because therein injury to living beings, such as seeds and sprouts, would occur.
He should walk avoiding living beings, drink water filtered through a cloth, speak words that cause no agitation, and never become angry with anyone at any time.

He should live with himself as his only companion, independent and without support, constantly devoted to the inner self, with hair, nails, and beard clipped short, and having his senses under control.
Clad in safflower-dyed garments, carrying a staff, subsisting on alms, and devoid of worldly fame; a vessel made of gourd, wood, clay, or bamboo is recommended, but not a fifth.
A mendicant should never accept a vessel made of metal; for if even a single cowrie shell is accepted here and there day after day, [it leads to further attachment].
The sin of killing a thousand cows is this eternal Vedic revelation: if one should ever look upon a woman with an affectionate heart in one's mind.
For two billion Brahma-kalpas, one will undoubtedly dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell; one should wander for alms only once a day and should not engage in elaboration therein.

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the eating bowls is completed, the ascetic should always go forth for alms. (28)
Eating little, dwelling in solitude, not covetous for the objects of the senses, and free from passion and hatred, a mendicant is fit for liberation. (29)
If an ascetic may rest for even a moment in someone's hermitage, what need has he for many sacred sites? He becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. (30)
Whatever sin has been accumulated by a householder until the end of his life, an ascetic who has stayed for even a single night will surely consume it all.
Having seen the unbearable onset of old age, the affliction of disease, the abandonment of the body, and once again the womb and the terrible suffering within the womb; (32)
Dwelling in various wombs, separation from those who are dear, union with those who are unpleasant, and the arising of suffering from unrighteousness—[all these he beheld]. (33)
Furthermore, dwelling in hell and the various torments of the hells—the manifold destinies of men arising from the defects of their own karma—[are experienced]. (34)
Having perceived the impermanence of bodies and the permanence of the Supreme Self, one should exert effort for liberation, regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) one is devoted to.
Known as a "hand-bowl" (karapātrī), she is devoid of an alms-bowl; for them, merit indeed increases a hundredfold day by day. (36)
Having thus sequentially attended to the four stages of life, the wise man, free from dualities and having abandoned all attachments, becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.
The self of those with evil intellects, when unrestrained, leads to bondage; yet that same self, when restrained by the wise, can bestow the state free from all affliction.
The Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, as well as the Vidyās and Upaniṣads; the verses, mantras, commentaries, and whatever other verbal compositions exist anywhere—(39)
The study of the Vedas, knowledge, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint, faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the realization of the Self. (40)
For that very Self is what must be sought after by all those abiding in the stages of life; it is to be heard, reflected upon, and beheld with diligent effort. (41)
Liberation comes through self-knowledge, and that cannot be attained without yoga; and that yoga is perfected only through long-term practice. (42)
Yoga is not attained by resorting to the forest, nor by contemplating various scriptures, nor by gifts, nor by vows, nor even by austerities or sacrifices. (43)

Neither through the lotus posture and such yogic postures, nor by gazing at the tip of the nose; neither through ritual purity, nor through silence, nor even through the propitiation of mantras [is liberation attained]. (44)
Through persistent application, constant practice, firm conviction in that very [object], and repeated effort without despondency, yoga is perfected; and not otherwise.
For one who constantly sports with the Self, who is always united with the Self, and who is perfectly satisfied in the Self alone, the perfection of yoga is not far off. (46)
He who does not perceive a second thing here apart from the Self—that lord of yogis, delighting in the Self, becomes one with Brahman in this very world. || 47 ||
The wise declare that the conjunction of the self and the mind is yoga; some, however, say that yoga is the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Even the unlearned claim that the union of the senses with their objects is yoga; for those whose minds are attached to sense-objects, both knowledge and liberation are far away. (49)
As long as the activity of the mind, which is difficult to restrain, has not ceased, how can one say that yoga is near? How could it be so? (50)
Having rendered the mind free from fluctuations and having unified it with the Kṣetrajña, the Supreme Self, one who is thus engaged in yoga is said to be liberated.
Having indeed turned all the external openings inward, one should unite the collection of senses within the mind, and the mind with the Self.

One should dissolve the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is liberated from all states of being, into Brahman; for this is both meditation and yoga—everything else is merely an expansion of books.
To say that something which does not exist in all the worlds exists is a contradiction; yet when it is spoken by another, it remains fixed in the heart. (54)
For that Brahman is to be personally realized, just as a young girl [realizes] the pleasure of a woman; one who is not a yogi does not know it at all, like one born blind [who does not see] a lamp.
For one whose nature is constant practice, that indeed becomes self-evident; because of its subtlety, it is the supreme, eternal Brahman, which cannot be described. (56)
Just as water does not remain still for even a single moment, so too is the mind struck by the wind; therefore, one should not place trust in it. 57.

Therefore, one should restrain the vital air for the sake of achieving steadiness of the mind; for the purpose of restraining the breath, one should practice the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga). || 58 ||
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these are the six limbs of yoga. (59)
There are as many postures here as there are species of living beings; this one is declared to be Siddhāsana, which bestows the perfection of yoga upon the yogi.
By constant practice of this, one shall attain firmness of the body.
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh, the knower of yoga knows this to be the lotus posture (padmāsana).
One should then hold the two thumbs with both hands using a firm grip; from this practice of padmāsana, one's body becomes firm.
Alternatively, the knower of yoga, having sat upon whichever seat—such as the svastika posture—brings him ease, should practice yoga.
Not near water or fire, nor in a dilapidated forest or a cow-pen; not where gadflies and mosquitoes abound, nor at a shrine, nor at a crossroads. (69)
One should not practice in a place defiled by hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, bones, and the like; nor in a place with a foul odor, nor in a place crowded with people.
Free from all affliction, bringing pleasure to all the senses, generating clarity of mind, and gladdened by the fragrance of garlands and incense; (67)
One who knows yoga should practice yoga when he is neither over-satiated nor afflicted by hunger, nor oppressed by excrement and urine, nor exhausted by travel, nor distressed by anxiety. (68)
With the feet placed flat on the thighs, the right hand resting upon the left, slightly raising the face with the palms turned upward, and bracing the chest; (69)
With eyes closed, established in sattva, he should not let his teeth touch one another; with the tongue fixed on the palate and the mouth closed, he should remain perfectly motionless.

Having fully restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high, one should then undertake the middle and the highest forms of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
When the breath moves, everything moves; when it is still, everything is still. Therefore, by restraining the breath, the yogi attains the state of a pillar (immobility).
As long as the vital breath remains in the body, so long is it called life; when it has departed, that is death; therefore, one should restrain the vital breath. (73)
As long as the breath is bound within the body, as long as the mind is without support, and as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, how can there be any fear of death? (74)
Out of fear of death, Brahmā always practiced breath control (prāṇāyāma); through the complete restraint of the vital breaths, yogis have attained perfection. (75)

The slow [tempo] consists of twelve *mātrās*, where a *mātrā* is considered to be the duration of a short syllable; the medium [tempo] is double that of the former, and the fast [tempo] is triple that.
This [practice] gradually produces perspiration, trembling, and despondency; one should overcome perspiration with the first [stage] and trembling with the second. (77)

Indeed, by the third [stage], the vital breath (prāṇa) of the yogi becomes perfected; then, gradually restrained, the perfected vital breath of the yogi, when practiced in due order, leads him wherever he desires.
If this prāṇa is forcibly restrained, it may escape through the pores of the skin; it tears the body apart and even gives rise to diseases such as leprosy. (79)
He must be brought to confidence gradually, like a wild elephant in the forest; for a wild elephant or even a lion attains gentleness only through a gradual process. (80)

He carries out the instruction of the Teacher and does not transgress it; likewise, this vital breath (prāṇa) residing in the heart, when grasped by the yogi through the yoga of successive stages and being cultivated, attains a state of confidence.
The *haṃsa* (the vital breath) moves thirty-six finger-breadths outside; because it moves by way of the left and right paths, it is called *prāṇa*.
When the entire wheel of channels becomes pure and undisturbed, at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of restraining the vital breath.
Seated firmly, one should fill the breath with the moon (inhale) according to one's capacity, and then exhale it through the sun; this is called prāṇāyāma.
Meditating upon the moon accompanied by a flowing torrent of nectar, the lord of yogis attains bliss in that very instant through breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 85 ||
Having drawn in the breath with the sun (the right nostril), the yogi should fill the cavity of the abdomen; having retained it, he should then slowly exhale through the moon (the left nostril).
Meditating in his heart upon the "Heat" (ūṣmagu) stage, which has the brilliance of a mass of blazing fire, the lord of yogis shall become a partaker of bliss through this southern extension.
Thus, through three months of practice and the cultivation of both types of *āyāma*, the yogi whose multitude of channels is purified is called one who has mastered the vital breath (*siddhaprāṇa*).
The retention of breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and health result from the purification of the channels (nāḍī). 89.
Prāṇa is the wind residing within the body; āyāma is that which is dependent upon it. A single measure (mātrā) consisting of one breath is defined as prāṇāyāma.
In the lowest stage of breath control (prāṇāyāma), there is heat; in the middle stage, trembling occurs; and in the highest stage, the body, seated in the bound lotus posture, repeatedly rises up.

One should burn away defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sin through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra); one attains steadiness of mind through concentration (dhāraṇā), and the vision of the Lord through meditation (dhyāna). 92.

One attains liberation through meditative absorption (samādhi) by abandoning both auspicious and inauspicious phenomena; through the posture (āsana), the firmness of the body is achieved—this is proclaimed as the six-limbed [yoga]. 93.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is said to be accomplished by twelve rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma); by twelve rounds of withdrawal, concentration (dhāraṇā) is proclaimed.
For the sake of union with the Lord, meditation consists of twelve dhāraṇās; by means of those twelve meditations alone, samādhi is said to be attained.
Beyond meditative absorption (samādhi) lies an infinite light that is self-luminous; when that is perceived, the cycle of coming and going—the realm of ritual action—comes to an end.
When the wind reaches the ether, a great sound arises from bells and other instruments that are being played; from that, success is not far off.
Through the proper practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases; through improper practice of yoga, however, all diseases arise. || 98 ||
Hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes.
Various disorders arise from the derangement of the wind (vāta).
One should exhale the breath properly, fill it properly, and bind it properly; in this way, the knower of yoga attains perfection. 100.
When the senses wander among their objects at will, the skillful withdrawal of them is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). || 1 ||
He who withdraws the senses from all sides, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, shall become free from impurity through the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
The sun resides in the region of the navel and the moon in the region of the palate; the downward-facing moon rains, while the upward-facing sun devours.

That practice must be performed by which that nectar is attained: the navel above and the palate below, the sun above and the moon below; this practice called "inversion" arises only through constant repetition.
With a mouth like the beak of a crow, the yogi who knows the method of controlling the vital breath should drink it very slowly; thus he becomes ageless.
Placing the tongue in the cavity of the palate and facing upwards, one who drinks the nectar will undoubtedly attain freedom from old age within six months.
The knower of yoga who, having become steady, performs the drinking of soma with the tongue turned upward, undoubtedly conquers death within half a month.
Pressing the great cavity of the upper teeth with the tip of the tongue and meditating upon the Goddess composed of nectar, one becomes a poet within six months.
For the yogin whose body is filled with nectar, after two or three years, semen begins to flow upward, bringing about the manifestation of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
The poison does not spread in the body of that yogi who is perpetually filled with the digits of the moon, even if he has been bitten by Takṣaka.
Endowed with the proper posture and joined with breath control, and perfected in sensory withdrawal, he should then practice concentration.
That which consists of the individual concentration upon the five elements within the heart through the immobility of the mind is called dhāraṇā.
One should meditate in the heart upon the earth, resembling yellow orpiment, marked with the letter *la*, together with its presiding deity, and shaped as a quadrangle; this is the earth-dhāraṇā.
Meditating on the syllable 'va', which is the essence of water, resembling a half-moon, joined with Viṣṇu, and white as a jasmine flower—one should thus conquer the lotus-born [Brahmā].

Having meditated upon the fire-element situated in the palate, which has the luster of an indragopa insect, is triangular, conjoined with the letter *ra*, and presided over by Rudra, one shall conquer the fire. || 15 ||

One should conquer the wind by meditating on the air-principle (vāyutattva) located between the eyebrows, circular and resembling collyrium, with the seed-syllable *yaṃ* and Īśa as its presiding deity. || 16 ||

Space, which resembles a mirage of water, resides in the *brahmarandhra*; it is accompanied by the Lord Sadāśiva, is peaceful, and is the syllable *Ha*. Having drawn the vital breath (*prāṇa*) there for five *ghaṭikās* and maintaining concentration, one should practice this; it is called the "Meditation on Space" (*nabhodhāraṇā*), which is skillful in shattering the door of liberation.
The five concentrations (dhāraṇās) for living beings are: the paralyzing, the flooding, the burning, the wandering, and likewise the pacifying. || 18 ||

The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally remembered as meaning "thought" (*ciṃtā*), which is a perfectly steady contemplation upon reality; this is declared here to be meditation (*dhyāna*), which is twofold: with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*).

That which is with qualities (saguṇa) is considered [the form] differentiated by the forest; that which is without qualities (nirguṇa) is held to be absolute. Know that which is accompanied by mantras to be with qualities, and that which is devoid of mantras to be without qualities.
Having established the mind within and the eyes without upon a comfortable seat, and maintaining equanimity of the body, this meditation posture bestows supreme accomplishment.
Neither by the horse sacrifice nor by the Rājasūya does one obtain that merit which a yogi of steady posture gains through a single moment of meditation.
As long as the subtle elements of sound and the rest remain within the ears and other sense organs, so long is it considered *dhyāna*; beyond that is *samādhi*.
Retention (dhāraṇā) consists of five nāḍīs; meditation (dhyāna) would be sixty nāḍīs; and here, it is said that absorption (samādhi) occurs after twelve days.
Just as the union of water and salt occurs through their combination, so too the unification of the self and the mind is here called samādhi. (25)
When the vital breath is completely diminished and the mind dissolves, that state of equanimity which arises is here called samādhi.
That state of equality between these two—the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—in which all volitional constructions have perished, is designated as samādhi. || 27 ||
The lord of yogis, absorbed in samādhi, perceives neither himself nor another, neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor that which is other than pleasure.
The yogi who is disciplined in meditative absorption is not driven away by time, is not smeared by karma, and is not pierced by weapons or missiles. (29)
The yogi who is moderate in diet and conduct, disciplined in his actions, and balanced in sleep and wakefulness, perceives the ultimate reality.
The knowers of Brahman know Brahman as the bliss of the realization of reality, devoid of causes and examples, and beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Therein, through the method of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), the yogi merges into the supreme Brahman, which is without support, free from fear, and free from affliction.
Just as clarified butter poured into clarified butter becomes indeed that very butter, and milk [poured] into milk likewise [becomes that very milk], so too the yogi attains identity with that.
One should perform limb-massage with water that has not been boiled; one should avoid lukewarm water and salt, and should always subsist on a diet of milk. (34)
A practitioner of celibacy who has conquered anger, subdued greed, and is free from envy—by constant practice in this manner for a year, he is called a yogi. (35)
He who knows Mahāmudrā, Nabhomudrā, Uḍḍīyāna, Jalandhara, and Mūlabandha—that yogi possesses the perfection of yoga.
The purification of the network of channels, the union of the moon and the sun, and the thorough drying up of the bodily fluids—this is designated as Mahāmudrā. (37)
Pressing the perineum with the left foot and placing the chin upon the chest, one should hold the outstretched right leg with both hands for a long time.
Having filled the abdomen with the vital breath (prāṇa), one should slowly exhale it for a long time; this is declared to be Mahāmudrā, the destroyer of the flood of great sins. (39)
Having practiced on the lunar part, one should practice again on the solar part; when the count has become equal, one should then release the mudrā.
For indeed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all tastes are not devoid of flavor; even dreadful poison, when drunk, is digested like nectar.
Consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, indigestion, and other such ailments—these defects of his go to destruction for one who practices Mahāmudrā. (42)
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse, and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that is the Khecarī Mudrā. (43)
He who knows the Khecarī mudrā is not afflicted by a shower of arrows, nor is he tainted by karma; he is not oppressed by time. (44)
Because the mind moves in the void and the tongue has gone to the void, this mudrā is called Khecarī, practiced by the perfected ones (siddhas). || 45 ||
As long as the bindu remains within the body, whence can there be fear of death? As long as the space-seal (nabhomudrā) is bound, the bindu does not depart. (46)
Because this great bird flies upward day and night, it is therefore called Uḍḍīyāna; therein, the lock (bandha) is prescribed.
One should maintain the posterior contraction in the abdomen and above the navel; this is indeed the Uḍḍīyāna Bandha, by which one may abandon even the fear of death.
For it binds the network of vessels through which the water from the sky flows downward; this is the Jālandhara-bandha, which destroys the flood of suffering in the throat. (49)
When the Jālandhara band, characterized by the constriction of the throat, is performed, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital breath (vāyu) rush upward. || 150 ||
Pressing with the heel, one should contract the anus; drawing the *apāna* upward, the *mūlabandha* is thus performed. (51)
When the downward breath (apāna) and the upward breath (prāṇa) are unified, there is the cessation of urine and feces; even an old man becomes young through the constant practice of mūlabandha.
Under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the individual soul runs up and down; flickering along the left and right channels, it finds no stability.

Just as a bird bound by a string is drawn back even though it has flown away, so too the individual soul (jīva) bound by the qualities (guṇas) is drawn [toward the heart] by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma). 54.
The apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna; the knower of yoga unites these two which are situated above and below. (55)
With the sound *ha* it goes out, and with the sound *sa* it enters again; thus the mantra "Haṃsa, Haṃsa" is constantly recited by the living soul.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times—endowed with this number—the individual soul constantly recites the mantra day and night. (57)
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogis; by the mere intention of this [mantra], a person is released from sins. (58)
In this world, obstacles arise for the yogin that cause the destruction of his yoga; it is heard that news from afar reaches him, and what is far away appears before his eyes. (59)
One would have the power to travel a hundred yojanas in half a moment; indeed, even unthought-of scriptures would become committed to memory by rote. (160)
The power of retention is exceedingly fierce; the great burden becomes light. In one moment he is emaciated, in one moment stout, in one moment small, and in one moment great. (61)
He enters the bodies of others, understands the speech of animals, bears divine fragrance upon his body, and utters divine words. || 62 ||
"Divine maidens entreat him, and he maintains a divine body"—such signs as these are the obstacles that indicate the perfection of yoga. (63)
If his mind is not distracted here by these obstacles, then he attains before him that state which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to reach.
O Pot-born One, that which, once attained, one does not return from, and having attained which one does not grieve—that is obtained through yoga consisting of six limbs.
How can such a yoga be accomplished in a single lifetime? And without the perfection of yoga, how can liberation be attained here?
"O Pot-born One, both indeed are surely paths to Nirvana; whether it be the casting off of the body at Kāśī, or such a yoga as this. (67)
Due to the restless activity of the senses, the expansion of the impurities of the Kali age, and the short lifespan of men, where in this world can there be the great success of yoga? (68)
For this very reason, that Lord of the Universe, an ocean of compassion who bestows the state of supreme exaltation upon all living beings, remains eternally present in Kāśī. (69)
In Kāśī, absolute liberation (kaivalya) is attained by living beings with ease through the means of yoga-practice and other methods, in a way that it cannot be attained anywhere else. || 170 ||
In Kāśī, union with one's own self is declared to be the perfect yoga; one is not liberated here so quickly by any other kind of yoga.
Viśveśvara, Viśālākṣī, the celestial river Gaṅgā, Kālabhairava, the illustrious Ḍhuṇḍhi, and Daṇḍapāṇi—this indeed is the six-limbed Yoga.
He who constantly practices this six-limbed yoga in Kāśī attains the long yogic sleep and enjoys immortality.
Oṃkāra, Kṛttivāsas, Kedāra, Triviṣṭapa, Vīreśvara, and Viśveśa—this is another group of six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) here.
The confluence of the Pādodaka and Asī rivers, Jñānoda, Maṇikarṇikā, the Ṣaḍaṅga Mahāyoga, as well as the lakes of Brahma and Dharma—these are [the sacred sites]. 75.
O best of men, by virtue of this practice of the six limbs in Vārāṇasī, a living being is never again born within the womb of a mother. (76)
The Gaṅgā-bath is the Mahāmudrā, which destroys great sins; even by practicing this mudrā, one may attain immortality. (77)
Moving through the streets of Kāśī is the Khecarī Mudrā; by means of this Khecarī Mudrā, one certainly becomes a sky-walker (khecaro).
Flying up from all regions and proceeding toward Vārāṇasī—this is the Uḍḍīyāna Mahābandha, which leads to liberation. (79)
O Lord of the Universe, holding upon the crown of the head the water born from bathing—this is the Jālandhara-bandha, difficult for all the gods to attain. (180)
That a wise person does not abandon Kāśī even when surrounded by hundreds of obstacles is indeed known as the "Root-Bond" (mūlabandha), for it cuts away the very root of suffering.
Thus, O Sage, this twofold yoga has been fully described by me to you—the one with its six limbs and the ocean-like [yoga]—as spoken by Śambhu for the sake of liberation. (82)
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, as long as disease does not afflict, and as long as there is time remaining, one should remain devoted to yoga. (83)
Between these two yogas, this Kāśī-yoga is the most excellent; by practicing the Kāśī-yoga, one shall attain the supreme yoga.
Recognizing that death is imminent through old age, which is accompanied by mental and physical ailments and bears the very signs of mortality, one should take refuge in the Lord of Kāśī.
Having taken refuge in Kāśīnātha, from where can men have fear of Time? Even though Time is enraged and a taker of life, that very Time is most auspicious in Kāśī. (86)
Just as a virtuous man would await a guest with hospitality, so does the fortunate one await the arrival of time in Kāśī. || 87 ||
The Kali age, the [degenerate] time, and deeds performed in the past—this triad known as "the three thorns"—has no power over those who dwell in Ānandavana.
Elsewhere, time will undoubtedly seize one unexpectedly; if one desires freedom from fear of time, then one should take refuge in Kāśī. (89)

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of Yoga," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 41.
Agastya said: "O son of Hara, how is the nearness of the end of time known? Tell me, who am asking you, some of those signs."
The youth said: "O sage, listen to those signs of Time that arise for embodied beings when death has drawn near."
If the breath flows continuously through the right nostril day and night, his lifespan indeed diminishes by exactly three years.
The sun flows continuously for one day and night, for three days and nights, and for one full year; this is said here to be the limit of his life.
If the wind flows continuously through both nostrils for ten days, and there is a transit [of the breath] along with it, one shall live for three days.
Except for the two nostrils, the wind does not blow from the mouth; therefore, one should predict his departure on the road within two days.
At any moment, death may suddenly draw near; therefore, one who fears death should strive diligently to contemplate that time.
When the sun is situated in the seventh zodiac sign and the moon is in the natal asterism, that time should be regarded as Pauṣṇa, when the sun moves toward the southern path.
He who suddenly beholds a man who is dark-brown in complexion shall live for two years, provided he remains formless at that very moment.
If the seed, excrement, urine, sneeze, or even feces of anyone should fall here on a single occasion, his lifespan is held to be one year.
He who sees a multitude of serpents resembling sapphire in the sky, spreading here and there, does not live for six months.
If one with a mouth full of water on a cloudy day turns his back to the sun and, upon blowing, does not see a rainbow, he has six months to live.
One whose death is imminent does not behold Arundhatī, Dhruva, the three steps of Viṣṇu, or the fourth, the circle of the Mothers.
Arundhatī is the tongue, and Dhruva is said to be the tip of the nose; the steps of Viṣṇu are between the eyebrows, and the circle of the Mothers is in the eyes.
If one suddenly perceives a change in the colors such as blue or in the tastes such as bitter and sour, he will meet death within six months. (15)
For a mortal whose death is six months away, the throat, lips, tongue, and teeth constantly wither, and likewise the palate as the fifth becomes lusterless.
If the semen, nails, and the corners of the eyes possess a dark blue tint, then that man shall go to the city of Yama in the sixth month.
If a man sneezes during the midst of sexual intercourse, it is certain that in the fifth month he will become a guest of the King of Dharma (Yama).
If a three-colored lizard quickly climbs onto someone's head and moves about there, that person's life will come to an end within six months.
If the heart, feet, or hands of one who has even bathed well quickly become parched, his life remains for only three months.
He whose reflection appears in the form of a foot or a half-footprint in either dust or mud lives for five months.
If one's shadow trembles even when the physical body is motionless, the messengers of Death bind that man in the fourth month.
He who does not see the head of his own reflection in water, a lamp, a mirror, or similar objects, will perish in its entirety.
One's intellect shall fail and one's speech shall falter; Indra’s bow shall be seen without arrows, two moons in the night, and two suns in the day. (24)
By day there was the circle of stars, and by night the sky was devoid of stars; and simultaneously in the four directions appeared the circle of Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
A tree upon a mountain peak, a city of the Gandharvas, and the dancing of Piśācas even during the day—these are the causes of death.
If one observes even a single one of all these signs, then death should be expected within the limit of one month, and not longer. (27)
When one whose ears are blocked by the hands does not hear sound, then—whether being stout or thin, or thin and stout—one returns from that delusion.
He who sees his own shadow situated in the southern direction shall live for five days and then meet his death.
It is cast away or even devoured by piśācas, asuras, and crows; by bhūtas, pretas, dogs, vultures, jackals, donkeys, and pigs. (30)
Having abandoned his life at the end of the year, he beholds Yama in a dream by means of donkeys, young camels, monkeys, hawks, mules, and cranes.
That man who, during the time of a dream, beholds his own body adorned with red perfumes, flowers, and garments, shall live for eight months, alas, only for a short while.
He who indeed climbs a heap of dust, an anthill, or even a sacrificial post in a dream perishes in the sixth month.
He who sees himself in a dream mounted upon a donkey, smeared with oil, shaven-headed, and being led toward the direction of Yama along with his ancestors; || 34 ||
If a man in a dream sees grass or dry wood upon his own head or even upon his body, he does not survive the sixth month.
If one should see a black man clad in black garments, holding an iron staff, standing before him in person, he shall not exceed three months [of life].
If a young girl named Kālī should bind one with her arm-nooses in a dream, he shall behold within a month a city as desired by his mind.
A man who, while sleeping, dreams that he has mounted a monkey and travels toward the eastern direction, shall behold the city of Saṃyaminī in just five days.
If a miser were to become generous, or a generous person were to become miserly—if such a transformation of nature were to occur—then one meets with death. (39)
These are the signs of the time; though there are many others as well, having recognized them, a person should practice yoga or else take refuge in the Akāśikā [state]. (40)
I do not know of any other means for deceiving Time than the Lord of Kāśī, who grants victory over death and prevents rebirth in a womb. (41)
Sins roar as long as they can, and King Yama roars as long as a man does not devotedly go for refuge to the Lord of the Universe. 42.
Who that has reached the abode of Viśveśvara, drunk from the waters of the northward-flowing [Gaṅgā], and touched the excellent Liṅga of Viśveśa, does not deserve to be honored? 43.
What can even an enraged Time (Death) do to the men who dwell in Kāśī, where Śiva himself whispers the instruction of mantras into their ears at the time of death? || 44 ||
Just as childhood passes away and youth has gone, so too does youth and old age pass swiftly and are destined to depart. (45)
As long as one is not overcome by old age and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should the wise person abandon all that is trivial in nature and take refuge in Kāśī.
O Pot-born one, let other signs of time remain aside; old age itself is the first sign, and it is strange that there is no fear even of that.
For one who is overcome by old age is despised by all, like a man deprived of his wealth whose ruby of youth has been stolen. 48.
They do not utter words of welcome, their wives abandon even their affection, and kinsmen no longer respect a man embraced by old age. (49)
Seeing him embraced by old age, a loving woman, fearing another's wife, would constantly turn away from him, even though he is her beloved. (50)
There is no disease equal to old age; there is no suffering like that of old age. Old age alone brings about humiliation for men, and it is indeed death itself.
Time cannot be overcome by asceticism or the methods of yoga in the same way that it is overcome by residing in Kāśī for even a long period of time. 52.
Who would desire to reach Kāśī without sacrifices, without gifts, without vows, recitations, and the like, and without a vast accumulation of merit? (53)
Attaining Kāśī is this yoga; attaining Kāśī is this austerity; attaining Kāśī is this gift; attaining Kāśī is oneness with Śiva.
What is the Kali age, or what is Time; what is old age, and what is evil action? What are diseases, or what are obstacles, if one has taken refuge in Vārāṇasī? (55)
The Kali age would afflict them alone, and Time itself seeks to destroy them.

Those who have not taken refuge in Kāśī are afflicted by sins and their consequences; however, those who have taken refuge in Kāśī and by whom Viśveśvara has been worshipped, having attained the liberating knowledge (tāraka-jñāna), are released from the bonds of karma. || 57 ||
Wealthy men never obtain such happiness anywhere as the imperishable bliss one attains through death in Kāśī.
Better is one who dwells in Kāśī than one who sits upon the station of the gods; the former attains the end of suffering, while the latter attains the end of happiness.
O Lord, although the Sovereign remained on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, he found no pleasure there without Kāśī, which is inhabited by King Divodāsa.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Means of Deceiving Time," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 42.
Agastya said: O Blessed One, tell this narrative for the delight of the listeners: how did the three-eyed God cause King Divodāsa to abandon Kāśī, and how did he come from Mount Mandara? || 1 ||
Skanda said: Out of respect for the words of Brahmā, the Lord went to Mount Mandara; he was pleased by the penance of that very mountain, Mandara.
When the god Viśveśvara had departed for Mandara, the beautiful mountain, all the inhabitants of heaven also went along with Giriśa.
Having indeed abandoned the Vaiṣṇava fields here on earth, Viṣṇu himself departed for Mandara, where Umādhava, the God of gods, resides.
O best of Brahmins, Gaṇeśa also departed from there for the abodes of the Gaṇapatyas; I too, having left, went toward Mount Mandara.
The Sun, having abandoned his solar duties, departed from his abode; and the other gods as well, leaving their respective places on earth, went away.
When the hosts of gods had departed, the powerful lord of the earth, Divodāsa, ruled his kingdom free from all opposition.
Having established his capital at Vārāṇasī as a firm and stable seat, that one of great intelligence caused it to prosper while protecting his subjects in accordance with righteousness.
Like the sun, he scorched the hearts and eyes of his enemies; like the moon, he dwelt in the minds of his friends and even in those of his own kin.
Wielding his unbroken bow like Indra in battle, he was beheld by the cloud-like enemy forces as they fled.
Born like a king of dharma, he was a discriminator between dharma and adharma; as king, he honored those who deserved no punishment and strictly punished those who deserved it.
Like Dhanañjaya, he repeatedly consumed the enemy forests; like Varuṇa, though remaining at a distance, he bound the circle of his foes with his noose.
There was a lord of virtuous people, who increased his enemies' demons; he was equal to the life-breath of the world and was intent upon giving life to the world. (13)
He alone became the king of kings, the bestower of wealth upon all virtuous men; he alone was the very form of Rudra, whom his enemies beheld in battle.
For he assumes the forms of all the gods through his ascetic power; therefore, the Viśvedevas praise him and worship him. || 15 ||
For he is indeed beyond the reach of those who can be accomplished; superior to the Vasus in wealth, he is the wielder of form among the planets, a son of the Aśvins who possesses an eternal beauty.
Disregarding the hosts of Maruts while delighting the Tuṣitas with his virtues, he was indeed the sovereign of all Vidyādharas among all the Vidyādharas. (17)
He humbled even the Gandharvas with his own songs; meanwhile, the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas guarded that fortress, which was like a brother to heaven.
The Nāgas committed no offenses against him who was exceedingly powerful like a Nāga; and having assumed the forms of men, the Danujas served him.
