O King, since the Guhyakas, who move in secret among men, have been born all around you, we Asuras shall serve you with our own splendors.

Since even the abode of the gods is difficult to attain within your domain, we have come here; for it was there that the swift wind, stationed upon the purifying path, taught the king’s horses the art of rapid movement.
Seeing his elephants—born not from elephants, possessing the stature of great mountains, and constantly exuding rut—others too became generous donors.
In the arena of debate he was a victor, and in the arena of conduct he was a warrior; he was never, anywhere, conquered by anyone through either scriptures or weapons.
The enemies of that king never set foot within the range of his vision; thus, his subjects were always "unfallen from their station" (anaṣṭapadāḥ). || 24 ||
In the triple heaven of the gods, there is but one who possesses the arts; yet on this earth, all the people of that king are repositories of the arts. (25)
For there is indeed only one desire in heaven, and even that is devoid of limbs; whereas on that earth, all desires of everyone exist with all their primary and secondary parts.
Not even in his vicinity was a single mountain known as Gotrabhid anywhere; however, in heaven, the Lord of the dwellers of heaven is celebrated as Gotrabhid.
Moreover, no one in his realm heard of anyone who was subject to decay; for even in heaven, the lord of the night (the moon) is observed to wane day by day. || 28 ||
In heaven there are the nine planets; on earth, his territories are free from planetary afflictions.
In the heavenly world, Hiraṇyagarbha alone shines; all the inhabitants of that city here have their abodes within Hiraṇyagarbha.
In the heavenly world, the sun alone, possessing seven horses, shines intensely; yet the inhabitants of that city possess many horses and are always clothed in fine garments. (31)
Just as Svarbhū has six apsarases, so too does his city have six apsarases; Padmā alone is in Vaikuṇṭha, while he has a hundred lotus-lakes.
In that village, there were no calamities and no royal officials anywhere; here, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) resides in every house, while he alone is the lord of Alakā in heaven.
While that very Divodāsa was thus ruling the kingdom in Kāśī, eighty thousand autumns passed by, becoming as if mere days.
Then the gods, who follow the path of dharma, desiring to take retaliatory action against him, consulted with their preceptor.
O Sage, for those who practice dharma like you, the gods generally bring forth long successions of great calamities. (36)
Although that lord of the earth was excessively afflicted by diseases that were difficult to withstand, he remained a performer of sacrifices; nevertheless, they were not his friends.
Intolerance of the excellence of others is indeed the very nature of the gods; what wrong was done here by Bali, Bāṇa, Dadhīci, and the rest? (38)
Obstacles surely arise at every step even for one's own duty; nevertheless, those whose minds are fixed on dharma do not abandon their innate duty.
The unrighteous prosper with abundance of wealth and grain, yet through unrighteousness alone they go to the lowest state, utterly uprooted.
As Ripuñjaya protected his subjects like his own biological sons, there was not even the slightest accumulation of unrighteousness on his part.
The gods could find no vulnerability in him, who understood the sixfold policy, whose mind was strengthened by the three powers, and who was skilled in the four expedients.
Even the wise gods, though intent on causing opposition, were not able to do even the slightest harm to that Lord.
All the men in his realm were devoted to the vow of having only one wife; among the women, there was not a single one who did not observe the dharma of being faithful to her husband.
He was not a Brahmin who had not studied; nor was he a Kṣatriya who was not a hero; nor was he a Vaiśya who lacked knowledge regarding the activities for acquiring wealth. (45)
In the kingdom of King Divodāsa, the Śūdras were devoted solely to the service of the twice-born.

In that kingdom, those practicing the life of a religious student (brahmacārins) never violated their celibacy; they remained constantly dependent upon the teacher's family and were devoted to the acquisition of the Vedas.
Devoted to the duty of hospitality and expert in the treatises on dharma, his householders everywhere were constantly engaged in virtuous conduct. 48.

In that [place], those belonging to the third stage of life (the forest-dwellers) take delight in the forest way of life; they are free from desire for village affairs and follow the path of the Vedas. (49)
Completely liberated from all attachments, free and without possessions, the ascetics there are devoid of longing and rich in the restraint of speech, mind, and action. (50)
Even those born in the inverse order of castes, though produced through the reverse succession, did not abandon even slightly the path seen by their own lineage.
In that kingdom, there was no one childless, nor anyone lacking wealth; no one failed to serve their elders, and no one suffered an untimely death.
They were neither flatterers nor loquacious chatterers; they were neither deceivers nor harmful; they were neither heretics nor jesters; they were neither widows nor liquor-sellers.
Indeed, everywhere there was the sound of Vedic chanting and the discourse of the scriptures at every step; everywhere there were auspicious conversations and joyful songs of benediction. (54)
The sounding of lutes and flutes, and the sweet-toned drums—except for the drinking of Soma, no other convivial gathering of drinking reached his ears. 55.
Meat-eaters are never found anywhere else than at the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice; nor are there gamblers, debtors, or thieves where it is performed. || 56 ||
For a son, the worship of his parents' feet is the worship of the gods; it is fasting, it is a vow, it is a pilgrimage, and it is the supreme propitiation of the deities. (57)
For women, the worship of their husband's feet and the listening to his words [are paramount]; likewise, younger brothers constantly honor their elder brother.
Joyful servants attend upon the lotus feet of their master; those of lower caste are extolled by those of the highest caste on account of the weight of their virtues. (59)
The deities of Kāśī shall again worship [him] at the three times of day; everywhere, all learned men shall be honored with their heart's desires.

By the learned, those devoted to austerity are honored; by those devoted to austerity, those who have conquered their senses; by those who have conquered their senses, those devoted to knowledge; and by the wise, the yogis of Śiva.
Day and night, an offering—purified by mantras, highly precious, prepared according to ritual, and well-consecrated—is poured into the fire of the mouths of the Brahmins.
Where there are numerous builders who, at every step, construct ponds, wells, tanks, and groves with abundant and pure materials.
In that kingdom, all classes of people were seen to be joyful and well-nourished, devoted to blameless service, with the exception of hunters and butchers.
Thus, for that lord of the earth who conducted himself with purity in all matters, even the gods, though they watch with unblinking eyes, could find no opening whatsoever.
Then the preceptor of the immortals spoke to the gods who desired to do harm, while that most righteous king, the best among those who know the mantras, was ruling.
The Guru said: "Neither alliance, nor war, nor marching, nor seeking shelter, nor the state of double-dealing—none here understands these as that king does. (67)
O gods, there is only one means here among the four; for if that which is called "division" were to succeed, it would indeed be possible only against one powerful through asceticism.
Therefore, although the gods of the earth have been exiled from the land by that lord of the earth, nevertheless, there are still many there who are partial to our side. (69)
Even a moment of time without them passes not happily; they are honored there by us as well as by him.
They move constantly within and without, being the ground of all confidence; when they have assembled here, everything dear to us will be accomplished.
Having heard what was spoken by Bṛhaspati, all those gods determined its meaning; then, having honored him, they all said, "Let it be so," regarding those who move within and without.
Then Śakra, having summoned Vītihotra who stood before him, spoke with sweet words and great respect: || 73 ||
O Havyavāhana, withdraw quickly that form of yours which is established there from the domain of that king.
When that form has been restored, all subjects, with their foremost leaders destroyed and devoid of the performance of rites for the gods and ancestors, will become alienated from the king.
When the subjects have become indifferent toward the kingdom that once yielded all desires, the title of "king" will become meaningless, acquired only with great hardship.
The etymological derivation of "king" (rājā) as one who "delights" (rañjana) his subjects has been acquired; if that derivation is lost, the kingdom itself will perish. (77)
A king who is bereft of his subjects, though he may be prosperous in terms of treasury, fortresses, and forces, will soon perish like a tree standing on the edge of a riverbank.
For a lord of the earth, the subjects are the primary means for accomplishing the three goals of life; indeed, when the subjects' livelihood is exhausted, the three goals themselves perish.
When the threefold aim is exhausted, the goal consisting of both worlds is utterly destroyed.
At these words of Indra, Agni, endowed with the power of yogic illusion (yogamāyā), quickly withdrew his own form from the circle of the earth.
By the word of the wielder of the thunderbolt, the Lord Agni did not merely lead away the Tretā age, but also his own digestive fire, endowed with his innate power.
When Vahni had ascended to the heavenly world and midday had arrived, O King, the monarch, having performed his midday rites, quickly entered the dining pavilion.
Then the superintendents of the kitchen, trembling repeatedly, softly informed the king, though he was afflicted by hunger, as follows: || 84 ||
The cooks said: "O you of exceedingly great splendor and heat, who have surpassed the fire with your majesty! O expert in battle, we wish to make a certain request of you, though it is untimely."
O King, if you would grant us the boon of safety, then we shall address you with our hands joined in reverence. (86)
Having received instructions by a sign from the eyebrows of that praiseworthy king, the officials in charge of the kitchen made their request gently. (87)
"O Lord, we do not know by what deceitful means the wise Vaiśvānara, afflicted by the fear of your majesty, has vanished from the city. (88)
When the fire has become weak, how can the act of cooking take place? Nevertheless, some form of cooking is indeed accomplished through the heat of the sun. (89)
"Having received our master’s command, we shall bring her right here; and we consider, O King, that today's meal will be auspicious. (90)
Having heard the words of the Andhasika, that great being of great intelligence, the king, reflected: "This has surely been done by the gods."
Meditating there for a moment, he beheld by the power of his asceticism that the consumer of oblations (Agni) had abandoned not only his home, but even the caves within his own belly.
"He has departed from this world and gone to the abode of the gods; for what loss could there be to us here by his having entered the fire? (93)
It is precisely due to their lack of discernment that this ruin has befallen the gods; and by what strength was this kingdom accepted by me? (94)
As that Indra of the middle world was thus reflecting, "This has been bestowed by my grandfather out of great respect," (95)
The citizens, together with the people of the provinces, gathered at the gate; then, by the king's command, they were ushered inside by the doorkeeper.
Having offered appropriate gifts, they bowed down to the king, the wielder of the earth; some were addressed by the king with words that were like a brother's.
Some were dismissed by the king with a mere glance, and some with a gesture of the hand; all were sent away with great respect.

They all shone and flocked together in that place attended by the luster of jewels, which surpassed the mass of fragrance from the scents of celestial trees, and was made auspicious by the shade of the king’s hundred-ribbed parasol.
Then the lord of the people (the king), perceiving that intention from the expression on her face, spoke; for the citizens were overcome with great fear.
If Anala were brought down to earth by those writings that cause transformation, would their defeat over me be accomplished by this much alone? (1)

"O citizens, it was I myself who previously desired to accomplish this task; however, for the most part, it was neglected. By good fortune, it has been brought to my mind again after a long time by you. (2)
"May Anala go; may the Wind, the life-breath of the world, also depart from here for your welfare. May Varuṇa depart from here without delay along with the two Sun-gods. (3)
"Indeed, by the power of my asceticism, I myself shall become the rain-cloud, bestowing the abundance of all crops for the joy of the people. (4)
Having conceived myself through the power of asceticism and yoga, I am the supreme performer of the cooking, the sacrifice, and the manifestation of results, existing in three forms as fire.
"Moving both within and without in two ways, following the path of the wind, I shall know the activity of the inner faculties of all beings. (6)
"Having fashioned a watery form that is the sole life-sustainer for all living beings, I shall revive the subjects; what need have I for inert objects? (7)
When the moon and the sun are swallowed by darkness in the sky, O citizens, do we not live on this earth without them? (8)
Having attained the lunar splendor, I shall delight all creatures; for what is the use here of this night-stalker, which is subject to waning and possessed by a stain?
Bhāskara is indeed venerable to us as the very root of our lineage; let him remain here in comfort and carry out his coming and going.
He alone is the Self of the worlds and, in particular, the tutelary deity of the lineage; yet he does not even know how to do him a favor, for this is his supreme vow.

Thus, having drunk in the flood of the nectar-like flow of the king’s words with the vessels of their ears, the multitude of citizens, their lotus-faces blossomed and their minds liberated from anxiety, departed for their respective homes. 12.

The lord of the earth, having performed that accordingly, reflected: "What is there in these three worlds that cannot be accomplished by asceticism? Possessing a splendor exceeding fire and the sun, he became like a thorn in the side of the gods. (13)

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Prowess of Divodāsa," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Skanda said: Now, in a jewel-palace shining with intense luster within the interior of the caves of Mount Mandara, where the gods were stationed on all sides and the sky was made into a canopy by its own peaks— (1)
Dwelling there, Hara, the Lord of the World, who is as enchanting as a digit of the slender moon, found no peace; for Śaṅkara was consumed by the spreading fever born of separation from Kāśī. || 2 ||

That very sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains, which was once smeared even by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) for the sake of quenching the fire of his separation, has now become thirsty for water.

The serpents, though soft and capable of removing the heat from lotus ponds, were turned into bracelets; since these things were spoken by the Lord, it became true: "Indeed, the will of Maheśvara is infallible."

The full moon, the soft essence drawn forth by the gods after churning the ocean of milk, became emaciated as its body withered from the heat of the Lord’s head, which was scorched by the pain of separation.
When Śiva, afflicted by the heat of birth, took refuge within the thick bower of his matted locks, he has not even now abandoned that celestial river which removes all torment.

Śaṅkara, who is the master of all, was forcibly brought under his control despite his great separation [from her]; he was surrounded by various gods seated in the assembly hall and encircled by his own sons.

How truly extraordinary it is that this Lord of the Three Worlds, though pure by his very nature, should be tormented by the fire born from the separation from his own city—the fire produced by the sacrificial hearth! (8)
He who constantly adorns the surface of his own forehead with a digit of the moon even tormented that very Lord; indeed, when alone, the moon behaves quite perversely.
Poison does not blaze within the hollow of his throat, nor is he scorched by it; rather, it is a marvel that he is scorched solely by the masses of cool rays from the nectar-rayed moon.

For her heart was tormented by even the spray of water from the shimmering sandalwood paste intended to dispel the pain of separation from him, and not at all by the heat arising from the spreading hoods of the serpent.
Hara destroys all delusion arising from the instruction that a garland is not harmful; yet this is his wonder: that even in a manifest garland, there arises the delusion born of a great serpent.
The Unborn One, who utterly dispels the threefold suffering even when he has merely entered the path of memory, spoke something within himself while tormented by the pain of separation from Kāśī.
Even if the breeze from Kāśī were to come here and embrace my limbs, the fever of my passion would find relief; it cannot be soothed even by plunging into the waters of the Mānasa lake.

Otherwise, how could this great torment have increased for the daughter of Dakṣa? Indeed, the creeper that is the very life of my soul would not have become so quickly extinguished had the daughter of the Himalayas not existed.

My mind was not so pained by the departure of the daughter of Dakṣa, who had cast off her body, as it would be tormented by a great heat born from the separation from one who has not yet been released. 16.
O Kashi, when shall I again joyfully obtain from you that happiness born of bodily contact, by which my limbs, though already exceedingly cooled, become instantly filled with wonder? (17)
O Kashi, destroyer of the multitude of sins, the fire born from separation from you increases most wonderfully, as if by an oblation of the soft, liquid nectar from the digits of the moon. 18.

The fever born of separation from me first came upon Dakṣa’s daughter, which was quelled by the medicine that is the daughter of Himavat; now, indeed, it would not reach peace at all if I were not to behold Kāśī immediately. (19)

Then Śiva, speaking thus with his mind, was completely freed from the agitation of his distress; he was somehow perceived by the Mother of the World as one who had been separated from the Mother of Intellects.

Even by this beloved half of his body, who remained unaware of the cause of their separation, he—who dispels the heat of the suffering of all living beings with his prostrations—was served with words of consolation.

Śrī Pārvatī said: O all-pervading one, everything exists in your hand; what joy or sorrow can there be for you? Oh, your very ashes bestow prosperity, and even the entire earth, though a source of calamities and strife, is the sustainer of all beings.

O Lord, in an instant, through not being beheld by you, the worlds go to destruction like something pitiable; even the other powers of the Lord fall away from even a mere fragment of your compassion, yet they are established in their own roles by you alone.

O Three-eyed One, the moon, the sun, and fire—which are the causes of distress for others—do not cause you distress; for these are fixed within your eyes, while they are merely objects of affection on your head, along with the water dripping from the tilaka.
O Blue-throated One, these serpents and their serpents are always yours, and yet poison does not pass to you; and I am Vāmadeva, O beautiful one, your lovely body here is joined with consciousness.
When this beneficial composition of words, which is the mother of the seed of cyclic existence, had been thus spoken, Giriśa also took up the speech to speak.

Īśvara said: "O Kāśī! Bhava, whose form consists of eight aspects, has become the eightfold manifestation of existence. Śiva quickly understood the command; surely Hara has been drawn here by Kāśī. (27)
Then, having become a childhood friend to the various creepers of that forest, she introduced Śivā to the city that grants liberation and from which she had been released.

Pārvatī said: O Bhava, let us go to the city of Kāśī, the destroyer of Smara, which possesses the splendor of white lotuses and is held aloft by your trident even during the dissolution when the waters have met the surface of the sky. 29.
O Dhūrjaṭi, even the most beautiful land of Dharādharendra does not delight me as much as Kāśikā, the preeminent city among yours, which, though situated on the earth, is certainly not of this world.
In Kāśī there is no fear born of the Kali age; in Kāśī there is no rebirth after death; in Kāśī there is no fear arising from impurity. O Lord, how can she become a guest for my eyes? (31)

Are there not thousands of places before us at every step that are lands of all-encompassing prosperity? But, O Śiva, I swear to you, nowhere has anything like Kāśī ever come within the range of my sight.

In heaven, are there not hundreds of cities that serve as the birthplace of every kind of wonder? Yet, O Enemy of Tripura, those cities become as mere blades of grass before each of your cities, which are the abodes of those who hate worldly existence.
It is not only the fever born of separation from Kāśī that afflicts you as it does me here; rather, O Nidāgha, the remedy for the cooling of this fever is either that city or my own birthplace.

I did not realize that the burning heat born of separation from my birthplace had seized me, even after reaching Kāśī, which bestows peace on all sides and is the cause for the destruction of every affliction. (35)

Nowhere has the splendor of liberation been beheld by any embodied being here before their very eyes; O bestower of bliss, I understand that this Kāśī is indeed Liberation personified, the giver of all happiness. (36)

There is no liberation here through such meditative absorption, nor through that concentration which abandons the steadiness of the senses; neither by sacrificial rites nor by Vedic knowledge is it attained in the way it is found in Kāśī, having cast off the body.

There is no such happiness in the world of the gods, much less in the exceedingly beautiful realm of Pātāla; even the mere mention of a refuge for happiness is absent in the mortal world—how could it exist in Kāśī, where one attains liberation by the mere assumption of a physical form? 38.

O Trident-bearer, in your sacred field of Avimukta, which is never devoid of the splendor of liberation, that best of living beings who applies even his mind to the six-limbed yoga is always truly engaged in it. (39)

O Śiva, such perfection of the body cannot be attained suddenly by men here through the sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) as that which is obtained with ease by reaching Kāśī and fixing one's two eyes upon You for even a moment.

Indeed, it is better to be an animal whose intellect lacks power than to be a human being who possesses great intelligence yet finds the sight of the Lord of Kāśī to be fruitless—a state that is like a bubble upon a lotus leaf in every respect. (41)

Her two eyes were fulfilled in having seen Kāśī; her body was fulfilled by dwelling in the auspicious Kāśī; her mind was fulfilled by taking refuge in Kāśī; and her face was fulfilled by being turned toward Kāśī. || 42 ||

Indeed, that dust of Kāśī is a supreme purifier which destroys passion and ignorance, radiant with the luster of the moon; it is held in high esteem by the gods who, having offered their salutations, bear it upon their foreheads as they touch the ground at Maṇikarṇikā.

Neither the world of the gods, nor the world of truth, nor the world of the nagas can equal Manikarnika, where the sound of those who have made the great departure (mahaprayana) is heard, and which is the abode of the elixir of Brahman.

The ground of Maṇikarṇikā is a source of great splendor, where the mass of darkness meets its destruction; though it has increased over more than a hundred births, it cannot be overcome even by the rays of the sun, fire, or the moon.

Is it the auspicious throne of the state of Nirvāṇa, or the soft couch of the Goddess of Liberation? Or perhaps it is the site of Maṇikarṇikā, the birthplace of the beautiful lotus-stalk of supreme bliss? (46)

There, people sitting at ease count the number of beings liberated in the past, while glistening, fine sands—eager for the great festival of their own bodies falling [into them]—serve as the counting-marks.
Skanda said: O Sage, having thus described the city of Vārāṇasī, Aparṇā again made a request to the wielder of the Pināka bow for the sake of attaining Kāśī.
Śrī Pārvatī said: O Lord of the Pramathas, Sovereign of All, You who always act according to Your own will, O Bestower of Boons, act in such a way that I may go to Ānandavana. 49.
Skanda said: Then, having heard these words of the Daughter of the Mountain—beautiful as a hymn to Kāśī and surpassing the sweetness of nectar—the Lord of the Mountain was filled with joy.
The illustrious God of Gods said: "O beloved Gaurī, I have been thoroughly nourished by the spray of the nectar of your words; now I shall strive to attain Kāśī."
O Great Goddess, you know that great vow of mine: I consume no object that has not been previously tasted by another, nor anything else. (52)
"While King Divodāsa, acting in accordance with dharma, rules the city by the command of his grandfather, what means should be devised? (53)
How was that most righteous king, Divodāsa, the lord of the earth who was devoted to the protection of his subjects, separated from the city of Kāśī? (54)
"Since an obstacle would arise for one who lives unrighteously, but not for another, therefore, O Sovereign, whom shall I dispatch who might separate him from Kāśī? (55)
O you who increase love, for those who follow the path of Dharma, he who would create an obstacle for them instead encounters an obstacle himself. 56.
"Without a flaw [in my conduct], O King, I am unable to destroy him; for it is by me alone that those who bear the burden of dharma must be protected, my dear. (57)
Neither old age can overcome him, nor does death seek to destroy him; the threefold afflictions of disease do not oppress him who maintains the path of Dharma.
While reflecting thus, the Lord beheld before him a circle of yoginīs, exceedingly mature and the means for accomplishing his profound task.
Then, O great sage, after consulting with the Goddess, Hara, whose hair is the sky, summoned the host of Yoginīs and spoke these words.
"O Yoginīs, go quickly to my city of Vārāṇasī, where King Divodāsa rules his kingdom perfectly according to dharma."
O wise ones, endowed with the power of yogic illusion, act in such a way that the king, having fallen away from his own duty, shall quickly abandon Kāśī.
"O Yoginīs, act quickly so that I may depart from here after having renovated the city of Vārāṇasī. (63)
Having thus attained serenity and bearing the teaching upon his head, the host of yoginīs then departed after having offered their salutation.
Entering the sky with a speed exceeding even that of the mind, those yoginīs, filled with joy, traveled along while conversing with one another.
Today we are indeed most fortunate, since we have been personally favored by the God of gods and sent to the glorious Ānandakānana.
Today, two great gains have occurred immediately, both of which are very difficult to attain: the honor bestowed by the Three-eyed King and likewise the sight of Kāśī.
Thus, with a joyful mind, that multitude of yoginīs, having made light their speed of travel through the sky from the groves of Mount Mandara, presented that city as a guest to his eyes.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Kāśī," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Then, casting her gaze from afar toward that multitude of Yoginīs, she praised the fruitfulness of the creation of the length of her own eyes.
The banners on the rows of divine palaces, with their fluttering fronds like hands, seemed to call out respectfully from afar to the travelers standing on the road.
The sky, though naturally deep blue, appeared perfectly clear as it was gazed upon by the expanding rays of light from the shimmering rubies of the palaces.

Having concealed her divine nature through illusion and assumed the attire appropriate for a wandering mendicant, she entered Kāśī along with a circle of yoginīs in a manner that transcends sequential order.
One yoginī had become a spirit, another was born as an ascetic woman; one became a maidservant, and another was one who fasted for a month.
One was the wife of a garland-maker, another was a beautiful woman skilled in hairdressing; one was knowledgeable in the care of childbirth, and another was an expert in medicine.
There was a certain Vaiśya woman who was keen on buying and selling; another became a snake-catcher, and yet another was a maidservant and a nurse.
One was skilled in dancing, another was proficient in singing; another was knowledgeable in playing the flute, and yet another held a lute.
One was skilled in playing the mṛdaṅga drum, another was proficient in the rhythms and measures of time; one knew the secrets of magical arts, and another was a stringer of pearls.
One was an expert in the methods of preparing perfumes, another was devoted to the arts of dice; one was skilled in the delight of conversation, while another frequented the public squares.
One was skilled in climbing bamboo poles, while another moved along a rope-path; a certain one acted like a madwoman on the road, her robes wrapped around her.
She was the bestower of offspring to the childless; she lived there in that city and was well-versed in the marks of the lines on the hands and feet.
One woman there wandered about, captivating the minds of people through her skill in painting, while another moved about, knowing the mantras for subjugation.
One bestows the perfection of pills, another bestows the perfection of collyrium; another is skilled in the alchemy of metals, and yet another bestows the perfection of sandals.

She taught him the immobilization of fire, the immobilization of water, and the immobilization of speech; one [goddess] granted him the power of moving through the air (khecarī), while another granted him invisibility.
One granted the power of attraction, another that of eradication; yet another, through the beauty of her own limbs, enchanted the hearts of young men.
"Someone grants the desired object; someone else possesses the art of light," and so forth, they imitated [these roles] everywhere through various costumes and modes of speech.
The host of Yoginīs entered every courtyard and every house; thus those Yoginīs wandered through the city day and night for a year.

Those who sought to create obstacles for the king could find no opening anywhere. Then all those yoginīs, their desires frustrated, gathered together and remained right there after consulting one another; they did not go back to Mount Mandara again.
Who, having failed to accomplish his master’s business, could stand before his lord with his honor unimpaired, even if he were exalted by the assembly’s esteem? (20)
Furthermore, O Sage, this was thought by those yoginīs: "We may live even without our Lord, but never without Kāśī. (21)

Even when greatly enraged, a good master merely takes away the livelihood of a servant; however, Kāśī snatches away the four aims of human existence from the hand of one who has fallen [from her]. 22.
O great sage, from that time onwards, the Yoginīs have not abandoned Kāśī even today; though they wander through the three worlds, they remain elsewhere [only] after leaving Kāśī.
Even having reached the glorious Kāśī, that evil-minded person who remains indifferent to it is, on the contrary, abandoned by virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Having reached Kāśī, what person of base intellect would desire to go elsewhere—having placed the vessel of liberation in his hands while his mind is set on trivial wealth? (25)
"Even though our Lord was previously turned away from us, by the merit of serving Kāśī he will become present before us; we have fulfilled our purpose through that merit. (26)
In just a few days, even the Omniscient One will arrive; for the Three-eyed Lord does not take delight anywhere other than Kāśī.
This Kāśī is a certain power of Śambhu, beyond the reach of all; indeed, only Śambhu himself knows her supreme bliss. (28)
Having thus resolved in her mind, the host of yoginīs remained in the Forest of Śambhu’s Bliss, concealed by a certain illusory power (māyā).
Vyāsa said: Having heard this, the sage again questioned the six-faced one: "O Lord, tell me what those various names of theirs are. (30)
What fruit arises from the worship of the Yoginīs in Kāśī? On which festival are they to be worshipped, and how are they to be worshipped? Tell me that. (31)
Having heard this question concerning the refuge of the Yoginīs, O Sage, Aumeya then replied: "I shall speak; may you listen with focused attention. (32)
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, I shall declare the names of the Yoginīs, by hearing which the sins of living beings perish in an instant. (33)
Gajānanā, Siṃhamukhī, Gṛdhrāsyā, Kākatuṇḍikā, Uṣṭragrīvā, Hayagrīvā, Vārāhī, and Śarabhānanā. || 34 ||
Ulūkikā, Śivārāvā, Mayūrī, Vikaṭānanā, Aṣṭavaktrā, Koṭarākṣī, Kubjā, and Vikaṭalocanā. (35)
Śuṣkodarī, Lalajjihvā, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Vānarānanā, Ṛkṣākṣī, Kekarākṣī, Bṛhattuṇḍā, and Surāpriyā. (36)
Holding a skull in her hand, red-eyed, she is Śukī, Śyenī, and Kapotikā; holding a noose and a staff in her hands, she is Pracaṇḍā of fierce prowess.
Śiśughnī, Pāpahaṃtrī, Kālī, Rudhirapāyinī, Vasādhayā, Garbhabhakṣā, and Śavahastāṃtramālinī. || 38 ||
Sthūlakeśī, Bṛhatkukṣi, Sarpāsyā, Pretavāhanā, Daṃdaśūkakarā, Krauñcī, Mṛgaśīrṣā, and Vṛṣānanā. (39)
With her mouth wide open, exhaling smoke, she moves alone through the sky with one foot raised and eyes looking upward; she has a scorching and withering gaze, a hollow body, and a thick nose.
Vidyutprabhā, Balākāsyā, Mārjārī, Kaṭapūtanā, Aṭṭāṭṭahāsā, Kāmākṣī, Mṛgākṣī, and Mṛgalocanā. || 41 ||
The mortal who recites these sixty-four names every day at the three junctions of the day, his afflictions caused by evil spirits in this world shall be pacified. (42)
Neither ḍākinīs, nor śākinīs, nor kūṣmāṇḍas, nor rākṣasas can cause him affliction who recites these names. (43)
These bring peace to children and secure the well-being of the fetus; they grant victory in battle, in the royal court, or even in dispute. (44)
One who serves the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of the Yoginīs shall obtain the desired accomplishment; even while reciting other mantras, one becomes a possessor of success at those seats. (45)
Through offerings of oblations, worship, and gifts, and by the presentation of incense and lamps, the Yoginīs will quickly become pleased and grant one's heart's desires. (46)
Having performed the great worship there according to the prescribed rite during the autumn season, and having offered oblations, the knower of mantras shall attain great success.

Beginning from the auspicious first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, a person should perform worship until the ninth day (navamī), and shall obtain whatever they have desired.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that best of men who observes a fast and performs a vigil there shall attain great success.
A devoted person, having performed an oblation one hundred and eight times for each name at night, using names preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending in the dative case; || 50 ||
With guggulu mixed with clarified butter in the measure of a small jujube fruit, whatever accomplishment a person may desire, that he shall attain. || 51 ||
On the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, a pilgrimage should be undertaken there with great effort by meritorious people for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the sacred field.
If anyone, out of contempt, does not perform the annual pilgrimage (yātrā), the Yoginīs dwelling in Kāśī shall inflict obstacles upon him.
Having placed Maṇikarṇikā in Kāśī at their forefront, all of them remained there; by merely bowing to it, a person is not afflicted by obstacles. (54)

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Sixty Yoginīs," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Pot-born one, when the host of Yoginīs had departed, the God of gods, desiring to know the news of Kāśī, dispatched the Sun-god.
The God of Gods said: "O Saptāśva, go swiftly to the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī, where that king Divodāsa, the embodiment of dharma, resides."
Act quickly so that this territory may become deserted through opposition to righteousness; do not hold that king in contempt. (3)
Whatever humiliation is inflicted upon one who has set out on the path of Dharma will surely recoil upon oneself, and a great sin is thereby produced.
O Bhānu, if that city should fall away from its dharma due to the expansion of your intellect, then it must be expelled by you with unbearable rays.
Lust and anger, greed and delusion, as well as envy and egoism—these do not exist there; for even Time cannot conquer that place.
As long as the intellect remains firm in the Dharma and the mind remains steady in the Dharma, how could there be the arising of obstacles for men, even in the midst of calamity? It is like the sun.
"You know the movements of the sun regarding all living beings here; therefore, O Eye of the World, go for the accomplishment of our purpose."
Having received the command of the gods and assumed another form that travels through the sky day and night, Ravi became directed toward Kāśī. || 9 ||
In his mind he became exceedingly restless, longing for the sight of Kāśī; even though he possessed a thousand feet, he then desired to have only one foot in the sky.
Then, the state of being a swan attained fulfillment for that Sun, who always travels through the sky and desires to go toward Kāśī. (11)
Then, having reached Kāśī and moving both within and without, the Sun did not perceive even the slightest destruction of dharma among its people.
The Fire-god dwelt in Kāśī for a year in various forms; yet he found no opportunity there with that most virtuous queen.
Once, having become a guest and requesting something difficult to obtain, the Sun-god did not see anything at all that was unattainable within the realm of that king.
At times he became a beggar, and at other times he was a great donor; at times he fell into a state of wretchedness, and at times he was even an astrologer. || 15 ||
At times he even established practices outside the Vedas, and at other times he established worldly matters based on perceptible evidence.
At times he became a matted-haired ascetic, and at times a naked mendicant; at times he was a snake-charmer, an expert in the science of poisons.
Knowing the doctrines of all heretical sects, he was at times a proponent of Brahmanism; and at other times he was a magician, deluding the people.
On various occasions, he repeatedly attempted to disturb those devoted wives by instructing them in diverse vows and by telling stories accompanied by illustrative examples.
At times that twice-born man was a bearer of the Kāpālika vow; at other times he was a possessor of realized knowledge, and at yet other times an alchemist.

In one place he was a Brahmin, in another a prince, in another a Vaiśya or an outcaste; in one place he became a student of sacred knowledge, in another a householder, and in another a forest-dweller.
Sometimes the ascetic deluded people with his similar forms; at other times, he became skilled in all sciences and was regarded as omniscient.
Thus, moving about in Kāśī in various forms, the Lord of Planets never found any vulnerability whatsoever among the people at any time.
Then the son of Kaśyapa, afflicted by anxiety, censured himself: "Fie upon this service to others, in which no fame whatsoever can be obtained! (24)
Mārtaṇḍa said: "If I go to Mandara today, the Lord will immediately become angry with me for not having accomplished the task, as if I were an ordinary servant."
Even if I were to go there somehow by deliberately provoking his anger, how could I then stand before him like a foolish servant? (26)
If, however, having uttered "Om," I should somehow go away with disregard, or if the Three-eyed Lord should look upon me with anger, then poison must be drunk by me. (27)
If my father has truly become a moth in the fire of Hara’s wrath, then even the Grandfather (Brahmā) will certainly not be able to protect me.
I shall remain right here forever and never abandon it, having established my hermitage in Vārāṇasī according to the rite of renunciation in a sacred field (kṣetrasaṃnyāsa).
Whatever sin shall accrue to me by remaining here without first informing the Lord of the Cities (Śiva) for the sake of my body—may there be atonement for that sin committed against Kāśī.
Furthermore, all other sins—whether great or small—that belong to virtuous people perish entirely upon entering Kāśī.
"This sin was not intentionally committed by me; indeed, in former times, Purāri himself commanded that dharma must be protected. (32)
For by him who has protected the Dharma while the body is fleeting and transitory, the three worlds have been protected; what is the use of well-guarded sensual pleasures and wealth? (33)
If desire were something to be protected by the Enemy of Desire (Śiva), how could it have been reduced to a bodiless state in an instant, even though it brings happiness to many? (34)
Some have declared that wealth must be protected by all means; how then did Hariścandra fail to protect it when it was with the son of Kuśika? (35)
Indeed, Dharma was protected by all, even at the cost of their own bodies, by kings such as Śibi and by brahmins headed by Dadhīci.
For this very dharma, born from the service of Kāśī, will protect me even from an enraged Rudra; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Having attained Kāśī, which is so difficult to reach, what conscious person would abandon it? Who, having cast away a jewel held in their own hand, would desire to grasp a piece of glass? (38)
He who, having abandoned Vārāṇasī, desires to go elsewhere, is like one who wishes to seek wealth by begging after kicking away a treasure with his foot. (39)
Sons, friends, wives, fields, and wealth are obtained here in every birth; however, Kāśī alone is never obtained.

By him who has obtained the city of Kāśī, which is capable of uplifting the three worlds, that great bliss has been attained which is difficult even for the sovereignty over the three worlds to reach. || 41 ||

For even if Rudra were to become angry with me, he would only cause a diminution of my splendor; moreover, I shall obtain that splendor in Kāśī which indeed arises from the realization of one's own Self.
Indeed, all other lights here shine only so long as the splendor born of Kāśī has not yet expanded, appearing like the glow of fireflies.
Thus, the knower of the power of Kāśī, the eye of the world who dispels darkness, divided himself twelvefold and established himself within the city of Kāśī.
Lolārka and Uttarārka, as well as Sāṃbāditya; the fourth is Drupadāditya, and Mayūkhāditya as well. (45)
Khakholka, Aruṇāditya, and those known as Vṛddha and Keśava; the tenth is Vimalāditya, and likewise Gaṅgāditya. (46)
And the twelfth is Yamāditya in the city of Kāśī, O Ghaṭodbhava; these [twelve] always protect the sacred field from the wicked who are dominated by darkness.
Because that mind of the Sun became restless at the sight of Kāśī, the name Lolārka was given to Vivasvat in Kāśī.
Lolārka, situated in the southern direction at the confluence of the Asi river, shall always provide for the welfare and security of the people residing in Kāśī.
On the seventh or the sixth lunar day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or on a Sunday, a man who performs the annual pilgrimage is liberated from sins.
Whatever sins have been committed by men over the course of a year perish in an instant upon seeing Lolārka on the sixth lunar day of the month of Āṣāḍha.

Having bathed at the confluence of the Asi and having satiated the ancestors and the gods, a man who performs the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule attains freedom from his debt to the ancestors.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Lolārka, whatever action is performed—whether it be giving gifts, offering oblations, or the worship of the gods—that leads to infinite results.
During a solar eclipse at Lolārka, ritual acts such as bathing and giving gifts become ten times more meritorious than at Kurukṣetra; of this there is no doubt. (54)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Sī at Lolārka on the Rathasaptamī day, one is instantly liberated from the sins committed during seven lifetimes.
Whoever, observing pure vows, beholds Lolārka on every Sunday, for him no suffering shall ever arise in this world.
Neither suffering, nor scabies, nor ringworm, nor eczema shall afflict him who beholds the Lolārka and Arka [suns] and partakes of the water used for washing their feet.
Even though he dwells in Vārāṇasī, if a man does not serve Lolārka, surely the afflictions arising from hunger and disease will attend him.
Among all the holy places on earth, Lolārka is the foremost head; all other sacred sites are its limbs, for they are indeed bathed by its waters.
All other holy places, even those situated throughout the entire circle of the earth, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the holy site at the confluence of the Asi.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing and other rites at all sacred fords (tīrthas), that fruit is fully attained by men at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sītā.

"O Sage, this which has been uttered is not a mere figurative statement, nor is it a panegyric; it is the truth, a statement of things as they are, and should be accepted with respect by the virtuous. (62)
Where Viśveśvara is present in person and where the celestial river flows, there even the envious logicians must admit that [all else] is false.
Those fools who, arrogant with the power of fallacious reasoning, proclaim that everything concerning Kāśī is mere figurative praise—they are vermin-like worms from age to age.
O Sage, surely even the pavilion of the three worlds could not equal the greatness of this certain sacred bathing place (tīrtha). 65.
One should not describe Kāśī in the presence of atheists, those outside the Vedic fold, those devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, and those born of the lowest castes. || 66 ||
Scorched by the rays of the Lolārka sun and severed by the edge of a sword in the southern quarter of Kāśī, great impurities shall not enter [the city]. (67)
Having heard this majesty of Lolārka, the best of men shall never become miserable anywhere within this ocean of worldly existence.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Lolārka," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Now, in the northern direction, there is an excellent pool named Arka; there, the Sun-god, garlanded with rays, resides by the name Uttarārka.
Scorching the mass of suffering and nourishing even the virtuous, the sun of great splendor, Uttarārka, protects Kāśī at all times.
In this regard, listen to the history that occurred, O observer of noble vows: there was a certain Brahmin named Priyavrata, born of the lineage of Atri.
In Kāśī there lived one named Śubhācāra, who was always beloved by his guests; his wife was Śubhavratā, who was exceedingly beautiful.
Devoted to serving her husband and skillful in domestic duties, she gave birth to a daughter endowed with auspicious marks.
When Jupiter was in the first quarter of the Mūla constellation and likewise in a quadrant (kendram), she grew in her parents' home like the moon during the bright fortnight.
She was beautiful, well-mannered in her conduct, and did what was pleasing to her parents; she became exceedingly skillful in cleaning and arranging the household utensils.
In whatever manner that maiden grew up in her father’s house, in that same manner her father’s anxiety increased all the more.
To whom should this most beautiful girl, endowed with auspicious marks, be given? Where can I find a most excellent groom who is a worthy match for her? (9)
To whom should she be given so that, endowed with noble lineage, youth, virtuous conduct, learning, beauty, and wealth, she may find happiness? (10)
As he was thinking thus, a most terrible fever seized him—that fever called "anxiety" which does not subside even with medicines for men.
Due to the ripening of the asterism that was his root-cause, and by means of a fever known as "anxiety," that Brahmin met his death, abandoning everything including his home.
When her father had passed away, her mother, Śubhavratā, also abandoned that daughter and followed her husband.
This is the law: whether her husband be living or even deceased, a woman devoted to her husband must always remain together with him.
Neither offspring, nor mother, nor father, nor even kinsmen protect a woman; only service to her husband’s feet can truly protect a woman. (15)
Although Sulakṣaṇā was afflicted by grief when her parents had met their death, she performed their funeral rites and completed the ten-day period of mourning.

Deprived of her protector and fallen into a state of wretchedness, she fell into great anxiety, wondering: "How shall I, alone and destitute of father and mother, cross the ocean of worldly existence? (17)
I shall reach the further shore of this womanhood which is difficult to cross and overcomes all; yet I have not been bestowed by my parents upon any suitor. (18)
How could I, having not been given by him, choose another husband of my own accord? Even if chosen, he would be of no noble lineage, nor possessed of virtue or good character.
"Even though he is under my own control, what would be gained by choosing him?"—thus she reflected, she who was endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue.
Although she was constantly sought after again and again by many young men, the maiden did not grant entrance to anyone’s heart.
Seeing the passing away of his parents and their such profound affection, he censured himself in many ways and indeed condemned the cycle of worldly existence.
Where have those two parents gone, by whom I was brought forth and by whom I was nurtured? Alas for the transience of embodied beings! 23.
"Ah! Even this body is a limb, just as it was before my parents. Having thus resolved, that young girl conquered her senses and her mind.
Having made her vow of celibacy firm, she practiced severe austerity with a steady mind in the presence of the god Uttarārka.
While she was performing penance there, a certain small female goat would come every day and stand motionless before her.
Having consumed some grass, leaves, and such at evening, and having drunk water from that pool, she would go to her own husband's dwelling.
Then, after five or six excellent years had passed in this manner, the Lord, wandering about playfully, arrived there together with the Goddess.
In the vicinity of the sun Uttara, Sthāṇu beheld Sulakṣaṇā performing austerities; she was motionless like a pillar, emaciated by her penance.
Then Śambhu was entreated by the compassionate Girijā: "Favor this slender-waisted woman, who is bereft of kinsmen, with a boon. (30)
Having heard the words of Śarvāṇī, Śarva, the ocean of compassion, Hara, the bestower of boons, then spoke to her as she sat with eyes closed in meditative absorption.
"O Sulakṣaṇā of noble vows, I am pleased with you; choose a boon. You have long been exhausted by your ascetic penance; what desire do you have here? (32)
She too, having heard the speech of Śambhu—which rained down nectar from his mouth and pacified her great anguish—opened her eyes.
Beholding the three-eyed Lord directly before him, intent on granting boons, and the Goddess situated at his left side, he bowed with palms joined in reverence.
While that woman of beautiful waist was thus reflecting, "What shall I choose?", that wretched she-goat was seen by her standing right before her.
In this world of living beings, what man does not live for his own sake? Only he who lives for the sake of helping others truly lives.
"Since I have been served for a long time by this practice of penance acting as my witness, I therefore choose the Lord of the World as my husband for her sake."
Reflecting thus in her mind, Sulakṣaṇā spoke to the Three-eyed Lord: "O Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, if a boon is to be granted to me... (38)
"Let this wretched she-goat be favored first; being a beast, she does not know how to speak, yet she is tenderly devoted to me. (39)
Having heard these words, which were characterized by benevolence toward others, the Lord, who removes the distress of those who bow before him, was exceedingly pleased with Sulakṣaṇā.
Then Devadatta said: "O Goddess, daughter of the Lord of Mountains, behold! Such is the intellect of the virtuous, strengthened by their desire to benefit others. (41)
They are blessed in all worlds, and they are the refuge of all dharmas—those who strive with their whole being for the benefit of others. (42)
The accumulation of all things does not remain anywhere for long; however, O beloved, that which is beneficial to others alone endures for a very long time.
"She is blessed and possesses auspicious marks; she is fit for the act of bestowing grace. Speak, O Goddess, what boon should be granted to her, and what is desired by her, O Beloved? (44)
The Goddess said: O Creator of all creators, O Omniscient One who removes the distress of those who bow before You, let Sulakṣaṇā, of auspicious conduct and noble resolve, be my companion. 45.
Just as Jayā and Vijayā, and likewise Jayantikā; Śubhānandā and Sunandā, and Kaumudī as well as Ūrmilā.
Just as Caṃpakamālā, just as Malayavāsinī, just as Karpūralatikā, and just as the auspicious Gandhadhārā; || 47 ||
She is free from sorrow and beyond grief, like the Malaya breeze that bears fragrance; she is like the exhalation of sandalwood, like the finest musk.
Just as the song of the cuckoo, just as she who speaks so sweetly, and just as that treasury of prose and verse who understands even what is unsaid—so too was she.
Just as a woman who understands hints from a mere glance fulfills her desires, and just as one captivates the mind through song, so too may this Sulakṣaṇā be.
"She will become exceedingly dear to me, for though she is a young female student of sacred knowledge (brahmacāriṇī), she shall be adorned with divine limbs even in this very body. (51)
Clad in divine garments, possessing divine fragrance, and endowed with divine knowledge, may Samaya always remain by my side, holding a shimmering chowrie.
This Barkarī, the daughter of the King of Kāśī, shall likewise attain enjoyments right here and obtain unsurpassed liberation.
By her, however, in this solar fire-pit during the month of Puṣya on a Sunday, she bathed before the sun had risen, with a mind undisturbed by the cold.
Therefore, O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, by the power of the granting of the boon, let this princess of auspicious eyes be born through your merit. (55)
"Let the name of this Arka-kuṇḍa be Barkarī-kuṇḍa; the image of this goddess shall be worshipped here by human beings. (96)
In the month of Puṣya, on a Sunday coinciding with the Uttarārka festival of the deity, that annual pilgrimage must be undertaken by those who desire the fruit of Kāśī. || 57 ||
Having done all this, the all-pervading Lord of the Universe, the omnipresent one, entered the palace unobserved by Mṛḍānī. || 58 ||
Skanda said: "O twice-born one, O highly fortunate one, the majesty of Lolārka and Uttarārka has been told to you; now listen to that of Sāmbāditya."
Having heard this meritorious and auspicious narrative of Lolā and Uttarārka, one shall not be overcome by diseases nor afflicted by poverty.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Uttarārka," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 47.
Skanda said: Listen, O son of Mitrāvaruṇa; for the sake of slaying the Dānavas and for the removal of the earth's burden, the upholder of the Yadu lineage [will manifest] in Dvāravatī.
Kṛṣṇa himself, the abode of the universe, Vāsudeva, whose splendor is like that of fire, appeared from Vasudeva and Devakī.
O Pot-born One, he had eighty thousand sons with the luster of the sun; such virtuous boys as these do not exist even in heaven, O Agastya.

They were exceedingly endowed with beauty, exceedingly possessed of great strength, exceedingly skilled in the knowledge of weapons and treatises, and exceedingly marked with auspicious signs. || 4 ||

To behold her, the mind-born son of Brahmā, a treasure-house of austerities, arrived; he was clad in bark garments and a loincloth, wearing a black antelope skin as his upper garment; he held the staff of a Brahmin and wore a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass, and was adorned with a garland of tulasī resting upon his chest.
His limbs were anointed with the shining paste of Gopīcandana, and though all his limbs were emaciated by ascetic penance, he blazed like a personified fire.
The sky-traveler Nārada arrived at the city of Dvārakā, which was fashioned by Viśvakarman and surpassed the splendor of the celestial city of Svarga.
Seeing Nārada, all the descendants of Vṛṣṇi, with their necks deeply bowed and their palms joined over their heads, prostrated themselves before him.
Sāmba, infatuated by the entirety of his pride in the beauty of his own form, did not bow to the sage there, laughing at the perfection of the sage's appearance.
Having understood that intention of Sāmba, the great sage Nārada entered the exceedingly beautiful temple of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa, seeing Nārada approaching, went out to meet him, honored him with the madhuparka offering, and seated him upon his own throne.
After engaging in conversations of diverse meaning, Nārada, remaining in a secluded place, whispered into Kṛṣṇa’s ear about the conduct of Sāmba.
"O increaser of Yaśodā’s joy, there must certainly be something here; for generally, O Lord, that which is impossible does not occur among women. (14)
Among the youths dwelling in the three worlds, Sāmba was exceedingly handsome; yet the mental disposition of women, naturally fickle-eyed, is extremely volatile. (15)
Those with bewildered eyes, deluded by the god of love, do not consider family, character, learning, or wealth; they look only at physical beauty. (16)
Or perhaps you already know the conduct of the cowherd girls: O Kṛṣṇa, these frail women desire him even without the eight heroines. (43)
Due to the natural disposition of those fair-browed women and from the words of Nārada, Kṛṣṇa also understood the entire account as it truly was.
The fortitude of women remains steady and their minds retain their discernment only so long as no seeker stands before them in solitude; once a seeker is present, it is not otherwise.
Thus reflecting in his mind, the wise Kṛṣṇa, having stilled the torrent of the river of anger with the dam of discernment, dispatched Nārada.
Even though he was watching day and night, Kṛṣṇa did not perceive any change whatsoever in Sāmba once that divine sage had departed.
After some time had passed, the sage returned once more; he perceived that Kṛṣṇa was standing in the midst of the playful women.
Calling out to Sāmba as he was playing outside, Nārada said to him: "Go quickly to Kṛṣṇa and tell him of my arrival."
Sāmba also thought thus for a moment: "Should I go, or should I not go? How can I approach my father, who is in private with his female companions?"
And how could I not go at the word of this celibate student, who resembles a blazing coal and whose splendor flashes from every limb? (25)
Once, he was ashamed before me while bowing down to those who were very delicate; even now, I would not go because of the word of this great sage.
"There is a great danger here due to the sight of those two sins; even my father’s anger toward me is praiseworthy, but that of a Brahmin is not. (27)
Those consumed by the fire of Brahma’s wrath never sprout again; those consumed by any other fire may grow back, like trees burnt by a forest fire.
Having meditated thus for a moment, the son of Jāmbavatī entered his father’s inner apartments, which were filled with women, while Kṛṣṇa remained in their midst.
Having bowed from afar, he made a request full of apprehension; at that moment, Nārada followed after him for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
Then Kṛṣṇa, seeing Sāmba and Nārada, rose up in haste, putting on his yellow silken garment.
When the son of Devakī had risen, all those gopīs, filled with shame, stood up while each taking hold of her own garment.
Holding that great sage by the hand, Kṛṣṇa seated him upon a costly couch, while Sāmba went away to play.
Observing their stumbling as they stood before him, the sage sang of Hari to those whose beautiful limbs had been softened by the play of Kṛṣṇa.
"Look, look, O one of great intelligence! Having seen the son of Jāmbavatī, these women have become agitated at heart by his beauty and have stumbled. (35)
Kṛṣṇa also, having summoned his son along with Samba, suddenly cursed him, even though he was looking on, at the hand of adverse fate: "May all [your wives] be like Jāmbavatī. (36)
"Since these cowherd girls have stumbled upon seeing your form, therefore, by virtue of this unseasonable arrival, become a leper immediately. (37)
Trembling from the terrible fear of a great disease, Sāmba also propitiated Kṛṣṇa many times for the sake of pacifying his sin.
Kṛṣṇa, recognizing him as his own legitimate son along with Sāmba, said: "Go to the city of Vaiśveśvarī for the sake of being freed from leprosy."
There, having propitiated Bradhna, you shall regain your own nature; for there is no destruction of great sins except in Vārāṇasī. (40)

Where Viśveśvara is personally present and where that celestial river flows, there is indeed purification for those great sins for which no atonement was seen even by the sages, once one has reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
For it is not only from great sins that one is liberated in Vārāṇasī; by the command of Śaṅkara, one is liberated even from ordinary sins. (42)
In ancient times, Purāri created Avimukta for the sake of liberation for all living beings who cast off their bodies there at the end [of their lives], out of his compassion. (43)
"There, in that Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana), the removal of Śambhu’s curse shall take place; O Sāmba, go there as instructed by the Truth, for otherwise there is no cessation of the curse."
Then, having taken leave of Kṛṣṇa, Nārada—his activities now liberated from karma and his purpose fulfilled—departed by way of the sky.
Having reached Vārāṇasī and propitiated the Sun-god, Sāṃba, having placed that pool behind him, regained his own natural form.
From that time forward, the Sun-god Sāṃbāditya became the remover of all diseases; he bestows freedom from illness and all forms of prosperity upon all his devotees.
Having bathed at Sāṃbakuṇḍa on a Sunday at the break of dawn, and having worshipped Sāṃbāditya, a man is not overcome by diseases.
A woman does not suffer widowhood by serving Sāmbāditya; even a barren woman shall give birth to a son endowed with a pure form.
O twice-born one, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, when it falls on a Sunday, it is declared to be a great festival, auspicious and equal to the festival of the Sun.
Having bathed there at the break of dawn and having worshipped Sāmbāditya, one shall be liberated from great disease and shall attain imperishable merit.
Whatever merit is gained at the Sannihati-tirtha in Kurukshetra during a lunar eclipse, that same merit is obtained on Ravisaptami in Magha at Kashi; of this there is no doubt.
On the day of the Sun in the month of Madhu, the annual pilgrimage should take place; having worshipped there with Aśoka flowers and bathed in the pool according to the prescribed rite. (53)
A person who visits Sāṃbāditya is never overcome by sorrows; he is instantly liberated from the sins committed throughout the year.
To the west of Viśveśa, the auspicious form of Āditya was perfectly propitiated here by the high-souled Sāmba.

"O Agastya, this future form of mine was described before you. By worshipping it, bowing down to it, and performing eight circumambulations, a man becomes free from sin and obtains the fruit of residing in Kāśī. (56)
O high-minded one, the greatness of Sāṃbāditya has been recounted to you; having heard it, a man shall never again behold the world of Yama.
Now, O sinless one, I shall describe the Sun-god Draupadāditya; thus the Sun-god Draupadāditya, who bestows the perfection of devotion, should be worshipped. (58)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of Sāṃbāditya," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 48.
Sūta said: O Sage Vyāsa, son of Parāśara, when Kumāra related this story to the one born from a jar (Agastya), where was the daughter of Drupada at that time?
Vyāsa said: O Sūta, he recites the Purāṇa compendium, a narrative pertaining to the three periods of time; no doubt should be entertained here, since everything is within its scope.
Skanda said: Listen, O sage; formerly, Hara himself, the five-faced one, for the welfare of the world, manifested on earth by dividing himself into five forms.
And Umā, the sustainer of the world, also appeared as a beautiful woman from the sacrificial fire-pit of King Drupada as he was performing the sacrifice.
All five sons of Pāṇḍu, who bore the very forms of Rudra himself and were the agents of the destruction of the wicked, descended here from heaven.
Nārāyaṇa also, having attained the state of Kṛṣṇa and acting in association with him, pacifies those of overbearing conduct and establishes others in virtuous behavior.
Shining upon the earth, those sons of Pṛthā moved about individually; for in him resided both the rise and the fall of prosperity and adversity alike.
Once, those great heroes, having encountered a massive calamity brought about by their kinsmen, became dwellers of the forest.
And his wife, the princess of Pañcāla, tormented by her husband’s misfortune, being slender-limbed and knower of dharma, intensely propitiated the Sun.
Then, having been propitiated by that daughter of Drupada, Savitṛ gave her an inexhaustible cooking pot together with its ladle and its lid.
And with a gracious soul, Bhāskara spoke to the daughter of Drupada.
She was propitiating [him] with devotion, her mind pure in every respect.
"O highly fortunate lady, as long as you do not eat, so many people who seek food shall obtain satisfaction from this vessel. (12)
When you have eaten, this vessel, though now empty, will become full of food; it is a treasury of flavorful side-dishes that grants whatever food one desires.
O Sage, thus was the boon obtained by her from the Sun at Kāśī; and another boon was granted to her by the radiant Lord.
The Sun said: "The man who shall worship me, standing here before you on the southern side of Viśveśa, his affliction by hunger shall perish. (15)
"O devoted wife, another boon was granted to me by Viśveśa, who was fully satisfied with my ascetic penance; listen to it as I tell you. (16)
"O Prāgrava, having propitiated you, whatever man shall behold me, do you dispel his darkness of suffering with your own rays. (17)
Therefore, having obtained this boon from Viśveśvara, I shall eternally destroy the accumulation of sins for those beings who reside in Kāśī and are dear to Dharma.
Those men who, endowed with faith, shall worship me here while you stand with hand extended to grant boons, to them I shall give whatever they desire.
"You, who are devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira, shall remain near me, to the south of Viśveśa and in the vicinity of Daṇḍapāṇi. (20)
Whether they be men or women, those who shall worship with devotion will never experience fear born of separation from their beloved.
O sinless one, beloved of Dharma, by beholding Draupadī at Kāśī, there shall never be for you any fear born of disease, nor any arising from the afflictions of hunger and thirst.
Having thus granted boons, the Sun-god, the bestower of all upon the virtuous, propitiated Śambhu; and Dharma approached Draupadī.
The sin of that man who shall listen with devotion to this account of Āditya, who was indeed propitiated by Draupadī, shall come to an end. (24)
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, I have now related to you in brief the majesty of Draupadāditya; listen now to the majesty of Mayūkhāditya. || 25 ||
Formerly, at the Pañcanada Tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds, the Lord of a thousand rays performed most rigorous penance.
Having installed the great Liṅga known as Gabhastīśvara, and Gaurī named Maṅgalā, who always bestows auspiciousness upon her devotees; || 27 ||
O Sage, for a thousand divine years multiplied by a hundred, he propitiated Śiva, the Moon, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
By its very nature, however, the sun is capable of scorching the three worlds; therefore, O Sage, it blazed forth exceedingly through that most intense ascetic heat.
At that time, the entire space between heaven and earth was pervaded by the rays of the sun, which were capable of burning the three worlds.
And the inhabitants of the celestial mansions abandoned their coming and going at the station of Viṣṇu, as if out of fear of becoming moths in the intense heat of the sun.
Only the rays of the sun are seen—obliquely, upwards, and even downwards—but not the sun itself, just as one sees the position of the nīpa flower but not the tree.
At the intense majesty of that mass of splendor, that mass of austerity, and those flames of penance, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, trembled with violent fear.
The Sun is proclaimed in the Vedas as the soul of this world; if he himself is the one who sets it ablaze, who here could be our protector? (34)
This Sun is the eye of the world; this Maker of Light is the very soul of the world, for every morning he awakens the world that was nearly dead. (35)
Rising day by day, He shall extend His arms in all directions and rescue the multitude of living beings fallen into the blind well of darkness.
When he has risen here, we always rise; when he sets, we go to our setting. Therefore, whether there is his rising or his non-rising, the Sun is the cause of our own.
Seeing the universe thus thrown into confusion, the Lord of the Universe himself, the protector of the world, approached the one of fierce rays (the Sun) to grant him a boon.
Beholding the garlanded with rays (the Sun) standing perfectly motionless, Śambhu was amazed at his asceticism, for he had forgotten himself in deep meditative absorption.
And Śrīkaṇṭha, whose soul was gracious and who removes the distress of those who bow before him, said: "Enough of your asceticism; choose a boon, O Sun, O treasury of splendors! (40)

Because the functions of his senses had been suppressed by meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*), Bradhna did not grasp Śambhu’s words; though spoken twice or thrice, he was like one who has no ears.
Knowing him to have become like a log of wood, Śiva touched him with his hand, which rained down the nectar that quenches the heat born of great austerity.
Then Viśvalocana opened his eyes, just as a forest of lotuses does at dawn upon the rising of the sun.
Through the touch of the Lord, the sun, its heat entirely dispelled, shone forth like a cloud that has released its rain, causing the beauty of the crops to flourish.
Having made the three-eyed Lord his guest before his very eyes, Mitra prostrated himself like a staff before the wielder of the Pināka bow and praised him aloud.

Ravi said: O God of gods, Lord of the worlds, All-pervading One, Bharga, Bhīma, Bhava, Moon-adorned One! O Lord of beings, Dispeller of the fear of worldly existence, I bow to You, the Granter of the desires of those who prostrate.

O Moon-crested One, O Mṛḍa, O Dhūrjaṭi, O Hara, O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice! O Peaceful, Eternal Lord of Śivā, O Śiva, I bow to you, the granter of the desires of those who prostrate before you. 47.

O blue-and-red one, O burner of desired objects, O you with two eyes and one eye, O you with deformed eyes; O sky-haired one, O destroyer of the bonds of the individual soul, I bow to you, the granter of the desires of those who prostrate. 48.

O Vāmadeva, Śitikaṇṭha, wielder of the trident, moon-crested one, adorned with the lord of serpents; O Paśupati who fulfills desires, O Maheśvara, I bow to you, the bestower of the wishes of those who prostrate. 49.

O Three-eyed One, Lord of the destroyer of Tripura, you who grant protection, composed of the three Vedas, O ender of Death himself who crushed the Kālakūṭa poison; I bow to you, the granter of the desires of those who prostrate.

O Śarva, who is free from the night; O omnipresent one, who bestows the happiness of the path to heaven and liberation; O enemy of the demon Andhaka, wearer of matted locks; O granter of the desires of those who bow to you—I bow down to you. 51.

O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the fierce Girijā, O Lord of the universe, praised by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; O You who are known through the Vedas as the Knower of all limbs and principles, I bow to You, the bestower of the desires of those who prostrate before You. 52.

O You who possess the universal form yet are devoid of any other form, O Brahman free from crookedness, O bestower of immortality; O You who have gone far beyond the reach of speech and mind, I bow to You, the granter of the desires of those who prostrate.
Having thus circumambulated the god Mṛḍa, Mārtaṇḍa, with a delighted soul, then praised Mṛḍānikā, who occupies the left half of Śiva’s body.

The Sun said: O Goddess, that man who is skilled in prostration and bears upon the surface of his forehead the dust of your lotus feet—verily, even in another birth, the beautiful crescent of the moon makes that forehead exceedingly fair for him. (55)

O Śrī Maṅgalā, source of all auspiciousness; O Śrī Maṅgalā, fire that consumes the cotton of all impurities; O Śrī Maṅgalā, destroyer of the pride of all demons; O Śrī Maṅgalā, protect this entire universe! 56.

O Sovereign of the Universe, you are the creator of all people; you are their protector, and likewise, at the time of dissolution, you are their destroyer. The river of pure merit, shimmering with the chanting of your name, sweeps away the trees upon its banks that are our sins.

O Mother Bhavānī, you who remove the vast accumulation of intense suffering—there is no other refuge here but you. Blessed indeed are those in the worlds, and they alone are worthy of honor, upon whom your auspicious glance of compassion shines.

May the Destroyer of Smara remember those who constantly meditate upon You—the innate radiance, residing in the city of Kāśī, the very embodiment of the fortune of liberation for those who bow—those who possess pure intellect and have become worthy vessels skilled in protecting others in the state of Nirvāṇa. (59)

O Maṅgalagaurī, for him whose stainless pair of feet, O Mother, resides in his heart, the entire world is held in the palm of his hand; and as long as he does not abandon Your name and splendor, the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) never leave his home.

O Goddess, you are the mother of the Vedas, whose nature is the syllable Om; you are Gāyatrī, indeed the wish-fulfilling cow for the twice-born. You are the three Vyāhṛtis here for the accomplishment of all rites; you are Svāhā and Svadhā, the cause of satisfaction for the gods and the ancestors.

O Gaurī, you alone are Sāvitrī to the moon-crested Brahmā; you are the beautiful Lakṣmī to the wielder of the discus; and in Kāśī, O you of stainless form, you are the Lakṣmī of liberation. O Mother Maṅgalagaurī, you are my refuge here. 62.

Having thus praised her, who possesses the splendor of half the body of the Destroyer of Smara, with the great hymn of the Eight Verses of Auspiciousness (Śrī-Maṅgalāṣṭaka), the Sun-god bowed repeatedly all around the Goddess and the God; then Savitṛ became silent before Śiva and Śivā.
The God of gods said: "Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O high-minded one; I am pleased. I always behold that friend who has entered my eyes, along with all things moving and unmoving."
O Sūrya, you shall become my very form; be omniscient and all-pervading, a mass of all splendors, and the knower of all actions of all beings. || 65 ||
Dispel all the sufferings of all your devotees; for you have proclaimed that group of eight [names] from among your sixty-four names.
By praising me with this, a person shall attain devotion to me; it is the eightfold hymn of Maṅgalā-Gaurī, known as the *Maṅgalāṣṭaka*.
By praising Maṅgalā-Gaurī with this, one shall obtain auspiciousness; [this includes] the hymn of sixty-four verses, the hymn of eight verses, and indeed the Maṅgalāṣṭaka.
This excellent hymn of praise is meritorious and destroys all sins; even if staying in a distant land, the best of men who recites it constantly [attains the goal]. (69)
With a purified soul, by reciting this pair of hymns every day, men shall attain the difficult-to-reach Kāśī at the three junctions of the day.
Daily sin is washed away by this; of this there is no doubt. Never shall there be a persistence of evil within the body of that embodied being.
One should constantly recite these two auspicious hymns three times a day; for what is the use of many other prayers that bestow only fleeting prosperity upon men? (72)
One should offer these two hymns at Kāśī to obtain the glory of ultimate liberation; therefore, men who desire emancipation should do so with every effort. (73)

Having abandoned these two hymns for recitation and [recited] many other hymns, [you have failed to realize that] this entire phenomenal world, including all things moving and stationary, belongs to us alone. (74)
Then, through this hymn of praise by us two, people shall become free from worldly elaboration (niṣprapañca) after attaining great prosperity here, consisting of sons and grandsons. (75)
At the end, a person reciting this hymn attains nirvāṇa. Listen to something else, O Seven-Horsed One, King of Planets, Maker of Day! (76)
