The Liṅga known as Gabhastīśvara, which bestows all supernatural powers, was installed by you and has been worshipped with a spirit of devotion. || 77 ||
O Bhāskara, because you have worshipped the Lord’s Liṅga with all your being, using your rays which possess the luster of Campaka flowers and lotuses; || 78 ||
Then that linga shall obtain the name Gabhastīśvara; having bathed at Pañcanada and worshipped Gabhastīśa, a man [attains his goal]. (79)
Having shaken off all impurities, neither woman nor man shall ever again be born from a mother’s womb; this is the blessing of Maṅgalāgaurī. (80)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, being intent on fasting, one should worship [the deity] with great offerings, such as silk garments, ornaments, and the like.
Having kept a vigil at night with songs, dances, stories, and the like, one should worship twelve young girls in the morning with garments and other offerings.

Having fed others with the finest foods fit for a communal meal and having given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule with the verse beginning "jātavedase."
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter at dawn, and having given a pair of cattle to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family, [he attains the fruit].
Having adorned the Brahmin couple with ornaments out of faith and having fed them with costly foods, may the two Lords of Auspiciousness (Maṅgaleśvara) be pleased.
Having recited this mantra and performed the breaking of the fast in the morning, one never encounters misfortune nor poverty at any time. (86)
Indeed, she never experiences the severance of her lineage nor the cessation of her enjoyments; a woman does not incur widowhood, nor does a man suffer the loss of his wife.
Sins go to dissolution and a heap of merit is obtained; even a barren woman may give birth by performing this auspicious vow.
By performing this vow, ugliness shall never arise; a maiden shall find a husband endowed with ultimate excellence of character and form. (89)
The prince also, having performed a vow, obtained an excellent wife; for there are many vows that bestow wealth and fulfill desires. (90)
Minds shall never attain equality with the auspicious vow; and on that lunar day in the month of Caitra, the annual pilgrimage must be performed by men.
For the sake of pacifying all obstacles, I shall always speak further to you, O Sun, as you perform penance here while residing in Kāśī.
Only the rays were seen in the sky, and the physical body was not seen; therefore, O son of Diti, they were called "the Sun of Rays" (Mayūkhāditya).
Due to your worship, no disease shall prevail among men; nor shall there be poverty, through the sight of you on Sundays.
Thus, having granted many boons to Mayūkhāditya, Śiva vanished right there; the Sun remained in that very place.
Having heard this meritorious narrative concerning Mayūkhāditya, together with Draupadāditya, a person shall not go to hell.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Draupadāditya and Mayūkhāditya," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 49 ||
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, out of affection for you, I shall now describe those Ādityas who reside in Vārāṇasī and others as well; they are all destroyers of every sin.
The Lord Āditya is celebrated by the name Khakholka; situated in the northern part of Triviṣṭapa, he is the destroyer of all diseases and obstacles.
Listen to that which is called the "Sky-Lightning" (Khakholka) of that Sun; formerly, Kadrū and Vinatā were the two auspicious daughters of Dakṣa.
O sage, once those two wives of Kaśyapa, the son of the ancient progenitor Mārīca, were sporting with one another when they spoke thus to each other.
Kadrū said: O Vinatā, if you know that, tell it before me; for your movement remains unimpeded within the expanse of the sky.
That horse Uccaiḥśravas who is heard of as being on the chariot of Savitṛ—what is his form? Is he brindled or white? Tell me quickly.
"Make a wager, O auspicious and sinless one, whatever pleases you; for this [time] does not pass away in this manner without a game of chance."
Vinatā said: "O sister, what is the point of a wager here? I shall speak of it exactly as it is: what joy would I have in your victory, and what happiness would there be for you in mine?"
One who desires mutual affection should not engage in a wager after considering this: when one side is certain to be victorious, anger inevitably arises here in this world.
Kadrū said: "O sister, there is no cause for anger here; this is merely a game, and whatever is spoken regarding the stake is simply part of the play. (10)
Vinatā said: "O eater of winds, act in such a way that you may have satisfaction. Then Kadrū, whose mind was crooked, spoke to that Vinatā.
"Whichever of us is defeated by the other, she shall become the other's slave; and in this wager, all these friends of ours shall be witnesses. (12)
Having thus made a mutual wager, Kadrū, the female serpent, and Vinatā, the bird-lady, spoke to Garuḍa regarding the dappled horse and the white one.
They established a limit for their departure, saying, "When shall we return? Then, ceasing their play, they went each to his own abode.
When Vinatā had departed, Kadrū summoned her own offspring and said: "Go, my sons, quickly at my command. (15)
The horse Uccaiḥśravas emerged from the ocean of milk while it was being churned by the gods and demons out of fear of the impact of Mount Mandara.
It perceives a similarity between the nature of cause and effect; therefore, O sons, make that [being], which resembles the color of milk, variegated.
Having settled upon his tail, they turned his black hair into a mass of curls; likewise, by their venomous hissing, they caused the hairs on his body to stand erect.
Having heard these words of their mother, the sons of Kadrū consulted one another and, having assumed hideous forms, spoke to their mother Kadrū. (19)
The Nāgas said: "O Mother, at your call we have come here joyfully, leaving our play by force, thinking that today our mother will give us delicious food. (20)
Let that delicious food remain far away; it is more bitter than even poison. For that which you have spoken cannot be pacified by mantras or medicines.
"We shall not go; let whatever is destined to happen here befall us"—thus was it spoken then by those crooked-moving ones, who were full of malice.
Skanda said: Furthermore, those others who move crookedly, who seek out the vulnerabilities of others, who are deaf to counsel and cruel-hearted—they bring shame upon their parents.
Those who, being exceedingly arrogant, disregard the words of their parents, shall encounter great calamity in this world and soon go to their destruction.
Having heard their words, "We shall take them away," the serpent-maiden, overcome with anger, cursed those snakes who had come to her with such transgression.
"Because you have transgressed my word, may you become food for Tārkṣya; and as soon as they are born, may the female serpents devour their own young. (26)
Thus, some, terrified by the fire of the curse, took refuge in Pātāla; others, desiring to live, carried out the words of their mother.
Having obtained the horse Uccaiḥśravas, those highly intelligent ones made his tail resemble the luster of deep blue hair and his body variegated.
By the masses of smoke from the fire of his roar, emitted through the force of his hissing, they were not consumed by the rays of the sun, due to the merit born from the form of the Mother’s speech.
Then, having mounted the back of Vinatā out of affection, Kadrū adorned the path of the sky and beheld the orb of the sun.
Her mind agitated by the power of the sun’s fierce rays, Kadrū then said to Vinatā: "O Vinatā, go confidently as a bird."
My body is intensely scorched by the hot rays of the sun; I am naturally confident, whereas you are full of apprehension on all sides. (32)
By your own nature you are a female bird, and this male bird has a thousand eyes; therefore, there is no affliction for you in the sky arising from the heat.
This sky is a lake and you are a female swan moving with the grace of a swan; therefore, the fire of the fierce-rayed sun's heat does not afflict you here.
As she was being sung about by the birds in the sky, the serpent dwelling in the hole spoke again: "Sister, save me, save me here, as long as there is still space in the path of the sky! (35)
O winged one, why do you not protect me, Vinatā, who am bowed down? I shall become your slave, subsisting upon the remnants of your food. (36)
"As long as I live, may I be one who drinks the water from your feet; let this Khakholkā fall, speaking with a very faltering voice. (37)
Having fainted, the female serpent covered her wings with her hands; "O friend, she might fall upon the torches!"—thus she spoke in agitation. (38)
When the speech "Khakholka" was uttered by Kadrū with a bewildered mind, the sun named Khakholka was then praised extensively by Vinatā.
When the sun had reached a slightly oblique position in the sky, a horse with a few speckled markings was seen by the two of them in the chariot.
This cruel female serpent, whose eyes were afflicted by heat, was addressed thus by Vinatā herself, who was truthful and honored by the whole world.
"O auspicious Kadrū, you have won, since this horse Uccaiḥśravas, though possessing the luster of moonbeams, appears as if he were dappled. (42)
O serpent, it is a marvel that destiny is more powerful in victory and defeat; for sometimes even the cruel one is victorious, while even the non-cruel one is defeated.
Speaking as she had been instructed, Vinatā, who was the support for those who were not humble, arrived at the dwelling of Kadrū and performed the service of her slave.
Once Vinatā was seen by Suparṇa with tearful eyes, lacking luster, soiled, dejected, and sighing deeply.
Suparṇa said: "O Mother, day after day, where do you go every morning? And from where do you return in the evening, so pale and dejected in spirit? (46)
Why do you sigh so loudly with eyes filled with tears, like a woman whose son is impotent, or like one who has been insulted by her husband? (47)
"Speak, O mother bird! Why are you so distressed today? While I, your child, am alive, even though Time has struck fear into us? (48)
O ascetic woman, what is the reason for shedding tears? Among women of virtuous conduct, nothing inauspicious is ever desired here. (49)
Fie upon those sons, while whom their mother suffers grief; it would be better for her to be barren, whose sons have rendered her hopes barren. (50)
Having heard these powerful words of her son Garuḍa, Vinatā spoke to that son who was filled with devotion toward his mother.
"O fool, I am indeed the slave of the cruel-minded Kadrū; O dear son, I constantly carry her on my back, as well as her sons. (52)
Sometimes I go to Mount Mandara, sometimes to the Malaya mountain; at other times I may wander among the islands of the oceans.
"O son, wherever those exceedingly arrogant sons of Kadrū may lead you, there I too shall go, for I am dependent upon you."
Garuḍa said: "O Mother, O lady of auspicious marks, what was the cause for your becoming a slave? O daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati, O sinless beloved of Kaśyapa? (55)
Vinatā spoke to Garuḍa the entire account of what had occurred in the past, namely the reason for her servitude and how she had gazed upon the horse of the Sun.
Having heard this, Garuḍa said to his mother: "Go quickly; O Mother, ask those wicked sons of Kadrū these words today."
"Whatever is difficult for you to obtain, and in which you have such great delight—that very thing ask me for, in order to release you from my state of servitude; I shall grant it. (58)
Vinatā did exactly so; and having heard what she had said, those serpents consulted together and, with joyful hearts, spoke to Vinatā.
"If he gives us nectar for the sake of releasing us from our mother's curse, then let your desire be fulfilled; otherwise, if he does not give it, you shall. (60)
Having thus addressed Kadrū and taken her leave, the bird, moving with swift speed, informed Garuḍa upon seeing that his mind was filled with joy.
Then Nāgāntaka said to his mother, who was distressed with anxiety: "Know, O Mother, that the nectar has been brought; give me my food. (62)
With the hair on her body bristling with joy, Vinatā said to her son: "O Suparṇa, go quickly to the ocean; may it be auspicious for you! (63)
There also dwell many Niṣādas, fishers who live upon the shore; devour those evil-minded ones.
In this world, those of wicked intellect nourish their own lives with the lives of others; they must be restrained with effort, for such restraint is the supreme good.
Violence committed against those who have perpetrated much violence may indeed be a means to attain heaven, because by harming the wicked, the world is extensively protected. (66)
O son, even if there is some Brahmin among the Niṣādas, he must be protected with effort and never devoured.
Garuḍa said: "How am I to recognize a twice-born man living among fish and other such creatures? Tell me some sign by which that whom you have declared unfit to be eaten may be known. (68)
Vinatā said: He who has the sacrificial thread around his neck and a spotless upper garment, whose clothes are constantly washed, and whose forehead is marked with a tilaka; (69)
He whose hands hold the sacrificial grass (pavitra), whose waist-knot contains kuśa grass, and whose head bears the topknot with its knot intact—he should be recognized by you as a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever here recites even a single verse of the Ṛg, Yajur, or Sāma Vedas, or even merely the Gāyatrī mantra, he should be recognized by you as a twice-born (dvija). 71.
Garuḍa said: O Mother, if a twice-born man should always dwell in the midst of Niṣādas, I do not consider even one of these [marks] to be indicative of his status as a twice-born.
O Mother, tell me another mark that reveals a Brahmin, by knowing which I might release even one who has reached my throat. (73)
Having heard that, Vinatā said: "O son, drive far away anyone who, like a charcoal of khadira wood, might burn you as he remains in your throat."
For any violence committed even against a mere twice-born is not conducive to spiritual welfare; in time, it utterly uproots one's country, lineage, prosperity, and oneself.
Having heard this from the feet of his mother Kāśyapi and having prostrated before her, the lord of birds, having received her blessing, departed swiftly through the path of the sky.
Shaking his wings and filling heaven and earth with dust, the lord of birds beheld from afar the Niṣādas who live by fishing.
Having blinded the quarters of the sky, he sat upon the shore of the ocean, opening his terrible mouth which resembled a vast cave.
The Niṣādas, fleeing in all directions, entered there of their own accord; and while they were seeking a path, even as they were entering their throats, [the situation unfolded]. (79)
The touch of his tongue set the Brahmin’s throat-crevice ablaze; then Tārkṣya entered the internal cavity of the hunters who had previously entered there.
Having caused it to enter and clearly perceiving that it was stuck at his throat and palate, he quickly vomited it out, constrained by the words of his mother and overcome by fear. (81)
Seeing that man disgorged, the king of birds addressed him: "Who are you by birth? Tell me, for you have caused a burning sensation in my throat. (82)
Being questioned thus in the presence of Garuḍa, that brahmin said: "I dwell among these Niṣādas, subsisting by my caste alone. (83)
Having sent him far away and having devoured him in great abundance, Garuḍa then agitated the sky like the wind at the time of universal dissolution.
Seeing him of fierce splendor, with flames spreading through the quarters of the sky like a blazing forest fire upon a mountain, the inhabitants of heaven were struck with fear.
Having donned their armor and equipped themselves with weapons, all those gods, clad in mail, quickly mounted their mounts for the sake of battle.
"This is not the river of the animal realm, nor is this fire accompanied by smoke; this is certainly not even a flash of lightning—what being is this that approaches before us? (87)
"Such a distinction is not found among the Daityas, nor is this form seen among the Dānavas; who is this that causes such great terror and makes our hearts tremble? (88)
Even as the wise gods, well-versed in policy, were still deliberating, the mighty king of birds spread his two wings.
By the wind from their wings, they fell along with their weapons and mounts; it was not known where they had gone, carried away by that whirlwind like dry leaves upon the ocean.
Then, when they had disappeared, the king of birds, having understood through his intellect, saw the treasury of nectar and its guards there.
Having shaken off all those gods who held weapons and missiles raised in their hands, he beheld the Kartari machine situated above the nectar.
Whirling with great speed by the force of the wind of the mind, it shatters even a mosquito into millions of pieces upon merely touching it.
Having sat down near that machine, the fearless lord of birds reflected for a moment: "Alas, what shall I do here? (94)
This cannot even be touched, nor can the wind prevail against it here; what means should be employed in this matter? My effort has been in vain.
Neither strength nor any human effort whatsoever could prevail here; oh, how great is the exertion of the gods in guarding this nectar!
If my devotion to Śaṅkara is free from duality and exceedingly steadfast, then may that God of gods unite me with supreme wisdom.
If I am devoted to my mother even more than to my lord Śaṅkara, then let my intellect be capable of carrying away the nectar from this place.
This effort is not for my own sake; the All-pervading One, dwelling within the heart, knows this. I strive toward immortality in order to liberate my mother from her state of servitude.
For a man whose parents are aged, who has young children, and who has a virtuous wife, there is no fault even in an improper act if it is for their nourishment.
As that high-souled one was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind.
Having made his form a thousandth part of an atom, he created a most wonderful body that was even more minute than an atom.

Having entered the mechanism of the scissors due to the lightness of his body, and either fearing that mechanism or evading it by fragmenting through the air, he swiftly uprooted the root and seized the vessel of nectar.
He set out upon the purifying path while the inhabitants of heaven cried out.
Then those drinkers of nectar went to the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha and said: "O Discus-wielder, our very life is the nectar that is being carried away by them after they have conquered us."
Having heard this, Hari granted them fearlessness and, filled with haste, engaged in a very great battle for two ghaṭikās of twenty-four minutes.
Just as he brought forth the two goddesses Śumbha and Niśumbha, Garuḍa was superior there; then the Blessed One, the giver of all, was pleased by that great battle.
Having gone there, he said this to Garuḍa: "I am pleased, O Lord of Birds; choose a boon, may it be well with you, you who have conquered the hosts of the gods led by Indra."
Having laughed, Garuḍa said to Viśvarūpa Janārdana: "I myself am pleased; ask for two boons."
Then the Conqueror of Kaiṭabha, filled with joy, said to Vainateya: "O most noble one, grant, grant two boons for each boon requested."
Having heard what was spoken by Viṣṇu, the king of birds said, laughing: "Why delay? Speak it; the two boons have been granted. (11)

When the gain of what was not previously obtained has arisen through victory in gambling and the like, a wise person should always give to a worthy recipient; for where else can such gain and victory truly reside? (12)
Śrī Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of Birds, you are powerful; therefore, become my vehicle. This is one boon, O giver of boons; now hear the second, O Kāśyapa. (13)
O wise one, having shown them the nectar that brings liberation from servitude to their mothers, act in such a way against the double-tongued ones that they shall not consume it immediately.
"Let nectar be given to the drinkers of nectar; let this be my second boon. Having promised "So be it," the king of birds departed from heaven.
Having liberated his mother from slavery, that son of Kāśyapa held up a great vessel of nectar before the Nāgas.
To those who desired to drink the nectar, the high-minded one said: "O Nāgas, having attained purity, this auspicious ambrosia must be consumed. (17)
Otherwise, if it is touched by impure persons who have been excluded from bathing and other purifications, this nectar—guarded by the gods with unblinking eyes—will vanish from sight. (18)
Even that which is generally fit to be seen or touched may at times be defiled by impurities; the gods take away its essence, and it remains devoid of flavor.
Having spoken thus, the son of Vinatā departed together with his mother; and he was addressed by them while seated upon a grass mat, holding the vessel of nectar.
Just as the serpents went to bathe, Viṣṇu took the vessel of nectar and gave it to them, like life itself bestowed upon the gods.
Having arrived and bathed, the serpents did not see the vessel of nectar; they cried out, "Alas! We have been deceived; the nectar has been taken away! (22)
Then, longing for the touch of nectar, they licked the darbha grass; let alone the nectar itself, their tongues were split in two.
Even those who merely desire to enjoy wealth acquired through unjust means—such food will not reach its proper digestion; it cannot even be swallowed by the winds [of the throat]. (24)

By Tārkṣya, who stands firm in the path of justice, the nectar—so exceedingly difficult to obtain—was attained; yet though it was obtained, when seized by the Nāgas through unjust means, it vanished in an instant upon being seen.
Then, released from slavery, Vinatā said to the sky-traveler: "O son, I shall go to Kāśī for the removal of the sin of servitude."
Sins accumulated over various births continue to flourish as long as Kāśī, the destroyer of rebirth, does not reside within one's heart. (27)
What wonder is there that sin should perish by the mere remembrance of Kāśī? Even dwelling in the womb is destroyed through the supreme grace of Viśveśa. (28)
There, Viśveśvara himself, adorned with the moon as his crest-jewel, shall ferry [devotees] across the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence by means of the vessel that is Tāraka.
The inclination toward Kāśī arises only for those favored by Viśveśa whose entire karma has been severed; it never arises for others.
O King, those men whose minds are directed toward Kāśī and whose sins have been washed away without remainder are truly the living among the dead in this world. (31)
By those alone has Time been conquered, for they alone have indeed become free from sin; they have reached Vārāṇasī here, and for them there is no further dwelling in a womb. 32.
One should not lead this human birth—which is the vessel for all that is auspicious—in vain, except through the sight of Kāśī, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (33)
What is the Kali age, or what is time, or what are the manifold types of karma, when Avimukta—the field that bestows supreme bliss—is beheld?
They remain dwelling in the womb; indeed, they are dwellers in the womb who do not serve the Varaṇā, that sword which cuts through the forest of the womb.
Having heard these words, Tārkṣya bowed to his mother and said: "I too shall come to see Kāśī, which is worshipped by Śiva. (36)
Then, having received his mother's command, the king of birds reached Vārāṇasī—the ground for the deposit of liberation—in an instant, together with his mother.
Both of those great-minded ones performed fierce austerities; having established a Śiva-liṅga, the lord of birds, with his senses unshaken, remained steadfast.
Having established the auspicious Āditya Khakholka by name, Vinatā, through their great asceticism, in a very short time— [attained her goal]. (39)
The two gods Śaṅkara and Bhāskara became devoted to Kāśī; from the liṅga installed by Garuḍa, Umāpati manifested. || 140 ||
He granted many boons, exceedingly difficult to obtain, to Garuḍa: "O Lord of Birds, you are my devotee; knowledge shall arise within you. (41)
"You shall know my secret, which is not even known by the gods. This Liṅga established by you is named Garuḍeśvara. (42)
It bestows supreme knowledge upon men when seen, touched, or worshipped. Listen to something else as well, O Lord of Birds; I shall now speak what is for your benefit.
"I am he; I am indeed Viṣṇu. Let there be no perception of difference between us two. Thus [he spoke] to that very one, O Lord of Birds, the destroyer of the strength of the lord of Daityas.
"O bird, having attained the status of a noble vehicle, you too shall become worthy of worship. Having thus granted this boon to his devotee Garuḍa, Śambhu—
Vanishing right there, Garuḍa also went to Hari; having attained the status of being Hari’s vehicle, he too became worthy of worship on earth.
Then, once upon a time, the Lord Khakholka by name—the sun and the supreme form of Śiva himself—beheld Vinatā as she was performing penance.
Having granted the boon that destroys sin and is endowed with the knowledge of Śiva, he brought about the destruction of the sins of many beings residing in Kāśī.
The Sun known as Vinatāditya is situated there; thus, the Sun Khakholka is the dispeller of the darkness of obstacles in Kāśī. 49.

By the mere sight of him, one is liberated from all sins; by beholding Khakholka at the Paiśaṅgila Tīrtha in Kāśī, a man obtains his heart's desire and becomes free from disease in an instant. || 150 ||
Having heard this narrative concerning the origin of Khakholka-Āditya together with Garuḍeśa, a person is liberated from all sins. (151)

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Khakholkāditya and Garuḍeśa," in the first half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Now begins the second half of the glorious Kāśī-khaṇḍa. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Agastya said: "O Lord, who brings joy to the heart of Pārvatī, O Master born from the body of the Omniscient One! My mind is desirous of asking something; O Svāmin, you ought to speak upon that."
How did that virtuous woman—the daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati, the wife of Kaśyapa, and the mother of Garuḍa—fall into servitude? || 2 ||
Skanda said: O high-minded one, listen as I also relate how that ascetic Vinatā attained the state of being a *haṃjikā*.
In ancient times, Kadrū gave birth to one hundred sons from Kaśyapa; Vinatā gave birth to three: Ulūka, Aruṇa, and Tārkṣya.
O Sage, although Kauśika had obtained the kingdom due to his superiority among birds, he was deposed from that kingship by all of them because of his lack of virtue.
"This one has cruel eyes; he is blind by day; and he always has crooked claws. His speech causes extreme agitation to everyone. (6)
Having thus praised his multitude of virtues in many ways, the birds, who roam at their own will, have even now not chosen anyone for the kingdom.
O Kauśika, when things had thus occurred, Vinatā, longing to behold her son, then split open the middle egg.
When a full thousand years had passed, O Pot-born One, having burst [the egg], out of an eagerness inseparable from that [state], he [entered] the eighth century of the cosmic age (aṇḍa).
Meanwhile, all the limbs of that exceedingly lustrous infant were positioned upon the thighs of the Siddha who resided within the staff.
As soon as he emerged from the egg, with the beauty of his face crimson with rage and his body only half-formed, the infant made a solemn vow against his mother.
O Mother, having seen the sons of Kadrū playing with ease upon your lap, you broke that egg in two by your mere sport.
"O bird, since all my limbs are not yet perfected, I curse you: may you become a slave to those very wives of mine who have come here as co-wives. (13)
Trembling from that curse, the bird spoke this: "O Anūru, son of my mother, tell me the end of my curse."
Anūru said: "Do not break this third egg, for it is as yet unformed, just like mine. Whoever is destined to arise within this egg will take service from you. (15)
Having spoken thus, that crow flew up and went to the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana), where Viśveśvara grants an auspicious destination even to the lame.
This cause of Vinatā’s slavery has been explained to you as you asked; O Sage, I shall now speak incidentally of the origin of Aruṇa and Āditya.
Because he was without thighs (an-ūru), he is called Anūru; since he was ruddy with anger, he is Aruṇa. Having performed austerities in Vārāṇasī, he propitiated the Sun-god. || 18 ||
He too, being pleased, granted boons to that Anūru; thus, by his name, he became known as Aruṇāditya.
Arka said: "O Anūru, son of Vinatā, always remain upon my chariot, destroying the darkness before me for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
But for those men who shall worship the image installed by you here, O Mahādeva, what fear can there be for them in Vārāṇasī? (21)
For those who shall constantly worship me here under the name Aruṇāditya, there shall be neither suffering, nor poverty, nor sin.
They are not overcome by diseases, nor by any calamities; indeed, they are not consumed by the fire of grief through the service of Aruṇāditya. (23)
Then, having placed Aruṇa upon his chariot, the Sun led him away; even today, he rises at dawn while still situated on that vehicle of Sūrya.
For one who, having risen in the morning, should offer salutations day after day to Aruṇa together with Sūrya, from where could there be fear of suffering? (25)
Whatever supreme among men shall hear this majesty of Aruṇāditya, no evil deed whatsoever shall ever befall him. (26)
Skanda said: Listen, I shall tell you the majesty of Vṛddhāditya, by the mere hearing of which a person shall not partake in evil deeds.
In ancient times, the venerable Hārīta, a man of great asceticism, propitiated the Sun here in Vārāṇasī for the sake of attaining the perfection of his great penance.
Having installed the auspicious image of the Radiant One, endowed with favorable characteristics, he remained to the right of the large-eyed goddess, filled with firm devotion.
Pleased with that ascetic of advanced age, the Sun granted him a boon: "Enough of delay; ask for what boon should be given to you by me."
Then, from the gracious Sun-god, the sage chose a boon: "If the Blessed One is pleased, grant me back my youth once more. (31)
"Since I, being old, lack the capacity to perform austerities, I shall regain my youth and practice the highest penance. (32)
Austerity alone is the supreme dharma; austerity alone is the supreme wealth; austerity alone is the supreme desire; for austerity alone is indeed nirvāṇa.
The perfections of sovereignty are obtainable somewhere through truth and austerity; the station [of heaven] was attained by Dhruva and others solely by the power of austerity.
Then, having obtained through your granting of a boon youth esteemed by all, I shall practice asceticism that bestows greatness in both worlds. (383)
Fie on old age here among living beings, by which everyone becomes disenchanted; for when the collection of senses is afflicted by old age, even women bring themselves under one's control.
Death itself would be better than old age, which causes extreme lamentation; death brings suffering for but a moment, whereas old age brings suffering at every single moment. (37)

Those who have conquered their senses long for long austerity, they long for long life; they long for wealth for the sake of giving, a wife for the sake of a son, and an intellect for the sake of liberation.
At that very moment, Bradhna indeed stripped away the old man's decrepitude and bestowed upon him youth, the cause of beauty and the means for the accumulation of merit.
Thus, that great sage Vṛddhahārīta, having attained youth from the Sun-god in Vārāṇasī, performed fierce ascetic penance.
Because he was propitiated by the aged ascetic Hārīta, Āditya is therefore remembered as Vṛddhāditya, the "Averter of Old Age."
O Pot-born One, in Vārāṇasī, many have attained perfection by propitiating Vṛddhāditya, who destroys old age, misfortune, and disease. (42)
Having paid homage to Vṛddhāditya at Vārāṇasī on a Sunday, a man shall obtain his desired success and shall never encounter an evil fate.
Skanda said: Listen further, O Sage, to the supreme Keśavāditya, and how Savitṛ attained knowledge upon reaching Keśava.
Once, while traveling through the sky on his seven-horsed chariot, Adikeśava was worshipping the Liṅga of Īśvara with a spirit of devotion.
As if descending from curiosity, O Hari, the sun descended and sat down, silent, motionless, composed, and filled with great wonder.
Waiting for an opportunity to ask something of Hari, he bowed with palms joined in reverence to Hari, whose worship had been concluded.
"Welcome to you," Hari said with great respect; he had the radiant one, whose neck was bowed, sit near him.
Then, perceiving the opportune moment, the Eye of the World, having been granted permission by the Enemy of the Asuras, bowed to Adhokṣaja and made this request.
Ravi said: "O Viśvambhara, O Lord of the world, you are the inner self of all worlds. Yet, O Mādhava, you who are worshipped by the world, there is someone even more worthy of worship than you."
From you this world emerges, and into you everything is dissolved; you alone are the protector of the entire universe, O treasury of the worlds.
Having observed this wonder, I have come here into your presence. O Lord, what is this that is being worshipped by you, which removes the torment of worldly existence? (52)
Having heard these words spoken by the thousand-rayed sun, Hṛṣīkeśa loudly exclaimed, "Blessings! while warding off the seven-horsed chariot with a gesture of his hand.
The illustrious Viṣṇu said: "The God of gods, Mahādeva, the blue-throated Lord of Umā, is indeed the one alone to be worshipped here, the cause of all causes. (54)
In this matter, that person of small intellect who worships anyone other than Trilocana should be known as one devoid of eyes, even though he possesses eyes. (55)
The one who conquers death, the remover of birth, death, and old age, is to be worshipped; indeed, by worshipping Mṛtyuñjaya, Śveta became a conqueror of death.
Having propitiated Kālakāla, Bhṛṅgī indeed conquered Death; even Śailādi’s Death abandoned him who was a worshiper of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Who would not become most worthy of worship after honoring that Lord of Beings (Śiva), who conquered Tripura with ease by discharging a single arrow? 58.
Who would not worship the enemy of Smara, the essence of the sun, the three-eyed one, who is the supreme cause for conquering the three worlds? (59)
He by whose contraction of eyelashes this world undergoes contraction, and by whose expansion it becomes expansive—who could not be most worthy of worship? (60)
By worshipping the Liṅga of Śambhu here, a person immediately attains the four aims of human existence; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (61)
By worshipping the Śāmbhava Liṅga here, a person certainly abandons the mass of sins accumulated over hundreds of births in an instant.
What indeed cannot be attained here through the worship of the Śiva-liṅga? Sons, a wife, fields, heaven, and even liberation—of this there is no doubt. (63)
O thousand-eyed one, the attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds has been achieved by me solely through the worship of Śiva’s Liṅga; this is the truth, the truth, again and again.
This alone is the supreme application, this alone is the highest austerity, and this alone is the supreme knowledge: that the Sthāṇu-liṅga is worshipped. || 65 ||
For those by whom the liṅga of the Lord of Pārvatī has been worshipped here even once, whence could there be fear of suffering in this saṃsāra, which is a vessel of misery? (66)
O Sun, sins do not afflict him who, having renounced everything, has gone for refuge to your linga, even though those sins be great.
O Bhāskara, there shall be prosperity in the worship of the Liṅga for those whom Maheśvara desires to bring about the end of rebirth in this world. (68)

There is no other merit in the three worlds greater than the worship of the Liṅga; by partaking of the water used for bathing the Liṅga, one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Therefore, O Arka, you too should worship the Liṅga of Maheśvara; it has attained supreme splendor that expands through great majesty.
Having heard these words of Hari, the thousand-rayed one (the Sun) began from that time to fashion a crystal linga and worships it even today, O Sage.
Considering him to be his guru, Vivasvān even today remains stationed there, to the north of Ādikeśava.
Therefore, that Keśavāditya, the dispeller of the darkness of his devotees in Kāśī, when duly worshipped, shall always grant the desired fruit of the heart. (73)
By worshipping Keśavāditya in Vārāṇasī, the best of men attains supreme knowledge, by which he shall partake in Nirvāṇa.
There, having performed all the water-rites at the Pādodaka Tīrtha and beholding Keśavāditya, one is liberated from the sins committed throughout one's life.
O Agastya, when Sunday falls on Rathasaptamī, then, at the Pādodaka Tīrtha in the presence of Ādikeśava— || 76 ||
Having bathed at dawn and observed silence, a man is instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes by worshipping Keśava and the Sun.
Whatever sin has been committed by me throughout seven births, may the seventh lunar day of the month of Makara destroy that, along with my disease and grief.
Whatever sin has been committed in this life, and that which was acquired in other births; whatever arose from mind, speech, and body; and furthermore, those sins both known and unknown.
Thus, O Saptamī, O maker of no harm, remove from me this sevenfold sin, accompanied by the seven diseases, through my bath on the seventh day.
Having recited these three mantras and bathed in the water from [the Lord's] feet, a person who beholds Keśavāditya shall become free from all impurity in an instant.
A person who listens to the majesty of Keśavāditya endowed with faith is not tainted by sins and attains devotion to Śiva. || 82 ||
Skanda said: O Sage, hear hereafter of the supreme Vimalāditya, who is established in the delightful Harikeśavana forest within Vārāṇasī. (83)
Formerly, there was a Kshatriya named Vimala who lived in a high region; due to the connection of his past actions, he remained established even on the pure path. (84)
Having contracted the disease of leprosy, that wise man abandoned his wife, home, and wealth, and having reached Vārāṇasī, he propitiated the Sun-god.
With *karavīra* flowers, *japā* blossoms, fragrant *kiṃśuka* flowers, auspicious *raktotpala* lotuses, and *aśoka* trees, he worshipped the Sun-god.
With flower garlands of various arrangements made from *pāṭala* and *caṃpaka* blossoms, and with red sandalwood mixed with saffron, agallochum, and camphor; || 87 ||
With incense that deludes the gods, which fills the sky with great fragrance, with lamps of camphor wicks, and with food offerings of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
By offering water for honor according to the rules and by reciting hymns and prayers to the Sun, as he was thus propitiating him, the Sun became a granter of boons.
And he said: "Choose a boon, O you of pure and stainless conduct! Let this leprosy depart from you; ask for another boon once more. (90)
Having heard this discourse of the Sun (Raśmimālin), Vimala, his hair standing on end with joy, prostrated himself upon the ground like a staff.

They slowly made this request to Ravi, who possesses a single-wheeled chariot, the eye of the world, the immeasurable self, and the dispeller of great darkness: "O immeasurable self, O dispeller of the great darkness! (92)
If you are pleased, O Blessed One, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then let there be no leprosy in the lineage of those who are devoted to your service.
O Lord of a thousand rays, may no other diseases befall them, may they have no poverty, and may there be no suffering whatsoever for your devotees.
The illustrious Sūrya said: "So be it," O highly wise one; listen to another supreme boon: "O great-minded one, this very form has been worshipped by you thus in Kāśī. (95)
I shall never abandon her presence here; moreover, this image shall become renowned by your name. (96)
Known by the name Vimalāditya, she is always the granter of boons to her devotees; she is the destroyer of all diseases and the cause of the destruction of all sins.
Having thus granted these boons, Sūrya vanished on the spot; Vimala too, his body now stainless, went to his own abode.
Thus, that Vimalāditya, the bestower of auspiciousness in Vārāṇasī, causes leprosy to perish merely by the sight of him. 99.
And whatever man should hear this story of Vimalāditya, he attains stainless purity and is freed from the impurities of the mind. (100)
Skanda said: There is another [deity] there called Gaṅgāditya, indeed to the south of Viśveśa; by the mere sight of him, a person attains purity in this world.
When the Gaṅgā arrived, preceded by Bhagīratha, Ravi remained right there in order to offer praise to the Gaṅgā.
Even today, day and night, the Sun-god, with a gracious soul, facing the Gaṅgā, offers praise to her who bestows boons upon her devotees.
Having propitiated Gaṅgāditya in Vārāṇasī, that best of men never at any time encounters an evil fate, nor does he suffer from disease.
Skanda said: Listen to another [account], O illustrious one, concerning the origin of Yamāditya, by hearing which a man never beholds the world of Yama.
O Sage, by beholding Yamāditya on the western side of Yameśa and to the east of Vīreśa, a person does not see the world of Yama.
Having bathed at Yamatīrtha on the fourteenth lunar day (bhūtā) falling on a Tuesday, and having beheld Yameśvara, a man is swiftly liberated from all sins.
In the past, Yama, having performed most pure penance at Yamatīrtha, installed Yameśa and Yamāditya, who grant the fulfillment of the devotees' desires.
O Pot-born One, because the Sun was established there by Yama, it is therefore called Yamāditya; he removes the torments of Yama’s realm.
Bowing down to Yameśa and Yamāditya, who were established by Yama, and having performed his bath at Yamatīrtha, one does not behold the world of Yama.
By performing libations and offering funeral cakes at Yamatīrtha on the fourteenth lunar day, under the asterism Bharaṇī, on a Tuesday, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
The ancestors dwelling in hell constantly long for this most excellent conjunction, if it occurs on a Tuesday, under the asterism Bharaṇī, and on the fourteenth lunar day (Bhūtā).
O wise one, if someone at the Yamunā-tīrtha in Kāśī performs a bath and even offers libations with sesame seeds, it leads to liberation. (13)
What is the use for men of journeys to Gayā, or of Śrāddha rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, if this Śrāddha can be obtained here at the Yama-tīrtha in Kāśī during this Yoga? (14)
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) at the Yamatīrtha, having worshipped Yameśvara, and having paid homage to Yamāditya, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
Skanda said: Thus have these twelve Ādityas, the destroyers of sin, been described to you; by hearing of their origin, a man shall not fall into hell.
There are also many other Suns established in Kāśī, fashioned from clay and divided by the number of the suns, such as Guhyakārka and others. (17)
Having heard these meritorious chapters that indicate the twelve Ādityas, or having caused them to be heard, a mortal never goes to an evil state anywhere.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Description of Aruṇa, Vṛddhakeśava, Vimalagaṅgā, and Yama-āditya," in the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, of the Uttara-ardha of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 51 ||
Skanda said: O Sage, when the garlanded one (the Sun) had departed for Kāśī, which deludes the three worlds, Hara, staying on Mount Mandara, again fell into deep reflection.
Even now the yoginīs have not arrived; even now the sun of fierce rays has not risen. It is a marvel that news of Kāśī itself is so exceedingly difficult for me to obtain.
What wonder is there in this, that Kāśī makes even my own mind—which was once steady—unsteady? What need is there to mention other gods? || 3 ||
With my glance, I scorched Kāma, the conqueror of the three worlds; yet, alas, this longing for Kāśī torments me even more intensely. (4)
Whom shall I send from here to seek news of Kāśī? For who indeed is skilled enough to know it, since even he [Brahmā] has four faces? (5)
Having thus addressed the Creator with great respect and having seated him there, Śrīkaṇṭha spoke to the four-faced one.
The Yoginīs were sent previously, and then Sahasrārcis was sent; yet even now they do not return from Kāśī, O Pot-born One (Agastya).
O Lokeśa, that Kāśī agitates my mind, just as some fickle-eyed woman does to an ordinary man. (8)
My delight here on Mount Mandara is not intense in this beautiful cave, which has clear yet meager water, like that of a crocodile in a small puddle.
The torment arising from that hālāhala poison did not afflict me so greatly as this suffering born of separation from Kāśī afflicts me here.
Even though the cool-rayed moon stays upon his head, showering him with droplets of nectar, he is not able to dispel the fever born of separation from Kāśī.
O wise one, leader of the noble, perform my task! Go quickly from here to Kāśī and strive for my welfare.
O Brahman, you alone know the reason for abandoning Kāśī; even a dull-witted person would not abandon Kāśī, so how much less one who knows something of its nature?
O Brahman, why should I not go to Kāśī this very day by means of my own power of illusion? Yet, I do not venture to transgress against Divodāsa, who stands firm in his own dharma.
O Ordainer, since you alone ordain all that is to be ordained—both "this" and "that"—everything else spoken of is therefore meaningless in your regard. (15)
"Go safely; may your path be filled with auspicious results. Having received this command upon his head from Brahmā, he went joyfully to Vārāṇasī.
Having swiftly reached the city of Vārāṇasī on his vehicle of white swans, the Self-born One then considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose.
Today, the fruit of traveling by swan has been attained through my arrival at Kāśī; for it is said that obstacles arise at every step upon reaching Kāśī. (18)
The root *dṛś* (to see) has truly attained its etymological essence upon reaching her, since this Garden of Bliss has now clearly come within the range of my vision. (19)
There, the celestial river herself waters [the trees] with her own sweet waters; there the trees consist of bliss, and there the people consist of bliss.
In Kāśī, fruits that are full of bliss always ripen; Kāśī is eternally a land of bliss, and Śiva is eternally the bestower of bliss.
For this reason, living beings in Kāśī are born in the form of bliss; indeed, it is only for the fortunate ones here that their feet are eager to wander [through the city].
Those two feet which wander upon the earth through the cities of the Lord of the Universe—those very feet are your ears, made profoundly learned by your consciousness in order to hear. (23)
In this world, for those wise men possessed of learning by whom Kāśī has been heard even once, that alone is considered the entirety of their mind.

By which this Kāśī, the source of all authority, is authorized; that intellect perceives everything here among the wise and virtuous, by which this abode of Dhūrjaṭi was sustained and made its own object.
Better are the grasses and grains, even those blown by the wind, which fall here in Kāśī, than people who have not seen Kāśī. (26)
Today my life, lasting for two parārdhas, has become fruitful, since while it endures I have reached the city of Kāśī, so difficult to attain.
"Oh, what a perfection of dharma for me! Oh, what weightiness of my fortune! That today I have beheld Kāśī, which I have longed for for so very long. (28)
Today my tree of self-discipline, watered by the water of devotion to Śiva, has indeed borne exceedingly great fruit in the form of the fruits of my heart's desires. (29)
While expanding the creation, I have fashioned it in many ways; yet Kāśī is something else entirely, being the direct manifestation of Viśveśvara himself. (30)
Thus, with a joyful heart, the Creator, having beheld the city of Vārāṇasī, appeared before the king in the guise of an elderly brahmin.
With his hands moist with water and unbroken grains (akṣata), having pronounced words of blessing for the lord of the earth and offered his salutation, he then took the seat offered by the king.
Honored by the king with rising from his seat, offering a seat, and other courtesies, the brahmin informed the monarch—who had asked the reason for his arrival—of his purpose.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O protector of the earth, I have been here for a very long time; I am ancient. You do not know me at all, yet I indeed know you as Ripuñjaya. (34)
I have seen more than a hundred kings who gave profuse sacrificial fees, who were victorious in many battles, who were devoted to performing sacrifices, and who had conquered their senses. (35)

Having completely cast off the group of six internal enemies, they were well-disciplined, endowed with courage, having seen the further shore of sacred learning, and expert in the science of royal policy. || 36 ||
They were skilled in compassion and courtesy, devoted to the vow of truth, equal to the earth in forbearance, and surpassed the ocean in profundity. (37)
Having conquered the torrent of anger, these heroes were the very ground of gentleness and beauty; thus endowed with such qualities, they had well-accumulated the wealth of their fame. (38)
O royal sage, only two or three of your pure and excellent qualities have, for the most part, not yet come within my sight among these kings. (39)
You are the progenitor of your own family, and you are the deity of the Brahmins; you are the companion of great asceticism, whereas other kings are not like this on their path.
You are blessed and worthy of honor among the virtuous, and you are to be revered for your excellent qualities; even the gods, O Divodāsa, do not stray onto wrong paths out of fear of you.
O King, what use have we for praise of you, who are free from desire even toward the twice-born? What can we do? Your multitude of virtues compels us to act as your panegyrists. (42)
Let this conversation stand for now; I shall speak of the matter at hand. O King, I desire to perform a sacrifice and therefore choose you as my assistant.

"O King, through you this earth possesses its true ruler and becomes a vessel for all prosperity; and I too, O King, am one whose wealth truly exists, possessing great riches acquired through righteous means. (44)
And this capital city of yours is unsurpassed in the land of karma; for the deeds performed within it do not perish even at the end of an aeon. (49)
Whatever wealth has been accumulated by men who have walked the path of righteousness should be expended at Kāśī; otherwise, it will lead only to suffering.
O King, no one knows the supreme majesty of Kāśī except for the three-eyed Śambhu, the bestower of all knowledge. (47)
I believe you are most fortunate, for by means of meritorious deeds accumulated over hundreds of births, you protect Kāśī, the supreme body of the Lord of the Universe. 48.
Kāśī is indeed the essence of the three worlds, the very essence of the three Vedas, and the supreme essence of the three goals of life; so it has been determined by the great seers. (49)
"By the grace of Viśveśvara alone is this city protected by you; by the protection of even a single person in Kāśī, the three worlds would be protected. (50)
Furthermore, O sinless one, I shall tell you another beneficial word if it pleases you: the Lord of the Universe alone should always be propitiated with all your actions.
O King, do not ever look upon the Lord of the Universe with the thought that he is anyone else; for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun are merely His playthings, O Dhūrjaṭi.
Since kings must be instructed by Brahmins who desire their ultimate welfare, your benefit has already been proclaimed; what, then, is the use of this anxiety of mine? (53)
To the Brahmin who stood thus in silence, the best of kings replied: "O best of the twice-born, everything that you have said has been held in my heart."
The king said: "I am your servant in the task of assisting you who desire to sacrifice; I alone am capable of bringing all the sacrificial requisites."

"O Brahmin, you are the master even over that which exists within the seven constituent parts of the universe; therefore, perform the sacrifice with a single-minded focus and consider your desire already accomplished. (56)
O Brahmin, that kingdom which I rule does not serve my own interest even in the slightest; I strive for the benefit of others through my sons, my wife, and my body. (57)
The wise have declared that for kings, even more than sacrificial rites or pilgrimages from every quarter, the sole duty is the protection of their subjects. (58)

The fire of the heat of subjects is more terrible even than the thunderbolt-fire; while the thunderbolt-fire burns only two or three [trees], the former consumes the kingdom, the lineage, and the body. (59)
O best of the twice-born, whenever I am desirous of performing the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), then I perform my consecration with the water from the feet of Brahmins.
O best of the twice-born, O high-minded one, that oblation which I perform through the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa, I consider to be superior even to the performance of Vedic sacrifices.
Among all my desires, one alone remains awake here in my heart: even today, some seeker must still be seen, even at the cost of my own body. (62)
"Oh! After many days, my heart's desire has borne fruit, since you have arrived at my house today, O twice-born one, seeking something. (63)
O Brahmin, know that with a one-pointed mind you have performed many sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, and that you have rendered assistance in all matters.
Having heard these words spoken by King Mahābuddhi, who was of virtuous character, the Creator, with a joyful mind, gathered the requisites for the sacrifice.
Having obtained the assistance of the royal sage Divodāsa, the Lotus-born One performed ten great horse-sacrifices in Kāśī.
Even today, because the interior of the sky has been pervaded by the masses of sacrificial smoke since that time, this firmament does not abandon its blueness.
From that time forward, there existed in Vārāṇasī that famous holy site named Daśāśvamedha, which bestows auspiciousness upon the surface of the earth. 68.
O Pot-born One, that sacred ford formerly known as Rudrasaras later became known as Daśāśvamedhika due to its formal consecration by Brahmā.
Then the celestial river arrived there through her meeting with Bhagīratha; because it became exceedingly meritorious, that supreme sacred site (tīrtha) was thus established.
Having installed the Liṅga known as Daśāśvamedheśa there, Vidhi indeed remained; even now he has not gone anywhere else, having never left Kāśī.
He could not find even the slightest flaw in that king who delighted in righteousness; therefore, having gone before the Enemy of Tripura, what could Fate possibly say?
Having understood the power of the sacred field and meditating upon Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, Brahmā established Brahmeśvara and remained right there.
"It is certain that this Kāśī is the supreme body of Viśveśa; because of her service, Śambhu will not be angry with me here. (74)
O you of dull intellect, who would wish to abandon Kāśī once more after reaching it—she who is capable of uprooting the karma produced over many lifetimes? (75)
It is only fitting that the body of the Lord of the Universe, who removes the suffering of the entire world, should be intensely tormented by the great fire born of separation from Kāśī. (76)
He who, having reached Kāśī, which destroys the entire flood of sins, should abandon it, is to be known as a beast among men, turned away from supreme bliss.
He who desires the glory of Nirvana after abandoning the miserable states of saṃsāra must not abandon Kāśī, provided he has obtained its grace through the Lord’s favor. 78.
If a person of wicked mind should abandon Kāśī and go elsewhere, the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life shall depart from the palm of his hand.
Who, having reached Kāśī—which destroys the flood of sins, increases great merit, and bestows the bliss of liberation—would abandon it, being of dull intellect? (80)
Where is that happiness in Satyaloka, and where is that happiness in the station of Viṣṇu, compared to the happiness which is obtained in Kāśī by serving [it] for even half a moment? (81)
O Sage, having thus determined the multitude of Vārāṇasī’s virtues, Brahmā turned back toward Mount Mandara and did not return again.
Skanda said: O son of Mitra and Varuṇa, I shall describe to you the greatness of Daśāśvamedha in Kāśī, the crest-jewel of all holy places.
Having reached Daśāśvamedhika, the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas), whatever action is performed here is said to be inexhaustible.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, worship of the deities, the twilight devotions, libations, the ancestral rites, and the honoring of the ancestors. || 85 ||
Having bathed even once at the Daśāśvamedhika tīrtha, the best of men [attains the fruit].
Having seen the Lord of Daśāśvamedha, one is liberated from all sins. || 86 ||
Having reached the first lunar day (pratipad) in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who bathes at Daśāśvamedhika is liberated from the sins of birth.
Having bathed in the Rudrasarovara on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the sin committed in two lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Thus, bathing in sequence on all lunar days, that best of men shall cast off the sins of his entire lifetime by the tenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having reached the Daśaharā lunar day, which removes the sins of ten births, one who has bathed at Daśāśvamedhika shall not behold the torments of Yama.
Having beheld the Liṅga of Daśāśvamedheśa on the lunar day known as Daśaharā, one is abandoned by the sins accumulated over ten births; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having bathed on the Daśaharā day, worships with devotion the supreme Liṅga, the Lord of Daśāśvamedha—him the state of being in the womb shall not touch.
A person who performs the annual pilgrimage during the month of Jyeṣṭha, in its bright fortnight, at Rudrasaras, is not overcome by obstacles.
Whatever fruit is fully obtained through the ten purificatory baths (avabhṛtha) of the horse-sacrifice, that is surely attained by bathing at Daśāśvamedha on the Daśaharā lunar day. 94.
Having bowed to Daśahareśvara on the western bank of the celestial river (Svarṇadhunī), a most meritorious man never encounters a state of misfortune anywhere.
That which is celebrated as the southern gate of the inner sanctuary in Kāśī—by beholding Brahmeśvara there, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 96 ||
Thus, in the guise of a brahmin, the great-minded Druhiṇa remained in Vārāṇasī until the arrival of Viśveśvara.
Divodāsa, the lord of kings, also provided a Brahma-hall for the Brahmin who had performed the sacrifice, appearing in the form of an elderly Brahmin.
Near Brahmeśvara, however, was a captivating Brahma-hall; there Brahmā dwelt, filling the sky with the resonant chanting of the Vedas.
Thus, O Brahmin, has been narrated to you the exceedingly great majesty of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha, which destroys the entire multitude of sins. 100.
Having heard this meritorious chapter and likewise having caused it to be heard, the best of men attains the world of Brahmā through faith.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Daśāśvamedha," in the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, of the Uttara-ardha (latter half) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 52 ||
Agastya said: O best among the knowers of Brahman, this unprecedented story of Brahmā has been told; what did Śambhu do next while Brahmā remained there?
Skanda said: Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya; while Brahmā remained in Kāśī, Giriśa, his mind deeply agitated, began to reflect. || 2 ||
That city Kāśī, which is the ground for subjugation, was not seen by me anywhere else in this world to be quite like it; indeed, this is almost certain.
Whoever goes to that city remains right there; those who were formerly practitioners of yoga became non-practitioners upon reaching Kāśī. || 4 ||
Even though he possesses a thousand rays, the sun became utterly powerless; and although Fate is skilled in ordaining, it did not come to my side.
Thinking thus, the Lord of the Gods summoned his hosts in great numbers and dispatched them, saying, "O, go quickly to the city of Vārāṇasī."
What do the Yoginīs do, and what does that Sun-god do? Go and find out with haste; and what is Brahmā doing? (7)
Then, preceded by great respect, he called out their names: "Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahākāla, Ghaṭākarṇa, Mahodara! (8)
Somanandin, Nandiṣeṇa, Kāla, Piṅgala, Kukkuṭa, Kuṇḍodara, Mayūrākṣa, Bāṇa, Gokarṇa, and Tāraka.
O Tilaparṇa, Smṛtakarṇa, Dṛmicaṇḍa, Prabhāmaya, Sukeśa, Chāga, Kapardin, and Piṅgalākṣaka! 10.
Vīrabhadra, Kirāta, Caturmukha, Nikumbhaka, Pañcākṣa, Bhārabhūta, Tryakṣa, Kṣemaka, and Lāṅgalin.
Virādha, Sumukha, and Āṣāḍha—you are my sons, just as these two, Skanda and Heraṃba, and this Naigameya are mine.
Just as Śākha and Viśākha, and just as these two, Nandi and Bhṛṅgin, [are protected], so too are we while you, who possess great prowess, are present.
"I know nothing of the news from Kāśī, nor of King Divodāsa, nor of the yoginīs, the sun, and the moon; therefore, let two of you go to your own abode. (14)
Śaṅkukarṇa and Mahākāla, who cause even Time itself to tremble, arrived together at the crossroads to learn the news of Vārāṇasī.
Having quickly reached the city of Vārāṇasī, those two, Śaṅkukarṇa and Mahākāla, who had made their vow, forgot the word of Śambhu.
Just as a discerning person, upon seeing a magician's illusion here, falls into delusion in an instant, so too do those two upon beholding Kāśī. || 17 ||
Oh, the greatness of delusion! Oh, the reversal of fortune! For, having reached Kāśī, which is a mass of liberation, the ignorant depart for elsewhere. (18)
For those by whom this Kāśī, the ground of great blessings, was abandoned, liberation—though already attained—has slipped away from their very palms. (19)
Where even the mere act of bathing is superior to all ritual purificatory baths (avabhṛtha), who would abandon that Kāśī, even with its waters merely warmed? (20)
Who would abandon that Kāśī, where by the offering of a single flower upon the head of the Śiva-liṅga, one gains the merit of ten gold pieces?
Who would abandon that Kāśī, where even by a single prostration with staff-like limbs before Śiva, they say the position of Indra is but trivial? (22)
Who would abandon that Kāśī, where by feeding even a single twice-born man according to one's desire, one gains merit exceeding that of the Vājapeya sacrifice? (23)
Whereby, by giving even a single cow to a brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the merit of ten thousand cows—what wise person would abandon that Kāśī? || 24 ||
Who would abandon that Kāśī, where even a single liṅga has been installed, as if it were the entire three worlds? || 25 ||
Having thus reached a firm conclusion and established themselves upon that merit-bestowing Liṅga, they attained their final abode right there; even today, they do not leave Kāśī.
Having beheld the Śaṅkukarṇeśvara Liṅga, which is worshipped by the Gaṇa Śaṅkukarṇa, a living being is never again born within the great womb of a mother.
Having worshipped Śaṅkukarṇeśvara to the northwest of Viśveśa, a person shall not enter this terrible ocean of worldly existence.
Having worshipped, bowed down to, and praised the Mahākāleśvara Liṅga, which is adored by the Mahākāla Gaṇas, from where can there be fear of Time (Death)? 29.
Skanda said: Having learned that Śaṅkukarṇa and Mahākāla were lingering for a long time, the Lord of the All-Knowing then spoke to two other attendants.
"O Ghaṇṭākarṇa, come here! O Mahodara of great intellect! You two must go quickly to Kāśī to ascertain the activities taking place there. (31)
Thus, O Agastya, those two attendants went to the great city of Kāśī, but even today they have not returned; they remain stationed right there.
Having duly installed the Ghaṇṭākarṇeśvara Liṅga in Kāśī, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, the most excellent of Gaṇas, himself attained liberation right there.
Having established a water-pool right there for the purpose of bathing the Liṅga, he did not yet leave Kāśī, for he continued to meditate upon the Liṅga in that very same manner.
Mahodara, too, being devoted to the meditation on Śiva in that eastern direction, meditates upon the Mahodareśvara Liṅga even today, O Pot-born One (Agastya).
O best of the twice-born, having seen Mahodareśvara in Vārāṇasī, one shall never again enter the cavity of a mother's womb.
Having bathed in the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake and beheld the omnipresent Vyāseśvara, even if one should perish anywhere else, he shall be as if dead in Vārāṇasī.
By performing a Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules at the great pilgrimage site of Ghaṇṭākarṇa, one may deliver seven generations of ancestors, even if they have fallen into a miserable state.
Even today, whoever immerses themselves in that pool and remains attentive for a moment hears the sound of the bell during the great worship of Viśveśvara.
The ancestors say: "In Kāśī, at the pure waters of Ghaṇṭākarṇa, may someone be born in our lineage who offers even water with sesame seeds. (40)
O Pot-born One, the sages of his lineage, having performed their water-rites at the great lake Ghaṇṭākarṇa in Kāśī, attained supreme perfection.
Skanda said: When Ghaṇṭākarṇa had departed and Mahodara had gone forth, the enemy of Smara (Śiva) was filled with wonder, repeatedly shaking his head.
And Hara, smiling again and again, said within his mind: "O Kāśī, you are the sword of great deluding magic; I have fully understood you."
Those who know the past praise Kāśī as the remover of great delusion; yet they do not realize that she herself is this very abundance of great delusion.
"I shall send them all; you will bewilder them. Thus do I fully understand you, O Kāśī, to be a bewildering herb.
Nevertheless, I shall send whatever retinue I possess; for here, the wise do not desist from effort when a task remains to be accomplished.
The wise should never desist from effort in any undertaking; for even an adverse fate may become exhausted by one’s constant exertion.
Although the sun and the moon were seized by Rahu in the expanse of the sky, even now they do not abandon their course, having exerted themselves in their appointed task.
In one case, fate repeatedly destroys undertakings due to its adverse nature; in another case, those very tasks will succeed through intense exertion. (49)
Fate is said to be one's previously performed karma, and nothing else; therefore, a wise person should personally exert effort to dispel it.
Food placed in a vessel may, by chance, enter his mouth of its own accord; but it enters the cavity of his belly only through the exertion of his hands and mouth.
Having thus justified his exertion and firmly concluded that destiny is conquerable, the Lord again dispatched the Gaṇas of the five great powers.
Somanandin, Nandiṣeṇa, Kāla, Piṅgala, and Kukkuṭa—like those who have attained the nectar of life, they do not return even to this day from Kāśī. || 53 ||
Having installed lingas under their own names with the desire for the gratification of Śambhu, they remained in Kāśī, the source of universal liberation.
Having beheld the supreme Liṅga Somanaṃdīśvara in Nandavana, a devoted man shall attain supreme bliss in the world of Soma.
Then, having beheld Nandiṣeṇeśvara to the north of that, and having reached Ānandasenā, a man may conquer even death in an instant.
Having bowed to the great Liṅga Kāleśvara, located to the northwest of the Gaṅgā, one shall never be bound by the noose of Time (Kāla). || 57 ||
Having worshipped Piṅgaleśvara, located slightly to the north of Kāleśa, one obtains the knowledge of Piṅgala, by which one attains identity with Him.
Those who extend their devotion here to the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga, which has the form of a hen’s egg, shall not enter a womb again.
Skanda said: O Sage, when the five groups of attendants, beginning with Somanandi, had reached Ānandakānana and were stationed there, Sthāṇu spoke.
If this matter is properly reflected upon, it is indeed our own task; by means of this pretext, let these men of mine remain there as well. (61)
Even though the Pramathas, great in their illusory power, have entered, I myself have undoubtedly entered Vārāṇasī.
"I shall gradually dispatch whatever personal attendants I have; once they have all departed, I myself will go there afterwards. (63)
Having deliberated thus in his heart, the trident-bearing God of gods then dispatched four groups of Pramathas.
Kuṇḍodara, the one named Mayūra, Bāṇa, and Gokarṇa—these Gaṇas entered Kāśī, relying upon the power of their illusory magic (māyā).
Having employed hundreds of stratagems during the agitation caused by them to Divodāsa, when not even a single one was capable [of prevailing], he remained right there.
"By what action can the Lord be pleased despite hundreds of offenses? Having deliberated thus, they performed the supreme worship of the Liṅga.
When a single Liṅga of Śambhu is worshipped here according to the prescribed rite, the Three-eyed Lord forgives a hundred offenses and bestows liberation.
Śambhu is not so pleased by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, or vows as He is when a liṅga has been worshipped even once according to the prescribed rite.

One who knows the procedure for the worship of the Liṅga and is always devoted to the worship of the Liṅga should be recognized as truly three-eyed, even if that person is a mere mortal with only two eyes. (70)
That fruit which is obtained by men from worshipping a liṅga even once is not attained by the gift of a hundred cows, nor by the gift of a hundred pieces of gold. (71)
That fruit which is obtained by mortals through the constant worship of the Liṅga is not attained even by sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha. (72)
Having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, whoever drinks the water used for bathing the Liṅga three times, his threefold sin is swiftly destroyed in this world.
He who performs an ablution upon his head with the waters used for bathing the Liṅga shall obtain here, O sinless one, the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Whoever, upon seeing the well-worshipped Liṅga, should perform even a single prostration—for such a person, no doubt arises regarding being bound again to a physical body. (75)
Whoever installs a *liṅga* with devotion is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt, and being purified, he shall become a partaker of heaven.
Having deliberated thus, the Gaṇas established Liṅgas in Kāśī for the pacification of the offense against their master, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
Having beheld the Kuṇḍodareśvara Liṅga in the vicinity of Lolārka, one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 78 ||
Having worshipped Mayūreśvara on the bank of the Asi river to the west of the Kuṇḍodareśvara Liṅga, one does not enter a womb again.
To the west of Mayūreśa is the great Bāṇeśvara Liṅga; by the mere sight of it, one is liberated from all sins.
Having worshipped Gokarṇeśa, the great Liṅga at the western door of the inner sanctum in Kāśī, one is indeed not overcome by obstacles.
For a devotee of Gokarṇeśvara, at the time of death, no loss of knowledge shall occur, even when reaching the ultimate end.
Skanda said: While these four excellent Gaṇas were lingering, the Lord of the Gaṇas described the greatness and majesty of that Kāśī.
By which Vaiṣṇava Māyā the entire universe is made to wander here, that very one is certainly this Kāśī, the sole enchantress of the world, appearing in embodied form. (84)
Casting aside brothers, wives, sons, fields, homes, and wealth—even accepting death—they all resort to Kāśī.
In Kāśī, there is not even the slightest fear even of death; how then could the Gaṇas dwelling there be afraid even of me? || 86 ||
Where death is auspicious and where nakedness is an ornament, where a loincloth is like silk—how can Kāśī be compared to anything else?
In that place, Nirvāṇa, the beloved, chooses as her ornament one from the borderlands—whether he be a pauper or a nobleman, a Brahmin or an outcaste.
Even the gods, such as Śakra and others, are not equal—even by a ten-millionth part—to those beings who, having died there, attain the state of Nirvāṇa. (89)
Wherever in Kāśī a living being dies, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and the other gods bow down with great effort, their heads bowed and palms joined in reverence. || 90 ||
In Kāśī, even in the state of a corpse, a living being does not become impure; therefore, I myself shall personally touch his ear.
But that meritorious person who mutters "Kāśī, Kāśī" twice or thrice is greater and more pure than even all other purifiers. (92)
By whom Kāśī is meditated upon in the heart, by whom Kāśī is served here, by him I am meditated upon in the heart, and by him I am always served.
That living being who serves Kāśī with a mind free from conceptual construction, him I constantly hold within my heart with great effort. (94)

Even if one is unable to reside there oneself, one should cause a resident of a sacred site (tīrtha) to dwell there; by providing even a single person with the necessary means, one who provides the residence will certainly partake in the fruit of that residence.
Those wise ones who dwell in Kāśī, having reached the certainty of non-duality, should be known as liberated while living; they alone are indeed worthy of salutation and worship. (96)
Having reflected thus many times upon the virtues of Vārāṇasī, Sthāṇu summoned his other attendants and dispatched them with affection.
"O you of pure mind, come and depart as a savior; go to that excellent city which Divodāsa, whose dwelling is righteousness, governs. (98)
O Tilaparṇa, Sthūlakarṇa, Dṛmicaṇḍa, Prabhāmaya, Sukeśa, Chāga, Kapardin, and Piṅgalākṣaka! 99.
Vīrabhadra, the one named Kirāta, Caturmukha, Nikumbhaka, Pañcākṣa, the one named Bhārabhūta, Tryakṣa, Kṣemaka, and Lāṅgalin. 100.
O Virādha, Sumukha, and Āṣāḍha, let all these highly fortunate hosts, who are devoted to their master and firm in their vows, go forth individually. || 1 ||
Having displayed many kinds of diverse illusions, those clever ones stood with unblinking eyes, longing for a vulnerability in the king.
Their flaws exposed and their wealth of fame scattered, they cried out, "Alas! What is this that has happened? and there they reviled themselves.
The Gaṇas said: "Fie upon us, who have been constantly honored by our Lord again and again, yet among whom not even a single ordinary mortal has been brought under control!"
Fie upon us, who have betrayed that task, even though we were shown favor by the Three-eyed Lord through his great honor, his gifts, and his immense affection! || 5 ||
What will be our destiny here, we who have been negligent in our master’s duties? Our dwelling will surely be in a world of blinding darkness.
Alas, for those who sustain their lives without having accomplished the duties of a master, and whose sensory faculties remain unimpaired, there is misfortune at every step.
The desires of servants who have received great honor yet been humiliated in their master’s service, and who enjoy abundant rewards, are destined to be fragile.
Alas, this earth is burdened by those shameless ones who look toward the face of their master even though they have not accomplished the task for which they were sent.
Neither the burden of mountains, nor of oceans, nor of great trees is as heavy as that of those who betray their master. 110.
"Aha! An irreproachable ancient verse has been remembered by us; relying upon its meaning, we shall remain here with our resolve firmly made. (11)
For those who have not accumulated merit, whose wealth and lifespan are exhausted, and who are devoid of all other means, the city of Vārāṇasī is their refuge.

For those exhausted by the burden of demerit, for those who have attained repentance, and for those whose movements are otherwise directed everywhere upward, the city of Vārāṇasī is the ultimate refuge.
For those who betray their master, those who are ungrateful, and those who destroy trust, there is no refuge anywhere except for the city of Vārāṇasī.
Having thus determined the meaning of the verse, the Pramathas remained there, their true nature unknown to King Divodāsa. (15)
Although he was exceedingly wise, that king did not perceive the gods who stood there in various forms by the power of the Lord.
It is marvelous that even Citragupta does not know the creatures residing in Vārāṇasī; what need is there to mention others who dwell in the world of mortals? (17)
Even the King of Dharma cannot reach the end of those whose power is uninterrupted, whose splendor is boundless, and who have performed the consecration of a liṅga.
Thus, O great sage born from a jar, all those Pramathas, having performed the worship of the Linga, do not even today abandon Kashi, the bestower of bliss. (19)
O Sage, the supreme Gaṇa named Tāraka even today worships the great Liṅga called Tārakeśa, which bestows the knowledge of liberation upon men.
By establishing firm devotion toward the Tārakeśvara Liṅga, that supreme among men easily attains the knowledge of Tāraka.
The Tilaparṇeśvara Liṅga was established by Tilaparṇa; by seeing it here, even a sin the size of a sesame seed cannot remain.
Having fully worshipped the Sthūlakarṇeśvara Liṅga, the best of men does not meet with an evil fate and attains supreme merit. || 23 ||
By worshipping the Dṛmicaṇḍeśvara Liṅga as well as the Prabhāmaya Liṅga to its west, one is not overcome by sins.
Having seen the Prabhāmaya-Īśvara Liṅga, even if situated elsewhere, the wise man shall go to the world of Śiva by means of a radiant vehicle.
Having worshipped Sukeśeśvara in the Harikeśa forest, a person shall not again and again assume a body composed of the six sheaths.
A man who worships Īśa in the vicinity of Bhīmacaṇḍī finds Him; having abandoned even the most terrible sin, he attains eternal liberation. || 27 ||
Having beheld the great Liṅga Chāgaleśa, situated near Pitṛīśvara, no one—even one like a beast—shall be touched by worldly sin.
