Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Vārāṇasī and the Dispatching of Gaṇas," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Pot-born one, I shall speak; listen attentively to the supreme and great majesty of the Liṅga Kapardīśa.
The leader of the Gaṇas named Kapardin, who is extremely dear to Śambhu, installed a Śambhu-liṅga in the region to the north of Pitṛīśa.
He dug a sacrificial pit before it, named Vimalodaka, by the mere touch of whose water a man becomes pure.
O Pot-born One, I shall relate an ancient history that occurred there in the Tretā Yuga; as it truly happened, its hearing removes all sins.
There was a preeminent Pāśupata known by the name Vālmīki; that sage practiced austerities while worshipping Kapardīśa.
Once, during the winter month of Mārgaśīrṣa, that ascetic, having bathed at midday in that great sacred ford of pure water, [proceeded on his way].
Having performed his midday rites, he bathed with sacred ash from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head on the southern side of the Liṅga.
Having placed the dust from [the sage's] head upon his own, he meditated on the spiritual twilight (sandhyā), recited the five-syllabled mantra, and contemplated the Lord with matted hair.
Having performed a circumambulation with its proper measure by way of reabsorption, he should utter "huḍuṃ" three times loudly.
Having placed the *praṇava* (Om) at the forefront, and having performed a joyful song distinguished by the six musical notes (*ṣaḍja*, etc.), accompanied by dance and hand gestures (*hastaka*).
Captivating with his *aṅgahāras* and *cārīs*, and joined by *maṇḍalas*, that great ascetic sat there for a moment on the bank of the lake.
He beheld a terrible Rākṣasa of exceedingly deformed appearance, whose mouth had cheeks like dry conch shells and whose tawny eyes were sunken deep.
The tips of his hair were coarse and split, his neck was very long, his nose was exceedingly flat, and his lips were dry and extremely protruding. || 13 ||
He had a very broad crown and hair standing erect on his head; he possessed long earlobes and was terrifying with his tawny beard.
With a long, dangling, and lolling tongue, an exceedingly prominent nape of the neck, and a structure of thick clavicles, it was formidable with its pair of long shoulders.
With the hollows of his armpits sunken, his two arms were withered and short; the tips of his hands had widely spaced fingers, and the rows of his nails were curved and thick.
With its chest parched and covered in dust, the skin of its belly clinging to its back, formidable with its broad hips, and its sacral joint devoid of flesh; (17)
He possessed a pair of pendulous buttocks, with shriveled testicles and a small penis; his thighs were long and fleshless, and his skeletal frame was characterized by thick knees.
With only bone and skin remaining, his body was covered in a network of veins; he was veiny, with long shanks, and terrifying with his thick ankles and bones. || 19 ||
His feet were excessively broad, with long, crooked, and thin fingers; his body was reduced to mere skin and bone, its form scarred by prominent veins.
He was hideous and of terrifying appearance, emaciated by hunger, excessively hairy, resembling a tree scorched by a forest fire, and possessed of extremely restless eyes.

Seeing that ghost, who was embodied and as if terrifying, causing fear to all living beings, making the heart tremble, and possessing an extremely wretched face, the aged ascetic asked him with composure, "Who are you? (22)
"From where have you arrived here, and why is your gait such as this? O Rākṣasa, out of a compassionate mind I ask you; speak without fear. (23)
For us ascetics, who have fashioned our armor from the ashes of the thousand names of Śiva, there is not even the slightest fear of those such as you. (24)
Having heard those words uttered by the ascetic with affection, that Rākṣasa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that compassionate one whose wealth is penance.
The Rākṣasa said: "O Blessed One, O best of ascetics, if you have compassion for me, then I shall tell you my own story; listen attentively for a moment. (26)
There is a place named Pratiṣṭhāna on the banks of the Godāvarī; there I was a Brāhmaṇa who took pleasure in accepting gifts at sacred fords.
By the ripening of that karma, I have reached such a state as this: in a most terrible desert, utterly devoid of trees and water. (28)
O Sage, a very long time has passed while I have been dwelling there, hungry, afflicted by thirst, and enduring cold and heat. (29)
Even when a great cloud rains down torrents day and night, and when the wind blows during the rainy season, I have not even the slightest covering.
Those who fail to give gifts on festival days and accept offerings at sacred fords, they enter this womb, which is the source of great suffering. (31)
O Sage, after a long time had passed, I once saw a certain descendant of a Brahmin who had arrived in the desert region.
Having reached sunrise, he neglected the ritual of the twilight prayers; having voided urine and excrement, he omitted the purification and ceremonial rinsing. || 33 ||
Seeing him with his lower garment untucked, impure, and devoid of the twilight rituals, I entered his body out of a desire for enjoyment.
O Sage, that twice-born man, out of greed for wealth, arrived at this meritorious city along with a certain merchant due to my misfortune. (35)
O best of sages, that twice-born man entered the inner apartments, while I emerged from his body along with my sins in an instant.
O treasure of asceticism, by the command of Śiva, there is no entry for us pretas or for those who have committed great sins in Vārāṇasī. || 37 ||
Even now, those sins remain outside, desiring to exit; they stay at the very boundary out of fear of the Pramathas.
"Either today, tomorrow, or the day after, he will go outside"—it is with this hope, O ascetic, that we have remained until this very day. (39)
"Even now he has not gone outside, and even now our hope does not depart; thus we remain without support, bound by the noose of hope. (40)
O ascetic, listen to this wonderful account of today; for I believe that even now there will surely be great auspiciousness in the future. (41)
Day after day we travel as far as Prayāga, yet being hungry, though we long for food, we obtain nothing at all. (42)
Everywhere, in every forest, there are fruit-bearing trees; and on this earth, at every step, there are reservoirs of water with clear waters.
Moreover, oh, all kinds of foods are easily available to everyone; there are also many diverse drinks everywhere. (44)
Alas, O Sage, though our eyes have never even caught sight of them, they wander far, ever further away; yet today, by fate, we beheld a single pilgrim approaching.
Afflicted by hunger, I reached his presence and, thinking "I shall devour him," I proceeded with haste. (46)
Just as I was about to seize him, from his lotus-like mouth there issued forth speech, purified by the name of Śiva, which removes all obstacles.
"By the remembrance of Śiva’s name, even my sin became diminished; therefore, by that means, I obtained entrance. (48)
I was not immediately perceived by the Pramathas stationed at the boundary, for even Yama does not look upon those who have heard the name of Śiva.
Having now reached the boundary of the inner chamber along with him, that pilgrim has entered the middle [of the house], while I remain here.
O Sage, having now beheld you, I hold myself in high esteem; O Compassionate One, deliver me from this most dreadful womb.
Having heard these words of the preta, that compassionate ascetic reflected in his mind: "Fie upon those men who strive only for their own sake!"
Fill your own belly; for among all beings—beasts, birds, wild animals, and the rest—he alone is truly blessed in this world who is ever intent upon the welfare of others. (53)
By my own ascetic power, I shall today undoubtedly deliver this deceased man, afflicted by sin, who has come to me alone for refuge.
Having reflected thus, that most excellent being spoke to the demon in his mind: "O you, bathe in this lake Vimaloda for the removal of your sins!"
O Piśāca, by the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha), your state as a Piśāca will, upon the sight of Kapardīśa today, perish and be utterly destroyed in an instant.
Having heard these words of the sage, the preta bowed to him and, with a joyful heart and palms joined in reverence, spoke to the one whose mind was pleased.
O best of sages, I would not even obtain water to drink; O Lord, what need is there to mention bathing? The deities of the water would guard it. (58)
"What talk can there be of drink here? Even the touch of water is difficult to obtain. Hearing these words spoken by the preta, he became exceedingly joyful. (59)
And the ascetic, capable of uplifting the world, said to him: "Accept this divine power and place it upon the surface of your forehead."
Due to this greatness of my power, no ghost anywhere causes any affliction to anyone, even to one who is a great sinner—oh, how wonderful!
Beholding his forehead made white with sacred ash, even the servants of Yama flee in fear from him, as if from the Pāśupata weapon.
Just as travelers, seeing a body of water marked by bones, flee from afar, so do the servants of Yama avoid one who bears the mark of ashes upon his forehead.
Even predatory creatures do not approach from any direction that best of men who has donned the armor of protection through the mantras of Śiva. (64)
Those who, out of devotion, wear on their forehead, chest, and the roots of their arms ashes purified by the Śiva-mantra—those indeed are not harmed by violent beings.
Since she protects from all wicked beings day and night, she is called Rakṣā; and since she bestows prosperity, she is called Vibhūti.

Because it causes burning (bhāsana), because it causes scorching (bharṣaṇa), because it bestows the state of being dust (pāṃsutva) through dust (pāṃsu), and because it cauterizes (kṣāraṇa) sins, it is thus etymologically defined as "Buddhi" (the Intellect). 67.
Taking it from the middle of the stream, he placed the ashes into the hand of the preta; he too, receiving them with reverence, applied them to the region of his forehead.
Seeing that Piśāca wearing divine ornaments and intent on plunging into the water, the water-deities did not restrain him.
Having bathed and drunk, as soon as he emerged from that reservoir of water, he attained the state of a Piśāca and obtained a divine body.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes, he mounted a divine vehicle and then reached the holy path.
As he was departing through the sky, he paid homage to that ascetic and spoke aloud: "O Blessed One, O sinless one, I have been liberated by you!"
Therefore, due to the majesty of this sacred site, he has obtained a divine body, escaping from that exceedingly censured state of birth as a miser.
From this day forward, this sacred ford shall be known by the name Piśācamocana; it shall remove the state of being a Piśāca even for others through bathing here.
Those men who bathe here at this highly meritorious tīrtha, and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) preceded by the twilight libations (saṃdhyā) and water-offerings (tarpaṇa), [shall attain great merit].
By fate, their fathers and grandfathers have fallen into the state of Piśācas; they too, having cast off that Piśāca-state, shall go to the supreme goal.

O storehouse of austerity, on this fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform rites such as bathing here for the sake of liberation from the state of a Piśāca.
Those men who shall perform this annual pilgrimage will emerge from the sin incurred by accepting gifts at sacred fords.
Having bathed at Piśācamocana and worshipped Kapardīśa, and having given gifts of food there, men remain fearless even elsewhere.
Having bathed on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa in the presence of Kapardīśvara—or even dying elsewhere—they shall not attain the state of a Piśāca.
Having spoken thus and bowing repeatedly to that ascetic rich in penance, the illustrious divine being attained his celestial destination.
O Pot-born one, even that ascetic, having beheld that great marvel and having propitiated Kapardīśvara, attained liberation in due course of time.
O great sage, from that time forward, the holy site of Piśācamocana in Vārāṇasī attained supreme renown as the remover of all sins.
By properly feeding a Śiva-yogin at the Paiśācamocana tīrtha, one obtains the fruit of feeding ten million people for every single individual fed.
Having heard this meritorious chapter, a man with a disciplined mind is never overcome by spirits, ghosts, or piśācas. (85)
This supreme and great narrative should be recited with diligence for the sake of bringing peace to children who are overcome by seizing spirits. (86)
Having heard this narrative, a man traveling to another land shall never be overcome by thieves, tigers, piśācas, or other such dangers anywhere. (87)

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of Piśācamocana," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 54 ||
Skanda said: There are other Gaṇas as well who established Liṅgas there in Kāśī; I shall describe them to you, O Pot-born One—listen! (1)
By the Gaṇa named Piṅgala, the Liṅga of Śambhu known as Piṅgalākhyeśa was installed to the north of Kapardīśa.
Merely by the sight of him, the destruction of sins occurs; Vīrabhadra is greatly pleased with the trident-bearing God of gods.
One should meditate with unwavering focus even today upon the Vīrabhadreśvara Liṅga; by the mere sight of it, the siddhi of a hero (vīrasiddhi) is produced.
After worshipping Vīrabhadreśvara to the west of Avimukteśvara, a man shall never suffer defeat in battle.
O Sage, Vīrabhadra himself, manifesting in his heroic form, shall destroy the multitude of Brahmins residing in Avimukta.
By worshipping Vīrabhadra, who is accompanied by his auspicious wives Bhadrā and Bhadrakālī, a man obtains the fruit of residing in Kāśī.
The Kirāta established the Kirāteśa Liṅga in Kāśī, located to the south of Kedāra, which bestows fearlessness upon devotees.
The glorious four-faced Gaṇa remains motionless even today, meditating upon the Caturmukheśvara Liṅga in the presence of Vṛddhakāleśa.
The devotees of the Lord of the Four-Faced One, like the four-faced Brahmā himself in heaven, are honored by hosts of gods and endowed with all enjoyments.

Having beheld Nikumbheśvara, who is worshipped by the Gaṇa Nikumbha, and having worshipped him, one who proceeds to the village shall attain the fulfillment of his purpose; and in the vicinity of Kubereśa, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
By duly worshipping the great Pañcākṣeśa Liṅga to the south of Mahādeva in Kāśī, a person shall attain the recollection of past births.
Having meditated upon the Bhārabhūteśvara Liṅga, worshipped by the hosts of Bhārabhūtas, at the northern door of the inner sanctum, one shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
Those by whom the Bhārabhūteśvara Liṅga has not been beheld in Kāśī are a burden to the earth, like trees devoid of fruit. 14.
O Pot-born One, even today the supreme Liṅga known as Tryakṣeśvara is worshipped by the Gaṇa named Tryakṣa in front of Trilocana.
Those who are devotees of that Liṅga are born as three-eyed ones at the end of their bodies; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
The leader of the Gaṇas named Kṣemaka, who personally assumed a form in Kāśī, even today remains motionless as he meditates upon Viśveśvara, the omnipresent Lord. (17)
Whoever worships the great host of Kṣemaka in Vārāṇasī, his obstacles are dissolved and there shall be security at every step.
For one who has gone to another land, Kṣemaka should be worshipped here with the desire for his return; thus he shall quickly return in safety. (19)
Having beheld the Liṅga Lāṅgalīśvara, worshipped by the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), located to the north of Viśveśa, a man shall not be subject to disease.
By worshipping Lāṅgalīśa even once, one obtains in its entirety the supreme fruit arising from the gift of five ploughs, which bestows all prosperity.
Having propitiated Virādheśvara, who is worshipped by the host of Virādhas, one does not commit any offense anywhere, even if one is possessed of every possible transgression.
Whatever offense is committed day after day by those residing in Kāśī, that quickly goes to destruction through the thorough worship of Virādheśa. (23)
In the southwest, by bowing with great effort to Virādheśa, who holds a staff in his hand, one is liberated from all offenses; of this there is no doubt.
Having beheld the great Liṅga Sumukheśa, worshipped by the Gaṇa named Sumukha—a Liṅga facing the west—one is liberated from all sins. (25)
Having bathed at the Pilipilā tīrtha and beheld Sumukheśa, one shall always see Dharmarāja with a gracious countenance and never with a frowning face.
Having seen the Liṅga known as Āṣāḍhīśvara, which was worshipped by Āṣāḍhi, a man who beholds it with devotion on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha is liberated from all sins.
Worshipping Āṣāḍhīśa, located to the north of Bhārabhūteśa, on the fifteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one is indeed not tormented by sins.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, or even on the fifteenth, by performing the annual pilgrimage, a man becomes free from sin.
Skanda said: O Sage, while these Gaṇas were thus stationed in Vārāṇasī, they installed Liṅgas under their own names for the satisfaction of Viśveśvara.
The Lord of the Universe reflected again on how Kāśī might be restored: "Whom shall I send as a messenger today for the welfare [of all], so that I may enjoy supreme bliss? (31)
The yoginīs, the fierce-rayed suns, and the hosts with faces like Śaṅkukarṇa have returned from Kāśī, like rivers flowing toward the ocean.
Those who have entered Kāśī have certainly entered my own belly; for them there is no exit, just as there is none for oblations cast into a blazing fire.
For those whose established state is in Kāśī, their souls devoted to the worship of the Liṅga—they alone are my mobile Liṅgas; of this there is no doubt.
In Kāśī, all things—whether immobile or mobile, insentient or sentient—are my very own liṅgas; yet those of wicked intellect bear malice toward them. || 35 ||
Those in whose speech Vārāṇasī resides and in whose hearing dwells the story of the Lord of the Universe—they alone are the venerable Liṅgas of Kāśī, just as I am.
For those from whose mouths the words "Vārāṇasī," "Kāśī," and "Rudrāvāsa" have clearly emerged, Yama shall have no power. (37)
Those who, having reached Ānandakānana, desire even in their hearts another state devoid of bliss, shall remain forever joyless here.
Whether death occurs this very day or after a long interval of time, Kāśī must never be abandoned by men out of fear of the Kali age. (39)
Inevitable events will occur at every step; how could those of sound intellect abandon Kāśī, the abode of prosperity? (40)
It is better to endure thousands of obstacles at every step in Kāśī than to desire even a kingdom free from obstacles anywhere else. 41.
How brief are the enjoyments of fortune at every step! But what is Kāśī, which provides uninterrupted happiness both here and in the hereafter? 42.
For I am Viśvanātha, the Lord; Kāśī is the illuminator of liberation; and the celestial Gaṅgā has waves of nectar—what does this triad not bestow? (43)
This city of mine is five krośas in extent and immeasurable; its boundless prosperity is the cause of liberation for those devoted to it.
For those who are constantly exhausted by the burden of saṃsāra and subject to the cycle of coming and going, Kāśī alone is surely my city, the firm ground of rest. 45.
This place named Kāśikā is always like a pavilion for the wish-fulfilling creepers, fully bearing fruit in the form of the fulfillment of the desires of those traveling on the path of saṃsāra. (46)
This is the variegated parasol of the Universal Monarch, which removes all suffering; it stands like the lofty staff of my trident for the King of Kāśī, who has attained Nirvāṇa.
Those meritorious men who effortlessly desire the glory of Nirvana should never abandon Kāśī for the sake of attaining uninterrupted happiness. (48)
Those who indeed dwell perpetually as forest-dwellers in my Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana) obtain here the most delicious fruits of the fortune of liberation (mokṣalakṣmī).
By whom should that Kāśī, the deluder of the universe, not be remembered—that which, being free from possessiveness and free from delusion, might even delude me? (50)
By what merits is the name of Kāśī—not even the name itself, which is sweet and reveals supreme bliss—not chanted by anyone? (51)
For those who constantly drink the nectar named Kāśī, their path indeed becomes a celestial path composed of earth.
"Even though I am devoid of possessiveness, I am the Self of all; therefore, those in this world who chant the name 'Kāśī' are truly mine. (53)
Knowing it to be a secret, the lords of the Gaṇas, along with Brahmā, the Yoginīs, and the suns, remained right there in Vārāṇasī; it is not otherwise.
Otherwise, how could those Yoginīs, along with the Sun and the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as those Gaṇas, remain elsewhere after abandoning me? (55)
"Truly, a great blessing has arisen while they remain in Kāśī; for even a single dissension would cause a rift in the kingdom, were it not for the presence of other kings. (56)
All those who have obtained entry shall become identical in form to me; for they will certainly strive for the sake of my arrival.
I shall also dispatch others who attend upon me; even those excellent ones who are stationed there, I myself will go from there.
Having reflected thus, Mahādeva summoned Gajānana and dispatched him, saying: "Go from here to Kāśī, my son."
"Even while remaining there, strive for success together with your hosts; ensure that we remain free from obstacles, and create obstacles for the king. (60)
Then, placing the command of Dhūrjaṭi upon his head, the Lord of the Gaṇas, who knows the proper course of action, set out swiftly for Kāśī in order to establish stability.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Kāśī and the Dispatching of Gaṇeśa," in the latter half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Then, having received the command of the Lord, the elephant-faced one set out from Mount Mandara, contemplating the means for Śambhu’s arrival at Kāśī.
Having quickly reached Vārāṇasī, the Lord, traveling in his chariot, assumed the form of a mare and entered [the city], praised by auspicious omens.
Having become an elderly reciter of the *nakṣatra* texts, he frequented the inner quarters of the palace and wandered through the midst of the city, bringing joy to the citizens.
Manifesting dreams to people during the night himself, he goes to their houses in the morning and tells them of their strengths and weaknesses.
"Whatever dream-activity was seen by you tonight, that very thing I shall relate for the sake of arousing your curiosity. (5)
While you were sleeping at night during the fourth watch, a great lake was seen by you; and there, as you were repeatedly sinking, you reached the bank.
Then you sank and rose repeatedly many times in mud made slippery by water; and the ripening of this bad dream is great and most terrifying. (7)
"Alas! Even you have seen him, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes; this will produce a great and terrible anguish within you. (8)
A solar eclipse observed at night is certainly a sign of great misfortune; likewise, the appearance of two rainbows at night is not auspicious.
The sun, having come from the west, caused the moon rising in the sky to fall upon the surface of the earth; this was an omen indicating fear for that kingdom.
That pair of comets seen fighting with one another simultaneously was not auspicious; it portended nothing but the destruction of the kingdom. (11)
That you saw yourself being led toward the south with your hair and teeth falling out, appearing terrifying even to your family; || 12 ||
"That collapse of the palace flagstaff which you witnessed at the end of the night, know it to be certain to cause the destruction of the kingdom and a great portent. (13)
In my dream, the city was flooded by the waves of the ocean of milk; I suspect that within three or four fortnights, it will cause great alarm among the city-dwellers.
"O high-minded one, because you were carried toward the south by a monkey-vehicle in a dream, therefore the means to deceive him is the abandonment of the city. (15)
The woman whom you saw weeping at the end of the night—her hair disheveled and her garments stripped away—that lady rose up like the goddess Śrī herself.
"Since the pinnacle of the temple was seen by you falling, the destruction of the kingdom will occur within just a few days. (17)
A city surrounded on all sides by herds of deer crying out excessively in a dream will become desolate within a single month.
"Something ominous has surely been indicated for the inhabitants here by the hawks, owls, vultures, and other birds that frequent the vicinity of the city. (19)
Repeatedly proclaiming many dreams and portents here and there, that Lord of Obstacles caused many inhabitants of the city to flee.
To some, the proponent might demonstrate the movement of the planets, saying: "Saturn, Venus, and Mars situated in a single zodiac sign are not auspicious. (21)
This smoke-grasping [comet], having pierced the circle of the Seven Sages in the sky, has proceeded toward the western quarter for the destruction of the lord of men. (22)
One who has entered a retrograde motion, is slow, or is situated on a retrograde path, and is conjoined with a malefic planet—such a one is not considered suitable here. (23)
O citizens, this earthquake that occurred yesterday causes even my heart to tremble exceedingly.
This meteor which has sped from the northern direction toward the southern quarter and has dissolved right there in the sky is an ill omen; it is not auspicious.
This sacred tree at the crossroads, which possessed great roots, has been uprooted by the force of a mighty wind; it portends a great calamity.
Having reached sunrise in the eastern direction, this crow Karaṭa shrieks loudly atop a withered tree, portending fierce and terrible fear. (27)
In the midst of the marketplace, two forest-dwelling deer, seeking their prey, quickly moved before the eyes of the citizens like an ill omen. || 28 ||
That this mango bud is seen in autumn—I consider this to be a portent of great danger for the city-dwellers, even though it is out of season. (29)
Having thus instilled fear, certain city-dwellers who were creating obstacles were driven away by him, who had assumed the guise of a deceitful brahmin.
Then, having entered the inner apartments by means of his own illusory power, he became the object of the women's confidence, speaking only of matters already perceived.
O lady of auspicious marks, ninety-seven sons were born to you; among them, one, mounted upon a horse, fell dead in the outer courtyard.
"This maiden is pregnant and will give birth to a beautiful child; for she was previously unfortunate, but now she has become fortunate. (33)
For she was exceedingly dear to the king and the queens here; the pearl ornament from his own chest was given to her by the king.
"It is conjectured here that she has been born for only five or seven days; by the king's favor, two villages were announced to be given to her. (35)
Thus, by speaking of matters witnessed by him, the twice-born man became honored by the queen; and they, in turn, described the many virtues of the king even in his absence.
"Oh, what a Brahmin he is! He is exceedingly discerning in all matters; he is of excellent character, handsome, truthful in speech, and moderate in his talk. (37)
Free from greed, noble, of virtuous conduct, and with senses subdued, he is content even with very little and turns his back on accepting gifts.
Having conquered anger, with a serene countenance, free from malice and deceitful, grateful, pleasant-faced with affection, and averse to slander; || 39 ||
He was a teacher of merit, meritorious in soul, and devoted to all vows; he was pure, of pure conduct, and learned in the Śruti and Smṛti.
He was steadfast, conversant with sacred histories, all-seeing, and honored by all; he was skilled in the entire range of arts and the most eminent among those who know the science of astrology.
"Patient, of noble birth, not miserly, an enjoyer of life with a stainless mind—someone endowed with such qualities has not been seen anywhere. (42)
Thus, describing her multitude of virtues at every step, the women dwelling in the inner apartments passed the time.
Once, having found an opportunity, the queen named Līlāvatī informed King Divodāsa of that matter.
O King, there is one who is aged in virtues, an aged and highly discerning Brāhmaṇa; he alone is to be seen as the supreme, embodied treasury of Brahman. 45.
Having received permission from the king, the queen sent a wise female attendant and brought that brahmin in, who was like the spiritual power of Brahmā embodied in form.
The king also, seeing that Brahmin approaching from afar, rejoiced in his heart, saying to himself: "Where there is such a form, there excellence must reside."
Honored by the king with a formal rising from his seat and other marks of respect for two or three steps, he gladdened him with blessings born of the four Vedas.
Having offered his salutation, he occupied the seat respectfully offered by the king; then that monarch was asked about his welfare by the other king.
O best of the twice-born, the two lords of the earth were well with one another and skilled in the art of conversation; they were satisfied by means of questions and answers.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the king then dismissed the twice-born man to his home; having received great honor and worship, he entered his own hermitage.
When the brahmin had departed for his own hermitage, King Divodāsa described the brahmin extensively before Līlāvatī.
"O Great Queen, O highly wise Līlāvatī, you who are fond of virtue! Just as the Brahmin described her, she is even more virtuous than that. (53)
He knows the past in its entirety and understands the present; indeed, he should be consulted tomorrow morning regarding whatever is yet to come.
With various great riches and abundant enjoyments, that king, when the night had passed, summoned a brahmin in the morning.
Having honored that twice-born man with devotion by presenting him with fine silk garments and other gifts, the king questioned him in private about what was dwelling in his own heart.
The king said: "It is certain that you alone appear to me as the foremost of the twice-born; my mind is of the opinion that no one else possesses an intellect so endowed with truth as yours. (57)
O Brahmin, having seen you—highly wise, peaceful, self-controlled, and a treasure-house of austerity—I am minded to ask something; therefore, explain it to me according to the truth.
This earth has been ruled by me in a manner not achieved by other kings; for as long as I have lived, I have enjoyed manifold divine pleasures. (59)
Day and night, without weariness, this progeny has been protected by forcibly subduing the wicked—even more so than one's own biological sons.
"I know of no merit other than a little gained from worshipping the feet of the twice-born; what is the use to me here of this which remains unspoken? (61)
"O noble one, my mind is now as if devoid of confidence regarding all undertakings; therefore, O best of beings, having deliberated upon what results in auspicious consequences, please tell me. (62)
The twice-born said: Even if a task be exceedingly small, it should always be spoken by a wise man when questioned in private by kings in this world. (63)
Even if unasked, a minister should not say even the slightest thing before the king, being fearful of great dishonor. (64)
If you ask, I shall tell you here; do not harbor doubt regarding that matter. For your sake, it will indeed become a cause for despondency in your mind.
Listen, O King of great intellect; I do not speak anything that is untrue. You are valiant, you are exceedingly heroic, and you have always been fortunate. (66)
In merit, fame, and wisdom, you are as perfected as no one else; I believe that even the Lord of the Thirty-three in Amarāvatī is not like this.
With a clear intellect, I consider you my preceptor; by your grace you are the moon, by your splendor you are the sun, and by your majesty you are fire. (68)
By your strength you are Prabhañjana; by bestowing prosperity you are Śrīda; by your command you are Rudra; and on the field of battle you are Nirṛti.
As the binder of the wicked, you are Pāśī; as the restrainer of the unrighteous, you are Yama. Because of your sovereignty, you are Mahendra; because of your forbearance, you are Kṣamā.
In terms of propriety you are the ocean; in greatness you are the Himalaya; in statecraft you are Bhārgava; and in kingship you are equal to Manu. (71)
Like a cloud, he removes the heat of suffering; like the Gaṅgā, he is pure; and like Kāśī, he bestows a happy rebirth upon all living beings.
As Rudra, you exist in the form of dissolution; as the four-armed one, you are the protector. You are the Ordainer according to the sacred law, and Bhāratī shall dwell within your lotus-like mouth.
In your lotus-hand resides Kamalā; in your anger lies the Halāhala poison; your speech alone is nectar; and your two arms are the two sons of Aśvinī.
Therefore, O King, since you are indeed composed of all the gods, I have come to know through reality that the outcome for you will be auspicious. (75)
O King, starting from this day, on the eighteenth day, a certain northerner will arrive and will surely instruct you. (76)
O King, his word must be carried out by you without hesitation; then, O high-minded one, everything residing in your heart will surely be accomplished.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, the best of the twice-born, having received permission, entered his own hermitage contented; the king, too, was filled with wonder. (78)
In this manner, the conqueror of obstacles brought the entire city under his own control by means of his own illusory power—along with its citizens, its harem, and its king.
Then, considering himself as one who had accomplished his purpose, that conqueror of obstacles (Vighnajit) manifested himself in many forms and established his residence in Kāśī.
O Pot-born One, when that Divodāsa was no longer present, the Lord of the Gaṇas adorned his own original station from that time forward.
When King Divodāsa had been expelled by Viṣṇu, and the city had been restored to its former state by Viśvakarman, [the following occurred].
Having come in person from Mount Mandara to the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī, the Lord first praised Gaṇanāyaka.
Agastya said: How was Vighnajit praised by the Blessed One, the God of gods? And how did that Vināyaka multiply himself in many forms? 84.
By what name indeed was he established in the city of Kāśī? O Six-faced One, tell all of this to me in brief. (85)
Having heard what was thus spoken by the pot-born sage (Agastya), the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) duly related the auspicious story of the king of the Gaṇas.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Gaṇeśa’s Māyā," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O best of sages, Viśveśa, together with Viśvā and myself, preceded by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin, along with Mahāśākha and Viśākha— || 1 ||
Accompanied by Naigameya, surrounded on all sides by the Rudras, joined by the celestial sages, and praised by Sanaka and the others.

He was greeted with acclaim by all the lords of the spheres and the guardians of the directions; he was shown the way to the sacred fords by the holy sites themselves, and his auspiciousness was celebrated in song by the gandharvas.
He was honored by celestial nymphs with dances of sprout-like hand-gestures, and applauded from all sides by unstruck musical instruments resounding in the sky.
The quarters of the sky were deafened by the resonant chanting of the sages; he was praised by throngs of celestial bards and surrounded on all sides by divine chariots.
Mahādeva was showered from all sides with parched grain falling from the fists of the women of Triviṣṭapa, and his hair stood on end with joy.
Having been presented with offerings of garlands by hosts of many vidyādharīs, he was celebrated by yakṣas, guhyakas, siddhas, and other sky-dwellers.
Having entered, he was preceded by beasts and birds, and praised by Kinnaras with joyful faces and by Kinnarīs.
And by Viṣṇu, Mahālakṣmī, Brahmā, Viśvakarman, Nandin, and Gaṇeśa, a great festival was inaugurated.
Having performed the rite of lustration (nīrājana) by the Naga women on all sides, Mahādeva entered the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī.
While all the gods were looking on, he descended from his lordly bull, embraced the Lord of the Gaṇas, and spoke. || 11 ||
That I have reached the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī, which is exceedingly difficult for even me to attain—that is indeed the grace of that child.
"For that which is indeed difficult to accomplish even for a father on the surface of the three worlds can be easily accomplished by his son; I am here the illustration of this. (13)
By means of this elephant-faced one, through the power of my own intellect, some practice has been performed here so that I may attain Kāśī.
"I alone am truly possessed of a son, for that which I have long contemplated—I have, through my own prowess, made my desire come into the palm of my hand. (15)
Having spoken thus, the destroyer of Tripura, praised by Indra and the other gods, being greatly pleased and filled with joy, lauded Gajānana with clear words.

Śrīkaṇṭha said: Victory to you, O primordial one among the creators of obstacles, who brings about the removal of obstacles for your devotees; O pacifier of obstacles that cause no hindrance, the sole creator of great obstacles! 17.
Victory to you, Lord of all the Gaṇas; victory to you, the leader of all the Gaṇas! O you whose lotus feet are bowed to by the Gaṇas, you whose excellent qualities transcend all calculation! 18.
Victory to you, O omnipresent one, Lord of all, the sole treasure-trove of all intellect! O Knower of the entire expansion of illusion, who are worshipped at the forefront of all rites! 19.
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, victory to you, O All-Auspicious One! You are the pacifier of inauspiciousness and the cause of the greatest auspiciousness.

Victory to you, O one worshipped by the creators of the universe! Victory to you, who are bowed to by the sustainers of the world! Victory to you, the praiseworthy destroyer! Victory to you, the bestower of success in virtuous deeds! 21.
O you whose lotus feet are worshipped by the Siddhas, O bestower of victory and success! O sole abode of all accomplishments, O indicator of great siddhi and prosperity! 22.

O creator of all virtues without exception, O you who transcend qualities, O leader of virtues! O you whose purpose is fulfilled through conduct, victory to you who are praised for your excellences! 23.
Victory to you, O Lord of all powers, enemy of Bala, bestower of strength! You who are radiant with the white crane, with the tips of your tusks, and with the prowess of a child yet beyond childhood.
O support of infinite majesty, O upholder of the earth, O rending one! You who have fixed the serpent king upon the tip of your tusk, you who are adorned by the vanquished serpents. || 25 ||

O Compassionate One, O Divine Form, those who bow down to you on this earth become partakers of liberation even from all their sins; for them, you always remove great calamities and bestow upon them both heaven and final emancipation.

O King of Obstacles, those who on this earth are gazed upon by you for even a moment with compassionate side-long glances—indeed, all their sins perish, and Lakṣmī casts her glance upon those supreme men. (27)

O Lord who destroys the obstacles of those who bow before you, O fierce-rayed sun to the lotus-heart of Dākṣāyaṇī—those who praise you are indeed already renowned here; this is no wonder. But what is truly marvelous in this regard, O Lord of the Gaṇas, is that they themselves [become] such [renowned ones]. 28.

Those who constantly worship the pair of Your feet become possessed of abundance in sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain; having fully honored Your lotus feet, they obtain the stainless prosperity enjoyed by kings along with a multitude of servants. (29)

You are the cause of the causes of the supreme causes; you alone are eternally the object of knowledge for those who know the Vedas. You are that which is to be sought by the words of the root-scriptures, O divine one whose form transcends both the moving and the unmoving, and who is beyond the reach of speech.

The Vedas do not know you as you truly are, nor do Brahmā and the other gods, O Architect of all that moves and is stationary! You alone create, protect, and destroy everything; what possible undertaking of praise could there be for you, who are inaccessible even to the mind? (31)

I shall slay the Daityas, headed by Tripura, Andhaka, and Jalandhara, who have been struck down by the arrows of your evil glances. For who else here, besides you, possesses the power to accomplish even the most insignificant collection of tasks that grant success?

The verbal root *ḍhuṃḍh* is renowned in the sense of "searching"; because you have searched for the welfare of all, your name is *ḍhuṃḍhi*. O Vināyaka, King of *ḍhuṃḍhis*, what embodied being here can even obtain entry into Kāśī without your favor? 33.

O Ḍhuṇḍhi, having bowed before your lotus feet, whatever man dwelling here in Kāśī pays homage to me, I shall approach the root of his ear and impart that certain knowledge by which there is no longer any rebirth for him in this world.

Having first bathed with his clothes on at Maṇikarṇikā, a man should quickly sprinkle his two feet with dust, offer libations to the gods, sages, humans, and ancestors, and then, having reached the Jñānoda-tīrtha, he should worship you.

Having propitiated you—who are skilled in bestowing the fruits of the city of Kāśī—with loads of fragrant sweetmeats, excellent incense and lamps, garlands rich in scent, and unguents, who here, O Ḍhuṇḍhi, would not attain perfection after addressing me thus? (36)

O Ḍhuṇḍhi, even one who accomplishes other holy sites here in a manner that disregards the proper sequence, having had the multitude of obstacles that destroy his own welfare removed by the side-glances of Your compassion, shall obtain the complete fruit in this Kāśī.

For one who bows daily at dawn in Kāśī to you, O Ḍhuṇḍhi Vināyaka, the entire host of obstacles is warded off; for such a person, nothing whatsoever existing on the surface of this world—whether in this life or the next—is ever difficult to attain. (38)

Whoever mutters the name of that Ḍhuṇḍhi-Vināyaka, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) indeed dwell daily within his heart; having enjoyed various pleasures fit for the gods, he is finally chosen by Nirvāṇa-Kamalā.

O Ḍhuṇḍhirāja, bestower of all perfections, he who remembers the footstool of your feet day after day, even while standing far away, shall obtain the fruit equal to staying in Kāśī; it is not otherwise, for my word is never in vain.
O highly fortunate one, you remain here in various forms in order to destroy the countless obstacles of this sacred field in manifold ways. (41)
O sinless one, whatever forms he assumes and wherever they appear, I shall describe them all; let these dwellers of heaven listen. (42)
First, you are Ḍhuṇḍhirāja; you are slightly to my right. Having searched thoroughly, you bestow all desired objects upon all devotees. (43)

O Gaṇeśa, those who, having reached this fourth lunar day falling on a Tuesday, have performed various worship for you with heaps of joy-inducing modakas and with perfumes and garlands—those I establish here as my sons within the Gaṇas. (44)

Those wise and accomplished ones who worship you here on the fourth lunar day with profound devotion, O Ḍhuṇḍhi, having placed their left foot upon the heads of all calamities, truly attain the state of being "Gajānana" (the Elephant-faced One), O Gajānana. 45.

Those who, devoted to the *nakta-vrata* on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, shall worship you, O Ḍhuṇḍhi, they shall become worthy of worship by the enemies of the Asuras. (46)

Having performed the annual pilgrimage and reached the fourth day dedicated to the ascetics, the observer of the vow, having fasted during the bright fortnight, should eat sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) bound with white sesame seeds.

A pilgrimage should be undertaken with great effort by those desiring the spiritual perfection of this sacred field; for on that fourth lunar day, O Ḍhuṇḍhi, you remove all calamities out of affection for me.
One should not undertake that pilgrimage without offerings of sesame-seed sweets; by my command, he shall be struck down by thousands of calamities.
The knower of mantras who performs a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds and clarified butter with devotion on that fourth lunar day, his mantra shall become effective.
O Gajānana, whether Vedic or non-Vedic, whatever mantra is recited in your presence, O Ḍhuṇḍha, it will grant the desired perfection.
Īśvara said: "The wise person who shall recite this hymn composed by me will certainly never be afflicted by floods of obstacles. (52)
Whoever searches for and recites this meritorious hymn in the presence of Dhuṇḍhi, all supernatural powers shall constantly attend to him, remaining in his proximity.
Having recited this hymn of praise with a supremely restrained mind, a person shall never again be overcome by those mental sins. (54)
A man reciting the *Ḍhuṇḍhi-stotra* shall obtain sons, a wife, fields, excellent horses, a magnificent residence, as well as wealth and grain. (55)
This hymn named *Sarvasaṃpatkara* (The Bestower of All Prosperity) has been recited by me; it should always be recited with effort by one who desires liberation. 56.
For a man who has recited this meritorious hymn while departing for any undertaking, all perfections will certainly come before him.
Furthermore, I shall speak here; let these dwellers of heaven listen: wherever Dhuṇḍhi established his presence for the sake of protecting the sacred field.
At the confluence of the Kāśī and Gaṅgā, there is the deity named Arkavināyaka; when seen by men on a Sunday, he brings about the pacification of all afflictions.
The leader of the Gaṇas named Durga, the destroyer of all miserable states, should be worshipped with great effort in the southern part of the sacred field.
Near Bhīmacaṇḍī is Bhīmacaṇḍavināyaka; situated in the southwestern region of the sacred field, when seen, he destroys great fear.
In the western part of the field is that Dehalīvināyaka; he wards off all obstacles for his devotees—of this there is no doubt.
In the north-western quarter of the field resides the elephant-faced one named Uddaṇḍa; he shall always punish even the most formidable multitudes of obstacles for his devotees.
In the northern direction of Kāśī, there is the noose-handed Vināyaka; through devotion, he binds those who would obstruct the residents of Kāśī.
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Varaṇā stands the beautiful Kharva-Vināyaka; he diminishes even the massive floods of obstacles for the virtuous devotees.
To the east, for the protection of the sacred field, resides Siddhivināyaka, a perfected being; to the west of Yamatīrtha, he bestows swift success upon practitioners.
These eight Vināyakas, residing in the outer enclosure at Kāśī, drive away those who are non-devotees and bestow all accomplishments upon the devotees. (67)
And those Vināyakas who protect this field of Avimukta within the second enclosure—I shall describe them now.
On the western bank of the celestial river, north of Arkavināyaka, may Gaṇādhyakṣa Laṃbodara wash away the mire of obstacles.
To the west of that, at Kūṭadanta, located to the north of Durgavināyaka, may he who destroys the afflictions of distress always protect this sacred field.
Slightly to the northeast of Bhīmacaṇḍa, the leader of the Gaṇas, is Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, the leader of the hosts of Kṣetrapālas, who is to be worshipped.
To the east of the entrance-gate of Vighneśa, the Vināyaka named Kūśmāṇḍa should always be worshipped with devotion for the pacification of great calamities. (72)
Situated in the south-eastern direction from the Gaṇapati named Uddaṇḍa, the highly renowned Muṇḍavināyaka is to be worshipped by devotees. (73)
His body is in Pātāla, while his head is situated in Kāśī; therefore, he is celebrated in Kāśī as the deity Muṇḍavināyaka.
Having worshipped Vikaṭadvija, the Gaṇapati located to the south of Pāśapāṇi Gaṇeśāna, one shall attain the station of a leader of the Gaṇas.
In the south-western direction from the one named Kharva is the Vināyaka Rājaputra; when worshipped, he restores to his kingdom a king who has been deprived of his realm. (76)
On the western bank of the Gaṅgā is the lord of the Gaṇas named Praṇava; by bowing to him to the south of Rājaputra, one shall be led to heaven.
In the second enclosure, these eight Vināyakas at Kāśī shall destroy the multitudes of obstacles for those residing in the city of Kāśī. (78)
In the third enclosure of the field, there are always those who act as guardians of the field; those kings of obstacles who are present here shall now be described by me. (79)
On the beautiful bank of the celestial river Udagvāhinī, to the north of Lambodara, resides Vakratuṇḍa, the Lord of Obstacles, who removes the multitude of calamities.
To the north of Gaṇapati Kūṭadanta is Ekadantaka; may he protect Ānandakānana from constant contact with calamities.
To the northeast of Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, there is the Lord of Obstacles named Trimukha, who has the faces of a monkey, a lion, and an elephant, and who eternally removes the fear of Kāśī.
To the east of Kūśmāṇḍa is the Lord of Obstacles named Pañcāsya; with his excellent five-faced chariot, he protects the city of Vārāṇasī. (83)
The one named Heraṃba, located to the southeast of Muṇḍavināyaka, should always be worshipped; like Ambā, he fulfills the desires of all residents of Kāśī.
For the sake of attaining perfection, the wise man should worship the ineffable Vikaṭadanta, the King of Obstacles, Gaṇapati, the destroyer of all impediments.
To the northeast of Vināyaka, from the prince, there dwells the leader of the Gaṇas named Varada; he is worthy of worship and bestows boons upon his devotees. (86)
To the south of Praṇava-Vighneśa, Gaṇeśa, who is fond of modakas, is to be worshipped at the Piśaṅgilā Tīrtha on the auspicious bank of the Devanadī.
In the fourth enclosure at Kāśī, the eight Vināyakas, who destroy obstacles to food, are clearly to be beheld by those with joyful minds. (88)
To the north of Vakratuṇḍa, situated on the bank of the celestial river, stands Vināyaka, the bestower of fearlessness and the destroyer of the fears of all.
In the north, because he has but one tusk, the Vināyaka Siṃhatuṇḍa destroys the elephants of calamities for the inhabitants of Vārāṇasī.
May the leader of the Gaṇas, with squinting eyes and three faces, stationed in the northeast direction, constantly protect the great cremation ground from evil glances.
To the east, may Kṣipraprasādana protect the city from the five-faced one; through the worship of Kṣipraprasādana, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are swiftly attained.
To the southeast of Heraṃba is the Vināyaka Cintāmaṇi, who is the literal wish-fulfilling gem for his devotees, bestowing whatever desired object is thought of.
To the south of Vighnarāja is Gaṇeśvara Dantahasta; he records the thousands of obstacles for those men who harm Vārāṇasī.
And the god named Piciṇḍila, surrounded by a host of Yātudhānas, shall protect the city day and night, along with Varadā and Ātudhānī.
Seen at the Pilipilā-tīrtha to the south of Modakapriya, does Heramba, with his staff-like trunk and shaven head, not bestow everything upon his devotees? (96)
In the fifth enclosure at Kāśī, there are Vināyakas in groups of two and four; I shall now describe those who provide protection for the sacred field (kṣetra). || 97 ||
On the northern bank of the celestial river, at the bestower of fearlessness, stands the lord of the Gaṇas, Sthūladaṃta; he shall grant great supernatural powers to the virtuous.
To the north of Siṃhatuṇḍa is the Vināyaka Kalipriya; he constantly causes quarrels among those who are hostile toward fellow followers of other paths. 99.
Likewise, from Kūṇitākṣa to the northeast is the four-tusked Vināyaka; by the mere sight of him, the multitude of obstacles perishes of its own accord.
Because he quickly inspires faith, the leader of the Gaṇas has two trunks in the eastern direction; he possesses an equal splendor both in front and behind.
From the sight of him, men shall attain all-encompassing prosperity. He is the leader of the Gaṇas named Jyeṣṭha, and he is my eldest son in terms of excellence.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, he should be worshipped for the attainment of seniority; he is situated in the south-eastern direction from Cintāmaṇi Vināyaka.
In the direction of the elephant (the east), Gajavināyaka, who has tusks and a trunk, is to be worshipped; by worshipping him with devotion, one attains prosperity ending in elephants.
To the south of Piciṇḍila Gaṇapati is Kālavināyaka; by serving him, men have no fear born of the power of Time.
Having seen the elephant-headed Gaṇeśa situated in the northwestern direction at Uddaṇḍamuṇḍa, one is glorified in the world of the Nāgas.
Now, the leaders of obstacles (vighnanāyakas) residing in the sixth enclosure are described; by the mere hearing of their names, success (siddhi) arises for men. (7)
Maṇikarṇa Gaṇapati, the destroyer of obstacles, is in the east; Āśāvināyaka stands in the southeast, fulfilling the hopes of his devotees.
In the south is Sṛṣṭigaṇeśa, who indicates both creation and dissolution; in the southwest is Yakṣavighneśa, the supreme remover of all obstacles.
In the west is Gajakarṇa, the bringer of welfare to all; and Citraghaṇṭa, the lord of the Gaṇas, shall protect the city in the northwest.
And Sthūlajaṅgha in the north shall pacify the sin of those who practice self-restraint; in the northeast, the Auspicious Vināyaka shall protect the city of Īśāna. || 11 ||
To the north of Yamatīrtha, Mitravināyaka is to be worshipped; I shall now describe those Vināyakas who reside in the seventh enclosure.
Moda and the others are the five Vighneśas; the sixth is Jñānavināyaka; the seventh is Dvāravighneśa, who presides over the great gateway.
The eighth is Vināyaka, who liberates from the floods of all misfortunes; he shall remove [obstacles] for those whose minds are bowed in devotion within my field, Avimukta.
Whoever shall remember these fifty-six elephant-faced [deities], even while staying in a distant foreign land, shall attain knowledge upon death.
The meritorious soul who shall recite this highly auspicious hymn to Ḍhuṇḍhi, consisting of fifty-six verses addressed to Gajānana, shall attain success at every step.
All these lords of the Gaṇas should be remembered wherever one may be; they protect the man who is falling into the midst of an ocean of great calamity.
Having heard this highly meritorious hymn of praise to these Vināyakas, one shall never be afflicted by obstacles and shall be liberated even from sins. (18)
Having spoken thus, even the God of gods, his mind filled with great joy, was consecrated by Brahmā and the others, and having granted them their desired wishes, [he departed].
Having propitiated everyone as was appropriate, he, who was skilled in all that was fitting, entered the royal palace constructed by Viśvakarman.
Skanda said: Thus praised by the Blessed One, the God of gods, Vināyaka, the conqueror of obstacles, manifested himself in many forms in this manner.
O Pot-born One, by chanting these names of Ḍhuṇḍhirāja, a person shall obtain his own desired object.

O Divodāsa, we are even more blessed than those who are near you; yet they too are most blessed among mortals who proclaim your name.
Smiling again and again, the Brahmin sang while repeatedly shaking his head; inwardly thrilled as if greatly rejoiced, the hair on his body stood erect with delight.
Oh, what a rise of his fortune! Oh, what purity he possesses! For the Lord of the Universe, who is to be meditated upon by all, meditates upon him incessantly. (89)
Oh, the excellence of this person's future! No one can equal it; for that which is distant even for us is, for him, not far at all.
Having reflected in his heart and described the lord of the earth, the brahmin revealed all that he had perceived during his meditative absorption.
The Brāhmaṇa said: "O King, today the great tree of your desire has borne fruit; with this very body, you have gone to the supreme state. (92)
Just as Viśveśvara constantly contemplates you alone within his heart, so too does he regard us and others, O twice-born ones, whose eyes are fixed upon his feet.
Indeed, on the seventh day from today, a divine celestial chariot belonging to Śambhu shall arrive to take you away, once you have performed the consecration of the Liṅga.
"O King, you know for which meritorious deed this is the ripening; I understand it to be from your thorough service to the city of Vārāṇasī. (95)
O best of kings, even for one who protects but a single person staying here in Vārāṇasī, such is the ripening of the fruit at the end of the body.
Having heard this, the powerful royal sage Divodāsa, being pleased, granted the desired boon to the Brāhmaṇa and his disciples.
Then, having bowed down again and again to the Brahmin who was thus gratified, the king, filled with joy, said: "I have been rescued from the ocean of worldly existence."
The Brahmin too, his soul delighted and his desires fulfilled, took leave of the lord of the earth and departed for his own desired land.
Having surveyed Kāśī on all sides in the form of a Māyā-brāhmaṇa, Hari reflected again and again: "What here is most purifying? (200)
And by occupying this place, I shall lead all my devotees without exception to the supreme abode through the highest grace of Viśveśa.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, upon seeing the Pāñcanada lake, performed his ritual bath there and remained right there.
Waiting for a swift meeting with the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva), the Lord of Lakṣmī dispatched Tārkṣya, who was well-acquainted with the affairs of kings.
Divodāsa, the lord of kings, while praising the eminent brāhmaṇa, summoned all his subjects, along with his ministers and the regional lords.
He also gratified all the superintendents appointed over the treasury, horses, elephants, and so forth, as well as his five hundred sons and his eldest son, Samarañjaya.
The domestic priest, the doorkeeper, the officiating priests, the astrologers, the twice-born, the vassal lords, the princes, the cooks, and the physicians; || 6 ||
He also [saw] many foreigners who had gathered for various purposes, as well as Queen Sāṃtapurā and the elderly cowherds and boys.
With a joyful heart and palms joined in reverence, he spoke to them all exactly as that Brahmin had stated regarding his stay for a period of seven days.
While they were listening in amazement and with dejected faces, I myself took the prince to Rājagṛha and delighted him.
Having consecrated [him] and having gratified both the citizens and the people of the countryside, the king of great intelligence and meritorious soul returned once more to Kāśī. || 210 ||
Having arrived at Kāśī, that wise king Ripuñjaya caused a palace to be constructed on the western bank of the celestial river.
Having crushed his enemies in battle, that king constructed a temple of Śiva with as much wealth as he had acquired.
Since all the royal fortune (*bhūpālalakṣmī*) was bestowed upon her there, she became auspicious and was thereafter known as Bhūpālaśrī.
Having installed the Divodāseśvara Liṅga, King Ripuñjaya considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Then one day, after the king had worshipped that Linga according to the prescribed rites and paid homage to it, he began to offer praise to the bestower of satisfaction.
Then, from the expanse of the sky, a divine vehicle swiftly descended, surrounded on all sides by attendants holding tridents and skull-topped staffs in their hands.
With forehead-eyes possessing a brilliance exceeding that of the sun and fire, with matted locks, and with limbs resembling pure crystal, they illuminated the expanse of the sky.

[The serpents] were honored by their bodies with the light of the jewels on their hoods as their ornaments; their necks, which had once taken refuge in darkness, were now terrified by that eternal radiance. || 18 ||
Then the king was surrounded by hundreds of Rudra-maidens with yak-tail whisks held busy in their fingertips, as well as by his attendants adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
Filled with joy, they adorned him with divine silk garments and ornaments, making his noble forehead appear as if it had three eyes and his neck darkened.
Whose entire body was made exceedingly white, whose hair on the head was formed into matted locks, whose form was endowed with four arms, and who had adorned himself with serpents as ornaments.
The attendants led him, whose head was adorned with the crescent moon, to heaven.

From that time onwards, that sacred ford became known as Bhūpālaśrī; having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies there, and having given gifts according to one's capacity, [one attains merit]. || 23 ||
Having beheld Divodāseśvara and having worshipped him with devotion, and having heard the narrative of the king, a man shall not enter a womb again.
Having read or even caused others to read this purifying narrative of King Divodāsa, a person is liberated from sins.
Whoever enters into battle after hearing the auspicious narrative of Divodāsa shall never at any time experience fear caused by enemies. (26)
The meritorious story of Divodāsa, which cuts away great calamities, should be recited with effort for the pacification of all obstacles. (27)
There, no drought occurs, nor is there fear of untimely death; for there exists the story of Daivodāsa, which destroys all sins. (28)
By reading this narrative, one's desires will reach fulfillment just like those of Viṣṇu, who fulfills the thoughts of Śambhu. || 229 ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Nirvāṇa by Divodāsa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: O omniscient one, delighter of the heart, whose hair is kissed by Gaurī; O destroyer of Tāraka, six-faced one, savior, and doer of good! || 1 ||
Homage to you, the treasury of all knowledge, the son of the Omniscient One; homage to the Great-Souled Youth who has utterly conquered Māra. || 2 ||

Salutations to you, who, even as a youth, conquered Māra after beholding the Lord who is half-woman and half-man (Ardhanārīśvara), the crusher of the enemy of desire, and who was himself indeed made of desire.
O Skanda, as you have said, Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin through his illusory power (māyā), occupied the exceedingly purifying Pañcanada Tīrtha in Kāśī.
Among the regions of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, Kāśī is supremely purifying; even there, the supreme Pañcanada Tīrtha was recognized by Hari.
O Six-faced One, why is that sacred ford named Pañcanada, and why was it considered the supreme purifier among all sacred fords?
And how is it that the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the inner self and lord of the universe, is the protector, creator, and destroyer of all worlds by his divine play?

Though formless, he has entered into form; though unmanifest, he has attained manifestation. Though devoid of shape, he possesses shape; though free from conceptual proliferation, he partakes in proliferation.

You are unborn and yet possess many births; you bear no name and yet bear names clearly manifest; you are without support and yet the support of all; though devoid of qualities, you are the abode of all qualities.
Though devoid of senses, Janārdana is the lord of the senses; though without feet, he is omnipresent. Having withdrawn his own form, the all-pervading one [remained].
O Six-faced One, tell me this as you have heard it from the Five-faced One: how he remained at the supreme sacred ford of Pañcanada by means of his entire being.
Skanda said: Having paid homage to Maheśvara, I shall relate this narrative, which pacifies the flood of all sins and bestows all that is auspicious.
Just as the Pañcanada Tīrtha has attained renown at Kāśī, by the mere utterance of its name, sin is shattered into a thousand pieces.
And Prayāga, the lord of sacred fords, is himself personally present there, forcibly destroying the mass of sins of the wicked by means of his own splendor.
Indeed, all holy fords are surpassed by the power of Prayāga; all those holy fords [are present] during the month of Māgha when the sun is situated in Capricorn.
Every year, through the arrival at the King of Tīrthas, they shall become stainless; for Prayāga is the Lord of Tīrthas, and it removes the impurity deposited by all other Tīrthas.

The Lord of Tīrthas forcibly removes from the land of Pañcanada the great burden of the sins of the wicked; whatever flood of sin one accumulates throughout the year, that he certainly casts off by a single immersion in the month of Kārttika at Pañcanada.
Just as the Pañcanada originated, so shall I relate it; listen, O illustrious one, son of Mitra and Varuṇa. (18)
In ancient times, there was a sage named Vedaśiras, a man of great asceticism, born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, who was like another Veda incarnate. (19)
As that sage was performing penance, there appeared before his very eyes Śuci, the most excellent of the Apsarases, endowed with beauty and grace.
At the mere sight of her, the sage’s mind became deeply agitated; he emitted his seed immediately, and then that excellent apsaras was terrified.
Having offered salutations from afar, she addressed that sage, her limbs trembling violently out of fear of his curse, though she remained pure.
"I have committed no offense whatsoever, O treasure-house of most formidable asceticism; it must be forgiven by me, O support of forbearance, for ascetics are the very embodiment of forgiveness. (23)
O best of beings, the minds of sages are generally softer even than a lotus; women, however, are hard-hearted by their very nature.
Having heard these words of that pure Apsaras, the sage, by means of the bridge of discernment, stemmed the torrent of his great anger.
And with a serene soul, he said: "O pure one, you are certainly pure; for there is not even the slightest fault in me here, nor is there any fault in you, O beautiful lady. (26)

"The woman is of the nature of fire and the man is like butter; those who say they are ignorant [of this] speak thus because of a lack of reflection, for there is a great difference [between them]. (27)
Even wood from which the essence has been extracted becomes moist upon contact with fire; yet it is a marvel that a man, having taken up what is called "woman," becomes moist even from afar. 28.
Therefore, O Śuci, you need not fear, O Śuci who dwells in my mind; for it was I who stumbled because of you, who appeared unexpectedly.
The sage’s loss of ascetic power due to a lapse committed unintentionally was not as great as the loss caused by the enemy’s anger, which blinded him for a moment.
Through anger, the merit accumulated through great hardship goes to ruin, just as the light of the two suns is obscured upon encountering a mass of clouds.
Where is the flourishing of true goals when there is anger that brings about misfortune? And where is the growth of the virtuous when there is the exaltation of the wicked? (32)
When indignation drags the mind away, how can the mind-born [god of love] arise? When Rahu violently afflicts the moon, where is the moonlight?
Where could there be the existence of a tree of peace amidst the blazing forest fire of anger? Has anyone ever seen anywhere the security of a young elephant in the presence of a lion? (34)
Therefore, with every effort, the wise man should avoid that which is adverse and obstructive to the fourfold aims of the body. 35.
Now listen, O auspicious and pure lady, to that which must be done by you; for our seed is never in vain—therefore, accept this seed. (36)
When this vigor has been preserved and purified by your gaze, a single jewel of a maiden, exceedingly pure, shall belong to you from you. || 37 ||
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the Apsaras felt as if she were born again; saying, "This is a great favor," she swallowed the semen of the sage. (38)
Then, in due course of time, the celestial woman gave birth to a jewel of a daughter, who was exceedingly pleasing to the eyes and a treasure-house of the perfection of beauty. (39)
Having deposited her in that very hermitage of Vedaśiras, that purest of Apsarases departed as she desired.
And Vedaśiras nurtured that fawn-eyed maiden with affection, feeding her with the milk of a doe living in his own hermitage.
The sage gave her a meaningful name, Dhūtapāpā; by the mere utterance of that name, the multitude of sins trembles.
Richly adorned with the beauty of all the primary marks and beautiful in every limb, the sage did not leave her from his lap even for a single moment.
Beholding her increasing day by day, he rejoiced greatly, like one gazing upon the lovely digit of the moon in the night, which is as beautiful as the ocean of milk.
Then, seeing that eight-year-old girl, the lord of sages reflected, "To whom shall she be given? and questioned her very self.
Vedaśiras said: "O daughter, O highly fortunate one, O you whose sins are washed away, O lady of auspicious gaze! To which bridegroom shall I give you? You yourself tell me who that groom is."
Having heard these words spoken by her father, whose heart was moist with excessive affection, she, Dhūtapāpā, spoke with a downcast face.
Dhūtapāpa said: "O mother, if I am to be given by you to a noble and handsome husband, then bestow me upon him as I shall describe to you. (48)
And it pleases you as well, dear one; may your lordship listen attentively: he who is the most pure among all, and who is saluted by all. (49)
That which everyone desires, from which the arising of all happiness occurs, which never perishes, and which always persists—[that is this]. (50)
He who certainly protects [this] from the arising of great calamities both here and in the hereafter—for from him all desires indeed become completely fulfilled. (51)
And day by day, good fortune increases in the presence of him who serves [her] continuously; for one who performs her service without interruption, there is no fear anywhere.
Merely by uttering whose name some do not cause any obstruction, and upon whose support the fourteen worlds abide. (53)
"O father, bestow me upon that bridegroom who possesses such qualities as these and whose conduct is excellent; this will bring happiness to both me and them. (54)
Having heard this from her, she indeed attained great joy, thinking: "I am blessed; blessed are my ancestors, in whose lineage this daughter has appeared. (55)
For she whose intellect is of such a kind is surely steadfast and cleansed of sin; who indeed in this world could equal her in the weightiness of such a multitude of virtues? (56)
"Or else, how can he be obtained without the arising of a great mass of merit? Having thus composed his mind for a moment, that bull among sages—
Having examined him with wisdom as one in whom such excellent qualities arise, he spoke to the blessed maiden: "Listen, O child who desires what is auspicious. (58)
The father said: "O wise one, regarding these qualities which you have described as belonging to the bridegroom, it is certain that the bridegroom is the possessor of these qualities. (59)
Yet he is not easily obtained, nor is his form exceedingly beautiful; he is to be purchased at some marketplace of sacred fords by means of the price of asceticism. (60)
O maiden, he is easily attained through the weight of sacred fords, not through noble lineage, nor by the study of the Vedas and Shastras, nor indeed by the power of sovereignty. (61)
Neither by beauty of form, nor by intellect, nor by prowess, but solely through purity of mind and the conquest of the senses. || 62 ||
"Only through the aid of great austerity, joined with self-restraint, charity, and compassion, can that highly wise and worthy husband be obtained; not otherwise. (63)
Having heard this, the maiden then prostrated before her father and, having made her resolve, requested permission to practice asceticism.
Skanda said: Having received permission from her father, she performed supreme penance in that most holy field—a penance that is unattainable even for other ascetics.

Where is that girl with limbs so exceedingly tender, and where is such asceticism, which must be accomplished by a body hardened by hardship? Oh, how great is the fortitude of those with virtuous minds!
During the well-timed rains, accompanied by great winds and falling in torrents, she spent many nights on spacious rocky surfaces. (67)
Having heard the terrible roar of thunder and seen the flashes of lightning, she was moistened by the spray of the downpour, yet she did not tremble even slightly.
In the darkness of the penance grove, the lightning flashes repeatedly, as if it were coming and going to observe the state of that asceticism.
Indeed, Kumārī herself is performing penance here in the penance grove under the pretext of being a maiden, having surrounded herself with the five fires.
Though tormented by the five fires, that young woman, longing for water, did not drink even a single drop from the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Clad in a bodice of horripilation and with her garment trembling, she, emaciated by asceticism, spent the wintry nights.
In the nights of the cold season, partaking of the essence of the autumnal waters, she thought: "Who is this lotus-pond that has risen up today along with the cranes? (73)
In the springtime, which evokes passion even in the minds of the wise, the redness was stolen from her bud-like lips by the sprouts of Mākaṃda trees.
Dwelling in the forest during the spring, that young woman, whose mind was unshakable even while performing austerities, was captivated by the warbling of the cuckoo.
Having deposited, as it were, the luster of her lips in the bandhujīva flowers and the grace of her gait in the kalahamsa swans, she became devoted to ascetic penance in the autumn season.

Having cast off contact with enjoyments and adopted the way of life of those who possess them, this ascetic woman, whose sins have been shaken off, practices penance for the sake of awakening and suppressing her hunger.
Though emaciated by the hempen garment and the jewel-licking vine, her body attained a priceless state; nevertheless, though wasted by asceticism, that body of hers shone all the more brightly. (78)
Beholding her performing penance with a perfectly purified mind, Brahmā approached and said, "O woman of excellent wisdom, I am pleased; choose a boon."
Beholding the four-faced one seated upon his swan-vehicle, she, being delighted, bowed with joined palms and then addressed the Lord of Creatures.
Dhūtapāpā said: "O Grandfather, O bestower of boons, if a boon is to be granted to me, then make me more purifying than all other purifiers. (81)
Having heard that which was desired by her, the Creator, his mind exceedingly pleased, then replied to that pure girl who sought purity.
Brahmā said: O Dhūtapāpā, among all the purifying things that exist here everywhere, may you become incomparably more purifying than them by virtue of my boon.
O maiden, there are three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, each more purifying than the last.
"By my word, let all those sacred fords dwell within your body in reverse order; thus, become the purifier of all. (85)
Having spoken thus, the Creator vanished; she too, her impurities shaken off, reached the hut of her father Vedaśiras, now cleansed of sin.
Once, beholding her playing in the courtyard of the hermitage, Dharma, drawn by her ascetic power, made a request to the maiden.
Dharma said: "O lady of broad hips, large eyes, slender waist, and beautiful face! I have been purchased by you through the perfection of your own form; grant me privacy."
"O fair-eyed one, because of you, desire torments me intensely; that man of unknown name has repeatedly made his request. (89)
She said to him, "O evil-minded one, pray to my father, who is the giver; for this is the eternal Vedic injunction that a daughter is to be given away by her father. (90)
Having heard these words concerning a future matter, Dharma, out of respect for what was to come, again constrained her who possessed fortitude, though she was devoid of self-restraint.
Dharma said: "O fortunate one, O beautiful lady, I do not desire your father; do you fulfill my wish through the Gāndharva form of marriage. (92)
Having heard these persistent words, the young girl, wishing to grant her father the fruit of having a daughter, spoke again to that brahmin.
"O dull-witted one, do not speak thus again; go away from here! Though addressed in this way by the maiden, he, tormented by passion, did not desist.
Then the young woman, through the power of her intense asceticism, cursed him: "Since you are utterly dull-witted, become a river, a reservoir of water! (95)
Having been cursed thus by her, he, filled with rage, then cursed her in turn: "O hard-hearted one, you of wicked mind, become a stone! (96)
Skanda said: O Sage, by this mutual curse, Dharma became a river; in the great sacred field of Avimukta, he became renowned as the great Dharmanada.
Terrified, she too told her father the reason for her own stoniness; then the sage, having understood the matter through meditation, spoke to the maiden.
"Do not fear, daughter; I shall bring about everything auspicious for you. That curse cannot be otherwise: become a moonstone (caṃdrakānta-śilā)."
Then, upon the rising of the moon, her body having become liquefied, O virtuous daughter, she became a river known as Dhūtapāpā.
And that Dharmanada, O maiden, shall be your most excellent husband; his limbs are fully endowed with those very qualities which were sought by you.
Listen further, O one of virtuous intellect: by the power of my asceticism, you two shall come to possess a dual form—both solid and liquid.
Having thus consoled his daughter Dhūtapāpā, who had become like a moonstone (caṃdrakānta-śilā), the wise father, the scorcher of foes, showed her favor.
From that time on, O Sage, the lake in Kāśī became famous as Dharmanada; it is Dharma itself in liquid form, the destroyer of great sins. || 4 ||
