Then there is Vṛṣabhadhvaja-tīrtha, and after that the Paitāmaha-tīrtha; then the one called Gadādhara, and beyond that the Pitṛ-tīrtha.
Then indeed Kāpiladhāra, and again this Sudhākhanī; thereafter, this auspicious holy site known as Śivagayā is to be known. 64.
O grandfathers, these ten names of this sacred ford bring you satisfaction even without the performance of ancestral rites or libations.
Those who, desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, shall feed Brāhmaṇas at the conjunction of the sun and the moon, their Śrāddha rite shall be infinite.
Those who will give an auspicious tawny cow (kapilā) at a Śrāddha ceremony for the satisfaction of the ancestors, their host of ancestors shall dwell there on the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
By those who have performed the rite of releasing a bull at this sacred ford of Vārṣabhadhvaja, their ancestors have been gratified by the sacrificial cakes of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
O Grandfathers, at this sacred ford of Kapiladhārikā, on the new moon day joined with the moon, the merit of the śrāddha offerings is eight times that of Gayā.
For those whose miscarriage occurred in the womb and those who died before the eruption of teeth, there will surely be satisfaction at the Kāpiladhārika Tīrtha.
For those who have not received the gift of the *mauñjī* cord and for those who have not taken a wife, the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) offered here indeed attains imperishability for them.
Those who have died by fire, and those for whom there was no cremation by fire—all of them attain satisfaction at the Kapiladhārika Tīrtha.

Those who have been deprived of the funeral rites for the deceased and those who have been excluded from the sixteen śrāddhas attain satisfaction through the offering of libations poured into a stream of clarified butter.
Even those who have died childless, for whom there is no one to offer the funeral water libation, attain supreme satisfaction when they are satiated at Madhusravas.
For those who have indeed died an untimely death through thieves, lightning, water, and so forth, a Śrāddha performed here for them results in the granting of a good rebirth.
Even those wicked men who meet their end here by committing suicide obtain satisfaction through the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) offered at Śivagayā.
For those who have died in the paternal lineage and those who have died on the maternal side, the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered here shall grant them inexhaustible satisfaction.
Those who have indeed died among the circle of wives and those who have died among the circle of friends—all of them attain satisfaction when they are gratified before the Bull-bannered Lord. (78)
Whether they belong to the lineages of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, or to the Śūdra lineage or among the lowest castes—by uttering their names here, those to whom gifts are given are uplifted.
Those who have indeed died in the animal womb, or those who have attained the state of a piśāca—they too attain an upward course when they are satisfied at Kāpiladhārika. (80)
But those ancestors in this world of men who are of mortal birth shall indeed become of divine birth when they are satiated at Madhusravas.
Those ancestors who, through their merits, attained the status of gods in the divine world, go to the world of Brahmā, being satisfied at the Vṛṣadhvaja Tīrtha.

In the Kṛta age it is a holy ford consisting of milk; in the Tretā age, moreover, it is full of honey; in the Dvāpara age it is filled with clarified butter; and in the Kali age, it becomes composed of water.
This auspicious Tīrtha should be known as being outside the sacred boundary (sīmā), yet it is the most excellent within Vārāṇasī for men due to my presence there. (84)
"Since the banner marked with the signs of a ram and a bull was seen by those residing in Kāśī, I shall therefore remain here by the name Vṛṣadhvaja, O Grandfathers."
Accompanied by the Grandfather (Brahmā) and joined by Gadādhara (Viṣṇu), together with Ravi and his attendants, [may he come] for your satisfaction, O Grandfathers.
While the bull-bannered Lord was thus granting boons to the ancestors, the river approached, prostrated before the Lord, and made this request: || 87 ||
Nandikeśvara said: "Let the chariot be prepared and ready; let there be the emergence of victory, wherein eight lions and eight auspicious bulls are stationed."
Where eight elephants shine, where there are eight swift horses, where the reins are the controller of the mind, and where the whip is held in hand. (89)
The wind-god fashioned the two wheels from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; the pure celestial sphere, O Māyā, became the parasol at dawn and dusk.
The spikes are composed of the Tārāvalīs; the Upāyikas are the serpents; the Śrutis are the guides of the path; and the Smṛtis are the protections of the chariot. || 91 ||
Where the southern pole is firm, where the sacrifices are the protectors, where the seat is the Praṇava, and where the Gāyatrī is the footstool; || 92 ||
Where the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis) along with their auxiliary parts serve as auspicious flights of stairs, and where the sun and moon are the constant guardians of the gate.
Agni was the makara-head of the chariot, and the ground of the chariot was composed of moonlight; Mount Mahāmeru was the flagpole, and the banner possessed the radiance of the sun.
Where the Goddess of Speech herself stands, holding a waving fly-whisk; Skanda said: Thus addressed by Śailādi, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, [spoke]. 95.
After the rite of lustration (nīrājana) had been performed by the eight divine mothers, the wielder of the Pināka bow rose up, with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow placing his hand upon him as support.
The sound of divine musical instruments filled the heaven and earth, further augmented by the Cāraṇas with songs of auspicious hymns.
With the quarters of the sky deafened by that divine sound, the inhabitants of all the worlds arrived from every direction as if they had been summoned. || 98 ||
There are thirty-three crores of gods, two hundred and ninety million Gaṇas, nine crores of Cāmuṇḍās, and one crore of Bhairavīs. (99)
And the six-faced Kumāras, mounted upon excellent peacocks, followed me; eight crores of them, possessed of great strength, arrived as my attendants.
Seven crores of elephant-faced deities arrived, their trunks throbbing as they held axes in their hands; they were pot-bellied, possessed of great speed, and the destroyers of obstacles. || 1 ||
Eighty-six thousand sages who discourse on Brahman, as well as householders from that region, also assembled there.
There were thirty million nāgas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, and twenty million dānavas and daityas who had Śiva as their soul.
There were eight million Gandharvas, fifty million Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, and twelve thousand Vidyādharas.
Likewise, there were sixty thousand auspicious divine apsarases, eight hundred thousand Gomātṛs, and sixty thousand Suparṇas.
The seven oceans arrived, bestowing various kinds of jewels and gifts; and there were thirty-five thousand rivers as well.
Eight thousand mountains, three hundred lords of the forest, and the eight elephants of the quarters came to where the god who wields the Pināka bow resided.
Accompanied by these, satisfied and being praised from all sides, Śrīkaṇṭha mounted his chariot and entered the supreme city of Kāśī.
That three-eyed one, the son of the Lord of Mountains, the abode of joys and the mine of delights, gazed with great joy upon Kāśī, which was as magnificent as heaven itself.
Skanda said: Having heard this meritorious narrative, which destroys the sins of ten million births, and having read it or caused it to be read, one shall attain union with Śiva.
This should be recited with special effort, particularly at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony; thus the Śrāddha becomes inexhaustible and brings supreme satisfaction to the ancestors.
By reciting the majesty of Vṛṣabhadhvaja in the presence of Śiva every day for the duration of a year, even one who is sonless shall indeed become possessed of sons.
That entry into Kāśī which has been proclaimed for the Lord of the Universe is certainly the seed of the root of supreme bliss. 13.
Whoever enters a new house after reciting this joyful narrative shall indeed become an abode of all happiness; of this there is no doubt. || 14 ||
This supreme narrative generates joy for the three worlds; by the mere hearing of it, the Lord of the Universe becomes well-pleased. (15)
For the King has indeed attained here that supreme gain which is unattainable; therefore, let this excellent narrative known as "The Entry into Kāśī" be recited. 116.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vṛṣabhadhvaja," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: O destroyer of Tāraka, tell me what was done by the Enemy of Tripura after he beheld Kāśī—the delight of the eyes—which had been attained through many long-cherished desires.

Skanda said: O Lord of the chaste wives, O Agastya, listen; I shall tell you everything in its entirety. Kāśī, which causes longing even for the one marked by the deer (the Moon), has been made a guest of my eyes. || 2 ||
Then the Lord of the Omniscient, whose heart is compassionate toward his devotees, beheld Jaigīṣavya, the best of sages, standing within the cave.
Beginning from Yamanaha, he proceeded toward Mount Mandra, together with Rudra—who was mounted upon the lord of bulls—and the daughter of the king of mountains.
O Pot-born one, on that very day, the highly intelligent and great-souled Jaigīṣavya took up a firm vow.
"When shall I behold again the lotus-feet of the Three-Eyed One? Then, alas, I shall consume even a single drop of water [from them]. (6)
O Sage, due to the power of concentration from some source, or perhaps through the grace of Śambhu, the yogi Jaigīṣavya remained there without eating or drinking.
Śambhu alone knows it; no one else knows it at all. For this very reason, the Lord of the Pramathas first obtained it from him.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when it falls on a Monday and under the asterism Anurādhā, a great procession (mahāyātrā) should be performed there by human beings on that festival day.
Then, in Kāśī, that place of Jyeṣṭha also became a bestower of merit; there, a Liṅga manifested itself, known by the name Jyeṣṭheśvara.
Upon seeing that Liṅga, the sin of men accumulated over hundreds of births perishes in that very instant, just as darkness vanishes upon the rising of the sun.
Having bathed in the Jyeṣṭhavāpī and offered libations to his ancestors, and having beheld Jyeṣṭheśvara, a man is not born again on this earth.
Gaurī, the bestower of all perfections, the most excellent Jyeṣṭhā, manifested herself there in every direction in the vicinity of Jyeṣṭheśvara. || 13 ||
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, a great festival should be celebrated there; a vigil should be kept at night for the sake of the increase of all prosperity.
Having bowed to Jyeṣṭhā-Gaurī and bathed in the Jyeṣṭha-vāpī, a woman shall become a vessel of good fortune, and even a man shall partake in good fortune.
Since Śambhu himself made his dwelling in that place, the supreme Liṅga there is therefore renowned as Nivāseśa.
By the service of the Nivāseśvara Liṅga, all riches dwell constantly in the home, indeed at every single step. || 17 ||
Having performed the Śrāddha according to the prescribed rite at Jyeṣṭhasthāna, that best of men surely grants supreme satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
By giving gifts according to his ability at Jyeṣṭha-tīrtha in Kāśī, a man attains the highest heavens and goes to liberation.
Jyeṣṭheśvara should be worshipped first in Kāśī by men seeking their own welfare; thereafter, Jyeṣṭhā-Gaurī should be worshipped by those desiring the highest of all forms of excellence.
Then Dhūrjaṭi, that treasure-house of compassion, having summoned Nandin, spoke these words while all the gods were listening: ||| 21 ||
Īśvara said: O Śailāda, enter quickly; there is a captivating cave here, and within it dwells my devotee Jaigīṣavya, whose wealth is his asceticism.
"Bring here my devotee who observes the great vow, whose skin, bones, and sinews alone remain, and who is firm in his resolve for the sight of me. (23)
From the time I went from Kāśī to the all-beautiful Mandara mountain, he has remained observant of great vows and has abstained from food ever since.
"Take this playful lotus, which nourishes with nectar; touch his limbs with it immediately, for it is a source of great growth."
Then Nandī, taking that play-lotus of the Lord and bowing to the God of gods, entered the deep cave.
Then Nandī, seeing him there with a mind firm through concentration, his limbs withered by the fire of austerity, touched him with his lotus hand.
Like a frog in a hollow at the end of the heat through contact with rain, that lord of yogis leaped up from the mere touch of that lotus-born one.
Then Nandī, taking up that bull among sages with haste, prostrated at the feet of the God of gods and set him down.
Then Jaigīṣavya, filled with wonder upon seeing Śaṅkara before him with the Daughter of the Mountain seated on his left side, prostrated himself.
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and rolled about on all sides, that sage praised the moon-crested Lord with supreme devotion.
Jaigīṣavya said: Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the omniscient, the auspicious-souled; to the root of the world’s joy, the cause of supreme bliss. (32)
To the formless one, to the one with form, and to the bearer of manifold forms; to Virūpākṣa, to the Ordainer, and to the one praised by Brahmā and Viṣṇu. || 33 ||
Salutations to you who are the stationary; salutations to you who are the moving. Salutations to you, the soul of all; salutations to you, the supreme soul.
Salutations to the one desired by the three worlds, and to the one who burns away the limbs of desire; salutations to you, the excellence of all that remains, and to you whose limbs are the remnants.
Salutations to you, O Śrīkaṇṭha; salutations to you, whose throat bears the poison. Salutations to him whose feet are worshipped by Vaikuṇṭha, and who possesses unimpeded power.
Salutations to the one whose body is half Śakti, who is bodiless yet possesses a beautiful body, and who, by a single prostration alone, prevents the embodiment of embodied beings.
To Kāla, to the Death of Death, to the consumer of the Kālakūṭa poison; to him who has a serpent for a sacred thread, to the wearer of serpents as ornaments. || 38 ||
Salutations to you, O wielder of the broken axe; salutations to the bearer of the severed head; salutations to the one who has destroyed all suffering, and to the bearer of the sword and shield.

To the Lord whose praises are sung by the gods, who wears the surging waves of the Gaṅgā as a garland, the Lord of Gaurī, the Lord of the Mountains, the Dweller on the Mountain, who sports in mountain caves.

Salutations to you who are adorned with the pure crescent moon, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; salutations to you who wear a hide as a garment, salutations to you who have the directions as your clothing.

Salutations to you, the Lord of the World, who has transcended old age, who removes both decay and birth; salutations to you, the Life-giver, who takes away the repetitive chanting of those who mutter prayers.
Homage to you who hold the hand-drum; homage to you who hold the bow. Homage to you, the three-eyed one; homage to you, the eye of the world. 43.
Salutations to the one who holds a trident in his hand, the bearer of the triple-pathed river (Ganges), the sovereign lord of the three heavens, and the one praised by the three Vedas. || 44 ||

Salutations to you who consist of the three Vedas, to you who are satisfied, and to you who bestow satisfaction upon your devotees; salutations to you, the initiated one, salutations to you, the God of gods.
Salutations to you, the far-sighted one, who has torn asunder all sins; salutations to the distant one, difficult to attain, and the destroyer of faults.
O source of faults, O holder of the digits [of the moon], and to you who have abandoned the arrival of defects—salutations to you, Dhūrjaṭi, who are fond of the Dhattūra flower.
Homage to the steadfast Dharma, homage to you, the protector of Dharma; O Blue-necked One, homage to you; homage to you, O Blue-and-Red One. 48.
O you who fulfill the sovereignty of the three worlds for those who merely remember your name, homage to the Lord of the Pramathas, whose hand wields the Pināka bow! 49.
Salutation to the Lord of the bound souls (Paśus), for the sake of liberating them from their bonds; to Him who removes even the greatest sins by the mere utterance of His name. (50)

Salutations to the one who is higher than the highest, the further shore, and the supreme beyond both the high and the low; salutations to the one whose conduct is boundless and whose story is most purifying.

Salutations to Vāmadeva, who bears the beautiful left half [of the body], who rides upon the bull; salutations to Bharga, to the Terrible One, and to the remover of the fear of those who bow before him. || 52 ||
Salutation to the one who brings about existence and the destruction of existence, the Lord of all beings; O Mahādeva, salutations to you, O Maheśa, O Lord of splendors! 53.
Salutations to the Lord of Mṛḍānī; salutations to you, the conqueror of death. Salutations to you, the enemy of sacrifice, and to the beloved of the king of Yakṣas.
To the one who frequently performs sacrifices, to the sacrifice itself, to the bestower of the fruits of sacrifices, to Rudra, to the Lord of Rudras, to the auspicious Rudra, and to Rama. || 55 ||
Salutations be to you, the trident-bearer, the eternal Lord, who wanders through the cremation grounds, who is dear to Śivā, the destroyer Śarva, and the omniscient one.

Salutations to you, the destroyer, whose form is forbearance, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the creator of patience, the embodiment of forgiveness, the remover of the earth, and who is as white as milk. || 57 ||
Salutations to you who are in darkness, and who are devoid of beginning and end; to the Lord who is the support of the *iḍā* [vital breath], and who is praised by Upendra and Indra.
Salutations to you, the beloved of Umā, the fierce one, whose vital energy flows upwards; to the one who is both singular in form and alone, and whose nature is great sovereignty.
Salutations to you, the performer of infinite deeds, the Lord of Ambikā; you indeed are the syllable Oṃ, the Vaṣaṭ-call, and you are truly Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
O Mādhava, whatever exists here, whether visible or invisible, all that is you; I do not know how to offer praise, for you alone are the one who praises.
You are the expressed, you are the expresser, and you are speech itself; I bow down to you. O Mahādeva, I know no other; O Maheśvara, I praise no other.
O Lord of Gaurī, I bow to no other; O Śiva, I utter no other name. I am mute in pronouncing the names of others, and deaf in hearing the talk of others. (53)
"I am lame in approaching another and blind in looking toward another; O Lord, you alone exist, for you alone are the sole doer. (64)
You alone are the protector and the destroyer; diversity is but the imagination of the deluded. Therefore, you alone are my refuge—again and again, over and over. (65)
"O Maheśvara, lift me up who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra! Having thus praised Maheśāna, the great sage Jaigīṣavya—
"Restraining his speech before Sthāṇu, he stood motionless like a pillar. Having heard this praise from the sage, the moon-crested Lord, with a gracious soul, said to that sage, "Choose a boon."
Jaigīṣavya said: "If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, then [grant that] from your lotus feet, O Bhavānīśa, giver of distant stations, may I not be far away."
And another boon, O Lord, should be granted by you without hesitation: may you be present there where this linga has been installed by me. (69)
Īśvara said: O Jaigīṣavya, O highly fortunate one, O sinless one, let all that which has been requested by you be so; I grant you another boon as well.
I have bestowed upon you this Yoga-śāstra, which brings about liberation; indeed, may you become a master of yoga among all yogins. (71)
O you whose wealth is asceticism, through my grace you shall come to know the secret of the science of yoga exactly as it is, by which you will attain liberation.
Just like the river, just like the female bee, and just like Somanandin, you shall become my devotee, freed from old age and death.
There are many vows, there are various kinds of observances; there are diverse austerities here, and gifts are manifold. (74)
In this matter, the means for attaining the highest good are in every way destroyers of sin; indeed, supreme and most excellent is this very vow which has been undertaken by you.
For this is indeed a supreme rule: that which is eaten after beholding me; whereas that which is eaten without beholding me is eaten as mere sin alone. (76)
And that fool who eats even leaves, flowers, or fruits without first offering them [to the deity] shall become a consumer of semen for twenty-one births.
Indeed, compared to this great discipline practiced by you, other disciplines and restraints do not merit even a sixteenth part.
Therefore, you shall dwell in every way in the vicinity of Maccaraṇa; thus, you will certainly attain the glory of supreme liberation right there.
The Liṅga named Jaigīṣavyeśvara in Kāśī is very difficult to attain; by serving it for three years, one shall obtain Yoga, without a doubt. (80)
Having reached the cave of Jaigīṣavya and being intent on the practice of yoga, one shall obtain the desired perfection within six months through my grace. 81.
This Linga of yours should be worshipped with great effort by devotees, and this beautiful cave should be visited by those desiring supreme perfection. (82)
In this field of Jyeṣṭheśvara, your Liṅga bestows all perfections; when seen, touched, or worshipped, it destroys the multitude of sins.
In this sacred field of Jyeṣṭheśvara, by properly feeding even a single Śiva-yogin, one obtains the merit equivalent to feeding ten million.
The Jaigīṣavyeśvara Liṅga must be guarded with great effort, especially from those of defiled intellect in the Kali age. || 85 ||
"O ascetic, I shall maintain my presence here in this liṅga forever, for the sake of bestowing the perfection of yoga upon practitioners. (86)
Listen, O highly fortunate one, Jaigīṣavya, I grant you another boon: this supreme hymn which has been composed by you brings about the perfection of yoga. (87)
It pacifies the flood of great evils, increases great merit, allays great fears, and augments great devotion. || 88 ||

For men, there is nothing whatsoever that is unattainable through the recitation of this hymn; therefore, it should be recited with every effort by those who are well-established in their practice. 4 || 89 ||
Having thus granted him the boon, the enemy of Smara, with eyes smiling, beheld the Brahmins dwelling in that sacred field who had assembled there.
Skanda said: Having heard this incomparable narrative with diligence, a wise mortal becomes free from sin and is no longer afflicted by calamities.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Jyeṣṭheśa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: O Six-faced One, having seen Śambhu, what did the earthly deities (Bhūdevatās) say? And what are the various Liṅgas there? Tell me those as well.
O Six-faced One, tell us what wonder occurred there at that time in the most meritorious abode of Jyeṣṭha, which is dear to the God of gods?
Skanda said: Listen, O Agastya, to that which you have asked; I shall tell it to you. When the Lord went to Mount Mandara out of reverence for Brahmā, [he spoke]. || 3 ||
Then, O brahmins, those sinless ones who had renounced their homes for the sacred field were rendered destitute, as they were incessantly deprived of the acceptance of gifts from that great field.
O Sage, those who subsisted on roots and other such things dug the earth repeatedly with the tips of their staffs and created a beautiful lotus pond known as Daṇḍakhātā.
Having established numerous great liṅgas all around that sacred bathing place, they, intent on the worship of Maheśa, performed penance with great effort.
They constantly wear sacred ashes, they constantly wear rudrākṣa beads, they are always devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, and they constantly recite the Śatarudriya.
O Sage, having heard of the return of the God of gods, they—already emaciated by their austerities—became exceedingly overflowing with joy.
Five thousand twice-born ones, performing extensive penance, came from the great holy site of Daṇḍakhāta to behold the God.
O twice-born ones, ten thousand ascetics observing the Pāśupata vow, who were solely devoted to the worship of Śiva, gathered from the sacred ford named Mandākinī.
Ten thousand three hundred were obtained from Haṃsatīrtha, and eleven hundred more from Durvāsas’s Tīrtha.
Indeed, six thousand [brahmins] came from Matsyodarī, and seven hundred brahmins arrived from Kapālamocana.
O Sage, from the holy ford of Ṛṇamocana, more than twelve hundred [brahmins] were liberated; and from Vaitaraṇī as well, fifty thousand brahmins were saved.
Then, from the Pṛthūdaka pool which had been excavated by Pṛthu, thirteen hundred brahmins departed.
In the same way, two hundred Apsarases were obtained from the pool named after Menakā, and one thousand two hundred from the pool of Urvaśī. || 15 ||
Likewise, from the Airāvata-kuṇḍa, three hundred Brāhmaṇas, seven hundred Gandharvas, and two hundred Apsarases [emerged]. || 16 ||
Three hundred and ninety arrived from the Vṛṣeśa Tīrtha; one thousand three hundred reached from the Yakṣiṇī Kuṇḍa. (17)
O best of the twice-born, from Lakṣmītīrtha they proceeded further for sixteen hundred yojanas, and from Piśācamocana for seven thousand.
From Pitṛkuṇḍa there are more than a hundred; from Dhruvatīrtha there are six hundred; and from the lake named Mānasa there are three hundred and two.
O twice-born ones, ten thousand Brāhmaṇas came from the Vāsuki-hrada, and likewise eight hundred came from the Jānakī-kuṇḍa to behold [the Lord].
They reached Kāśīnātha, who bestows supreme bliss; likewise, nine hundred arrived from Gautama-kuṇḍa.
From that holy ford which destroys miserable rebirths, eleven hundred Brahmins set out to behold the Lord who is the consort of Umā.
O Pot-born One, the twice-born residing on the banks of the Gaṅgā, starting from Asīsaṃbheda and extending there to Āsaṃgameśvara, have arrived at that place.
Eighteen thousand and five hundred Brāhmaṇas, as well as fifty-five, arrived from the banks of the Gaṅgā.

With Brāhmaṇas who held fresh dūrvā grass and unbroken rice in their hands, who carried flowers and fruits in their palms, who bore fragrant garlands, and who were proclaiming cries of victory; || 25 ||
Praised with hymns of auspiciousness and prostrated to again and again, Śambhu granted them freedom from fear and joyfully inquired after their welfare.
Then those brahmins, with their hands joined in a gesture of reverence, said: "O Lord, for those dwelling in this sacred field, may there always be the arising of well-being through Your gifts. (27)
We have especially brought you directly within the range of our vision—you whose true nature the Vedas do not know in its ultimate reality. (28)
Unwholesome is it always for those who turn their backs on your field; indeed, even all fourteen worlds are eternally turned away from them. (29)
O Tāśīviṣāgada, for those in whose hearts Kāśī always resides, the poison of the serpent of saṃsāra shall never prevail against them anywhere.
The mantra consisting of two syllables of Kāśī is the jewel that protects the fetus; for him in whose throat it always resides, whence could there be any misfortune? (31)
He who constantly drinks the nectar consisting of the two syllables of Kāśī, having abandoned the state of old age, becomes nectar itself. || 32 ||
He by whom the two syllables "Kā-śī," which are nectar for the ears, have been heard, shall never again hear the story of birth in a womb. (33)
Even a particle of dust from Kāśī that might fall upon one's head, driven by the wind, would cause that head to become like the head of Candraśekhara, marked by the crescent moon.
Even by chance, if Ānandakānana comes within the range of your vision, those who go there shall not be born again, nor shall they behold the realm of the ancestors.
Whether walking or standing, sleeping or waking, he by whom this great mantra "Kāśī" has been recited becomes free from fear. (36)
For one who holds in the heart the pair of seed-syllables "kā-śī," indeed, the seeds of karma become truly seedless.
For one whose state of being consists in the constant chanting of "Kāśī, Kāśī, Kāśī," liberation shines forth before them even if they are elsewhere. 38.

This Kāśī is the embodiment of security; you, O Bhava, are the embodiment of security; and the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) is the embodiment of security—nowhere else is there this triad of security. (39)
Having heard these words of the Brahmins, which were amplified by their devotion to the sacred field, Hara, the beloved of Girijā, was exceedingly pleased.
And with a serene soul, he said: "Blessed are you, O bulls among the twice-born, who possess such devotion here in my most purifying field. (41)

I know that they have become composed of pure being (*sattva*) through the cultivation of this field; free from passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), they have reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Those who are devotees of Vārāṇasī are certainly my devotees; they are indeed liberated while living, truly graced by the side-glances of the Goddess of Liberation. (43)
And by those who have provoked even a single creature residing in Kāśī, the entire earth has indeed been provoked by them along with me. (44)
Whoever hears even the praise of Vārāṇasī and rejoices in it has, for certain, rejoiced in the entire cosmic egg. (45)
Indeed, those mortals who dwell in this Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana) shall dwell within my own heart, free from all taint.
I teach only those who dwell in my field, who practice devotion to me, and who bear my liṅga.
Those who dwell in my field but do not practice devotion to me, even though they bear my emblem—I do not instruct them.
Those in whose hearts Kāśī, the city of liberation, shines forth, appear resplendent before me, enveloped in the glory of supreme beatitude.
Those to whom this Kaśī, the glory of liberation, does not appeal, while they long for the glory of heaven—they have fallen; of this there is no doubt. (50)
O twice-born ones, by my grace, the four aims of human life shall stand before those who desire them, like servants. (51)
For here in Ānandakānana, I am a blazing forest fire; I incinerate the seeds of karma of living beings so that they do not sprout.
One must dwell constantly in Kāśī, worship me with great effort, conquer the Kali age and Time itself, and take pleasure in the maiden that is liberation.
Even having reached Kāśī, if one of wicked intellect does not serve me, the glory of absolute liberation (kaivalya), though already within his grasp, quickly perishes.
Blessed are the Brahmins dwelling in Kāśī, who bear the marks of devotion to me; for you, neither I nor Kāśī are beyond the reach of the mind's inclination.
"A boon must be granted to you; choose from me whatever you desire, since you, my beloved ones, have performed the renunciation of this field. (56)
Having thus drunk the nectar born from the milk-ocean of Maheśāna’s mouth, all the twice-born were completely satiated and chose an unsurpassed boon.
The Brahmins said: "O Lord of Umā, O Maheśāna, O Omniscient One, this is our boon: Kāśī must never be abandoned by you, O remover of the affliction of worldly existence. (58)
By the word of the Brahmins, may the curse of any of them never have power here in Kāśī to create an obstacle to liberation at any time. (59)
May we have unwavering devotion toward the pair of your lotus-like feet; and may we dwell in Kāśī day and night until the fall of our bodies.
O Lord, what need is there for any other boon? This alone should indeed be granted to us: O destroyer of Andhaka, take heed; we choose no other boon. (61)
"Since we, permeated by devotion to you, have established these lingas as your representatives, may your presence abide here. (62)
Having heard their words, the wielder of the Pināka bow said, "So be it," and granted them another boon as well: "Knowledge shall also be yours."
The Lord of the Gods spoke again: "Listen, O twice-born ones! I shall tell you what is for your benefit; let that certainly be carried out."

The river flowing northward should be constantly resorted to, and the Linga should be worshipped with great effort; self-restraint, charity, and compassion must always be practiced by those who desire liberation.
This very secret has been told to the inhabitants of the sacred field: one's mind should be intent on the welfare of others, and one should not utter words that cause distress.
In this matter, even in thought, one who desires victory must not perform [forbidden acts]; for whatever is done here—whether virtuous or otherwise—is inexhaustible.
Whatever sin has been committed elsewhere perishes in Kāśī; a sin committed in Vārāṇasī perishes within the Antargeha.
Sin committed within the inner quarters leads to the state of a Piśāca and to hell; even if one goes outside, the attainment of the Piśāca state and hell certainly follows.
Karma committed at Kāśī is not effaced even by ten million eons; rather, one is born here as a Rudra-piśāca for thirty thousand years.
He who indeed dwells in Vārāṇasī, even if he is always devoted to sinful acts, shall obtain a Piśāca birth for thirty thousand years. (71)
Furthermore, dwelling right here, he shall attain unsurpassed knowledge; once that knowledge has been fully attained, he will obtain unsurpassed liberation. (72)
Having committed evil deeds here and then met their death outside [the city], I shall describe their destination; listen, O best of the twice-born! (73)
My hosts known as the Yāmas are terrible and of deformed appearance; they first blow upon those who have committed evil deeds against the sacred field within a crucible.
Then they lead them toward the eastern region, which is mostly marshy and difficult to traverse; during the rainy season, they cast those of evil conduct into the great waters.
They are bitten day and night by winged leeches, water-born serpents, and mosquitoes that are difficult to ward off.
Then, during the winter season, they were led by the Yāmas to Mount Himālaya; deprived of food and shelter, they were tormented day and night.
Then, in a desert region devoid of water and trees during the summer, those who were thirsty were scorched by the intense rays of the sun.
Afflicted on all sides by fierce hosts and by torments, they are led here after having spent such an incalculable period of time.
Then those Yāmas report them in the presence of Kālarāja; and Kālarāja, having seen them, causes them to remember their evil deeds.
He also forcibly unites them with other Rudra-piśācas—those who are naked, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and whose backs and bellies are covered with skin.
Then those Rudra-piśācas, the constant attendants of Bhairava, endure excessive exhaustion arising from hunger, thirst, and ferocity. (82)
Occasionally they obtain food mixed with blood; thus, for a period numbering thirty thousand years, they remain there in extreme misery.
Bound by nooses around their necks, they are led all around the pillars of the cremation ground; though they are parched with thirst, they do not obtain even the touch of water. (84)
Then, their sins being completely exhausted by the sight of Kālabhairava, they become embodied beings right here and are liberated by my command. (85)
Therefore, one should not desire anything here, even through speech, mind, or action, O destroyer of evil; those who desire great gain should always abide on the pure path. 86.
No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell; having obtained my grace, he surely attains the supreme goal.
My devotee who, firm in his vows, practices fasting here in this world, shall not return again even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Knowing this human condition to be impermanent and full of many evils, one should always resort to Avimukta, which grants liberation from the fear of saṃsāra. 89.
I see no other means for living beings in the Kali age to pacify all their sins as an expiation than the city of Vārāṇasī.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of previous births, all of that goes to destruction for one who has entered Avimukta.
That which a yogi might attain by practicing through thousands of other births, that supreme liberation is reached here and now, even beyond death.
Even those beings born in the animal realm who have made liberation their abode reach the supreme goal when they meet their end in due time. || 93 ||
Those fools, shrouded in darkness, who do not resort to Avimukta, dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen.
Having reached Avimukta, the wise person who installs a linga shall not undergo rebirth even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
The falling of planets, lunar mansions, and stars is certain to occur in time; however, for those who have died in Avimukta, no such falling exists at all.
A man who, having committed the murder of a Brahmin, later casts off his life-breaths at Kāśī with a restrained mind, is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (97)
O Brahmins, those women who are devoted to their husbands and absorbed in devotion to me, when they die at Avimukta, attain the supreme goal.
O best of the twice-born, at the time of departure from this world, I myself shall impart the Tāraka Brahman, by which the embodied soul becomes one with That. (99)
One who has me as their mind, is my devotee, and has dedicated all their actions to me—such a person attains liberation here in this world in a way that cannot be attained anywhere else. 100.
Knowing that death is certain and that the destination [after death] is of an unpleasant nature, and that everything is unstable and adventitious, one should therefore take refuge in Kāśī. || 1 ||
The glory of liberation shall take refuge here in those of stainless intellect who have resorted to Kāśī through the actions of their mind, speech, and body.
Whoever gratifies even a single person residing in Kāśī with wealth acquired through righteous means, by him the entire three worlds, together with me, have been gratified.
O Brāhmaṇas, I always please that meritorious soul who delights the man for the city of Nirvāṇa by means of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
The royal sage Divodāsa also, while protecting Kāśī with righteousness, attained my abode in his very body, from which there is no return.
In this place, yoga as well as knowledge and liberation are attained in a single lifetime; therefore, having reached Vimukta, one should not go to another penance grove.
Knowing liberation to be extremely difficult to attain and cyclic existence to be most terrifying, one should strike one's feet with a stone and await the time for death right here.
When those of wicked intellect depart, abandoning Avimukta, then all beings will laugh at one another, striking their palms together.
Having reached the meritorious Vārāṇasī, the unsurpassed field of spiritual perfection, what living being would have the mind to depart elsewhere? || 9 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained by men elsewhere through great acts of charity, that is attained by giving even a single kārṣāpaṇa at Avimukta.
One person may worship a single liṅga, while another may perform austerities; between those two, he who worships the liṅga here is the superior one.
He who bestows ten million cows according to the prescribed rites at another sacred site, and he who should dwell for even a single day in Kāśī—the resident of Kāśī is superior to those two.
Whatever fruit is obtained by feeding ten million Brahmins elsewhere, that same fruit is attained in Vārāṇasī by feeding just one.
At Sannihatya in Kurukṣetra, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, alms received in Kāśī shall be equal to the gift of one's weight in gold (tulāpuruṣa-dāna).
Here, my supreme light, assuming the form of a Liṅga, stands established from the netherworld (Pātāla) upwards, transcending the seven worlds and extending to infinity.
Even those who remember my Liṅga Avimukta, even at the end of the earth, are certainly liberated from their great sins. (16)
But those in this field who have not seen me, touched me, or worshipped me—even after attaining the saving knowledge (tāraka-jñāna), they are born again. || 17 ||
Whoever worships me here and dies elsewhere, even in another birth, shall attain me and become liberated.
Having thus spoken of the greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra) before the twice-born, Hara vanished right there while they were looking on.
Having directly beheld Virūpākṣa with their own eyes, those Brahmins, their minds exceedingly delighted, departed for their respective abodes.
Having fully resolved upon the words of Śambhu, the omniscient storehouse of compassion, the brahmins abandoned all other duties and worshipped only the Liṅgas.
Skanda said: Having read and having caused others to read this supreme narrative of the secret, the faithful person, liberated from sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Secrets of the Sacred Field," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, the five thousand liṅgas that surround Jyeṣṭheśvara are fully capable of bestowing spiritual perfection upon sages.
The great Parāśareśvara Liṅga is located to the north of Jyeṣṭheśa; by the mere sight of it, stainless knowledge is attained.
In that very place is the Liṅga known as Māṇḍavyeśvara, which bestows success; by the sight of it, a man shall never again fall into evil thought.
And the Liṅga named Śaṅkareśa is always there, bestowing auspiciousness; and Bhṛgunārāyaṇa is there, granting all perfections to his devotees.
And there is the Liṅga known as Jābālīśvara, which bestows supreme Siddhi; by the mere sight of it, a living being shall never fall into an evil state.
The most excellent Āditya was installed there by the sage Sumantu; by the mere sight of him, the disease of leprosy is pacified.
There, the goddess named Bhairavī, possessing a terrifying form, shall destroy all that is fearsome in the sacred field when she is worshipped with devotion.
There, at Upajaṅghana, is the Liṅga known as Karmabandhavimokṣaṇa; when served with devotion by men for six months, it bestows supreme perfection.
The Bhāradvājeśvara Liṅga and the excellent Mādrīśvara Liṅga—these two, situated in one place, should be beheld by one of virtuous soul.
O Pot-born One, the Liṅga installed by Aruṇi is located in that very place; through the service of that Liṅga, one shall attain all prosperity.
There exists a most enchanting Liṅga known as Vājasaneya; by the sight of it, men obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 11 ||
The auspicious Kaṇveśvara Liṅga, the Kātyāyaneśvara Liṅga, the Vāmadeveśvara Liṅga, and also the Autathyeśvara Liṅga.
The Liṅga known as Hārīteśvara, Gālaveśvara, the highly meritorious Kumbhe-liṅga, and likewise Kausumeśvara; || 13 ||
Agnivarṇeśvara, Naidhruveśvara, the great Liṅga Vatseśvara, and Parṇādeśvara; || 14 ||
The Saktuprastheśvara Liṅga, as well as the Kaṇādeśa [Liṅga], and another great Liṅga there dedicated to Māṇḍūka; || 15 ||
The Vābhraveyeśvara Liṅga, as well as the Śilāvṛttīśvara, the Cyavaneśvara Liṅga, and the Śālaṅkāyanakeśvara. || 16 ||
The Kaliṃdameśvara Liṅga, the Akrodhaneśvara Liṅga, the Kapotavṛttīśa Liṅga, the Kaṅkeśa Liṅga, and the Kuṇṭaleśvara Liṅga. || 17 ||
Kaṇṭheśvara, Kaholeśa, the Liṅga worshipped by Tuṃburu, Matageśa, Marutteśa, and likewise Magadheyeśvara; || 18 ||
The Jātūkarṇeśvara Liṅga, as well as Jambūkeśvara, Jārudhīśa, Jaleśa, Jālmeśa, and Jālakeśvara; || 19 ||
O Pot-born One, there are fifty thousand such signs resulting from remembering, seeing, touching, worshipping, bowing down to, and praising [the deity]. (20)
For a person who is pure, the arising of defilement never occurs at these auspicious signs in the holy Jyeṣṭhasthāna.
Skanda said: O great sage, I shall relate to you what occurred there once at Jyeṣṭhasthāna; listen to that which destroys all sins.
While the Great Lord was sporting there at his ease in his supreme station, Śivā playfully engaged in the game of ball out of mere curiosity.
Displaying the agility of her limbs as they rose and fell, her eyes were agitated by bees aroused by the fragrance of her sighs.
The ground was made uneven by her falling hair-crests and flower-garlands; the decorative paintings on her cheeks were moist with sweat, shining with trickling drops of water.
Her body was covered by the radiance of her limbs emerging from her transparent colā-garment; her lotus-like hands were intensely red from the repeated striking of the shimmering ball.
With her gaze following the ball and the tips of her dancing eyebrows flickering, Mṛḍānī, the Mother of the Universe, was indeed seen playing. (27)
And by two sons of Diti who moved through the intermediate space, Manoharā was, as it were, glanced at with side-long looks by those whose death had indeed arrived.
By virtue of a boon from Brahmā, those two arrogant men known as Vidala and Utpala treated the three worlds as mere straw through the strength of their own arms.
Desiring to avoid the goddess and being tormented by the arrows of the god of love, the two of them quickly resorted to the Śāmbarī illusion and vanished from sight.
Having assumed the form of attendants, they approached the presence of Ambikā; meanwhile, those two were extremely wicked in conduct and possessed exceedingly fickle minds.
The All-Knowing One fully recognized her due to the flickering arising from her eyes; then the Lord cast a sidelong glance at Durgā, the slayer of formidable enemies.
Having understood the signal of the eyes, she who possesses half the body of the Omniscient One then struck both of them simultaneously with that very same ball.
Struck by the ball of the Great Goddess, those two of great strength, being wicked, whirled around again and again and fell down.
Like a ripe fruit falling from its stalk when shaken by the wind, or like the peak of a great mountain struck down by the thunderbolt. || 35 ||
Having struck down those two great Daityas who were intent on performing an evil deed, the ball then underwent a transformation into the form of a Linga.
And at that time, that Liṅga became known by the name Kaṇḍukeśvara; it is situated near Jyeṣṭheśvara and wards off all evils.
For that devotee who, filled with joy, shall hear the origin of Kaṇḍukeśa and shall worship him, from where can there be fear of suffering? (38)
May Bhavānī, the destroyer of fear, always provide for the welfare and security of those sinless men who are devotees of Kaṇḍukeśvara. (39)
One should always perform the worship of that Liṅga with Mṛḍānī; for right there resides the presence of the Goddess Pārvatī, which grants success to her devotees. (40)
How can Bhavānī and Īśa become the granters of all desires for those by whom the great Liṅga Kaṇḍukeśa has not been worshipped in Kāśī? || 41 ||
And that Liṅga Kaṇḍukeśvara, which is the supreme destroyer of all multitudes of calamities, should be beheld with great effort.
Upon hearing even the name Kaṇḍukeśvara, a succession of sins quickly comes to an end, just as darkness perishes upon encountering the sun.
Skanda said: Listen, O highly fortunate one, to the account that occurred near Jyeṣṭheśvara, O Brahmin, which was truly a source of supreme wonder.
At the great sacred ford (tīrtha) called Daṇḍakhāta, which brings satisfaction to the gods, sages, and ancestors, the Brahmins were performing supreme penance free from desire.
The wicked Daitya Dundubhinirhrāda, the maternal uncle of Prahlāda, reflected on a means [to achieve his ends], thinking: "How might the gods be easily conquered? (46)
"What are the powers of the deities, what is their sustenance, and what is their support? Having reflected thus many times, the Daitya understood the truth and reached a certainty.
Upon reflection, the Brahmins were certainly the cause in this matter; therefore, he repeatedly made an effort to kill the Brāhmaṇas.

Since the gods are the consumers of sacrifices and sacrifices originate from the Vedas, and those Vedas are dependent upon the Brahmins, therefore, O twice-born ones, the power of the gods rests with the Brahmins.
It is certain that all the Vedas, along with Indra and the gods, have the Brahmins as their support; the deities possess the power of the Brahmins—of this there is no need for doubt. (50)
If the Brahmins were lost, then the Vedas themselves would be lost; when the sacred scriptures (Āmnāyas) have perished, the hundred-threaded sacrifices are destroyed. (51)
When the sacrifices were destroyed, the gods would then be deprived of their food; being weakened, they would become easy to conquer, and once the thirty deities were defeated— || 52 ||
"I alone shall become the venerable lord of the three worlds; I shall bring forth for the gods all imperishable riches. (53)
"I shall enjoy only pleasures in a kingdom where all thorns have been removed. Having thus resolved, O Sage, that evil-minded one thought again: || 54 ||
Where are there many twice-born ones, greatly augmented by Brahmanic splendor, perfected in the study of the Vedas, and endowed with the power of austerity? (55)
Vārāṇasī shall be the abode of the majority of Brāhmaṇas; having first gathered them together, I shall then proceed to another sacred site.
For wherever there are holy fords (tīrthas) and wherever there are hermitages (āśramas), all those twice-born ones (agrajanmans) beginning with me are present there on every side.
Thus, having formed a resolve appropriate to his lineage, the deceitful and evil-natured Dundubhinirhrāda reached Kāśī and began to slaughter the twice-born.
Wherever those best of the twice-born go to gather sacrificial fuel and kuśa grass in the forest, there that evil-minded one devours them all.
He remained concealed once more so that no one would know him at all; he became a forest-dweller in the woods and took the form of water in the reservoirs.
Invisible in form, a master of illusion, beyond the reach even of the gods, he should remain absorbed in divine meditation like a sage, dwelling in the midst of sages.
Observing the entry and exit of the huts, he would devour many Brahmins in the form of a tiger during the night.
"He would carry [the victim] away silently, not even discarding a single bone; in this manner, many Brahmins were slain by that wicked man. (63)
Once, on the night of Śivarātri, a certain devotee, having performed the worship of the God of gods in his own hut, remained absorbed in meditation.
And that lord of the Daityas, Dundubhinirhrāda, arrogant in his strength, assumed the form of a tiger and set his mind on seizing him.
Seeing that Bhakta absorbed in meditation, his mind fixed on the vision of Śiva, and having performed the ritual placement of the Astra-mantra, he was unable to overcome him.
Then Śambhu, the all-pervading Hara, having understood the intention of that demon of wicked form, set his mind upon his destruction.
Just as the tiger was about to seize him, Hara appeared—He who is the jewel that protects the world, the three-eyed one, whose intellect is expert in protecting His devotees. (68)
Seeing Rudra approaching, the Daitya, from the Liṅga worshipped by his devotee, grew to resemble a mountain in that very same form.
Then, as soon as the Dānava beheld the Omniscient One with contempt, he seized him as he approached and crushed him within the mechanism of his armpit.
Then the five-faced one struck the five-faced one on the head with his fist; and he [the latter] did so with that very same form and by the crushing of the armpits.
The tiger, extremely distressed, let out a roar that filled both heaven and earth; by that sound, their minds were suddenly made to tremble.
The ascetics, following the sound, arrived there at night; having beheld the Lord there with the king of beasts held within his mouth.
Bowing down, they all praised Śarva with cries of "Victory! Victory!", saying: "O Protector of the World, you have rescued us from this terrible obstacle. (74)
O Lord, O Teacher of the World, grant us your favor; remain right here in this very form, known by the name Vyāghreśa. (75)
O Mahādeva, always provide protection for the site of Jyeṣṭha; protect us, who dwell at this sacred ford (tīrtha), from all other calamities as well. 76.
Having heard their words, the god adorned with the moon said, "So be it," and spoke again: "Listen, O best of the twice-born! (77)
Whoever here indeed beholds me with faith in this form, I shall undoubtedly destroy the multitude of his afflictions.
If a person travels on a journey after having duly worshipped this Liṅga, how could there be any fear for him arising from thieves, tigers, or other such dangers? (79)
Having heard this account of my conduct and having remembered this Liṅga in his heart, a mortal entering into battle attains victory; it is not otherwise.
Having spoken thus, the God of gods entered into dissolution within that liṅga; then the Brahmins, filled with wonder, departed in the morning as they had come.
Skanda said: From that time forward, the Linga born from the pitcher, known by the name Vyāghreśvara, located to the north of Jyeṣṭheśa, removes fear when seen or touched. || 82 ||
The servants and even the exceedingly cruel Yāmas fear those who are devotees of Vyāghreśvara; instead, they cry out, "Victory! Live long! (jayajīva).
Having heard of the origin of the Lingas here, such as Parāśareśvara and others, a person shall not be smeared by the mud of great sins.
Having heard of the origin of Kaṇḍukeśa as well as his manifestation on the tiger, a man is never again afflicted by calamities. (85)
The Uṭajeśvara Liṅga is situated to the west of Vyāghreśa; having worshipped it, which has manifested for the sake of protecting devotees, one becomes fearless. (86)

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Liṅgas such as Parāśareśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: I shall describe to you those other liṅgas which are situated all around Jyeṣṭheśvara; listen, O subduer of Vātāpi!
To the south of Jyeṣṭheśa is the auspicious Liṅga of the Apsarases; right there is the well of the Apsarases known as Saubhāgyodaka (the Water of Good Fortune).
Having bathed well in the water of that well and beheld the Lord of the Apsarases, neither a woman nor a man shall suffer misfortune.
Right there, near the step-well, is the Liṅga known as Kukkuṭeśa; by worshipping it, the family of men prospers.
The auspicious Pitāmaheśvara Liṅga is situated on the bank of the Jyeṣṭhavāpī; by performing a Śrāddha ceremony there, a man shall bestow joy upon his ancestors.
To the southwest of Pitāmaha, one should diligently worship the Gadādhareśvara Liṅga, which bestows complete satisfaction upon the ancestors.
O Sage, in the direction known as Puṇyajana, from the Jyeṣṭheśvara Liṅga, the Liṅga named Vāsukīśvara is to be worshipped on all sides.
There, at the Vāsuki-kuṇḍa, rites such as bathing and giving gifts remove the fear of snakes for men, through the power of Vāsukīśa.
For one who has bathed on the fifth day of the lunar fortnight (Nāgapañcamī) in the pool known as Vāsuki, there shall be no contact with poison arising from serpents.
A procession should indeed be performed there during the rainy season on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa (Nāgapañcamī); by that, the Nāgas will always remain well-disposed toward his family.
To the western part of that pool is the Liṅga known as Takṣakeśvara; it should be worshipped with great effort, for it bestows all perfections upon devotees.
To the north of that sage is the pool known as Takṣaka; one who performs the water-libation rites there is not overcome by serpents.
To the north of that pool is the sacred field Kṣemakara, which always destroys the fear of devotees; there resides the Bhairava named Kapālī.
That is indeed the great field of Bhairava, which bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner; the mantras mastered there attain their perfection within six months.
And there, Caṇḍī Mahāmuṇḍā, who bestows the pacification of obstacles for her devotees, should be worshipped with offerings, oblations, and gifts for the attainment of one's own desired goals. (15)
That best of men who performs her procession on the Mahāṣṭamī day becomes illustrious, enriched with sons and grandsons, and endowed with prosperity. (16)
In the west is Mahāmuṇḍā, which has four ocean-like ponds; one who bathes there becomes as one who has bathed in all four oceans.
That place is highly renowned and known as Catuḥsāgara; there, four liṅgas were installed by the oceans.
On the four sides of that pond, there are worshiped shrines that burn away sin; to its north is the great Liṅga known as Vṛṣabheśvara.
That [liṅga] was established by Hara himself through his own devotion upon his bull; by the sight of it, liberation arises for men within six months.
To the north of Vṛṣeśvara is the one known as Gandharveśvara; to the east of that is the Gandharva-kuṇḍa. Having bathed there, the best of men [attains merit].
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gandharvas and given gifts according to his ability, and having gratified the ancestors and the gods, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
To the east of Gandharveśvara, there is a Nāga named Karkoṭa; there is the Karkoṭa-vāpī and the Karkoṭakeśvara Liṅga.
Having bathed in that pond and worshipped Karkoṭeśa, and having propitiated the Naga Karkoṭaka, a man is glorified in the world of the Nagas.
For those by whom the Naga Karkoṭaka was seen while performing water-rites in that pond, no poison—whether stationary or mobile—spreads within their bodies.
To the west of Karkoṭeśa is the one named Dhundhumārīśvara; by worshipping that liṅga, men shall have no fear arising from enemies.
To the north of that is situated the Purūravasvara Liṅga; it should be visited with great effort, as it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
In front of that city was the Liṅga worshipped by the world-elephant Supratīka; it is known by the name Supratīkeśvara and increases fame and strength.
And before it shines the great lake named Supratīka; having bathed there and beheld that Liṅga, one attains the status of a guardian of the quarters. || 29 ||
Therein resides one Mahāgaurī named Vijayabhairavī; she stands at the northern gate for the sake of protection and for the attainment of the supreme siddhi. (30)
On the beautiful bank of the Varaṇā, the two Gaṇas Huṇḍa and Muṇḍa perform the protection of the sacred field; they are the ones who cause the obstruction of obstacles.
Those two should be visited with effort for the sake of ensuring the field is free from obstacles; having seen Huṇḍaneśa and Muṇḍaneśa there, one shall become happy.
Skanda said: O enemy of Ilvala, listen attentively to one story, that most excellent account of what occurred in the past on the delightful bank of the Varaṇā.
Once, beholding the Lord of Mountains with a joyful mind, the devoted wife Menā remembered Umā, sighed, and spoke thus: (34)
Menā said: "O noble son, O Lord of the Mountain, I do not know even the slightest news concerning that Gaurī since the time of her marriage."
Where is that god now, who moves with the gait of a lordly bull, who is adorned with ashes and serpents, whose dwelling is the great cremation ground, and who is clothed in the directions? (36)
O beloved, those eight mothers who were seen, beginning with Brāhmī, I consider them to be the young girls themselves in their own forms, acting as the cause of my distress. (37)
For that unique wielder of the trident, who has no other equal, there exists no second; therefore, O Lord, let an effort be made to obtain news of his activities.
At the words of his beloved, the Mountain—fond of that offspring, his voice choked with paternal affection—spoke these words to Umā with tears.
The King of Mountains said: "I myself shall go in search of her, O Menā; my love, scorched by the fire of not seeing her, afflicts me intensely."
Ever since that Gaurī departed from my house, I believe the lotus-dwelling Lakṣmī herself has gone forth.
O beloved mistress of my life, from that time forward, my two ears, which drank the nectar of your conversation, shall no longer perceive other sounds. (42)
Since the life-giving moonlight has become distant from my eyes, alas, that very life-giving moonlight now torments me intensely. (43)
Having spoken thus, the lord of mountains took various jewels and garments and departed at the rising power of an auspicious moment.
Agastya said: O Six-faced One, what were those various jewels and how many were they, which he took and set out with? Tell them to me as I ask.
Skanda said: Two crores of measures (tulā) of pearls, as well as a hundred measures of water-clear diamonds, [were offered]. 46.
O Brahmin, there are more than nine hundred thousand highly radiant six-sided [mountains], and two hundred thousand Vidūra mountains with the pure luster of scales.
O Sage, five crores of rubies were brought; and one hundred thousand lakhs of topazes, multiplied by nine, [were brought]. (48)
Likewise, O Sage, there were one hundred thousand *tulās* of *gomeda* gems, and fifty million *tulās* of sapphire (*indranīla*) jewels.
There were millions of measures of gems resembling the outpouring of a garuḍa, and nine crores of measures of pure coral gems.
O Sage, it is impossible to calculate the number of eight-limbed ornaments, as well as the various soft garments. (51)
O Sage, there were also many chowries, fragrant substances, and countless items such as gold, male servants, and female servants.
Taking all of them with him, the Lord of Mountains set forth; having reached the bank of the Varaṇā, he beheld Kāśī from afar.
Its entire ground was inlaid with heaps of many jewels, and the sky was overspread by the radiance of the rubies from its various palaces.
With the various golden domes atop its palaces illuminating the quarters of the sky, it resembled the celestial realm with its multitude of Jayantī and Vaijayantī banners.
It is a wondrous playground for even the eight great Siddhas, with groves of all-fruiting trees that have surpassed the forest of the wish-fulfilling kalpa-tree.
Thus, having beheld the prosperity of Kāśī, he became ashamed; and that lord of mountains spoke these words within his own mind: || 57 ||
In palaces, in gateways, in ramparts, and in houses; in variegated city-gates, on door-panels, and even upon the riverbanks. || 58 ||
By which this [place] is seen to be matted together with networks of light from the rising, beautiful radiance of gems, rubies, and jewels. 59.
"I understand it thus: the space between heaven and earth is exactly like this; even in the house of Kubera, there is no such abundance of wealth."
"Or even in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha—what need is there to mention anyone else here?"—even as the Lord of Mountains was thus reflecting in his mind, [the Lord appeared]. (61)
Just then, a certain pilgrim came within the range of his vision; the Lord of Acala summoned him with great honor and questioned him.
Himavat said: "O best of travelers, sit upon this seat here; O wayfarer, tell me the news of your own city—is there anything extraordinary here?"
Who is the presiding authority here now, and what is the activity of that presiding authority? If you know all this, tell it to me right here in my presence. (64)
Having heard those words of the king of mountains, that pilgrim, O Sage, began to speak.
The pilgrim said: "Listen, O Indra among kings, to everything that I have been asked by you; only five or six days have passed, O giver of honor. (66)
When the Lord of the Universe, the husband of the daughter of the King of Mountains, had arrived from the beautiful Mount Mandara, and Divodāsa had departed for heaven; (67)
He who is indeed the presiding lord of the universe is the omnipresent presiding lord here; how is it that Śarva, the all-seeing, the giver of all, and the All-pervading Lord, is not known? 68.
I think you are of the very nature of stone, with an intellect even harder than stone, since you do not recognize the Lord of the Universe, the husband of Girijā, in Kāśī. (69)
It would be better for that Himalaya mountain, though its very nature is hardness, to have gladdened the Lord of the Universe by the gift of his daughter, who was dearer to him than life itself. (70)
Possessing innate hardness, the father of Gaurī was born as a great mountain; yet, by worshipping Śambhu with his daughter as a garland, he surpassed even the Preceptor of the Universe.
Who knows the activity of that Lord, who is to be known through the Vedas? Yet, I understand even slightly that this world is His very activity.
The presiding deity has been described by me, as well as the activity of that presider; now listen as I relate that which you asked about, which is unprecedented.
In the auspicious place of Jyeṣṭheśvara, that Lord of Umā, having reached Kāśī, now dwells with joy together with the daughter of the King of Mountains as his companion.
Skanda said: Whenever that traveler would utter the nectar of the soft syllables of Girijā’s name, the lord of mountains would rejoice at each such instance.
O Pot-born One, he who has drunk the nectar named Umā here on the surface of the earth shall never again drink the breast-milk of a mother.
O twice-born one, Citragupta does not remember him who recollects this two-syllabled mantra day and night, even if he has committed sins.
Furthermore, the delighted Himavat heard what was spoken by the pilgrim. The pilgrim said: "O King, this temple for Viśveśvara was built by Viśvakarman. (78)
A most excellent emanation was manifested by the one who bestows nirvāṇa upon those born in saṃsāra; such a thing as that I have never before heard with my own ears.
There, the walls of the palaces were constructed from jewels, rubies, and gems, which, with their exceeding brilliance, shone like shafts of light on all sides.
Therein are one hundred and twelve radiant pillars, each set of eight being fashioned to support a single world.
Whatever splendor exists throughout the fourteen worlds, that very splendor, increased a hundred-fold by ten million times, resides here in this celestial chariot.
And the stone pillars and foundations of the moonstone gems were supported by columns made of variegated jewels, which held back the mass of their radiance.
Where graceful statues carved from rubies and sapphires perform the lustration ceremony day and night with lamps made of gold dust.
Upon the smooth surface of lotus-stones fashioned from shimmering crystal, various forms of many jewels were scattered on all sides. (85)
With colors of reddish-yellow, madder-red, blue, and variegated hues, they appear as if painted by a skilled artist upon a canvas. (86)
Rows of ruby pillars are seen, slippery to the sight, because in this sacred field of Avimukta they are like the sprouts of the beauty of liberation.
From all the jewel-mines, the hosts brought together many great accumulations of gems and formed heaps that resembled mountain peaks.
There, from the depths of Pātāla, from the treasuries of the Nāgas, all the hosts of jewels were gathered by the attendants and fashioned into mountains.
There, the devotee of Śiva, Paulastya himself, brought ten million peaks of gold by means of his Rākṣasas from his own mountain peak.
O King, having heard of the construction of the palace, devotees residing in other continents brought rubies in great numbers, beyond all counting! (91)
Where the wish-fulfilling gem itself, for the sake of the architect of the universe (Viśvakarman), bestows various desired jewels day and night upon whatever task he undertakes. || 92 ||
And there, where the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpamahīruha) stand, they—endowed with constant devotion—provide in no small measure banners of various colors.
Where the oceans constantly bathe [the Lord] day after day with jars of the five nectars—curd, milk, sugarcane juice, and clarified butter.
There, the wish-fulfilling cow constantly bathes the Lord of the Universe, who exists in the form of a linga, with her own milk and with a stream of honey through her own devotion. (95)
And the Malaya mountain serves him with the juices of sandalwood; the Karpūrarambhā plant serves him with devotion through floods of camphor.
"O one of hard heart, how is it that you do not know that Umāpati resides daily in the temple of Śaṅkara, where such unprecedented things occur? (97)
O Pot-born Sage, having seen that prosperity of his son-in-law, the King of Mountains was utterly overcome with shame.
Then, having given a reward to that pilgrim, the king of mountains became once again lost in thought after the pilgrim had departed. (99)
With eyes wide open in wonder, he spoke thus within his mind: "Oh, what a blessing has arisen that you, a partaker of happiness, have heard this!"
Indeed, as much as the collection of his perfections is heard of and seen here, so too is the divine play of the Lord of the three worlds present here in the home of his son-in-law.
Therefore, the gift which I brought for the sake of the daughter, intended to please the son-in-law, now appears to me as utterly insignificant. (2)
I believe that he is exactly as he appeared to me before: possessing nothing more than the stature of an old bull, and averse to all worldly activity.
No one shall ever know him, nor his lineage at any time; he has not even a single name, and it cannot be inferred from which country he hails.
Of what character and what conduct was he, who was "Lord" in name only, and for whom not a single object indicative of sovereignty could be observed? (5)
Oh, he bestows the attainment of Nirvana even upon a beggar; that Sumukha makes all actions bear fruit.

For he who is the object of Vedic knowledge is the omniscient one, whose continuum is the entire universe; he whom no one [else] knows at the beginning of the Vedas—he indeed is the one to be known through the Vedas.
He who is not known by the higher knowledges (abhijñās) is always unknown; he alone is indeed the Omniscient One, whose single name cannot be known by any man whatsoever.

Then the Gandharvīs, as if struck with wonder, said to one another: "Is this a dream, or is it real? Or is it the play of Ratneśvara? (65)
"Or perhaps we ourselves are deluded; are we not indeed Gandharvas? We do not understand what this is—it is like the play of a magician. (66)
"This must clearly be the Ganges flowing northward here; this is the pond of Śaṅkhacūḍa, and that is his abode. (67)
This is the Pañcanada Tīrtha, this is the abode of Vāgīśvara; by the mere sight of which the power of speech unfolds.
And this is Śaṅkhacūḍeśvara, installed by Śaṅkhacūḍa; by the mere sight of whom, men have no fear arising from the serpent of Time.
This is the long pond named Mandākinī, a source of meritorious water; mortals who have performed their water-rites therein do not enter the world of mortals again.
This is the goddess Āśāpurī, who was praised on the auspicious bank of the Mandākinī by Tripurāri, who desired to conquer Tripura.
Even today, when worshipped by mortals, she fulfills the hopes of supplicants; and to the west of Mandākinī is this Siddhyaṣṭakeśvara.

In whose house there may clearly be the eightfold accomplishment (siddhyaṣṭaka) through worship, right there shall be the water free from dust known as the eightfold accomplishment of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍasiddhyaṣṭaka).

Having bathed there and performed the śrāddha rite, one becomes free from passion and ascends to heaven; those eight supernatural powers (siddhis) which reside in Kāśī as its forms bestow all accomplishments.
He is the bestower of all accomplishments and the great leader of the Vināyakas; for those men who bow down to him, the obstacles (Vināyakas) perish. || 75 ||
This lofty temple of Siddheśvara is radiant with gold; its jeweled banners and flags constitute the very attainment of perfection (siddhi) for one who beholds them.
In the middle portion of the field, this is indeed Madhyameśvara; by the sight of whom one would not dwell in the midst of the middle and lower worlds. || 77 ||
By duly worshipping Madhyameśa in the central realm, a man shall become a sovereign of the earth extending to the oceans, and thereafter he attains liberation.
To the east of that is the Airāvateśvara Liṅga, which grants the fulfillment of one's desires; it is seen as the beautiful elephant Airāvata upon its banner. (79)
This temple of Vṛddhakāleśvara is constructed of jewels; there the moon dwells every new moon night together with the stars. || 180 ||
By the mere sight of whom, Time shall have no power over men in this world; neither shall the Kali age prevail, nor shall there be falsehood or heaps of impurity. (81)
While the young girls, as if bewildered, were thus engaged in conversation, that Gandharva Vasuvibhūti departed with haste.
Having heard from Nārada the account of Subāhu’s birth as a Dānava, and how his daughter Ratnāvalī was joyfully abducted along with her companions; 83.
As she was returning from Ratneśvara along the empty path of the sky, he brought her to Pātāla just as before, and once again a battle took place.
Just as that Subāhu, whose body was born of a Danava, was slain by Ratnacūḍa—the devotee of Ratneśa—with a great bow and an arrow. (85)
And just as he had been asked about his history, he led him by way of the pond to that pond of Śaṅkhacūḍa which extends through the netherworlds (pātālas).
And just as the young girls, having reached and seen Kāśī, fell into a state of great bewilderment—even while looking on, they remained full of longing; || 87 ||
Seeing her, along with her companions, possessing the exquisite beauty of a lotus-face that was never withered, the king of the Gandharvas regarded her as if she were his own daughter born again.
Having embraced him and repeatedly smelled the surface of his forehead, he placed him upon his lap and respectfully inquired about the entire account of events.
Then she related the story of her abduction by the son of Danu, as well as her attainment of boons from Ratneśvara, excluding the state of her dream.
Then, having understood Ratnāvalī’s state of mind through her facial expressions and gestures, Śaśilekhā related everything in detail with clear words.
Then that virtuous lord of the Gandharvas was exceedingly pleased and joyfully described the power of Ratneśvara.
Skanda said: Listen, O best of sages, you who cause the growth of the Vindhya mountain; every day, even Ratnacūḍa, being self-restrained, [would go] by way of the pond.
Having returned from the world of the Nāgas and bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī, he indeed worshipped Ratneśvara with eight handfuls of jewels.
Once, during the time of a dream, Ratneśa, assuming the form of a liṅga, joyfully presented him with eight golden lotuses.
He spoke thus to Ratnacūḍa, his own devotee of firm vows: "You shall liberate the maiden who has been carried off by the Dānava."
"Having conquered that Dānava in battle, she shall become your wife. Remembering this boon, the high-minded King of Nagas then [acted].
Having slain that Dānava and liberated the maiden through his own prowess, he brought her back from Pātāla to the earth once more by way of the well.
And that wise man himself performed his daily observance every day, having worshipped the Liṅga and also performed circumambulation. || 99 ||
Just as he emerged from the beautiful pavilion of Ratneśa and came outside, they [presented him] to Vasubhūti, the king of the Gandharvas.
"This is he, this blessed youth, pointed out with the tip of the forefinger"—seeing that prince of the Naga kings, the King of the Gandharvas [spoke].
With eyes exceedingly smiling and the hair on his body bristling with joy, he described that form along with its age and lineage within his mind.
I am blessed and favored by the Lord of Jewels for the granting of this boon; and this maiden is even more blessed, since she has a worthy husband.
Having deliberated thus, having summoned that handsome man into his heart, having inquired after his name and lineage, and having calculated his strengths and weaknesses; || 4 ||
Having taken her to the world of the Gandharvas and performed the auspicious marriage rites, he joyfully gave his daughter to him in the presence of Ratneśvara.
Having honored him with the madhuparka offering, he then caused him to take her hand; according to the nuptial rites, he gave him numerous jewels.
O Pot-born Sage, Śaśilekhā, Anaṅgalekhā, and Citralekhā also requested their own fathers and chose him as their husband.
Having taken all four beautiful daughters of the Gandharva as his wives, Ratnacūḍa then departed for his father's palace with them.

Just as the sacred syllable *praṇava* is auspicious when accompanied by the four Vedas, so too that king of the Nāgas, having bowed at the feet of his parents along with his newly-wedded brides, was likewise auspicious.
Having reported the account of Ratneśa’s grace, he lived happily with them, welcomed by his parents.
Īśvara said: O Girijā, the power of this Liṅga of mine, Ratneśvara, which is of a stationary form and bestows everything upon all, is incomparable.
In this liṅga, thousands of perfected ones (siddhas) have attained supreme accomplishment; yet, O woman of beautiful waist, this liṅga remained hidden until today.
By your father Himavat, who is my devotee in every way, Ratneśa has been manifested through great jewels acquired by merit.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, my affection for this Liṅga is absolute; this Liṅga in Vārāṇasī should be worshipped with great effort. (14)
O Umā, O beloved, various jewels are obtained through the grace of the Lord of Jewels—such as the jewel of a wife, the jewel of a son, and even heaven and liberation. (15)
Whoever dies here after bowing to Ratneśvara, even if they die in another land, shall not return from heaven to this world even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Goddess, by fasting on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and keeping a vigil at night in the presence of Ratneśa, one shall attain my proximity.
O beloved, in a previous birth, this Liṅga was installed by you to the east of this one as the Dākṣāyaṇīśvara Liṅga out of devotion to me.
By the mere sight of him, a person does not go to an evil state; you are Gaurī named Ambikā, and there I am Aṃbikeśvara.
O slender-waisted Umā, your son Ṣaḍānana is present there in embodied form; having seen these three, a man shall not enter a womb again.
I have proclaimed to you the majesty of Ratneśvara; it should be guarded with great effort from those whose minds are defiled by the impurities of the Kali age.
