Whoever shall always recite this narrative called the Ratneśvarākhyāna will never at any time be separated from sons, grandsons, or cattle.
Having heard this account of the origin of Ratneśvara along with its history, an unmarried man of noble character shall truly obtain a jewel of a maiden worthy of his lineage. (23)
A maiden who hears this delightful history with faith shall obtain a virtuous husband and become a devoted wife.
Having heard this history, whether a woman or even a man, one shall never be tormented by the heat of the fire of separation from what is beloved.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Praise of Ratneśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Listen further, O best of Brahmins, to another account that occurred there, which produces great wonder and removes even the most heinous sins.
While Maheśvara was thus engaged in conversation with Ratnaśekhara, a great clamor arose from all sides, crying out, "Save us! Save us! (2)
This Gajāsura, the son of Mahiṣāsura, approaches, arrogant with the pride of his own prowess, crushing all the Pramathas.
Wherever on earth he set his foot, O descendant of Bharata, there the son of Bhṛgu caused the mountains to tremble.
By the force of his thighs, trees fall along with their peaks; by the blow of his staff-like arms, even mountains are reduced to powder.
Even though the clouds abandon the blueness of the sky due to friction with his crown, they have not yet relinquished that blueness born from contact with his distress.
By the mass of whose breaths the great oceans become surging with high waves, and even the rivers, along with their whales, possess fierce billows.
The height of this illusory being is nine thousand yojanas, and the extent of his body is exactly as much.
That tawny hue in his eyes, as well as their flickering quality, have not been abandoned by lightning even until today; he is approaching with great haste.
Whichever direction this Dānava Duḥsaha approaches, that very quarter surely becomes level with him, as if out of sheer awe.
Having obtained a boon from Brahmā, he has treated the three worlds as mere straw; he is invulnerable to men and women who are conquered by desire.
Then, recognizing that bull among the Daityas—who was approaching with a trident as his weapon—was incapable of being slain by any other means, he struck him with his own trident.
Pierced by that trident, the Daitya Gajāsura, regarding himself as if he were being held over his head like a parasol, addressed Hara.
Gajāsura said: "O wielder of the trident, Lord of Gods, I know you as the destroyer of Smara; O Destroyer of Cities, death at your hands is indeed for my ultimate welfare."
I wish to say something; attend to what I have spoken. I speak the truth, not falsehood; O Conqueror of Death, reflect upon it. (15)
"You alone are worthy of veneration by the worlds, established above the universe; and I am situated even above you—thus, victory is mine! (16)
I am blessed and I am graced, standing as I am upon the tip of your trident; for all must die in time, yet such a death as this leads to the highest good.
Having heard these words of his, Śambhu, the god of gods and treasure-house of compassion, laughed and spoke to Gajāsura, O Pot-born One (Agastya).
Īśvara said: "O Gajāsura, treasury of great manliness, I am pleased with you! O wise Asura, ask for a boon that is favorable to you; I shall grant it."
Having heard this, that lord of the Daityas replied to Maheśvara. Gajāsura said: "O sky-clad one, if you are pleased, then dwell with me forever."
"O Virūpākṣa, take this hide, purified by the fire of your trident, which is of your own size, pleasant to the touch, and offered as a stake upon the field of battle. (21)
May she always possess a pleasing fragrance; may she always be exceedingly tender; may she always be stainless; and may she always be a source of supreme adornment.

O Lord, although it has been exposed for a very long time to the flames of the fire of great austerity, this skin of mine has not been burnt; therefore, it is a treasure-house of meritorious fragrance.
O naked one, if this woman were not so meritorious as to have been cut by me, then how could her contact with your body have occurred on the field of battle? (24)
And grant me another boon, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased: let "Kṛttivāsas" (Clothed-in-Skin) be your name, beginning from this very day.
Having heard these words of his and saying "So be it," Śaṅkara spoke again to that Daitya, whose mind was purified by devotion.

Īśvara said: Listen, O Daitya, treasure-house of merit, to another boon that is very difficult to obtain: [the granting of liberation] when you cast off your body in battle within the great field of Avimukta.
"May this meritorious body of yours become my linga here in this field that accomplishes liberation, bestowing liberation upon all. (28)
The one named Kṛttivāseśvara is the destroyer of great sins; it is the most excellent, the very head of all liṅgas. (29)
Whatever great sacred emblems exist in Vārāṇasī, this one is the most excellent among them all, as supreme as the head itself.

"For the benefit of human beings, I shall remain here together with my retinue. By seeing this Linga, by worshipping it, and by praising it, a mortal shall have fulfilled his purpose and shall not enter into saṃsāra again. (31)
The Rudras, the Pāśupatas, the Siddhas, and the sages who contemplate reality—calm, self-controlled, having conquered anger, free from dualities, and without possessions.
But those who abide in Avimukta, my devotees seeking liberation, are equal toward honor and dishonor, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
I shall remain here for his grace at the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga; ten thousand crores of holy places [will reside] there every day.
Men born in the Kali and Dvāpara ages, whose intellects are defiled by sin, will undoubtedly come to Kṛttivāsa at the three times of day. (35)
They are devoid of virtuous conduct, averse to truth and purity, and are possessed of deceit, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, and egoism.
Brahmins who consume the food of Śūdras are greedy for the tongue; they have driven their minds and intellects far away from the twilight prayers, ritual bathing, silent recitation, and sacrifice.
Having reached Kṛttivāseśvara, freed from all sins, they shall attain liberation with ease, just like those of meritorious deeds.
Therefore, the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga should be worshipped by men in Kāśī; elsewhere, liberation is very difficult to attain even in thousands of future births. (39)

At the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga, [liberation] is attainable in a single birth. Sins committed in previous lives, which might otherwise perish only gradually through penance, charity, and other means, are destroyed instantly by the mere sight of Kṛttivāseśvara. (40)
Those men who shall worship the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga have entered my very body; for them there is no rebirth.
One must dwell here in Avimukta, recite the Śatarudriya, and behold the Lord Kṛttivāseśvara again and again. (42)
Whatever fruit may arise from the excellent recitation of seven crores of Mahārudra mantras, that same fruit is obtained in Kāśī by worshipping Kṛttivāsas.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should keep vigil at night; he who worships Kṛttivāseśa shall go to the supreme goal.
Whoever performs a great festival at the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra shall not enter a womb again.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods, whose garment is the sky, took up that great hide of Gajāsura and donned it.
O Pot-born One, on that day a great festival took place, wherein the Lord, who was naked, attained the state of being clothed in the hide of an elephant.
Where the Daitya, having been impaled upon a trident, was made into a parasol over the earth, a very great pool was formed there from the uprooting of that trident.
Having bathed in that pool and performed the libations for the ancestors, and having beheld Kṛttivāseśvara, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Skanda said: O Agastya, listen to what occurred at that sacred ford; by the power of that tīrtha, crows attained the state of swans.
Once, in ancient times, a festival took place on the full moon day of Caitra at Kṛttivāsa; there, food produced as an offering was heaped into a great mound.
O Brahmin, seeing that [food], many temple-attendants (devalakas) and birds gathered together, fighting one another in the path of the sky for the sake of that food. || 52 ||

The crows, their limbs emaciated, shrieked harshly at the cranes whose bodies were nourished by offerings; and the weak ones were struck down by the strong cranes with their beaks, whose own limbs were exceedingly well-fed.
Being struck down, they fell from the expanse of the sky into that pit; saved by the remainder of their lifespan, the crows were transformed into female swans.
The people gathered there for the festival were filled with wonder; pointing with their fingers, they said, "Aha! Look, look! (55)
While we were looking on, those crows that fell into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) there were born as Dhārtarāṣṭra cranes through the power of this sacred ford (tīrtha). || 56 ||
O Agastya, from that time forth, that pool near Kṛttivāsa became famous in the world by the name Haṃsatīrtha.
Those whose souls are exceedingly defiled by great impurities attain stainlessness in an instant by performing ablutions at Haṃsatīrtha.
One should always reside in Kāśī, bathe at Haṃsatīrtha, behold Kṛttivāseśa, and attain the supreme state. || 59 ||
O Sage, there are many lingas at Kashi at every step; the Krittivaseshvara linga is remembered as the crown of all lingas. (60)
By propitiating Kṛttivāsa with a mind endowed with devotion, one obtains in Kāśī the fruit arising from the worship of all liṅgas.
Recitation, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, libations, and worship of the deities—all these, when performed in the presence of Kṛttivāsa, become infinite.
O Pot-born Sage, this sacred ford (tīrtha) was established from time immemorial; it has become manifest once again through the presence of the Great Lord.
These marks of the Siddhas remain concealed in age after age; indeed, having attained the proximity of Śambhu, they manifest once again.
O Sage, around Haṃsatīrtha there are ten thousand and two hundred liṅgas installed by the best of sages.
Each individual liṅga, beginning with Kātyāyaneśa and ending with Cyavaneśa, bestows spiritual perfection upon men residing in Avimukta.
The great Liṅga Lomaśeśa was installed by Lomaśa; to the west of that is Kṛttivāsas—having seen those, what fear can there be of Death? (67)
Having worshipped that great and auspicious Liṅga of Mālatīśa, located to the north of Kṛttivāsa, a king shall become a lord of elephants.
And the Liṅga known as Antakeśvara is situated in the direction of that Rudra; even one who has committed great sins becomes sinless by beholding it. (69)
To the side of that is the great Janakeśa Liṅga, the supreme bestower of knowledge; by worshipping that Liṅga, the knowledge of Brahman is attained. (70)
To the north of that is the great form of the Bhairava Asitāṅga; by the sight of him, men shall no longer behold Yama.
And there is the goddess Śuṣkodarī with fierce eyes; she dwells to the north of Kṛttivāsa and consumes those who create obstacles for Kāśī.
The Vetāla named Agnijihva is located to the southwest of that goddess; when worshipped on a Tuesday, he grants the desired accomplishment.
There is the Vetālakuṇḍa there, which destroys all diseases; by contact with the water of that pool, the pain of wounds and boils shall depart.
Having bathed well in Vetālakuṇḍa and having prostrated before Vetāla, one shall obtain the desired perfection that is difficult for all embodied beings to attain.
There is a herd there consisting of two arms, four feet, and five heads; by the mere sight of it, sin is shattered into a thousand pieces.
To the north of that, O Sage, is the terrifying Rudra, who has four horns, three feet, two heads, and indeed seven hands.
O Pot-born One, he who takes the form of a bull and is bound in three ways cries out repeatedly; so too do those who create obstacles for Kāśī and those whose minds are set on evil within Kāśī. (78)
And I, holding an axe, am here to cut them down—those who create obstacles in Kāśī and those whose minds are set on worldly things in Kāśī. (79)
I am the one who holds the jar of nectar and the one who sprinkles that lineage; having seen that Vṛṣarudra and having worshipped him with devotion, [one attains the goal]. || 80 ||
And by means of great and extensive offerings, one is not overcome by obstacles; there is a serpent named Maṇipradīpa to the north of that Rudra.
In front of that is Maṇikuṇḍa, which is supreme for removing poison and disease; having performed his bath in that pool and having gazed upon that Nāga, [he should proceed].
One shall obtain a kingdom filled with jewels and rubies, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and enriched with the treasures of women and sons.
Those by whom the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga in Kāśī has not been beheld have undoubtedly become a burden to the earth in the world of mortals. 84.
Skanda said: Those men who here shall hear of the origin of Kṛttivāsa will obtain welfare from the sight of that Liṅga; there is no doubt in this matter.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Kṛttivāsa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Listen, O Agastya, you who are a mass of asceticism, to those liṅgas which indeed exist in Kāśī; when served by men of purified souls, they lead to liberation. || 1 ||
Where the Lord playfully made his garment of animal skin, that place became renowned as Rudrāvāsa, bestowing all spiritual perfections.
While the wearer of the elephant hide remained there at his own will together with Umā, Nandin arrived and made this representation preceded by a prostration.
O Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord of the universe, sixty-eight beautiful and most enchanting temples, composed of all kinds of jewels, have appeared here.
Indeed, whatever auspicious sanctuaries exist throughout the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, even those that grant liberation, have all been brought here by me from every quarter.
O Lord, please attend for a moment to that which has been brought from wherever it came, and where it has established its seat; this I shall relate. (6)
The great liṅga named Sthāṇu, which bestows liberation upon the God of gods, originated from Kurukṣetra; indeed, only a fraction of it remains there.
In front of that is the auspicious great lotus-pool named Sannihatī; to the west of Lolārka is that very site of Kurukṣetra.
Whatever bathing, fire-offerings, recitations, austerities, or gifts are performed there by those seeking auspicious results, it is truly more than ten million times superior to Kurukṣetra.
O Lord, the God of gods departed from Naimiṣa accompanied by Brahmāvarta; having established a mere portion of himself there, he manifested in Kāśī.
To the north of Ḍhuṇḍhirāja is indeed the Liṅga named Devadeva, which grants success to the practitioner; in front of it is an excellent well.
Known as Brahmāvarta, it removes the cycle of rebirth for men; having performed one's ablutions with the waters of its wells and having worshipped the God of gods, [one attains liberation].
That merit is remembered as being ten million times ten million times greater than that of the Naimiṣa forest; here, the Great One manifested himself from the shrine of Gokarṇa.
Near Sāṃbāditya is the Liṅga named Mahābala; by the sight or touch of which, great sin is destroyed in an instant.
Having seen the Mahābala Liṅga in the city of Kapālamocana, one flees from afar like a heap of cotton struck by the wind. || 15 ||
One obtains great strength and shall go to the city of Nirvāṇa from the excellent sacred field of Prabhāsa, located to the east of Ṛṇamocana.
The Liṅga known as Śaśibhūṣaṇa is established here; by serving that Liṅga, a mortal shall attain the state of being adorned by the moon.
One obtains ten million times the merit of a pilgrimage to Prabhāsa-kṣetra; the omnipresent Lord Mahākāla has come here in person from Ujjayinī. (18)
Merely by remembering the name of that great Liṅga called Praṇava, which destroys impurity and is situated to the east, there shall be no fear of the Kali age.
The Liṅga named Mahākāla bestows supreme liberation through its mere sight; and from Puṣkara, the most excellent of holy places, comes the Ayogandheśvara Liṅga.
Then, together with Mahatpuṣkara, Matsyodarī appeared here on the northern side, having seen the Lord Īśvara who is free from worldly attachment.
Having bathed in the Ayogandhakuṇḍa, one delivers one's ancestors from worldly existence; the Mahānādeśvara Liṅga has come here from Aṭṭahāsa.

To the north of Trilocana, that Liṅga known as Mahotkaṭeśvara is considered to grant liberation when seen; it came here from Marutkoṭa and, when beheld in the northern part of Kāmeśvara, bestows pure perfection.
The Liṅga known as Vimaḷeśvara, which bestows pure perfection, was seen here having come from its station in Viśva, located to the west of Svarlīna.
The Mahāvrata-Mahāliṅga is established here starting from Maheṃdra; it is situated near Skandeśvara and bestows the fruit of the Great Vow (Mahāvrata). || 25 ||
In the first age, that great liṅga which was born, having pierced the earth so difficult to penetrate, while the hosts of gods were offering praise.
Because they addressed him as "Mahādeva" for fulfilling their desires, he became known as Mahādeva from that time forth in Vārāṇasī.
By him, through the Great Liṅga, Kāśī has been made a field of liberation; that mortal who shall behold Mahādeva here in Avimukta [shall likewise attain it]. || 28 ||
For one who dies anywhere, there is indeed a journey to the world of Śambhu; therefore, those seeking liberation should diligently resort to Avimukta. (29)
Even in another kalpa, the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana) was never abandoned by Mahādeva, who exists there entirely in the form of a Liṅga.
This incomparable, auspicious shrine, composed of all kinds of jewels, is the protector of the sacred field (kṣetra) located to the west of Hiraṇyagarbha-tīrtha.
The presiding deity of Vārāṇasī is Sābhilāṣadā; she is indeed known by the name Mahādevī, whose very nature consists of all liṅgas.
By those who have seen Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī assuming the form of a liṅga, the liṅgas of the three worlds have undoubtedly been seen here. || 33 ||
Having worshipped Mahādeva even once in Vārāṇasī, a person shall dwell joyfully in the world of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings.
By diligently offering a sacred thread (*pavitra*) to the Great God (Mahādeva) during the *Pavitraparvan* festival in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one is never again subject to rebirth in a womb.
The Pitāmaheśvara Liṅga has come here from the Gayā-tīrtha, accompanied by eighty million holy sites beginning with Phalgutīrtha.
Where, indeed, for ten million times a hundred ages, penance was performed by Dharma, having made the great Liṅga named Śrī Dharmeśvara his witness. (37)
Having joyfully worshipped the Pitāmaha-īśvara Liṅga there, a person is liberated along with twenty-one generations of his lineage; of this there is no doubt. || 38 ||
From Prayāga, the king of holy places, Maheśvara, bearing the trident-mark, arrived in person and remained there together with the king of holy places.
From the delightful pavilion of Nirvāṇa, in the inexpressible [state], there is a most pure palace, radiant with gold, which vies with Mount Meru.
A boon was granted by the God himself in a former age: "Maheśvara, the remover of impurities, is to be worshipped first in Kāśī. (41)
He who bathes here at Prayāga and pays homage to Maheśvara, having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with extensive and grand preparations; || 42 ||
From the merit born of bathing at Prayāga and from the sight of Śūlaṭaṅka, he shall obtain merit a crore times greater; of this there is no doubt.
From Śaṅkukarṇa, the great field, the Liṅga known as Mahātejas manifested here, which bestows an increase in great splendor.
His palace, a treasury of great splendor, was exceedingly pure; its flames matted the sky, as if it were constructed entirely of rubies.
Through seeing, touching, praising, and fully worshipping that Liṅga, one attains that supreme abode, having gone to which one does not grieve.
By worshipping Mahātejas to the east of Vināyakeśvara, one goes to the state of Maheśvara by means of a vehicle composed of light.
From that supremely purifying holy site known as Rudrakoṭi, the Supreme Lord himself manifested the Liṅga Mahāyogīśvara.
Near the Pārvatīśvara Liṅga is the bestower of all perfections; by the sight of that Liṅga, men obtain the fruit of ten million Liṅgas. || 49 ||
Surrounding that temple, temples equal in number to ten million Rudras, with beautiful structures, were constructed by the forms of Rudra himself.
That place is recited by the exponents of the Vedas as Rudrasthalī in Kāśī; indeed, those worms, insects, and moths who die in Rudrasthalī [attain liberation]. || 51 ||
Whether they be domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, mortals, or even barbarians, once they have been initiated and have become one with Rudra, there is for them no returning here again.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of previous births, all of that goes to destruction for one who has entered Rudrasthalī.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, even one who has entered the womb of an animal, by casting off his life-breaths at Rudrasthalī, shall attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Having come here from the field of Ekāmbara, he who is clothed in animal skin (Kṛttivāsas) has himself established himself here in this Liṅga as Kṛttivāsas.
In this place, the omnipresent Lord Sāmba, together with the hosts of sages, shall personally instruct his own devotees in the Brahman praised by the Vedas in the Śruti.
Having arrived at this field that grants success, Caṇḍīśa, from Marujāṅgala, shall shatter a multitude of most fierce sins in a hundred glances.
He who beholds the great Liṅga Caṇḍīśvara in the presence of the Lord of Gaṇas, Pāśapāṇi, attains the supreme goal. || 58 ||
From Kālañjara, the all-pervading Lord Nīlakaṇṭha himself resides here, the destroyer of worldly existence, near the Gaṇeśa known as Daṃtakūṭa.
Those by whom the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara Liṅga has been fully worshipped in Kāśī shall themselves become blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭhas) and shall themselves be adorned with the moon as their ornament.
The Liṅga known as Vijaya, which has come here from Kashmir, always bestows victory upon men; it is situated to the east of Śālakaṭaṃkaṭa.
In battle, in the royal court, in gambling, and in dispute—indeed, at all times—victory arises for men through the worship of Vijayeśa. (62)
The omnipresent Lord himself, whose semen is drawn upward, arrived here bearing the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) and stood present, placing Kūśmāṇḍaka at the head of his attendants.
One attains an upward course by beholding one whose vital energy is drawn upward; for those who are devoted to such a person of sublimated energy, there is indeed no downward course.
From the sacred field of Maṇḍaleśvara, the Liṅga known as Śrīkaṇṭha is situated to the north of the Vināyaka named Maṇḍa.
Those men who are devotees of Śrīkaṇṭha are indeed Śrīkaṇṭhas themselves; they are never separated from prosperity, neither in this world nor in the next.
From the great pilgrimage site of Chāgalāṇḍa, the omnipresent Lord known as Kapardīśvara manifested himself at the Piśācamocana Tīrtha.
Having duly worshipped Kapardīśa, a man shall not go to hell; nor does he fall into the state of a Piśāca, even after committing the most grievous sin here.
From the sacred field of Āmrātakeśvara, the Liṅga known as Sūkṣmeśa has come here of its own accord to this field, which is the abode of all auspicious things.
Having seen the Sūkṣmeśvara Liṅga near the Gaṇeśa known as Vikaṭa-dvija, one shall attain a subtle state of existence.
Having arrived here from Madhukeśvara, he beheld Jayanta, the Lord of Gods, stationed there in front of Gaṇapati Lambodara.
Having beheld Jayanteśvara and bathed in the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā, one shall attain the desired perfection and become victorious everywhere.
The Lord of Gods, the Destroyer of Tripura, manifested [himself] from Śrīśaila; indeed, the fruit that is proclaimed for beholding the peak of Śrīśaila—[he produced that]. (73)
Beholding Tripurāntaka, its fruit is obtained with ease. To the western part of Viśveśvara is the Lord Tripurāntaka.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion, a man shall not enter a womb again; for the Lord Kukkuṭeśvara has come here from his gentle abode.
He stands near Vakratuṇḍa, the leader of the Gaṇas; by seeing him and by worshipping him, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are held within one's hand.
And from Jāleśvara, the Lord himself came as Triśūlī; he who bestows all perfections stands before Gaṇapati at Kūṭadanta.
From the great sacred field of Rāmeśvara, Jaṭīdeva arrived; situated on the northern side of Ekadanta, he is worshipped as the granter of all desires.
From the sacred field of Trisaṃdhya, the god Tryambaka has arrived; from Trimukha in the eastern direction, he who has assumed the state of Tryambaka was worshipped.
Hareśvara has come here from the Hariścandra-kṣetra; worshipped in front of Hariścandreśvara, he always bestows victory.
Here Śarva has arrived from the abode of Madhyamakeśvara and remains stationed, having placed the Caturvedeśvara Liṅga before him.
Having worshipped every single *liṅga* in Kāśī, which grants supreme perfection, a human being shall never again attain the state of a transmigrating creature anywhere.
From Sthaleśvara, however, a supreme great Liṅga manifested here, where the Yajñeśvara Liṅga, which bestows the fruits of all Liṅgas, is located. (83)
Having worshipped the Mahāliṅga endowed with great faith, one attains great prosperity both in this world and in the next.
Here is the thousand-eyed Liṅga, which came from Suvarṇākhyā; by the sight of it, the eye of knowledge arises for men. (85)
To the south of Śaileśvara, having beheld the omnipresent Lord Sahasrākṣeśvara, one shall abandon the sins of hundreds of thousands of births. || 86 ||
From that which was joyful, there appeared here another joy-bestowing Liṅga that dispels darkness, which grants delight to men through both sight and touch. (87)
Near Maṃtreśvara is the temple of Harṣiteśa; from the sight of it, a continuous succession of joy arises for men at all times. 88.
Here Rudra has come in person from Rudramahālaya; by the sight of him, men clearly go to the world of Rudra.
Those mortals by whom the Rudreśvara Liṅga has been worshipped here in Kāśī should be known as being of the very form of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Having seen the omnipresent Lord Rudreśvara near Tripureśa, those who are alive as well as those who are dead should be known as being like Rudras themselves.
Mahādeva, the lord of the bull and whose banner is the bull, always came here from Bāṇeśvara-liṅga to bestow his boons.
One who has come here should behold the deity known as Kedārādīśāneśvara, and also the Liṅga situated to the west of Prahlādakeśava.
Having worshipped Īśāneśa and bathed in the waters flowing northward, one shall dwell in the city of Īśāna with a splendor equal to that of Īśāna himself.
From Bhairava, the captivating form of Bhairavī has arrived here; he who is named Saṃhārabhairava should be beheld with great effort. (95)
Through worship for the sake of all accomplishments, he [is worshipped] to the east of Kharvavināyaka; may Saṃhārabhairava in Kāśī destroy the succession of sins.
The fierce [deity] Ugra, the bestower of perfection, manifested here from the sacred ford of Kanakhala; by beholding him, the terrible sins of men are destroyed. (97)
The Ugra Liṅga, located to the east of Arkavināyaka, should always be worshipped; even the most terrible calamities perish through its adoration. (98)
O Lord, from the great sacred field of Vastrāpatha, the omnipresent Lord named Bhava himself manifested here near Bhīmacaṇḍī. 99.
Having worshipped Bhaveśvara, a man shall manifest as Bhava; he becomes the lord of all kings here who carry out his commands.
From the Devadāru forest, Daṇḍī, the all-pervading Lord who punishes multitudes of sins, arrived at Vārāṇasī and remained there in the form of a Liṅga.
In the east, Daṇḍīśvara is to be worshipped, located from Dehalivināyaka; by worshipping him, rebirth is not seen for mortals.
From the Bhadrakarṇahrada lake, Śiva himself, accompanied by Bhadrakarṇahrada and worshipped as the bestower of auspiciousness upon all, has come here in person.
To the east of the Gaṇapati named Uddaṇḍa is that supreme holy place; having bathed in the Bhadrakarṇahrada lake and having worshipped the Liṅga called Śiva, [one attains the fruit]. || 4 ||
One attains auspiciousness everywhere through the worship of Bhadrakarṇeśa; one hears the welfare of all beings and beholds auspiciousness with one's own eyes.
Śaṅkara and Hari appear before you from the Candrā [river]; by worshipping them, people are not born again in a mother's womb.
From the great tirtha of Yamaliṅga, Kālaliṅga is situated here; it is renowned as Kalaśeśa and is located to the west of Candreśa.
Having bathed at Yamatīrtha, situated to the south of Mitrāvaruṇa, and having beheld the Kālaliṅga, whence can there be any fear of the Kali age?
Whoever undertakes a journey there on the fourteenth day of the lunar month of Bhādra, even if burdened by sins, shall not go to the journey of Yama.
And from the great sacred field of Nepal, Paśupati came here, where the Pāśupata yoga was taught by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
By you, the God of gods, for the sake of liberation from Brahmā and the others, one is released from the bonds of Paśu merely by the sight of him. || 11 ||
From the Karavīraka Tīrtha, Kapālīśa has come here; he should be visited with great effort at the Kapālamocana Tīrtha.
By the mere sight of it, the sin of killing a Brahmin is dissolved; the Lord of Umā, having come here, has established himself at Devikā. (13)
Lord Paśupati, seen in the east, removes sins accumulated over a long time; this Liṅga here in the field of Maheśvara is known as Dīpteśa.
One should remain devoted to Upomāpati for the sake of splendor both in this world and the next; the Liṅga Dīpteśa, situated in the heart of Kāśī, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (15)
From the mountain Kāyārohaṇa, the teacher Nakulīśvara stands surrounded by disciples who observe the great Pāśupata vows. || 16 ||
For when seen to the right of Mahādeva, he bestows knowledge; he swiftly destroys ignorance, which is the cause of the cycle of existence within the womb. || 17 ||
From the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean comes that which is called Amareśa; by the mere sight of which, indeed, immortality—which is otherwise difficult to attain—is secured.
From the Saptagodāvarī tīrtha, the Lord Bhīmeśvara shines forth in the form of a liṅga for the sake of enjoyment and liberation of men here.
If one beholds the Lord Bhīmeśvara in front of Nakulīśa, indeed great and terrible sins perish at that very moment.
From Bhūteśvara, the Bhasmagātra [Liṅga] manifested here spontaneously; having worshipped it with great effort on the southern side of Bhīmeśa, [one attains the fruit]. || 21 ||

Whatever fruit is obtained from practicing for a hundred years in the Samyak-Pāśupata and other such disciplines, that same fruit shall be attained simply by beholding one whose limbs are smeared with ashes.
From Nakulīśvara, the Lord known as Svayaṃbhū became manifest by himself; in Kāśī, Hara exists in the form of a Liṅga.
Having bathed in the Siddhihrada lake and worshipped the Svayambhū Liṅga before Mahālakṣmīśvara, a man shall not be subject to birth again.
On the very bank of the Prayāga tīrtha stands this great temple of Vārāha, which possesses the luster of coral and belongs indeed to the one named Dharaṇī.
Having heard that the Lord had arrived from Mount Mandara with his retinue and the gods and sages, he came from a cave here at the Vindhya mountain.
In Kāśī, that Earth-Boar should be beheld with diligent effort; he shall rescue the one who has sought refuge when submerged in the ocean of calamity.
From Karṇikāra comes Gaṇādhyakṣa, who has the luster of a Karṇikāra flower; he is to be worshipped with a mace in hand, and he removes thousands of calamities.
Therefore, by worshipping Gaṇādhyakṣa, who is situated in the western direction from that Earth-boar [temple], one shall attain the station of the Lord of Gaṇas. || 29 ||
From Hemakūṭa, the Liṅga named Virūpākṣa manifested here; it was seen to the south of Maheśvara and is the savior from saṃsāra.
From Gaṅgādvāra, one should behold the Lord of Himastha, a Liṅga with a luster like snow, situated to the west of Brahmanāla; it bestows spiritual perfection in this world.
And the Lord of the Gaṇas, along with other mighty Gaṇas numbering seventy million, arrived from Mount Kailāsa, O Lord. (32)
Fortresses were built by them here, equal to the seven heavens, provided with excellent gates, mechanical devices, and formidable door-panels.
They were enriched with millions upon millions of soldiers and possessed every supernatural power, as well as [vessels] made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, brass, and lead.
Then, with those [stones] which were attractive, firm, and even sky-scraping due to their magnetism, they constructed a great fortress of rock all around Kāśī.
A deep moat was also constructed, filled with the waters of the Matsyodarī; that Matsyodarī then became divided into two, flowing both outside and inside.
And that great and famous sacred ford (tīrtha) is joined with the waters of the Gaṅgā when the water of the Gaṅgā flows here by way of the path of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Then, by the weight of one's merit, the Matsyodarī Tīrtha is attained; it possesses a hundred times ten million times the merit of both the Sun and the Moon.
Indeed, all sacred festivals are right there, all holy fords are truly there, and all Lingas are right there because of the Gaṅgā and Matsyodarī.
For those men who bathe anywhere at Matsyodaryā and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas), they shall never again lie within a mother’s womb.
This field, being unliberated, shall assume the form of a fish; it is seen on all sides surrounded by the flowing waters of the celestial river.
Those men who have performed their ablutions at Matsyodarī are the best of men; even after committing many sins, they do not behold the city of Yama.

What is the use of bathing in many sacred fords, or what is the use of performing difficult austerities, if one has bathed in the Matsyodarī? From that, whence can there be any fear of rebirth in a womb? (43)
For wherever there are lingas established by human beings, gods, or sages, one who reaches Matsyodarī and bathes well there becomes a vessel for liberation.
There are many sacred fords (tīrthas) belonging even to the realms of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar; yet it is certain that they are not equal to this one, even by a ten-millionth part.
Thus, O Lord, this great holy ford was established by that Gaṇādhipa, the dweller of Kailāsa, who performs most exalted and noble deeds.
The Liṅga known as Bhūrbhuvaḥ manifested itself here from Mount Gandhamādana, to the east of Gaṇādhipa.
Having beheld the Bhūrbhuva-liṅga, meritorious people dwell for a very long time in the realms of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Mahaḥ, as well as in the higher worlds, enjoying divine pleasures.
O Lord, the great Liṅga Hāṭakeśa, accompanied by Bhogavatī, came here of its own accord from the depths of the seven netherworlds.
And by Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and other principal [nāgas], that great temple here was diligently constructed with a multitude of jewels, gems, and rubies. (150)
That tall linga, made of gold and adorned with garlands of jewels, situated to the east of Īśāneśvara, should be worshipped with great effort. || 51 ||
Having worshipped that Liṅga with devotion, a man becomes possessed of all prosperity; after enjoying countless pleasures, he attains liberation in the end.
From the star in the sky, a linga of luminous form has come here; that Tārakeśvara Linga is situated in front of the Jñānavāpī pond.
Salvational knowledge is attained through the worship of that Liṅga; and having bathed in the Jñānavāpī and beheld Tārakeśa, a man [attains the same].
Having performed the observances such as the twilight prayers and having fully gratified the ancestors, the wise one maintained the vow of silence until he beheld the Liṅga.
One is liberated from all sins and attains eternal merit; and at the end, one obtains the liberating knowledge (tāraka-jñāna), by which knowledge one is finally released.
And from Kirāta, Kirāteśa manifested here; it was there that the Lord formerly became a deity in the form of a Kirāta.
After bowing down to that Kirāteśvara Liṅga, which follows Bhārabhūteśvara, a man shall never again lie within a mother's womb.
Coming from the city of Laṅkā, he reached the Liṅga known as Marukeśvara, by worshipping which men shall have no fear of Rākṣasas.
In the southwestern direction is that Liṅga known as Nirṛteśvara; worshipped after Paulastya-Rāghava, it removes all evils.
The Liṅga, which is fond of the water of merit, arrived even from the site of the Jalaliṅga and became established in the midst of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In the middle of the Gaṅgā, that most wonderful palace is seen; it is excellent, composed of all metals, auspicious, and consisting of all jewels.
Even today, due to the weight of their accumulated merit, some see this most excellent Liṅga, which has come here even from the Koṭīśvara Tīrtha.
The merit gained from beholding that Liṅga at Koṭiliṅga in a single moment is superior even to Jyeṣṭheśvara; it is the most excellent and bestows supreme accomplishment.
The Liṅga named Analeśvara, which emerged from the mouth of the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha), is located here in front of Naleśvara; when worshipped, it bestows all spiritual perfections.
Having arrived from Viraja-tīrtha, the three-eyed God of gods established himself in the beginningless, eternally perfected Liṅga at Triviṣṭapa.
At the meritorious Pilipilā tīrtha, which grants liberation to all, the Lord himself manifested the syllable Oṃ from Amarakaṇṭaka.
That was the primordial field of Tāraka when the Gaṅgā had not yet arrived; it was then that Kāśī manifested for the sake of uplifting the three worlds.
Then, a great liṅga of that very form manifested itself; no one else understands the majesty of that omnipresent Lord except for him.
O Lord, he brought these great abodes and left behind only a mere portion of each in their respective fields.
"O Lord, meritorious deeds have come here in their entirety and not otherwise; moreover, their beautiful palaces rise up on all sides, scraping the very clouds. (71)
They consist of many elements, variegated, and resplendent with all kinds of jewels; by the mere sight of even a single jar of them, liberation is attained. (72)
O best of gods, even by merely hearing the names of these lingas, heaps of sins arising from thousands of births are destroyed. (73)
"Now, what command of yours, O Lord, should be carried out by me here? Let it be graciously granted; for once accomplished, it must indeed be considered as already achieved."
Skanda said: Having heard these words of Nandin, Hara, the Lord of the God of Gods, being pleased with Śailādi’s faith, spoke this, O Pot-born One (Kumbhaja).
The illustrious God of Gods said: "Well done by you, Nandin, O bestower of eternal bliss! Carry out my command and now dispatch the Caṇḍīs."
Indeed, ninety million Cāmuṇḍās reside there together with their own deities, along with Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Bhairavas.
For the purpose of protecting that city, you who possess vehicles, forces, and weapons, and who are yourselves like fortresses, station yourselves all around every stronghold.
Skanda said: Having thus instructed Nandin, Mṛḍa, accompanied by Mṛḍānī, went to the realm of the three gods (Traiviṣṭapa), which is the place where the seeds of liberation sprout.
The son of Śilāda, having also placed the command of Īśa upon his head, summoned the Durgās from all sides and stationed them at every fortress.
And by hearing this chapter, which contains the womb of meritorious shrines, a person shall attain heaven and liberation in due order through faith. (81)
Having heard of these sixty-eight [deities] who take refuge in the great shrines, a mortal shall never again enter the cave of the mother's womb.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Assembly at the Sixty-Eight Sanctuaries," in the latter half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 69.
Agastya said: O son of Kātyāyanī, Nandin, delighter of the universe, tell me how the goddesses were dispatched by the command of the God of gods.
O Lord, for the sake of protecting one who is not yet liberated, please show me favor and tell me truly which deities reside wherever [he may go].
Having heard what was thus spoken by Agastya, the son of Mahādeva joyfully recounted where and how she remained in Ānandavana.
Skanda said: In Vārāṇasī, Viśālākṣī, the bestower of the supreme boon upon the sacred field, established herself on the bank after having created the Viśāla-tīrtha in the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed at the Viśāla-tīrtha and having bowed to Viśālākṣī, one obtains vast fortune that bestows happiness both in this world and the next.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, men intent on fasting should keep a vigil at night in the presence of Viśālākṣī.
On the morning of the fourteenth day, fourteen young girls should be diligently fed and adorned according to one's means with garlands, garments, and ornaments.
O Pot-born Sage, after performing the breaking of the fast together with one's sons and servants, the full fruit of residing in Vārāṇasī shall be obtained.
On that lunar day, a great procession (mahāyātrā) should be performed by the residents of the sacred field for the sake of pacifying calamities and for the attainment of the lotus of Nirvāṇa.
In Vārāṇasī, Viśālākṣī should be worshipped with diligence by means of incense, lamps, auspicious garlands, and charming offerings. 10.
With ornaments such as jewels and pearls, with variegated canopies and chowries, and with auspicious, unused silk garments scented with perfumes; || 11 ||
Whatever, even if it be very little, has been given by the best of men—wherever they may dwell—to Viśālākṣī for the sake of attaining the abundant glory of liberation; [that shall not perish]. 12.
O Sage, at that time, everything given, recited, offered in sacrifice, and praised at the great seat (pīṭha) of Viśālākṣī indeed bears fruit for infinity in both worlds.
Liberation is its full fruition; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. From the worship of Viśālākṣī, one obtains a husband endowed with excellence of form. (14)
In this world, young maidens obtain husbands adorned with virtues and good character; pregnant women obtain sons; and barren women obtain the birth of offspring. (15)
By those who are unfortunate, great good fortune is attained; and by widows, widowhood shall never again occur in any future birth.
Whether by women or by men desiring supreme liberation, she who is heard of, seen, or worshipped in Kāśī grants the fulfillment of the desires of the large-eyed ones. (17)
Beyond that is Lalitātīrtha, in the vicinity of Gaṅgākeśava; there resides the supreme goddess Lalitā, the protector of the sacred field.
She should be worshipped with great effort for the sake of the abundance of all prosperity; and for those who worship Lalitā, no obstacle ever arises. (19)
Having worshipped Lalitā on the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, whether a woman or a man, one indeed attains the desired state.
Having bathed in the Lalitā-tīrtha and having prostrated before Lalitā, one shall obtain grace everywhere, regardless of whatever one may utter.
O Sage, the fair-complexioned Gaurī stands before you with wide eyes, always dispelling great obstacles for those who possess devotion to this sacred field.
During the autumnal Navarātra, a pilgrimage must be performed with great effort for the sake of fulfilling all desires, indeed for the sake of the Goddess Viśvabhujā. (23)
If a man does not bow to the goddess Viśvabhujā in Vārāṇasī, how can there be peace for that evil-minded one from great calamities? (24)
But for those by whom the goddess Viśvabhujā was praised and worshipped in Vārāṇasī, no multitude of obstacles shall afflict them, for they are of virtuous nature. (25)
There is another Vārāhī in Kāśī, in the vicinity of Kratuvārāha; by bowing to her with devotion, a person does not sink into the ocean of calamity. (26)
Śivadūtī, the destroyer of calamities, is to be beheld right there; for the protection of the Forest of Bliss, she holds her trident raised and points with her threatening finger at the enemies.
Likewise, Vajrahastā and Aindrī, seated upon a chariot drawn by a king of elephants, are worshipped on the southern side of Indreśa; they always bestow prosperity.
Near Skandeśvara, Kaumārī resides upon a peacock; she should be visited with diligence for the sake of attaining an abundance of great fruits. (29)
To the south of Maheśvara, the goddess Māheśvarī, who possesses a bull as her vehicle and bestows the prosperity of great bulls, should be worshipped by men. (30)
Near Nirvāṇanarasiṃha, those desiring liberation should worship Nārasiṃhī, whose beautiful arms raise a discus.
Brahmī, who possesses a swan-vehicle, is situated to the west of Brahmeśa; she is auspicious when struck by the handfuls of water falling from her water-pot.
For the sake of awakening to the knowledge of Brahman, she should be worshipped daily in Kāśī by Brāhmaṇas and ascetics who constantly seek the realization of their own true nature. (33)
One should take refuge in Nārāyaṇī at Kāśī, who destroys all obstacles by means of great arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow here and there.
He who bows to Nārāyaṇī—who has her limbs turned westward, whose wheel is whirling, and who has raised her finger—attains great prosperity in Kāśī.
Then, having worshipped Gaurī Virūpākṣā in the northern direction from Devayānī with devotion, a man obtains his desired prosperity. || 36 ||
Śaileśvarī, who dwells near Śaileśvara, should be worshipped; she threatens with her forefinger the contact born of calamities.
Having bathed in Citrakūpa, which bestows wonderful fruits upon men, and having beheld Citragupteśvara and worshipped Citraghaṇṭā; || 38 ||
Even if he is burdened with many sins or has abandoned the path of dharma, a man who worships Citraghaṇṭā shall not be subject to the recording of Citragupta.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever does not worship Citraghaṇṭā in Kāśī, thousands of obstacles attend upon him at every step.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a pilgrimage should be undertaken with diligence; a great festival must be celebrated, as well as a vigil at night. (41)
Having worshipped Citraghaṇṭā with great articles of worship, one does not hear here the bell of Antaka (the God of Death) hanging from the neck of his buffalo.
Having bowed to Citragrīvā to the east of Citrāṅgadeśvara, a living being shall never behold the wondrous torments of Yama.
Having seen Bhadrakālī, a man never beholds anything inauspicious; he who has performed his water-libations at the Bhadravāpī pond in front of Bhadranāga [attains the same].
Having worshipped Harasiddhi with diligence, the best of men attains great success from Siddhivināyaka in the east.
Having worshipped Vidhi according to the prescribed rites with various offerings, one attains manifold success that leads into the presence of Vidhīśvara.
A person who has bathed well at the Prayāga tīrtha and has worshipped Nigaḍabhañjanī is never again oppressed by fetters. (47)
On every Tuesday, the goddess Nigaḍabhañjanī should always be worshipped with devotion by one who has observed a single meal, desiring the liberation of prisoners.
When worshipped, she even grants the severance of the bonds of saṃsāra; what account can there be for chains and the like when she herself is worshipped? (49)
For even a kinsman who is far away shall quickly come together with those men who take refuge at the feet of Bandī with faith; of this there is no doubt. (50)
If she is resorted to by adhering to even some small restraint, Kāśī—the dispeller of doubt—swiftly fulfills all desires.
The Goddess, who holds a heavy chisel in her hand and severs the bonds of her devotees, fulfills which desire indeed when she dwells near the King of Tīrthas?
The Goddess, situated behind the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati) in the presence of Amṛteśvara, should be diligently saluted after bathing in the Amṛta-kūpa.
Having worshipped the goddess Amṛteśvarī with devotion, a person shall indeed attain immortality by serving her lotus feet.

Who, having meditated upon Mahāmāyā holding the pitcher of nectar in her [upper] right hand, granting fearlessness with her [lower] right, and [holding the same] in her left, would not partake in immortality? 55.
Siddhalakṣmī, the sustainer of the world, is worshipped as the bestower of perfection in the west, in front of the Prapitāmaha Liṅga and Amṛteśvara.
Who, having beheld the palace of Siddhalakṣmī, which is shaped like a lotus and is known as Lakṣmīvilāsa, would not attain prosperity? (57)
Then Kubjā, the Mother of the World, is to be worshipped in front of the Nalakūvara Liṅga and to the west of Prapitāmaha. 58.
When worshipped, Kubjā removes all remaining obstacles; therefore, those seeking welfare should worship Kubjā in Kāśī with great effort. (59)
To the west of Nalakūbara is the Kubjāmbarēśvara Liṅga; there Gaurī, known as Trilokasundarī, should be worshipped, for she bestows all desired objects.
The goddess Trailokyasundarī bestows the perfection of being beautiful throughout the three worlds; by the worship of that goddess, widowhood is never encountered anywhere. (61)
The great Śakti named Dīptā resides near Sāṃbāditya; by worshipping her, those possessed of radiant splendor are born.
In the presence of Śrīkaṇṭha, the Goddess Mahālakṣmī, the mother of the world, bathed in the Śrīkuṇḍa Tīrtha and worshipped the Mother of the Universe.
Having duly gratified the ancestors at the sacred ford known as Śrīkuṇḍa, and having given gifts according to the prescribed rites, one is never abandoned by Lakṣmī.
The field of Lakṣmī is a great seat (mahāpīṭha) that bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner alone; by practicing mantras there, a man shall attain success.
There are many sacred seats (pīṭhas) in Kāśī that grant spiritual accomplishments; yet there is no other supreme seat equal to Mahālakṣmīpīṭha for bestowing prosperity.
Having reached the Mahālakṣmyaṣṭamī, for those men who perform a pilgrimage there and worship Padmā according to the prescribed rites, she does not abandon their abode.
To the north, however, Mahālakṣmī, wielding a horse-necked spear and an axe, cuts down the great trees that obstruct Kāśī every single day.
The power of the Tortoise, Mahālakṣmī, holding a noose in her right hand, binds the multitude of obstacles in this sacred field at every moment. (69)
Worshiped and praised by mortals, she bestows the perfection of the sacred field (kṣetra-siddhi). And in the northwest is the fierce Śikhī, the supreme guardian of the field.
Devouring the multitude of obstacles, she utters a shrieking sound; by the mere sight of her, all diseases of men perish.
Bhīmacaṇḍī always guards the northern gate without weariness; she stands before Bhīmeśvara, bearing a noose and a mallet.
Having beheld Bhīmacaṇḍī and performed the water-libation at Bhīmakuṇḍa, a virtuous man shall never again behold the Yama-messengers of fearsome appearance.
To the right of the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) is the goddess Chāgavaktreśvarī; day and night she devours the sprouts of the tree of the multitude of obstacles.
By the grace of that goddess, residence in Kāśī is obtained; therefore, one should worship the goddess Chāgeśvarī on the Mahāṣṭamī day.
The goddess Tālajaṅgheśvarī, who has made a palmyra tree her weapon, destroys the multitudes of obstacles situated within Ānandavana.
Having bowed to Tālajaṅgheśvarī, who has a formidable countenance, to the south of the Saṃgameśvara Liṅga, one is not overcome by obstacles.
To the south of the Uddālakeśvara Liṅga is the holy site named Uddālaka; and there is the one called Yamadaṃṣṭrā, which chews away the multitude of obstacles.
Having prostrated before Yamadaṃṣṭra at the sacred ford named Uddālaka, even those who have committed a multitude of sins do not fear Yama here.
At the Dārukeśvara Tīrtha, near Dārukeśa, she has the surface of Pātāla for her face, the sky for her lips, and the earth for her lower lip.
She holds a skull and a scythe in her hands, is fond of devouring the cosmic egg, has a withered belly, is bound by sinews, and is renowned as Carmamuṇḍā.
Protecting the eastern quarter of the field from the host of obstacles, she possesses shimmering thousand-fold staff-like arms and blazing, squinting eyes.
Her hands extend across the near and far shores, holding sweets for her enemies; she is clothed in a leopard skin and laughs with a fierce, loud, and terrifying laugh.
[She saw] the bodies of the wicked, those who committed treachery against sacred fields and were impaled on the points of stakes, being violently chewed like lotus stalks by the sinners. 84.

Having bowed to her who is adorned with a garland of skulls, who possesses a most terrifying form, and who holds a hide and a severed head, a person is not afflicted by obstacles within the sacred field (kṣetra). || 85 ||
Just as this Carmamuṇḍā is, so too is this Mahāruṇḍā; the only difference between them is that she is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
"O two goddesses of great power, protect the field! Laughing and clapping your hands with the stretching out of your arms against one another. (87)
At the Hayagrīveśvara Tīrtha, always situated to the north of Lolārka, resides Mahāruṇḍā, who has a fierce face and removes the obstacles of her devotees.
O deities, between those two who have been described as Carmamuṇḍā and Mahāruṇḍā stands Cāmuṇḍā, who has the form of a severed head.
These three should be worshipped with great effort by the residents of the sacred field; they bestow wealth and grain, and these grant sons and grandsons.
When remembered, seen, touched, or worshipped with faith by men, they destroy misfortunes and bestow the glory of ultimate liberation.
And in the west is the auspicious goddess Mahāruṇḍā, the sovereign of dreams; she shall declare in a dream the future, both auspicious and inauspicious, before her devotee.
There, having bathed at the meritorious confluence of the Asī, one should visit the Svapneśvara Liṅga and likewise the goddess Svapneśvarī on any lunar day whatsoever.
Whether a woman or a man, the wise person intent on fasting, having performed worship and sleeping upon the bare ground, shall behold what is to come in a dream.
Even today, one who possesses discernment should place their trust in this: the Mistress of Dreams speaks of everything—past, future, and present—at night. (95)
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth day, by night or by day, she should be worshipped with great effort in Kāśī by men seeking knowledge.
And Durgādevī is established in the western direction of Svapneśvarī; she always protects the southern part of the sacred field. || 97 ||

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Abode of the Deities," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 70 ||
Agastya said: "O son of Umā, how did the name 'Durgā' come to belong to the Goddess? And how is she to be worshipped in Kāśī? Explain this to me here."
Skanda said: O one of great intelligence, I shall tell you how the goddess came to be named Durgā and how she is to be worshipped by spiritual practitioners.
A great Daitya named Durga was born as the son of the Daitya Ruru; having performed intense penance, he attained invincibility against men.
Then, having conquered all the worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar in battle through the power of his own arms, he brought them under his own control.
He himself was Indra, he himself was Vāyu, he himself was Candra, and he himself was Yama; he himself was Agni, he himself was Varuṇa, and he himself became the powerful Kubera.
He himself assumed the station of Īśāna, Rudra, Arka, and the Vasus; and out of fear of him, the ascetics abandoned their austerities.
Afflicted by fear of him, the Brahmins did not engage in the study of the Vedas; the sacrificial enclosures were utterly destroyed by his unbearable soldiers.
Those virtuous women were repeatedly devastated by those who had taken refuge in unrighteous paths; and having forcibly seized the property of others, they became difficult to approach.
Those of evil conduct, who had embraced cruel deeds, drank [the waters]; the rivers flowed out of their courses, and the fires blazed up unlike before.
Alas! The luminaries do not shine, being agitated by fear; the garments of the quarters, like women, have become lusterless on all sides.
Those very ones who had abandoned the performance of dharma and were engaged in evil deeds became clouds and rained down by their own playful power. 11.
Out of fear of him, the earth produced crops even though they were not sown; and even trees that were previously barren became constantly fruit-bearing.
By that exceedingly arrogant one, the wives of the celestial sages were taken captive; by him, all the inhabitants of heaven were turned into forest-dwellers.
Mortals, afflicted by fear and beset by calamities, do not honor even the immortals who have arrived at their own homes, even with a mere word of greeting.
Skanda said: Neither noble birth nor virtuous conduct conduces to greatness; indeed, a single state is superior, for falling from one's position is a cause of humiliation.
For even in misfortune, those are truly fortunate who, though driven by wretchedness, never at any time seek the company of those with defiled minds for the sake of wealth.
Indeed, even death in this world is better if it is free from humiliation; immortality, however, is not desirable if it is accompanied by humiliation. (17)
Only they truly live in this world and only they are partakers of merit, whose ocean-like mind does not abandon its profundity even in times of calamity.
Sometimes there is the rise of prosperity, and sometimes the emergence of adversity; having encountered both through fate, a wise man should not abandon his fortitude. (19)
The wise should observe the rising and setting of the two suns; their constant uniformity is never abandoned, whereas joy and sorrow are therefore transient.
He who, having encountered misfortune, falls into ruin overcome by dejection, has lost both worlds; therefore, one should avoid dejection. || 21 ||
For even when misfortune occurs, those who are wise in this world and the next shall not be touched by it again, since it has been cast aside by their steadfastness.
Having been deprived of their kingdom, the gods went for refuge to Maheśa; then, urged by the Goddess, the Omniscient One set out to crush the asuras.
Having approached Bhavānī, the consort of Maheśvara, he joyfully received her command; then, granting fearlessness to the immortal one, he proceeded toward battle.
Having summoned Kālarātri, who was more beautiful than the three worlds, Rudrāṇī sent her to invite the enemy of the gods.
Having approached that Daitya of wicked conduct, Kālarātrī said: "O Lord of the Daityas, relinquish the prosperity of the three worlds!"
"Let Indra obtain the three worlds, but you go to the netherworld (rasātala). Let all the rites prescribed in the Vedas proceed for those who speak the Veda."
If, however, there is even a trace of pride in you, then come to the assembly; or else, if you desire to live, then go for refuge to Indra.
Thus, by the Great Goddess, who is the embodiment of supreme auspiciousness, I have been sent to your presence; for she disregards your death.
Therefore, O great asura, do whatever is appropriate to be done; if you desire the ultimate welfare, listen, and then depart while we are still alive.
Having heard these words of the goddess Mahākālī, that king of the Daityas then blazed with anger and cried out, "Seize her! Seize her! (31)

For she, who enchants the three worlds, has been obtained through the weight of my good fortune; she is the great fruit of the creeper of prosperity consisting of sovereignty over the three worlds. (32)
"For this very purpose, O divine sage, the king and the captive were seized by me; through the dawning of auspiciousness, she has come to my home without effort. (33)
Whatever is destined for someone will inevitably come to them here, whether in the forest or in the home, because of the weight of one's fortune. (34)
"Let these women of the inner apartments lead her to the great inner apartment; by her being present here, my kingdom has been made truly adorned. (35)
"O high-minded one, today a great prosperity has arisen for me—not only for me alone, but for the entire lineage of the Daityas. (36)
"Let the ancestors dance today, and let my kinsmen rejoice in happiness; let Death, Time, the Ender, and the gods themselves experience fear from me this day! (37)
Thus, just as the chamberlains arrived to lead her away, that bull among the Daityas was addressed by her, who was like the Night of Doom.

Kālarātri said: "O King of the Daityas, O one of great wisdom, this is not fitting for those such as you. We are messengers subject to another's will, O best among those who know the science of statecraft. (39)
Even a person of little means should never cause distress to messengers, much less those who are great, powerful lords like you. (40)
"O Great King, what affection can there be here for these insignificant female messengers? By their arrival, we shall come [to you] without any effort. (41)
"O Lord of the Daityas, having conquered my mistress in battle, enjoy thousands like me as you desire. (42)
This very day, through the sight of you who have been meditated upon, there shall be great happiness for you; today there will be joy for your kinsmen together with your ancestors.
Today all those desires that you have long contemplated shall be fulfilled; she is weak and innocent, and there is no one to protect her.
And you ought to behold her who consists of all forms; for I shall show you where that mine of the world resides.
"And even if only one were held, what desire of yours would remain? I shall not abandon your presence until this very day. (46)
"Then ward off these chamberlains who wish to seize me from me. Having heard her words, he, deluded by lust, anger, and delusion, [acted accordingly]. (47)
The Asura regarded that single messenger alone as sufficient, just as Death does; and let these pure ones quickly bring him to her, who is pure and has a pure inner self.
Thus instructed by him, O Sage, all those excellent sages, being exceedingly powerful, made an effort to seize her by force.
She quickly reduced them to ashes by means of the fire generated from her *huṃkāra*. Then the lord of the Daityas, seeing them turned to ashes, became enraged. (50)
In an instant, by means of that female messenger, she cast her gaze upon thirty thousand Daityas—namely Durdhara, Durmukha, and Khara.
Sīrapāṇi, Pāśapāṇi, the subduer of Surendra, Hanu, Yajñāri, Khaṅgaloman, Ugrāsya, and Devakampana.
"O Dānavas, bind this wicked woman with nooses and bring her here quickly, with her hair and ornaments disheveled and her garments fallen away. (53)
Thus, by the command of the lord of the Daityas, those led by Durdhara, bearing nooses, swords, and mallets, then made an effort to seize her.
With bodies as massive as the king of mountains and weapons and missiles raised in their hands, they reached the ends of the quarters, struck by the wind of his breath.
When those Daityas, numbering one hundred crores, had flown up, that Kālarātri then emerged, traveling through the sky.
Then, as she was departing, thousands of millions upon millions of great asuras followed her, filling both heaven and earth.
A great Daitya named Durga was surrounded by a hundred crores of chariots and encircled by two hundred arbudas of elephants.
Accompanied by ten billion horses with the speed of the wind, and by innumerable foot soldiers who had pulverized mountain peaks, [he advanced].
Accompanied by those most formidable beings who held raised weapons and struck fear into the three worlds, that great Daitya Durga went forth in a rage.
Then, having seen the Great Goddess whose abode is on the Vindhya mountain, Kālarātri approached her and reported that transgression.
She was endowed with a thousand great arms, augmented by immense splendor, wielding various terrible weapons, and intent upon the excitement of battle.
Her auspicious face was polished by the rays of a thousand full moons, and she was like the singular moonlight emerging from the surging ocean of loveliness.
Her form was inlaid with the radiance of a great mass of rubies; she was a brilliantly shining lamp for the beautiful city of the three worlds. || 64 ||
She is the medicinal creeper that revives the life of Kāma, who was consumed by the fire from Śiva’s eye; she is the great elixir that deludes the world with her radiant abundance of beauty.
His heart pierced by arrows in the uneven parts of his body, that bull among Daityas, who commanded the great army, issued orders to his generals.
O Jambha, Mahājambha, Kujambha, you of the hideous countenance! O Laṃbodara, Mahākāya, Mahādaṃṣṭra, Mahāhana! || 67 ||

O tawny-eyed one, O buffalo-necked one, O you of most fierce and extremely terrible form! O cruel-eyed one, O wrathful one, O you who cause others to cry out, O you who roar, O source of great fear! 68.
O conqueror of Death, O mighty-armed one, O great-faced one, O upholder of the earth! O Dundubhi, O you whose roar is like a drum, O you with a nose like a great drum!

With a fierce face, long fangs, and hair as thick as a boar's bristles, you have the face of a wolf, the face of a lion, and the face of a boar; you are exceedingly terrible with the howl of a jackal.
O you with a parrot’s beak, fierce face, and terrifying eyes; O you of voracious mind, owl-eyes, heron-beak, crow-beak, and formidable speech! 71.
O long-necked one, O great-thighed one, O camel, O upholder of the head; O you with blood-drops, with eyes like hibiscus flowers, with a tongue like lightning, and who heats like fire! 72.
O Dhūmrākṣa, O Dhūmaniḥśvāsa, O Caṇḍacaṇḍāṃśutāpana, and you who are led by Mahābhīṣaṇa, listen to my command with respect! 73.
Among you, these others, or anyone else, he will bring this Vindhyavāsinī here by means of fortitude, intellect, force, or even through deception.
"Today I shall undoubtedly grant him the station of Indra; having seen this beautiful woman today, my mind has become agitated. (72)
"Let them go quickly; otherwise, my mind, afflicted by the arrows of the five-arrowed god [Kāma], will fall into a state of agitation due to the impossibility of attaining her. (76)
Having heard these words of Durga, the lord of the Danujas, all the Daityas then spoke with their hands joined in reverent salutation.
Listen, O Great King: what is so difficult in this deed? It is for one who is helpless, alone, and especially a woman. (78)
O Lord, what is this method of great effort for bringing her here? Who are we, compared to the great masses of flames of the fire at the time of universal dissolution? (79)
By your grace, he would withstand those who exert themselves against him throughout the three worlds; if the command should be given today, then let him [conquer] Indra along with the host of Maruts.
Having brought her along with the women of the inner apartments, we shall cast her at your feet; for this entire realm—Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar—is subject to your command. (81)
O great Asura, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka are all under your authority; yet even there, nothing is impossible for us by your command.
The eternal lord of Vaikuṇṭha, who faithfully carries out your commands, joyfully dispatched whatever beautiful gems there were.
Indeed, that lord of Kailāsa was abandoned by us alone; because of his extreme poverty, he became the Vipāśī, smeared with ashes and adorned with snakes as ornaments.
Out of fear of us, a certain woman has hidden herself with only half her body; even in his entire village, there is not a single four-footed animal.
There is but one old bull, and even he does not subsist on anything other than others; all dwell in the cremation ground, and all are clad only in loincloths.
All are white with their supernatural splendor, and all have a single matted lock; such are the Gaṇas who dwell in his entire city.
"O Lord, what can we do for those hosts who are impoverished? The oceans send us a collection of jewels every single day. (88)
O Lord, these wretched nāgas themselves constantly light the jewel-lamps upon their hoods for us every evening. (89)
By your grace, even the wish-fulfilling tree, the cow of plenty, and numerous wish-granting gems abide within our very homes. (90)
The wind, having become a fan, serves you with great effort; and Varuṇa, oh wonder, fills [the vessels] daily with pure waters! 91.
May Agni wash his garments, may Candra himself hold the umbrella, and may Sūrya eternally illuminate the lotuses in the pleasure-pool.
Who among mortals, immortals, or serpents would not behold your grace? All—the gods, asuras, birds, and others—depend upon you for their livelihood. (93)
"Behold our prowess, O King; we shall bring her here by force! Having spoken thus, they all simultaneously became as agitated as the oceans.
Having reached the time of universal dissolution (saṃvartaka) to submerge this world, the sound of battle trumpets arose from all sides.
Because their hair stood on end upon hearing it, even those who were timid became fearless; consequently, the gods trembled with fear and the earth shook.
All the oceans were agitated and the garlands of stars fell; indeed, the entire circle of heaven and earth was pervaded by that sound of musical instruments.
Then the Blessed Goddess brought forth from her own body hundreds and thousands of Śaktis.
By those powers, the surging ocean of the army of these mighty sons of Diti was individually hemmed in on all sides.
The fierce weapons and missiles that were hurled by the great Daityas in the battle were instantly treated as mere blades of grass by those Śaktis and cast aside.
Then those enemies of the gods, led by Jambha and filled with extreme rage, [assailed him] with swords, discuses, *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons, maces, clubs, and lances.
With *bhiṇḍipāla* slings, iron clubs, spears, barbed arrows, javelins, crescent-headed shafts, razor-sharp arrows, iron bolts, and feathered shafts; || 2 ||
With great bhalla-arrows, axes, and bhindu-missiles that pierce the vital organs, they rained down like clouds with a great shower of trees and stones.
Then that Mahāmāyā, the Great Goddess whose abode is the Vindhya mountains, took up her formidable bow and, with ease, [discharged] the Vāyavya weapon.
He cast away the multitude of Daitya missiles and weapons to a distance; then the great asura Durga beheld his army rendered weaponless.
Taking up a blazing spear, he hurled it at that goddess; indeed, that spear came rushing toward him in the battle with great velocity.
She reduced it to powder with arrows discharged from her own bow; then, seeing the spear shattered, the great asura Durga [acted].
And he hurled a discus that brought great joy to the host of Daityas; but that was reduced to atoms by the Goddess with hundreds of arrows even before it could reach its mark.
Then, taking up the Śārṅga bow which was like the rainbow of Indra, that destroyer of the immortals pierced that goddess in the heart with an arrow.
O Sage, although that arrow was warded off by the goddess with her own exceedingly swift arrows, it still rushed impetuously toward the goddess.
Then, having struck that swift arrow with his own swift staff-like bow, he warded it off as if it were another staff of Death.
When that arrow had turned away, the Asura Durgama, enraged, took up a trident that shone like the fire of universal destruction.
The lord of the Daityas hurled it with great speed toward the goddess; but Caṇḍikā struck down that trident with her own trident.
Right there, he cut it down along with his hope for victory over the Daityas—even as that great trident was being disregarded by the Goddess’s own trident.
Taking up his mace, the lord of the Daityas suddenly rushed forward; and that one of great strength struck the goddess on the base of her arm.
That goddess as well, having reached his arm which was shaped like the peak of the king of mountains, shattered the mace instantly into hundreds and thousands of pieces.
Then that lord of the Daityas, struck by the goddess with the sole of her left foot, fell to the earth, his heart severely tormented.
At that very moment, the lord of the Daityas, having fallen, rose up again; he suddenly became visible like a lamp extinguished by the wind.
Then the powers belonging to the Mother of the World, being impelled by her, moved among the Daitya armies like the army of Death at the time of universal dissolution.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Prowess of Durga," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: O Skanda, delighter of Pārvatī’s heart, son of the Omniscient One! Tell me, who indeed are those Śaktis and what are their names? || 1 ||
Skanda said: O sage born from a jar, listen to the names of those supreme powers who were born from the limbs of Umā, as I recount them according to their true nature.
Trailokyavijayā, Tārā, Kṣamā, Trailokyasundarī, Tripurā, the Mother of the Three Worlds, Bhīmā, and Tripurabhairavī. (3)
Kāmākhyā, Kamalākṣī, Dhṛti, Tripuratāpanī, Jayā, Jayantī, Vijayā, Jaleśī, and Aparājitā. || 4 ||
Śaṅkhinī, Gajavaktrā, Mahiṣaghnī, Raṇapriyā, Śubhānandā, Koṭarākṣī, Vidyujjihvā, and Śivāravā. || 5 ||

She has three eyes and three faces, she has three feet, and she is the source of all auspiciousness; her weapon is the syllable *huṃ*, she is the mistress of the rhythmic beat (*tāla*), she has the face of a serpent, and she is the most beautiful of all.
Siddhi, Buddhi, Svadhā, Svāhā, Mahānidrā, Śarāśanā, Pāśapāṇi, Kharamukhī, Vajratārā, and Ṣaḍānanā. || 7 ||

She has the face of a peacock, she is the female crow, the female parrot, the female vulture, and the female garuḍa; she is Padmāvatī, she has hair like a lotus, a lotus-like face, and dwells in a lotus.

She consists of syllables and is three-syllabled; she is the thread, the mistress of the *praṇava*, and identical with the vowels. She comprises the three aims of life, is free from pride, and is the *ajapā* that takes away the need for recitation.

She is the perfection of recitation, the perfection of austerity, and the supreme nectar of yoga-perfection; she is the creator of friendliness, the one with eyes like a friend, the slayer of Rākṣasas, and the scorcher of the Daityas.
She is the paralyzer, the deluder, the illusory one, possessed of great illusion and fierce power; she is the expeller, with a face like a great meteor, the destroyer of the lords of the Danavas.
She who brings security, she who grants success, Chinnamastā of auspicious countenance, Śākambharī, the Fortune of Liberation, and the bestower of the fruits of the three aims of life.
Vārtālī, Jaṃbhalī, Klinnā, Aśvārūḍhā, Sureśvarī, Jvālāmukhī, and others—these nine crores are of great power.
By those [powers], the strengths of the powerful Dānavas were effortlessly compressed, as if by the flames of the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon.
Meanwhile, that powerful Durga, the lord of the Daityas, from within the clouds, unleashed a heavy downpour of hailstones accompanied by a forceful whirlwind.
Then, by the employment of the Śoṣaṇa weapon, the divine Bhagavatī instantly warded off the rain consisting of stones and hail.
Just as a woman full of desire becomes fruitless upon encountering a eunuch, so too did that shower of Daitya weapons become fruitless upon reaching the Goddess. || 17 ||
Then, by the king of the Daityas, out of anger at the contraction of his arms, a mountain peak was uprooted and hurled from the expanse of the sky.
Beholding the mountain peak, which was exceedingly vast, as it came rushing toward her, she shattered it entirely into millions of pieces with a blow from her thunderbolt.
Repeatedly shaking his head, which was adorned with two earrings, the asura quickly assumed the form of an elephant and rushed at the goddess in battle.
Seeing that elephant approaching with the form of a mountain, the Blessed Lady bound it with a noose and swiftly severed its trunk with her sword.
Then, having let out a great cry, that elephant, his trunk severed by the Goddess, became powerless and assumed the body of a buffalo.
Due to the assault of the gods, that powerful one made all mountains—both immovable and movable—shake; he repeatedly hurled heaps of rocks with his two horns.
Struck by the wind of his breath, great trees fell to the earth; even the seven oceans overflowed their bounds.
By him, in the form of a great buffalo, the pavilion of the three worlds was shaken by that powerful one, as if by a whirlwind at the end of an eon.
Seeing even the cosmic egg agitated by that sudden terror, the Blessed Lady became enraged and struck him with her trident.
Dazed by the blow of the trident, he fell down and rose again; abandoning that buffalo form, he became a possessor of a thousand arms.
That Durga appeared exceedingly difficult to overcome upon the field of battle, bearing thousands of weapons and resembling the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then that lord of the Daityas, possessed of great strength, quickly seized that goddess who was skilled in combat and swiftly carried her into the expanse of the sky.
Then, having hurled the Mother of the World from afar across the expanse of the sky, the swift one covered her in an instant with a mass of arrows.
Then the goddess moving through the intermediate space, situated in the midst of his search, shone like a garland of lightning held within a mass of great clouds.
Having thoroughly shaken off that shower of arrows with her own volleys, she then pierced that lord of the Daitya folk with a great shaft.
Pierced in the heart by that goddess and by that great arrow, he fell to the earth overwhelmed, his eyes rolling.
And causing a great stream of blood to flow as he fell upon that fortress, which possessed the prowess of a most formidable stronghold.
The celestial drums resounded and the worlds were filled with joy; the sun and the moon, along with fire, regained their own natural brilliance.
