The gods, accompanied by great sages, arrived showering flowers and reverently praised the Great Goddess with magnificent hymns.
The gods said: "Salutations, O Goddess, sustainer of the world, great forest-fire of the three worlds! O Maheśvarī, possessor of great power, axe for the trees that are the Daityas! (37)
Obeisance to you, O Śivā, who pervades the three worlds, who bear the conch, the discus, and the mace, with the tips of your hands occupied by your own bow, O you whose very nature is Viṣṇu!
Salutations to you, who ride upon a swan, the ordainer of all creation, the birthplace of the ancient speech, and the one whose form is the four-faced Brahmā. (39)
You are Aindrī, you are Kauberī, you are Vāyavī, and you are Ambupā; you are Yāmī, you are Nairṛtī, you are Aiśī, and you are Pāvakī.
You are the moonlight of the moon, and you alone are the solar power; you alone are the Supreme Goddess, the power consisting of all the gods.
You are Gaurī, you are Sāvitrī, you are Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; you are Prakṛti, you are Mati, and you are she whose form is Ahaṃkṛti.
O Ambikā, you are indeed the embodiment of consciousness; you are the embodiment of all the senses; you are the form of the five subtle elements, whose nature is the great elements.

You are indeed the embodiment of sound and the other [objects of sense]; you are the one who bestows grace upon the senses; O Goddess, you are the creator of the cosmic egg, for you alone exist within that cosmic egg.
You are the Supreme, O Great Goddess; and you, O Goddess, are both the Higher and the Lower. You are the highest among those who are higher and lower, having the nature of the Supreme Self.
O Īśānī, you are all forms; O omnipresent one, you are formless. You are the power of consciousness, O Mahāmāyā; you are Svāhā and you are Svadhā, O Immortal One.
You are the very nature of Vaṣaṭ and Vauṣaṭ; you alone are the essence of the Praṇava. You indeed consist of all mantras, and Brahmā and the other gods have originated from you.

You indeed consist of the fourfold aims of life, and you are the source of the arising of the fruits of those fourfold aims; from you comes this entire universe, and everything is contained within you, O treasure-house of the world. (48)
Whatever is visible and whatever is invisible, in its gross and subtle forms—in all that, you exist in the form of power; nothing exists anywhere apart from you.

O Mother, by slaying today the great lord of the asuras—Durga, who was surrounded by a host of daityas surrendered to the gods by nature—you have saved us, O Goddess, you who are the eternal refuge for those who bow before you; for who else is there in this world to whom we may go for protection? (50)

In this world, they alone possess the abundance of wealth and grain; they are endowed with sons, grandsons, virtuous wives, and good friends. O Lord, for those in whom you reside as the true vision, the entire universe becomes as bright as the spreading rays of the moon, and their fame shall spread far and wide.

O Consort of the Enemy of Tripura, where could even a trace of misfortune or affliction ever affect those people whose minds are devoted to You? And for those who take refuge in the cycle of Your names throughout their entire lives, how could there be rebirth here again? 52.

It is wonderful that in this battle, even that Durgadaitya, having encountered the fall of your glance which is a treasury of nectar, fell under the power of death; for it is known, O Bhavānī, that even a wicked person who comes within the range of your sight does not go to a miserable state.

Even the Daityas here, though reduced to the state of moths in the fire of your weapons, attain the splendor of birds and ascend to heaven; for the virtuous do not harbor ill-will even toward the wicked, but rather, like friends toward the good, they point out the right path.

O Mṛḍānī, always protect those who bow before you in the eastern direction; O Bhavānī, guard us at every step from calamities in the southern direction; O wife of the burner of Tripura, protect us in the western quarter; and O Maheśī, preserve your own devotees in the northern direction.

O Brahmāṇī, always protect the region of the crown of my bowed head; O Vaiṣṇavī, protect me from every direction below; may Mṛtyuñjayā, Trinayanā, Tripurā, and Triśakti protect me in the directions of Rudra, Agni, Nairṛti, and Sadāgati (Vāyu). (56)

May the stainless trident protect the region of your forehead born from your crown; may the crescent moon protect your gentle eyebrows; may the consort of the Three-eyed Lord protect your eyes; may Girijā protect your nose; may Jayā protect your upper lip; and may Vijayā protect the region of your lower lip. (57)
May Śruti protect our two ears, Śrī our row of teeth, Caṇḍī our pair of cheeks, and Vāṇī our tongue; may Jayamaṅgalā always protect our chin, and Kātyāyanī our entire facial orb. 58.

May the Blue-throated Goddess (Nīlakaṇṭhī) descend here upon the region of our necks; may the Earth-bearing Power (Bhūdāra-śakti) [dwell] constantly in the nape of our necks; may the Tortoise-form (Kaurmya) [protect] our shoulder-region constantly; and may the Indra-like Power (Aindrī) and Padmā [protect] the staff-like arms and the palms of those of us who offer salutation. 59.

May the hand-fingers protect us—those born from the lotus with stainless nails; may she who dwells in the solar orb protect the space between the armpits, destroying darkness; may the one moving on land protect the chest, and the Earth protect the heart; and may she who slays the night-stalkers protect our two thighs.

May the Mistress of the Universe, Daradarī, always protect our navel; may Nabhogati protect our back, and may Ajā protect our waist. May Vikaṭā protect our buttocks, Guhāraṇi our private parts, and Apāyahantṛ protect our anus.

May Vipulā protect the two thighs, Lalitā the knees, and Javā the shanks; may Kaṭhoratarā protect the ankles here, Ugrā the feet, Rasātalacarā the region of the toes, Cāndrī the nails, and Talavāsinī the soles of the feet. 62.
May Lakṣmī protect our home; may she who always brings security protect our field; may she who grants what is dear protect our sons; and may the eternal one protect our lifespan.
May Mahādevī protect my fame; may Dhanurdharī protect my dharma; may Kuladevī protect my lineage; and may Sadgatipradā grant me a good rebirth.
May Śarvāṇī protect me in every way—in battle, in the royal court, at dice, in combat, amidst the perils of enemies, in the home, in the forest, in water, and elsewhere. 65.
Having thus praised the Mother of the World, all the gods, including Indra, along with the sages, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, bowed down to her again and again.

"I am exceedingly pleased by this hymn of praise which is so true to the facts; I shall grant another boon, so listen to it, O best of gods. (68)

The cruel Jhoṭiṅga Rākṣasas, poisons, serpents, fire, and thieves; as well as Vetālas, Kaṅkālagrahas, and even Bālagrahas. (74)

"By my command, they shall provide protection for my devotees. Having thus granted these boons to the gods at that time, the Goddess then departed.

O Sage, these and others, who delight in the blood of the wicked, always protect the field on all sides, terrifying those of evil conduct.
O Sage, born from a water-jar, those powers beginning with Trailokyavijayā and ending with Jvālāmukhī have been described here by me.
They protect Kāśī from all four directions with weapons raised; they should be worshipped with diligent effort for the pacification of great obstacles. || 2 ||
The Bhairavas, headed by Ruru, who ward off great fear, should always be worshipped in Kāśī; they are the causes of all prosperity. (3)
Vetālas of fierce form, such as Vidyujjihva and others, when worshipped here, will remove even the most formidable multitudes of obstacles.
Likewise, O Sage, a multitude of beings here, numbering one hundred crores and possessing various terrifying forms with uplifted weapons, protect the city.
These deities, who protect at every step the field of the glory of Nirvana, are indeed to be worshipped in Kashi by those who desire liberation. (6)
Having heard this meritorious chapter named "The Conquest of Difficulties," which is endowed with various powers, a person shall swiftly cross over all hardships.
Having heard the names of these Bhairavas who have been mentioned and those Vetālas who have been described, a man is no longer tormented by the Brahmins.
Even those beings who have not been seen will protect with great effort the reciter of this narrative, along with the audience.
Therefore, with every effort, men devoted to the worship of Kāśī should listen to this narrative, which wards off great obstacles. (110)
In whosever home this shall remain written and honored, the deities will destroy thousands of his calamities.
He who has true love for Kāśī should listen with great reverence to this narrative, which is like a diamond cage.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Victory of Durgā," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Agastya said: Having approached Trilocana, what did the six-faced god, the deity of deities, do immediately upon being joined by the Mother of the Universe? Tell me that.
Skanda said: O Sage, listen to that which I declare in response to what you have asked; it is the sacred seat (pīṭha) named Viraja, which is said to bestow all perfections (siddhis).
Merely by beholding that sacred seat, a man becomes free from passion; for there exists that great Liṅga, Trilocana, in Vārāṇasī.
That sacred ford known as Pilipilā, famous for its waters in the celestial river, is celebrated in Kāśī as a holy site that embodies all sacred fords.
O Sage, those three worlds—containing gods, sages, humans, and serpents, along with rivers, mountains, and forests—that exist, they are all present there.
From that time forward, that sacred ford and that Trilocana Liṅga became exceedingly famous as Triviṣṭapa for this very reason.
O Sage, I shall relate the greatness of the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga as it was told by the wielder of the Pināka bow in the presence of the Mother of the World.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the world, Śarva, giver of all, omnipresent one, all-seeing, progenitor of all—whatever I ask, please tell me that. (8)
This field of yours is dear to you; it is a great medicinal herb for the seed of karma, the home of the glory of ultimate liberation, and a source of great joy even to me.

Whatever lingas exist here, all of them without doubt are indeed causes of liberation, even though they are self-manifested.

Where the Lord always resides, even during the dissolution of the universe, that beloved city has attained this renown as Kāśī, the city of liberation.
By the mere remembrance of whom even here the destruction of sin occurs, and by seeing and touching whom, heaven and liberation are attained.
O Lord, for those who worship even once in the midst [of this world], it is certain that all the Lingas shall have been worshipped in Kashi. (15)
O ocean of the nectar of compassion, having shown me mercy, tell me this, O Śambhu; I am prostrate at your feet.
Having heard these well-spoken words of that goddess, O best of beings, Maheśāna spoke of the great liṅgas, O enemy of Vindhya.
Merely by hearing its name, heaps of sins are destroyed; one attains a store of merit, and Kāśī is the cause of liberation. || 18 ||
The God of Gods said: Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, the cause of liberation in this sacred field; even Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and the others do not know this. (19)
In the Forest of Pārvatī’s Delight (Ānandakānana), there are innumerable lingas—both large and minute—and composed of various jewels.
O Sovereign, there are many [liṅgas] made of various elements, as well as numerous ones made of stone; indeed, there are many self-manifested ones and those established by divine sages. 21.
They were also honored by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, as well as by Asuras, Uragas, mortals, Dānavas, and hosts of Apsarases.
O Goddess, the world-regents (diggajas), mountains, holy fords (tīrthas), bears, monkeys, kinnaras, and the foremost of birds have indeed marked [the earth] with their respective names.
O beloved, even those things established here as causes for liberation—though they be invisible, visible, or in a wretched state—are likewise [subject to change].
O beautiful one, even those that have been broken over time are worthy of worship; once, I counted as many as a hundred parārdhas.
O Goddess, even those sixty crores of Siddha-liṅgas that remained within the waters of the Gaṅgā became invisible during the Kali age.
O beloved, there is no known number for those [liṅgas] that have been installed here by my devotees since the days of Gaṇanādi.
O beautiful one, I shall describe those lingas which you have asked about, by means of which this most excellent field [became such], and which are the causes of liberation.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, these [mantras] will become as secret as the arts (kalās); however, their power shall not depart from its respective locus.
Those who are nourished by the impurities of the Kali age—those who are wicked, nihilists, and deceitful—even they shall not know the names of these Siddha-liṅgas here on earth.
O lady of auspicious countenance, by merely hearing the names of these lingas here, sins go to destruction and heaps of merit increase. (31)
Oṃkāra is the first liṅga, and the second is Trilocana; the third is Mahādeva, and the fourth is Kṛttivāsas.
Ratneśa is the fifth Liṅga, and the sixth is named Candreśvara; Kedāra is the seventh Liṅga, and Dharmeśa is the eighth, O beloved.
They know Vīreśvara as the ninth and Kāmeśa as the tenth; the auspicious Viśvakarmeśvara Liṅga is the supreme eleventh.
The twelfth is Maṇikarṇīśa, and the thirteenth is Avimukta; the fourteenth is the Great Liṅga known by my name, Viśveśvara.
"O dear, beautiful one, these fourteen are the causes of prosperity; this collection of them is here called the Field of Liberation."
These supreme deities are the presiding powers of this sacred field; when propitiated, they bestow upon men the glory of the highest spiritual good.
O beautiful one, O beloved, these fourteen great liṅgas have been declared for the sake of liberation by embodied beings in Ānandakānana. 38.
Beginning every month from the auspicious first lunar day (pratipadā), one should diligently perform pilgrimages to these principal lingas.
O Pot-born One, without propitiating Mahādeva through these liṅgas, who in Kāśī attains liberation? This is the truth, the truth, again and again. (40)
Therefore, O Sage, those who desire the fruit of Kāśī should worship these Liṅgas with supreme devotion and every possible effort.
Agastya said: "O Six-faced One, are these alone the great liṅgas, or are there others here that cause liberation? If they exist, then speak."
Skanda said: "O observer of noble vows, there are indeed other great liṅgas here as well; however, due to the power of the Kali age, they shall certainly remain hidden."
Only he who possesses constant devotion to the Lord and who is the most excellent knower of the truth of Kāśī shall know these Liṅgas; no one else whatsoever.
By the mere utterance of whose names the impurities of the Kali age are destroyed: Amṛteśa, Tārakeśa, Jñāneśa, and Karuṇeśvara. (45)
Mokṣadvāreśvara and likewise Svargadvāreśvara; Brahmeśa and Lāṅgala, as well as Vṛddhakāleśvara. || 46 ||
Vṛṣeśa, Caṇḍīśa, Nandikeśa, and Maheśvara—the Jyotīrūpeśvara Liṅga is celebrated here as the fourteenth. || 47 ||
O beautiful one, these fourteen great Liṅgas in Kāśī are the causes of liberation; they are the Liṅgas in Ānandakānana. (48)
These [deeds] should never be told to those whose intellects are defiled by the Kali age; however, he who worships these fourteen Liṅgas here [shall attain success]. (49)
There is never again for him a return to the path of saṃsāra; therefore, this incomparable treasure-house of Kāśī must not be disclosed to just anyone.

O beloved, the reason for the renown that liberation is certain in this field is these fourteen Liṅgas of mine.

The letter *A* is endowed with the quality of goodness (*sattva*), the field of the Ṛgveda, and the protector of creation; it is Nārāyaṇa himself, established beyond darkness (*tamas*).
Then, before him, appeared the syllable *ukāra*, born of the *yajus* and having the nature of *rajas*, like the Creator himself reflected in his own form. (83)
Then, in front of him, he beheld the letter "Ma," which resembled a dwelling place for the darkness of a waterless desert, and which was particularly characterized by the nature of obscurity.
Then, meditating upon him who was the source of the Sāman, the cause of its dissolution, and whose very nature was that of Rudra, he made him the guest of his own eyes right before him.

He whose form consists of the universal manifestation, who is both with attributes and without attributes, whose abode is the inexpressible primordial sound (nāda), and whose very body is supreme bliss.
That which is renowned as Śabdabrahman, the cause of all verbal expression, is situated above the Nāda; it is in the form of a Bindu, higher than the highest.
Through his ascetic penance, Vidhi beheld that supreme cause of causes, the source of the universe, who had been brought within the range of his vision.
It is known as "Oṃ" because of its power over all this; since it elevates the devotee, it is therefore called "Oṃ. (89)

Although formless, he was made by the Creator to possess a beautiful form and was taken into the range of vision; because he would ferry across the ocean of worldly existence one whose mind is intent on his own recitation, he became known as Tāra (the Savior), whom Brahmā beheld.
Since it is praised by all who desire supreme liberation, the *praṇava* is therefore proclaimed by them to be superior to all else. (91)
Since he leads the person who serves him to the supreme state, Brahmā has directly perceived that peaceful Praṇava.

He who consists of the three Vedas, who is the fourth state, who transcends the fourth, who is the soul of all, whose nature is sound and the point (nāda-bindu)—he was beheld by the one who moves among the twice-born.
From him the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs—the source of all things—proceeded; he was beheld by the Lotus-born Brahmā at the very beginning of the Vedas.
The bull who, bound in three ways, bellows loudly as a mass of light, has been made the object of the eye by the supreme Parameṣṭhin within the wheel.
He who has four horns, seven hands, two heads, and three feet—that god was beheld by Vidhi.
When that seed—which contains within it all beings of the past, the future, and the present, yet is itself devoid of any seed—was beheld by Druhiṇa; || 97 ||
One should seek that in which this world—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is dissolved; therefore, that Liṅga is beheld by the virtuous as the object to be dissolved. 98.
That in which the five objects appear, which indeed consists of the five Brahmas, and which is the primordial form of the five—indeed, that was perceived by Brahmā.
Then, beholding the Lord in the form of a Liṅga, who is distinct from the phenomenal world, the Creator praised Śaṅkara with the five-syllabled mantra.
Brahmā said: Salutations to you whose form is the syllable Om; salutations to the bearer of the imperishable body; salutations, O Sadāśiva, to the source of the letters beginning with 'A'.
You are the letter *a*, you are the letter *u*, and you are the letter *m*, O Formless One! Salutation to You, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, yet who transcends all form.

Salutations to you, whose essence is the Nāda; salutations to you, whose essence is the Bindu and its Kalās; to you who possess the form of both the unmanifest and the manifest, and who are the very nature of all forms. || 3 ||
Salutations to you, the treasury of light, who are devoid of birth and death; salutations to Bhava, to Rudra, and to Śarva—salutations be unto you.
Salutation to the fierce one, to the terrible one, to the lord of animals; salutation to you who are the very form of the Savior, salutation be to you, O Source of all existence.
Salutations to you who are free from illusion; salutations to you, the most auspicious one. Salutations to you, the one with matted hair; salutations to you, O blue-throated one.

Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Mountain, most bountiful, who are manifest as Śipiviṣṭa; obeisance to the one who is not short, to the dwarf, to the vast, and to the one whose form is ever-increasing.
Salutations to you, the teacher of Kumāra, who possesses the form of a youth; salutations to the one who is white, black, yellow, and of ruddy form.
Salutation to the smoke-colored one, to the tawny one, and to him of variegated luster; salutation to the pale-red colored one, and salutation to him of green splendor. || 9 ||

Salutations to the one whose essential nature consists of various colors, the Lord of the letters; salutations to you who are the form of the vowels, and salutations to you who possess the form of the consonants. || 110 ||
Salutations again and again to the one who possesses the acute, the grave, and the circumflex accents; salutations to you, the lord of short, long, and protracted vowels, together with the visarga.
Salutations to you whose nature is the *anusvāra*, O you who possess nasalization; salutations to you who are devoid of nasalization, and who take the form of dentals and palatals.

Salutations to the one whose nature consists of labials and vowels; salutations to you who are the nature of the sibilants (ūṣman), to the semi-vowels (antaḥstha), and to the fifth [letter], the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Salutations to you, O Niṣāda; salutations to you, the Lord of the Niṣādas; salutations to you who take the form of musical instruments such as the lute, the flute, and the drum. || 14 ||
Salutations to Tārā, to Maṃdra, to Ghorā, and to the one whose form is Aghora; salutations to him whose nature is Tāna, and salutations to the Lord of Mūrcchanās. || 15 ||

Salutations to the one whose nature is the aesthetic emotions (bhāva), distinguished by the permanent and transitory moods; to the lover of rhythm, to rhythm itself, and to the source of the Lāsya and Tāṇḍava dances.

To you whose very nature is the triple symphony (tauryatrika), who are greatly beloved by the triple symphony; to you, the bestower of the glory of liberation upon those who practice the triple symphony with devotion. 17.
Salutations to You whose nature is both gross and subtle, whose form is both visible and invisible; salutations to You who are near, and salutations to You who are beyond.

Salutations to the one whose nature is the expansion of speech and who transcends the expansion of speech; to the one who is both one and manifold in his divisions, and to the Lord of existence and non-existence. || 19 ||
O Śabdabrahman, salutations to you; O Parabrahman, salutations be to you. Salutations to the one known through Vedānta; salutations to the Lord of the Vedas.
Salutations to you whose nature is the Vedas, whose form is the object of the Vedas; O Lord of Pārvatī, salutations to you; O Lord of the Universe, let there be salutations to you. (21)
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; O Divine One, bestower of celestial stations! Salutations to you, Śaṅkara; salutations to you, Maheśvara.
Salutations to you, O Joy of the World; salutations to you, O Moon-crested One. Salutations to you, O Conqueror of Death; and salutations to you, the Three-eyed One.
Salutations to the one who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, the bearer of the trident weapon; salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, and salutations to the slayer of Andhaka.
Salutations to the crusher of the pride of Kandarpa, to the enemy of Jalandhara; salutations to Time, to the Death of Death, who consumed the Kālakūṭa poison.
Salutations to You, the destroyer of the sorrow of devotees, yet the sole bestower of sorrow upon the non-devotees; salutations to You, the embodiment of knowledge, who are omniscient.
O best of yogis, you are the bestower of the perfection of yoga for yogis; O one whose wealth is austerity, you are the giver of the fruit of austerities to those who practice them.
You alone are the embodiment of mantras; you are the bestower of the fruits of mantras. You are indeed the fruit of great gifts; you are the giver of great gifts.
O Lord, you alone are the great sacrifice, the bestower of the fruits of the great sacrifice; you are everything, you are all-pervading, you are indeed the giver of all, and you are the seer of all.
You are the consumer of all, the creator of all, and the agent of the dissolution of all; O you who have made your abode in the space of the hearts of yogis, homage be to you! 130.
You alone, in the form of Viṣṇu, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, protect the three worlds; O Savior, embodiment of purity, salutations be unto you! (31)
Becoming the Ordainer yourself, you alone shall ordain that, being the knower of ordinances; O bestower of the stainless state, you shall do so by assuming the form of passion (rajas).
For you alone are Mahārudra; you are the fierce Mahogras, the wearer of serpents; you alone are indeed Mahābhīma, the wanderer in the great cremation ground.
O Kṛtāntaka, having assumed a tamasic body, you become Kālāgnirudra at the end [of the age], the one who sets in motion the dissolution.
O Unborn One, through the forms of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, you manifest the entire universe, beginning with Mahat, once again by the mere lifting of your eyelashes.
The opening and closing of your eyes are the sole causes of creation and non-creation; this play with a garland of skulls belongs to you who move according to your own will. 36.
O Dhūrjaṭi, this human skull that shines upon your neck is clearly a rosary of seeds for all those who have been consumed by the end.
O Śambhu, all this proceeds from you; in you resides everything, both moving and unmoving. Who is capable of praising you, who are beyond the reach of words from time immemorial? (38)
For you are the praiser, for you are the praise, and you alone are eternally the one worthy of praise; I know only "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," and I know nothing else at all. (39)
For you alone are my refuge, and you alone are my supreme goal; I bow to you alone, O Lord—salutations to you, salutations again and again.
Having spoken thus repeatedly, the Creator prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Maheśvara, who is known as Praṇava and whose form is that of the Great Liṅga.
Īśvara said: Then, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains, having heard that supreme hymn of praise by Brahmā, which is the cause for the attainment of supreme sovereignty, I was wonderfully pleased.
"Though I am formless, I have therefore assumed a Śaṅkara-form from that Liṅga; I am pleased, so choose a boon," he said to the four-faced one.
Then the four-faced one, having arisen and beheld me directly, again cried out "Victory! Victory! and bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Then the Lotus-Seated One, his eyes filled with tears of joy and the hairs on his body bristling with delight, spoke in a voice faltering with emotion.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then, O Śaṅkara, let your presence abide in this great Liṅga."
"This alone is the boon to be granted; I choose no other boon. Let this name 'Oṃkāreśvara' exist as the sole giver of liberation to devotees. (47)
Skanda said: O brahmin-sage, having heard that it was as ordained by Brahmā, the Lord (Ishita) spoke these words to the four-faced one: "So be it."
The omnipresent Lord, being highly pleased by that hymn of praise, immediately granted other boons as well to Vidhi, who had performed long penance, for he was exceedingly gratified by her.
Īśvara said: "O best of gods, O foremost in austerity, become the treasury of all the Āgamas; by my grace, may you possess the power to effect creation. (150)
"You are the grandfather of all, you are the one to be honored by everyone; this liṅga has arisen for the purpose of granting the fruit of your penance. (51)
O Creator, he is the supreme form of Oṃkāra and consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman); for men, the state of Brahman is not far off through his worship.
This linga is called the letter A; this supreme one is called the letter U; and this is named the letter M, as well as that which is designated as Nāda and Bindu.
Thus has this Īśāna, the five-fold abode, been described for the liberation of all living beings here in this Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana).
Having bathed in the Matsyodarī tīrtha and beheld the Lord Oṃkāra, a living being is never again born within a mother’s womb.
This is the Liṅga of Nādeśvara; this Liṅga is very difficult to attain. Seen and touched on the beautiful bank of the Matsyodarī, it bestows liberation.
Since this light of Kapila is seen within this liṅga, therefore this liṅga, known as Kapileśa, is very difficult to attain.
When the Matsyodarī Gaṅgā is in the vicinity of Kapileśvara, a man who bathes there at that time is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Having bathed in the waters of the Varaṇā, which overflow with water and mingle with the waters of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), and having beheld Nādeśvara, what cause for lamentation remains for a man? (59)
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, sixty thousand million holy fords, together with the oceans, indeed enter into the Matsyodarī.
When the Gaṅgā comes into the vicinity of Praṇaveśa, that time will be most meritorious, beloved by the gods, sages, and ancestors.
There, bathing, recitation, giving, fire-offerings, and worship of the deities performed at Matsyodarī in the presence of Oṃkāreśvara shall become inexhaustible.
Merely by the sight of Oṃkāra, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; therefore, Oṃkāra the Lord should be beheld with great effort in Kāśī.
Human birth, the sole means for achieving the four goals of life, is difficult to obtain; yet it would be as fleeting as a bubble on the water for one by whom the Lord has not been beheld. 64.
Having bathed in the waters of the Matsyodarī and beheld Kapileśāna, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors by performing the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Even after committing many great sins out of delusion, why indeed should one fear Yama upon beholding Oṃkāra in Kāśī? (66)
Seeing a man facing toward the pilgrimage of Oṃkāra, the ancestors dance with joy at the birth of one from their own lineage.
Whichever name he remembers again and again and pays homage to, by that very name the wise man leads his father to the state of Brahman.
Whatever fruit is properly obtained by chanting a million *niyutas* of the Rudras, that fruit one certainly attains simply by beholding the syllable *Oṃ* with devotion. (69)
The birth of that living being is indeed merely a burden to the earth, by whom the *Oṃkāra*, the granter of all desires, has not been seen in the Forest of Bliss (*Ānandavana*). || 170 ||
Having beheld even a single Oṃkāra throughout the entire circle of the earth, all the Liṅgas would undoubtedly be seen [therein]. || 71 ||
Having bowed to the Lord of Praṇava, if one should die elsewhere, one will attain the heavenly world and subsequently obtain liberation in Kāśī.
"O Brahman, it is firmly resolved that I shall always abide in this liṅga; and I shall indeed grant liberation forever to the worshipper of this liṅga. (73)
By bowing with effort even once here to the syllable Oṃ, a person will surely become one who has accomplished all that was to be done, through my supreme grace. (74)
To the western part of Oṃkāra is the unsurpassed Tāratīrtha; a man who performs the water-rites there crosses over the miserable states of existence.
Those who are devotees of Oṃkāreśa should not be known as mere humans; bound only by human skin, they are Rudras destined for liberation.
The greatness of this Linga cannot be understood by others here; for it has manifested in this place through the emergence of your own merit. (77)
And by the power of this Liṅga, you shall know everything in its true essence; therefore, O Brahmā, bring forth all this, both the moving and the unmoving.
Having thus granted that boon to Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, Śambhu became absorbed within that very same great liṅga.
Skanda said: O Pot-born one, even Brahmā worships that Liṅga even today, praising it with the Brahma-stava composed by his own self.
A mortal who recites the Brahmastava is liberated from all sins; he is filled with great merits and attains the most excellent knowledge.
By reciting this hymn to Brahmā three times a day for a full year, at the time of death one will attain that knowledge by which one is liberated from bondage.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Oṃkāra," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Listen, O destroyer of Vātāpi; I shall tell you of that which occurred in Kāśī during the Padma Kalpa, concerning the twice-born Damanaka, which destroys all sins.
The son of Bhāradvāja, known by the name Damana, having performed the rite of tying the girdle and having mastered the collection of sciences, [proceeded].
Having realized that life is full of the many sufferings of saṃsāra and is also fickle, the wise Damana departed from his own home.

Taking his stand in one direction or another, he fell into a state of supreme world-weariness, wandering from hermitage to hermitage, from mountain to mountain, from ocean to ocean, and from forest to forest.
Endowed with ascetic fervor, he wandered from sacred ford to sacred ford and from river to river, reaching as many shrines as exist here throughout the world.
He dwelt there for all that time with his senses and mind restrained; yet, he did not attain supreme stability of mind anywhere at all.
And nowhere at all was anyone seen who could instruct him in his desires; however, by the turn of fate, a certain ascetic named Damana appeared.
On the bank of the Revā, he beheld the holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka, where there was indeed a great and meritorious sanctuary of Oṃkāra as well.
Upon seeing them, his mind became joyful and he attained steadiness of heart; then, he observed those Pāśupatas there, whose wealth was their asceticism.
Their bodies were adorned with supernatural powers, they performed the worship of the Liṅga, they had secured their means of subsistence, and they engaged in the investigation of the Āgamas.
Having prostrated before the preceptor, who was seated comfortably with a steady mind directly in front of him, he then sat down there in his presence.
Then the great sage Garga, a teacher of the Pāśupata discipline, with his two hands joined and his neck bowed low in prostration— || 12 ||
Overcome by old age, his body emaciated by asceticism, he was devoted to the worship of Śambhu and was the most excellent among all ascetics.
And he asked Damana: "Who are you, and why have you come here? Though young, you are dispassionate; tell me, O best of beings, from where does this come? (14)
Having heard this with affection, Damana spoke: "O Blessed One, teacher of the Pāśupata, you who are dear to the worship of the Omniscient One! (15)
I shall tell you the true nature of my own mental activity: I am a descendant of Brahmins who has exerted effort in the study of the Vedas and the Shastras. (16)
Having realized the worthlessness of saṃsāra, I took refuge in the forest-dweller’s stage of life (vānaprastha), desiring to attain great siddhi with this very body.
He has bathed in many sacred fords, mantras have been recited by the millions, numerous deities have been served, and many oblations have been offered.
Many teachers have been served for a long time, and many nights have been spent even in great cremation grounds. (19)
Alas! I have dwelt upon the peaks of the lords of mountains, and I have also prepared thousands of divine medicinal herbs.
Furthermore, resorting to great courage, I have repeatedly consumed elixirs of rejuvenation in mountain caves inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas).
I have entered many times [into hells] resembling the mouth of Death (Kṛtānta), and great austerity has also been practiced by me through numerous observances and restraints.
O Lord, while wandering over the earth, I have not seen even a single sprout of success anywhere else; only now, having reached you, have I found it.
Like one who has attained perfection and reached a state of mental steadiness, words will inevitably flow forth from your lotus-like face. (24)
"By that alone shall great accomplishment be mine, and not otherwise; therefore, tell me the excellent instruction: how may accomplishment be mine? (25)
Having heard these words of Damanaka at that time, Garga Ācārya spoke thus regarding this very earthly body, which is exceedingly vast.

He spoke of a supreme and great wonder that he had seen with his own eyes, while all his disciples—whose minds were steady, who were seekers of liberation, and who maintained the Great Pāśupata vow—were listening there. (27)
Garga said: "If you desire perfection even with this very body, then listen attentively; I shall tell it to you. (28)
In the great field of Avimukta, which bestows all accomplishments upon the virtuous, and which is the supreme mine of the jewels known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (29)

To you, who resemble a lamp for all creatures dependent on you, who are the great enemy of the mass of darkness, and who [overcome] all the karmas of all beings—just as a lamp [dispels darkness] for moths.
In the forest fire of the tree of karma, in the submarine fire of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the milk-ocean of the glory of nirvāṇa, and in the abode of the rendezvous of bliss; || 31 ||
She who bestows the supreme awakening upon those fast asleep in the long slumber, and who is the tree on the path for living beings weary from the toil of coming and going. 32.
O wielder of the thunderbolt against the mountain of great sins accumulated over many births, you who bestow supreme welfare upon those men who utter your name! (33)
In the supreme abode of the Lord of All, which is the boundary between heaven and liberation, the celestial river with its restless waves eternally washes the ground.
O great-minded one, I shall relate what occurred before my very eyes in such a great field, which removes the flood of all suffering. (35)
Who is capable of fully describing the majesty of that sacred field where there is no fear of death and where there is no fear of sin? (36)
Whatever holy places there are in this world that destroy the sins of living beings, they all come constantly to Kāśī for the sake of purification. (37)
Even if one who eats all things and sells all things should dwell in Kāśī, the destination that mortal attains cannot be reached elsewhere by means of sacrifices or gifts. (38)
The great tree of saṃsāra, which has arisen from the seed of passion, having been cut down by the axe of long sleep in Kāśī, does not grow again. (39)
Of all barren lands, however, Kāśī is the most barren; this seed of the sower, when sown therein, does not sprout at all. (40)
Those virtuous ones who remember Kāśī here will certainly be liberated from the multitude of their sins and shall go to the supreme goal.
The splendor of all the worlds, beginning with truth, is fragile; yet that which is unfragile belongs to the liberated one, and it is obtained by the command of Śiva. 42.
The glory seen there for worms, insects, and moths who cast off their bodies in Avimukta—where else in the entire sphere of the universe is such glory found? (43)
"When Vārāṇasī is reached at some point in the course of time, that means must be devised by which we may go forth outside. (44)
Maṇikarṇīśa is in the east, Brahmeśa is situated in the south, Gokarṇa is in the west, and likewise Bhārabhūta is in the north.
This is the supreme field within Avimukta, which yields great fruit; having bathed in the Maṇikarṇī pool and beheld the omnipresent Lord Viśveśvara.
By circumambulating the sacred field, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice; and for the one who offers a śrāddha there, even the great-grandfathers are liberated.
Within the entire sphere of the universe, there is no field equal to Avimukta anywhere; this is the truth, the absolute truth, which bestows success upon the practitioner.
Where the fierce and great attendants, who possess minds free from cruelty despite their ferocity, constantly guard the field with nooses and swords in hand against those who are cruel.
And Aṭṭahāsa, at the eastern gate, surrounded by ten million attendants, shall protect this sacred field day and night from the wicked, being himself terrifying to behold.
In the same way, Gokarṇa, the lord of the supporter of beings (the earth) and the protector of the southern field, guards the western gate, surrounded by ten million attendants.
Likewise, the great host Ghaṇṭākarṇa should guard the northern gate; Chāgavaktra, the terrifying one, [guards] the northeast corner and the southeast quarter.
Rakṣa protects the quarter of Kaṣṭhā, Śaṅkukarṇa the quarter of Dṛmicaṇḍa, and Marut the quarter of the Wind; thus these exceedingly radiant Gaṇas always protect the field.
Kālākṣa, Uraṇabhadra, Kauleya, and Kālakaṃpana—these hosts stationed on the bank of the Gaṅgā protect [the region] to the east.
Vīrabhadra, Nabhas, and Kardamāliptavigraha—Sthūlkarṇa and Mahābāhu—were stationed at the edge of the sword.
Viśālākṣa, Mahābhīma, Kuṇḍodara, and Mahodara, stationed at the threshold, guard the western gate.
Naṃdisena, Pañcāla, Kharapāda, Karaṃṭaka, Ānanda, Gopaka, and Babhru protect [the site] on the bank of the Varaṇā.
In that field of great merit is the Liṅga known as Oṃkāra; there, practitioners have attained supreme perfection with this very body.
Kapila, Sāvarṇi, Śrīkaṇṭha, Pigala, and Aṃśumān—these are indeed the perfected ones (siddhas) of the Pāśupata school, for they attained perfection through the worship of that Liṅga.
Once, having performed the fivefold worship of that liṅga, all five of them attained absorption into that liṅga while dancing with the sound of hand-claps.
Moreover, O highly intelligent one, O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall relate to you another wonderful event that occurred there, O Damana. (61)
O Sage, a certain female frog, wandering there in the vicinity of the Liṅga, would always perform circumambulation while subsisting on the remains of the offerings and unbroken grains of rice.
She did not meet death there because she had consumed the remains of Śiva's offerings; her death occurred elsewhere than in that sacred field due to that sin.
It is better to consume even poison than to ever consume the property of Śiva; for poison kills only the individual, whereas the property of Śiva destroys one's sons and grandsons. (64)
Those whose limbs were nourished by Śiva were not to be touched by the virtuous; as a result of that karmic ripening, they became inhabitants of the Raurava hell.
A certain crow, having spotted that female frog as she was leaping here and there, seized her with its beak and went outside the field.
By that crow, the female frog was thrown outside the field. Then, in the course of time, she [remained] right there in that most excellent field.
By circumambulating and even by touching the Liṅga, the daughter of Puṣpabaṭu was born endowed with both merit and demerit in his house.
Though she possessed beautiful limbs and was marked with auspicious signs, she became a vulture-faced woman due to eating the remains of offerings and unbroken grains. (69)
She was an expert in the secrets of perfect singing and possessed an exceedingly sweet voice; she knew the seven notes, the three scales, and the twenty-one melodic modulations.
There are forty-nine tālas and one hundred and one rāgas; of these, there are exactly six rāgas, and each of them has five female counterparts (aṅganās). || 71 ||
The twenty-six types of passionate women who bring joy to the impassioned man, as well as another fifty-five types distinguished by differences of place and time, [make sixty-one]. (72)
"For as many palm trees as there may be, so many indeed are the passions. Thus, according to the Gītā Upaniṣad, she of auspicious vows [performed this] every day. (73)
Mādhavī, whose speech was sweet, constantly worshipped with the syllable Om; though she had attained priceless youth, she remained the daughter of Puṣpabaṭu.

Due to the connection with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of her previous birth, she indeed held the syllable Om (oṃkāra) in high esteem; for her mind was by nature fickle, yet through the service of that linga, it became steady.
The self-control of that great-souled one reached a state of steadfastness as if through yoga; hunger and thirst did not afflict him by day, nor did sleep disturb his daughter at night.
Her mind remained unwearied in gazing upon that liṅga; as many as were the twinklings of her eyes, so many passed for her day and night.

"By that virtuous woman, a great obstacle must be inferred for this duration of time; for every moment that has passed while I was distracted, how can there be an expiation for not having observed the linga? (78)
While reflecting thus, she abandoned her service to the Unmanifest; for she, longing for water, would drink the nectar of the name of the Liṅga. (79)
Her two eyes desire nothing else; even when reaching the ears, they do not leave the *liṅga* known as Oṃkāra, which resides in the heart-space of the virtuous.
Her two hands, intent on grasping sounds, were no longer merely capable of perceiving sound; they became exceedingly skillful, as if they were the very makers of her beautiful garlands.
Her feet wandered nowhere else out of a desire for pleasure, except upon the ground of the courtyard of Oṃkāra, which had been trodden by her who was intent on the state of Nirvāṇa.
Oṃkāra, the Praṇava, the essence that reveals the Supreme Brahman, whose form is the Śabdabrahman and the three Vedas, and which is the abode of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. || 83 ||

The six-syllabled one, whose form is the primordial, whose form is the universe, both supreme and inferior; the most excellent, the worthy of worship, the giver of boons, the eternal, the peaceful Lord.
The sole progenitor of all the worlds, the sole protector of all the worlds, the sole destroyer of all the worlds, and the one adored by all the worlds. || 85 ||

Devoid of beginning and end, eternal, auspicious, the benefactor Śaṅkara, immutable, transcending the single [quality] and the triad of qualities, He has made His abode in the hearts of His devotees. 86.
Without limiting adjuncts, formless, changeless, stainless, free from the sense of "I," beyond the phenomenal world, and self-manifesting. || 87 ||
He who delights in his own self, who is infinite, all-pervading, and all-seeing; who bestows everything, who is the enjoyer of all, who is everything, and the abode of all happiness. || 88 ||
His organ of speech, sounding day and night, never uttered the name of anyone else whatsoever. (89)
Tasting this nectar of the syllables of her name day and night, her tongue does not perceive any other flavor whatsoever.
One should always perform the sweeping and the decoration of the courtyard around the temple; there, Mādhavī should likewise attend to the worship and the cleansing of the vessels.
In that regard, those who are indeed Pāśupatas devoted to the worship of the Lord of Praṇava—one should always serve them with devotion, regarding them as one's own ancestors. || 92 ||
Once, on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, that Mādhavī, having observed a fast during the day, performed a night vigil (jāgaraṇa).
When the devotees who had gathered for the pilgrimage had departed in every direction at dawn, he performed the sweeping and other rites, and worshipped the Liṅga with joy. (94)
Singing a sweet song and dancing with her own playful grace, meditating upon the Oṃkāra-liṅga, she attained absorption into that very liṅga. || 95 ||
With this very earthly body, the one of great intelligence [attained his goal] while our chief teachers and the ascetics were looking on. 96.
From that liṅga there appeared a light that filled the sky with its massed flames; within that light, the young girl became one composed of light herself.
Even today, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, the residents of that sacred field perform a pilgrimage there preceded by a great festival.
Having kept vigil there and fasted on the fourteenth day, they attain supreme knowledge, even if they die anywhere at all.
Whatever holy places exist everywhere within the interior of the cosmic egg, they all come on the new moon day of Vaiśākha for the sight of Oṃkāra.
At the tip of the Liṅga is a most excellent cave named Śrīmukhī; it is the gateway to Pātāla, and indeed, the Siddhas dwell there.
Those of virtuous vows who remain in that cave for five nights shall behold the daughters of the Nāgas, and they shall speak of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
In the northern part of that cave, there is a well with water of nectar-like taste; having drunk that for six months, one should drink the elixir of Brahman.
There, having beheld the Liṅga Nādeśvara, which is the source of sound, the entire universe, consisting of all sounds, shall come within the range of one's hearing.
Having bathed there in the Matsyodarī, the celestial river (Svardhunī) where Varuṇa has immersed himself, a living being becomes one who has accomplished his purpose and never grieves anywhere.
Countless attendants of Oṃkāreśvara have attained perfection with their very earthly bodies becoming divine in that very instant.
Avimukta is the supreme field, even more so than the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); beyond that, Oṃkāra is said to be supreme on the bank of the Matsyodarī.
O limbs of the Lord of Praṇava, for what purpose have those been born who neither bowed nor worshipped [you] in Kāśī, yet robbed their mothers of their youth?
O best of beings, from the moment Viśveśa arrived at that dense thicket of bliss on Mount Mandara, from that time forward [it has remained so].
Then they quickly went to all the abodes, including the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, the sacred fords, and the islands.
Now, O Sage, I have been reminded by you through my own good fortune; I too shall come, and let us go slowly toward Kāśī.
These disciples of mine as well, who observe the great Pāśupata vow and are all seekers of liberation, are likewise desirous of going to Kāśī. (12)
Moreover, for those who have reached old age without ever having resorted to Kāśī, once this rare human birth has been lost, how can there be great happiness for them? (13)
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, and as long as there is no exhaustion of life, so long should the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana) of Śambhu be diligently resorted to.
May the goddess of immovable fortune never forsake those who have taken refuge in Ānandavana, the abode of Śambhu and the sanctuary of prosperity, for they are the sole repositories of great bliss.
Having thus related this delightful story, Garga, the foremost of the Pāśupatas, together with Bhāradvāja, reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
For the righteous Damanaka, accompanied by Gargācārya, having propitiated the illustrious Oṃkāra, attained dissolution within that very liṅga.
Skanda said: O enemy of Ilvala, in Avimuktaka there is the supreme station of Oṃkāra; there, O sage, many practitioners have attained the highest perfection.
Indeed, in this Kali age, the majesty of Praṇaveśvara must never be recounted in the presence of those with defiled minds, and especially not before atheists.
Those who revile Mahādeva, those ignorant ones who revile this sacred field, and those who revile the Purāṇa—these should not be spoken to anywhere at all. (120)
"A liṅga equal to the syllable Oṃ does not exist anywhere on the surface of the earth; thus was it definitively declared by the God of gods to Gaurī. (121)
Having heard this chapter, a man whose mind is absorbed in it shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Śiva. || 122 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Oṃkāra," in the latter half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 74 ||
Agastya said: O Viśākha, having heard this account of the syllable Om which destroys great sins, I am not yet satiated; now tell me the story concerning the inhabitants of heaven.
And how, O Six-faced one of great intelligence, was the supreme, meritorious manifestation of the three-eyed goddess described by the God of gods to the Goddess? (2)
Skanda said: Listen, O sage, I shall relate the story that dispels fatigue, just as it was told by the God concerning the origin of Triviṣṭapa.
That sacred seat (pīṭha) is indeed named Virajā, and there the Liṅga is Triviṣṭapa; by the mere sight of that sacred seat, a man becomes free from passion (viraja).
O Pot-born One, three rivers flow together there; indeed, to the south of the Three-eyed Lord, they are the three that carry away all impurities.
Sarasvatī, Kālindī, and Narmadā—who bestows supreme bliss—manifested in person as streams of water for the purpose of bathing the Liṅga.
For indeed, at all three junctions of the day, those three rivers, with jars in their hands, bathe that great, celestial, and supreme Liṅga.
He also installed lingas all around them under their own names; by the sight of these, men shall obtain the fruit of bathing in those [tirthas].
To the south of Triviṣṭapa is the Sarasvatīśvara Liṅga; when seen or touched, it bestows the station of Sarasvatī and removes dullness.
And Yamuneśa, worshipped with devotion by men in the western quarter, wards off the realm of Yama even for those who are burdened with sins.
To the east of Trilocana, the Narmadeśa site was seen, which bestows great peace; by worshipping that Liṅga, the womb-dwelling of men is prevented.
Having bathed at the Pilipilā Tīrtha near Triviṣṭapa and having beheld the Trilocana Liṅga, why should one grieve any further? (12)
By the mere remembrance of the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga, a human being shall become the lord of heaven; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (13)
They shall undoubtedly become beholders and creators of the third heaven; they alone here have accomplished their purpose, and they alone here possess great intelligence.
Those of pure intellect who have bowed to the Liṅga at Ānandakānana, which is situated in Triviṣṭapa, and by whom even the name of Trilocana has been heard; || 15 ||
They shall be purified from the sins accumulated over seven births; of this there is no doubt. Whatever fruit is obtained when all the lingas on earth are beheld, [that fruit is attained here].
I consider that [merit] which exists when Triviṣṭapa is seen to be even greater when Kāśī is seen; for when Kāśī is seen, all of Triviṣṭapa is seen. || 17 ||
In an instant, his sins are shaken off, and he shall not again enter a womb; he has bathed in all sacred fords and performed all ritual ablutions at the conclusion of sacrifices.
He who, having bathed at the Pilipilā tīrtha in the waters flowing northward, [reaches] the three rivers of great merit where [the deity] always dwells in person.
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other duties there, what will he do at Gayā after bathing in the Pilipilā Tīrtha and offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa)? || 20 ||
Having seen the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga, one obtains the fruit of ten million holy fords (tīrthas). Whatever sin has been accumulated elsewhere departs upon the sight of Kāśī.
But whatever sin is committed in Kāśī bestows the state of a Piśāca; having committed a transgression through negligence in Śambhu’s Ānandakānana—
Upon seeing the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga, even that sin will vanish; for among all the surface of the earth, Ānandakānana is the most excellent.
Even there, all sacred fords (tīrthas) are surpassed; even more so than those is the ground of Oṃkāra; and even more than Oṃkāra is the true Liṅga, which illuminates the path to liberation.
The most excellent Liṅga, which is the embodiment of spiritual welfare, has three eyes. || 25 ||
Just as the sun is among all luminous bodies and the moon is among all visible objects, so too is the three-eyed supreme Liṅga among all Liṅgas.
For those who worship the Three-Eyed One, that state is not far off—the state of the lotus of supreme liberation, which is the sole treasure-trove of great bliss. (27)
The spiritual merit that is fully acquired by worshipping Trilocana even once cannot be obtained by worshipping other lingas throughout one's entire life.
Those of great intelligence who worship the Trilocana Liṅga in Kāśī should be honored by the inhabitants of the three worlds who desire my favor.
Even after performing the renunciation of everything and undertaking the Pāśupata vow, why do men fear even when they have slipped from their observances? (30)
While the great Liṅga exists—the remover of floods of great sins, a mass of merit in Triviṣṭapa, and the abode for the deposit of liberation—(31)
By worshipping the great three-eyed Liṅga even once, one is liberated from all impurities accumulated over hundreds of births. || 32 ||

Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—even one associated with such persons—is proclaimed a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātakin) for a year. || 33 ||
Even one who is devoted to another's wife, or even one who delights in harming others, or one whose habit is to slander others, as well as one who betrays trust; || 34 ||
Even one who is ungrateful, a killer of an embryo, or the husband of a low-caste woman; even one who abandons his mother, father, or guru, or a giver of fire, or a giver of poison— (35)
Whether he be a killer of cows, a killer of women, a killer of Śūdras, or a defiler of virgins; whether he be cruel or even a slanderer, or one who has turned his back on his own duty (36).
One who is a reviler, or an atheist, or one who speaks false testimony; one who eats what is not fit to be eaten, or likewise one who sells what should not be sold. (37)
Thus, even one of sinful character—provided he avoids the reviler of Śiva—obtains purification from his sins by bowing to the three-eyed Liṅga.
For that fool who delights in reviling Śiva and who censures the scriptures of Śiva, no expiation has been seen anywhere, even by anyone in any scripture. (39)
He who reviles Śiva should be known as a self-destroyer and a perpetual destroyer of the three worlds; that lowest of the low is not even to be spoken to. (40)
Those who are devoted to reviling Śiva, as well as those who revile the devotees of Śiva, go to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Those who desire liberation in Kāśī should worship the devotees of Śiva with great effort; when they are honored, Śiva himself becomes pleased, without a doubt. (42)
Desiring to perform atonement for all sins here, those who know the authoritative means of knowledge should speak these words without any hesitation. (43)
If you desire the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), or if you are afraid of sin, or if you consider our words to be true according to the authority of the scriptures; || 44 ||
Therefore, renouncing everything and making a firm resolve in your mind, go to Ānandakānana, where Viśveśvara himself resides.
In that field, for those men who have entered with resolute minds, no accumulation of sin causes affliction, and the supreme excellence is attained. || 46 ||
There, even today, is a great sacred ford named Pilipilā, situated at the confluence of the three extremely pure rivers; it is meritorious and attended by the three streams.

Having bathed according to the ritual prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras at that place of great merit surrounded by the casting of glances from the eyes of Trilocana, and having offered libations to those who are to be satisfied; || 48 ||
Having given what is to be given according to one's ability, free from stinginess regarding wealth, and having beheld the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga, one should worship it with supreme devotion. (49)
With various perfumes and garlands, preceded by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), garments, and many ornaments. || 50 ||
With articles for worship and ritual substances, with bells, mirrors, and chowries; with variegated banners and flags, and with dances, instrumental music, and excellent singers. || 51 ||
Having performed worship in this manner with recitations, circumambulations, and joyful prostrations, as well as by satisfying the attendants; || 52 ||
Afterwards, speaking the words "May I be free from sin," he should cause the Brahmins to recite [the mantras]. By acting in this way, a wise man becomes sinless in an instant.
Then, having bathed at Pañcanada and then in the Maṇikarṇī pool, and thereafter having worshipped Viśveśa, one attains great merit.
This expiation has been proclaimed as the purifier of great sins; it must not be taught to an atheist or to one who reviles the majesty of Kāśī.
And if one bestows this auspicious expiation out of greed for wealth, O Pot-born One, the giver attains hell; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Whatever fruit is fully obtained by circumambulating Kṣamā, that same fruit is attained at Trilocana in Kāśī seven times during Pradoṣa.
Having seen the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga at Kāśī, which has serpents for its girdle, one shall be liberated even in another birth, should death occur elsewhere.
In all other liṅgas, the auspicious time is distinguished [by specific occasions]; however, at Triviṣṭapa, the auspicious time for men exists always, day and night.
The Lingas, headed by Oṃkāra, are fully capable of destroying all sins; yet, O Pārvatī, there is another supreme power, that of Trailocanī.
Since this Liṅga is the most excellent among all Liṅgas, listen to its cause, O Parṇa; place it upon your ear, for I shall speak.
Formerly, while I was absorbed in yoga, this great Linga emerged from the surface of the earth, piercing through the seven netherworlds, and appeared before me.
O Gaurī, in this very place, while I was dwelling in secret long ago, I gave you three eyes; thus you beheld that which is most excellent.
From that time onwards, O Goddess of gods, this Trilocana Liṅga has been praised by those dwelling within the three worlds as the bestower of the vision of knowledge.
All those who are devotees of Trilocana are themselves three-eyed; they are my attendants and are indeed liberated while living.
O Maheśānī, no one truly knows the greatness of the Trilocana Liṅga; it has been kept secret by me alone.
Having bathed in the Pailipila lake on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, they remained devoted to fasting and were engaged in keeping a vigil at night with devotion.
Having bathed there in the morning and worshipped Trilocana, one should again worship the Liṅga and also offer water-pots of righteousness (dharmaghaṭas).
O Goddess, having joyfully offered food along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) intended for the ancestors, one should thereafter perform the breaking of the fast together with the devotees of Śiva.
Having cast off their earthly bodies, O Goddess, impelled by that merit, they certainly become my Gaṇas who march at my head.
O Gaurī, gods, mortals, and great serpents wander in this cycle of existence as long as they do not behold the three-eyed Liṅga at Kāśī.
Indeed, a living being who has once beheld Triviṣṭapa and bathed in the Pailipila pool shall never again be born here as one who drinks from a mother’s breast.
O beautiful lady, every month on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) come to behold the Lord Triviṣṭapa.
Having bathed in the waters of the Pailipila to the south of Triviṣṭapa and having performed the twilight devotions there once, one obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice.
Right there is a well known as Pādodaka, which destroys all sins; by drinking its water, a mortal is no longer born as a mortal again.
Beside that Liṅga, however, there are many other Liṅgas; they grant liberation here even through sight or touch.
There, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, stands the Śāṃtanava Liṅga; by beholding it, a man tormented by the sufferings of saṃsāra attains peace.
To the south of that, O Sage, is the great Liṅga known as Bhīṣmeśa; neither Kali, nor Time (Kāla), nor Desire (Kāma) can cause any affliction upon beholding it.
To the west of that is the great Liṅga celebrated as Droṇeśa; by worshipping that Liṅga, Droṇa regained his form of light once again. (79)
In front of that is the Aśvatthāmeśvara Liṅga, which bestows great merit; by virtue of worshipping it, the son of Droṇa does not fear even Time (Death).
To the northwest of Droṇeśa is the supreme Vālakhilyeśvara; by beholding that Liṅga with faith, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. || 81 ||
To its left, one should behold the Liṅga known as Vālmīkeśvara; by the mere sight of it, a man becomes free from sorrow.
Furthermore, O Pot-born One, I shall relate what else occurred in this very place: the greatness of Triviṣṭapa as it was told by the Lord to the Goddess. (83)
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 75 ||
Skanda said: Listen, O son of Mitrāvaruṇa, to this history that occurred in a former age during the Rathantara [Kalpa] at the sacred seat known as Viraja.
In the palace of Trilocana, constructed of jewels and rubies, rich with windows of various designs, it appeared like the peak of Mount Meru.
Even at some point at the end of a kalpa, when the world and heaven fall away in destruction, he remains as a supporting pillar, established by the Creator himself.
O Sage, with its banners whose tips are tossed by the wind here and there, the city seems to ward off the floods of sin entering it.
It was resplendent with a shining golden pitcher, as if the full moon had taken refuge there out of exhaustion.
There, a pair of pigeons, having made their home, dwelt at their own will; they performed circumambulation daily in the morning, evening, and at midday.
Day after day, it flew about, driven here and there by the wind from its wings, clearing away the dust clinging to the palace.
The name "Trilocana" is constantly uttered by devotees, and likewise, "Triviṣṭapa" should become a guest in their ears. (8)
The four kinds of musical instruments, which greatly please Śambhu, reach the caves of their ears and produce resonant echoes.
The light of the auspicious *ārārtika* lamp, entering the corners of the eyes of those two birds at the three junctions of the day, constantly manifests the activities of their devotion.
Sometimes, even neglecting their search for food, those two birds, with steady minds, would not fly away to their desired destination, but remained watching the spectacle with curiosity.
There, O Sage, moving about rice and other offerings all around the temple crowded with devotees, the two of them performed circumambulations.
O Brahmin, once two birds, afflicted by thirst, drank the water of the four rivers located in the southern quarter of the gods while they were bathing there.
As those two brahmins of virtuous conduct were thus wandering in the vicinity of the Three-eyed Lord, a great deal of time passed.
Then, as they sat comfortably within the lattice window on the roof of the temple, they were spotted by a certain hawk with a cruel gaze.
Then that pair of pigeons, pursued by a hawk desiring to seize them, quickly descended from the sky and entered another temple of Śiva.
Then he surveyed the entry and exit points of that fortress, wondering by which path these two birds were entering this inaccessible place.
By which path have they departed, at what time, and what are they doing? How shall those two be captured by me simultaneously and at my own will? (18)
"Since these two have entered a fortress and are under my control, why does the hawk remain with a fixed gaze for a moment?"—thinking thus, he stood still. (19)
"O wise ones, it is for this reason that they say the strength of a fortress is indeed formidable; even a weak enemy cannot be overcome with ease. (20)
The accomplishment of that king's task by means of a single fortress cannot be equaled even by a thousand elephants or a hundred thousand excellent horses. (21)
One situated in a fortress cannot be overcome by any adversary anywhere, provided that the fortress is independent and its secrets are not revealed to those who know its vulnerabilities. (22)
Thus praising the strength of his fortress, Śyena, his eyes red with rage, beheld the two fearless sparrows and flew up into the expanse of the sky.
Then Pārāvatī, skilled and possessing formidable strength, beholding her husband the bird with his wings clipped and his power gone, spoke to her lord, the pigeon: || 24 ||
Kalaravi said: "O dear pigeon, wise one, you who desire all things and coo so happily, a powerful enemy in the form of a hawk has come within the range of your vision. (25)
Having heard those contemptuous words of the female pigeon, her husband spoke this to her: "O dear one, what is the cause of your anxiety? (26)
The pigeon said: "O fortunate one, how many sky-dwellers are there not here? Indeed, how many birds do not perch upon these temples? (27)
And how many, O beloved, do not see us two established here in happiness? If one must fear them here, from where could that happiness of ours come, O beloved? (28)
"Rejoice with me; cast aside this anxiety, O auspicious one. This wretched hawk does not even enter my thoughts. (29)
Having thus heard the words of the male pigeon, the female pigeon then remained observing silence, her eyes fixed upon the feet of her husband.
Even when instructed in the path of what is beneficial, a virtuous woman, out of a desire to do what is pleasing, should remain silent and always carry out the word of her husband.
Then, having arrived on another day, the hawk beheld that couple with an unobstructed gaze, just as Death beholds one whose life has reached its end.
Then, wandering around that palace in a circular motion, he beheld those two who had come and gone by way of the path of the sky.
Then, when the hawk had departed into the sky, the female pigeon spoke again to her beloved husband: "O Lord, has that wicked enemy been seen by you? (34)
Having heard her words, Kalarava spoke again: "O innocent one, what can he do to me, who roam the sky? (35)
And this fortress of mine is equal to heaven, wherein there is no fear of enemies; he does not know those paths in the expanse of the sky that I know.
Praḍīnā, uḍḍīnā, saṃḍīnā, kāṇḍā, vyāḍā, kapāṭikā, sraṃsanī, and maṇḍalavatī—these eight modes of movement have been described. || 37 ||
Just as I possess skill in these [modes of flight] here on earth, O dear Pārāvatī, no bird anywhere possesses such skill in the sky.
"Stay in happiness; what anxiety is there while I, your beloved, am alive? Having heard these words of his, that virtuous woman remained silent like a dumb cow.
On the following day as well, the hawk, having approached a certain distance from that rocky surface, sat down there appearing exceedingly delighted.
Having stayed there for a while and observed that nest, the hawk departed once more; she too, being afraid, spoke again.
"This beloved place must be abandoned, for it is defiled by the evil gaze of this cruel man who sits nearby, appearing exceedingly joyful. (42)
He spoke again with contempt: "O beloved, what will he do? For this is generally the nature of deer-eyed women—they are mostly of a timid disposition. (43)
On the following day as well, that mighty hawk arrived and remained there facing them for the duration of two watches.
Having looked back once more at that path, he quickly departed as he had come; and when that bird had gone, the female bird spoke:
"O Lord, let us go elsewhere, for death is near to us here. O dear one, when this wicked man has perished, we shall find happiness again. (46)
If the movement of one who has allies is everywhere conducive to success, why would that wise man meet with destruction through attachment to his own country? (47)
If one abandons one's own country when it is beset by calamities and does not go elsewhere, he perishes like a tree standing on the riverbank—he is as if lame. || 48 ||
Having heard what was thus spoken by his beloved, he, afflicted by destiny, spoke again with pride: "O beloved, do not fear that bird."
Then on another day, that hawk arrived at the gateway early in the morning and remained there until evening, O Balarāma.
When the sun had reached the peak of the western mountain and the bird had departed, the female dove came outside her nest and spoke to her husband: || 51 ||
"O Lord, this is not the time for your departure; the time is still very far off. Therefore, O noble-minded one, depart now, even leaving me behind. (52)
While you live, nothing on the surface of the earth is difficult to obtain: again a wife, again a friend, again wealth, and again a home. (53)
If the self is protected by a man, even at the cost of his wife and wealth, then everything is obtained here, just as it was by King Hariścandra.
This self is one's dear kinsman; this self is great wealth. This self is the supreme achiever of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. 55.
As long as there is security for oneself, so long is there security in the three worlds; yet even that security is desired by Sumati along with glory. (96)
But that security which is devoid of fame is worse than death; therefore, fame is attained by men through proceeding upon the path of policy.
Therefore, O Lord, having heard this path of policy, depart from this place; if you do not go, then tomorrow morning you will remember my words.
Although thus addressed by his wife Pārāvatī, who was possessed of great wisdom, he did not depart from Pratiṣṭhāna, being restrained by destiny.
Then, O Sage, at dawn, a powerful hawk carrying some prey arrived and blocked the path by which he was to depart.
Having stayed there for a few days, the high-minded hawk said this to the pigeon: "Fie on you, who are devoid of manliness! (61)
Or else, O evil-minded one, fight, or else depart at my word; otherwise, wasted by hunger, you will surely die and go to hell hereafter. (62)
There are two states and I alone am the third; victory and defeat are both unstable. For the sake of one's position, beings fight with their vital energy for either heaven or a difficult hell.
For those of great intellect who strive while firmly grasping the goal of human endeavor, fate itself—impelled by their own inner essence—will surely provide assistance.
Thus addressed by the hawk and encouraged by his wife, that bird took refuge at the gate of his own fortress and fought with that hawk.
