In the winter he stayed in the midst of water, during the rains he lived under the open sky, and in the heat of summer he stood amidst five fires; thus he practiced asceticism at various times.
He remained for a long time with the tips of his big toes touching the ground; at other times, he also stood on one leg for a great length of time.
He subsisted on air and partook of much that was divinely ordained; yet, being thirsty, he drank only droplets of water from the tips of kusha grass.
Thus he spent a divine cycle of four yugas performing austerities, desiring to behold me through supreme meditative absorption multiplied fourfold.
Then, being well-pleased by the austerity of that high-souled Śamana, whose mind was steadfast, I went to him to grant boons.
There was a banyan tree named Kāñcanaśākhā, which, providing excellent shade and serving as a refuge for many birds, drove away the succession of ascetics performing austerities.
With her sprout-like hands—fresh shoots trembling in the gentle breeze—she, the remover of distress, beckons like a divine woman the travelers scorched by the journey.
He who fully gratifies the multitude of supplicants with his own fruits—his own livelihoods—which are fragrant with their own passion, sweet, and fully ripened; || 25 ||
Looking further down from there, I beheld that son of the Sun, his body as motionless as a pillar, with his eyes fixed upon the tip of his nose.
Surrounded on all sides by his rising splendors of asceticism, he was like the sun in the deep blue sky with its own radiance. || 27 ||
Having installed the great Liṅga marked with his own name with supreme devotion, it was worshipped as if with masses of radiance from pure sun-crystals.
As if having personally witnessed that great penance being performed by that Liṅga, I addressed Dharmarāja while the Sun was present, saying, "Choose a boon."
"Enough of your asceticism, O highly fortunate one; I am pleased with you, O observer of auspicious vows. Having heard this and having seen me, Yama indeed bowed down.
And the lord of the senses, the son of the Sun, having cast aside his sincere meditative absorption, offered praise with his faculties fully delighted.

Dharma said: Salutations again and again to the cause of causes; salutations again and again to Him who is devoid of any cause. Salutations again and again to You who consist of effects; salutations again and again to You whose form is distinct from all effects.

Salutations to you, the moon-crested one, who possesses both form and formlessness, who embodies all forms, who is of the nature of the supreme atom, who is both transcendent and immanent, who is the shoreless beyond yet the further shore itself, and who bestows the far shore of the ocean of the Supreme.

You are without a lord, yet you are the Lord of the universe; you consist of the qualities (guṇas), yet you are devoid of qualities. You are beyond time and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); salutations to you, who are the time of time and the source of nature.

You alone are the state of Nirvana; you alone, O possessor of infinite power, are Nirvana itself. You are the form of the self and the form of the Supreme Self; you are the inner soul of all that is moving and unmoving.

From you the world arises, you are the world itself, and the world is truly yours, O sole kinsman of the universe; you are the destroyer, the protector, and the primordial creator—O Viṣṇu, Īśa, the Ordainer, salutations, salutations unto you!

You alone are Mṛḍa (the compassionate one) toward those who walk the path of the Vedas; you alone are Bhīma (the terrible one) toward those who do not walk the path of the Vedas. You are Śaṃkara (the bestower of happiness) to those who possess excellent devotion to Soma; O Rudra, you are Ugra (the fierce one) to those who lack devotion.

You alone are the wielder of the trident for enemies; you alone are Śiva through the words of those whose hearts are humble. You are the one Śrīkaṇṭha for those who have taken refuge at your feet, yet you are the one with a throat fierce as halāhala poison for the wicked-minded.

Homage be to you, O Śaṅkara, O peaceful Śambhu; homage be to you, whose crest-jewel is the digit of the moon. Homage be to you, who are adorned with serpents; salutations to the wielder of the Pināka bow, the enemy of Andhaka.

He alone is blessed, he alone possesses the fortune of devotion to you, and he alone is the virtuous worshiper of you, who always offers praise to you; he is praised by the gods, beginning with Duścyavana.

O You of infinite power, who is like me, with such meager intellectual capacity, able to praise You here? For You are beyond the reach of the ancient words of the sages; toward You, this "praise" is nothing more than a prostration.
Skanda said: Having uttered the name of the Sun’s son with great devotion, and chanting "Obeisance to Śiva," he, his head touching the ground, bowed down to Śambhu a thousand times with extreme joy.
Then the Lord Śiva, having restrained him who was utterly exhausted by his asceticism from those prostrations, granted boons to the son of the seven-horsed one: "May you be Dharmarāja even by name."

"You alone have been appointed by me today as the overseer of dharma for all embodied beings, both stationary and moving; perform your duties from this day forward and govern them all according to my command. (44)

You are the lord of the southern quarter; be the witness of the deeds of every living being. May those of high and low station, following the path shown by you, depart from here to the destination appropriate for their own karma.
O Dharma, since this Liṅga has been propitiated here by you, who are devoted to me, men shall attain perfection through seeing it, touching it, and worshipping it before long.
That mortal of pure intellect who, having bathed here in the Dharmatīrtha before you, beholds Dharmeśvara even once, for him the attainment of the goals of human existence is not far off.

Even one who has committed a thousand sins here may, by the turn of fate, behold Dharmeśvara; that conscious being shall never experience the agony of hell, for even the gods in heaven speak only of his story.

That mortal who, having obtained this seat of Dharma in Kāśī, does not strive for his own spiritual welfare—how can he, though possessing great luster, consider himself to have accomplished his purpose, like Dharmatva? Just as your desires were attained here, O King of Dharma, through your heavy ascetic penances, so too shall the desires of those devoted to the Lord of Dharma bear fruit; there is no doubt in this.

Even after committing great sins here on earth, one who performs worship of the Lord of Dharma even once—O Beloved One, how can that devotee of the Liṅga worshipped by you fear, for he is indeed your own kinsman? (51)
Whoever shall worship Dharmeśvara with a leaf, a flower, water, or dūrvā grass, him the gods, who feed upon nectar, will most joyfully honor with garlands of mandāra flowers.

Those who have committed sins will fear you, yet for them there shall never be any fear; for those who perform the worship of Dharmeśvara and offer him their minds as a bond of kinship, no fear shall ever arise.

Whatever men, having bathed in the celestial river, shall offer here at the Seat of Dharma, that will become inexhaustible even in another age, provided they have offered salutations to your Dharmaliṅga.

Those men who, having fasted, shall perform a pilgrimage on the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, and keep a vigil at night with great festivities before Dharmeśvara, shall not be born again on this earth.
And those men who shall recite this hymn uttered by you in your presence at any time, being freed from sin, they shall go to my world and, through your power, attain friendship with me. (56)
"Speak another boon as you desire, O son of the treasury of splendor, O King of Dharma; there is nothing here that cannot be given to you. Make your request with the mere effort of speech alone."

Beholding Śaṅkara, whose form was serene, full of compassion, and the very embodiment of his own heart's desire, he was submerged in a lake of overflowing bliss and was unable to say anything for a moment.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Dharmeśa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Beholding him with his throat choked by tears of joy, Mṛḍa—the ocean of nectar—touched him with both hands that were like two palaces.
Then, through the pleasure of that touch, Dharmarāja, the great ascetic, once again caused his body—blazing with the fire of penance—to sprout anew.
Then that son of Bhrigu spoke to the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, whose face was serene, who was peaceful, and who was surrounded by his tranquil attendants.
If you are pleased, O Īśāna, omniscient one, ocean of compassion, what need is there for any other boon here, since you have been directly perceived by me? (4)
O Lord, that which the Vedas do not know correctly, nor even those two Veda-puruṣas, for that very reason I am worthy of Your choice; therefore, I pray for that.
Of these children born from Śrīkaṇṭha’s loins, who speak so sweetly, whose births have occurred before me, and whom I have long witnessed through my ascetic penance; || 6 ||
Be the bestower of boons upon the parrots—who, though learned in the narratives of ancient lore, have been deprived of their parents and abandoned their food and recreation.
At the time of this birth, the female parrot, tormented by disease, met her death; the male parrot was devoured by a hawk.
O Lord of the helpless, by you—who are the very embodiment of the remainder of their lifespan—those who were once unprotected, yet always beheld my face, have now been protected.
O Sage, having heard these words of Dharma, which were stainless with benevolence toward others, Śambhu summoned them, whose faces were bowed in humility.
Delighted, Śuka spoke these words to the young parrots: "O winged ones, you who are virtuous and devoted to dharma, speak! (11)
O Lord of Dharma, what boon should be granted by you to your attendants, whose great sins from previous births have been utterly destroyed through association with the virtuous? (12)
Having heard these words of Maheśa, those birds bowed to the Lord of Gods and said: "Salutations to you, O destroyer of Bhava! (13)

The birds said: "O Lord of the helpless, O Omniscient One, what boon do we desire? Even more than this, O Three-eyed One, is that we have been beheld by you in person, even though we are in the state of animals."

May hundreds of other gains accrue here to those who possess effort through the Lord of Mountains; however, this is the supreme gain among them all: that you have come within the range of my vision. (15)
O Lord, all that is seen here is momentary and subject to decay; You alone are imperishable, and service unto You is likewise imperishable. (16)
The memory of millions of diverse births does not manifest here [in others] due to the sight of this Linga-worship performed by an ascetic. (17)
O Lord, we have long attained birth as gods; there, by our own play, we enjoyed thousands of celestial women. (18)
The womb of an Asura, a Dānava, a Nāga, a Nairṛta, a Kinnara, a Vidyādhara, and a Gandharva has been acquired by us. (19)
In the state of being human, sovereignty has been attained many times; likewise, there has been the nature of aquatic creatures in the water and the nature of land-dwellers on dry land.
Those born in the forest dwell in the forest, while those born in villages dwell in villages; there are givers and beggars, as well as protectors and slayers. (21)
We were born happy, yet we have also been miserable; we have become victors, and likewise, we have been vanquished. (22)
Even those who have studied the scriptures may be fools, and even masters may be servants; among the four classes of living beings, there are the superior, the inferior, and the middling. (23)
O Śambhu, we have existed many times, yet we have never attained stability anywhere; from this womb to that womb, and from that womb to another.

O wielder of the Pināka bow, not even the slightest trace of happiness was obtained anywhere; but now, through the accumulation of merit, by virtue of beholding the Lord of Dharma, [all has been attained]. (25)
Having beheld you in person, O Three-eyed One, we have become fulfilled—our sins incinerated by the fire of the intense penance of Tāpani. (26)
Nevertheless, O Dhūrjaṭi, if a boon is to be granted to us who are animals, then grant that knowledge, O Omniscient One, even to us who are wretched and pitiable. (27)

By that knowledge through which we have been liberated from this bond of saṃsāra, which was previously constrained by the bonds of material nature that are so difficult for those like me to break. (28)
O Śambhu, we do not desire the station of Indra, nor that of the Moon, nor indeed any other; we desire only death at Kāśī, which brings about non-rebirth.
O Omniscient One, through Your proximity we understand everything, just as all trees become fragrant through contact with sandalwood.
This alone is the supreme knowledge that causes the destruction of saṃsāra: that you have cast off your body at the proper time in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana).
Having thoroughly churned the entire web of speech, this supreme essence was formerly uttered by Brahmā: that in Kāśī, liberation awaits those who cast off their bodies. (32)
That which is expressed by many books was spoken by Hari in eight syllables before the Sun, concerning the attainment of liberation while residing in Kāśī.
The eminent sage Yājñavalkya declared in an assembly of sages: "Having studied the Vedas from the Sun, one attains the supreme state at the end in Kāśī. (34)
Long ago, on Mount Mandara, the Lord of the universe himself declared before [the gods] that this very place is Kāśī, the birthplace of liberation.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana will also say this regarding Śambhu, and not otherwise: "Where Viśveśvara is present in person, there liberation is at every step. (36)
Other ancient sages as well, such as Lomaśa and others who have renounced worldly life at sacred fords, declare that Kāśī is the illuminator of liberation.
We too know this: where the celestial river flows in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana), O Śambhu, liberation is certainly attained right there on earth.
Whatever has been, whatever is, and whatever will be—in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld—all that we know through the supreme grace of the Lord of Dharma. (39)
Therefore, O Śambhu, we understand all that has been spoken by Hiraṇyagarbha, proclaimed by Hari, uttered by the sages, and declared by you.
This entire cosmic egg is as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; it exists within the range of our speech precisely because of our devotion to the seat of Dharma.
O Lord, through the ascetic power of the King of Dharma, even we, though animals, have indeed become vessels for all-encompassing knowledge beyond doubt. (42)
Having heard the well-spoken words of the bird—sweet, gentle, truthful, measured, well-refined, beneficial, concise, and illustrated with examples—[he was moved]. (43)
Overcome with devotion and wonder, he described the greatness of the sacred seat (pīṭha): "In this city of the three worlds, the palace of the King of Kāśī is my home. (44)
There too, my abode of enjoyment, constructed of priceless jewels and known as the palace named *Mokṣalakṣmīvilāsa*, is a source of bliss. (45)
Even the winged deities who move through the sky roam at their own will, yet they too are liberated by performing circumambulation of this place.
By beholding the temple named Mokṣalakṣmīvilāsa, even the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa departs from the body at a distance; it is not otherwise.
For those by whom the vessel of the playful splendor of the Fortune of Liberation has been beheld, the jars of treasure do not leave them at every step.
Even from afar, those by whom even a banner atop my palace has been made a guest of their eyes are my constant guests. (49)
Having burst through the earth and arisen of its own accord under the guise of that temple, this is surely some supreme sprout of the bulbous root named Ānanda.
Wherein the various forms beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary beings constantly worship me alone—even those depicted in paintings, though they are diverse. (51)
In this world of Mekhila, she is my palace, the abode of supreme bliss; she is my delightful chamber of love, and she is my ground of trust. (52)

Although I am omnipresent, this temple is my supreme abode; for I, who am formless and proclaimed by the words of the highest Upaniṣads as the Supreme Brahman, have become embodied out of compassion for my devotees. (53)
That sacrificial pavilion of mine, situated in the southern direction, is the abode of the glory of ultimate liberation; there I dwell eternally—that sacrificial pavilion of mine.
He remains motionless for a period of time measuring half a blink; therein, he indeed has practiced yoga for a hundred years.
That place on the surface of the earth is named Nirvāṇamaṇḍapa; by worshipping there and reciting [the mantra] even once, one obtains the fruit of all that has been heard.
If one should perform even a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in the Pavilion of Liberation, by that the eight-limbed yoga is fully practiced, whereas elsewhere it would take ten thousand years.
Whoever should mutter even a single six-syllabled mantra in the pavilion of Nirvana shall obtain that same fruit which is gained by reciting ten million Rudra-mantras.
He who, being pure and having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, should mutter the Śatarudriya, is to be known as Rudra himself wearing the guise of a twice-born. (59)
Having performed the Brahma-yajña even once in my southern pavilion, one attains the world of Brahmā and thereafter reaches the Supreme Brahman.
He who recites the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas there, remaining free from worldly desire, shall dwell in my abode. (61)
The virtuous person who, having restrained the fickleness of the senses for even a moment, stands [steadfast] in the pavilion of Nirvana, has performed great austerity elsewhere.
Whatever merit is gained by subsisting on air alone for a hundred autumns, that merit is obtained in half a ghaṭikā by observing silence in the southern pavilion.
He who gives even a single *kṛṣṇalaka* of gold in the Muktimaṇḍapa shall travel through heaven in a golden celestial vehicle.
Whoever, on any day whatsoever, observes a fast and worships the Liṅga by keeping a single vigil, shall partake in the merit of all religious vows.
Having bestowed great gifts there, having performed great vows there, and having studied the entire Veda there, a man does not fall from heaven.
If one's life-breaths depart while in my Liberation Pavilion, he shall remain here, having entered into Me, for as long as I myself exist.
May I always perform water-sports with Umā in the pool of knowledge, by the mere drinking of whose waters stainless wisdom may arise. (68)
That place for sporting in water is a great source of joy to me; in this royal palace, it is filled with water that removes all dullness.
In front of that palace is my Śṛṅgāramaṇḍapa; that indeed should be known as the Śrīpīṭha, which bestows fortune upon those who are destitute of it. (70)
O wonder! Whoever should give there for my sake pure silk garments, and most variegated garlands perfumed with yakṣakardama paste; || 71 ||
Various articles for attire and implements for worship—wherever that most excellent man may stay, he remains adorned with splendor. (72)
The splendor of Nirvana chooses him for the attainment of the state of Nirvana; he shall certainly attain it, even if he meets his death anywhere at all. (73)
To the north of my palace named Mokṣalakṣmīvilāsa, there is a beautiful pavilion of sovereignty; therein, I bestow sovereign power. (74)
In the eastern direction from my temple, there is a pavilion of knowledge; there I constantly bestow wisdom upon the virtuous who meditate upon me.
O Bhavānī, in the palace of the king there is indeed a kitchen; whatever merit is offered there, I enjoy that with great joy. (76)
In the great mansion of Viśālākṣī, there is my place of rest; there, I grant repose to those weary from the cycle of worldly existence. (77)
The Niyamasnāna-tīrtha and my Cakrapuṣkariṇī are there; I bestow that purity upon those men who bathe therein.
That which they call the supreme reality, that which they call the highest Brahman, and that which they call self-realized—toward that very end I direct [myself]. (79)

That which they call saving knowledge, that which they call exceedingly pure, and that which they call delighting in one's own self—I impart that very thing at the conclusion of this [instruction]. (80)
There, at Maṇikarṇikā—the supreme ground of auspiciousness for the world—I shall liberate the bound souls who are fettered by their karmas.
Wherein one need not consider who is worthy or unworthy in the bestowing of nirvāṇa—that Forest of Bliss is my place for giving, day and night.
Having become the helmsman for living beings who are sinking in the exceedingly deep ocean of worldly existence, I shall ferry them across at the end.
Maṇikarṇikā is indeed renowned as the abundant ground of good fortune and prosperity; in that place, I give away my entire possession to one who is either the eldest-born or the lowest-born.

Liberation, which is difficult to attain elsewhere even for those who are sorrowful, is obtained here by those endowed with great meditative absorption (mahāsamādhi) and devoted to the meaning of the Vedānta.
Whether he be a consecrated Divākīrti or a learned man or even an unlearned one, all are equal to me in the initiation for liberation once they have reached Maṇikarṇikā.
Whatever I was miserly in giving away elsewhere, having reached Maṇikarṇikā, I give all that long-accumulated wealth to every living being.
If, by the power of destiny, this extremely rare triple conjunction has been attained here, then one's entire long-accumulated wealth should be given away without hesitation. 88.
The body, then prosperity, and then that Maṇikarṇikā—this triple conjunction is unattainable even by the gods, Indra and the rest.
Having reflected again and again, I bestow the glory of Nirvāṇa upon all living beings, provided they always dwell at Maṇikarṇikā.
That earth which grants liberation is not as great to me as the earth of Vārāṇasī; even the three worlds together could not equal the dust of that land.
But the supreme place for the worship of the Liṅga is Avimukteśvareśvara; by performing worship there even once, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
In the evening, I shall perform the Pāśupata twilight rite before the Lord Paśupati; by wearing the sacred ashes there, one is no longer bound by the fetters of the bound souls (paśu-pāśa).
I perform the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) constantly in that abode of the syllable Om; even a single saṃdhyā performed there cuts asunder all sins.
I always dwell here in Kṛttivāsa on every fourteenth day; having performed a vigil here on the fourteenth day, one does not enter a womb again.
One who worships Ratneśvara with devotion shall bestow great jewels; by worshipping that Liṅga with gems, a man obtains the jewel of a woman and other such treasures.
Although I reside within the three worlds, I dwell eternally in the Triviṣṭapa Liṅga for the fulfillment of the desires of my devotees.
Having visited the great seat Virajaska there, a person who has performed the water-libations at Caturnada certainly becomes free from passion (viraja).
At Mahādeva is my great seat (mahāpīṭha), which bestows success upon the practitioner; merely by beholding that seat, one is liberated from great sins. (99)
The sacred seat known as Vṛṣabhadhvaja bestows delight upon the ancestors; one who performs libations there for the ancestors causes them to be liberated in an instant.
At the seat of Ādikeśava, I, assuming the form of Ādikeśava, lead my most beloved Vaiṣṇava devotees to Śvetadvīpa.
In that very Maṅgalāpīṭha, which bestows all auspiciousness, at the holy site of Upapañcanada, I deliver my devotees across [to liberation].
In the form of Bindumādhava, I shall lead those Vaiṣṇava people who have bathed in the Pañcanada to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
For those who serve Vīreśvara at the great seat (pīṭha) of Pañcamudrā, supreme nirvāṇa arises in a short time.
There, at the Siddheśvarī-pīṭha near Candreśvara, success shall come within six months to those who remain in close proximity.
And in Kāśī, at the Yoginī-pīṭha which bestows the accomplishment of yoga, what excellent practitioners have not attained the supernatural powers, such as eradication and the rest? (6)
There are many sacred seats here in Kāśī at every step; yet, the power of the Dharmeśa-pīṭha is uniquely unsurpassed.
There, these young parrots became vessels for stainless knowledge; through my virtuous instruction, they cried out, "Save us! Save us! || 8 ||
From this day forward, I abandon this seat of Dharmeśvara; never again shall I leave your supreme penance grove, O son of the Sun.
"O son of the Sun, behold these parrots through my grace; having ascended a divine celestial chariot, they shall go to my great city."
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and having attained the knowledge proclaimed by me, they shall obtain liberation in this world, purified by their association with you.
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, a divine celestial chariot, resembling the peak of Kailāsa and adorned by the daughters of Rudra, arrived.
Those birds of excellent divine form did not travel by vehicle; having approached Kailāsa, those stainless ones took leave of Dharma.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dharmeśa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, having witnessed that marvel, the Mother of the Universe, bowing down, spoke to Śambhu, the supreme remover of the distress of those who prostrate before him.
Ambikā said: O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, tell me the majesty of this sacred seat (pīṭha), by which even animals attained the knowledge that liberates one from the cycle of worldly existence.
Therefore, O Dhūrjaṭi, having recognized the power of the Seat of Dharma (Dharmapīṭha), I shall remain here today until the end of this day in the presence of Dharmeśvara.
"However, for those who are devotees of this Liṅga, whether they be women or men, I shall always bring about their desired perfection."
Īśvara said: "O Goddess, you have done well by accepting this seat of Dharma, which fulfills the desires of the virtuous in this world."
For those very men who shall worship you here, O Viśvabhujā, will indeed be the enjoyers of the universe and honored by the entire world.
O All-pervading One, O Giver of sustenance, origin, and dissolution to the universe, men who worship you here shall become pure in soul.
Whoever shall offer devotion on the Manoratha-tṛtīyā day, the fulfillment of that person's desires shall come to pass through my grace.
O beloved, whether it be a woman or a man, by practicing your vow, they shall attain their heart's desires in this world and obtain knowledge at the end.
The Goddess said: O Lord, what is the nature of the vow on Manoratha-tṛtīyā, and how is its narrative? What is its fruit, and by whom has it been performed? Please tell me this; have mercy. (10)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, deliverer from worldly existence, to that which you have asked; this is the Manoratha-vrata, the supreme secret more hidden than the hidden.
In former times, the daughter of Puloman performed supreme austerity; yet, though she sought to attain a certain desire, she did not obtain the fruit of her penance.
Then she worshipped me with supreme devotion and joy, indeed with a song full of secret meaning and as sweet as the warbling of a cuckoo.

He was exceedingly pleased by that singing, which was soft and sweet, performed with excellent rhythm (*tāla*), beautiful melody (*svara*), and possessed of the proper musical modes (*dhātu*), measures (*mātrā*), and time-units (*kalā*).
He said to her, "Choose a boon, O daughter of Puloma; I am pleased with this beautiful song and with this worship of the Liṅga. (15)
Pulomajā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased with me, then fulfill that desire of mine, O Mahādeva, O Great God, O most beloved one. (16)
"May he who is honored among all the gods, who is the most beautiful among all the gods, and who is the best among all those who perform sacrifices, be my husband. (17)
O Bhava, being pleased, grant me whatever form I desire, whatever happiness I desire, and whatever lifespan I desire. 18.
And whenever I might have union with my husband out of a desire for the happiness of the heart, at each such time, having abandoned this body, may I obtain another body. (19)
And may I always possess unsurpassed devotion toward the worship of the Liṅga; O Bhava, destroyer of worldly existence, may it be the remover of old age and death. (20)
"O Mahādeva, even upon my husband's death, let there not be widowhood for me here for even a moment; and let my devotion to my husband never depart. (21)
Skanda said: Having heard this desire of Paulomī, the Lord, the destroyer of cities, smiled for a moment and spoke, filled with wonder.
Īśvara said: "O daughter of Puloman, whatever desire has been formed by you, you shall obtain it through the performance of vows; therefore, O lady of subdued senses, carry it out."
It shall come to pass through the practice of Manorathatṛtīyā; I shall describe the vow for its attainment—perform it exactly as prescribed.
O young girl, by the performance of that vow which bestows great good fortune, your heart's desire shall surely be fulfilled.

The daughter of Puloman said: "O Śambhu, ocean of compassion, bestower of all upon those who bow before you, what is the nature of this [power], what is its power, and which deity is to be worshipped therein? (26)
"And when should that be performed, and what is the procedure?"—having heard these words, Śiva spoke to her.
Īśvara said: O Paulomī, on the day of Manoratha-tṛtīyā, that auspicious vow [should be observed]; Gaurī, who possesses twenty arms and has faces on all sides, is to be worshipped. (28)
Bestowing boons and holding the gesture of fearlessness, with a rosary and water-vessel, Āśāvināyaka should be worshipped by the practitioner in front of the Goddess. (29)
Having performed the cleaning of the teeth on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, and having completed the evening rites, one should partake of a meal without excessive satiety.
One who has conquered anger and subdued the senses, having abandoned contact with the untouchable, being pure and with a mind fixed upon that [practice], should undertake the observance as well.
"O sinless Mother Viśvabhujā, I shall perform my vow in the morning; please be present there for the fulfillment of my heart's desire. (32)
Having taken up this rule, he should sleep at night while recollecting auspicious things; then, having risen in the morning, the wise man should perform his necessary daily rites.
Having performed purification and the ritual rinsing of the mouth, he should take up an auspicious tooth-stick from the Aśoka tree, which destroys all sorrows.
Having performed the daily rite, that best among those who know the ordinances, having bathed and wearing clean garments, should perform the worship of Gaurī in the evening.
Having first worshipped Vināyaka and offered him cakes filled with ghee, one should thereafter worship Viśvabhuj with auspicious Aśoka flowers.
Having first anointed [the deity] with saffron, one should offer oblations of ashoka flowers and incense made from aguru, and thereafter observe the practice of eating only once a day.
With charming *ghṛtapūras* accompanied by *aśokavartis*, O daughter of Puloman, when the third day of the month of Caitra has thus passed; (38)

One should observe the vow on the third lunar days beginning with Rādhā (the full moon of Vaiśākha) and ending with Phālgunī (the full moon of Phālguna). O sinless one, I shall describe to you the tooth-sticks in their proper sequence. (39)
O lady of auspicious vows, these are the substances for unguents, as well as flowers and food offerings for the elephant-faced god and the goddess.
And hear now the foods for the single meal that lead to the attainment of fruit: the jambu, apāmārga, khadira, jātī, mango, and kadamba. (41)
The Plakṣa, Udumbara, Kharjūrī, Bījapūra, and Daḍima—these trees are declared to be suitable for the tooth-stick of one observing a vow.
Sindūra, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, red sandalwood, gorocanā, devadāru, lotus seeds, and the two types of turmeric (niśā). || 43 ||
O child, the ointment of *yakṣakardama* is produced from *prīti*; and even when all [other ingredients] are unavailable, *yakṣakardama* alone is praised. (44)
Two parts of musk, two parts of saffron, three parts of sandalwood, and indeed one part of camphor. (45)
This is known as yakṣakardama, beloved by all the gods. Having anointed [the image] with this, one should worship it with flowers; I shall now describe those as well. (46)
With *pāṭalā*, *mallikā*, *padma*, *ketakī*, and *karavīraka*; with *utpala*, *rājacaṃpa*, *naṃdyāvarta*, and *jāti* flowers; || 47 ||
One should worship with jasmine flowers, karṇikāra flowers, and alābū leaves; or, in the absence of all these, one should worship with heaps of fragrant blossoms.
Karaṃbha, rice with curd, maṇḍakas with mango juice, pheṇikās, vaṭakas, and milk-rice with sugar. (49)
In the month of Kārttika, one should offer cooked rice with ghee in a covered vessel; in Māgha, one should offer iṇḍerikās, laḍḍūkas, and auspicious lampsikās.
Fist-sized balls filled with sugar and cooked in clarified butter should be joyfully offered to the Goddess, together with the Conqueror of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), in the month of Phālguna.
Whatever food one offers, that indeed is remembered as the "single meal. If a deluded person offers one thing but eats another while consuming, he shall fall downward.
Having thus performed worship every month on the third lunar day for a year, one should perform the worship of the fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the completion of the vow.
The observer of the vow should perform one hundred and eight oblations according to the prescribed rite, using sesame seeds and clarified butter while reciting the Jātavedasa mantra.
Worship is always prescribed for the night; indeed, eating is always at night. This fire-oblation is performed only at night, and the rite of seeking forgiveness is likewise only at night.
Accept my worship with devotion, O Mother, together with Vighnajit; salutations to you, the wielder of the universe, quickly fulfill my heart's desire! 56.
Homage to you, the creator of obstacles; homage to you, Āśāvināyaka! Together with Viśvabhujā, grant my heart’s desire. (57)
Having recited these two mantras, Gaurī and Vināyaka are to be worshipped; at the conclusion of the vow, a couch provided with a cotton mattress should be given as a gift.
Provided with secondary grains and joined with the leaves of the *dīpī* tree, he should seat the preceptor together with his wife upon a couch.
Observing the vow, he should joyfully worship with garments, ornaments for the hands and ears, fragrant sandalwood, garlands, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
For the completion of the vow, one should give a milch cow, as well as articles of enjoyment such as an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.
This vow of Manorathatṛtīyā has been performed by me; may it be complete, with nothing deficient or redundant, by your word.
Having thus taken leave of the teacher and being told by him, "So be it," he followed him as far as the boundary and gave gifts to others also according to his ability.
At night, with a well-pleased mind, he should perform the rites together with his dependents; and in the morning, on the fourth lunar day, he should feed four young boys.
Having worshipped even the twelve young maidens with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, this stainless vow thus reaches completion. (65)
This auspicious vow should be performed by all for the attainment of their heart's desires: namely, a beautiful wife of noble lineage who acts in accordance with one's own disposition. (66)
By performing this vow for a year, a youth will clearly attain Tāriṇī, the devoted wife who delivers one from the ocean of the cycle of suffering.
A maiden obtains a husband who is wealthy and preeminent in all virtues; a married woman shall obtain sons and unbroken happiness from her husband.
One who is unfortunate shall become fortunate; one who is wealthy shall become poor; and even a widow shall never again encounter widowhood anywhere. (69)
A pregnant woman obtains an auspicious son of long life, and a Brāhmaṇa obtains knowledge that bestows all good fortune. (70)
One fallen from his kingdom shall regain his kingdom, and a Vaiśya obtains profit; by the observance of this vow, a Śūdra attains whatever he has contemplated.
One who seeks righteousness attains righteousness; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth; one who seeks desire attains desires; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation. || 72 ||
Whatever desire one may have, that very thing the practitioner of the vow certainly attains by performing the observance of Manorathatṛtīyā. (73)
Skanda said: Having thus heard this from Śiva, Pārvatī, her mind filled with satisfaction, again questioned the Lord of the Universe with her hands joined in reverence.
O Sadāśiva, how will those others who perform this vow worship me, Āśāvināyaka? (75)
Śiva said: Well asked by you, O Goddess, who dispels all doubts! You are to be worshipped in Vārāṇasī, manifesting yourself in visible form to the entire universe.
Together with Āśā, the conqueror of obstacles, who fulfills all hopes, captivates endless impediments, and seeks the welfare of my field. (77)
Having caused even those who had gone far away to arrive quickly and having bowed to them, he then fulfilled their desires with thoughts that were in perfect accord with their wishes.
Except for those observing a vow, O Viśvā, an image of you made of gold should be fashioned even by one who removes obstacles, weighing no less than five kṛṣṇalas.

At the conclusion of the vow, the practitioner should give two images to the preceptor; once this has been performed, the practitioner shall have fulfilled his duty and become one who has completed his vow.
Then, O Goddess, having heard of this supreme vow, the daughter of Puloma fulfilled her heart's desire and attained that which she had longed for in her mind.
Vasiṣṭha was obtained by Arundhatī, and Atri by Anasūyā; likewise, Dhruva, the best of sons, was obtained by Sunīti from Uttānapāda.
And Sunīti’s state of being difficult to conceive was also removed by this vow; her husband, born from the ocean of milk, attained four arms. (83)
O lady of beautiful hips, what is the use of much speaking? By him who has performed this vow, all vows have certainly been performed by that observer of vows.
Having heard this meritorious narrative, the wise man, with his mind once again absorbed in it, attains auspicious understanding and is liberated even from sins.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manoratha-Tṛtīyā Vow," within the "Praise of Viśvabhujāśā-Vināyaka" in the "Account of Dharmeśvara," in the latter half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-Khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 80 ||
Agastya said: O Skanda, please show me your grace and tell me what kind of majesty of Dharmatīrtha was described by Lord Śambhu to the Goddess.
Skanda said: O highly wise one, listen as I describe the origin of Dharmatīrtha, which removes the elevation of the Vindhya mountains, exactly as it was spoken by the Lord.
Having slain Vṛtra, the enemy of Vṛtra incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin; then, filled with remorse, he questioned his domestic priest regarding the means of expiation.
Bṛhaspati said: "If you wish to dispel this brahmin-slaughter, which is so difficult to cast off, O King of the Gods, then go to Kāśī, which is protected by the Lord of the Universe."
O Śakra, no other great medicine for the sin of killing a Brahmin has been seen anywhere than this supreme capital city of the Lord of the Universe.
Even from the tip of Bhairava’s hand, the head of the son of Vidhi fell; go quickly, O enemy of Vṛtra, to that Ānandavana where it lies.
Indeed, even upon reaching the boundary of Śakrānandavana, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter would flee, trembling and without refuge.
Kāśī, presided over by Viśveśa, is the supreme destroyer of all other sins, even for those who have committed great crimes.
O Śatakratu, liberation from the great sins occurs only in Kāśī; liberation from the great cycle of existence occurs only in Kāśī and nowhere else.
Kāśī is the city of Nirvāṇa; Kāśī removes the entire mass of all sins. Kāśī is the beloved of the Lord of the Universe; there is no heaven equal to Kāśī.
For one who fears the slaughter of a Brahmin, or for one who fears worldly existence, Kāśī—the illuminator of liberation—should never be abandoned from the heart.
Wherever living beings cast off their bodies, the seeds of their karma never sprout again once they have been dried up by the power obtained through the glance of Hara.
O enemy of Vṛtra, having reached that Kāśī, propitiate Viśveśa, the bestower of universal liberation, for the sake of removing the sin of slaying Vṛtra.
Having heard these words of Bṛhaspati, the thousand-eyed one [Indra] went very swiftly to Kāśī, which destroys great sins.
Having bathed in the northward-flowing river and standing around Dharmeśa, he propitiated Mahādeva for the removal of his sin against a Brāhmaṇa.
Then Sutrāman, intent on the recitation of the Mahārudra, beheld the Three-eyed Lord situated within the center of the Liṅga, illuminating the sky with his own radiance.
He praised him again in many ways with the Rudra-sūktas declared in the Vedas; then, emerging from the Liṅga and manifesting himself, Bhava spoke.
"O Lord of Śacī, I am pleased; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows! Tell me quickly what should be given, O you who have made your abode upon the seat of Dharma! (18)
Having heard these words of love from the God of gods, Hari, the slayer of Vṛtra, spoke thus to him: "O Omniscient One, what is unknown to you? (19)
Then, impelled by compassion for him, the Lord established a holy site (tīrtha) there through his attendance at the Seat of Dharma (dharmapīṭha), and said, "O Indra, bathe here."

There, by the mere act of bathing, Indra instantly became endowed with divine fragrance and regained his former beautiful luster, which had been lost during the performance of the Śatayajña sacrifice.
Then, having witnessed that wonder, the sages headed by Nārada, filled with joy, bathed in the Dharmatīrtha, which removes all sins.
They gratified the divine ancestors and performed śrāddha rites with faith; they bathed Dharmeśa with jars filled with the waters of that sacred ford.
From that time onwards, that holy place became renowned as Dharmāndhu; it is the supreme means for washing away sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, without any difficulty.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to come from bathing in the King of Tīrthas, that same fruit shall be multiplied a thousandfold merely by bathing in Dharmāndhu.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains at Gaṅgādvāra, Kurukṣetra, or at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, that he shall obtain at Dharmatīrtha.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by bathing in the Narmadā, the Sarasvatī, or the Gautamī when Jupiter is in Leo, that same fruit one shall obtain at Dharmakūpa.
Whatever fruit may be obtained by bathing at Mānasa, Puṣkara, Dvārakā, and likewise at the ocean, that same fruit shall be obtained at the Dharmajalāśaya.

Whatever fruit is obtained at Śaṅkhoddhāra on the day of Hari (the eleventh lunar day) during the month of Kārttika at Sūkarakṣetra, or during the month of Caitra at Gaurīmahāhrada—that same fruit is indeed obtained here.
The ancestors await two sacred bathing places—the Gaṅgā and Dharmakūpa—expecting men who desire to bathe with the hope that they will offer them funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
In the presence of the Grandfather (Brahmā), or before Dharmeśa, or at Phalgu and Dharmakūpa, the great-grandfathers rejoice.
Having bathed in the Well of Dharma and fully satiated his ancestors, what more could a man do upon going to Gayā that would bring such joy to his forefathers? (32)
Just as the ancestors become satisfied by the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā, so too shall they be at Dharmatīrtha—neither less nor more.
They are blessed and devoted to their fathers; by them the grandfathers have been gratified—those sons who have fulfilled the debt to the ancestors at the Dharma-tīrtha.
By the power of that holy place, he became free from sin in an instant; having bowed to the Lord of the gods, Indra went to Amarāvatī.
O Pot-born Sage, the majesty of that Dharma-tīrtha is boundless; even by merely beholding one’s own reflection in its well, one obtains the fruit of performing a śrāddha offering.
Even there, if a man should offer as little as a single *kākiṇī* for the delight of his ancestors, he obtains inexhaustible fruit through the power of the Seat of Dharma.
In that place, whoever should feed Brahmins who are self-restrained and ascetic, he shall clearly obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice for every single grain of rice.
Having reached Amarāvatī, Śakra then described the great majesty of the Dharmapīṭha at Kāśī before the city-dwellers of heaven.
Having returned once more to this Forest of Śambhu’s Bliss, Hari, together with the hosts of eminent sages, installed a liṅga.
To the west of Tārakeśa is the one called Indreśvara; by the sight of it, the world of Indra is not far for men.
To the south of that is Śacīśa himself, installed by Śacī; by worshipping Śacīśa, women shall attain incomparable good fortune.
Near that is Raṃbheśa, who bestows abundant happiness and prosperity; and around Indreśvara is another supreme deity, Lokapāleśvara.

Through the worship of that [deity], the world-protectors (Lokapālas), who bestow prosperity, become pleased. To the west of Dharmeśa, Dharaṇīśa is celebrated; by beholding him, one shall possess fortitude in the kingdom, the royal family, and so forth.
To the south of Dharmeśa, the supreme [liṅga] known as Tattveśa should be worshipped by men; through the propitiation of that liṅga, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) shall arise.
One should worship Vairāgyeśa in the eastern direction from Dharmeśa; by the mere touch of that linga, there is the cessation of the mind's [worldly] inclinations.
Likewise, Jñāneśvara, the bestower of knowledge upon all embodied beings, is in the northeast; and Aiśvaryeśa is to the north of the auspicious Dharmeśvara Liṅga.
From the sight of them, men shall attain the sovereignty desired by their minds; O Pot-born One, these are the lingas that possess the forms of the five-faced one. (48)
By certainly resorting to these, a person attains the eternal state. O Sage, listen as I relate another account that occurred in that very place. 49.
Having heard this, even a man does not sink into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra; here on earth is the great foothill of the Vindhya range named Kadambaśikhara.
There was a king there named Durdama, the son of Dama; having obtained the kingdom upon his father's death, he remained one whose senses were unsubdued.
Deluded by lust, he would forcibly seize the wives of the citizens; the wicked became dear to him, while the virtuous fell into his disfavour.
He punished those who deserved no punishment and turned his face away from those who deserved punishment; he was constantly addicted to hunting and associated with hunters.
Those who bestowed sound counsel were banished from his own realm; the Śūdra officials of justice were made to pay tribute, while the Brāhmaṇas were reduced to the status of tax-payers.
Content with the wives of others and turning his face away from his own wife, he never once worshipped the two gods who bring an end to suffering.
The two lords, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śrīpati, who remove all sins, grant all desires, and are the essence of the entire world for everyone. (56)
Among his own subjects, that king named Durdama rose up like another comet for their destruction; indeed, he was a calamity in very deed.
Once, afflicted by the addiction to hunting, he entered the forests on horseback together with hunters, followed by a young cow.
By the turn of fate, that king Durdama, alone, armed with a bow and mounted on a horse, entered the Ānandakānana forest.
Then, having observed everywhere trees with fresh foliage, providing excellent shade and great breadth, he became as if his fatigue had vanished.
For a moment, the king was fanned with leaf-fans by the Kujas with fragrant, cool, exhilarating, and pleasant breezes.
The weariness born of hunting alone did not depart; rather, the weariness produced since birth vanished upon seeing that forest. (62)
In the middle of the forest, he beheld a palace that kissed the sky, like a single beautiful mine of great jeweled spikes.
Then, having dismounted from his horse, that king, filled with great wonder, reached the pavilion of Dharmeśa and praised himself.
I am blessed; I am filled with joy; my two eyes are blessed today, since I have beheld this land. (65)
Furthermore, by the power of Dharmapīṭha, he censured himself: "Fie on me, who have associated with the wicked and abandoned the company of the virtuous! (66)
One who causes distress to living beings, who is deluded yet considers himself an expert in oppressing his subjects, and who takes pleasure in seizing the wives and wealth of others; || 67 ||
Until this day, the life of me, one of small intellect, has passed in vain, since such places of dharma as these have never been seen by me anywhere. (68)
Having thus reproached himself in many ways and bowed to the all-pervading Lord of Dharma, King Durdaṃḍa mounted his horse and departed for his own kingdom.
Then, having summoned the long-standing ministers who had come down through succession, he dismissed the new ones and also called together the citizens.
Having paid homage to the brahmins and granted them their livelihoods, and having entrusted the kingdom to his son and established the subjects in righteousness; || 71 ||
Having punished those deserving of punishment and having gratified the virtuous, he even renounced his wife, turning his back upon the objects of the senses.
Then, traveling alone, he arrived at Kāśī, which causes the blossoming of the highest good; having propitiated Dharmeśvara, he attained nirvāṇa in due course of time. || 73 ||
Through the constant vision of Dharmeśa, that Durdamas became such as he was; he became the best among the self-controlled and attained liberation in the end. || 74 ||
Thus, O Pot-born One, the greatness of Dharmeśa has been described by me in brief; who indeed can fully know the majesty of Dharmapīṭha?
That best of men who hears this narrative called Dharmeśvara shall, in an instant, be liberated from the sins accumulated since birth.
At the time of the Śrāddha ceremony, the wise man should especially cause the Brahmins to hear this supreme narrative called Dharmeśa, which is the cause of satisfaction for the ancestors.
Even one who stands at a distance, being wise, shall be liberated from all sins upon hearing this discourse on Dharma and will go in the end to the abode of Śiva.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dharmeśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 81.
Pārvatī said: O Maheśāna, the great majesty of Vīreśa is heard of; there, more than a hundred perfected ones (siddhas) have attained supreme success and are fully satisfied. || 1 ||
O Lord of the World, tell me how that most excellent Liṅga, which bestows swift accomplishment in this world, manifested itself here in Kāśī. || 2 ||
Maheśvara said: Listen, O Great Goddess, to the supreme manifestation of Vīreśa; by hearing of it, O Śivā, a person attains abundant merit. (3)
There was a king named Amitrajit, a conqueror of enemy cities, who was righteous, endowed with courage, and devoted to pleasing his subjects.
He was named Yaśodhana, generous, wise, and devoted to the Brahmins; his hair was always moistened by the ritual bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice.

Disciplined and endowed with statesmanship, he was skilled in all undertakings; having reached the further shore of the ocean of knowledge, he was virtuous and affectionate toward those possessed of virtue.
Grateful, sweet-spoken, and averse to evil deeds; truthful in speech, an abode of purity, sparing in words, and having his senses conquered.

On the field of battle he was like the God of Death, yet in the assembly hall he was a man of refined learning; though a youth, he was an expert in the amorous sports of lovely women and was beloved by the elderly.
His treasury was increased by righteousness and wealth; he possessed abundant forces and vehicles; he was fortunate and handsome; he was highly intelligent and a refuge for his excellent progeny.
Endowed with steadfastness and fortitude, skilled in discerning place and time, always bestowing honor upon others, and forever free from all faults. || 10 ||
Having fixed his mental faculty upon the pair of feet of Vāsudeva, he ruled the kingdom free from dualities and devoid of all worldly talk.
The illustrious one, whose commands were inviolable and who was devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu, enjoyed abundant pleasures that had been entirely surrendered to Viṣṇu.
In the auspicious kingdom of that treasury of great fortune, there were lofty temples of Hari on every palace and at every step.
O Govinda, protector of the cowherds and guardian of the cattle, you who enchant the hearts of the gopīs; O mace-wielder, beyond all qualities yet rich in virtues, whose banner bears Garuḍa.
O enemy of Keśin, Hṛd, and Kaiṭabha; O foe of Kaṃsa; O Lord of Kamalā! O Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, lotus-eyed one, destroyer of the fear of Death! 15.
O Supreme Person, O Destroyer of Evil, O Lotus-eyed One! O You clothed in yellow silk, O Padmanābha, O Higher than the Highest!
O Janārdana, Lord of the Universe, you who were born from the waters of the Ganges; O remover of the birth of living beings, O destroyer of the sins of those who constantly mutter prayers! 17.

O you whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa, O beloved of Śrī, O bringer of prosperity, O treasury of all blessings; O Śauri, whose bow is the Śārṅga, whose abode is Śrīraṅga, and whose eyes are like the cool-rayed moon.
O enemy of the Daityas, O foe of the Dānavas, O Dāmodara, O ender of all things! O delight of Devakī's heart, O you who recline upon the lord of serpents! 19.
O Viṣṇu, whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha; O enemy of Bāṇa; O Viṣṭaraśravas; O Viṣvaksena; O support of Virādha; O wearer of the forest garland; O lover of the forest!
"O Trivikrama, O Lord of the three worlds, O wielder of the discus, O four-armed one"—such pure names [should be recited] in every temple. (21)
But wherever one may hear the delightful words of the enemy of Madhu uttered by women, the elderly, children, or even cowherds, [one should listen]. (22)
In every house, only the groves of Surasā trees are seen, as well as the wonderful and purifying deeds of the Lord of the Ocean-born Goddess.
On the walls of the palaces, however, only those things created by painters are seen; no other discourse is heard except for the stories of Hari.
Out of fear of that king, even hunters did not pierce those who bore the portions of Hari’s own name and lived happily wandering in the forest.
Neither fish, nor tortoises, nor boars were killed anywhere by anyone out of fear of him, even by those who eat the flesh of fish. (26)
Moreover, in the kingdom of that Mitrajit, even those lying on their backs never suckle at the breast upon reaching the day of Hari.
Even animals, abandoning their diet of grass on the day of Hari, have become intent upon fasting; what then need be said of other men? (28)
While he was ruling the earth, when the day of Hari arrived, a great festival was celebrated by all the citizens.
On this earth, he alone became subject to punishment by King Mitravijit—whosoever was devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, even at the cost of their lives or their wealth.
Even the outcastes in that kingdom, having received the Vaiṣṇava initiation, shone like those who had been consecrated, bearing the marks of the conch and the discus.
Whatever auspicious deeds are performed daily by people, they are offered to Vāsudeva by those who desire no fruit for them.
Except for Mukunda, Govinda, the supreme bliss, the infallible one, no other should ever be chanted, meditated upon, or worshipped by people anywhere. (33)
Kṛṣṇa alone was the supreme deity; Kṛṣṇa alone was the ultimate refuge; Kṛṣṇa alone was the supreme kinsman of that lord of the earth. (34)
While that protector of the earth was thus governing the kingdom properly, once the illustrious Nārada arrived, desiring to see him.
Then, duly honored by the king with the offering of madhuparka according to the prescribed ritual, Nārada described that king, the conqueror of enemies.
Nārada said: "O lord of the people, you are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are worthy of honor even among the gods, for you perceive Govinda in all living beings."
He who knows that Puruṣa Viṣṇu, who is Hari, the Person of Sacrifice; he who is the inner self of this world, the all-pervading creator, destroyer, and protector. || 38 ||
O best of kings, as I beheld the universe as being composed of that [Brahman], I attained supreme purity upon receiving your auspicious vision. (39)
For in this world, which is subject to momentary destruction, there is indeed only one essence: devotion to the lotus feet of the Beloved of Kamalā, which bestows everything. (40)
For indeed, all objects of value resort to that person of great intelligence who, having renounced everything, always worships Viṣṇu alone.
Alas, he whose senses have attained stability in Hṛṣīkeśa alone attains stability in this exceedingly fickle universe.
Knowing that youth, wealth, and life are exceedingly fickle—like drops of water upon a lotus leaf—one should take refuge in Acyuta alone. (43)
He in whose speech, mind, and everywhere else dwells the Lord Janārdana—he alone, in human form, is always to be worshipped as Janārdana.
Who on this earth has not attained the state of Supreme Person by emulating the Lord of Śrī with sincere resolve? (45)
