Even more meritorious for men than that is the holy site of Citraratheśvara; having bathed and given gifts there, one does not behold Citragupta.
Beyond that is the meritorious Dharmatīrtha situated in front of Dharmeśa; by performing the śrāddha and other rites there, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors. || 1 ||
Then there is the pure Viśālatīrtha, which bestows abundant fruit; having bathed there and beheld Viśālākṣī, one is not born again from a womb. || 2 ||
There is also the Jarāsaṃdheśa Tīrtha in the vicinity of Jarāsaṃdheśa; one who bathes there is not deluded by the afflictions of the fever of worldly existence.
Beyond that is Lalitātīrtha, which increases great good fortune; having bathed there and worshipped Lalitā, one becomes neither poor nor a partaker of suffering.
Then, having bathed at Gautama-tīrtha, which purifies all sins, and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) there, one grieves nowhere at all.
Then there is the Gaṅgākeśava-tīrtha and the tīrtha known as Agastya; after that is the Yoginī-tīrtha, and beyond that is the one called Trisaṃdhyā.
Then there is the Nārmada Tīrtha, then the Āruṃdhateyaka; then the Vāsiṣṭha Tīrtha, and the unsurpassed Mārkaṇḍeya.
These sacred fords (tīrthas) should be known as bestowing merit in an ever-increasing degree; and after that is the unsurpassed sacred ford named Khurakartari.
There, by performing acts such as ancestral rites (śrāddha), one is liberated from sins; thereafter is the Bhagīratha Tīrtha, which bestows great merit upon royal sages.
Whatever small amount one may give there shall indeed remain inexhaustible even at the end of a kalpa; for it is superior even to these sacred fords and even to thirty million lingas.
The Vīravīreśvara Liṅga shall become most excellent; having bathed in the Vīra-tīrtha and having fully worshipped Vīreśa, a man [attains the supreme goal]. || 11 ||
One becomes as if bathed in all these sacred fords (tīrthas) and not otherwise; he who shall worship the Vīreśvara Liṅga at night has indeed worshipped here Liṅgas numbering three crores.
But he who desires prosperity that bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment, by him the Vīreśvara Liṅga should be worshipped with great effort.
Having performed a single vigil while worshipping Vīreśa on the fourteenth lunar day (bhūtā), a man does not again assume a body composed of the five elements.
This Liṅga should always be worshipped by the Siddhas who desire complete perfection; for it shall fulfill all desires pertaining to both this world and the next.
The man who performs an ablution with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) at Vīreśa shall obtain, for every single pala, the fruit produced by ten million water-pots.
Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere by offering ten million flowers at a linga, that same fruit is attained by offering a single flower at Vīreśa; of this there is no doubt.
By offering even a single oblation in the vicinity of Vīreśvara, one fully obtains the fruit of ten million homas; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
For every single grain of rice offered as a sweetened oblation, there shall be the fruit of ten million grains; even a very small act performed for Vīreśa becomes inexhaustible.
If one recites even a single Mahārudra in the presence of Vīreśa, or causes it to be recited, he will certainly obtain the fruit of ten million Rudras.
Whatever rites, such as the concluding ceremony of a vow, are performed at Vīreśa by men observing vows, that indeed becomes multiplied ten millionfold; of this there is no doubt. (21)
Whoever has performed eight prostrations before Vīreśvara obtains the fruit of eighty million prostrations; of this there is no doubt.
"O Hero, by virtue of my granting this boon, this Liṅga shall become the abode of all prosperities; it will be Vīraśivara, of this there is no doubt. (23)
By my command, the knowledge known as Tāraka shall arise within men; this Liṅga must be worshipped by those seeking auspicious goals while they are still alive.
Having heard this, the hero, the son of Mitrajit, his desires completely fulfilled, bowed to the Lord of the gods and spoke again.
"O Lord of Gods, these sacred fords which have been mentioned before me by you—out of compassion, O Lord, please speak of others as well. (26)
Beginning from Ādikeśava up to that Bhagīratha Tīrtha—by the mere hearing of which names a man becomes free from sin. (27)
Having heard what was spoken by the son of the king, Maheśāna again began to describe the holy sites along the Gaṅgā.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Vīreśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Listen, O Brahmin, to how Sthāṇu made the ground of the holy site from the meritorious confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Varaṇā. || 1 ||
Having bathed there at the confluence and having worshipped Saṅgameśa, a man shall never again enter the womb of a mother.
Therein lies the Pādodaka Tīrtha, where the feet of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow were first washed when he had come from Mount Mandara.
He who performs the water-rites at the sacred ford of Viṣṇupādodaka during the Vyatīpāta yoga will certainly not again experience the cycle of worldly existence.
Having performed his ablutions with the water used for washing the feet [of the deity] and having worshipped Keśava, that best of men dwelt in Kāśī, free from the attachments of worldly existence.
In Kāśī, that ground is designated as Śvetadvīpa by the twice-born; having performed the accumulation of merit there, one shall become the lord of Śvetadvīpa.
Then, from the Pādodaka Tīrtha, one proceeds to the Tīrtha known as Kṣīrābdhi; having acquired great merit there, one may dwell upon the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
To the south of the Kṣīroda [ocean] is the unsurpassed holy site named Śaṅkha; one who bathes there will surely become the lord of the treasures, beginning with Śaṅkha.
And indeed, the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha is located on this side of Śaṅkhatīrtha; by bathing in the water of that tīrtha, one shall not fall into the wheel of worldly existence.
In front of that is Gadātīrtha, which destroys the disease of saṃsāra; by performing śrāddha and other rites there, one shall behold the Lord Gadādhara.
In front of that is Padmākṛti and Padmatīrtha, which brings satisfaction to the ancestors; by performing ablutions and other rites there, one attains the destruction of sins.
Next is the sacred site of Mahālakṣmī, which bestows the fruit of great merit; by worshipping Mahālakṣmī there, one shall attain the lotus of liberation.
Then there is the Gārutmata Tīrtha, which destroys the poison of saṃsāra; having performed the water-rites there, one obtains residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
Then there is Nāradatīrtha, the sole cause for the knowledge of Brahman; by bathing there and beholding Nāradakeśava, one shall be liberated.
To the south of that is the Prahlāda-tīrtha, which bestows the fruit of great devotion; merely by bathing there, one becomes most dear to Viṣṇu. (15)
Next is the Ambārīṣa Tīrtha, which destroys great sins; there indeed, people of auspicious deeds do not become vessels for the womb.
Before that is the supreme holy site named Ādityakeśava; having performed an ablution there as well, one shall obtain the consecration of heaven.
There exists the Tīrtha of Dattātreya, which purifies the three worlds; one attains perfection in Yoga there by merely bathing with devotion. (18)
In front of that is the Bhārgava Tīrtha, which bestows great knowledge; by performing the rite of bathing there, one becomes a partaker of the world of Bhārgava.
Then there is Vāmanatīrtha, which is the cause of Viṣṇu’s presence; by performing the śrāddha rite there, one is liberated from the debt owed to the ancestors.
Indeed, that auspicious holy site known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa exists there; by bathing in that tīrtha, rebirth in a womb becomes very difficult for men to attain. (21)
And to the south of that is the auspicious Yajñavārāha-tīrtha, where for men who have bathed, the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice is certain.
There is a purifying holy site there known as Vidāranārasiṃha, where by a single bath, the sin accumulated over hundreds of births may perish. (23)
And then there is Gopīgoviṃda-tīrtha, which bestows the world of Viṣṇu; having bathed there, a wise man shall not experience the suffering of the womb again.
To the south of Gopīgoviṃda is Lakṣmīnṛsiṃhatīrtha, where the best of men is chosen by Nirvāṇalakṣmī.
In that southern direction lies the unsurpassed Śeṣatīrtha, where even the remnant of a multitude of great sins does not remain after one has immersed oneself there.
And to the south of that is the excellent Śaṅkhamādhava-tīrtha; by resorting to that holy place, how could there be any great fear of sin for men? (27)
Even more purifying than that is the incomparable holy site named Nīlagrīva, which grants success at that very moment; one who bathes there is always pure.
Therein is the Uddālaka-tīrtha, which destroys the flood of all sins; by merely bathing there, it bestows great prosperity upon men. (29)
Then there is the holy ford named Sāṃkhya, in the vicinity of Sāṃkhyeśvara; by resorting to that holy ford, the yoga of Sāṃkhya becomes manifest for men.
Since the Lord himself, the husband of Umā, merged into this world from the heavenly realm (Svarloka), therefore, in the vicinity of Svarlīneśvara, there is the Svarlīna Tīrtha.
There, through bathing, giving gifts, faith, feeding the twice-born, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, everything indeed becomes inexhaustible for men.
And near that is the purifying Mahiṣāsura-tīrtha, where that lord of the Daityas, having performed austerities, conquered all the gods.
Even today, the servant of that sacred ford is not overcome by women, nor by great sins; and he shall obtain the fruit that was prayed for.
And nearby that is Bāṇatīrtha, which bestows a thousand arms; a man who bathes there shall attain firm devotion to Śambhu.
In front of that is an excellent sacred site named Gopratāreśvara, where even one who is childless may cross the Vaitaraṇī river with ease after bathing there.
To the south of that is the sacred ford named Hiraṇyagarbha, which removes all sins; one who bathes there is never again separated from gold.
Then there is the Praṇavatīrtha, the most excellent among all holy places; by merely bathing there, a human being becomes liberated while living.
"Therefore, O Sage Agastya, that holy ford Piśaṅgilā—which removes sin even by its mere sight—is indeed my own abode and bestows supreme perfection."
Having bathed at the Piśaṅgilā tīrtha and given some gift, why should one grieve over committed sins even if one dies elsewhere? (40)
"Whoever bathes at the Piśaṅgilā tīrtha and worships me, he shall become my friend, equal in splendor to the radiance of Mitra. (41)
Then there is the sacred ford named Pilipilā, which has been made perfectly pure by the gaze of the inhabitants of heaven and which destroys the impurities of the mind.
There, by performing acts such as the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and by satisfying the poor and the helpless, a human being attains great and exceedingly stable prosperity. (43)
Beyond that is the Nāgeśvara Tīrtha, which purifies great sins; by merely bathing in that Tīrtha, there shall be the destruction of all evil.
To the south of that is the supreme and highly meritorious holy site named Karṇāditya, where a mortal who bathes shall attain the splendor of the Sun-god.
Then there is Bhairavatīrtha, which brings about the destruction of the great flood of sins, causes the arising of the four aims of life, and wards off all obstacles. || 46 ||
Having bathed there on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight (Bhaumāṣṭamī), a man should offer libations to the ancestors; and by beholding Bhairava Kāla, he shall conquer both Kali and Time.
To the east of the Bharadvāja Tīrtha is the holy site named Kharvanṛsiṃha; for a man who has bathed there, whence could there be any fear born of the womb?
To the south of that is the extremely pure Tīrtha of the sage Mṛkaṇḍu; by bathing there, mortals never encounter untimely death.
Then there is the sacred site known as Pañcanada, frequented by all holy places; having bathed there, a person shall not be born again into the cycle of worldly existence.
Whatever holy places exist everywhere within the interior of the cosmic egg, they all come together here during the month of Kārttika for the complete removal of the flood of one's own sins.
Where all the most excellent holy places always remain for three days, beginning with the tenth day, for the sake of their own purification.
Abundantly, at every step within Kāśī, all sacred fords (tīrthas) exist; however, the greatness of Pāñcanada is not equaled by any of them anywhere.
Even if a single day of Kārttika is made fruitful there through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and gifts, they alone have truly accomplished their purpose.
And even all the sacred fords (tīrthas), though weighed together simultaneously, did not equal even a sixteenth part (kalā) of the Pañcanadī.
Having bathed at the Pāñcanada tīrtha and beheld Bindumādhava, the wise man is never again born upon the stage of his mother’s womb.
Beyond that is the sacred ford Jñānahrada, which removes the dullness even of the ignorant; a man who bathes there shall never suffer a loss of knowledge.
Having bathed there in the lake of knowledge and beheld Jñāneśvara, a person shall indeed attain that knowledge by which he is never again afflicted.
Therefore, there is the Maṅgala Tīrtha, which destroys all inauspiciousness; by bathing there, one shall become a vessel of auspiciousness. (59)
Inauspicious things shall perish and auspicious things shall come to pass for one who bathes in this auspicious tīrtha and for one who offers salutations to it. (60)
In front of that is the Malanāśana Tīrtha belonging to Mayūkhamālin; one who bathes there and beholds Gabhastīśa shall become pure.
Makhatīrtha is located right there, in the vicinity of Makhaiśvara; the best of men, having bathed there, obtains the merit born of sacrifice.
Beside that is Bindutīrtha, the cause of supreme knowledge; by performing śrāddha and other rites there, one obtains the highest merit.
And there is the holy ford (tīrtha) of the sage Pippalāda situated in the southern direction; having bathed there on a Saturday and having beheld Pippaleśvara, [one attains merit].
Having worshipped the Pippala tree there with the mantra "aśvattha," one does not suffer from the affliction of Saturn, and it also destroys bad dreams. || 65 ||
Then there is the exceedingly purifying holy site (tīrtha) named Tāmravarāha, where by bathing and giving gifts, one shall not sink into the ocean of sin.
At its head is the Kālagaṅgā, which destroys the impurities of the Kali age; by bathing in it, a wise man becomes free from sin at that very moment.
At the great pilgrimage site of Indradyumna, situated before the deity Indradyumneśvara, one who performs the water-rites there shall attain the world of Indra.
Then there is Rāmatīrtha, located in front of Vīrarāmeśvara; by merely bathing in that tīrtha, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. || 69 ||
Next is the Aikṣvāka-tīrtha, which destroys the flood of all sins; by bathing there, the best of men becomes purified in soul. (70)
At its edge, near Marutteśvara, is the Marutta-tīrtha; having bathed there and worshipped that Lord Īśa, one shall attain great sovereignty.
And beyond that is the Maitrāvaruṇa-tīrtha, which destroys all sins; by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) there, one becomes dear to the ancestors.
Thereafter, by bathing in the great and pure Agnitīrtha situated in front of Agnīśa, one attains the world of Agni.
Right there, in the vicinity of Aṅgāreśvara, is the Aṅgāra-tīrtha; by bathing there on the Aṅgāra-caturthī, one shall attain freedom from sin.
Therefore, indeed, by bathing at Kalītīrtha in the vicinity of Kalaśeśvara and worshipping that Liṅga, one does not fear the Kali age or Time.
And right there, in the vicinity of Candreśvara, is Candratīrtha; having bathed there and worshipped Candreśa, one shall attain the world of the Moon.
In front of that, near Vīreśvara, is the Vīratīrtha, which was previously described by you as the most excellent and supreme among all holy places.
And then there is Vighneśatīrtha, which destroys all obstacles; one who has bathed there at any time is never overcome by obstacles. (78)
Next is the unsurpassed tīrtha of the royal sage Hariścandra, where a man who has bathed never at any time deviates from the truth.
O hero, whatever merit is acquired at the holy site of Hariścandra yields inexhaustible fruit, both in this world and in the next.
Then, there is Parvatatīrtha near Parvateśa; by bathing there on a festival day or even when it is not a festival day, one obtains the fruit of all festivals.
There is the Kaṃbalāśvatara Tīrtha, which destroys all poisons; a mortal who bathes there becomes an expert in the science of music.
Then there is the Sarasvata Tirtha, which bestows all branches of knowledge; there the ancestors dwell together with the celestial rishis and human beings.
Umātīrtha, endowed with all powers, is located right there; it is certain that by merely bathing there, one shall attain the world of Umā. (84)
Then, O hero, there is that most excellent holy site, renowned throughout the three worlds and capable of uplifting the three worlds, whose name is Maṇikarṇikā.
At the very beginning, Viṣṇu established the Cakrapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha; by merely hearing its name, one is liberated from all sins.
The inhabitants of heaven indeed chant Maṇikarṇikā at the three junctions of the day; for the mere utterance of its name brings about the highest welfare for men.
O Hero, those by whom Maṇikarṇikā has been heard, remembered, or seen—they alone are the successful ones in this world; they alone have indeed accomplished their life's purpose.
O hero, those men of meritorious deeds in the three worlds who here recite the name of Maṇikarṇikā—I myself recite it for them at the three times of day.
He has performed great sacrifices with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees by whom the five-syllabled great vidyā of Maṇikarṇikā has been uttered. (90)
"O hero, great gifts were indeed bestowed by that performer of meritorious deeds, by whom I was honored upon reaching Maṇikarṇikā. (91)
By him whose great-grandfathers have been satiated with the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, śrāddhas have been offered at Gayā with honeyed milk-rice.
For one of pure intellect who has drunk the water of Maṇikarṇikā, what need is there for those soma-libations that result in rebirth? 93.
They have bathed extensively in all the sacred fords during the great festival occasions, and likewise, they have bathed at Maṇikarṇikā with all the ritual purificatory baths.
By them, all the gods, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, were honored with sacrifices; for they had worshipped Maṇikarṇikā with golden flowers and jewels.
Having received from him, along with Umā, the initiation pertaining to Śambhu, I was worshipped daily by him, through whom the Nava-ṇikarṇikā was honored.
By him penances were performed for a long time with withered leaves and such, and by him the glorious Maṇikarṇikā was served with faith. (97)

Having bestowed abundant gifts and performed numerous sacrifices, and having practiced austerities for a long time in the forests, they fall from the sovereignty of heaven back to the earth once again. (98)
On this vast surface of the earth, within a radius of five krośas, Maṇikarṇikā is enchanting; those who have resorted to her have gone from whence there is no returning.
I consider this alone to be the fruit of all gifts, vows, sacrifices, and even austerities: that Maṇikarṇikā is attained. 100.
This glorious Maṇikarṇikā is the manifest goddess of the fortune of liberation; indeed, even I cannot clearly know her greatness in its entirety.
To the south of Maṇikarṇikā is the supreme Pāśupata Tīrtha; beyond that is the Tīrtha known as Rudravāsa, and after that is Viśvatīrtha.
Beyond that is the delightful Muktitīrtha, and then the supreme Avimukta; then the Tāraka-tīrtha, the Skānda-tīrtha, and after that the tīrtha of Ḍhuṇḍhi.
Then there is Bhavānī, and then Aiśāna, the supreme Jñānatīrtha; then Naṃditīrtha, Viṣṇutīrtha, and thereafter the Paitāmaha-tīrtha.
This is the Nābhi-tīrtha, and beyond this is the Brahma-nāla; thereafter is the Bhāgīratha-tīrtha, which was previously described before you.
In the celestial river that flows toward the north, in the vicinity of Kāśī, there are many meritorious holy sites (tīrthas); however, I have described them to you only briefly.
Even there, O Prince, the Pañcatīrthī is preeminent; having bathed in it, a person shall no longer remember dwelling in a womb.
First is Asisaṃbheda, the supreme and most excellent of holy fords (tīrthas); then there is the one named Daśāśvamedha, frequented by all sacred sites.
Then there is the Pādodaka Tīrtha in the vicinity of Ādikeśava; thereafter is the meritorious Pañcanada, which removes the flood of sins merely by bathing.
O best of beings, among these four holy places, the fifth, known as Maṇikarṇikā, grants purification of the mind through mere remembrance.
I bathe here constantly with Umā on the festival days, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the divine sages headed by Indra.
Therefore, this verse, which is approved by the Vedas, is constantly sung here by those who dwell in the world of the Nagas as well as by the inhabitants of heaven.
Truth, truth, and again truth—this word is preceded by truth: there is no holy site equal to Maṇikarṇī within the entire sphere of the universe.
Having bathed at Pañcatīrthī in Kāśī, a man never again assumes a body composed of the five elements; rather, he is born as a lion (Pañcāsya).
Having thus granted these boons, Lord Hara vanished from the sight of Vīra; and that Vīra, having worshipped the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa), attained his desired object.
Skanda said: O Agastya, whoever should listen to this meritorious chapter on sacred fords (tīrtha), his sins accumulated even over a hundred lifetimes shall be destroyed.
Thus, the narrative of Vīreśvara has been told to you in connection with the description of the sacred fords; I shall now describe Kāmeśa.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vīreśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 84.
Skanda said: Just as that meritorious story was told by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) in the presence of Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, so shall I relate it to you.
Formerly, [he traversed] this entire earth, including its oceans, mountains, and forests; with its rivers and seas, and its villages, cities, and towns.
Having wandered about, the one of great splendor, great wrath, and great austerity, Durvāsas, arrived at Śambhu’s Ānandakānana.

Beholding the entire pleasure-garden adorned with many palaces, as well as numerous sacrificial pits and ponds, Durvāsas attained great satisfaction. At every step, seeing the beautiful huts of the sages who had conquered the great fear of Death, Durvāsas was filled with wonder.
Seeing trees laden with flowers of all seasons, possessing beautiful shade and glossy foliage, bearing fruit, and entwined by lovely creepers, the sage attained great joy.
And Durvāsas became exceedingly joyful upon seeing those supreme Pāśupatas, whose entire bodies were adorned with sacred ashes and whose heads were matted with locks of hair.

Wearing only their loincloths, they were intent on meditation upon the Enemy of Smara (Śiva); having girded themselves with large gourds, they surpassed the clouds with the sound of their *huḍut* grunts.
Having seen in some places Tridaṇḍins who were unattached and free from possessions, possessing only a basket, a staff, a water-pot, and a bowl; || 9 ||

They were free from fear even regarding Time (Death), having taken refuge in the Lord of the Universe; in some places, they were knowers of the secret of the Vedas who had observed celibacy since childhood.
Their hair was perpetually reddened by bathing in the Bhāgīrathī.
Having beheld the brahmins in Kāśī, Durvāsas rejoiced exceedingly.

The contentment found even among domestic animals, the splendor found even among wild beasts, and the joy found even among lower creatures—clearly, that is not to be found elsewhere than in Kāśī. (12)
This is the manifestation of supreme excellence; where else among the immortals in the triple heaven, or even among the animals dwelling there, does it increase the highest bliss? (13)
Better even than these are the animals wandering in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana), who are ever-blissful; whereas the gods, though residing in the Forest of Nandana, are not so.
Better indeed is even a barbarian residing in the city of Kāśī, for he possesses auspicious fortune; but one from elsewhere, though initiated, is not a fit vessel for liberation.
Just as this city of Vaiśveśvarī captivates my heart, neither the entire earth, nor heaven, nor even the realm of the Nāgas does so. (16)
The course of my mind, as it wandered over every part of the earth, found no stability anywhere, such as it has attained here.
"May this city be more beautiful even than the entire cosmic egg"; having praised it thus, Durvāsas indeed attained peace of mind.
For even though that great ascetic performed austerities for a very long time, when he did not obtain any fruit whatsoever, he then became exceedingly angry.
"Fie on me, a wicked ascetic! Fie on my difficult penance! And fie on this field of Śambhu, which deceives everyone! (20)
"Act in such a way that no one here may attain liberation"—when he was thus prepared to utter this curse, Śiva then laughed.
There, a single Liṅga became famous as Prahasiteśvara; by the sight of that Liṅga, men shall experience bliss at every step.
Overcome with wonder, the Great Lord spoke thus within his own mind, saying again and again: "Salutations to such ascetics! (23)
For wherever they perform austerities, wherever their hermitages are established, and wherever they have gained a firm footing, there indeed are those twice-born ones who are full of indignation.
If ascetics do not obtain even a slight portion of what they have merely thought of, they are instantly overcome by anger, which robs them of the glory of their austerities. (25)

Nevertheless, ascetics are to be honored by those who desire the increase of their own welfare; whether they are free from anger or prone to anger, for what concern is there regarding the conduct of ascetics?
While Maheśāna was thus reflecting within his mind, the fire born of his wrath pervaded the entire expanse of the sky.
The expanse of the sky, which was pervaded by the masses of smoke from the fire of his anger, still retains an even greater intensity of blueness today.
Then the hosts were agitated like the waters of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution; crying out to one another, "Ah! What is this? What indeed is this? (29)
Roaring and threatening, with weapons raised in their hands, the Pramathas stood all around the abode of Śambhu.
Who is Yama, or who is Kāla, who is Mṛtyu, and likewise who is Antaka? Who is the Ordainer (Vidhātṛ), who are the Scribes (Lekhas), and when we are enraged, who is our superior? || 31 ||
We shall drink up the fire like water, grind all the mountains into powder, and quickly turn even the seven oceans into desert land.
We could bring Pātāla upward or place it below, or even the heavens; indeed, we could make the entire sky a single morsel.
Or indeed, we shall shatter the vessel of the cosmic egg in an instant; or we shall strike one another like palm-fruit against Time and Death.
Or else we shall seize the world, having abandoned the city of Vārāṇasī, where living beings indeed become liberated the very moment they die. (35)
Whence comes this mass of smoke, and whence these rows of flames? Or who, deluded by pride, would not know Rudra, the conqueror of death? (36)

No one knows Him correctly; even one who knows is deceived. This has been declared by you as the state of perfection: who truly knows that Sadāśiva? (89)
You were deceived previously, and now you are deceived once again; having established a connection with him, you have become a participant in his incoherent prattle.
If you had thought otherwise of Śambhu, whom you described exactly as he is, why did you give me to him—him whom no one at all knows? 91.
Or rather, O dear one, if your mind does not consider that relationship to be a cause, then the sole weight of my merit was the cause in that matter.
Then, having spoken thus at great length, you shall be the progenitor of this body; moreover, with this heard body, the censure of her husband shall be experienced.

The very act of dismissing him is indeed a preliminary rite of purification for her; for a virtuous woman of noble birth, she should live only so long as the reproach of her husband’s master is not heard. 94.
Having spoken thus, into the fire blazing with anger, which was the very form of Mahādeva, he offered the fuel of his body according to the rite of breath-restraint (prāṇarodha).
Then all the gods, including Indra, became pale; and the fire did not blaze as it had previously when offered oblations of clarified butter.
The mantras instantly became powerless; "Alas! What is this most undesirable thing that has occurred? (97)
Some of the best of the twice-born, desiring to go around, said to one another: "A great storm wind has arrived, capable of shaking the mountains. (98)
In an instant, the ground of the sacrificial pavilion was made uneven by him; an unexpected flash of lightning struck, and the earth began to tremble. 99.
Meteors fell from the sky during the day, and piśācas began to dance; above in the heavens, vultures scorched by the heat formed circular patterns.
Below the sun was inauspiciousness, yet even there the auspicious goddesses showered down; the clouds produced a torrential rain there with showers of blood.
A thunderous roar arose from the earth, causing the heart to tremble; and divine weapons fought one another most terrifyingly.
The great sacrificial materials intended for the oblation were defiled by jackals and dogs; meanwhile, *cakora* birds and crows roamed about there in the sacrificial pavilion.
In an instant, that sacrificial enclosure became like a cemetery; whatever was situated there, all of it remained fixed right where it was.
The multitude of objects there appeared as if fixed in a painting and was beautiful; the wielders of the discus and the other gods seemed as if they had been covered over or enclosed.
O twice-born ones, Dakṣa too, having experienced the exhaustion of his face along with his retinue, somehow resumed the sacrifice once again.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Satī’s Body," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: Once again, that Nārada approached Agastya and the Goddess, and then departed to report that entire account in its entirety to Hara.
Having seen Śambhu engaged in some conversation with Nandin, preceded by the gesture of the raised index finger, Nārada bowed down to him.
And Śailādi sat down upon the excellent seat offered to him; manifesting a slight sense of embarrassment, he remained silent for a moment.
By his very appearance, Śambhu, the omniscient one, understood the circumstances of that event; he spoke to the sage: "Why have you resorted to silence? (4)
This state of embodied beings consists of birth and dissolution; even divine bodies are likewise subject to time and the like. (5)
Everything visible is perishable, especially that which lacks a sovereign lord; therefore, O Brahmā, what wonder is there in this, that Time indeed does not consume even a skeleton?
For the existence of a non-existent entity is never possible anywhere; nor is there non-existence for that which is destined to exist. Therefore, the wise are not deluded.
Having heard what was uttered by Śambhu, that bull among sages spoke thus: "What has been spoken by the Lord is indeed the truth."
Whatever is destined to happen will certainly come to pass; there is no doubt in this matter. However, a single anxiety, which greatly afflicts my mind, troubles me exceedingly.
Nothing whatsoever would diminish you, nor would anything truly increase you; because of your immutability and perfection, how could there be decline or growth in you?
Alas, how wretched is this saṃsāra; where will it go, being powerless, since from this very day no one at all shall worship you? (11)
Since Dakṣa Prajāpati did not invite you to the sacrifice, therefore, having seen him today, even the gods, sages, and men revile him.

Will they show contempt for you? What is the use of sovereignty to those who are contemptuous? Having met with humiliation in this world, even though they have conquered the fear of Time, will they—though endowed with sovereignty—ever become worthy vessels of honor? (13)
Of what use is a very long life or abundant wealth to those who, possessing pride as their only riches, are mocked at every step?
Even if they were alive, I would not praise those who are insentient, contemptible, and whose only wealth is pride; rather, it is better for a woman to be a truly virtuous wife.
"Having heard the censure of you, she held her own life as cheap as a blade of grass. Having heard this and having fully understood the passing away of Satī, Mahākāla—
"O Sage, it is true that the virtuous goddess held her own life as lightly as a blade of grass while the sage remained silent there out of fear of Mahākāla. (17)
Rudra became exceedingly fierce, inflamed by the fire of his great wrath; then, from that anger, a fire of immense luster manifested.
Manifest in the form of an image, causing even Time and Death to tremble, he bowed to the Lord and spoke while wielding his great *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon.
"Give me your command, O Father; what supreme service may I perform for you? By your command, I shall make the entire universe into a single morsel. (20)
I indeed drink even the seven oceans with a single mouthful; or the Rasātala as Pātāla, or Pātāla as Rasātala.
"O Lord, at your command, I shall bring him here with ease, having exchanged him for Indra along with the world-protectors, or even seizing him by the hair."
Or if even the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha should provide him assistance, then by your command I shall render his weapons blunt.
Who indeed are these Danujas and Ditijas, so weak for such a cause? Among them, whoever displays arrogance, him I shall slay.
Either I shall set a deadline in this battle, or I shall seek death from Death himself; for when I am enraged on this field of combat, nothing here—whether stationary or moving—is safe.
O Great Lord, by your power no one shall remain steady; indeed, this entire circle of the earth shall [be shaken] by a blow from the sole of my foot.
The surface of the earth trembles from the wind like the leaf of a plantain tree; I shall pulverize these great boundary mountains with the blows of my staff-like arms.

What is the use of speaking at length? Grant me your command; there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Know that, having relied on the power of your feet, I have today achieved what was previously unthought of.
Having heard this vow of his, the Lord considered it as already accomplished; and as if he had attained his ultimate goal, He replied to him with great joy.
"O noble one, you are a great hero among all my hosts here; indeed, attain supreme renown by the name Vīrabhadra. (30)
"Quickly perform my task: bring about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. As for those who disregard you there, provide assistance to them. (31)
"They must not be disregarded even by you; go, my son, may auspiciousness arise for you. Having thus received this command of the Supreme Lord upon his head, he then [departed].
Having circumambulated Hara, he departed with extreme speed; then Śambhu [beheld] his followers, who had been produced from his own breath.
He dispatched another host of attendants numbering one hundred crores; some of those attendants went ahead of Vīrabhadra as he marched forward.
Some were born as his followers, while others went by his side; the sky was completely pervaded by them, who shone with splendor like suns.
Indeed, the peaks of the mountains were uprooted by some, while by others the mountain masses were torn out from their very summits to their foundations. (36)
Having uprooted great trees, some reached the sacrificial courtyard; by some the sacrificial posts were pulled out, while others filled the ritual pits.

Some hosts, fierce with rage, demolished the pavilion; some, bearing tridents in their hands, dug up the altars; others devoured the sacrificial offerings, while still others drank the speckled clarified butter (pṛṣadājya).
Some ate heaps of food as large as mountains; some indeed subsisted on milk-rice, and some drank only milk. || 39 ||
Some, their limbs nourished by cooked food, crushed the sacrificial vessels; others, possessing arms as sturdy as staffs, snapped the handles of the *sruva* ladles.
Some dismantled the carts; some swallowed the animals; and some extinguished the fire, which was otherwise of exceeding brilliance. || 41 ||
Others, filled with joy, personally donned fine silken garments (dukūla), while some took up the mountain of jewels that had been prepared beforehand.
With one [eye], the Lord, seeing, made [the sun] two-eyed; with the other, being enraged, he knocked out the row of teeth of Pūṣan.
The sacrifice was seen fleeing by someone in the form of a deer; it was beheaded from afar by him with that discus.
One, seeing Sarasvatī going along, made her noseless; another, out of anger, cut off Aditi’s lips.
Another likewise tore out the pair of arms of Aryaman, while someone else forcibly tore out the tongue of Agni.
Another powerful attendant cut off the testicles of Vāyu; having bound Yama with a noose, someone else asked, "Who is Dharma? (47)
In that place where Maheśa is not worshipped first, another, having seized Nairṛta by the hair, repeatedly dragged him along. 48.
"O consumer of oblations, you have eaten the sacrificial offering without the Lord's permission! saying this, he struck him with his foot; another, seizing Kubera by the feet, shook him violently.
He repeatedly vomited up the sacrificial oblations that had been consumed; even those eleven Rudras who stand in a single row as guardians of the world.
By the power of their meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), those Pramathas were treated with contempt by the one named Rudra; another Pramatha, moreover, forcibly compressed the belly of Varuṇa.
Having assumed the form of a peacock, the high-minded thousand-eyed one vomited out that which had been given [to him] while devoid of the Lord's grace. (52)
Flying up and taking refuge on a mountain, he watched with curiosity from his concealment; having bowed to the Brāhmaṇas and the Pramathas, they cried out, "Go! Go! (yāta yāta).

The Pramathas drove away the other supplicants as well. When the sacrifice had been thus disrupted by the Pramathas who had arrived first, Vīrabhadra himself arrived, surrounded by an army of Pramathas.
Having previously seen the sacrificial enclosure—which had been reduced to a most pitiable state by those Pramathas and resembled a cremation ground—Vīrabhadra then spoke.
O Gaṇas, behold! For those of evil conduct who have begun their actions without being masters of themselves, such a state of affairs is inevitable; why then this hatred toward Maheśvara?
Those who hate Mahādeva, the sole witness of all actions, even while engaged in righteous deeds, shall meet with such a fate as this. || 57 ||
Where is that wicked Dakṣa, and where are the gods who partake of the sacrifice? Go, O Gaṇas, and bring them all here with the utmost speed! || 58 ||
Having received this command from Vīrabhadra, those Pramathas quickly went forward; just as they were proceeding, they beheld the enraged Gadādhara.
By him, all those Pramathas of great strength and prowess were reduced to the state of withered leaves and grass, as if by a whirlwind.
Then, when all the Pramathas had perished out of fear of Hara, Vīrabhadra, resembling the fire of universal destruction, became enraged.
And he beheld the wielder of the Śārṅga bow before him, surrounded by his own hosts and praised by countless four-armed beings who had conquered the great power of the Daityas.
Then Vīrabhadra, seeing that slayer of demons who was attended by those bearing discuses, maces, swords, and even bows, spoke.
But you here are the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa), the initiator of the great sacrifice; by your own prowess, you are the protector of Dakṣa, who was an enemy of the Three-eyed One (Tryakṣa).
Either bring Dakṣa here and give him to me, or fight with me; but if you do not give up Dakṣa, then protect him with every effort.
Since you are generally proclaimed as the foremost among the devotees of Śambhu, you formerly gave away your lotus-eye when one short of a thousand eyes remained. (66)
The delighted Śambhu has granted you the Sudarśana discus, by obtaining whose assistance in battle you shall conquer the lords of the Danujas.
Having heard those powerful words of Vīrabhadra, Viṣṇu, desiring to test his strength, spoke to Vīrabhadra.
O son of Śambhu, you are indeed the foremost among the Gaṇas; having received the king’s command, you are even greater and more powerful than before. (69)
"Since you are capable of protecting Dakṣa, I too shall watch here with an intellect skilled in guarding him; let me see your power—how will you carry off Dakṣa? (70)
Thus addressed by that wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Vīrabhadra indeed urged on the Pramathas in the battle with a mere glance of his eye.
Then those followers of Viṣṇu were addressed by the Pramathas in the battle; seizing blades of grass with their mouths, they were reduced to the state of bound victims.
Then Tārkṣyaratha, enraged, struck each one at the forefront of the battle in the heart with a thousand arrows.
With their chests all torn open and raining blood, those hosts attained the beauty of *vāsantī* and *kaiṃśukī* flowers upon the courtyard.
Like elephants exuding rut and like mountains discharging streams, the hosts shone with ichor mixed with the red hue of mineral ores.
Then, laughing, the leader of the Gaṇas said to the Lord of Kuṇṭha: "O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, I know you; you are an expert on the field of battle."
"But you fight with the lords of the Daityas and the lords of the Dānavas, not with my attendants. Thus addressed by Vīrabhadra, she held a bhuśuṇḍī weapon in her hand.
Then, with his mace, he quickly struck the mace-wielder—who was covered in the dust from the mountain of the lord of the Daityas—with a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon. || 78 ||
Upon coming into contact with his limbs, the Kaumodakī mace shattered into a hundred pieces as it struck the radiant Vīrabhadra. (79)
Vāsudeva also swiftly struck Ajñātavedana; then [the latter], seizing his khaṭvāṅga staff, rushed at Gadādhara, who held a mace in his hand.
Striking the mace with his left arm, he cast it upon the ground; then this enraged enemy of Madhu struck him with his discus.
Seeing the discus approaching, he remembered Śaṅkara; and by the remembrance of Śaṅkara, the discus acquired a slight curvature and, reaching the throat of the hero, became perfectly Sudarśana.
With that discus, that Lord of the Gaṇas shone exceedingly, as if he were encompassed by the Fortune of Heroism with a garland of victory in battle.
Then, seeing that Sudarśana as an ornament upon his neck, Hari smiled slightly with a touch of wonder and took up the Nandaka sword.
As the Siddhas in heaven were looking on, she paralyzed with a roar of "hum" the hand of that enemy of Madhu, which was raised together with Sanandana.
And seizing a blazing trident, he rushed forward with speed; just as he was about to strike Hari, a voice from the sky spoke: || 86 ||
That king of the Gaṇas was restrained with the words, "Do not commit such a rash act! Thereupon, Vīrabhadra, the best of the Gaṇas, quickly left him.

Having reached Dakṣa, he cried out loudly, "Shame on you, the reviler of the Lord! How can one who possesses such prosperity and for whom the gods themselves are allies, not perform a rite dedicated to the Lord while maintaining his skill? (88)
"With that very mouth by which you have reviled Śiva, I shall now crush that mouth of yours on all sides with my slaps. (89)
Having spoken thus, the hero struck off the face of that Dakṣa, who had spoken harsh words to Hara, with hundreds of blows from his palms.
Then, during the great festival of the assembled goddesses headed by Aditi, he tore off their ears and other major and minor limbs.
The staff-like braids of some were severed by him in his great rage; the hands of some were cut off, and the breasts of others were lopped away.
The attendant, the beloved of Śiva, likewise tore open the nostrils of others and even cut off the fingers of yet others.
Whosoever reviled the Lord of Gods and whosoever listened to them at that time, he angrily cut off their tongues and ears and split them in two.
Some, having been bound firmly by the neck with nooses and suspended from the sacrificial posts, hung head-downwards; O Lord of Gods, they abandoned him and took that great oblation.
The king of the twice-born, Dharma, and the foremost among the descendants of Bhṛgu and Marīci were made by him to become objects of extreme contempt.
These were the sons-in-law of that evil-minded Dakṣa; for, having abandoned Maheśvara, he regarded them as superior to Śiva.
Those sacrificial pits, those sacrificial posts, those pillars, and that pavilion; those altars, those vessels, and those various kinds of oblations—[all these were present]. (98)
Those very materials for sacrifice, those very initiators of the sacrifice, and those very protective mantras—all of them perished with ease. || 99 ||
For in a very short time, wealth acquired through the deception of others perishes quickly, even if it was gained through skill and accompanied by prosperity, yet remains inauspicious.
When that great sacrifice had been brought to such a state by him and his followers, Vidhi, through the destruction of the ritual procedure, informed Hara and restored it.
In that place where such a sacrifice had taken place, devoid of Śiva, Mahādeva arrived; then Vīrabhadra was overcome with great shame.
Having bowed, the god said nothing, for he understood everything by himself; then, having propitiated the Lord of the gods of gods, the eldest of the deities spoke again.
O Treasure of Compassion, O Śaṅkara, even though this Dakṣa has committed an offense, he should be propitiated; restore all these [beings] once again to their former state.
O Śambhu, let such a command be given so that the Vedic rite may proceed according to the rules; for when accompanied by a Lord, the ritual succeeds.
O Supreme Lord, in all actions that lack a presiding master, it is exactly thus that thousands of obstacles arise.
Upon reflection, this wretched man is clever and most devoted to you; for by performing a rite that acknowledges no Lord, he has become a living example for others to behold.
Furthermore, whoever shall perform ritual action while disregarding Maheśāna, the success of that action will be like that of Dakṣa.
Therefore, having heard of his conduct, no one anywhere will perform any rite whatsoever without Śiva, thinking, "Dakṣa is capable of such an act."
Having heard the words "It is ordained," the Lord Maheśvara smiled and commanded Vīra: "Arrange it as it was before."
Vīrabhadra, having received all those commands from Śarva, restored everything to its former state, with the exception of Dakṣa’s face.
Those who revile the Lord are certainly mute beasts; therefore, the attendant Vīrabhadra made Dakṣa face like a ram.
Having taken leave of Brahmā, the god, fallen from his righteous state of household life, went to the Doḍhimaprastha mountain to perform austerities, accompanied by his sin.

Since even a moment of time should not be spent in vain by a man who does not belong to a stage of life (āśrama), one should always apply oneself to spiritual exertion for the sake of the highest good.
Therefore, Maheśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all austerities, performed penance along with his attendants; meanwhile, Brahmā instructed Dakṣa in the practice of austerity.
If you desire to wash away the mire of sin arising from censuring others—which is so difficult to abandon—then go to Vārāṇasī.
Having reached the holy Vārāṇasī, which removes the flood of great sins, perform the installation of a Liṅga; by that, Śambhu will be pleased.
When Maheśvara is pleased, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pleased; there is no other place for your sins to go except for the city of Vārāṇasī.
The wise have prescribed expiations for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; however, there is none for the reviling of Hari, for in that regard, Kāśī alone is the remedy.
Those virtuous souls who have established a *liṅga* here in Kāśī have performed all religious duties; they alone are truly seekers of the goals of human life. (120)
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Dakṣa then quickly reached the great sacred field of Avimukta and performed supreme austerity.
Having installed the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites and being intent upon its worship, he perceives nothing else on the surface of the earth apart from the Liṅga.
Day and night, the skillful Dakṣa Prajāpati praises, worships, bows down to, meditates upon, and beholds Maheśāna.
For twelve thousand measured years, the concentrated mind of that skillful one remained absorbed in meditation upon the supreme sign of the Lord.
When Satī, having attained Menā, became the devoted wife of Himācala, she assumed the form of Umā through intense austerity and obtained the wielder of the Pināka bow as her husband.
Meanwhile, that Dakṣa worshipped the Liṅga, remaining steadfast in his penance; then Girīndrajā (Pārvatī), together with her husband, arrived at Kāśī.
Seeing Hara with an unwavering heart, devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, the Goddess addressed him: "O Lord, he is emaciated by his ascetic penance."
"O Ocean of Compassion, propitiate this Prajāpati with a boon. Thus addressed by Aparṇā, Śambhu, the Lord, spoke to that Dakṣa.
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one; I shall grant whatever is desired by your mind. Having heard these words spoken by the Lord, he bowed repeatedly to Hara.
Having praised Śaṅkara with various kinds of hymns and seeing that he was pleased, he spoke to the Lord of the gods: "If a boon is to be granted to me... (130)

"O You who are the Reality, may my devotion be fixed upon Your pair of feet, free from all dualities. And this great liṅga of Yours which has been installed here by me—O Lord, You must indeed reside within this liṅga forever. (31)
"O Lord, O treasure-house of compassion, whatever offense I have committed must be forgiven; let these alone be my boons—what need is there for any other supreme boons? (32)
Having heard this, Mahādeva Bhava became exceedingly pleased and said: "Let that which has been spoken by you be so, and not otherwise."
Furthermore, O Prajāpati, listen as I grant you another boon: this liṅga which has been installed by you shall be known by the name Dakṣeśvara.
"By serving this, I shall forgive even a thousand offenses of men; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, this must be honored by people. (35)
But you, through this worship of the Liṅga, shall become honored by all; then, at the conclusion of two Parārdhas, you shall attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods merged into that liṅga; Dakṣa also returned home, having attained his heart's desire.
Skanda said: Thus has the origin of Dakṣeśvara been fully recounted by Agastya; having heard this, a living being is liberated even from hundreds of transgressions.
Having heard this meritorious narrative concerning the origin of Dakṣeśvara, a man is not tainted by sins, even if he is a repository of offenses.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Dakṣeśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 89.
Agastya said: O Lord of Pārvatī, bringer of joy to Pārvatī’s heart, please tell me here that which was previously indicated by you as the destroyer of sins.
Skanda said: Listen, O Agastya, when Menā, the devoted wife of Himācala, spoke to her daughter, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains: "O daughter, regarding this Great Lord..."
What is your place or where is your dwelling? Do you know anyone at all? Generally, this son-in-law has no home, nor does he have anyone anywhere.
Having heard these words of her mother, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains was overcome with great shame; finding an opportunity, Gaurī approached Śambhu, bowed down, and addressed him thus.
"O beloved, it has been decided by me that I must go to my mother-in-law's house today; O Lord, I must not stay here at all—take me to your own home. (5)

Having heard the voice of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, he who knew the truth, thinking "it is the Lord of the Mountain," left the Himālaya mountain and arrived at his own Ānandakānana grove.
Having reached Ānandavana, the cause of supreme bliss, the Goddess forgot her dwelling with her father and became the very embodiment of bliss.
Then, on one occasion, Gaurī made this request to Giriśa: "Tell me, why is there an unbroken abundance of bliss here in this sacred field?"
Having heard what Gaurī had said, the wielder of the Pināka bow replied: "In this sacred field, a sanctuary of liberation measuring five krośas in extent—"
O Goddess, there is not even the space of a sesame seed anywhere without a liṅga; indeed, every single liṅga extends for a distance of one krośa all around, as far as the earth reaches.
For even elsewhere that goddess would be a cause of bliss; but here in this Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana), O Goddess, which gives rise to supreme bliss— || 11 ||
Indeed, there are numerous Liṅgas in the form of supreme bliss throughout the fourteen worlds where those who are perfected dwell.
"O Great Goddess, even though they have made lingas here in their own names, they have not achieved their purpose; for it is he by whom a linga of mine has been installed here. (13)
Even Śeṣa does not know the number of those who possess that excellence, for he is not a knower of distinctions.
Because it is the supreme cause of bliss that transcends all limitations, this is therefore the supreme field (kṣetra), O Adrijā, abounding with numerous liṅgas.
Having heard this, the Great Goddess bowed her head again at his feet and said, "O Mahādeva, grant me permission to install a linga."
Having received her husband’s command, whatever welfare a devoted wife bestows, there shall never be any loss of that welfare for her, even at the time of universal dissolution.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods and obtained the command of the Great Ruler, Gaurī installed a Liṅga in the vicinity of Mahādeva.
By the sight of that Liṅga, the sins of men such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa are dissolved; of this there is no doubt, nor is there even the bondage of the body again.
Furthermore, O Sage, listen to that boon which was granted at that Linga by the God of gods out of a desire for the welfare of his devotees.
Whoever shall worship the Liṅga known as Pārvatīśa in Kāśī, upon reaching the end of that body, he shall become a Liṅga of Kāśī.
Having attained the state of being the Liṅga of Kāśī, he shall enter into me alone by virtue of worshipping Pārvatīśa on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, by propitiating Pārvatīśvara, one attains good fortune in this world and an auspicious state in the next. (23)
One shall not enter a womb again; one becomes a vessel of good fortune even by grasping the name of the Linga of Pārvatī’s Lord. (24)

The supreme man who hears this majesty of the Lord of Pārvatī shall, at that very moment, destroy the sins of a thousand births; that highly intelligent one shall attain all desires pertaining to both this world and the next.

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatīśa," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 90 ||
Skanda said: O sinless sage, the greatness of Pārvatīśa has been recounted by me to you; now listen to that which arises from Gaṅgeśvara.
Having heard this, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā wherever one may be, when the Gaṅgā arrived at the Cakrapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha.
Together with that Dailīpi, having recognized the incomparable power of this Ānandakānana due to its being accepted by Śambhu, [he remained] in this forest of bliss.
Recalling the world-transcending fruit of the installation of a Liṅga at Kāśī, Gaṅgā established an auspicious Liṅga to the east of Viśveśa. || 4 ||
The sight of the Gaṅgeśvara Liṅga in Kāśī is very difficult to obtain; yet, he who worships Gaṅgeśa on the Daśaharā lunar day [attains great merit].
The sin of a thousand births is destroyed in an instant; in the Kali age, the Gaṅgeśvara Liṅga will become almost hidden from view.
The sight of that [liṅga] arises for men as a cause of merit, by whom the Gaṅgeśvara Liṅga, so difficult to obtain even in Kāśī, has been seen. (7)
By him, Gaṅgā in her manifest form was undoubtedly seen; for in the Kali age, Gaṅgā, the remover of all impurities, is very difficult to attain.
There will be no doubt of this, O son of Mitra and Varuṇa; even more so when the Kali age (Tiṣya) has arrived, Kāśī will become extremely difficult to attain.
Even more difficult to attain than that is the Liṅga named Gaṅgeśvara in Kāśī, the sight of which indeed leads to the destruction of the sins of men.
Having heard the majesty of Gaṅgeśa, a man shall not go to hell; he shall obtain a multitude of merits and attain whatever he has desired. || 11 ||

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Greatness of Gaṅgeśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 91.
Skanda said: O Sage, I shall relate to you the majesty of Narmadeśa, by the mere remembrance of which there is the destruction of great sins.
At the commencement of this Vārāha-kalpa, the preeminent sages inquired about which river was the most excellent; O son of Mṛkaṇḍu, tell us that.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Listen, all you sages; there are more than a hundred rivers, all of which remove sin and all of which bestow merit.
Of all rivers, those that flow to the ocean are the best; yet even among those, the most excellent rivers are the supreme among rivers.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Narmadā, and the Sarasvatī—O best of sages, this quartet is the most meritorious among rivers.
Gangā is the embodiment of the Ṛgveda, and Yamunā is certainly the Yajurveda; Narmadā is the embodiment of the Sāmaveda, and Sarasvatī is the Atharvaveda.
The Gaṅgā is the source of all rivers and the one that fills the ocean; no other excellent river here can attain equality with the Gaṅgā.
But previously, O best of beings, after Revā had performed austerities for a very long time, the Creator was entreated by her as he was about to grant a boon. (8)
"O Creator, if you are pleased, O Lord, grant me equality with the Gaṅgā. Then Brahmā spoke to Narmadā with a smile: ||| 9 ||
If equality with the Three-Eyed One (Śiva) could be attained by anyone else, then equality with the Gaṅgā might likewise be attained by some other river. || 10 ||
If another man were to exist anywhere equal to Puruṣottama, then only would another river attain equality with the Gaṅgā. (11)
If there were to be another woman here on earth equal to Gaurī, then only would she attain equality with the celestial river Gaṅgā.
If there were ever a city equal to this city of Kāśī anywhere, then another river might attain equality with the celestial river of heaven. 13.
Having heard these words of the Creator, Narmadā, the most excellent of rivers, abandoned the boon of the Ordainer and reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Indeed, among all meritorious acts, no other deed has been declared by anyone to be more conducive to spiritual welfare than the installation of a Liṅga in Kāśī. || 15 ||
Then that holy Narmadā established her shrine according to the prescribed rites at the Pilipilā-tīrtha, in the vicinity of Triviṣṭapa.
Then Śambhu became pleased with that auspicious river and said, "O fortunate one, O sinless one, choose a boon, whatever pleases you."
Having heard this, Revā, the best of rivers, said to Maheśvara: "O Lord of Gods, O Dhūrjaṭi, what is the use of such a trivial boon here? (18)
"O Maheśvara, may I have devotion toward Your pair of feet that is free from the pairs of opposites. Having heard these unsurpassed words of Revā, He was exceedingly pleased.
And he said: "O best of rivers, let that which has been spoken by you be so. Accept it, O abode of merit; I grant you another boon. (20)
"As many stones as there are upon your banks, O Narmadā, so many shall become embodied as Liṅgas by my boon. (21)
Moreover, I shall grant you another boon; listen to that most excellent one, which is in truth difficult to attain even through multitudes of sacrifices and austerities. (22)
The Gaṅgā removes sins instantly; the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) does so in seven days; the Sarasvatī and the Revā do so in three days; but you, O Reva, [remove them] by the mere sight of you.
Furthermore, O Narmadā, who purifies sins through the mere sight [of you], I shall grant another boon: the Liṅga installed by you shall be known by the name Narmadeśvara.
That Liṅga, which is of great merit, will grant eternal liberation; having seen those who are devotees of this Liṅga, the son of the Sun (Yama) [will show favor]. || 25 ||
They will bow down with great effort for the sake of increasing their supreme welfare; O Goddess, there are many Lingas in Kashi at every step.
"Indeed, the greatness of Narmadeśa is supreme and truly wonderful. Having spoken thus, the Lord of the gods merged into that very liṅga.
Narmadā too was greatly delighted, having attained wonderful purity; she reached her own region, removing sins merely by being seen.
Having heard those words of the sage born from Mṛkaṇḍu, the lords of sages became joyful at heart and then performed what was beneficial for each of them.
Skanda said: Having heard the majesty of Narmadeśa, a man endowed with devotion shall cast off the cloak of sin and attain supreme knowledge.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Narmadeśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 92.
Agastya said: "The majesty of Narmadeśa, which destroys all impurities, has been heard. Now, O Skanda, tell me about the origin of Satīśvara."
Skanda said: O you who were born from Mitra and Varuṇa, listen as I relate the story of how the Satīśvara Liṅga manifested in Kāśī. || 2 ||
O sage, in ancient times Śatadhṛti performed a very great penance; by that penance, the Lord of Gods was satisfied and became a bestower of boons.
And he who is exceedingly fond of Brahmins, the omniscient Lord, the Soul of the worlds, and the Creator of the universe, spoke to Brahmā: "Choose a boon, O Maker of the world! (4)
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased and will grant the desired boon, then may you become my son, and may the Goddess be the daughter of Dakṣa."
Having heard this boon from Brahmā, Mahādeva, the giver of all, smiled, looked toward the face of the Goddess, and spoke to the four-faced one.
"O Brahmā, may your desire be fulfilled; what is there that cannot be given, O Grandfather? Having spoken thus, the Moon-bearer appeared from the forehead of Brahmā.
Weeping while lying on his back, he gazed at the face of Brahmā; then Brahmā, too, beheld that child as he was weeping.
"Why do you weep again and again even after having obtained me as your father? Hearing this, the child replied with the words spoken by the Supreme Lord (Brahmā).
"I weep for my name; O Grandfather, give me a name! Because of this weeping, let the child receive the designation 'Rudra'. (10)
Agastya said: O Six-faced One, even though he had attained the state of childhood, why did the Lord weep? If you know, then tell me, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Skanda said: "O Pot-born One, because I am omniscient due to my nature as Kumāra, I understand everything; I shall tell you the cause of his weeping—listen."
The thought arose in the mind of the Lord, the Supreme Soul: "Oh, how great is the power of the intellect of this Parameṣṭhin, whom I have come to observe! (13)
Thus, from the joy of the four-faced Brahmā, the lord of Satyaloka, a flood of tears arose from the Great Lord (Maheśvara). 14.
Agastya said: What was the extent of the Creator’s intellectual power that Śambhu envisioned in his mind, by which even in childhood there arose such a flood of tears of bliss for the Lord? (15)
"O wise one, who increases the bliss of all-knowledge, tell this to me. Having heard the words spoken by Agastya, the enemy of Tāraka spoke indeed.
"O Sage, O Pot-born One, since it was not meditated upon by the god in his mind, who here is capable of rescuing one's progenitor in the absence of offspring? (17)
This is one desire, and this second one is most certain: that when he has become my offspring, I may remember him as he takes me away from birth.
Moment by moment he shall behold her; moment by moment he shall receive the touch of her limbs; and moment by moment he shall obtain a single bed, seat, and meal with her.
What is this which is nowhere within the range of either speech or mind; having become my offspring, what desired object will it not grant me?
Whatever creature should touch this once, or whoever should behold it with joy even once, shall not be born again and shall become overflowing with bliss.
If that [state] should somehow become my plaything in the home, then I would undoubtedly be a treasury of supreme happiness. (22)
And knowing that this was the desire of the Creator, he, the omniscient one, surely fixed his three eyes, filled with tears of joy. (23)
Having heard these words of Skanda, Agastya was filled with joy; he bowed at his feet and said, "Victory to you, O son of the Omniscient One! (24)
The intention of Vidhi as well as the thought within the mind of Śambhu have been perfectly understood by you; salutations to you, the conscious self! (25)
Skanda too was exceedingly pleased at seeing the joy of the listener: "Blessed are you, O Agastya! Blessed are you! You know how to listen according to the truth. (26)
"My labor has not been in vain as I have related this story before you," having thus addressed Agastya, the six-faced one spoke again.
When the god had attained the state of Rudra, the goddess became the daughter of Dakṣa; she too, desiring a boon, performed intense penance at Kāśī as Satī.
He beheld Hara manifested before him in the form of a *liṅga*, clearly saying, "O Great Goddess, enough of this penance. (21)
This *liṅga* shall be known by your name as Satīśvara; for your desire here has been fulfilled, O daughter of Dakṣa.
Likewise, by worshipping this Liṅga, even another shall indeed obtain fruit; a maiden shall obtain a husband who is superior even to her own imagination.
Having propitiated this Liṅga, even Kumāra obtained a beautiful woman; for whatever desire anyone may have, that indeed becomes certain for each of them.
There will be no doubt; through the worship of Satīśvara, whatever anyone desires after having worshipped Satīśvara, that shall come to pass.
For each of them, that respective desire shall quickly be fulfilled. || 34 ||

"On the eighth day from now, your progenitor Prajāpati will give you, his daughter, to me; thus your heart's desire shall be fulfilled. Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished on that very spot.
Having returned to her own abode, that daughter of Dakṣa was filled with joy; and on the eighth day, her father gave her to Rudra.
Skanda said: Thus, O Sage, the Satīśvara Liṅga manifested in Kāśī; even by its mere remembrance, this Liṅga bestows the supreme quality of sattva.
Having beheld the Satīśvara Liṅga in the eastern quarter from Ratneśa, one is instantly liberated from sins and gradually attains knowledge. || 38 ||

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Satīśvara," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Skanda said: O great sage, I shall also describe other lingas, beginning with Amṛteśa, the mere name of which bestows immortality.
In ancient times, there was a sage named Sanāru who lived here as a householder; he was constantly devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman and always regarded guests as deities.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga and never accepting gifts at sacred fords, that sage Sanāru had a son named Upajaṅghani.
Once, having gone to the forest, he was bitten there by a serpent; then, by his companions, he was brought back to his own hermitage.
Sighing deeply, Sanāruṇa led Upajaṅghani to a region of the great cremation ground near the Gate of Heaven.
There, a single Linga shaped like a bilva fruit lay well-concealed; while the wise man placed the corpse there, he reflected upon it.
"How is the ritual for one bitten by a snake performed?"—even as he asked this, Aupajaṅghani rose up alive, just like one who had been asleep.
Then, seeing that Upajaṅghani together with Nārada had once again been endowed with life, that sage was filled with supreme wonder.
What is the reason for my son Upajaṅghani still being alive here? For that serpent, having bitten her outside the sacred field, did not cause her to pass away.
While he was thus forming a thought solely intent on his own life, a single ant happened upon a dead ant somewhere.
And having brought him right there and placed him down, he too departed from that spot; then that sage, realizing the truth indicated by the [signs of] life, [acted accordingly].
While the sage was indeed digging with his soft palm, he beheld a linga the size of a bilva fruit.
Then, having become reddish-brown, that Liṅga was worshipped there by him; he also gave a name to the long-standing Liṅga that was consistent with its lineage.
This Liṅga named Amṛteśvara is in Ānandakānana; by the touch of this Liṅga, one shall certainly attain immortality.
Having worshipped Amṛteśa, that sage, whose sons were indeed living, returned to his own abode, where he was beheld by the people as if he were a marvel.
O Lord of Sages, from that time forward, that Liṅga Amṛteśa shall remain hidden again in Kāśī during the Kali age, yet it bestows spiritual perfection upon men.
By the touch of Amṛteśvara, those who are dead come back to life at that very moment; even while living, they attain immortality here through mere contact.
There is no Liṅga equal to Amṛteśa anywhere on the surface of the earth; that Liṅga was established by Śambhu during the Kali age and has been diligently concealed.
Even those who take up the name Amṛteśvara in Kāśī shall never experience any fear arising from calamities.
O Sage, there is another great liṅga known as Karuṇeśvara, located near Mokṣadvāra, in front of Mokṣadvāreśvara. || 20 ||
Indeed, upon seeing that most compassionate Liṅga, no one ever departs from the sacred field to go outside.
One should bathe at Maṇikarṇikā and behold Karuṇeśvara; the fear born of obstacles to the sacred field should be abandoned with supreme joy.
Having reached Monday, one should observe the vow of eating only once a day; the Lord of Compassion (Karuṇeśvara) should be worshipped by the observer of the vow with flowers of compassion.
Satisfied by that vow, the Lord of Compassion will never cause him to go outside the sacred field; therefore, this vow must indeed be performed.
Lord Karuṇeśvara is to be worshipped with those leaves or even those fruits; yet he who does not know that Liṅga is devoid of perfect knowledge.

"Therefore, the Lord of Gods, who is the tree of compassion, should be worshipped with the thought, 'May He be pleased. Thus, O twice-born one, he who performs this vow on every Monday for a year [attains the fruit]. (26)
The Lord of Compassion here, being pleased, will grant his desired wish; therefore, the Lord of Compassion here in Kāśī should be visited with effort by human beings.
Thus has the most exalted majesty of the Lord of Compassion been told; having heard which, no fear arising from calamities shall exist in Kāśī.
Having beheld both Mokṣadvāreśvara and Svargadvāreśvara in Kāśī, a man attains both heaven and liberation. (29)
Another Liṅga, Jyotīrūpeśvara, shines forth in Kāśī; indeed, by worshipping it, devotees become embodiments of light.
Having duly worshipped the supreme Jyotīrūpeśvara on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī, a mortal shall undoubtedly attain the form of light.
When the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, arrived there, from that time forward the celestial river joyfully worshipped that Liṅga daily.
Formerly, while Viṣṇu was performing penance here, that radiant Liṅga manifested itself; therefore, this sacred field is auspicious.
Then, for one who meditates upon Jyotīrūpeśvara on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī pond—even if staying far away—success is not distant.
And among these fourteen liṅgas, O best of men, eight liṅgas possess great power and are like a forest fire to the seeds of karma.
The fourteen lingas beginning with Oṃkāra that have been mentioned, as well as the eight great lingas beginning with Dakṣeśvara; || 36 ||
The Śailēśa and other Liṅgas, as well as those fourteen, and furthermore these thirty-six, are for the sake of attaining perfection in the sacred field (kṣetra). || 37 ||
Sadāśiva, whose nature consists of the thirty-six principles, dwells eternally within these lingas in this sacred field; residing here, he imparts the liberating knowledge.
Indeed, this is the true nature of the field (kṣetra), consisting of thirty-six forms of liṅgas; alas! By worshipping these, men shall never encounter an evil state of existence.
O Sage, these liṅgas are certainly of a secret nature; and by the power of these liṅgas, liberation here is well-ascertained. (40)
O high-minded one, this Kāśī is the field of liberation because of these liṅgas; others such as these also come into being in age after age.
This field of Śambhu, Ānandakānana, is beginningless; those who have established their residence here are undoubtedly liberated. (42)

The perfection of yoga exists here indeed; for the perfection of austerity is found right here. The perfection of vows, the perfection of mantras, and the perfection of sacred fords are certainly attained here. (43)
This very place, the pleasure garden of Śambhu, is the birthplace of that most exalted group of eight supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā), which has been described. 44.
This Ānandakānana is the abode of the glory of Nirvāṇa; having attained it through meritorious deeds, one who fears cyclic existence must never let it go.
This alone is the great gain, this alone is the supreme austerity, and this alone is the great merit, that one has obtained Vārāṇasī here.
Death will inevitably come to every living being, wherever it may be; thereafter, one attains a state—whether auspicious or inauspicious—in accordance with one's karma.
Having understood that death is certain and follows one's past actions and destiny, Kāśikā— which wards off all karma—must necessarily be resorted to. (48)
Having attained human birth, those fools who do not serve the city of Kāśī—whose life lasts but a moment—are deluded and dull-witted.
Human birth is difficult to attain, and the city of Kāśikā is difficult to reach; having achieved the union of both, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (50)
Where in this world is there such austerity, and where is there such supreme yoga, by means of which liberation—the highest of the high—is attained in Kāśī? || 51 ||
Truth, truth, and again truth; truth first and again and again: there is no other land on the surface of the earth equal to Kāśī for the sake of liberation. 52.
Viśveśa is the eternal bestower of liberation, and the northward-flowing [Ganges] leads to liberation; in Ānandakānana there is liberation, but liberation is not found anywhere else.
For the Lord of the Universe alone is the bestower of liberation, and indeed no other; he alone, having led one to Kāśī, grants liberation, and not from any other source.

Liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti) occurs right here, while proximity [to the deity] and other forms occur elsewhere; yet even that is certainly not easily attained elsewhere, whereas in Kāśī, liberation exists effortlessly.

Skanda said: Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya; I shall relate to you what will happen in the future. Hear that which Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa spoke in his great words, and hear what he, with a mind intent on certainty, will do hereafter.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Amṛteśa and Other Liṅgas," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O Sūta of great intelligence, to how the future was spoken by Skanda in my presence, O high-minded one born from a jar.
Skanda said: Listen, O illustrious sage, son of Mitrāvaruṇa, to how the eminent sage Pārāśarya will fall into delusion.

Having divided the Vedas into various distinct branches according to their different recensions, and having taught the eighteen Purāṇas along with the Sūta and other texts, he of great intelligence [acted].
He who composed the secret essence of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, as well as the work known as the Mahābhārata, which captivates the hearts of all people.
It is the supreme pacifier of all sins and the bringer of all peace; by the mere hearing of it, even the murder of a Brahmin is destroyed.
Once, that illustrious sage, wandering upon the surface of the earth, arrived at the Naimiṣa forest where the lords of sages reside.
Eighty-eight thousand ascetics, headed by Śaunaka, whose great foreheads were marked with the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra) and who wore shimmering rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.

[He saw those] who bore the marks of divine power (vibhūti), who were devoted to the chanting of the Rudra-hymns, who were intent on the worship of the Liṅga, and who held the name of Śiva in high esteem.
To those who were constantly speaking thus with their minds firmly resolved, "The Lord of the Universe alone, and no other, is the bestower of liberation," (9)
Having observed all those who were devoted to Giriśa, the sage Vyāsa raised his forefinger high and spoke these words once more: ||| 10 ||
Having thoroughly churned the web of words and having repeatedly ascertained them many times, this one thing alone has been fully understood: Lord Hari, the Sovereign of All, is to be served. (11)
In the Vedas, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata—in their beginnings, middles, and conclusions—Hari alone is here, and no other.
