Truth, truth, triple truth, and again truth—not a falsehood; there is no scripture other than the Veda, and no god higher than Acyuta.

The Lord of Lakṣmī is the giver of all, and none other; the Lord of Lakṣmī alone is also the giver of liberation. Indeed, there is only one Lord of Lakṣmī; therefore, He alone should be meditated upon, and no other.
In this world and beyond, there is no giver of enjoyment and liberation other than Janārdana; therefore, those who desire happiness should always serve the Four-Armed One.
Those of small intellect who, having abandoned Keśava, serve another, enter again and again into the dense wheel of worldly existence.
For Hṛṣīkeśa alone is the Lord of all, higher than the highest; by constantly serving Him, one becomes worthy of being served by the three worlds. (17)

Viṣṇu alone is the bestower of Dharma, while Hari alone is the bestower of many worldly objects; the wielder of the discus (Cakrī) alone is the bestower of desires, while the Infallible (Acyuta) alone is the bestower of liberation.
Those who, having abandoned the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, worship another deity, should be excluded by the virtuous, just like twice-born men devoid of the Vedas.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest, their hearts trembling, spoke these words in reply.
The sages said: O sage, son of Parāśara, you are worthy of our respect, O high-minded one, because the Vedas were arranged by you and you also know the Purāṇas.
And since you are indeed the author of the great Bhārata, you are certainly the one who has established the definitive conclusions regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
O son of Satyavatī, who else here besides you is a knower of reality, that you have made this firm vow and decisively raised your index finger? (23)
The young students there do not have faith in this; only when they have faith in the truth of your words will they have confidence in that promise.
When you indeed pledged your word in the Ānandavana grove of Śambhu.
Go to Vārāṇasī, O Vyāsa, where Viśveśvara himself resides; there the dharma of the ages does not exist, nor is the earth bound by worldly attachment.
Having heard this, the sage Vyāsa, feeling somewhat provoked in his heart, departed quickly accompanied by his disciples, who numbered ten thousand.
Having reached Vārāṇasī and bathed in the Pañcanada pool, Vyāsa worshipped the glorious Mādhava and then proceeded to Pādodaka.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites there, and having beheld Ādikeśava, he then observed the five-night vow, being honored by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Gladdened by conch shells being sounded before and behind him, [he cried out]: "Victory to Viṣṇu! Hṛṣīkeśa! Govinda! Madhusūdana! (30)
O Acyuta, Ananta, Vaikuṇṭha, Mādhava, Upendra, Keśava; O Trivikrama, wielder of the mace, wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Janārdana! 31.
O you who bear the Śrīvatsa on your chest, O beloved of Śrī, O wearer of yellow garments, O slayer of Mura! O enemy of Kaiṭabha, O destroyer of Bali, O enemy of Kaṃsa, O slayer of Keśin!
O Nārāyaṇa, enemy of the asuras, Kṛṣṇa, Śauri, four-armed one! O delighter of Devakī’s heart, increaser of Yaśodā’s joy! 33.
O lotus-eyed one, O enemy of the Daityas, O Dāmodara, O beloved of Bala! O Hari praised by Indra, O Vāsudeva, O bestower of wealth! 34.
O Viṣvaksena, O Tārkṣya, O you who wear a garland of chariots, O best among men, O Adhokṣaja, O support of the earth, O Padmanābha, O you who recline upon the waters! 35.
O Nṛsiṃha, O Yajñavārāha, O beloved of the cowherds and cowherd boys, O Lord of the gopīs, O You who transcend all qualities, O You whose banner bears Garuḍa, O Upholder of the Earth! || 36 ||

Victory to you, O crusher of Cāṇūra! Victory to you, O protector of the three worlds! Victory to you, the beginningless one! Victory to you, O bliss! Victory to you, whose luster is like that of the blue lotus!
O you whose chest is adorned with the Kaustubha gem, O dryer of the bodily fluids of Pūtanā, protect, protect us, O jewel for the protection of the world, O destroyer of Naraka! 38.
O thousand-headed Puruṣa, invoked by many, bestower of happiness! You alone are the Puruṣa who exists in that which has been and that which is yet to be. || 39 ||
Thus praising Vanamālin with such garlands of names, he sang and danced with supreme joy, moving in spontaneous play.
Vyāsa arrived at the temple of Viśveśa, greatly delighted, together with great devotees of the Lord, in front of Jñānavāpī.
His neck shining with garlands of excellent tulasī, he himself became the bearer of the cymbals and himself became an excellent dancer.
Having become one who knew the true principles of flute-playing and was himself possessed of a divine ear for music, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, concluded his dance in this manner. (43)
Again, standing in the midst of the disciples, he raised his right arm and recited those very same verses once more, as if singing them aloud.

Having thoroughly churned the web of words and having repeatedly and firmly determined it in many ways, this one thing alone is fully understood: Lord Hari, the sovereign of all, is to be served. (45)
While Vyāsa was reciting this collection of verses beginning with these words—which serve to awaken him to his own vow—he raised up his left arm.
Then that Śailādi effortlessly paralyzed his arm, and there was also a paralysis of speech for that sage Vyāsa, the virtuous muni.
Then, having approached him in secret, Viṣṇu spoke to Vyāsa: "O Vyāsa, a great offense has certainly been committed by you here."
Because of this offense of yours, my own fear has become even greater; for Viśveśa is indeed one alone, and there is no second whatsoever.
By his grace I am the wielder of the discus, and by his power I am the Lord of Lakṣmī; the capacity to protect the three worlds was granted by that very Śambhu himself.
"Through devotion to him, supreme sovereignty was obtained by me from that boon; now, if you desire my welfare, praise that Śambhu. (51)
"Even at other times, you should certainly not entertain such a thought. Having heard this, he replied by means of a sign, "O son of Parāśara! (Pārāśarya). 52.
The paralysis of his arms was brought about by Nandin through a mere glance; the paralysis of his speech arose out of fear of him. "Touch my throat-pit! [he said]. 53.
O Lord of Bhavānī, just as Viṣṇu was unable to praise the Destroyer of Existence (Bhavāntaka), he touched his throat and departed in secret.
Then the son of Satyavatī, his creeper-like arms thus paralyzed, began with noble resolve to praise Maheśāna.

Vyāsa said: Rudra is one, not a second; therefore, that Brahman alone is one, and there is no diversity here whatsoever. Even if someone else anywhere were to explain it, let him do so in my presence, provided he possesses the power to do so.

Who else besides Maheśa was able to endure that most terrifying Kālakūṭa poison, wreathed in flames, which arose from the churning of the milk ocean by Mount Mandara—the poison by whose fumes Viṣṇu turned black?

Who could be equal to Him, whose arrow was Śrīpati (Viṣṇu), whose charioteer was Lokeśa (Brahmā), whose chariot was the entire earth, whose horses were the Vedas, and by whom the cities of Tripura were burnt by the discharge of His arrow? 58.

Since even Kāma, beholding him as equal to the other gods, was himself reduced to ashes, who else besides the Conqueror of Desire could be praised as the sole victor over the entire universe with his flowery arrows? (59)

Indeed, that Lord of Gods, the Master of the Universe, whom neither the Veda knows, nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator, nor the mind, nor even speech can know—alas, how could one of dull intellect like me truly know him according to his true nature? (60)

I bow to Him in whom all exists, who is everywhere, who is everything; who is indeed the creator, the protector, and the destroyer; who has no beginning, yet is the sole origin of all; who has no end, yet is the bringer of the end.

The praise of whom is equal to a horse-sacrifice, and by a single gift of whom even the splendor of Indra is rendered insignificant; by whose praise the world of truth (Satyaloka) is attained, and by whose worship the fortune of liberation is not far off.
I know no other god than the illustrious Maheśa; I praise no other god than Śambhu; nor do I bow to any other god than the Three-eyed One. This is the truth, the truth, the truth; it is not false.
While the great sage was thus praising Śambhu, Nandin, through the grace of Śiva’s glance, released the paralysis of his arms and spoke with a smile: "Salutations to you, O Brahmins!"
Nandikeśvara said: O Vyāsa, this highly meritorious hymn has been proclaimed to you; Śaṅkara is pleased with that wise person who shall recite it.
This *Vyāsāṣṭaka* should be recited with effort every morning; it pacifies evil dreams and sins and brings about the presence of Śiva.

Whether one is a matricide, a patricide, a killer of cows, or even a murderer of children; whether a drinker of intoxicants or a thief of gold—one shall become sinless through the recitation of this hymn.
Skanda said: From that time forward, the son of Parāśara became devoted to the worship of Śambhu; having installed the Vyāseśvara Liṅga in front of the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake.
He was eternally adorned with supernatural powers, eternally adorned with rudrākṣa beads, eternally devoted to the Rudra-hymns, and was a constant worshiper of the Liṅga.
Having made a formal renunciation of the sacred field, he should not abandon Kāśī even now, once he has realized the true nature of that field which bestows the state of Nirvāṇa.
Having bathed in the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake and beheld Vyāseśvara, a man—wherever he may die—will be as if dead in Vārāṇasī.
Having worshipped the Vyāseśvara Liṅga in Kāśī, the best of men never falls away from knowledge nor is he ever overcome by sins.
For those who are devotees of Vyāseśvara, there is no fear from the Kali age, nor from sin anywhere, nor from any affliction of the sacred field.
Vyāseśvara should be visited with great effort by those residing in Kāśī who have performed their ablutions at Ghaṇṭākarṇa and who fear the sin of violating the sacred precinct.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Paralysis of Vyāsa’s Arm," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 95.
Agastya said: O Skanda, if Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana is devoted to Śambhu, if he knows the secret of the sacred field, and if he has performed the renunciation of the field (kṣetrasaṃnyāsa); || 1 ||
If his power has been witnessed in such a manner, and if he is indeed the best among the wise, how could he possibly curse the preeminent city of Vārāṇasī? (2)
Skanda said: "This which you have asked is true; listen, O sage, as I relate the future life-story of that Vyāsa, since you have inquired of me."
Ever since Nandin paralyzed the arm of that Sage, he has praised Maheśāna with the utmost devotion.
In Kāśī there are numerous sacred fords (tīrthas) and manifold lingas; nevertheless, Viśveśa alone is to be served and Maṇikarṇikā is to be bathed in.
"Among all lingas, Viśveśa alone is supreme; among all holy places, Maṇikarṇikā is supreme"—thus Vyāsa spoke, holding those two in high esteem.
Having abandoned the vast web of words, he bathes every day at dawn and, in the Nirvāṇa-maṇḍapa, proclaims the majesty of the Great Lord.
That supreme seer Vyāsa constantly and joyfully expounds the great majesty of the sacred field in the presence of his disciples.

Whatever is done here in this field, whether auspicious or even inauspicious, there is no end to its consequences even at the time of universal dissolution; therefore, one should practice what is beneficial.
Those wise and accomplished people who desire the perfection of this sacred field must never abandon Maṇikarṇikā as long as they live.
One should bathe every day at the holy ford of Cakrapuṣkariṇī; Viśveśvara should always be worshipped with flowers, leaves, fruits, and water.

One's own dharma according to caste and stage of life must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree; every day, the greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra) should be heard with faith at least once.
And gifts should be given here according to one's ability, keeping them well-concealed; even food should be given by one who desires to ward off obstacles.
A wise person should always perform acts of assistance for others here, and especially on sacred festival days, perform rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts. (14)
A special worship should be performed preceded by a grand festival; likewise, extensive processions should be conducted and the deities of the sacred field (kṣetradevatā) should be honored.
In this matter, a wise person should never disclose the secrets of anyone to anyone; one should renounce another's wife, another's wealth, and doing harm to others. (16)
One should not speak ill of others, nor should one cause envy toward others; one must never utter untruth, even if one's life-breaths are at the throat. 17.
For the sake of protecting the living beings here, one may speak even what is untrue, by whatever means possible, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (18)

Every living being here must be protected with great effort. When even a single creature is protected here in Kāśī with diligence, one obtains the merit that comes from protecting the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. (19)
Those who always dwell in Kāśī, having made their renunciation in this sacred field, should be considered Rudras themselves; they are liberated while living, without a doubt. || 20 ||
They are to be worshipped, they are to be saluted, and they are to be gratified with effort; for when they are truly satisfied, the Lord of the Universe himself shall be pleased.
For the pleasure of the Lord of the Universe, the welfare and security of those mortals who dwell in Kāśī must be ensured by virtuous men, even from afar. || 22 ||
Furthermore, the outward wandering of the senses must be restrained here by the residents; for even the fickleness of the mind must be diligently checked in this place. (23)
One should not long for death, nor indeed should one long for liberation; a wise person should certainly not employ means for the emaciation of the body.

Physical excellence is to be desired for the successful accomplishment of vows, ritual ablutions, and other rites; indeed, a long life must be sought here for the attainment of abundant great fruits. (285)
In this matter, one must protect oneself for the sake of increasing great spiritual welfare; one should not, even in thought, contemplate means of abandoning one's life here. (25)
Whatever spiritual merit is obtained even on a single day at Kāśī, that cannot be attained anywhere else even in a hundred years. (27)
Whatever merit is acquired elsewhere through the practice of yoga throughout one's entire life, that is obtained in Vārāṇasī by means of a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma). || 28 ||
Whatever merit is earned by bathing in all the sacred fords throughout one's entire life is obtained by a single immersion in Maṇikarṇikā at Ānandavana.
Whatever merit is acquired over the course of an entire lifetime by worshipping all other lingas, that is obtained by worshipping Viśveśa once with faith.
The vision of the Lord of the Universe may occur through the exchange of that stainless merit which has been accumulated over a thousand births. (3)
Whatever fruit is obtained from the perfect gift of ten million cows, that same fruit is fully attained by beholding Viśveśvara. 32.
Whatever merit is proclaimed by the great seers as resulting from the sixteen great gifts, that same merit arises for men through the offering of flowers to Viśveśa.
Whatever fruit is obtained by all through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, that is attained by bathing the Lord of the Universe with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices properly performed, that is exceeded a hundredfold by offering once highly precious food-oblations to the Lord of the Universe.
He who offers a banner, an umbrella, and a chowrie to the Lord of the Universe shall indeed obtain sovereignty over the earth under a single umbrella. (35)
Whoever offers great articles of worship to the Sustainer of the Universe, the abundance of his wealth shall never forsake him anywhere in this world. (37)
And whoever creates a flower garden rich with blossoms of all seasons, in its courtyard the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) provide cooling shade.
For one who indeed offers a cow to the Lord of the Universe for the purpose of a milk-bath, his ancestors shall dwell upon the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Whoever causes a palace to be whitewashed or painted with various colors in the abode of Viśveśarāja, his own residence shall become like Mount Kailāsa adorned with paintings.
Likewise, one should feed those who follow other Brahmanical paths as well as Śiva-yogins; in this case, at Kāśī, each individual should be fed according to their respective order.
The fruit of feeding ten million people belongs to him through his faith; there is no doubt in this matter. One should perform penance here and cause gifts to be bestowed here.

The Lord of the Universe is to be propitiated here through baths, fire-oblations, recitations, and other rites. Whatever fruit is obtained by men elsewhere through ten million recitations is attained here by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. (43)
Whatever fruit has been proclaimed by the wise elsewhere for a *koṭi-homa*, that is obtained here in the Forest of Bliss (*Ānandakānana*) from one hundred and eight oblations.
Whoever recites the Rudra-sūktas in Kāśī in the presence of Viśveśa obtains the fruit of the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) of all the Vedas. || 45 ||
I do not know the extent of his merit when the supreme syllable is meditated upon; one should dwell constantly in Kāśī and always serve the river that flows northward.
For even in the most terrible calamity, Kāśī must never be abandoned; because the Lord, the Master of the Universe, is the protector who removes all misfortunes. (47)
One should make each day fruitful through bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and other such acts; for whatever action is performed in Kāśī leads to greatness. (48)
Austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa should be performed with great effort; likewise, the disturbances of the senses shall never cause any affliction there. (49)
If the senses cause the embodied beings here to undergo transformation, then success is never attained due to obstacles arising from those very influxes.
Agastya said: O Skanda, please describe the nature of those penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa which Vyāsa will indeed speak of, for the sake of purifying the senses.
Skanda said: O one of great intelligence, I shall describe before you the kṛcchra penances and others, by performing which a person here attains supreme purification of the body. (52)
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting for one day—this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra* (one-quarter penance). || 53 ||
The fig leaf, the udumbara leaf, the lotus leaf, the bilva leaf, and kuśa water—each of these, when drunk daily, is proclaimed as the Parṇakṛcchra penance. (54)
The consumption of one of these—oil-cake, ghee, buttermilk, water, or barley meal—each for one day, followed by a fast on the next, is proclaimed as the Saumya-kṛcchra.
One should eat sacrificial food (havis) in the morning and likewise in the evening; however, having eaten food obtained by begging, one should observe a fast for three days.
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat only a single morsel for three days as before, and fast for the final three days. (57)
The Kṛcchrātikṛcchra consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days; the Parāka is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days. || 58 ||
A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance eats in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, eats food obtained unasked for three days, and fasts during the final three days.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with kuśa grass, along with a fast for one night, is known as the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance. || 60 ||
When each of these six substances is consumed separately over six days, followed by a day of fasting, this seven-day rite is known as the Mahāsāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
A Brahmin performing the Taptakṛcchra penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air—each for three days—bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind.
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk; having consumed hot clarified butter for three days, one should subsist on air for three days.
Having drunk one pala of milk, two palas of clarified butter, and one pala of water, this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Whoever should employ barley-gruel mixed with cow urine performs what is called the "one-day kṛcchra," which is a purification of the body. || 65 ||
Having kept one's hands upturned throughout the day while subsisting on air alone, and remaining in water during the night until dawn, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.

One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight; performing ritual ablutions at the three sessions of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight; one should eat nothing at all on the new moon day—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A composed Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; this is known as the Śiśu-Cāndrāyaṇa.
When the sun has reached midday, one who is self-controlled should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food; this is remembered as the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating three hundred and sixty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in a month, with a concentrated mind in whatever manner possible, one attains the same world as the Moon.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth; the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
And that knowledge shall arise for men through the perfect service of Kāśī; by the service of Kāśī, the dawn of Viśveśvara’s compassion occurs. (73)
From that comes the attainment of great prosperity, which is capable of uprooting karma; therefore, one should diligently perform bathing, giving, austerity, and recitation at Kāśī. (74)
The vow consists of listening to the Purāṇas, following the path prescribed by the Smṛtis, and contemplating the feet of the Lord of the Universe at every moment and every day. (75)
Worship of the Liṅga at the three times of day, the consecration of a Liṅga as well, conversation with the virtuous, and the chanting of "Śiva, Śiva. (76)
There is also the hospitable reception of guests by those dwelling at the Tīrtha of Maitrī; a mind of faith, humility, and equanimity toward honor and dishonor. (77)
Freedom from desire, lack of restlessness, absence of passion, non-violence, the practice of non-acceptance, and a mind characterized by benevolence—these are [the qualities]. || 78 ||
Absence of hypocrisy, absence of envy, the arrival of wealth without being asked for it, freedom from greed, lack of laziness, absence of harshness, and lack of dejection. (79)
In this manner, the resident of the sacred field (kṣetravāsin) must perform virtuous activities and shall daily instruct his disciples in the true Dharma. (80)
In former times, Vyāsa lived in this manner: constantly bathing at the three periods of the day, always subsisting on food obtained through alms, and perpetually worshipping and honoring the Liṅga.
Once, in order to test him, Hara said to the Goddess: "Today, while the supremely righteous Vyāsa has gone out for alms—" || 82 ||
"O beautiful one, do not ask for alms from anyone, even though he is omnipresent. Having been told "So be it," Bhavānī [spoke] to Bhava, the remover of worldly existence.
Having paid his respects, he forbade alms from every house; that sage, accompanied by his disciples, was distressed at not obtaining any alms. (84)
Observing that the time had passed, he wandered again through that city; alms were obtained by him at every house, just as they were by all the other mendicants.
On that day, that sage, together with his disciples, could not obtain alms anywhere; then, having performed the evening rites along with his students, [he sat down]. || 86 ||
Devoted to fasting, he remained seated in that very manner day and night. Then, on another day, the sage Vyāsa, having performed the midday rites, [proceeded].
Accompanied by his disciples, he went about the city to beg for alms; he wandered everywhere, repeatedly visiting every palace.
Like one devoid of fortune who finds no wealth, he obtained no alms anywhere; then Vyāsa, exhausted from wandering about, reflected thus: (89)
"What is the reason that alms which were preserved with great effort cannot be obtained? Having summoned all his disciples, Vyāsa questioned them. (90)
"It is evident that you too have not obtained alms; what has happened here in this city? Go, two or three of you, at my command. (91)
On the second day as well, when alms could not be obtained despite great effort, [he realized] that some misfortune had occurred here arising from the fall of his great preceptor.
In an instant, there was a total depletion of food throughout the entire city, and simultaneously, the king’s punishment fell upon all the inhabitants of the town. (93)
Or perhaps alms were withheld from us by someone out of envy; or the residents of the city have become distressed due to some calamity. (94)

"Why have you all come here so hastily without knowing this entire situation? Then, two or three of them, having obtained permission from their preceptor whose feet were pure, returned and reported what they had seen regarding the prosperity of the inhabitants of that city.
The disciples said: "O venerable masters, listen; there is no calamity whatsoever here, nor is there any depletion of food anywhere in this entire city. (96)
Where Viśveśvara is present in person, where the celestial river herself flows, and where there are sages such as you—where could there be any fear born of calamities?
Whatever prosperity belongs to householders here in the city of the Lord of the Universe, even that prosperity does not exist in Vaikuṇṭha; Alakā and other such realms are but a small fraction of it.
O Great Sage, the jewels found in the oceans are not as numerous as those which exist in the homes of those who enjoy the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the Lord of the Universe. 99.
Furthermore, such heaps of grain as were found in every single house here were never seen anywhere in the city of Indra, even those bestowed by the wish-fulfilling trees. || 100 ||
In that entire city where the large-eyed goddess herself, who bestows most extensive fruits, resides, there is never anywhere a man who is destitute.
In this Forest of Bliss, which is the abode of the splendor of Nirvāṇa, even liberation is easily attained; what else could be difficult to find there?
All the women of the city were devoted to their husbands; they all possessed the form of Bhavānī, having dedicated their virtuous deeds to the Lord of the Universe.
All the men in Kāśī are indeed leaders of hosts; all are truly Kumāras, and all possess the gaze of Tāraka.

Those whose foreheads are marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) are all bearers of the moon upon their crests; so too are those here who, though being tormented by thousands of calamities, [wear it].
All those who never abandon Kāśī are indeed omniscient; even in every house, there are young students engaged in debates concerning the discourse of Brahman.
Here dwell the four-faced ones who have shaken off all impurities by the celestial river; they are lords of the fortune of liberation and have taken up the renunciation of the sacred field.
All of them are indeed Hṛṣīkeśas, all are truly Puruṣottamas; they are to be known as none other than Acyutas who have taken possession of this field. || 8 ||
Whether they be women or men, all of them without exception—of this there is no doubt—are three-eyed and all are four-armed.
All here are indeed Śrīkaṇṭhas; all are certainly conquerors of death (Mṛtyuñjayas). Since they are Ardhanārīśvaras, the glory of liberation has taken refuge in their bodies. 110.
Herein lies the supreme mass of Dharma; here are the great masses of wealth; all desires bear fruit here, and here is stainless liberation.
For those who dwell in Kāśī, there is no contact with dwelling in a womb; neither the Kali age nor time itself can cause them any affliction here.
Sins do not afflict those who seek refuge in the Lord of the Universe, where Viśveśvara himself is present in person, consisting of the essence of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā.
For there exists the Praṇava, whose form is sound and whose body is mantra; therefore, it is certain that the Vedas here possess embodied forms.
For Sarasvatī exists here in the form of a river; thus, this entire Ānandakānana is the abode of the scriptures and the dwelling place of those who have composed the Dharmaśāstras. || 15 ||
"As many gods as there are in heaven, so many serpents are here; they are not false. Every night, the serpents always perform the lustration ceremony for the Lord of the Universe. (16)
Having reached Kāśī from the netherworld (rasātala) by means of the lamps of the jewels on their own hoods, all the oceans arrived there accompanied by herds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu).
Indeed, Mandāra, Pārijāta, Saṃtāna, and Haricandana bathe Viśveśa with five streams of nectar.
And the Kalpavṛkṣa—these five always [shine] together with the trees. || 19 ||
All the hosts of gods and all the great seers, as well as all the yogins, worship the Lord of Kāśī here.
Kāśī is the abode of all sciences; Kāśī is the supreme residence of Lakṣmī; this Kāśī is the field of liberation; Kāśī consists entirely of the three Vedas.
Having heard this, the best of sages, Pārāśarya of great asceticism, spoke thus to those disciples: "Recite this verse once more."
The disciples said: "Kāśī is the refuge of all sciences; Kāśī is the supreme abode of Lakṣmī; this Kāśī is the field of liberation; Kāśī consists entirely of the three Vedas. (23)
Skanda said: Having heard this, O Pot-born One, Vyāsa—his eyes blinded by rage and his form blazing like a fire of hunger—will then curse Kāśī.
Vyāsa said: "May there be no learning for three generations; may there be no wealth for three generations; may there be no liberation for three generations—thus Vyāsa cursed Kāśī. (25)
In this place, there is pride regarding various branches of knowledge, and indeed, great pride regarding wealth; because of their pride in liberation, the residents here do not even grant alms.
Having thus formed this resolve, Vyāsa then pronounced a curse upon Kāśī; yet even after pronouncing the curse, that sage, filled with anger, went forth to beg for alms.
Entering every house in haste with his gaze fixed upon the sky, he wandered through the entire city but did not obtain alms anywhere.
Beholding the sun garlanded with rays, its orb slightly reddened, he cast aside his alms-bowl and set out toward the hermitage.
Then, as he was walking along, he was requested for alms by the Great Goddess, who was seated at the door of her house in the form of an ordinary woman.
The housewife said: "O Blessed One, no mendicants have been seen anywhere today; my husband will never eat without having first honored a guest. (31)
"Having performed the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, the master of the house must wait for the path of a guest; therefore, you become my guest. (32)
That householder who, without a guest, consumes food alone, consumes great sin along with his ancestors. (33)
Therefore, come quickly and fulfill the desire of my husband, who wishes to make his life as a householder fruitful through the honoring of guests.

Having heard this, Vyāsa, his resentment gone and filled with wonder, said to her: Vyāsa said: "O blessed lady, who are you? From where have you come? You have never been seen by me anywhere before. (35)
I believe you are some unique embodiment of the Dharma, possessed of a pure mind; by the sight of you, my senses have attained supreme delight. (36)
O you who are beautiful in every limb, you would likely have become nectar itself, had you not abandoned your residence in the Ocean of Milk out of fear of the Mandara mountain's strike.
Then, let Kuhū, afflicted by the fear of Rāhu, remain in Kāśī in the form of Sīmantinī, free from fear. 38.
Or rather, you are Kamalā; having left your lotus-abode which closes at night, you may dwell forever in Kāśī, which is ever-blossoming. (39)
Or rather, who here among the inhabitants of Kāśī is the very embodiment of compassion, the remover of the flood of all miseries, and the bestower of supreme bliss? (140)
Are you perhaps the presiding deity of Vārāṇasī, or are you the Goddess of Liberation who is celebrated in Kāśī? (41)
Whether it be a dog-cooker (outcaste) or one who performs sacrifices constantly, she adorns them equally at the end; this must surely be my own destiny ripening in the form of a woman.
Or rather, she must surely be that Bhavānī, the destroyer of worldly existence, who is celebrated as being present in the sacred field, bestowing devotion, food, and protection with her own devotion.
In every respect, you are certainly not a human woman, nor an asura woman, nor a kinnarī; you are not a vidyādharī, nor a nāgī, nor a gandharvī, nor a yakṣiṇī.
"You are surely some beloved deity of mine who removes my delusion; or rather, what is this anxiety of yours? O beautiful one, simply be here. (45)
"Having now been born dependent upon you through this meeting with you, I shall certainly carry out whatever you command; therefore, give me your orders. (46)
O fair-eyed one, setting aside this single loss of my ascetic merit, whatever else you shall command me to do, that very thing I will perform as your obedient servant.
Indeed, the speech of virtuous women like you does not diminish their greatness; however, who are you, O fortunate one? Tell me the truth before me. (48)
"Or rather, O pure-eyed one, where is truth in this body of yours? Thus questioned by the sage, she replied, "O Agastya, [it is] Viśvāyu. (49)
"O Sage, I constantly behold you, a householder, wandering here for alms while surrounded by a multitude of disciples. (150)
"You alone do not know me, for I indeed know you. O ascetic, what is the use of much speaking? [Let us go] before the sun sets. (51)
"First, make my hospitality to the lord of my life fruitful. Hearing that, the sage, his neck bowed in humility, said:
Vyāsa said: "O auspicious lady, I have a certain vow; if it should attain fulfillment, then I shall indeed accept a single alms-offering, and never otherwise. (53)
Having heard what was uttered by the ascetic, she then spoke these words: "Speak without hesitation, O wise sage; what is your religious observance? (54)
"By the grace of my husband, there is nothing lacking here. Hearing this, that ascetic, his soul filled with joy, said to her: (55)
"I choose to eat together with my ten thousand disciples; as long as the sun has not set, I shall eat, and not otherwise. (56)
Having heard this, her face beaming with joy, she then spoke to the sage: "Why delay? Go now and summon all the disciples."
Again he said to her, "O virtuous lady, such is your spiritual power that all my disciples shall attain complete satisfaction through it. (58)
Then, having smiled, she said to him: "O sage, by the grace of my husband, everything is already eternally accomplished within my abode. (59)
As long as every single person seeking wealth attains complete satisfaction in every way, we women are not like that—those who cause doubt regarding their husbands. (160)
When a seeker comes to the house, the task is indeed accomplished at that very moment; all directions are fulfilled, and all desires are completely satisfied.
"By the grace of my husband's feet, the entire house is now full; go quickly and return as soon as possible along with those who seek food. (62)

My husband has been away for a long time; he does not endure delay for long. He is a lover of guests and most dear to me; therefore, for the sake of providing him with a bountiful reception as a guest— || 63 ||
"Go quickly and return before the sun has set! Thus, being greatly delighted, he hurriedly summoned his disciples from all sides. (64)
Having returned and seen her looking toward the path, he spoke again: "O Mother, everyone has arrived; give us food quickly! (65)
"The sun has indeed reached the Sunset Mountain," saying this, those whose wealth is austerity entered within the temple. (66)
As soon as those ascetics reached the middle of that palace, which possessed the splendor of day due to the light of the jewels in its pavilion, they entered quickly.
Having washed their feet and been honored by some here and there, several were seated down to eat the food that had been served to them.
Having seen those preparations for the divine cooking, those who witnessed them attained supreme satisfaction in an instant through the rows of fragrances from their nostrils.
They attained complete satisfaction from partaking of that food; having sipped water for purification, they were adorned with sandalwood paste, garlands, and garments.
Then, having performed the twilight rites and sat down before him, they greeted him with great blessings and prepared to depart.
At that moment, an elderly householder cast a sidelong glance at his wife and asked: "What indeed is the primary duty for those dwelling at a sacred pilgrimage site?"
"Likewise, following that, we shall abide at the sacred ford. Having heard those words of his wife, he who was the best among all knowers of dharma [spoke]. (73)
Then, satiated by the taste of the great food moistened with the nectar of her devotion, the sage Vyāsa smiled and replied to her, the most knowledgeable of all.
Vyāsa said: O mother, you whose inner heart is pure and who take great delight in food; this very dharma which is being practiced by you is the only one that exists, and there is no other.
"You alone know the dharma, being devoted to the service of your husband; if you ask me the truth, then I shall say something to you. (76)
One who understands even slightly must certainly speak when questioned; O blessed lady, that alone is the Dharma, and there is no other Dharma whatsoever.
"By what means does this ancient husband of yours attain satisfaction? The wife replied: "This must surely be dharma; it is performed according to one's own ability. (78)
"I ask about the qualities common [to all]; tell them to me. Vyāsa said: "Speech that causes no agitation, and tolerance for the excellence of others. (79)

"Having reflected, one should always perform actions and contemplate the rising of one's own station. The householder said: "O learned one, among these duties, which one resides within you? Tell me that. (180)
Then Vyāsa stood as if paralyzed and said nothing at all; thereafter, that ascetic was addressed once more by the householder.
If these very principles have indeed been expounded by you, then self-restraint alone has been observed by you as the supreme form of giving and the highest form of cursing.
For compassion exists perfectly in you alone, and supreme fortitude likewise resides in you; in you alone is there the capacity to restrain desire and anger.
Only you know how to speak without agitation; only in you is seen the true capacity to endure the excellence of others. (84)
Having deliberated upon what must be done, you alone are the great refuge; you should certainly contemplate the arising of your own abode.
Tell me this one thing, O learned one: upon whom should that curse fall, uttered in anger by one who failed to achieve his own purpose due to misfortune? (86)
Vyāsa said: He who, failing to achieve his own purpose due to misfortune, utters a curse in anger—that curse, on the contrary, falls upon the cursing one himself, for he is lacking in discernment.

The householder said: "O Brahmin, when alms were not obtained by you while wandering—even though it was your own fault—then what offense have these wretched inhabitants of the field committed here? (88)
"O ascetic, hear my words: whoever here in my capital is unable to behold my prosperity is indeed one who has been cursed. (89)
"From this day forward, O wrathful sage, do not dwell in my field which is free from curses; you have no fitness to reside here."
Depart this very moment; leave this field. This field, which is the sole means for attaining liberation, is not fit for those such as you.
Whatever slight wickedness has been committed here by those dwelling in my field, the full ripening of that wickedness is indeed the state of being a Rudra-Piśāca.
Having heard that, trembling and with his lips and palate parched, he went for refuge to Gaurī, rolling at her feet.
And he spoke these words while weeping bitterly: "O mother, save me! Save me! I am helpless, yet I have you as my protector; I am a fool, your young child. (94)
Protect me who have come for refuge; guard me, who have sought your shelter. My evil-minded self is the abode of many transgressions. (95)
Even you are not able to alter the curse of Śambhu; and since I have come to you for refuge, O Śivā, let that one thing at least be done.
O Pārvatī, on every eighth day, he shall always appear in that field; I grant you permission to enter [the city], for the Lord would never transgress your word.
Thus addressed by that sage, Bhavānī, the source of compassion, looked at the face of Maheśvara and, by his command, said, "So be it."
Then those two auspicious ones, who bring welfare to the sacred field, vanished; Vyāsa also departed from the field, confessing his own transgression.
Beholding day and night that field which is not far from his vision, he should always enter the middle of the field on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
Standing even today on the eastern bank of the celestial river in the south-eastern direction from Lolārka, he beholds the row of palaces of Kāśī. || 1 ||
Skanda said: "O Pot-born one, in this manner that Vyāsa shall bestow a curse upon the sacred field; and by the bestowing of that curse upon the field, he shall depart from it at that very moment."
Therefore, for this sacred field of Avimukta which proclaims auspiciousness, there shall always be prosperity; otherwise, indeed, it would be quite different.
Having heard this meritorious chapter on the release from Vyāsa’s curse, he shall have no fear from anywhere regarding great calamities or afflictions.
Agastya said: O son of Śiva, having heard this account of the future from Vyāsa, I have become a vessel for wonder; now, please describe the sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas).
O Six-faced One, tell me in my presence what those [shrines] are that exist in Ānandakānana, and in what form they exist as liṅgas.
Skanda said: "O Pot-born one, listen as I relate exactly what this very same question was asked by the God to the Goddess at that time."
The Goddess said: "O Maheśvara, O Lord, tell me here which various holy places (tīrthas) exist wherever they may be; tell me that they are all present here in Kāśī."

The God of gods said: Listen, O large-eyed goddess, to that which is proclaimed as a *tīrtha* and a *liṅga*. Even in a reservoir of water, the designation "tīrtha" arises from its assumption of a physical form.
The forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, Śiva, Vighneśvara, and others, as well as that which is known as the Śaiva Liṅga—wherever these are found, that very place is a sacred tīrtha.
In Vārāṇasī, Mahādeva is said to be the first sacred site (tīrtha); to its north is the great well that bestows the station of Sarasvatī.
In the north-eastern part of that field, it is seen as the remover of the bonds of bound souls (paśu-pāśa-hṛt); thereafter, Vārāṇasī, possessing a physical form, is to be worshipped by men.
Always worshipped with great effort and bestowing happiness and well-being, it is the supreme *liṅga* called Goprekṣa, located to the east of Mahādeva.
From seeing that [image], one obtains the full fruit born of the gift of a cow; for previously, cows were sent from Goloka by Śambhu himself.
Having arrived at Vārāṇasī, Goprekṣa was heard of by him; to the south of Goprekṣa is the one known as Dadhīcīśvara.
From the sight of that, men obtain the fruit arising from sacrifice. To the east of that is Atrīśvara, which was worshipped by Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
By beholding the Liṅga with effort, one attains the station of Viṣṇu. To the east of Goprekṣa, there is a Liṅga known as Vijvara.
By worshipping him, a mortal becomes free from fever in an instant. To the east is Vedeśvara, who bestows the fruit of the four Vedas. (14)
To the north of Vedeśvara is Kṣetrajña-Ādikeśava; by beholding him, the entire three worlds are certainly seen. || 15 ||
Upon beholding Saṅgameśvara, one becomes sinless; to the east of that is Caturmukha, which was fashioned by the four-faced Brahmā to its east.
The Liṅga known as Prayāga, when worshipped, bestows the world of Brahmā; there, Gaurī, who brings peace, when worshipped, shall grant peace.
On the eastern bank of the Varaṇā, Kuntīśvara is to be worshipped by men; from worshipping him, sons who illuminate their own lineage are born.
To the north of Kuntīśvara is the sacred site of the Kāpila lake; by merely bathing there and worshipping the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva), [one attains the fruit]. || 19 ||
The fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice shall be obtained in its entirety. Whatever ancestors there may be among those such as the Roravas, numbering in the tens of millions— || 20 ||
O Sage, when a śrāddha is performed there by their sons, they go to the world of the ancestors; that is the Ānusūyeśvara Liṅga, located to the north of Goprekṣa.
By seeing him, the fruit of wifely devotion (pātivratya) becomes manifest for women. To the east of that Liṅga, Siddhivināyaka is to be worshipped. || 22 ||
Whatever accomplishment anyone may desire, they obtain it by bowing to that [Liṅga]; from Gaṇeśa, to the west of that, is the Liṅga of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
There exists a golden well there, which brings about the prosperity of golden horses.
To the west of that is the Muṇḍāsureśvara Liṅga, which bestows spiritual perfection; and to the southwest is Goprekṣā-Vṛṣabheśvara, which grants all desired objects.
O Sage, the Skandeśvara Liṅga is located to the west of Mahādeva; by worshipping that Liṅga, men shall attain residence in my own world. (26)
Indeed, by its side are Śākheśa and Viśākheśa; Naigameyeśvara is there, as well as the other Gaṇas such as Nandin and the rest.
For there are indeed thousands of their emblems present there; by beholding them, men shall attain residence in the same worlds as those respective Gaṇas.
To the west of Nandīśvara is the region of Śilā, which removes evil intellect; there, the auspicious Hiraṇyākṣeśvara bestows great strength.
To the south of that is the Liṅga named Aṭṭahāsa, which bestows all happiness; to its north is the auspicious Liṅga named Prasannavadaneśa.
A devotee should remain there with a serene countenance due to the auspiciousness of that vision; to the north of that is the Prasannoda pool, which bestows purity upon men.
In the west, at Aṭṭahāsa, there are two names, Mitra and Varuṇa; these two are to be worshipped in the Liṅga as bestowers of that world and removers of great sins.
In the southwest is the Liṅga known as Vṛddhavāsiṣṭha, belonging to Aṭṭahāsa; by worshipping it, great knowledge arises in men.
Situated near Vasiṣṭheśa is Kṛṣṇeśa, who bestows the world of Viṣṇu; to the south of that is Yājñavalkyeśa, who increases the splendor of Brahman.
After worshipping Prahlādeśvara, one should then visit Bhaktivardhana, where Śiva himself remains absorbed [in meditation] out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.

Therefore, that Linga which is absorbed within itself (Svalīna) should always be worshipped with great effort by those established in knowledge who desire supreme bliss. Whatever goal is ordained for them when they cast off their bodies, that same goal belongs to those who have abandoned their bodies at Svalīna.
The Vairocaneśvara Liṅga is situated in front of Svalīna; to its north is Balīśa, which increases great strength.
In that very place is the Bāṇeśa Liṅga, which, when worshipped, grants all desires; and to the east of Candreśvara is the Liṅga named Vidyeśvara.
By serving that Liṅga, all forms of ignorance shall become serene; to its south is Vīreśa, the bestower of great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhi).

In that very place is the goddess Vikaṭā, who liberates one from the flood of all suffering; that great seat (mahāpīṭha) with five seals (pañcamudra) should be known as the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhi). || 40 ||
There, the great mantras recited quickly attain success; it is not otherwise. On that very seat, in the northwest corner, Sagareśvara is to be worshipped. (41)
From worshipping him, the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) shall indeed be obtained in its entirety. And in his northeast is Bālīśa, who wards off rebirth in animal wombs.
To the north of that is Sugrīveśa, the destroyer of the flood of great sins; there is Hanūmadīśvara, who bestows the fruit of celibacy.
There, Jāmbavatīśvara, the bestower of great intelligence, is to be worshipped; and on the western bank of the Gaṅgā, the two Āśvina-Īśvaras are to be worshipped.
To the north of that is the Bhadra Lake, filled with the milk of cows; it yields the same fruit as that obtained by properly giving away a thousand tawny cows (kapilā).
A mortal who bathes in the Bhadrahrada obtains that fruit for certain, when the full moon day is joined with the constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā. || 46 ||
At that time, it is the most meritorious period, bestowing the fruit of the horse sacrifice (vājimedha) simply by beholding Bhadreśvara on the western bank of the lake. || 47 ||
From that merit, O sage, one shall attain Goloka; of this there is no doubt. At Bhadreśvara, in the direction of Yātudhānī, Śiva is Upaśānta.
By touching that linga, one attains supreme peace; and by beholding the tranquil Śivalinga, [one destroys] the [karma] acquired over hundreds of births.
One should abandon the mass of what is inauspicious and find the mass of what is auspicious; thereafter, he becomes a lord of the wheel and a restrainer of the wheel of birth.
To the north of that is the Cakra-hrada, which increases great merit; having bathed in the Cakra-hrada and having fully worshipped Cakreśa, a mortal [attains the highest state].
One attains the world of Śiva with a purified inner self; and to the southwest of that, Śūleśa should be visited with great effort.
O lady of excellent complexion, a trident was formerly placed there for the purpose of bathing; a great lake has arisen there in front of Śūleśa. (53)
Having bathed there in that lake and beheld the omnipresent Lord Śūleśvara, men go to the world of Rudra, leaving behind the thicket of worldly existence.
To the east of that, Nārada performed most intense penance; he installed an excellent Liṅga and also created an auspicious Kuṇḍa.
Having bathed in that pool and beheld Nāradeśvara, a man shall cross over the most terrible ocean of worldly existence; of this there is no doubt, O Sañjaya.
Having seen Avabhrātakeśvara to the east of Nāradeśvara, one attains a stainless state and is liberated from the multitude of sins.
In front of that is a copper vessel; one who bathes there does not enter a womb again. To the northwest of that is Gaṇādhyakṣa, the remover of obstacles, who effectively dispels all impediments.
Therein is a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that removes obstacles; one who bathes there does not suffer from impediments. To the north of that is the excellent Anārakeśvara Liṅga.
There is indeed the pool named Anāraka; one who bathes there does not become a denizen of hell. On the beautiful bank of the Varaṇā, to the north of it, is Varaṇeśa.
There, O great sage, the Pāśupata Siddha Akṣapāda attained eternal perfection with this very body. || 61 ||
To the west of that is Śaileśa, who grants the desire for supreme nirvāṇa; and to the south of that is Koṭīśvara, a liṅga that bestows eternal siddhi.
Having bathed in the lake at Koṭitīrtha and having fully worshipped Koṭīśa, a person obtains the fruit of the gift of ten million cows.
There is a pillar in the great cremation ground situated in the south-eastern direction from Koṭīśa; on that pillar resides Mahārudra together with Umā.
Having adorned that pillar, a man shall attain that state; right there, in the vicinity of Kapāleśa, is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha).
There is the place named Kapālamocana; one who bathes there partakes in the merit of a horse-sacrifice. To the north of that is the beautiful Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha.
Having bathed at that sacred ford (tīrtha), a person becomes liberated from sin. Right there is the Aṅgāraka-tīrtha and the Aṅgāra-nirmala pool.

Having bathed at the Aṅgāraka Tīrtha, one shall not again enter a womb. That man who bathes on the fourth lunar day conjoined with Tuesday shall not be afflicted by diseases, nor shall he ever be miserable.
To the north of that is the Viśvakarmeśvara Liṅga, which bestows knowledge; and to its south is the auspicious Mahāmuṇḍeśvara Liṅga.
The well named Śubhodaka must certainly be bathed in; there, a most beautiful garland made of skulls was cast by me.
Then the goddess Mahāmuṇḍā, the remover of sins, arose; a khaṭvāṅga was held there, and from that the Khaṭvāṅgeśa came into being.
A mortal becomes sinless by beholding Khaṭvāṅgeśa. To the south of that is Bhuvaneśa, and the holy pool (kuṇḍa) named Bhuvaneśvara.
A man who bathes in that pool shall become radiant in this world; to the south of it is Vimaleśa and the pool of pure water (Vimalodaka).
Having bathed there and beheld the Lord, a man becomes pure; there, a Pāśupata ascetic named Tryambaka attained perfection.
By means of this very body, he attained the world of Rudra; to the west of that is the abode of Bhṛgu, which bestows exceedingly great merit.
Having worshipped that according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain the abode of Śiva; and to its south is Śubheśvara, who bestows great auspicious fruits. (76)
There, the Pāśupata Kapila Ṛṣi, a great ascetic, attained perfection; for there, in the vicinity of Kapileśvara, is a delightful cave. (77)
Whoever indeed enters that cave shall never again enter a womb; there lies the Yajnodaka well, which bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
This very syllable Oṃ is that [reality], consisting of the nature of the primordial phoneme; on the northern bank of the Matsyodarī, I myself am indeed the locus of the resonance (nāda).
Instruction is not the supreme Brahman; instruction is not the supreme goal; instruction is not the supreme state that liberates one from the suffering of saṃsāra. (80)
Sometimes the Jāhnavī flows into the sight of that deity; she is called Matsyodarī, and bathing there is attained through meritorious deeds.
O Great Goddess, when the Matsyodarī Gaṅgā comes together with the Kapileśvara in the west, that conjunction is very difficult to attain.
To the north of Kapileśvara is the Uddālakeśvara Liṅga; by beholding it, supreme perfection is attained by all.
To the north of that is the Bāṣkulīśa Liṅga, which grants the accomplishment of all goals; to the south of Bāṣkulīśa is indeed the Kaustubheśvara Liṅga.
By worshipping that Śaṅkukarṇeśvara Liṅga, located to the south of Kaustubheśvara, one shall never be deprived of a multitude of jewels at any time.
By serving [this deity], the practitioner may even today obtain supreme knowledge. Aghoreśa is at the entrance of the cave; to its north is an auspicious well.
The place known as Aghoroda bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; there are two auspicious Liṅgas there, Gargeśa and Damaneśa. (87)
In this very body, in that place where those two attained perfection, the desired success is achieved through the worship of those two lingas. || 88 ||
To the south of that is the great sacrificial pit known as Rudrāvāsa; by worshipping Rudreśa there, one obtains the fruit of ten million Rudras.
O Aparṇā, when the fourteenth lunar day is conjoined with the constellation of Rudra, that is the most meritorious time; at that moment, bathing in that pool yields great fruit.
Having bathed in the Rudra-kuṇḍa and beheld the omnipresent Lord Rudreśvara, a man shall attain the world of Rudra, even if he dies anywhere else.
In the south-western quarter of Rudra is the Mahālaya Liṅga; in front of it is Pitṛkūpa, the supreme abode of the ancestors.

Having performed a śrāddha there, a man should cast the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the well; accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, the performer of the śrāddha shall partake in the world of Rudra.
There, O Goddess, is a long pond named Vaitaraṇī facing the west; a man who bathes in it does not go to hell at all.
To the west of Rudrakuṇḍa is the Bṛhaspatīśvara Liṅga; by beholding it during the conjunction of Jupiter and the Puṣya asterism, one shall obtain divine speech.
To the south of Rudrāvāsa is the supreme Kāmeśa Liṅga; to its south is the great Kuṇḍa, which grants all desired objects through bathing.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a pilgrimage there bestows all desires; and to the east of Kāmeśvara is the auspicious Nalakūbara Liṅga.
In front of that is a purifying well which bestows abundance of wealth and grain; to the east of Nalakūbara are the two lords, Sūryācaṃdramasa.
Those two, who remove the thick veil of the darkness of ignorance, have been duly worshipped; and to their right, Dhvajeśa, the destroyer of delusion, was seen.
Therein is the Siddhīśvara Liṅga, which bestows great supernatural powers; and in that very place is Maṇḍaleśa, who grants the station of a sovereign of a province.
To the east of Kāmakuṇḍa is Cyavaneśa, who bestows prosperity; and in that very place is Sanakeśa, who grants the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And to the west of that is the Sanatkumāra Liṅga, which bestows the perfection of yoga; to its north is Sanaṃdeśa, the promoter of great knowledge.
And to the south of that is seen Āhutīśa, who bestows the fruit of the fire-oblation; to the south of that is the Liṅga Pañcaśikheśvara, which generates merit.
To the west of that is the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, which increases merit; having bathed in that lake, what more would a man have to grieve for? (4)
There, bathing and giving gifts shall yield inexhaustible merit; and to the north of that is Kuṇḍeśa, who is saluted by all the Siddhas.
O Brahmin, a mortal obtains that same fruit which is gained in twelve years by receiving the Pāśupata initiation simply by beholding Kuṇḍeśa.
To the east of the Mārkaṇḍeya lake is Śāṇḍilyeśa, who bestows great merit; and to its west is Caṇḍeśa, who removes the sins of those who witness a solar eclipse.
To the south of Kapāleśa is the sacrificial pit known as Śrīkaṇṭha; having bathed in that pit, a man shall become a donor through the power of Śrī.
Near that pool is the Mahālakṣmīśvara Liṅga; having bathed in the waters of that pool, one should worship Mahālakṣmī.

He is fanned by divine women whose hands hold chowries; when the celestial dwellers depart from the heavenly world for the womb of the Fish, they travel happily along that very same path, surrounded by women.
Therefore, O best of sages, that place is renowned as Svargadvāra; to the south of that pool is the Liṅga that bestows the state of Brahmā.
Gāyatrīśvara and Sāvitrīśvara should be worshipped with great effort; and on the beautiful bank of the Matsyodarī is the Liṅga Satyavatīśvara.
Having first worshipped Ugreśvara, the great liṅga situated to the east of Lakṣmīśa, which increases the glory of asceticism, one should worship those two [deities].
A mortal shall become a rememberer of past births by worshipping that Liṅga; and to its south is the Ugra-kuṇḍa, which is superior to Kanakhala for the purpose of bathing.
To the west of that pool is the Karavīreśvara Liṅga; by the sight of it, the destruction of diseases occurs for men. || 15 ||
In that very place is the Marīcīśa Kuṇḍa, which destroys the multitude of sins; and behind it, O Sage, is the Indrakuṇḍa and the Liṅga named Indreśvara.
To the south of Indreśa is the auspicious Karkoṭavāpikā; having bathed there in the waters of the tank and beheld Karkoṭakeśvara, [one attains merit].
One attains lordship over the Nāgas; of this there is no doubt. After that is Dṛmicaṇḍeśa, the Hara who removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
To the south of that is a great sacrificial pit (mahākuṇḍa) which bestows the fruit of the world of Rudra; to its west is a great Liṅga well-known as Agnīśa.
To the east of that is the pool named Āgneya, which bestows the same world as Agni; to the east of Āgneyeśvara is that auspicious pool, and to its south is another.
Having bathed in that pool, a man dwells in heaven together with his ancestors. To the east of that is Bālacaṇḍreśa, who bestows the attainment of the world of the Moon.
Having beheld Bālacaṃdreśa on all sides and the numerous Liṅgas of the Gaṇas, one shall attain the station of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya) by visiting those Liṅgas.
Near Bālacandra is a well beloved by the hosts of ancestors; having bathed there and offered the śrāddha rite, one shall deliver seven generations of ancestors.
To the east of Andha is the meritorious Liṅga named Viśveśvara; to the east of Viśveśvara is Hara, known as Vṛddhakāleśvara.
There is a well named Kāloda at its head, which removes all diseases; by those men and women who have drunk the water there according to their own past actions, [all ailments are cured]. (25)
For them, there is no turning back even in hundreds of millions of eons; by drinking that, a human being shall be liberated from the fear arising from the bondage of birth.
O Pot-born One, whatever gift is given there at that well by those whose souls are devoted to Śiva, there is no destruction of it even at the time of universal dissolution.
Those men who perform the restoration of what is broken or cracked there, reach the world of Rudra and always rejoice in happiness.
To the south of Kāleśa is Mṛtyvīśa, who removes untimely death; and to the north of that well is the Liṅga known as Dakṣeśvara. (29)
Indeed, a thousand offenses shall perish through his worship. || 130 ||
The great Mahākāleśa Liṅga is located to the east of Dakṣeśa; having bathed in the Mahākuṇḍa, a man should worship Mahākāla.
By him indeed this entire world, both moving and unmoving, was honored there; and upon beholding Antakeśvara to the south of that [place], one has no fear of Death.
O Sage, to the south of that is the Hastipāleśvara Liṅga; by worshipping it, one indeed attains the merit born from the gift of an elephant.
Therein is the Airāvata-kuṇḍa and the Airāvateśvara Liṅga; by worshipping that Liṅga, a mortal becomes a possessor of abundance in wealth and grain.
To the south of that, for the sake of prosperity, there is the Mālatīśvara Liṅga; and to the north of Hastīśvara is Jayaṃteśa, the bestower of victory.
To the north of the auspicious Mahākāla Kuṇḍa is Bandīśvara; and in Vārāṇasī, the famous Bandikuṇḍa is the destroyer of great sins. (36)

There, by means of bathing, giving gifts, and performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), one enjoys inexhaustible merit; for there is indeed the Dhanvantarīśvara Liṅga and the pool (kuṇḍa) bearing that same name.
Indeed, the name of that Liṅga is one thing, while the name of the Kuṇḍa is another; the name of the Liṅga is Tuṅgeśvara, and the name of the Kuṇḍa is Vaidyeśvara.

O highly intelligent ones, great medicinal herbs consisting of nectar were cast there; therefore, by bathing in that pool and by beholding that Liṅga, all diseases perish along with most dreadful sins. (39)
To the north of that is Halīśeśa, the destroyer of all diseases; and to the south of Tuṅga is Śiveśvara, the bestower of auspiciousness. (140)
The auspicious Jamadagnīśvara Liṅga is to the south of Śiveśa; to its west is Bhairaveśa, and to its north is an auspicious well.
Merely by touching it, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. To the west of that well is Sukeśa, who bestows the perfection of yoga. (42)
And to the southwest of that is Vyāseśa and the well of pure water; having bathed in Vyāsakūpa and offered libations to the gods and ancestors, a man [attains merit].
One obtains an inexhaustible world wherever one desires it; to the west of Vyāsatīrtha lies the great lake Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
By bathing in the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake and beholding Vyāsa, one becomes as if dead in Vārāṇasī, even if one dies anywhere else.
Near Ghaṇṭākarṇa is the Pañcacūḍāpsaras lake; having bathed in the waters of Pañcacūḍā and beheld that Lord Īśvara, [one attains the fruit]. || 46 ||
A man goes to the heavenly world and becomes beloved by Pañcacūḍā. To the north of that is Gaurīkūpa, which destroys all dullness.
In the northern part of Pañcacūḍā is the holy site named Aśoka; to its north is the great holy site of Mandākinī, which removes great sins.

O Sage, that holy place is meritorious even in the heavenly world, how much more so in the world of men! To the north of that, in the middle, Lord Madhyameśa sleeps in the center of the sacred field—how wonderful!
Having kept a vigil there on the Aśoka-aṣṭamī in the month of Madhu, a man never experiences sorrow; he shall become eternally filled with bliss. (150)
And the extent of the field of liberation is one *krośa* on every side, beginning from this meritorious *liṅga*, Madhyameśvara.
All the great-grandfathers indeed always say this: "Will someone born in our family ever bathe in the waters of the Mandākinī? (52)
A man, being purified, should feed Brahmins and also ascetics who follow the Pāśupata path, after having bathed in the Madākinī and beheld Madhyameśvara.
Endowed with twenty-one lineages, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra; and to the south of Madhyameśa is the auspicious Viśvedeveśvara.
By worshipping that [liṅga], the thirteen Viśvedevas become worshipped. To its east is Vīrabhadreśa, the bestower of the station of Mahāvīra. (55)
Bhadradā and Bhadrakālī are auspicious to his south; there is a lake named Bhadrākālahrada which bestows great merit. || 56 ||
To the east of that is the Āpastaṃbeśvara Liṅga, the supreme bestower of knowledge; to its north is the Puṇyakūpa (Meritorious Well), and to its west is the Śaunaka Hrada (Lake).
To the west of the lake is the Liṅga named Śaunakeśa, which bestows wisdom; having bathed in that lake and indeed beheld Śaunakeśvara, a man [attains his goal]. (58)
One obtains that divine knowledge by which he crosses over death; to its south is Jambukeśa, the warder-off of animal births.
To the north of that is Mataṅgeśa, the awakener of the science of song; to the northwest of Mataṅgeśa, there are various liṅgas on all sides.
Established here by the sages and bestowing all perfections, the Brahmarāteśvara Liṅga is located to the south of Mataṅgeśa.
By the sight of that Liṅga, one's life is never cut short prematurely. Therein lies the Ājyapeśvara Liṅga and numerous Pitṛ-liṅgas; by serving that Liṅga, all the great-grandfathers are satisfied.
To the south of that is Siddhakūpa, where there are thousands of Siddhas; those Siddhas who are of the nature of wind, and those Siddhas who move within the rays of the sun.
The Liṅga established by them is called Siddheśvara; by the mere sight of it, all pure supernatural powers (siddhis) shall be attained.
To the west of that is the Siddhavāpī, yellow in color; bathing there bestows success. To the east of the Siddhakūpa is the Liṅga named Vyāghreśvara.
By beholding that Liṅga, men have no fear arising from tigers or thieves. And to the south of that is Jyeṣṭheśvara, known as Jyeṣṭhasthāna, which bestows spiritual perfection.
To the south of that is the Liṅga Prahasiteśvara, the abode of joys; to its north is Nivāseśa, who bestows the fruit of residing in Kāśī.
There lies the confluence of the four oceans, which bestows the merit of bathing in the sea; there resides Goddess Jyeṣṭhā, who, when bowed to, grants the highest station.
To the south of Vyāghraliṅga is the Liṅga named Caṇḍīśvara; to the north of that is the Daṇḍakhāta lake, which brings joy to the ancestors.
The bath immediately following the eclipse at Daṇḍakhāta bestows great merit; there is the Jaigīṣavya cave, and in each of those places, there is a Liṅga bearing that same name.
Having fasted there for three nights, one shall obtain stainless knowledge; thereafter is the Liṅga Mahāpuṇyaprada, Devaleśvara.
O Pot-born One, at that time, the Lord of Kālānumāpati manifested a hundred forms near him; when that Liṅga appeared in Kāśī, he brought [all others] under his control.
From the sight of Talliṅga, one's life remains unbroken for a hundred years; Śātātapeśa, located to its south, bestows the fruit of great recitation (mahājapa).
To the west of that is Hetukeśa, who is the cause for the great fruit; to the south of that is Ikṣapādeśa, the one who sets forth great gnosis.
And at its front is the site of Kaṇāda; there is the holy water Prahi. Having bathed in the Kaṇāda-well, whoever should worship Kaṇādeśa [there], || 75 ||
He is never forsaken by wealth nor by grain; to his right is seen Bhūtīśa, the bestower of prosperity upon the virtuous.
To its west is the destroyer of sins known as Āṣāḍhīśvara, and to its east is Durvāseśa, who fulfills all desires.

To the south of that is Bhārabhūteśa, the remover of the burden of sins. To the east of Vyāseśvara are the two lords Śaṅkha and Likhita; these two, who promote great knowledge, should be visited with effort in Kāśī.
O Lord of the Universe, that merit which is attained upon the completion of the Pāśupata vow is attained here in an instant by beholding you even once.
The Lord of that [place] is Avadhūteśa, the promoter of the knowledge of Yoga; and the sacred ford (tīrtha) is indeed Avadhūteśa, which effects the destruction of all impurities. || 180 ||
To the east of Avadhūteśvara is the Liṅga Paśupatīśvara; by the service of that Liṅga, men attain liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa).
To the south of that is Gobhileśa, who bestows great desires; and behind that is the supreme Jīmūtavāhaneśa Liṅga.
The attainment of the status of a Vidyādhara results from the service of that liṅga; indeed, Mayūkhārka and Gabhastīśa are located there at Pañcanada.
To the north of that is the great lake named Dadhikalpahrada; bathing in that lake is difficult to attain, and beholding it is likewise difficult to attain.
To the north of Gabhastīśa is Hara, the Lord of Dadhikalpa; having beheld him quickly, a man shall dwell for a kalpa in the city of the Three-eyed One.
To the south of Gabhastīśa, however, one should feed a Brahmin couple, dedicating the offering to Maṅgalā Gaurī, the auspicious abode of Maṅgalā.

Even if one adorns it according to one's ability, the end of that merit can never be reached; a single circumambulation is uniquely auspicious, yielding the same fruit as circumambulating the entire earth.
Vadanaprekṣaṇādevī is to the north of Mukhaprekṣeśvara; near Maṅgalā is the auspicious Sarvasiddhikarī.
At Liṅga, Tvaṣṭrīśa, Vṛtteśa, Mukhaprekṣa, and Uttaraśubha, the fruit of seeing those two is equal to the merit of giving land along with gold.
To the north of that is the auspicious vision of the goddess Carcikā; and the Revateśvara Liṅga, situated in front of Carcikā, bestows peace.
In front of that Mahāśubhāyatanā is the Liṅga Pañcanadeśvara; to the west is the auspicious Maṅgaloda great well and Maṅgalā.
To the west of Upamanyu’s great Liṅga is the auspicious Maṅgalā; beyond that is the Vyāghrapādeśvara Liṅga, which removes the fear of tigers.
And in the southwest, from Gabhastīśa comes Śaśāṅkeśa, who removes the multitude of sins; to the west of that is the Caitraratha Liṅga, which bestows a divine state.
To the west of Revateśa is Jaiminīśa, the destroyer of great sins; there, O best of sages, are many lingas of the ṛṣis. (94)
To the northwest of Jaiminīśa is indeed the Liṅga Rāvaṇeśvara; by seeing it, men no longer face the great fear of Rākṣasas. || 95 ||
To the south of that is Varāheśa; then Māṇḍavyeśa in the direction of Yama (the south); to the south of that is Pracaṇḍeśa, and then Yogeśa to the south of that.
To the south of that is Dhāteśa, and Someśa is in front of it; to its southwest is Kanakeśa, who bestows great gold upon the virtuous.
To the north of that are five lingas of the Pāṇḍavas for the joy of the virtuous; Saṃvarteśa is in front of them, and Śveteśa is to its west.
After that is Kalaśeśa, a Liṅga that bestows fearlessness from Time (Kāla). O Sage, it arose from the pitcher when Śveta was bound by Kāla.
To the north of that is the Citragupteśvara Liṅga, which destroys sins; and to the west of Citragupteśvara is Dṛḍheśa, who yields great fruit.
To the south of Kalaśeśa is the supreme Liṅga Graheśa; beholding that Liṅga pacifies the afflictions caused by the planets. || 1 ||
To the west of Citragupteśvara is Yadṛccheśa, which yields great fruit; and to the south of Graheśvara is the Utathyavāmadeveśa Liṅga.
To its south are the two auspicious lords Kambala and Aśvatara; in that very place is the stainless Liṅga worshipped by Nalakūbara.
To the south of that is Maṇikarṇīśa, and to its north is Paliteśvara; Jarāhara is in that very place, and Pāpanāśana is behind it.
To the west of that is Nirjareśa, and to its southwest is Pitāmaha; there is also Pitāmahasrotikā, where a Śrāddha ceremony yields great fruit.
To the south of that is Varuṇeśa, and Bāṇeśa is to its south; at the Pitāmahasrotikā is Kūśmāṇḍeśa, who bestows success.
To the east of that is Rākṣaseśa, Gaṅgeśa is to its south, and to its north are the Nimnageśas; there are numerous liṅgas [there].
There is Vaivasvateśvara, who wards off the world of Yama; behind him is Aditīśa, and in front of him is Cakreśa.
At its head is the supreme site named Kālakeśa, which produces direct spiritual realization; there a shadow is clearly seen, and by beholding it, one becomes free from sin.
To the east of that is Tārakeśa, and to the east of that is Svarṇabhārada; to the north of that is Marutteśa, and Śakreśa is to the east of that.
To the south of that is Raṃbheśa, and right there is Śaśīśvara; to the north of that are the Lords of the Worlds (Lokapālas), and there are numerous Liṅgas in that place.
They bring about various supernatural powers even for Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases, as well as for the hosts of divine sages and the elders.
To the south of Śakreśa is Phālguneśa, the great remover of sins; and to the south of that is Mahāpāśupateśa, the supreme bringer of auspiciousness. (13)
To the west of that is Samudreśa, and to its north is Īśāneśa; to the east of that is Lāṅgalīśa, who bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 14 ||
Worshippers who are completely free from passion and hatred attain perfection; for them, liberation has been declared by me, but you, O Goddess, are not such human beings.
Madhupiṅga and Śvetaketu, the two ascetics at Lāṅgalīśa, attained supreme perfection with this very body.
In that very place are Nakulīśa and Kapileśa; both of them indeed observe my supreme secret vow.
In its vicinity is Prītikeśa; there, O beloved, my own affection resides. By a single fast observed there, one obtains a fruit greater than that of a hundred years.
Having kept a vigil and observed a fast on my festival day, Prītikeśa shall certainly attain the rank of a Gaṇa.
To the south of the Lord, there is a pond of auspicious water; drinking its water leads men to the state of no rebirth.
To the west of that Jalā mountain, Daṇḍapāṇi always dwells; to its east, south, and north are Tāra, Kāla, and Śilādaja.
One should offer even the three-fold Linga with faith into this heart-lotus; those best of men by whom that water there has been drunk have achieved their life's purpose.
One should worship Avimuktasamīpeśa, the Lord of Liberation who bestows the intellect of liberation, and Karuṇeśa, the abode of compassion, to the north of that [Avimukta]. (23)
Svarṇākṣeśa is to the east of that [Liṅga], and Jñānada is to its north; Saubhāgyagaurī should be worshipped for the sake of attaining abundant good fortune and prosperity.
To the south of Viśveśa, Nikuṃbheśa should be worshipped with great care as the bringer of security to the sacred field; behind him is Vighnanāyaka.
Virūpākṣa, the destroyer of all obstacles, who bestows excellent success when worshipped, is especially to be worshipped on the fourth lunar day in the southeast from Nikuṃbheśa.
To the south of that is Śukreśa, who increases one's sons and grandsons; to its north is the great liṅga known as Devayānīśvara.
To the east of Śukreśa, the deity known as Kaceśa is to be worshipped; having sipped water at Śukrakūpa, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Bhavānī and Īśa, who bestow boons upon their devotees, are auspicious and worthy of salutation; they are located to the west of Śukreśa and always grant protection to their own devotee. (29)
Alarkeśa, situated to the east of Śukreśa, is worthy of worship; Madālaseśvara is there to his east, the remover of all obstacles.
O Brahmin, having slain the Lord of Laṅkā, Raghunātha installed this supreme Liṅga, the Lord of the lords of Gaṇas, which bestows all spiritual perfections.
By touching that Liṅga, even a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is quickly purified. Furthermore, the destroyer of Tripura (Śiva) is worshipped there as another bestower of great merit.
To the west of that is the auspicious Dattātreyeśvara Liṅga; to its south is Harikeśeśa, and beyond that is Gokarṇeśa.
In front of that lake is the sin-destroying [site], and behind it is Dhruveśvara; in front of that is the Dhruvakuṇḍa, which is supremely pleasing to the ancestors.
Beyond that is Piśāceśa, who removes the state of being a Piśāca; then to the south of that is Pitṛīśa, and in front of him is Pitṛkuṇḍa.
There, the great-grandfathers of those men who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall be satisfied; for Vaidyanātha himself is indeed Tāreśa, located in front of Dhruveśa.
To the southwest of that is the Manoliṅga, which supremely increases one's lineage; and the Priyavrateśvara Liṅga is situated in front of Vaidyanātha.
To the south of that is Mucukundeśa, and by its side is Gautameśvara; to the west of that is Bhadreśa, and to the south of that is Ṛṣyaśṛṅgiṇa.
Brahmeśa is to the east of that, and Parjanyeśa is situated to its northeast; Nahuṣeśa is to the east of that, and Viśālākṣī is in front of it.
The Viśālākṣīśvara Liṅga is located right there, bestowing the prosperity of the sacred field; the Jarāsaṃdheśvara Liṅga is to its south, destroying fever.
To the east of that, the Hiraṇyākṣa-liṅga, which bestows gold, is to be worshipped; to its west is Gayādhīśa, and to the west of that is Bhagīratha.
And in front of that, O Sage, to the west of Brahmeśa, is the Linga of Dilīpeśa along with its sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which bestows the desired fruits upon the one who bathes there.
Therein is the Liṅga of Viśvāvasu; to the east of that is Muṇḍeśa; to the south of that is Vidhīśa; and to the south of that is Vājimedhaka.
