Having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika and beheld that supreme liṅga, a human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
To the north of that is Mātṛtīrtha, which removes the fear of rebirth for one who bathes there; whether it be a woman or a man, whoever should perform a bath there— (45)
One obtains the desired fruit through the grace of the Mothers; and to the south of your pool is the supreme Puṣpadanteśvara.
In that direction of Agni (the southeast), there are numerous lingas of the hosts of celestial sages; to the south of Puṣpadanta is Siddhīśa, the bestower of supreme perfection.
Through the five-fold worship (pañcopacāra-pūjā), one shall attain supreme accomplishment (siddhi) even in a dream; by serving Hariścandreśa, men shall obtain a kingdom.
To the west of that is Nairṛteśa, then Aṅgiraseśa to the south; to the south of that is Kṣemeśa, and then Citrāṅgeśa to the south.
To the south of that is Kedāra, which bestows the status of an attendant of Rudra; by kings of the lunar and solar dynasties, [the lineage] from Kedāra in the southern region—
Hundreds and thousands of Liṅgas are established to the south of Lolārka; it is worshipped as the fulfiller of all desires.
To the west of that is the Karaṃdhameśvara Liṅga, which yields great fruit; to its west is Mahādurgā, the destroyer of great difficulties.
And Śuṣkeśvara is to the south of that, worshipped by the river Śuṣkā; Janakeśa is to its west, and Śaṅkukarṇa is to its north.
To the east of that is the Mahāsiddhīśvara Liṅga, which bestows all perfections; having bathed in the Siddhakuṇḍa and beheld the great Siddheśvara, a man [attains his goal].
A person reaches the further shore of all spiritual accomplishments by worshipping the Liṅga known as Vāḍavya at Śaṅkukarṇeśa in the north-western quarter. || 55 ||
In front of that is Vibhāṇḍeśa, and to its north is Kaholeśa; there is the Liṅga Dvāreśvara, and the auspicious Goddess Dvāreśvarī.
From worshipping that [liṅga], O Sage, there arises perfection that bestows residence in Ānandāraṇya; and the Gaṇas there are its protectors, possessing various forms and weapons.
In that very place is the Haridīśa Liṅga, and then the Kātyāyana Liṅga; by its side is Jāṅgaleśa, and behind it is Mukuṭeśvara.
In that very place is a pure pool that bestows the fruits of all pilgrimages; having bathed in Mukuṭakuṇḍa and beheld Mukuṭeśvara, [one attains these results].
By visiting her, one obtains the fruit that comes from visiting all the *liṅgas*; she is the supreme earth who bestows the perfection of both austerity and yoga. 260.
O Sage, there are hundreds of thousands of liṅgas there for the sake of spiritual perfection; yet, O Goddess, the single northern direction in Vārāṇasī is dear to me.
Even there, my delight is exceedingly dear in the five-sensed body; at the time of its arising and its duration, I am always present therein.
Thus, he who understands this is not defiled by sins. Truth, truth, and again truth—this triple truth, O beloved, is found nowhere else.
If you desire my state, you must go there quickly; O sage, I have described the lingas to you only by way of brief indication.
Certain liṅgas have been established twice or thrice with devotion; they are not redundant, and they should be worshipped everywhere with faith. (65)
These lingas, these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), these fires (indhavas), and these step-wells (vāpīs)—all of these should be accepted with faith by the wise.
From seeing and bathing at these, the fruit becomes progressively greater; this applies to the liṅgas, the wells, and the lakes located here as well. (67)
Who would be able to count the ponds and the images? Even the blades of grass situated in Ānandakānana are most excellent. (68)
Even the dwellers of heaven seek nowhere else that which results in rebirth; Kāśī, composed of all liṅgas, is the sole birthplace for all sacred fords.
O Goddess, you alone, who bestow both heaven and liberation, have been seen through the power of penance as my most beloved when served at the end of one's life. 270.
By its very nature, however, this Kāśī is my land of blissful rest; for those who utter the name of Kāśī and those who indeed rejoice in it [attain the same]. (71)
Those who possess the appearance of Śākha and Viśākha, and those who resemble Skanda, Nandin, and Gajānana—they alone, O Goddess, are my devotees; they alone are my servants. (72)
Only those who desire liberation and those who dwell in Ānandavana have truly performed great penance and observed the great vow here.
And those who dwell in Ānandavana have given great gifts; they have indeed bathed in all the sacred fords and are initiated into all sacrifices.

All those who have practiced all dharmas and dwell in the Forest of Bliss (Ānandavana)—including gods, asuras, serpents, and humans—all of them serve as a burden to the earth; yet even here, they are my companions because they dwell in the Forest of Bliss. (75)

Even an outcaste is superior in Kāśī, but not elsewhere; one who has mastered the Vedas is inferior in Kāśī. The former (the Vedic scholar) reaches the end of saṃsāra, while the latter (the outcaste) is even lower than an outcaste.
He alone is surely omniscient; he alone indeed possesses the supreme vision, who, having cast off his earthly body, assumes a body made of nectar in Kāśī. (77)
Having heard this meritorious chapter, which contains the secret of all sacred fords (tīrthas), a person certainly attains the merit born from beholding Kāśī.
Whoever recites this chapter every single morning, day after day, has effectively visited all these sacred fords; it is not otherwise.
The wise person who constantly recites this chapter, which consists of all the *liṅgas*, is not afflicted by Yama, nor by his messengers, nor even by sin. (280)
The fruit of the Brahma-sacrifice arises for that person of virtuous soul who, being pure and with a mind focused upon it, should recite this chapter. (81)
He who recites this chapter here has bathed in all the sacred pools, has drunk the waters of all the step-wells, and is a worshiper of all the Lingas.
What is the use of many other hymns that yield very meager results? This chapter, which yields great fruit, should be recited by those who possess love for Me. 83.
Whatever fruit is indeed obtained here from giving great gifts, that is fully attained by this single recitation and great meditation. 84.
Whatever fruit is obtained by mortals after bathing in all the holy fords and beholding numerous Liṅgas, that same fruit is certainly attained through the recitation of this.
O Sage, this very collection of names of the Kāśī-liṅgas, which is being chanted as a chapter, is itself the most intense austerity and the greatest recitation.
This recitation must not be given to one who bears malice toward me, nor to an atheist, nor to one devoted to reviling the Vedas; it must not be given, it must not be given, it must not be given. 87.

By the recitation of this chapter, the sin arising from the killing of a Brahmin, as well as approaching those who should not be approached and the eating of what should not be eaten, [is destroyed]. (88)
[The sins] arising from violating the teacher’s wife, originating from the theft of gold, born from the killing of mother or father, and produced by the slaughter of a cow or an embryo. (89)
Great sins, minor sins, and numerous sins known and unknown, as well as secondary sins and those born of mind, speech, and body—(290)
By my command, all these—sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, wife, and even fields—will undoubtedly go to destruction without exception. (91)
By reciting this chapter, a wise person will surely attain everything desired by the mind, including heaven and the bliss of liberation; of this there is no doubt. (92)
While the Lord was thus narrating this story before the Goddess, Nandin arrived, prostrated himself, and made this request: || 93 ||
The completion of the construction of the great palace has been achieved; this chariot is ready, and the gods, beginning with Brahmā, have assembled. (94)
The lotus-eyed Lord, mounted upon Tārkṣya, stands at the gate with his attendants, awaiting the opportune moment while placing the lords of sages at his forefront.
Those of noble vows who dwell throughout the fourteen worlds, having heard of this great festival of entry, have assembled today.
Skanda said: Having heard these words of Nandin, the God, accompanied by the Goddess, mounted his divine chariot and departed from heaven.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Sacred Fields and Tīrthas," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta, to how the great festival of Śambhu was described by Skanda when he was questioned by the one born from a water-jar (Agastya).
Skanda said: Listen, O one of great wisdom, to the narrative concerning the entry of Śambhu, which generates joy for the three worlds and destroys even the greatest of sins.
Having come from Mount Mandara on the Damanaka festival in the month of Caitra, Śambhu reached Ānandagahana and wandered here and there.
Now that the temple, the playground of the Goddess of Liberation, had been completed, the Lord entered the inner sanctum from the Virajas-pīṭha.

On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, when Mercury is in conjunction with the lunar mansion Rādhā, the Moon is situated in its seventh house, and all the remaining planets are in their exaltations. || 5 ||
While musical instruments were being played and the quarters of the sky were serene, the sound of the Vedic recitations of the Brahmins drowned out all other sounds.
The entire path between the Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka resounded with echoes, and everything was filled with joy during Śambhu’s festival of entry.
Multitudes of Gandharvas sang and throngs of Apsaras danced.
The celestial bards offered hymns of praise, and the hosts of deities rejoiced.
Fragrant winds blew and clouds rained down flowers; all were adorned with auspicious ornaments, and all spoke auspicious words.
All beings, both stationary and moving, including all the gods and asuras, gandharvas, and uragas, became overflowing with bliss.
Among the Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Kinnaras, and humans—among all those born as both female and male—only these four shone forth.
O Sage, at every step the goals of human endeavor were rendered entirely free from obstacles; for the sky was then deeply suffused with the thick masses of incense smoke.
Even today, that deep blue luster never abandons it at any time; all those lamps which were then lit for the lustration ceremony remain awakened.
Even though they are being scorched by those lights, O King, the stars shine there under the guise of constellations; moreover, in every mansion, there are variegated banners of diverse forms.
Washed by the radiance of beautiful banners, they shone at every temple of Śiva; in some places those skilled in song sang, and in others dancers danced.
In various places, the four kinds of musical instruments were played; and on every path, the ground was made slippery by splashes of sandalwood juice.
In every courtyard, beautiful rows of colors shone forth, possessing many splendors—green, white, madder-red, blue, and yellow. (17)
The ground areas were paved with jewels, and the gate-towers shone brightly; the rows of mansions, radiant with plaster, attained the very name of "celestial palaces" (saudha).
O Pot-born One, even those things which are insentient then appeared as if they possessed consciousness—whatever auspicious objects are celebrated here on earth.
Indeed, for all of them, that very day became their day of birth; then the God of gods arrived and entered the pavilion of liberation.

Then the God of gods, having been consecrated by the four-faced Brahmā along with the hosts of great sages, sat upon an auspicious throne together with Bhavānī, surrounded on all sides by groups of Kumāras.
Then the hosts of gods and the great lords of the serpents joyfully worshipped Maheśa with countless jewels, many fine silken garments, various garlands, and radiant, desirable fragrances. (22)

O Pot-born one, Śambhu was worshipped there by the lords of mountains with jewels according to their respective means, as well as by others of meritorious intellect; then the Lord was honored with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by the hosts of Mothers.
Having first satisfied all the lords of sages with their respective heart-felt long-cherished desires, Śiva, who is worshipped by the hosts of all the immortals, addressed Brahmā and Viṣṇu and spoke.

"Please sit here. You have always been my equal; you are the sole cause of my entire sovereignty. Even though you remain far away, you alone are near to me; there is no one other than you who can accomplish my purpose.
O Divodāsa, that best of kings was instructed by you with such excellent guidance that he attained supreme perfection, and my entire desire has been fulfilled.
"O Viṣṇu, choose a boon that you desire; indeed, there is nothing here that should not be given to you. This Ānandavana which has been obtained by me—its cause was you and that Gaṇeśa. (27)
Nothing in the three worlds is as dear to me as this ground of supreme bliss, Vārāṇasī—the mine of the elixir of Brahman, where those who sleep long [in saṃsāra] find no further rebirth.
Having heard these words of the Lord of the Universe, Viṣṇu spoke to Maheśa, the giver of boons: "If you are pleased, O wielder of the Pināka bow, then may I never be far from your feet. (29)
Having heard these words of Madhusūdana, Purāri, being exceedingly pleased, said: "O Murāri, may you always remain in my presence; here, be the refuge of Nirvāṇa-ramā."

O Lotus-handed One, Supreme among the supreme, if one first fails to propitiate You here and then worships me, even though endowed with devotion, his desired goal will certainly not be accomplished. (31)

O Acyuta, for me who am stationed here in this pavilion of liberation, there shall be happiness everywhere; yet that [happiness] is not found on the perfectly pure Mount Kailāsa, nor even in the heart of a devotee whose splendor is unwavering.

Those whose mental fluctuations remain steady for even a mere moment while staying here in my southern pavilion—even if their devotion is directed toward no other and their minds are deeply focused—they shall never again undergo the state of being in a womb.
Those who, having bathed for a moment in the unfathomable Cakrasaras—the sole crowning ornament of all sacred fords—enter here with desireless minds, are indeed my attendants, freed from sin.

Those who remember me in the pavilion of liberation, give even a little of their own wealth according to their ability, and listen for a moment with steady minds to the meritorious stories, obtain the fruit of giving away ten million cows. || 35 ||

Those who have long performed penances under Upendra and have indeed bathed in all the multitudes of holy fords (tīrthas), yet remain here, having bathed in the lake of Maṇikarṇikā—the very abode and object of sight for those who seek liberation—[they alone are truly purified]. (36)

O Hari, there are holy places at every step here; where is Maṇikarṇikā to be compared with them? How many auspicious pavilions are there here, for this is the lineage of abodes for the beauty of liberation! 37.
O Hari, in the future Dvāpara age, this Kaivalyamaṇḍapa will become famous in the world by the name Kukkuṭamaṇḍapa.
Hari said: O Bhālanetra, tell me how Nirvāṇamaṇḍapa shall attain such renown as has been described by the Lord.

The God of Gods said: "There shall be a twice-born man here named Mahānanda, who will possess four arms, follow the conduct of the eastern altar, and have renounced the acceptance of gifts from holy places."
Free from hypocrisy and with a gentle mind, he was always fond of guests; then, having reached youth, his father indeed passed away.
Having established a friendship with him, he caused someone to place his foot upon an uneven path with sharp arrows, and then carried off that person's wife.
Urged by her and utterly deluded, he drank that which was undrinkable; infatuated by passion, he developed a craving for consuming what is unfit to be eaten.
Seeing wealthy Vaiṣṇavas, that foolish soul, momentarily assuming the guise of a Vaiṣṇava, reviles the Śaivas who are the cause of protection from hell.
Seeing devotees of Śiva who desire to give even a little, one who subsists on the Śiva-liṅga would indeed revile all the Vaiṣṇavas.

Thus, one who knows the dharma of heretics, averse to the twilight prayers and ritual bathing, wearing a broad sectarian mark, adorned with garlands, and radiant in clean, washed garments; || 46 || 27 ||
Śikhin was a receiver of improper gifts from everyone; two children were born to him, who followed the path of the insane.
While he was thus engaged, a wealthy man will arrive from a mountainous region for the purpose of accomplishing a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
Having bathed in the Cakrasaras lake, he will indeed say: "I am a most excellent Caṇḍāla by birth, desirous of giving wealth. (49)
"Is there anyone who might accept it, to whom I may give this wealth?"—having heard these words of his, some [responded] with a gesture of their fingers.
"This one who has been designated and is seated shall recite with the meditation-mudrā; he alone, and no other, shall accept a gift from you. (51)
Having heard these words of theirs, that outcaste went into their presence, prostrated himself like a staff, and then spoke to him.
"O great Brahmin, deliver me; make my pilgrimage fruitful. I have a certain object; please accept it and show me your favor. (53)
Then, placing his rosary against his ear and withdrawing his meditation, he asked him by means of a gesture with his hand, "How much wealth do you have here? (54)
Having understood his intention, he spoke with great joy: "I shall give you as much as will bring you complete satisfaction; it shall not be otherwise."
Having heard those words, Mahānanda, filled with joy, broke his silence and said: "I am indeed free from desire for receiving gifts. (56)
Nevertheless, for the sake of showing you favor, I shall accept [this gift]; moreover, O most excellent one, if you will carry out my word.
"Having deposited all the wealth I possess with someone among you, not even the slightest amount shall be given [to anyone else]; then I will give it, and not otherwise. (58)
The Cāṇḍāla said: "Whatever wealth I have brought for the pleasure of Viśveśa, all that I shall give to you, since Viśveśa is mine. (59)
O best of the twice-born, all those who dwell here in the capital of Viśveśa—whether they be small or large, mere creatures—they are indeed the subjects of Viśveśa.
Those whose nature is to uplift others, those who fulfill the desires of others, and those whose habit is to assist others—they are indeed the teachers of the lords of the universe. (61)
Having heard those words, with his senses and mind filled with joy, that twice-born man then spoke to that outcaste from the mountains.
"Come, take the darbha grass and perform the utsarga with haste! "So be it," replied that high-minded man from the mountains, and he did so immediately.
Saying, "May Viśveśa be pleased," he departed as he had come; and that twice-born man, though censured by other twice-born men, continued to dwell here.
But as soon as he has gone outside, he is despised by many: "This is a Brāhmaṇa who is a Cāṇḍāla; his wealth was taken from a Cāṇḍāla. (65)
"For he is indeed a Cāṇḍāla, excluded from all the world; thus they run after him on all sides, O Hari, spitting upon him. (66)
And out of fear of that, he would not emerge from his house anywhere, like a crow-fearing owl, with his face bowed down in shame.
Having reflected upon this one day, he, censured by his wife and reviled by the world, abandoned the city of Vārāṇasī and went to the Kīkaṭa countries.
As he was traveling along the road, he was indeed noticed carrying gold; even though he was among the pilgrims, he was stopped by those who were blocking the path.
Having led him into that vast forest along with his retinue, those thieves plundered him, took his wealth, and consulted among themselves.
This man possesses abundant wealth, yet it perishes when he does not live; therefore, this wealthy man, along with his attendants, must be slain with every effort. (71)
"Deliberate upon this," they said; "O traveler, remember what must be remembered! We shall certainly kill you along with your entire retinue."
Having heard this, that twice-born one reflected within his mind: "Aha! That for which I have accepted such abundant wealth has now been fulfilled."
My family is lost, and my acceptance of gifts is lost; my very life is lost, and my residence in the city of Kāśī is lost. (74)
All was instantly and swiftly destroyed by the act of that evil-minded one; he did not attain death in Kāśī because of his acceptance of that wicked gift.
In the end, due to his recollection of his family as well as his remembrance of Kāśī, even though he was killed by thieves, he then became a cock in Kīkaṭa.
That hen, however, gave birth to two sons who attained the state of being copper-crested cocks; in the end, through the remembrance of Kāśī, they gained supreme recollection of their past births.
Thus, after a great deal of time had passed, O best of pilgrims, four [of them] arrived upon that very path where the cocks were located.
Indeed, while those cocks were loudly conversing with one another about Vārāṇasī, they then heard the discourse concerning Kāśī.
By the power of their recollection of past lives, they emerged through that connection; and on the road, they were seen by those compassionate and eminent pilgrims.
Having been brought to that excellent field by means of offerings of rice and other grains, those four peacocks reached the sacred site.
Wandering here around the supreme Muktimandapa, they were those who had conquered their appetite, observed their vows, and turned their backs on desire and anger.
Laughing at my conversations and discourses, which were free from the delusion of gain, their hair was thoroughly cleansed and purified by bathing in the celestial river.
Having seen the residents of the sacred field intent on the utterance of my name, their fine ears dedicated to my stories, and their minds and virtuous conduct bestowed upon me; (84)

Then, having deliberated among themselves, those cocks of virtuous conduct honored them due to the influence of their past latent impressions (vāsanā); and by gradually restricting their food, they shall indeed renounce their lives right here.
O Viṣṇu, while all the worlds are watching, by my grace, quickly ascend a celestial chariot and reach Kailāsa, my own abode.
Having enjoyed unsurpassed divine pleasures for a very long time, they will thereafter become possessors of knowledge here and attain eternal liberation.
From that time forward, people everywhere will speak of this as "Muktimaṇḍapa," while this [other place] shall be known as Kukkūṭamaṇḍapa. || 88 ||
Furthermore, those men who shall remember even their conduct, having reached Muktimandapa, will indeed attain the highest good.
While Śambhu was thus narrating his future before Hari, a tumultuous sound of bells suddenly rang out.
Then the God of gods, the consort of Umā, summoned Nandin and said: "Nandin, having ascertained the matter, go and tell me from where this sound comes."
Then Nandin, having approached the Bull-bannered Lord, spoke with a joyful countenance, having offered salutations with his palms joined in reverence.
Nandin said: "O God of gods, O Three-eyed One, what unprecedented thing shall I tell you? Here, the playful splendor of the Fortune of Liberation (Mokṣalakṣmī) is worshipped by various individuals."
Then Śambhu, smiling, said, "May our desire be accomplished. Rising up together with the Goddess, the most auspicious Lord of the gods departed.

Then, together with Brahmā and Hari, he went to the theater pavilion. Skanda said: "Having heard this meritorious chapter, which is the cause of supreme bliss, a person shall attain great joy and will certainly reach Kailāsa. (95)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Journey to the Pavilion of Liberation," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 98 ||

Vyāsa said: Listen, O Sūta, to how the life-story of the God of gods, the Lord of the Universe, the Supreme Self, was told by the one born from a jar (Agastya) to the one born in a reed-thicket (Kārttikeya).
Agastya said: O Senānī, tell me what the Lord did after emerging from that pavilion of liberation, accompanied by the lords of the gods.
Skanda said: I shall now describe what Śambhu, preceded by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, did after reaching the Śṛṅgāramaṇḍapa from the Muktimaṇḍapa. || 3 ||
The Lord sat facing the east together with us and the Goddess; he was attended by Brahmā on his right side and by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow on his left side.
Fanned by Mahendra and surrounded on all sides by sages, he stood in silence with respect, while his attendants remained behind him.
Attended by those bearing raised weapons and by those abounding in honor, Śambhu, having raised his right hand, [bestowed it] upon Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The Lord of Gods revealed the Liṅga, saying: "Behold, behold! This alone is the supreme light; this alone is that which is higher than the highest."
For this very form of mine is stable and bestows great accomplishment; these Pāśupata Siddhas have been celibate students since childhood.

They had conquered their senses, were devoted to austerity, were purified by knowledge of the five objects of sense, slept upon heaps of ashes, were generous, possessed excellent character, and were chaste.
They were constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, with their senses and minds focused on no other; they were always perfectly pure through the two-fold ablutions, both Vāruṇa and Āgneya.
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, their eyes were fixed upon the supreme reality; they were truthful, having conquered anger, free from delusion, and without possessions.
They are effortless, free from conceptual proliferation, fearless, and free from disease; they are without divisions, without means, unattached, and pure in intention.

They have crossed over the formidable ocean of saṃsāra; they are free from conceptual construction, free from sin, free from dualities, certain of the ultimate truth, and devoid of the activity of egoism. || 13 ||
"Always greatly dear to me are these sons of mine, who are my very own form; they are to be honored and saluted with the thought that they are I myself by those who are devoted to me. (14)
When these have been honored, I shall be pleased; of this there is no doubt. In this sacred field of Vaiśveśvara, the Śiva-yogins are to be fed. (15)
By correctly counting each one by one, the fruit is a hundred million feasts; for this Lord of the Universe is manifest as the soul of all immobile beings and the sovereign of the world. (16)
I am the accomplisher of all perfections for all those who possess devotion here; at times I may be visible, and at other times I may be invisible.
And here in Ānandakānana, O deities, I dwell at my own will for the sake of bestowing grace upon all devotees here forever. (18)

"I shall remain in the form of a *liṅga*, bestowing the fruits of all desired objects. All *liṅgas* everywhere—whether self-manifested (*svayambhū*) or not self-manifested—shall always come to behold this *liṅga*. (19)
"I abide within all lingas, there is no doubt; however, this supreme form of mine is specifically in the form of a linga. (20)
O dwellers of heaven, by whomsoever this Linga has been seen with faith and pure vision, by him I have indeed been seen through direct realization.
"By hearing of this Liṅga, the sins accumulated over a lifetime perish in an instant; let the gods, together with the hosts of sages, listen! (22)
By the mere remembrance of this Linga, the sin accumulated over two lifetimes will certainly and swiftly perish; there is no doubt of this by my word. (23)
Aiming for this Liṅga, even great sin accumulated over three lifetimes dissolves from the very moment one steps out of the house.
O immortals, by the sight of this linga, one shall certainly obtain the merit arising from a hundred horse-sacrifices through my grace.
O gods, by the mere touch of this self-manifested Liṅga of mine, the Lord of the Universe, one shall obtain the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
By offering even a mere flower preceded by a handful of water, one obtains the merit of a hundred gold pieces through the application of devotion. || 27 ||
By performing even a mere act of worship with devotion toward this king of lingas, one obtains the fruit of worshipping with a thousand golden lotuses.
By performing a great worship preceded by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for this Liṅga, one obtains the four aims of human existence.
O immortals, having bathed my liṅga with water filtered through a cloth, that virtuous person obtains the merit produced by a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. || 30 ||
Having anointed the liṅga with devotion using the fragrant juices of sandalwood, he is himself anointed by celestial women with fragrant yakṣakardama pastes.
Through the offering of fragrant incense, one shall come to possess divine scents; and through the kindling of ghee lamps, one shall travel in a celestial chariot in the form of light.
By offering a single lamp with a camphor wick out of devotion, one shall possess the radiant white beauty of a body like camphor and come to have an eye upon the forehead.
By offering even a mere portion of the food offering, grain by grain, the wise man shall dwell on Mount Kailāsa for age after age, endowed with great enjoyments.
Whoever should offer supreme food with ghee and sugar to the Lord of the Universe, by him the three worlds—including gods, ancestors, and humans—are satisfied. (35)
He who offers mouth-perfume, a mirror, a beautiful fly-whisk, a canopy, or a comfortable couch, gains a great fruit of merit.
The number of oceanic jewels might somehow be calculated; but who could possibly calculate the number of gifts such as mouth-fresheners and the like given here? (37)
Whoever with devotion offers articles for worship, such as a bell, a water-pot, and so forth, in my temple, shall dwell here in my presence.
Whoever has performed even one of these—singing, instrumental music, or dancing—for my pleasure, before him there shall be a great triple symphony day and night. (39)

Whoever causes the work of painting murals and other such works to be performed here in my temple, shall remain standing before me and enjoy great pleasures accompanied by beautiful paintings. || 40 ||
A wise man who, having been born in the middle [land], bows even once to the Lord of the Universe, becomes a lord of the earth whose feet are worshipped by the three worlds. (41)
But he who, having seen Viśveśvara, meets with death even elsewhere, will certainly attain liberation in another birth; of this there is no doubt. || 42 ||

For one who has the name "Lord of the Universe" on the tip of his tongue, who hears the stories of Viśvanātha, and who contemplates the character of the Lord of the Universe in his heart—where is his rebirth? (43)
He who, having seen my Liṅga, Viśvanātha, rejoices in it, shall be counted among my Gaṇas, supported by the power of great merit.

O Lord of the Universe, O Lord of the Universe, whoever constantly mutters "Viśvanātha" at the three junctions of the day—I too certainly regard that virtuous person as one who has performed true recitation. 15.
O gods, this great Liṅga of mine is also always most worthy of worship; therefore, it should be worshipped with every effort by gods, sages, and humans. (46)
Those by whom Viśveśvara has not been seen and those by whom Viśveśvara has not been remembered have been seen by the messengers of Kṛtānta; by them the pain of the womb has been experienced.

Those by whom this Liṅga has been prostrated before are themselves prostrated by gods and demons alike. By even a single prostration to it, the station of a world-guardian (Dikpāla) becomes insignificant; for from the station of a world-guardian there is a fall, but from prostration to Śiva there is no fall.
May all the hosts of celestial sages listen; I speak the truth for the sake of helping others: nowhere within the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, or Jana is there a Liṅga equal to Viśveśa.
Neither in Satyaloka nor in Tapas, nor indeed among the gods in Vaikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, or Rasātala, is there any holy site equal to Maṇikarṇikā, nor any other Liṅga equal to Viśveśvara.
Indeed, there is no linga equal to Viśvanātha’s, nor is there any sacred ford other than Maṇikarṇikā; there is no penance grove anywhere else that is as auspicious as my Ānandavana.

Vārāṇasī is entirely composed of sacred fords (tīrtha), and even its name is indeed a ford among all sacred fords; yet within it, there is a certain ground of my own bliss, the most supremely pure Maṇikarṇikā.
From this place, my royal palace, proceeding slightly toward the east where the Lord resides, there are three hundred rays on the left and two hundred rays on the right, respectively.

Those five hundred hands of mine that serve this Maṇikarṇikā—the northern and southern banks of the celestial river Gaṅgā, the essence of the three worlds and the supreme treasury—indeed dwell within my heart.
In this Forest of My Bliss, this Linga—the abode of nectar, the source of nectar—has arisen spontaneously from the very depths of the seven netherworlds by virtue of its compassion for its devotees.

Those people who, through the notion that it is a fabricated state, shall worship this emblem with rationalistic arguments—for them, this indeed is the supreme punishment: they will certainly not cease from dwelling in the womb.

Whatever is beneficial for oneself should always be offered here at this Liṅga by those devoted to me; for that [merit] shall never perish, either in this world or the next, unlike the sin committed by sinners in this world.
May the glory of ultimate liberation dwell with those virtuous ones who, even while staying at a distance, have worshipped this Linga of mine here with auspicious articles provided by me alone. (58)

Listen, O Viṣṇu; listen, O Creator of the World; and let all the hosts of divine sages listen! For this Liṅga indeed bestows supreme perfection upon the virtuous; there is not the slightest difference here from my own presence. (59)

Indeed, to those who have dedicated to this Linga—the means for accomplishing all perfections—all the wealth acquired through their own meritorious deeds, I grant the state of Nirvana, which is the unsurpassed means for achieving every happiness and is entirely free from fear.

Raising my arm, I declare again and again: within this world consisting of the three Vedas, these three alone are the essence—the Liṅga of the Lord of the Universe, the water of Maṇikarṇikā, and the city of Kāśī; this is the truth, this is the triple truth.
Then the Lord, the powerful Īśa, having arisen and performed beautiful worship upon that liṅga, entered into dissolution; and those gods, crying out "Victory! Victory!", praised that Lord.
Skanda said: O high-minded son of Mitrāvaruṇa, this single portion of the power of the Vimukta-kṣetra, which removes all impurities, has been described.
In your presence, according to my understanding, even our separation from Kāśī shall not last long; before long, you too will reach the unsurpassed Kāśī.
This sun has reached the peak of the western mountain; indeed, this has become the time for silence for both you and me. (55)
Vyāsa said: O Sūta, having heard this, that sage went forth for his twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsti), having bowed repeatedly to the immeasurable Lord who was accompanied by Lopāmudrā.
Having fully understood the secret of the field of the moon-crested Lord, Agastya, with a resolute mind, became intent on meditation upon Śiva.
O Sūta, who here is capable of describing the exceedingly great majesty of Ānandakānana, even in hundreds of years? (68)
Just as it was narrated to the Goddess by Śiva, the Supreme Self, so too has this majesty been told by Skanda to the one born from a water-jar (Agastya).
O best of beings, this has been recounted before you and before Śuka and the others; now, whatever you desire to ask, ask that, and I shall tell it to you.
Having heard this meritorious chapter, which destroys all impurities and bestows the fruits of every desire, a mortal becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Viśveśvara Liṅga," in the latter half of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the fourth section of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 99.
Sūta said: Having heard this unsurpassed Kāśīkhaṇḍa from the Skanda Purāṇa, I am exceedingly satisfied and have retained it within my heart.
O son of Parāśara, please recount the chapter on the table of contents as well as the supreme majesty, exactly as it occurred in the past.
Vyāsa said: O virtuous Sūta Jātūkarṇya, listen attentively; let Śuka, Vaiśampāyana, and the other youths also hear this.
I shall proclaim the chapter on the table of contents and also the greatness arising from the sections, which destroys sins and increases great merit.
The dialogue between Vindhya and Nārada is proclaimed in the first [chapter]; the majesty of Satyaloka is set forth in the second. || 5 ||
Then there was the arrival of the gods at the hermitage of Agastya, the account of the devoted wife’s conduct, and the departure of the Pot-born Sage.
Then follows the praise of sacred fords (tīrthapraśaṃsā), after which the seven cities are recorded; next is the true nature of Saṃyaminī, and beyond that, the world of the Sun (Brahmaloka).
Then follows the attainment of the worlds by Indra and Agni, and thereafter the [attainment] of Śivaśarman; from Agni arises Kravyād, and from him the birth of Varuṇa.
The origin of the two lords of the cities of Gandhavatī and Alakā, and the attainment of the lunar world by the twice-born Śivaśarman.

Then follows the account of the world of the stars (Uḍuloka), from which the origin of Venus (Śukra) arises; thereafter is the description of the worlds of Mars (Māheya), Jupiter (Guru), and Saturn (Sauri).
Beyond that are the worlds of the Seven Sages and of Dhruva, attained through austerity; then follows the attainment of Dhruva’s station, and thereafter the abiding in the world of Dhruva. || 11 ||
The vision of Satyaloka by that Śivaśarman, his consecration as four-armed [Viṣṇu], and the final liberation of Śivaśarman. 12.
Then follows the dialogue between Skanda and Agastya and the origin of Maṇikarṇikā; thereafter, the majesty of the Gaṅgā and the hymn to Daśaharā. (13)
Then follows the power of the Gaṅgā, the thousand names of Gaṅgā, the praise of Vārāṇasī, and thereafter the manifestation of Bhairava.
Then follows the birth of Daṇḍapāṇi, and from that, the emergence of Jñānavāpī; next is the narrative of Kalāvatī, and after that, the account of virtuous conduct.

Then follows the section on the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), the characteristics of women, the section on what ought and ought not to be done, and the description of Avimukteśa. || 16 ||
Then follow the duties of the householder, then the exposition of yoga; thereafter the knowledge of time is proclaimed, and then the description of Divodāsa.
Then follows the description of Kāśī, after that the description of Yoginī, then the account of Lolārka, and thereafter the story of Uttarārka. || 18 ||
The greatness of Sāṃbāditya, the praise of Drupadāditya, then the narrative of Garuḍa, and thereafter Aruṇa, Arka, and the others. (19)
Then follows the holy site of Daśāśvamedhika, the arrival of the Gaṇas from Mount Mandara, the narrative of Piśācamocana, and thereafter the dispatching of Gaṇeśa.
Then follows the manifestation of Māyāgaṇapati as Ḍhuṇḍhi, the expansion of Viṣṇu’s Māyā, and the dismissal of Divodāsa. || 21 ||
Then follows the origin of Pañcanada and the birth of Bindumādhava; thereafter is the detailed description of the majesty of the Vaiṣṇava tīrthas.
The departure from Mandara to Kāśī of the trident-bearing Lord whose banner is the bull; and the conversation of Maheśvara with Jaigīṣavya at Jyeṣṭhasthāna. 23.
Next follows the narration of the secret of the sacred field, which destroys all sins; now, therefore, begins the origin of Kaṇḍukeśa and Vyāghreśa.
Then follows the narrative of Śaileśvara and the vision of Ratneśa; next, the origin of Kṛttivāsas and the arrival at the sanctuary.
The empowerment of the deities, the prowess of the demon Durga, the victory of Durga, and then the description of the syllable Om.
Furthermore, [it contains] the majesty of the syllable Oṃ, the origin of Trilocana, the power of Trilocana, and the narrative of Kedāra.
Then follows the greatness of Dharmeśa, then the auspicious story of the bird, then the narrative of Viśvabhū, and after that the story of Durdama.
Then follows the narrative of Vīreśvara and again the majesty of Vīreśa; thereafter is the majesty of Kāmeśa, joined with the holy sites (tīrthas) of the Gaṅgā.
The majesty of Viśvakarmeśa arising from the sacrifice of Dakṣa, the casting off of her body by Satī, and thereafter the origin of Dakṣeśvara. || 30 ||
Then follows the glorification of the majesty of Pārvatīśa, then the majesty of Gaṅgeśa, and then that which arises from Narmadeśa. || 31 ||
The manifestation of Satī and Īśvara, the description of Amṛteśa and others, the paralysis of Vyāsa’s arm, and his liberation from Vyāsa’s curse. (32)

Then follows the assembly of sacred fields and pilgrimage sites, the discourse on the pavilion of liberation, the manifestation of Viśveśa, and thereafter the ritual circumambulation during the festival procession.

This century of narratives has been proclaimed in sequence; by the mere hearing of it, one obtains the fruit of hearing all the sections (khaṇḍas). Even in this chapter of the table of contents (anukramaṇikā), there is a detailed account of the pilgrimage circuit.
Sūta said: O best of sons of Satyavatī, out of a desire for the welfare of people, please describe the pilgrimage and circumambulation as it truly is for those who seek spiritual perfection.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O highly wise Lomaharṣaṇa, I shall tell you how the pilgrimage should first be joyfully undertaken by those who go on pilgrimage.
Having first bathed with his clothes on in the waters of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī, he should offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, the Brahmins, and likewise to those who seek his aid.
Having paid homage to Āditya, Draupadī, Viṣṇu, Daṇḍapāṇi, and Maheśvara, one should then proceed to behold Ḍhuṇḍhivināyaka.
Having touched the waters of Jñānavāpī, one should then worship Nandikeśa; thereafter, having worshipped Tārakeśa, one should then worship Mahākāleśvara.
Then again, this group of five sacred fords (pañcatīrthikā) is known as Daṇḍapāṇi.
This daily rite should be performed by those desiring great fruit; thereafter, the pilgrimage to Vaiśveśvara should be undertaken, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
And one should diligently maintain the livelihood of the fourteen sense-bases (āyatanas), starting from the first day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth, according to the prescribed rule.
Alternatively, those desiring the perfection of the field as a surety should bathe in each respective sacred ford (tīrtha) and perform worship with each respective emblem (liṅga).
Performing his journey in silence, the pilgrim obtains the fruit; having offered water libations at Matsyodarī, he should first behold the syllable Om.
Then one should go to Triviṣṭapa, Mahādeva, and Kṛttivāsas; thereafter, one should proceed to Ratneśa, Candreśa, and Kedāra.
One should go to Dharmeśvara and Vīreśa, and then to Kāmeśvara; then to Viśvakarmeśvara and thereafter to Maṇikarṇīśvara.
Having seen Avimukteśvara, one should then worship Viśveśa; this pilgrimage must be performed with great effort by a resident of the sacred field.
But he who, having resided in the sacred field, does not perform this pilgrimage, obstacles arise for him, indicating his expulsion from the field. || 48 ||
Another pilgrimage to the eight sacred sites (aṣṭāyatana) should be performed for the pacification of obstacles: Dakṣeśa, Pārvatīśa, and likewise Paśupatīśvara; || 49 ||
Gaṅgeśa, Narmadeśa, Gabhastīśa, Satīśvara, and Tārakeśa as the eighth—these are especially [venerated] on every eighth lunar day (pratyaṣṭamī). || 50 ||
These visible lingas are for the pacification of great sins; there is also another auspicious pilgrimage that always provides security and prosperity.
And the destroyer of all obstacles must be worshipped by those residing in the sacred field, after first beholding Śaileśa and performing the ritual bath in the Varaṇā river.
Having performed his bath at the confluence, he should visit Saṅgameśvara; having well-bathed at Svalīna Tīrtha, he should behold the Lord Svalīneśvara.
Having bathed at the Mandākinī-tīrtha, Madhyameśvara should be visited; one who has performed the water-rites at that sacred site should behold Hiraṇyagarbheśa.
Then, having bathed at Maṇikarṇikā, one should behold the Lord Īśāna; thereafter, having sipped water from the well, one should gaze upon Goprekṣa.
Having bathed in the Kāpileya lake, one should behold the bull-bannered Lord; having offered water in the well there, one should gaze upon Upaśāntaśiva.
Having bathed in the Pañcacūḍā lake, one should then worship Jyeṣṭhasthāna; having bathed in the Catuḥsamudra well, one should worship the God.
After performing ablutions in the pond that is in front of the God, one should then behold Śukreśvara, having offered water from that very well.
Then, having bathed in Daṇḍakhāta, one should worship Vyāghreśa; and having performed a bath in Śaunakeśvara-kuṇḍa, one should then offer worship.
Having performed this pilgrimage after visiting the great liṅga Jaṃbukeśa, a person is never again born into this ocean of misery that is worldly existence.
Beginning from the first lunar day up until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, other sanctuaries should indeed be visited in this sequence.
Having performed this pilgrimage, a person is not born again; another pilgrimage must be performed, originating from the eleven shrines (ekādaśāyatana). 62.
Having bathed well in the Āgnīdhra pit, one should behold the Lord Āgnīdhreśvara; from there, one should go to Urvaśīśa, and then to Nakulīśvara.
Then, having seen Āṣāḍhīśa, and then Bhārabhūteśvara, and then having beheld Lāṅgalīśa, and thereafter Tripurāntaka; || 64 ||
From there, one should go to Manaḥprakāmeśa, and then to Prītikeśa; from there to Madālaseśvara, and then to Tilaparṇeśvara.
This pilgrimage of the eleven Liṅgas should be performed here with great effort; by undertaking this pilgrimage, a man shall attain the state of Rudra.
Hereafter, I shall describe the unsurpassed pilgrimage of Gaurī, which, when performed on the third day of the bright fortnight, bestows prosperity in every respect. (67)
Having bathed well at Goprekṣa-tīrtha, one should proceed to Mukhanirmālikā; having bathed in Jyeṣṭhāvāpī, a man should worship Jyeṣṭhāgaurī.
Having performed the water-rites at Jñānavāpī, one should worship Saubhāgyagaurī; then, having likewise performed the water-rites right there, one should worship Śṛṅgāragaurī.
Having bathed in the Viśālagaṅgā, one should then go to Viśālākṣī; having bathed well at Lalitātīrtha, one should thereafter worship Lalitā.
Having bathed at the Bhavānī-tīrtha, one should then worship Bhavānī; thereafter, Maṅgalā should be worshipped with water from the Bindu-tīrtha.
Then one should go to Mahālakṣmī for the sake of attaining stable prosperity; having performed this pilgrimage in this field, which is the source of liberation, a person [attains his goal]. (72)

One shall not be overcome by sufferings anywhere, either in this world or the next; one should always perform the "every-fourth-day" festival (praticaturthī-yātrā) for the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara).

For their delight, sweetmeats (modakas) should indeed be given to the Brahmins with that as the purpose; and on the day of Bhauma (Mars), the pilgrimage to Bhairava should be performed, which removes all sins.

On a Sunday, during the sun’s transit, or on the sixth lunar day joined with Sunday, and likewise on the seventh day of the sun (Ravi-saptamī), [one should perform worship] for the pacification of all obstacles.
The pilgrimage of Caṇḍī is considered auspicious on either the ninth or the eighth day; furthermore, the pilgrimage of the inner sanctum should be performed every single day.
Having first performed the morning bath and bowed to the five Vināyakas, and then having paid homage to Viśveśa while standing in the Nirvāṇamaṇḍapa; || 77 ||
"I shall indeed undertake the pilgrimage to Antargṛha for the pacification of the multitude of sins," he said, and having taken this vow, he then went to Maṇikarṇikā.
Having bathed and returned in silence, one should worship Maṇikarṇīśa; then, having bowed to Kambalāśvatara and prostrated before Vāsukīśa. (79)
Then, having seen Parvateśa, and then Gaṅgākeśava; then, having seen Lalitā, and then Jarāsaṃdheśvara.
Then one should go to Somanātha and then to Vārāha; having bowed to Brahmeśvara, one should then bow to Agastīśvara.
Having paid homage to Kaśyapeśa, one should then go to Harikeśavana; thereafter, having beheld Vaidyanātha, and then having gazed upon Dhruveśa.
Having worshipped Gokarṇeśvara, one should then proceed to Hāṭakeśa, and after visiting Kīkaseśvara at the Asthikṣepa tank.
Then, having bowed to Bhārabhūta, and thereafter to Citreśvara, and then having prostrated before Citraghaṇṭā, one should then [visit] Paśupatīśvara.
Having gone to Pitāmaheśvara, one should then go to Kalaśeśvara; then Candraśa, Vīreśa, Vidyeśa, and Agnīśa. (85)
Nāgeśvara, Hariścandra, Cintāmaṇi Vināyaka, and Senāvināyaka—these should then be visited, for they remove all obstacles.
Both Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, who have assumed embodied forms, should be visited with great effort in Kāśī; they are the destroyers of great obstacles.
Then one should go to Sīmāvināyaka and Karuṇeśa; then Trisaṃdhyeśa, Viśālākṣī, Dharmeśa, Viśvabāhukā, Āśāvināyaka, and then again Vṛddhāditya.
The Caturvaktreśvara Liṅga is there, and after that is Brāhmīśa; then follows Manaḥprakāmeśa, and after that is Īśāneśa. (89)
Then Caṇḍī and Caṇḍīśvara, as well as Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, are to be beheld; thereafter, having bowed to Ḍhuṇḍhi, one should worship the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
Then Lāṅgalīśa is to be worshipped, and after that Nakulīśvara; then, having bowed to Parānneśa, one should then [worship] Paradravyeśvara.
Having worshipped Pratigraheśvara, as well as Niṣkalaṅkeśa, Mārkaṇḍeyeśa, and then Apsaraseśvara; || 92 ||
Thereafter, one should worship Gaṅgeśa and perform a bath in Jñānavāpī; then [one should visit] Nandikeśa, Tārakeśa, and Mahākāleśvara.
Then one should bow to Maheśa holding the staff (Daṇḍapāṇi) and Mokṣeśa; having saluted Vīrabhadreśvara, one should then [salute] Avimukteśvara.
Then one should go to the five Vināyakas and thereafter to Viśvanātha; then, having released the vow of silence, one should utter this mantra: || 95 ||
May the omnipresent Lord Śambhu be pleased with this pilgrimage of the inner chamber which has been performed by me according to rule, even if it be deficient or excessive.
Having recited this mantra and rested for a moment in the Pavilion of Liberation (Muktimaṇḍapa), that man, freed from sin and endowed with merit, should proceed to his home.
Having reached the day of Viṣṇu, a pilgrimage should be undertaken with great effort at all the holy sites of Viṣṇu for the sake of attaining abundant great merit.
And on the fifteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, one should worship Kulastaṃbha; by worshipping him, the misery of becoming a Rudra-piśāca shall not occur.
These processions must be performed with faith by the residents of the sacred field; indeed, processions should be conducted everywhere, especially on the auspicious festival days.
A virtuous person should never spend a day fruitlessly without undertaking a pilgrimage; two pilgrimages should be performed with diligence every single day.
First from the celestial river, and then from the Lord of the Universe—verily, for one who dwells in Kāśī, every day that passes must not be in vain.
On that very day, his ancestors became hopeless; he was bitten by a black cobra and was clearly seen by Death itself.

He was robbed that day on which he did not behold Viśveśa; yet he bathed in all the holy fords (tīrthas) and performed every pilgrimage. But he who has bathed in Maṇikarṇikā and beheld Viśveśa—[he alone has truly accomplished his purpose].
Truth, truth, again truth; truth, truth, again and again: Viśveśvara is eternally visible, and Maṇikarṇikā must be bathed in.
Vyāsa said: O Sūta, having heard this supreme *Skānda* account of the majesty of Kāśī, a man does not go to hell even after committing a thousand sins.
O Sūta, whatever spiritual merit is acquired by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), that shall be attained simply by listening to the Kāśīkhaṇḍa; of this there is no doubt.
Having given all kinds of gifts and having performed numerous sacrifices, a mortal certainly obtains that merit simply by hearing this.
Whatever great fruit is obtained by performing fierce austerities, one attains that simply by hearing this section; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever fruit is obtained by studying the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, that same fruit is attained by men upon hearing the Kāśīkhaṇḍa.
Just as ancestors are satisfied by the offering of śrāddha at Gayā, so too do the grandfathers become satisfied for men by hearing this.
By those of steady intellect, all the Purāṇas have been heard; and by those who have heard the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, the state of all auspicious blessings has been attained.
And all the dharmas have been heard by those who possess a single great mass of merit—those of steady mind who have heard the supreme majesty of Kāśī. (13)
For this alone is proclaimed as the supreme worship of the gods; O twice-born ones, one should recite this entire section with faith, and it should be heard.
Whoever hears even a single narrative born from the Kāśī-khaṇḍa has, without doubt, heard all the treatises on dharma.
This *Kāśīkhaṇḍa* is remembered as the sole progenitor of the Great Dharma, the expounder of the supreme goal, and the cause for the attainment of all desires. (16)
For men, liberation is not at all far off from hearing this; all the ancestors are satisfied upon hearing this supreme section. (17)
All the immortals, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, are delighted; the sages, such as Sanaka and the rest, rejoice and exult.
Upon hearing of this greatness of Vārāṇasī, every member of the fourfold classes of beings will surely become joyful; of this there is no doubt. (19)
The wise man who should cause this to be heard—whether in its entirety, or even half, or a quarter, or half of that, or just one excellent exposition—[attains the fruit]. (120)
He is to be saluted with effort and worshipped like one's own chosen deity; for the constant pleasure of Viśveśa, one should always give to him with diligence.
When he is satisfied, the Lord of the Universe is indeed satisfied; of this there is no doubt—wherever this section, which is the refuge of supreme bliss, is recited.
No misfortune whatsoever shall arise there for that wise man who hears this, or for that intelligent person who causes it to be heard. (23)
Even those meritorious souls who merely recite it, they all become forms of Rudra; and he who, having had this beautiful book transcribed, should offer it [to a worthy recipient]. || 24 ||
All the Purāṇas were given by him, and not otherwise; indeed, as many narratives as there are herein, and as many verses as there are, [were all composed by him]. (25)
Likewise, indeed, as many words as there are, as many letters as there are, as many morae as there are, and as many rows of words as there are—|| 26 ||
As many threads as there are in the string, as many warp-threads as there are in the cloth, and as many variegated forms as there are upon the surface of this beautiful book; ||| 27 ||
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [in this section], the donor is glorified in heaven; so too for one who hears this supreme section twelve times.
Even the sin of killing a Brahmin shall quickly perish for him through the grace of Śambhu; so too for one who is sonless, provided he listens with faith after having properly bathed. (29)
By the power of Śambhu’s command, he indeed becomes his son; what need is there for much speaking? Here, whoever has a desire, that person shall be born.
Whoever hears this, that person shall always attain success; even from a distant land, whoever listens to this excellent Kāśīkhaṇḍa [shall likewise achieve their goal]. (31)

By the command of Śiva, he shall become a vessel for the merit of residing in Kāśī. From hearing this, men shall achieve victory everywhere; and one of pure intent shall also attain good fortune in all places. (32)
Only for one who is endowed with merit and possesses a great, stainless mind, and for whom Viśveśvara is pleased, does the inclination to hear this arise. (33)
It is the supreme and greatest auspiciousness among all auspicious things; when written and worshipped even in the home, it leads to the accomplishment of all auspicious goals. 134.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Index," in the latter half of the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. The latter half of the Śrī Kāśī-khaṇḍa is complete. And thus, this fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, is finished.
